data.title: Biomolecules: Classification, Structure & Physiological Functions

notes: Biomolecules are organic molecules essential to life: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, plus minerals, enzymes and water.

Carbohydrates (CH2O)n: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, ribose), disaccharides (sucrose=glucose+fructose, lactose, maltose), polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose). Provide energy (4 kcal/g) and structural support.

Proteins: polymers of 20 standard amino acids (L-forms; glycine is achiral) joined by peptide (-CO-NH-) bonds. Four structural levels (primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary). Functions: enzymes, transport (haemoglobin), contraction, defence, structural.
Lipids: hydrophobic; triglycerides (fat storage, 9 kcal/g), phospholipids (membrane bilayer), steroids (cholesterol, hormones). Not true polymers.
Nucleic acids: DNA (double helix, deoxyribose, A=T 2 H-bonds, G=C 3 H-bonds) stores heredity; RNA (single strand, ribose, A=U) in protein synthesis (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA).
Enzymes: biological catalysts (mostly proteins); work by the lock-and-key / induced-fit model; denatured by high temperature or extreme pH; show high substrate specificity.
Water (major solvent, ~70% of cell) and minerals (Ca, P, K, Na, Fe, I) act as structural, catalytic and osmotic regulators; deficiency causes deficiency diseases.
confusion: Cellulose is a structural polymer in plant cell walls, not an energy reserve; glycogen (animal) and starch (plant) are the storage forms.
Starch is unbranched amylose + branched amylopectin; both yield maltose on hydrolysis.
Ribose and deoxyribose differ only by one oxygen atom on C-2; hence RNA vs DNA sugars.
Denaturation unfolds protein (loss of secondary/tertiary structure); it is often reversible at low temperature.
Lipids are not polymers; they do not have repeating monomers like the other three macromolecule classes.
A peptide bond forms between the -COOH of one amino acid and the -NH2 of the next, releasing one water (condensation).

universalFacts: Carbon makes up roughly a fifth of human body mass and forms the covalent backbone of every biomolecule.
Hemoglobin binds about 1.34 mL of oxygen per gram; fully saturated blood carries roughly 20 mL of oxygen per 100 mL.
Water has an anomalously high specific heat and acts as a biological thermostat.
Human insulin (51 amino acids) was produced by recombinant-DNA technology in 1978 and approved in 1982 — the first approved recombinant-DNA pharmaceutical.

Cellulose (beta-glucose) forms the cell wall of green plants.

enrichedContent.summary: Biomolecules are the chemical basis of life. Carbohydrates supply and store energy and form structural fibres; proteins (from 20 amino acids) act as enzymes, transporters, contractile and defence molecules in four structural levels; lipids store energy and build membranes; nucleic acids (DNA/RNA) store and express genetic information; enzymes, water and minerals complete the set. Mastery of structure-function links and enzyme kinetics is a frequent NEB examination focus.
specialNotes: In NEB written answers, pair every macromolecule with BOTH its monomer and its key function to earn full marks.
Protein denaturation is a favourite "application" question (cooking an egg, or fever denaturing enzymes).
Stress that enzymes lower activation energy; they do NOT supply energy.
importantStatements: All cells share the same basic biochemical machinery of DNA→RNA→protein (central dogma).
The 20 naturally occurring L-amino acids differ only in their R-group (side chain).
Phospholipid bilayers form spontaneously because the head is hydrophilic and the tail is hydrophobic.
Enzyme specificity is explained by the induced-fit model.
Water is the universal biological solvent and a participant in hydrolysis and condensation.
importantNotes: Memorise monomer → polymer: glucose→starch, amino acid→protein, fatty acid+glycerol→triglyceride, nucleotide→nucleic acid.
Learn base-pairing and hydrogen-bond counts (A=T=2, G=C=3).
Do 2–3 diagram questions: phospholipid bilayer, peptide bond, a DNA nucleotide ladder.
Link enzyme inhibitors (competitive vs non-competitive) to drug design.

A-T two H-bonds (think "A" has 2 strokes), G-C three.
Enzymes are proteins that END in "-ase".
Starch test: iodine → blue-black; reducing sugar: Benedict's → brick-red.

Diagram-based marks: label a phospholipid bilayer and a DNA nucleotide.
Application: explain a disease caused by a biomolecule deficiency.

notes: **जैवअणु (Biomolecules) वर्गीकरण, संरचना र शारीरिक कार्य:** जीवनको लागि आवश्यक कार्बनिक अणुहरू: कार्बोहाइड्रेट, प्रोटीन, लिपिड, न्यूक्लिक एसिड, खनिज, एन्जाइम र पानी।

**कार्बोहाइड्रेट (CH2O)n:** मोनोस्याक्काराइड (ग्लुकोज, फ्रक्टोज, राइबोज), डाइस्याक्काराइड (सुक्रोज=ग्लुकोज+फ्रक्टोज, ल्याक्टोज, माल्टोज), पोलीस्याक्काराइड (स्टार्च, ग्लाइकोजन, सेल्युलोज)। ऊर्जा (4 kcal/g) र संरचनात्मक सहयोग प्रदान गर्छ।

**प्रोटीन:** 20 L-अमीनो एसिडको बहुलक जे पेप्टाइड (-CO-NH-) बन्डद्वारा जोडिएको छ। चार संरचनात्मक स्तर (प्राथमिक, द्वितीयक, तृतीयक, चतुर्थक)। कार्यहरू: एन्जाइम, परिवहन (हीमोग्लोबिन), संकुचन, रक्षा, संरचनात्मक।
**लिपिड:** जलविरोधी (hydrophobic); ट्राइग्लिसराइड (वसा संग्रह, 9 kcal/g), फस्फोलिपिड (झिल्ली द्विस्तर), स्टेराइड (कोलेस्ट्रल, हार्मोन)। वास्तविक बहुलक होइनन्।
**न्यूक्लिक एसिड:** DNA (दोहोरो हेलिक्स, डिअक्सीराइबोज, A=T 2 H-बन्ड, G=C 3 H-बन्ड) वंशागति सङ्ग्रह गर्छ; RNA (एकल फाँड, राइबोज, A=U) प्रोटीन संश्लेषणमा (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA)।
**एन्जाइम:** जैविक उत्प्रेरक (अधिकांश प्रोटीन); लक-अन्ड-की / प्रेरित-फिट मोडेलबाट कार्य गर्छ; उच्च तापमान वा चरम pH ले विकृत गर्छ; -S- (सब्सट्रेट) विशिष्टता पालना गर्छ।
**पानी (प्रमुख विलायक, ~७०% सेल) र खनिज (Ca, P, K, Na, Fe, I) संरचनात्मक, उत्प्रेरक र परासरण नियामकको रूपमा कार्य गर्छन्; अभावले अभाव रोगहरू ल्याउँछ।
importantStatements: मानव शरीरमा पृथ्वीमा बालुका कणको संख्याको बराबर कार्बन परमाणु हुन्छन्; कार्बन सबै जीवनको मेरुदण्ड हो।
हीमोग्लोबिन १०० mL पूर्ण सन्तृप्त रक्तमा १.४ g अक्सिजन वहन गर्छ।
पानीको विशिष्ट ताप असाधारण उच्च छ र यो जैविक थर्मोस्टेटको रूपमा कार्य गर्छ।
इन्सुलिन (५१ अमीनो एसिड) मानव चिकित्साको लागि बनेको पहिलो पुनर्संयोजक प्रोटीन थियो (१९७८)।

notes: Biomolecule (noun): organic molecule essential to life. Plural: biomolecules.
Macromolecule (noun): large biological polymer. Includes proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides.
Monomer (noun): repeating unit of a polymer. E.g., amino acid for protein, nucleotide for DNA.
Enzyme (noun): biological catalyst, usually protein. Suffix -ase indicates enzyme.
Peptide bond (noun phrase): covalent bond between amino acids (-CO-NH-).
Hydrolysis (noun): breaking bonds by adding water. Opposite of condensation.
importantStatements: In biology, 'polymer' means a chain of repeating monomers, not necessarily synthetic.
The term 'denature' means loss of native structure (unfolding), not destruction of the molecule.
Base-pairing rules: A pairs with T (or U in RNA), G pairs with C — this is specific, not random.

### 1. Biomolecules Overview

Biomolecules are organic compounds produced by living organisms. They are classified into four major groups: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids. Minerals and water are inorganic biomolecules essential for life.
### 2. Carbohydrates
- **Monosaccharides**: Simple sugars - glucose (C6H12O6), fructose, galactose
- **Disaccharides**: Two monosaccharides - sucrose (glucose+fructose), lactose (glucose+galactose), maltose (glucose+glucose)
- **Polysaccharides**: Many monosaccharides - starch (energy storage), glycogen (animal starch), cellulose (structural)
- Functions: Energy source, structural support, cell recognition
### 3. Proteins
- Built from amino acids (20 types) linked by peptide bonds
- **Primary structure**: Sequence of amino acids
- **Secondary structure**: Alpha helix, beta sheet (hydrogen bonding)
- **Tertiary structure**: 3D folding (disulfide bridges, hydrophobic interactions)
- **Quaternary structure**: Multiple polypeptide chains (hemoglobin)
- Functions: Enzymes, structural support, transport, immunity, signaling
### 4. Lipids
- **Fats and oils**: Triglycerides (glycerol + 3 fatty acids)
- **Phospholipids**: Cell membrane component (hydrophilic head, hydrophobic tail)
- **Steroids**: Cholesterol, hormones (testosterone, estrogen)
- **Waxes**: Water-proofing
- Functions: Energy storage (9 kcal/g), membrane structure, insulation, hormones
### 5. Nucleic Acids
- **DNA**: Deoxyribonucleic acid - double helix, stores genetic information
- **RNA**: Ribonucleic acid - single strand, protein synthesis
- Monomers: Nucleotides (sugar + phosphate + nitrogenous base)
- DNA bases: Adenine, Guanine, Cytosine, Thymine
- RNA bases: Adenine, Guanine, Cytosine, Uracil
### 6. Enzymes
- Biological catalysts (mostly proteins, some RNA = ribozymes)
- Lower activation energy, not consumed in reaction
- **Lock and key model**: Active site fits specific substrate
- **Induced fit model**: Active site adjusts to substrate
- Factors affecting enzyme activity: temperature, pH, substrate concentration, inhibitors
### 7. Water
- Universal solvent, high specific heat capacity, cohesion and adhesion
- Essential for all metabolic reactions, transport, temperature regulation
### 8. Minerals
- **Macrominerals**: Ca, P, K, Na, Cl, Mg, S (needed in large amounts)
- **Microminerals**: Fe, I, Zn, Cu, Mn, Se, F (trace amounts)
- Functions: Bone formation, oxygen transport, nerve transmission, enzyme cofactors
### 9. Entrance Exam Focus
MCQs: Identify biomolecule types; Enzyme properties; Carbohydrate classification; Protein structure levels.

# Biomolecules: Introduction and functions of carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, minerals, enzymes and water

## 1. Introduction
Every living cell is a chemical factory, and **biomolecules** are its machines, materials and messages. Carbohydrates and lipids store and supply energy; proteins build structures and run reactions as enzymes; nucleic acids carry heredity; minerals and water create the ionic, solvent world in which all of this happens. Remove any one class and the cell stops — which is why NEB gives this topic the heaviest weightage of the unit (15 hours for the unit, most of it here).

A Nepali kitchen demonstrates the whole chapter: rice and potato (starch), ghee and mustard oil (lipids), dal and egg (protein), lemon pickle (vitamin C and minerals), and the curd set overnight by *Lactobacillus* enzymes. Malnutrition surveys in the hills — stunting from protein-energy lack, goitre from iodine lack — are this chapter written on human bodies.

**What you will learn:** (i) what biomolecules are and how monomers build polymers by condensation; (ii) carbohydrates: classes, functions, key examples; (iii) proteins: amino acids, four structure levels, functions; (iv) lipids: classes, why they are not true polymers; (v) nucleic acids: DNA vs RNA, base pairing; (vi) minerals: macro vs micro with deficiency links; (vii) enzymes: action, specificity, factors; (viii) water: life's solvent properties.

**Learning outcomes.** You can: classify any biomolecule by monomer–linkage–function; give the Atwater energy values; state base-pairing rules with H-bond counts; explain enzyme specificity and denaturation; and relate mineral deficiency to a Nepali health example.

## 2. Hierarchy body — each class of biomolecule

### Carbohydrates
1. **Definition and elements.** Polyhydroxy aldehydes/ketones of C, H, O (general ratio H:O ≈ 2:1). Monomer: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, ribose, deoxyribose).
2. **Classes.** Monosaccharides (glucose — blood sugar, respiratory substrate); disaccharides (sucrose = glucose + fructose, maltose, lactose — each formed by condensation with loss of water); polysaccharides (starch = amylose + amylopectin in plants; glycogen in animals; cellulose structural in walls).
3. **Key bonds.** Glycosidic bond between sugar units (condensation; hydrolysis breaks it during digestion).
4. **Functions.** Instant/quick energy (glucose), transport/storage (sucrose, starch, glycogen), structure (cellulose, chitin), genetic material sugars (ribose in RNA, deoxyribose in DNA — differ at carbon-2).
5. **Energy value.** ≈ 4 kcal per gram (Atwater system; FAO) — same as protein, less than half of fat.

### Proteins
1. **Monomers.** 20 standard amino acids linked by peptide bonds (condensation); each has an amino group, a carboxyl group, H and a variable R group on the α-carbon. Glycine's R is H, so it is achiral; the rest are L-forms in proteins.
2. **Four structure levels.** Primary (amino-acid sequence) → secondary (α-helix, β-sheet, held by H-bonds) → tertiary (3-D folding by H-bonds, ionic, hydrophobic, disulphide links) → quaternary (multiple polypeptides, e.g., haemoglobin's 4 subunits).
3. **Functions.** Structure (keratin, collagen), catalysis (all enzymes are proteins — except ribozymes), transport (haemoglobin), defence (antibodies), movement (actin/myosin), hormones (human insulin, 51 amino acids — first approved recombinant-DNA drug, produced 1978, approved 1982).
4. **Denaturation.** Heat, strong acid/alkali or heavy metals break the weak bonds of 2°/3° structure; the chain stays but function is lost (boiled egg white never un-boils).

### Lipids
1. **Definition and catch.** Water-insoluble esters of fatty acids with glycerol (triglycerides), plus phospholipids, steroids and waxes. They are **not true polymers** — no repeating monomer chain, no single linkage type.
2. **Saturated vs unsaturated.** Saturated (ghee, single bonds, solid) vs unsaturated (mustard oil, double bonds, liquid); excess saturated fat links to cardiovascular risk.
3. **Functions.** Concentrated energy (≈ 9 kcal/g — more than double carbs/protein), insulation and padding, membrane bilayers (phospholipids), hormones (steroids: testosterone, oestrogen), waterproofing (waxes, cutin).
4. **Haemoglobin note (validity-kept).** Haemoglobin binds about 1.34 mL of oxygen per gram; fully saturated blood carries roughly 20 mL of oxygen per 100 mL — the unit is volume-per-mass, not grams.

### Nucleic acids
1. **Building blocks.** Nucleotide = pentose sugar + phosphate + nitrogenous base. DNA uses deoxyribose (lacks O at C-2) and bases A, T, G, C; RNA uses ribose and A, U, G, C.
2. **Chargaff pairing.** A=T with 2 hydrogen bonds; G≡C with 3. The double helix (Watson–Crick) stores heredity; RNA (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA) expresses it.
3. **Functions.** DNA: master blueprint, replication each S phase. RNA: transcription copy (mRNA), adapter (tRNA), machine (rRNA + proteins = ribosome); some RNAs catalyse (ribozymes — the exception to "all enzymes are proteins").

### Minerals, enzymes and water
1. **Minerals.** Macrominerals needed in quantity: Ca, P, K, Na, Mg, Cl, S (bones, fluids, cofactors). Microminerals (trace): Fe (haemoglobin), I (thyroxine — deficiency → goitre, seen in hill Nepal), Zn, Cu, Mn, F. Deficiency maps directly onto disease — the exam's favourite angle.
2. **Enzymes.** Protein biocatalysts with high substrate specificity (lock-and-key / induced-fit); lower activation energy; work in narrow pH/temperature optima; inhibited by poisons and denatured by heat. Named with -ase (amylase, catalase).
3. **Water.** Life's solvent: high specific heat (≈ 4.18 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹ — the cell's thermostat), high heat of vaporisation (sweating cools), cohesion/adhesion (xylem pull), universal solvent for ions and metabolites. A cell is ~70% water — biochemistry is water chemistry.

## 5. Worked examples and applications
1. **Energy maths (Atwater).** A meal gives 60 g carbohydrate + 20 g protein + 15 g fat. Energy = 60×4 + 20×4 + 15×9 = 240 + 80 + 135 = **455 kcal**. Fat gives the most per gram — the working behind every nutrition label.
2. **Lactose intolerance.** Lactase (enzyme) hydrolyses lactose → glucose + galactose. Adults making little lactase cannot digest milk sugar — bloating follows. Missing enzyme, missing reaction: specificity in real life.
3. **Goitre in the hills.** Iodine is the trace mineral of thyroxine. Iodine-poor hill diets → underactive thyroid → goitre. Iodised salt is mineral biochemistry as public health.
4. **Why ghee keeps, oil flows.** Ghee's saturated fatty acids pack straight and solidify; mustard oil's double bonds kink the chains so it stays liquid — structure decides property.
5. **Boiled egg.** Heat denatures egg-white albumin: 3-D shape lost, function and solubility gone, permanently. Denaturation is irreversible in the kitchen.
6. **ORS (oral rehydration).** Sugar + salt + water exploits glucose-coupled sodium absorption in the gut — carbohydrate transport physiology saving lives in diarrhoea wards.
7. **Glucose drip.** A 5% dextrose saline bottle feeds a patient who cannot eat: carbohydrate as instant respiratory substrate, minerals as fluid balance — the chapter on a stand.

## 6. Key terms and statements
- **Biomolecule** — molecule produced by living systems: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, plus minerals, vitamins, water.
- **Monomer / polymer** — single unit / chain of units (amino acid → protein; glucose → starch).
- **Condensation / hydrolysis** — joining monomers with water loss / splitting with water uptake (digestion).
- **Glycosidic / peptide / phosphodiester bond** — links of sugars / amino acids / nucleotides.
- **Essential amino acid** — cannot be synthesised by the body; must come from food (e.g., lysine, methionine).
- **Denaturation** — loss of 2°/3° protein shape (and function) by heat, acid/alkali or heavy metals.
- **Chargaff's rules** — A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds) in DNA.
- **Ribozyme** — catalytic RNA; the exception to "all enzymes are proteins".
- **Macromineral / micromineral** — needed in large (Ca, P, K) / trace (Fe, I, Zn) amounts.
- **Substrate specificity** — each enzyme fits only its substrate (lock-and-key / induced-fit).

## 7. Exam Zone
**NEB map.** Tables rule this topic: biomolecule master table, DNA vs RNA, protein levels, saturated vs unsaturated. One-markers: monomer names, Atwater values, base pairs. Standard long answers: protein structure levels with diagrams; nucleic acids (DNA vs RNA); enzymes (specificity + factors). Minerals come as deficiency-reason questions (iodine→goitre, iron→anaemia, calcium→bones).

**Short tricks.** "4-4-9" = carb–protein–fat kcal/g. "A=T(2), G≡C(3)". "Starch=plant, glycogen=animal, cellulose=wall". "Glycine is achiral" — the one-line exception examiners love.

## 8. Summary and self-check
Biomolecules are built by condensation and broken by hydrolysis. Carbohydrates (glycosidic links; 4 kcal/g) give quick energy and structure; proteins (20 amino acids, peptide bonds, four structure levels) build and catalyse — including enzymes with strict substrate specificity; lipids (esters, not true polymers; 9 kcal/g) store dense energy and build membranes; nucleic acids (A=T with 2 H-bonds, G≡C with 3) store and express heredity; minerals (Fe, I, Ca…) supply ions and cofactors; water (4.18 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹) is the solvent stage. notes: Cell theory (Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow): all organisms are made of one or more cells; the cell is the basic structural and functional unit; every cell arises from a pre-existing cell.
Cell = the smallest unit of life; bounded by the plasma membrane; size typically 1-100 µm.
Prokaryotic cell: no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles; 70S ribosomes; e.g. bacteria, cyanobacteria; smaller (1-10 µm).
Eukaryotic cell: true nucleus with a nuclear envelope, membrane-bound organelles, 80S ribosomes; e.g. plant and animal cells.
Key differences: nucleus, organelles, chromatin vs naked DNA, cell size, ribosome size, cytoskeleton.
Basic cell components: plasma membrane, cytoplasm (cytosol + organelles), genetic material, and (in prokaryotes) cell wall, capsule, pili, flagella.
confusion: A virus is not a cell and is not prokaryotic or eukaryotic; it is an acellular, obligate intracellular parasite.
Prokaryotes lack a nuclear membrane but still carry DNA (usually a single circular chromosome).
Mycoplasma has no cell wall and is among the smallest known free-living cells (~0.2–0.4 µm).
A eukaryotic nucleus is a true membrane-bound organelle; the nucleoid of a bacterium is not.
Cell walls are found in plants, fungi and most bacteria; they are ABSENT in animal cells.

Human ova (~0.12 mm) are visible to the naked eye; the sperm head is ~5 µm long.
A human body contains roughly 3.7×10^13 cells (published estimate; counts vary with body size).
examples: E. coli is a classic prokaryotic model organism.

Amoeba is a single eukaryotic cell that carries out all life functions.

Mastering their structural differences — nucleus, ribosome type, cell wall, organelles — is a core NEB examination point.

notes: DETAILED ORGANELLE ANALYSIS (plant + animal cell).

Plasma membrane: phospholipid bilayer (heads out, tails in) + integral proteins (channels, pumps, receptors) + peripheral proteins + cholesterol + glycocalyx (cell recognition). Fluid-mosaic model (Singer & Nicolson, 1972).

Mitochondrion: double membrane; outer smooth, inner folded into cristae; matrix with Krebs enzymes; own DNA + 70S ribosomes (endosymbiosis); aerobic respiration: glycolysis (cytoplasm) → Krebs (matrix) → ETS (cristae) → ~34 ATP.

Chloroplast: double membrane; thylakoids stacked into grana; stroma with Calvin-cycle enzymes; chlorophyll a + b; own DNA + 70S ribosomes; light reactions (grana → ATP, NADPH, O2) + Calvin cycle (stroma → glucose).
Nucleus: nuclear envelope (4 nm, two membranes, pores); nucleoplasm; chromatin (DNA + histone proteins); nucleolus (rRNA + ribosome assembly).
Rough ER (RER): ribosomes on outer surface → protein synthesis (secretory + membrane proteins); continuous with nuclear envelope.
Smooth ER (SER): lipid synthesis, carbohydrate metabolism, detoxification (liver), Ca2+ storage (muscle — sarcoplasmic reticulum).
Golgi apparatus: cisternae + vesicles; modifies (glycosylation), packages, sorts, and secretes proteins; forms lysosomes + cell plate (plants).
Lysosomes: 8–12 nm vesicle, hydrolytic enzymes (acidic pH); digest food particles, worn organelles (autophagy); "suicide bags" when damaged.
Vacuole: plant — large central (turgor, storage); animal — small (excretion, osmoregulation, contractile in protozoa).
Cytoskeleton: microfilaments (actin), intermediate filaments, microtubules (tubulin); shape, movement, intracellular transport, division (spindle).
Centrioles (animal): microtubule rings; form the spindle during mitosis; absent in most plants.
Cell inclusions: storage granules (starch, fat, glycogen), pigments (leuco-, chro-, heterochromoplasts), crystalloids.
Cell wall (plant): cellulose microfibrils (primary wall) + pectin; secondary wall with lignin; fully permeable; provides rigidity + protection.

# Detail structure of eukaryotic cells: cell wall, cell membrane, mitochondria, plastids, endoplasmic reticulum, golgi bodies, lysosomes, ribosomes, nucleus, chromosomes, cilia, flagella and cell inclusions

## 1. Introduction
If the last topic drew the two house-plans of life, this one walks through every room of the eukaryotic house — twelve named structures, each with its architecture, its job and its exam note. The mitochondrion burns the fuel, the chloroplast catches the light, the nucleus holds the blueprint, the ER and Golgi run the production line, lysosomes handle demolition, ribosomes build, the membrane guards the gate, the wall braces the plant, chromosomes pack heredity for moving day, cilia and flagella row and swim, and inclusions store the pantry.

Nepal hooks are close: the red of a *lali gurans* petal is chromoplast pigment; the sour of a lemon is vacuole acid; the stretch of dough gluten is protein structure; pond scum (*Spirogyra*) under a school microscope shows spiral chloroplasts and a nucleus in every cell — this whole topic visible in one drop.

**What you will learn:** the structure–function–exam-note of all twelve syllabus structures: wall, membrane (fluid-mosaic 1972), mitochondria, plastids, ER (rough/smooth), Golgi, lysosomes, ribosomes, nucleus, chromosomes, cilia/flagella (9+2), inclusions — plus the plant-vs-animal split and the endosymbiotic thread.

**Learning outcomes.** You can: draw and label an animal cell, a mitochondrion, a chloroplast and the fluid-mosaic membrane; state one structure, one function and one exam trap per organelle; and explain the 9+2 axoneme and the inclusion correction.

## 2. Hierarchy body — membranes, powerhouses and plastids

### Cell wall
1. **Structure.** Rigid outer coat outside the plasma membrane in plants (cellulose microfibrils in a matrix), fungi (chitin), bacteria (peptidoglycan) — absent in animal cells. Layers: middle lamella (pectin cement) → primary wall → secondary wall (lignin in wood); plasmodesmata are cytoplasmic bridges through pits.
2. **Function.** Shape, mechanical strength, protection, and turgor balance — the wall pushes back when the vacuole swells.
3. **Exam note.** Lignin, not cellulose, makes wood hard; "wall vs membrane" is a comparison favourite.

### Cell membrane (plasma membrane)
1. **Fluid-mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972).** A phospholipid bilayer sea in which proteins float like icebergs: integral (channels, carriers, receptors) and peripheral; cholesterol stiffens animal membranes; glycolipids/glycoproteins form the glycocalyx identity badge.
2. **Function.** Selectively permeable gate: diffusion, osmosis, facilitated transport, active transport (ATP-driven, e.g., Na⁺/K⁺ pump), endo/exocytosis.
3. **Exam note.** Draw it as two-tailed rows with protein blobs — label bilayer, channel protein, cholesterol, carbohydrate chain; "fluid" (lateral movement) + "mosaic" (protein patches) is the 1-mark meaning.

### Mitochondria
1. **Structure.** Double membrane: smooth outer + folded inner (cristae) enclosing the matrix. Own small circular DNA + 70S ribosomes; semi-autonomous, divides by fission.
2. **Function.** Aerobic respiration: Krebs cycle (matrix) + electron-transport chain with ATP synthase (cristae) — "powerhouse of the cell". Abundant where energy is spent (muscle, kidney tubules).
3. **Exam note.** Cristae = surface area for ETS; inner membrane is the ATP factory floor.

### Plastids
1. **Types.** Chloroplasts (green: grana stacks of thylakoids in stroma — photosynthesis), chromoplasts (carotenoid colours of petals/fruits), leucoplasts (colourless storage: amyloplasts store starch).
2. **Chloroplast anatomy.** Double envelope + stroma (Calvin cycle) + thylakoid/grana (light reactions, chlorophyll a and b) + own DNA and 70S ribosomes — a second endosymbiont.
3. **Exam note.** Grana ↔ light reactions, stroma ↔ dark reactions: location-function pairing is the standard 2-marker.

### Endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi bodies, lysosomes
1. **ER.** Membrane network continuous with the nuclear envelope. Rough ER (ribosome-studded) folds and ships proteins; smooth ER synthesises lipids/steroids and detoxifies (liver SER). Transport vesicles bud toward Golgi.
2. **Golgi bodies (dictyosomes in plants).** Stacked cisternae with cis (receiving) and trans (shipping) faces: glycosylation, packaging into vesicles, lysosome formation, and plant cell-plate material during cytokinesis.
3. **Lysosomes.** Single-membrane suicide bags of acid hydrolases: digest worn organelles (autophagy), food particles, and — when ruptured — the cell itself (autolysis). Abundant in white blood cells.

### Ribosomes, nucleus, chromosomes
1. **Ribosomes.** Protein builders: 80S in eukaryotic cytosol (60S + 40S subunits), 70S in mitochondria/chloroplasts; free ones make intracellular proteins, RER-bound ones make export proteins. A busy liver cell carries on the order of a million — valid order of magnitude, estimates vary.
2. **Nucleus.** Double nuclear envelope with pores + nucleolus (rRNA factory) + chromatin (DNA + histone proteins). Control centre: stores heredity, directs protein synthesis via mRNA.
3. **Chromosomes.** Condensed chromatin visible at division: centromere, telomeres, 붙 sister chromatids; human somatic cells carry 46. Karyotype (size-ordered set) reveals trisomies such as Down syndrome.

### Cilia, flagella and cell inclusions
1. **Motile axoneme = 9+2.** Nine peripheral microtubule doublets ring two central singlets, with dynein arms driving the sliding that bends the shaft (validity-kept correction: no 9+9 arrangement exists; primary/non-motile cilia are 9+0, centrioles 9+0 triplets). Cilia row in coordination (*Paramecium*); flagella undulate (*Euglena*, sperm).
2. **Cell inclusions (validity-kept).** Non-living storage and waste granules: oil droplets, glycogen granules, starch grains, crystal inclusions, pigments — never chromosomes, which are living heredity material.
3. **Exam note.** Draw axoneme as 9 dots ring + 2 centre dots in cross-section; the 9+2 vs 9+0 vs 9×3 triplet (centriole) triple is a favourite MCQ set.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Membrane systems: structure → function → exam note**

| Organelle | Structure | Function | Exam note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cell wall | Cellulose/chitin + lamellae | Strength, turgor balance | Lignin hardens wood |
| Plasma membrane | Fluid-mosaic bilayer (1972) | Selective transport | Draw bilayer + proteins |
| Rough ER | Cisternae + ribosomes | Protein folding, shipping | Continuous with nucleus |
| Smooth ER | Tubules, no ribosomes | Lipids, detoxification | Liver SER example |
| Golgi | Cis→trans cisternae stacks | Packaging, lysosomes, cell plate | Plant = dictyosome |
| Lysosome | Acid hydrolases, single membrane | Autophagy, autolysis | "Suicide bag"; WBC-rich |

**Table 2 — Energy and heredity organelles**

| Organelle | Structure | Function | Exam note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mitochondrion | Cristae + matrix; own DNA, 70S | Krebs + ETS → ATP | Inner membrane = ATP floor |
| Chloroplast | Grana + stroma; own DNA, 70S | Light reactions / Calvin cycle | Grana-light, stroma-dark |
| Ribosome | 80S cytosol (60S+40S); 70S inside organelles | Protein synthesis | Free vs bound split |
| Nucleus | Envelope + pores, nucleolus | Control, heredity store | Nucleolus makes rRNA |
| Chromosome | Condensable chromatin, 46 in humans | Carry genes at division | Karyotype detects trisomy |
| Cilium/flagellum | 9+2 motile axoneme | Movement | 9+0 primary cilia; centriole 9+0 triplets |

**Table 3 — Plant vs animal cell**

| Feature | Plant cell | Animal cell |
|---|---|---|
| Wall | Cellulose present | Absent |
| Plastids | Present (chloro/chromo/leuco) | Absent |
| Vacuole | One large central | Small or absent |
| Centriole | Usually absent | Present (9+0 triplets) |
| Lysosome | Rare | Common |
| Storage carb | Starch | Glycogen |

**Table 4 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
|---|---|---|
| Wall + membrane | Brace + fluid-mosaic gate | Draw-and-label favourite |
| Mitochondrion/chloroplast | Cristae/grana + own DNA | Location–function pairing |
| ER/Golgi/lysosome | Production line + demolition | Flow-sequence questions |
| Nucleus/chromosomes | Control + 46 carriers | Karyotype/trisomy link |
| Cilia/inclusions | 9+2 movers; storage granules | 9+2 vs 9+0 MCQ set |

## 4. Diagrams and figures

## 5. Worked examples and applications
1. **Onion vs cheek under the lens.** Same stain, same microscope: onion shows walls + big vacuoles, cheek shows bare membranes + small nuclei — plant/animal split (Table 3) in one period.
2. **Spirogyra pond drop.** Spiral green ribbons (chloroplasts) with a nucleus slung in each cell — photosynthesis machinery visible without any diagram.
3. **Why muscle tires then recovers.** Sprinting outruns oxygen delivery; mitochondria repay the oxygen debt after — cristae surface explains stamina differences between athletes.
4. **Lemon sour = vacuole.** Citric acid sits in the central vacuole's cell sap; the wall's turgor keeps the fruit firm until it rots — organelles you can taste and squeeze.
5. **Antibiotic targeting again.** Chloroplast/mitochondrial 70S ribosomes remind us why some antibiotics touch these organelles — endosymbiosis has clinical footnotes.
6. **Beetroot leak test.** Boiled beetroot leaks red betalain (membrane destroyed); fresh slices in cold water stay pale — selective permeability demonstrated with a vegetable.
7. **Wood vs rope.** Lignified secondary walls make timber load-bearing; unlignified fibres make rope flexible — wall chemistry decides the industry.

## 6. Key terms and statements
- **Fluid-mosaic model** — Singer–Nicolson (1972): proteins floating in a fluid lipid bilayer.
- **Selectively permeable** — lets some substances cross freely, others by carrier/energy, some never.
- **Cristae / matrix** — folded inner membrane (ETS) / inner fluid (Krebs) of the mitochondrion.
- **Grana / stroma** — thylakoid stacks (light reactions) / fluid (Calvin cycle) of the chloroplast.
- **Rough vs smooth ER** — ribosome-studded protein folders vs lipid/steroid and detox tubules.
- **Cisternae (cis/trans)** — Golgi stacks: receiving face to shipping face.
- **Autophagy / autolysis** — self-digestion of worn parts / of the whole cell by lysosomes.
- **80S = 60S + 40S** — eukaryotic cytosolic ribosome; organelles keep 70S.
- **Chromatin → chromosome** — loose working DNA condenses for division; 46 in human somatic cells.
- **9+2 axoneme** — nine doublet ring + central pair: the motile cilium/flagellum; 9+0 in primary cilia and centriole triplets.
- **Cell inclusions** — non-living stores (oil, glycogen, starch, crystals, pigments) — never chromosomes.

## 7. Exam Zone
**NEB map.** Draw-and-label questions come from this topic: animal/plant cell, mitochondrion, chloroplast, fluid-mosaic membrane, Golgi, 9+2 axoneme cross-section. Short notes: ER types, lysosome ("suicide bag" with reason), ribosome S-values, inclusions correction. Long answers: membrane + transport; mitochondrion vs chloroplast; nucleus + chromosomes. The 9+2 vs 9+0 vs triplet set is MCQ gold.

**Short tricks.** "Wall MEMBRANE order": outside→in = wall, membrane, cytosol. "Rough makes, Smooth synthesises lipids". "Grana-light, Stroma-dark; Cristae-ETS, Matrix-Krebs". "46-23": somatic 46, gamete 23.

**Sources for the facts above:** OpenStax *Biology 2e* §4 (cell structure); Raven Biology (membranes, organelles); CSHL cilia/axoneme review (9+2); Britannica *Ribosome*; unit validation card (kept corrections: 9+2, inclusions, ribosome abundance).

## 8. Summary and self-check
Twelve structures, one logic: bound the cell (wall, membrane), power it (mitochondrion: cristae-ETS, matrix-Krebs), feed it by light (chloroplast: grana-light, stroma-Calvin), build and ship (RER, SER, Golgi cis→trans, vesicles), recycle (lysosomes), synthesise (80S cytosol, 70S organelles), command (nucleus, 46 chromosomes), move (9+2 cilia/flagella) and store (inclusions: oil, glycogen, starch — never chromosomes). Plant adds wall/plastids/big vacuole; animal adds centrioles/lysosomes. Figures: membrane strip, organelle twin panel, three reference plates.

**Self-check.** (1) Draw the fluid mosaic and label six parts. (2) Pair each membrane (cristae, thylakoid, envelope) with its process. (3) Why does a muscle cell need more mitochondria than a skin cell? (4) Correct: "chromosomes are cell inclusions". (5) Sketch the 9+2 cross-section and name one 9+0 structure. (6) RER vs SER in two rows.

**Common confusions.** Middle lamella cements, primary wall grows, secondary wall (lignin) strengthens — three different layers · Golgi = dictyosome in plants (same organelle) · nucleolus makes rRNA, not mRNA · centriole triplets are 9×3, not 9+2 · leucoplasts store, chromoplasts colour, chloroplasts photosynthesise.

notes: DETAILED ORGANELLE ANALYSIS (plant + animal cell).

Plasma membrane: phospholipid bilayer (heads out, tails in) + integral proteins (channels, pumps, receptors) + peripheral proteins + cholesterol + glycocalyx (cell recognition). Fluid-mosaic model (Singer & Nicolson, 1972).

Mitochondrion: double membrane; outer smooth, inner folded into cristae; matrix with Krebs enzymes; own DNA + 70S ribosomes (endosymbiosis); aerobic respiration: glycolysis (cytoplasm) → Krebs (matrix) → ETS (cristae) → ~34 ATP.

Chloroplast: double membrane; thylakoids stacked into grana; stroma with Calvin-cycle enzymes; chlorophyll a + b; own DNA + 70S ribosomes; light reactions (grana → ATP, NADPH, O2) + Calvin cycle (stroma → glucose).
Nucleus: nuclear envelope (4 nm, two membranes, pores); nucleoplasm; chromatin (DNA + histone proteins); nucleolus (rRNA + ribosome assembly).
Rough ER (RER): ribosomes on outer surface → protein synthesis (secretory + membrane proteins); continuous with nuclear envelope.
Smooth ER (SER): lipid synthesis, carbohydrate metabolism, detoxification (liver), Ca2+ storage (muscle — sarcoplasmic reticulum).
Golgi apparatus: cisternae + vesicles; modifies (glycosylation), packages, sorts, and secretes proteins; forms lysosomes + cell plate (plants).
Lysosomes: 8–12 nm vesicle, hydrolytic enzymes (acidic pH); digest food particles, worn organelles (autophagy); "suicide bags" when damaged.
Vacuole: plant — large central (turgor, storage); animal — small (excretion, osmoregulation, contractile in protozoa).
Cytoskeleton: microfilaments (actin), intermediate filaments, microtubules (tubulin); shape, movement, intracellular transport, division (spindle).
Centrioles (animal): microtubule rings; form the spindle during mitosis; absent in most plants.
Cell inclusions: storage granules (starch, fat, glycogen), pigments (leuco-, chro-, heterochromoplasts), crystalloids.
Cell wall (plant): cellulose microfibrils (primary wall) + pectin; secondary wall with lignin; fully permeable; provides rigidity + protection.

notes: DETAILED ORGANELLE ANALYSIS (plant + animal cell).

Plasma membrane: phospholipid bilayer (heads out, tails in) + integral proteins (channels, pumps, receptors) + peripheral proteins + cholesterol + glycocalyx (cell recognition). Fluid-mosaic model (Singer & Nicolson, 1972).

Mitochondrion: double membrane; outer smooth, inner folded into cristae; matrix with Krebs enzymes; own DNA + 70S ribosomes (endosymbiosis); aerobic respiration: glycolysis (cytoplasm) → Krebs (matrix) → ETS (cristae) → ~34 ATP.

Chloroplast: double membrane; thylakoids stacked into grana; stroma with Calvin-cycle enzymes; chlorophyll a + b; own DNA + 70S ribosomes; light reactions (grana → ATP, NADPH, O2) + Calvin cycle (stroma → glucose).
Nucleus: nuclear envelope (4 nm, two membranes, pores); nucleoplasm; chromatin (DNA + histone proteins); nucleolus (rRNA + ribosome assembly).
Rough ER (RER): ribosomes on outer surface → protein synthesis (secretory + membrane proteins); continuous with nuclear envelope.
Smooth ER (SER): lipid synthesis, carbohydrate metabolism, detoxification (liver), Ca2+ storage (muscle — sarcoplasmic reticulum).
Golgi apparatus: cisternae + vesicles; modifies (glycosylation), packages, sorts, and secretes proteins; forms lysosomes + cell plate (plants).
Lysosomes: 8–12 nm vesicle, hydrolytic enzymes (acidic pH); digest food particles, worn organelles (autophagy); "suicide bags" when damaged.
Vacuole: plant — large central (turgor, storage); animal — small (excretion, osmoregulation, contractile in protozoa).
Cytoskeleton: microfilaments (actin), intermediate filaments, microtubules (tubulin); shape, movement, intracellular transport, division (spindle).
Centrioles (animal): microtubule rings; form the spindle during mitosis; absent in most plants.
Cell inclusions: storage granules (starch, fat, glycogen), pigments (leuco-, chro-, heterochromoplasts), crystalloids.
Cell wall (plant): cellulose microfibrils (primary wall) + pectin; secondary wall with lignin; fully permeable; provides rigidity + protection.
confusion: RER makes PROTEIN; SER makes LIPID. A cell secreting lots of protein has abundant RER + Golgi (e.g., pancreatic acinar cell).
The Golgi does NOT synthesise proteins; it MODIFIES, SORTS, and PACKAGES what the RER made.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their OWN DNA + 70S ribosomes — the key endosymbiosis evidence.
Lysosomes are animal-cell organelles; plants use the large vacuole for hydrolytic digestion.
Cilia and flagella share the 9+2 axonemal microtubule structure; centrioles (9+0) are related but lack the central pair.
The nucleus is NOT the only place with DNA: mitochondria + chloroplasts carry their own genomes.

notes: Cell wall (plant: cellulose; bacteria: peptidoglycan; fungi: chitin) — rigid, fully permeable outer support; in plants it can secondarily thicken (lignin).
Plasma membrane: phospholipid bilayer + integral/protein (fluid-mosaic model, Singer & Nicolson 1972); selectively permeable; controls transport (diffusion, osmosis, active transport).
Mitochondrion: site of aerobic respiration (Krebs + ETS → ATP); double membrane; cristae; "powerhouse of the cell".
Chloroplast (plastid): photosynthesis; double membrane; thylakoid grana + stroma; green pigment chlorophyll a & b.
Endoplasmic reticulum: rough (RER, ribosome-studded, protein synthesis) and smooth (SER, lipid synthesis, detoxification).
Golgi apparatus: modifies, packages and secretes proteins and forms lysosomes and cell plate.
Lysosome: hydrolytic "digestive" enzymes; self-digestion = autophagy.
Ribosome: 80S in eukaryotes (60S+40S subunits) — protein synthesis; free or attached to RER.
Nucleus: genetic control centre; nuclear envelope, nucleolus, chromatin/chromosomes.
Cilia and flagella: locomotion/transport; composed of 9+2 microtubules (axoneme).
Cell inclusions: storage granules and pigments (e.g. oil droplets, glycogen granules, crystal inclusions).
confusion: The cell wall is fully permeable; the plasma membrane is selectively permeable.
RER is rough because of ribosomes; it makes PROTEINS. SER makes LIPIDS and detoxifies — it has no ribosomes.
The Golgi packages proteins and lipids; it does not synthesise them.
Lysosomes digest the cell's own material when damaged (autophagy); they are not plant cells' organelles (plants use vacuoles).
Cilia and flagella both have a 9+2 microtubule axoneme; flagella are longer; in prokaryotes the flagellum has a different (no microtubule) structure.
Chromatin (diffuse, interphase) and chromosomes (condensed, division) are the SAME genetic material in two forms.

notes: DETAILED CELL DIVISION: the full cell cycle and every mitotic/meiotic phase.
Interphase (90% of the cycle): G1 (growth, organelle duplication, protein synthesis), S (DNA replication — each chromosome now has 2 sister chromatids), G2 (preparation for mitosis, checkpoint).
Checkpoints: G1/S (DNA damage, nutrients), G2/M (replication complete), M (spindle attachment) — failures cause cancer.

Mitosis phases (PMAT): Prophase (chromatin → chromosomes, spindle forms, nuclear envelope breaks), Metaphase (chromosomes align at the equatorial plate, spindle fibres attached to centromeres), Anaphase (centromeres split, sister chromatids pulled to opposite poles), Telophase (chromosomes decondense, nuclear envelopes reform, cytokinesis).
Cytokinesis: animal cells — cleavage furrow (actin); plant cells — cell plate → new wall.

Meiosis: two divisions. Meiosis I (reductional): Prophase I (chromosomes pair = synapsis; crossing over between non-sister chromatids), Metaphase I (homologous pairs at the equator; independent assortment), Anaphase I (homologs separate), Telophase I. Meiosis II (equational): like mitosis but no DNA replication; sister chromatids separate.
Outcome: meiosis → 4 haploid (n) genetically distinct cells; mitosis → 2 diploid (2n) identical cells.
Crossing over (Prophase I) + independent assortment (Metaphase I) = the two sources of meiotic variation.
Amitosis (direct division): simple karyokinesis; rare — described in some protozoans, yeasts/some fungi and certain pathological or regenerating cells.
Errors: mitotic errors → uncontrolled division = cancer; meiotic non-disjunction → aneuploidy (e.g., Down syndrome = usually trisomy 21).
Significance: mitosis = growth, repair, asexual reproduction; meiosis = gamete formation + genetic diversity.
NEB focus: the full cell cycle, all mitotic and meiotic phases, variation, and errors.
Cell cycle: interphase (G1 growth, S DNA replication, G2 preparation) + M phase (mitosis).
Amitosis (direct division): simple splitting of the nucleus; rare, described in some protozoans and fungi.
Mitosis: one division producing two genetically identical diploid (2n) daughter cells; phases — prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase (PMAT).
Meiosis: two successive divisions producing four genetically diverse haploid (n) gametes; involves crossing over (Prophase I) and independent assortment.
Chromosome: chromatin condensed; the centromere joins sister chromatids.
Significance of mitosis: growth, asexual reproduction, tissue repair.
Significance of meiosis: gamete formation, reduction of chromosome number, genetic variation (crossing over, independent assortment).
Errors in mitosis → uncontrolled division = cancer; errors in meiosis → non-disjunction (e.g. Down syndrome, trisomy 21).

# Cell division: Concept of cell cycle, types of cell division (amitosis, mitosis and meiosis) and significances

## 1. Introduction
Every cell in your body — all ~3×10¹³ of them — descends from one fertilised egg by repeated division, and every grain of rice starts as a zygote that divided the same way. **Cell division** is how life grows, repairs and reproduces; the **cell cycle** is the ordered programme (grow → copy DNA → split) that keeps it faithful. Get it right and a cut heals, a seedling rises, a species continues. Get it wrong and the failures have names: cancer (checkpoints broken), Down syndrome (chromosomes mis-segregated).

Nepal reads this chapter in its fields and clinics: onion root tips in a school lab show mitosis on demand; a maternity ward explains why a mother's age matters for trisomy risk; hybrid maize seed exists because breeders manipulate meiosis. NEB loves this topic — PMAT sequences, mitosis-vs-meiosis tables and significance lists return every year.

**What you will learn:** (i) the cell cycle and its checkpoints; (ii) amitosis (direct division); (iii) mitosis phase-by-phase with diagrams; (iv) meiosis I and II with crossing over and assortment; (v) cytokinesis (furrow vs cell plate); (vi) the significance of each type — with validity-kept corrections on oogenesis, Down syndrome and amitosis.

**Learning outcomes.** You can: draw the cell-cycle wheel with phase events; narrate PMAT and meiosis I/II in order; state what is reductional and what is equational; and explain two significance points per division type.

## 2. Hierarchy body — cycle first, then the three divisions

### Concept of cell cycle
1. **Two eras.** Interphase (the working life: G1 growth, S DNA replication, G2 preparation — roughly 90% of the cycle) and M phase (mitosis + cytokinesis). A cell spends most of its life *not* dividing.
2. **Checkpoints guard the order.** G1/S (is DNA fit to copy?), G2/M (is copying complete?), spindle assembly (are all chromosomes attached?). The p53 protein can halt or sentence a damaged cell — broken checkpoints are the road to cancer.
3. **Regulators.** Cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) drive the cycle forward; growth factors permit it. Onion root-tip cells cycle continuously; your neurons exited to G0 permanently.
4. **Chromosome arithmetic.** Human somatic cell: 2n = 46. S phase doubles DNA (still 46 chromosomes, each with 2 chromatids); division distributes them.

### Amitosis (direct division)
1. **Mechanism.** Nucleus elongates and pinches in two, then cytoplasm splits — no spindle, no chromosome condensation visible.
2. **Where.** Described in some protozoans, yeasts/some fungi, and certain pathological or regenerating cells (validity-kept: binucleate liver cells more often arise by cytokinesis failure, so liver is no longer cited as the classic example).
3. **Exam note.** One line suffices: define + contrast with mitosis (no phases, no spindle).

### Mitosis (equational division)
1. **Prophase.** Chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes; nucleolus vanishes; spindle forms (centrioles in animals, spindle-pole bodies in plants).
2. **Metaphase.** Chromosomes line the equatorial plate, centromeres on the line — the best stage to count chromosomes and see karyotypes.
3. **Anaphase.** Sister chromatids separate (now daughter chromosomes) and move to opposite poles — the defining motion of mitosis.
4. **Telophase + cytokinesis.** Nuclear envelopes reform; cytoplasm splits by furrow (animals) or cell plate (plants, built by Golgi vesicles).
5. **Result.** One 2n cell → two genetically identical 2n cells. Growth, repair, asexual reproduction.

### Meiosis (reductional division)
1. **Why two divisions.** One DNA replication (S phase) followed by meiosis I (homologues separate: 2n → n, reductional) and meiosis II (sisters separate: equational, like mitosis). No S phase between the two — the single most-tested fact of the topic.
2. **Prophase I (the long one).** Leptotene → zygotene (synapsis: homologues pair) → pachytene (crossing over between non-sister chromatids exchanges segments) → diplotene → diakinesis. Crossing over is variation's first engine.
3. **Metaphase I vs metaphase (mitosis).** Homologous *pairs* line up (not single chromosomes); orientation of each pair is random — independent assortment, variation's second engine.
4. **Anaphase I / telophase I.** Homologues separate (sisters stay together) → two haploid (n) cells, each chromosome still two-chromatid.
5. **Meiosis II.** Runs like mitosis in both n cells: sisters separate → four haploid (n) cells, each chromosome one chromatid.
6. **Gamete maths (validity-kept).** Spermatogenesis: 1 primary spermatocyte → 4 sperms. Oogenesis: 1 primary oocyte → 1 functional ovum (n) + usually 2–3 polar bodies — and meiosis II in the oocyte completes only if fertilisation occurs.
7. **Errors matter.** Non-disjunction (homologues failing to separate) yields aneuploid gametes: fertilisation can give trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) — usually full trisomy (~95% of cases; translocation and mosaic forms also occur).

### Cytokinesis and significances
1. **Furrow vs cell plate.** Animal cells pinch via an actin-myosin furrow; plant cells build a Golgi-vesicle cell plate from the centre out (the rigid wall cannot pinch).
2. **Mitosis significance.** Growth, repair/healing, replacement (skin, gut lining, blood), asexual reproduction, and genetic stability (identical copies).
3. **Meiosis significance.** Halves the number (2n → n) so fertilisation restores it; crossing over + assortment generate variation; the raw material of evolution and breeding.
4. **Amitosis significance.** Quick, cheap division where fidelity matters less — microbial growth spurts, some regenerating tissues.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Cell-cycle phases**

| Phase | Event | Checkpoint after it |
|---|---|---|
| G1 | Growth, organelle duplication | G1/S: DNA fit to copy? (p53 acts) |
| S | DNA replication (2n→2n, chromatids doubled) | — |
| G2 | Preparation, protein synthesis | G2/M: copying complete? |
| M (mitosis + cytokinesis) | Chromosomes split, cytoplasm divides | Spindle: all attached? |
| G0 | Permanent exit (neurons, muscle) | — |

**Table 2 — Mitosis (PMAT) at a glance**

| Stage | Chromosome behaviour | How to recognise it |
|---|---|---|
| Prophase | Condensation; spindle forms | Threads appear, nucleolus gone |
| Metaphase | Line the plate | Straight row — count here |
| Anaphase | Sisters separate to poles | V shapes moving apart |
| Telophase | Envelopes reform | Two nuclei forming |

**Table 3 — Mitosis vs meiosis**

| Feature | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| Divisions | One | Two (no S between) |
| Products | 2 diploid (2n), identical | 4 haploid (n), all different |
| Homologue pairing / crossing over | Absent | Prophase I: synapsis + crossing over |
| Metaphase line-up | Single chromosomes | Homologous pairs (assortment) |
| Anaphase separates | Sister chromatids | Homologues (I), then sisters (II) |
| Purpose | Growth, repair, asexual reproduction | Gametes, variation |
| Example site | Onion root tip, skin | Anther, ovary/testis |

**Table 4 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
|---|---|---|
| Cell cycle | G1-S-G2-M + 3 checkpoints | Wheel drawing + checkpoint reasons |
| Amitosis | Direct pinch, no spindle | One-line contrast |
| Mitosis | PMAT + furrow/plate → 2×2n | Stage ID + significance |
| Meiosis | No S between; crossing over; assortment | I-vs-II + variation logic |
| Errors | Non-disjunction → trisomy 21 (~95% full) | Qualified, not absolute |

## 5. Worked examples and applications
1. **Root-tip squash.** Onion root tip + acetocarmine stain + warm + squash: prophase threads, metaphase plates, anaphase Vs — all of Table 2 in one slide, because the meristem cycles continuously.
2. **Counting the 90%.** In 100 root-tip cells, ~90 sit in interphase. The wheel (Fig. 6.1) predicts the slide — phase duration reads as cell frequency.
3. **Karyotype reading.** A metaphase spread with three copies of chromosome 21 = trisomy 21 — diagnosis read straight off a metaphase plate.
4. **Hybrid maize.** Breeders cross inbred lines; meiosis shuffles parental genomes (assortment + crossing over), and the F1 out-yields both — variation monetised.
5. **Cutting propagation.** A rose stem cutting roots because mitosis rebuilds meristems genetically identical to the parent — cloning by PMAT.
6. **Cancer in one line.** A p53 mutation breaks the G1/S checkpoint: damaged DNA copies anyway — uncontrolled mitosis is the disease.
7. **Age and trisomy.** Non-disjunction risk rises with maternal age because oocytes pause in prophase I from foetal life until ovulation — decades of waiting, one segregation error.

## 6. Key terms and statements
- **Cell cycle** — G1 → S → G2 → M: grow, replicate, prepare, divide; interphase ≈ 90%.
- **Checkpoint** — G1/S, G2/M, spindle-assembly controls; p53 can halt a damaged cell.
- **Amitosis** — direct nuclear + cytoplasmic pinching without spindle or visible phases.
- **Mitosis (PMAT)** — prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase + cytokinesis; 2n → 2×2n identical.
- **Meiosis I / II** — reductional (homologues split, 2n→n) / equational (sisters split); no S phase between.
- **Synapsis / crossing over** — homologue pairing / non-sister segment exchange in prophase I.
- **Independent assortment** — random orientation of homologue pairs at metaphase I.
- **Cytokinesis** — furrow (animals) vs cell plate (plants).
- **Non-disjunction** — homologue segregation failure → aneuploid gametes (e.g., trisomy 21).
- **Polar bodies** — oogenesis discards 2–3 tiny cells per one ovum; meiosis II completes only on fertilisation.

## 7. Exam Zone
**NEB map.** Stage identification from diagrams (PMAT + meiosis I/II) is the top diagram question. Tables (mitosis vs meiosis, cycle phases) are long-answer staples. Significance lists (three divisions × two points) are short-note favourites. Reason questions: no S between divisions; variation from meiosis; cancer from broken checkpoints; maternal age and trisomy.

**Short tricks.** "PMAT = People Meet And Talk". "2n→n needs TWO divisions, ONE replication". "I reduces, II equates". "Furrow-animals, Plate-plants". Oogenesis: "1 + 2–3, only on fertilisation".

**Sources for the facts above:** OpenStax *Biology 2e* §11 (meiosis); U. Minnesota *Human Biology* §5.2; Oregon State cell-cycle checkpoints review; MedlinePlus Genetics (TP53); CDC (Down syndrome types); 2023 trisomy-21 review; hepatocyte polyploidisation review (amitosis wording); unit validation card (kept corrections).

## 8. Summary and self-check
The cycle runs G1–S–G2–M (≈90% interphase) under three checkpoints (p53-guarded). Amitosis pinches directly without a spindle. Mitosis walks PMAT and splits cytoplasm by furrow (animals) or cell plate (plants): 2n → two identical 2n — growth, repair, cloning. Meiosis runs one replication then two divisions with no S between: prophase-I crossing over and metaphase-I assortment create variation; meiosis I reduces (2n→n), meiosis II equates sisters; spermatogenesis yields 4 sperms, oogenesis 1 ovum + 2–3 polar bodies (II completes only on fertilisation). Non-disjunction gives trisomy 21 (usually full, ~95%). Figures: cycle wheel, PMAT/meiosis flows, three reference plates.

**Self-check.** (1) Draw the cycle wheel with one event per phase. (2) Why is there no S phase between meiosis I and II — what would happen if there were? (3) Contrast furrow and cell plate formation. (4) Derive "4 sperms, 1 ovum" from the two meiotic divisions. (5) Link p53 failure to cancer in two sentences. (6) Name the two engines of meiotic variation and their phases.

**Common confusions.** Chromatids ≠ chromosomes after anaphase (each chromatid becomes a chromosome) · 2n→n happens in meiosis I, not II · crossing over exchanges non-sister segments of homologues, not sisters · "reductional" describes number, not size · amitosis is rare and specific — never cite liver cells as the example.

notes: DETAILED CELL DIVISION: the full cell cycle and every mitotic/meiotic phase.
Interphase (90% of the cycle): G1 (growth, organelle duplication, protein synthesis), S (DNA replication — each chromosome now has 2 sister chromatids), G2 (preparation for mitosis, checkpoint).
Checkpoints: G1/S (DNA damage, nutrients), G2/M (replication complete), M (spindle attachment) — failures cause cancer.

Mitosis phases (PMAT): Prophase (chromatin → chromosomes, spindle forms, nuclear envelope breaks), Metaphase (chromosomes align at the equatorial plate, spindle fibres attached to centromeres), Anaphase (centromeres split, sister chromatids pulled to opposite poles), Telophase (chromosomes decondense, nuclear envelopes reform, cytokinesis).
Cytokinesis: animal cells — cleavage furrow (actin); plant cells — cell plate → new wall.

Meiosis: two divisions. Meiosis I (reductional): Prophase I (chromosomes pair = synapsis; crossing over between non-sister chromatids), Metaphase I (homologous pairs at the equator; independent assortment), Anaphase I (homologs separate), Telophase I. Meiosis II (equational): like mitosis but no DNA replication; sister chromatids separate.
Outcome: meiosis → 4 haploid (n) genetically distinct cells; mitosis → 2 diploid (2n) identical cells.
Crossing over (Prophase I) + independent assortment (Metaphase I) = the two sources of meiotic variation.
Amitosis (direct division): simple karyokinesis; rare — described in some protozoans, yeasts/some fungi and certain pathological or regenerating cells.
Errors: mitotic errors → uncontrolled division = cancer; meiotic non-disjunction → aneuploidy (e.g., Down syndrome = usually trisomy 21).
Significance: mitosis = growth, repair, asexual reproduction; meiosis = gamete formation + genetic diversity.
NEB focus: the full cell cycle, all mitotic and meiotic phases, variation, and errors.
confusion: Mitosis maintains the chromosome number (2n → 2n); meiosis halves it (2n → n).
Crossing over and independent assortment occur in MEIOSIS only, not mitosis.
In Anaphase I of meiosis, HOMOLOGOUS chromosomes separate; in Anaphase of mitosis and Anaphase II of meiosis, SISTER CHROMATIDs separate.
DNA replication happens ONLY in the S phase; meiosis has one S phase then two divisions.
G2 is not a "resting" phase; DNA has already doubled in S and the cell is preparing for M.
Non-disjunction = a homologous pair (or chromatid pair) fails to separate → one cell gets both, the other gets none.

Biomolecules are organic compounds (C,H,O,N,S,P) that make up living organisms
Carbohydrates: monosaccharides (glucose), disaccharides (sucrose), polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose)
Proteins: amino acids linked by peptide bonds; primary→secondary→tertiary→quaternary structure
Lipids: fats, oils, phospholipids, steroids; hydrophobic molecules forming cell membranes
Nucleic acids: DNA (double helix) and RNA (single strand); genetic information storage and transfer
Enzymes: biological catalysts that lower activation energy; specific to substrates
Cell theory: all living things made of cells; cells are basic unit of life; all cells from pre-existing cells
Prokaryotic cells: no nucleus, no membrane-bound organelles; bacteria and archaea

data.topicTitle: Animal adaptation: Aquatic (primary and secondary), terrestrial (cursorial, fossorial and arboreal) and volant adaptation
notes: Animal adaptation: structural, physiological, and behavioural features that allow an animal to survive in a particular environment.
Aquatic adaptation: primary aquatic (fishes, fully aquatic) and secondary aquatic (whales, seals — originally terrestrial).
Aquatic features: streamlined (fusiform) body, fins, gills (countercurrent exchange), lateral line (fish), webbed feet, dense bones, salt glands.
Terrestrial adaptation: cursorial (running — cheetah, horse), fossorial (burrowing — earthworm, mole), arboreal (tree-dwelling — monkey, sloth).
Terrestrial features: waterproof skin (fur, scales, feathers), lungs, internal fertilisation, nitrogenous waste (urea/ammonia), strong limbs.
Volant adaptation: flight; features: wings (feathers), hollow (pneumatic) bones, air sacs (double respiration), strong pectoral muscles, streamlined body, beak.
Adaptations increase survival and reproduction in a given habitat; they are the result of natural selection.
NEB focus: aquatic (primary + secondary), terrestrial (cursorial, fossorial, arboreal), and volant adaptations.
Nepal examples: fish (Terai), rhododendron forest birds (volant), snow leopard (terrestrial cursorial), pangolin (fossorial).

notes: Animal behavior: the actions and responses of animals to stimuli; includes innate (fixed) and learned behaviours.
Reflex action: an automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus, mediated by a reflex arc (receptor → sensory neuron → CNS → motor neuron → effector).
Taxes: orientation responses (movement toward or away from a stimulus). Phototaxis (light), chemotaxis (chemical), thigmotaxis (touch), geotaxis (gravity).
Taxis vs Kinesis: taxis is DIRECTIONAL movement toward/away from a stimulus; kinesis is NON-directional (random) movement in response to a stimulus.
Dominance and leadership: social hierarchies in group-living animals (primates, wolves, fish); the dominant individual has priority access to food, mates, and territory.
Fish migration: seasonal movement to feeding or breeding grounds; e.g., salmon (upstream spawning), mackerel (Nepal Terai rivers).
Bird migration: long-distance seasonal movement (e.g., Himalayan birds migrate to lower altitudes in winter; storks migrate to the Terai).
NEB focus: reflex action, taxes, dominance and leadership, fish and bird migration.
Migration is a behavioural adaptation; it is seasonal and genetically programmed.
confusion: A reflex arc is SHORT (spinal level); it does NOT involve the brain (faster response).
Taxis is DIRECTIONAL (toward/away from a stimulus); kinesis is NON-DIRECTIONAL (random movement).
Phototaxis: movement in response to light (positive = toward, negative = away).
Dominance hierarchies are ESTABLISHED through social interactions; they are not fixed by birth.
Fish migration is often seasonal (breeding, feeding); it is not random movement.
Bird migration is a BEHAVIOURAL adaptation; it is genetically programmed and often learned by first-year migrants.

universalFacts: The fastest reflex is the knee-jerk (patellar) reflex, with a latency of ~30–50 ms.
Some salmon (e.g., Atlantic salmon) migrate thousands of km upstream to spawn in the stream where they were born.
Honeybees use a "waggle dance" to communicate the direction and distance of a food source to nestmates.
Migration is one of the most spectacular animal behaviours; some birds fly >10,000 km per year.
examples: Reflex: touching a hot object → hand withdraws (reflex arc: skin receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → muscle).
Phototaxis: earthworms move AWAY from light (negative phototaxis).
Chemotaxis: bacteria move toward a nutrient source (positive chemotaxis).
Dominance: a dominant male lion has priority access to females in the pride.
Fish migration: mackerel in the Kosi and Gandaki rivers migrate seasonally to feed and breed.
Bird migration: Himalayan birds (e.g., bar-headed goose) migrate to the Terai in winter; storks migrate to lowland lakes.

notes: Environmental pollution: the addition of substances or energy to the environment at a rate that exceeds its capacity to dilute, degrade, or absorb them.
Air pollution: SO2 (coal), NOx (vehicles), CO (incomplete combustion), PM2.5/PM10 (particulates), ozone (ground-level), CFCs; sources: industry, vehicles, power plants, biomass burning.
Effects of air pollution: respiratory diseases (asthma, bronchitis), acid rain, smog, global warming, ozone depletion.
Kathmandu Valley: PM2.5 exceeds WHO limits ~10× in winter (stove smoke, vehicles, dust).

Water pollution: domestic waste, industrial effluent, agricultural runoff (pesticides, fertilisers), oil spills, thermal pollution; effects: eutrophication, oxygen depletion, disease (cholera, typhoid).
Soil pollution: heavy metals, pesticides, plastics, industrial waste; effects: reduced fertility, contamination of food, leaching to groundwater.
Pesticides: chemicals to control pests; types: insecticides, herbicides, fungicides, rodenticides; effects: biomagnification, resistance, non-target species death, soil/water contamination.
Control measures: reduce emissions, renewable energy, tree planting, waste treatment, organic farming, international agreements (Montreal, Paris).
NEB focus: sources, effects, and control measures of air, water, and soil pollution; pesticides and their effects.
Nepal: vulnerable to air (Kathmandu), water (river pollution), and soil (pesticide) pollution; deforestation and urbanisation are major contributors.
confusion: Acid rain (pH < 5.6) is caused by SO2 and NOx, NOT by CO2 alone.
Ozone is beneficial in the STRATOSPHERE (blocks UV) but harmful at ground level (smog, air pollutant).
Biomagnification: toxin concentration INCREASES at higher trophic levels (e.g., DDT in fish-eating birds).
Pesticide resistance: pests evolve resistance over time; higher doses are needed.
Eutrophication: excess nutrients (N, P) → algal bloom → O2 depletion → fish kill.
PM2.5 (fine particulates) are MORE harmful than PM10 because they penetrate deeper into the lungs.

DDT (banned in many countries) biomagnifies up food chains; it caused eggshell thinning in raptors (eagles, falcons).
Eutrophication is the #1 cause of "dead zones" (hypoxic zones) in lakes and coastal waters.
Nepal's community forestry program manages ~36% of the country's forest land.

data.title: Fish and bird migration
notes: [Remember] Migration is the periodic, seasonal, two-way movement of animals between breeding and non-breeding habitats — distinct from one-way dispersal or permanent emigration.

[Remember] Fish migration: anadromous fishes move from sea to fresh water to breed (e.g. Hilsa ilisha ascending Terai rivers in monsoon); catadromous fishes move from fresh water to sea to breed (e.g. eels, Anguilla).

[Understand] Bird migration types: latitudinal or north–south (Siberian ducks wintering at Koshi Tappu and Chitwan), longitudinal, and altitudinal (pheasants and thrushes descending from hills to Terai in winter).

[Understand] Causes and triggers: breeding urge, food scarcity, shortening photoperiod, falling temperature and hormonal change; navigation uses the sun compass, star patterns, Earth's magnetic field and geographical landmarks.
[Apply] Contrast table — anadromous vs catadromous (direction, breeding ground, one example each); resident vs migratory vs partial-migrant birds with one Nepali example of each.

[Analyze] Advantages (safe breeding grounds, abundant seasonal food) versus costs (enormous energy demand, predation, barriers such as dams and habitat loss); homing instinct and ringing/banding studies as evidence.

[Evaluate/Create] NEB answer frame: define migration → classify fish and bird types → causes and navigation → Koshi Tappu/Chitwan and Terai-river examples → one advantage–cost line → labelled route sketch.

data.topicTitle: Environmental pollution: Sources, effects and control measures of air, water and soil pollution
notes: Pollution is the addition of substances or energy to air, water or soil at a rate the environment cannot make harmless. A pollutant is harmful because of its amount, its toxicity, or both.

Air pollutants include sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from burning fuel, carbon monoxide from incomplete burning, smoke and dust, and ground-level ozone formed in sunlight from vehicle exhaust. They irritate lungs, damage leaves, and form acid rain when sulphur and nitrogen oxides dissolve in cloud water.

Water is polluted by untreated sewage, factory effluent, fertiliser washed off fields, and oil. Sewage and fertiliser add nutrients. Algae then bloom, die and are decomposed, and the decomposers use up dissolved oxygen. Fish die in that oxygen-poor water. This is eutrophication.

Soil is polluted by persistent pesticides, plastics and heavy metals from industry and dumps. DDT and similar fat-soluble poisons increase in concentration along a food chain, so top predators carry the highest dose. That increase is biomagnification.

Control follows the source. Use cleaner fuel and maintain engines for air. Treat sewage before it enters a river. Match fertiliser to the crop so the surplus does not run off. Prefer pesticides that break down, and do not burn plastic on fields.

Laws and local habits both matter. A treatment plant that is bypassed, or a pesticide that is sprayed on the day of harvest, undoes the technical control. Monitoring of river oxygen and of air smoke tells whether the control is working.

confusion: Eutrophication is caused by too many nutrients, not by a poison in the ordinary sense. The fish die from lack of oxygen after the algal bloom collapses.
Biomagnification is not the same as bioaccumulation. Accumulation is the build-up inside one organism. Magnification is the rise in concentration from prey to predator along the chain.
Carbon dioxide from ordinary breathing is not listed with the classical air pollutants such as sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide and particulates.
Biodegradable sewage is still a pollutant when there is more of it than the river can decompose without losing its oxygen.

Control means treating the source: fuel, sewage, fertiliser dose and pesticide choice.
importantStatements: A pollutant is defined by harm at the concentration present, not only by being unnatural.
Eutrophication kills fish by oxygen depletion after an algal bloom, not by the fertiliser burning them.

exercises.answer: The fish die from oxygen loss after the nutrient-driven algal bloom collapses and decays. This is eutrophication.

data.summary: Air, water and soil are polluted when harmful substances arrive faster than they can be made safe. Sulphur and nitrogen oxides acidify rain. Sewage and fertiliser drive eutrophication and oxygen loss. Persistent pesticides such as DDT biomagnify up food chains. Control works at the source: cleaner burning, sewage treatment, careful fertiliser use and pesticides that do not persist.

data.title: biota-and-environment Mindmap
notes: How animals adapt to their environment and the impacts of pollution on biota and ecosystems.
Adaptation: structural, physiological, or behavioral traits that improve survival and reproduction
Structural adaptations: body shape, coloration, camouflage, mimicry
Physiological adaptations: temperature regulation, toxin resistance, hibernation
Behavioral adaptations: migration, hibernation, courtship rituals, social organization
Pollution: introduction of harmful substances into environment — air, water, soil pollution
Air pollution: particulate matter, SO₂, NOₓ, CO, ozone; causes respiratory diseases and acid rain
Water pollution: industrial waste, agricultural runoff, sewage; eutrophication from nutrient excess
Soil pollution: pesticides, heavy metals, plastic waste; affects soil organisms and crop productivity

notes: Biodiversity: the variety of life at three levels — genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity.
Genetic diversity: variation in genes within a species; important for adaptation and survival.
Species diversity: number and abundance of species in an area; higher in tropics.
Ecosystem diversity: variety of habitats, biotic communities, and ecological processes in a region.
Biodiversity conservation: protecting and managing biological diversity; in-situ (in natural habitat) and ex-situ (outside habitat).
In-situ conservation: protected areas (national parks, wildlife reserves, conservation areas), community forests, sacred groves.
Ex-situ conservation: zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks, gene banks, cryopreservation.
Why conserve? Food, medicine, industry, ecological services (pollination, water, climate), aesthetic, ethical, and intrinsic value.
Threats: habitat loss/fragmentation, overexploitation, pollution, invasive species, climate change, illegal trade (poaching).
Nepal: global biodiversity hotspot (Himalaya); 64% of forests; community forestry (22,000+ groups manage ~36% of forest land); national parks and conservation areas.
NEB focus: concept of biodiversity, its conservation, and in-situ vs ex-situ strategies.
confusion: Biodiversity has THREE levels: genetic, species, ecosystem (not just "number of species").
In-situ conservation protects species IN their natural habitat; ex-situ conserves them OUTSIDE (zoos, seed banks).
Protected areas (in-situ) are the most effective large-scale conservation strategy.
Community forestry (in-situ) gives local communities rights and responsibility; it is Nepal's success story.
A biodiversity HOTSPOT has high endemic species AND severe habitat loss (both criteria).
Conservation is not just "protecting animals"; it includes genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity.

Biodiversity conservation involves safeguarding and scientifically managing diverse life forms to sustain their levels and provide lasting benefits for current and future generations.

It protects plant, animal, microbial, and genetic resources crucial for food production, agriculture, and ecosystem functions like soil fertilization, nutrient recycling, pest control, erosion prevention, and crop and tree pollination.
Conservation practices aim to manage nature and resources for present and future generations, ensuring the sustained well-being of humanity.
There are two basic strategies of biodiversity conservation: a.
In-Situ Conservation (within natural habitat): This method protects organisms in their natural habitats like national parks and other protected areas.
For instance, in Chitwan National Park, we have centers for Elephant Breeding, Gharial Conservation, and Vulture Conservation.

Ex-Situ Conservation (outside natural habitat): This type of conservation strategy includes protection of animals outside their natural habitats such as botanical or zoological gardens, cryopreservation, seed gene banks etc.

The one-horned rhinoceros in Nepal is found mainly in:

notes: Protected areas: designated areas for conservation; in Nepal: 10 national parks, 6 conservation areas, 1 hunting reserve, and Ramsar wetlands.

National parks: Chitwan (1973, Bengal tiger + one-horned rhino), Bardia, Banke, Shuklaphanta, Koshi Tappu, Parsa, Rara, Langtang (1976), Sagarmatha (1976), Annapurna (1986), Manaslu (1986), Makalu (1992), Kanchenjunga (1989). NEB commonly cites 10 national parks; several sources list 11–14 depending on inclusion of the newer parks.
Conservation areas (6): Kanchenjunga, Manaslu, Shey-Phoksundo, Khoratadi, Khaptad, and Barun.
Ramsar sites: Koshi Tappu, Rara, Chitwan (Terai wetlands) — internationally important wetlands.

data.title: Wildlife: Importance, Causes of Extinction and Conservation Strategies
data.topicTitle: Wildlife: Importance, causes of extinction and conservation strategies
notes: Wildlife includes all non-domesticated plants, animals, and microorganisms living in natural habitats, forming essential components of ecosystems.
Wildlife provides ecosystem services: pollination, seed dispersal, nutrient cycling, pest control, and maintenance of food webs.
Wildlife has economic value through ecotourism, medicinal resources, genetic diversity for agriculture, and sustainable harvest of timber and non-timber products.
Wildlife holds cultural, aesthetic, and ethical value, supporting indigenous knowledge and spiritual traditions.
Major causes of extinction: habitat destruction and fragmentation, overexploitation (hunting, poaching), invasive species, pollution, climate change, and disease.
Habitat loss is the leading cause of species extinction, driven by deforestation, agriculture, urbanization, and infrastructure development.
Overexploitation occurs when harvesting exceeds reproduction rates, as seen in ivory poaching and overfishing.
Invasive alien species outcompete native species for resources and alter ecosystem dynamics (e.g., Lantana camara in Nepal).
Conservation strategies include legal protection (CITES, national laws), protected areas, captive breeding, habitat restoration, community-based conservation, and international cooperation.
CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species) regulates cross-border trade in threatened species through Appendix I, II, and III listings.

notes: The IUCN Red List is the world's most comprehensive inventory of the global conservation status of biological species, maintained by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
Extinct (EX): no reasonable doubt that the last individual has died; no surveys can find it.
Extinct in the Wild (EW): survives only in captivity or cultivation, with no natural population.
Critically Endangered (CR): extremely high risk of extinction in the wild; e.g., population < 50 mature individuals or rapid decline.
Endangered (EN): very high risk of extinction in the wild; smaller populations or steeper declines than CR threshold.
Vulnerable (VU): high risk of extinction in the wild; larger populations than EN but still threatened.
Near Threatened (NT): close to qualifying for a threatened category.
Least Concern (LC): widespread and abundant; lowest risk of extinction.
Data Deficient (DD): insufficient information to assess extinction risk.
Not Evaluated (NE): not yet assessed against the criteria.

data.title: Endangered Species in Nepal
notes: Nepal's diverse geography (tropical to alpine) supports rich biodiversity, but many species are threatened by habitat loss, poaching, and human-wildlife conflict.
One-horned rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) — Vulnerable; found in Chitwan and Bardia National Parks; recovered from ~100 individuals in 1960s to ~750 today.
Bengal tiger (Panthera tigris) — Endangered; population ~355 in Nepal (2022 census), concentrated in Terai protected areas.
Snow leopard (Panthera uncia) — Vulnerable; inhabits high Himalayas; threatened by poaching and retaliatory killing.
Red panda (Ailurus fulgens) — Endangered; found in eastern and central Himalayan forests; threatened by habitat fragmentation.
Gharial (Gavialis gangeticus) — Critically Endangered; freshwater crocodile of river systems; fewer than 200 in Nepal.
Himalayan musk deer (Moschus chrysogaster) — Endangered; hunted for musk pod; found in high-altitude forests.
Wild water buffalo (Bubalus arnee) — Endangered; restricted to Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve.
Conservation efforts: protected areas, anti-poaching units, community forestry, transboundary cooperation (India, China), and captive breeding programs.
Nepal's National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP) guides species conservation priorities.
