data.title: Earthworm (Pheretima posthuma): Habit and habitat, extern…
data.topicTitle: Earthworm (Pheretima posthuma): Habit and habitat, external features; digestive system (alimentary canal and physiology of digestion)

visualization.desc: Pheretima in side view: prostomium at the front, clitellum on segments 14 to 16, gizzard in the gut, typhlosole as a fold in the intestine.

notes: Pheretima posthuma is a terrestrial oligochaete of moist soil. It is nocturnal, because a dry skin blocks the gas exchange that its body wall has to do, and it comes up to feed and to mate when the surface is damp. It burrows by pushing coelomic fluid forward and anchoring the swollen segments with setae. The food is decaying organic matter in the soil it swallows. The castings it leaves are the soil after that meal has passed through.

The body has about 100 to 120 segments. The first segment is the peristomium, and a small prostomium overhangs the mouth. A glandular clitellum covers segments 14, 15 and 16 and looks like a saddle. Setae are arranged in a ring on each segment, the perichaetine pattern, and they are missing on the first segment, the clitellum and the last segment. The arrangement is the external sign of Oligochaeta.

The ventral surface carries the openings used in reproduction, and they are asked as a labelled list. Spermathecal pores open in the grooves between segments 5/6, 6/7, 7/8 and 8/9. The female genital pore is a single mid-ventral opening on segment 14. A pair of male genital pores opens on segment 18. Genital papillae sit on segments 17 and 19. The anus is the last segment. Dorsal pores, from which coelomic fluid leaks out to keep the skin moist, begin behind the clitellum.

Absorption is across the typhlosole and the intestinal wall into blood that already contains haemoglobin dissolved in the plasma. Egestion is continuous. An earthworm that is feeding is also depositing castings.

Pheretima posthuma is a terrestrial oligochaete of moist soil. It is nocturnal, because a dry skin blocks the gas exchange that its body wall has to do, and it comes up to feed and to mate when the surface is damp. It burrows by pushing coelomic fluid forward and anchoring the swollen segments with setae. The food is decaying organic matter in the soil it swallows. The castings it leaves are the soil after that meal has passed through.

The body has about 100 to 120 segments. The first segment is the peristomium, and a small prostomium overhangs the mouth. A glandular clitellum covers segments 14, 15 and 16 and looks like a saddle. Setae are arranged in a ring on each segment, the perichaetine pattern, and they are missing on the first segment, the clitellum and the last segment. The arrangement is the external sign of Oligochaeta.

confusion: The clitellum is segments 14 to 16, not a random swelling in the middle of the body. The female pore is on segment 14, inside that region.
Earthworm blood is red. Haemoglobin is dissolved in the plasma. It is not carried in red cells, and it is not absent.
The typhlosole is a fold of the intestine, not a separate gland. The caeca at segment 26 are the glandular outgrowths.
Setae are not parapodia. Parapodia belong to Nereis. Pheretima has a ring of small setae.
keyPoints: Moist soil, nocturnal, burrowing, feeds on organic matter in swallowed soil.
About 100 to 120 segments. Clitellum on 14, 15 and 16. Perichaetine setae.
Spermathecal pores in grooves 5/6 to 8/9. Female pore on 14. Male pores on 18.
Gizzard grinds in segments 8 to 9. Calciferous glands neutralise acid in the stomach.
Intestinal caeca at segment 26. Typhlosole increases the absorptive surface.
importantStatements: The gizzard is the grinding organ. The mouth does not chew.
Calciferous glands neutralise humic acids. They are not digestive enzymes.
Haemoglobin of Pheretima is in the plasma, which is why the blood is red without red cells.
examples: A worm in a dry courtyard stays deep in the burrow because gas exchange through the skin fails when the cuticle dries.
Soil with leaf litter enters the mouth, is ground in the gizzard, and leaves as a casting richer in mineral nutrients.
Starch from plant debris is attacked by amylase from the intestinal caeca of segment 26.
universalFacts: Pheretima is perichaetine: the setae form a closed ring on a typical segment.
Dorsal pores release coelomic fluid onto the skin and help keep respiration possible.
formulas: Clitellum 14–16. Female pore 14. Male pores 18. Spermathecae open at 5/6, 6/7, 7/8, 8/9.
Buccal cavity 1–3, pharynx 4, oesophagus 5–7, gizzard 8–9, stomach 9–14, intestine from 15.
Caeca at 26. Typhlosole from about 27, absent near the rectum.

exercises.question: A student says the earthworm chews leaves in its mouth and that its blood is colourless. Correct both claims with the organs involved.
steps: The mouth and buccal cavity only take soil in. They do not chew.
Grinding is the work of the gizzard in segments 8 and 9.
Chemical digestion of the organic matter happens in the intestine, with amylase from the caeca at segment 26.
Absorption uses the typhlosole. The blood that receives the products contains haemoglobin dissolved in the plasma, so it is red.
There are no red blood cells. Colourless blood would mean no respiratory pigment, which is the wrong description of Pheretima.
exercises.answer: Grinding is gizzard, not mouth. Blood is red because haemoglobin is dissolved in the plasma.

notes: Digestive system: mouth (tongue) → buccal cavity → oesophagus → stomach → intestine (small + large) → rectum → cloaca; liver and gall bladder; pancreas; bile for fat digestion.
Circulatory system: 3-chambered heart (2 atria + 1 ventricle) → double circulation; oxygenated + deoxygenated blood partially mixed in the ventricle; systemic + pulmonary circuits.

Heart structure: right atrium (deoxygenated from body), left atrium (oxygenated from lungs/skin), single ventricle (partially mixed blood); ventricle has a spongy myocardium (crista ventriculi) that reduces mixing.
Respiratory system: lungs (pulmonary), moist skin (cutaneous), buccal cavity (buccal); tadpoles use gills.

Physiology of respiration: inhalation (buccal floor lowers → air enters through nostrils), exhalation (buccal floor rises → air pushed into lungs); skin respiration is significant in water and at night.
Working mechanism of the heart: atria contract first (fill ventricle), then ventricle contracts (pump blood to lungs + body); valves (atrioventricular, conus valves) prevent backflow.
NEB focus: digestive system, blood vascular system (heart structure + working), respiratory system (organs + physiology).
confusion: The frog heart is 3-chambered (2 atria + 1 ventricle), NOT 4-chambered like mammals.
Blood is PARTIALLY MIXED in the frog ventricle (unlike the 4-chambered heart of birds and mammals where it is fully separated).
The spongy myocardium (crista ventriculi) in the frog ventricle helps reduce mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.
Frogs use THREE respiratory surfaces: lungs, moist skin (cutaneous), and the buccal cavity; tadpoles use gills.
The cloaca is the common exit for digestive, excretory, and reproductive systems.
Bile (from the liver, stored in the gall bladder) emulsifies fat in the small intestine; it is not a digestive enzyme.

visualization.desc: The same body, read for excretion and nerves: septal nephridia from segment 15 discharge into the gut, and the ventral nerve cord runs along the floor.

notes: Nitrogenous waste in Pheretima is removed by nephridia, which are coiled tubes derived from mesoderm. The animal is terrestrial, so most of that waste is urea, and the design of the ducts also decides how much water is lost with it. There are three kinds, named by where they sit: septal, integumentary and pharyngeal.

Septal nephridia are fixed on both faces of the septa from segment 15 to the posterior end. Each has a ciliated nephrostome opening into the coelom of the segment in front, a short neck through the septum, and a nephridial body made of a straight lobe and a looped lobe. The terminal ducts of the nephridia on one septum join a septal excretory canal. Those canals feed a pair of supra-intestinal excretory ducts, which open into the intestine. The waste therefore leaves with the gut contents. This is enteronephric excretion, and it saves water that a soil animal cannot afford to pour away.

Integumentary nephridia are attached to the inner surface of the body wall in every segment except the first two. They have no nephrostome. Their ducts open on the skin, so they are exonephric. They excrete, and the fluid they release also helps keep the respiratory surface moist. Pharyngeal nephridia form three paired tufts in segments 4, 5 and 6. They are also closed, without a funnel, and they open into the pharynx, so they are enteronephric like the septal set. The septal nephridia are the main excretory organs. The other two sets are smaller and have extra jobs.

The nervous system is a ventral chain, the opposite of the frog's dorsal hollow cord. The central part is a nerve ring plus a cord. A pair of cerebral ganglia, the brain, lies on the pharynx in segment 3. Circum-pharyngeal connectives run around the pharynx to a pair of sub-pharyngeal ganglia in segment 4. From there a double ventral nerve cord runs to the last segment, with a fused ganglion in each segment. The cord looks single and is anatomically double.

Peripheral nerves leave those ganglia. The cerebral ganglia send nerves into the prostomium. Each segmental ganglion sends paired nerves into the body wall and the organs of its segment. There is no single spinal cord doing the whole body's work. Each segment can answer a stimulus, and the cord links the segments so the answer travels as a wave.

The working mechanism is a reflex. A touch or a strong light stimulates receptor cells in the skin. A sensory fibre carries that signal into the segmental ganglion. An association neuron hands it to a motor neuron, and the motor fibre brings about a contraction of muscle or a change in the setae. The brain does not have to approve every segment. It does bias the animal: Pheretima moves away from strong light and coordinates the swell-and-thin wave of peristalsis so the burrow is dug backward from the front, rather than as a spasm of every segment at once.

confusion: Enteronephric ducts open into the gut. Exonephric ducts open on the skin. Septal nephridia are enteronephric. Integumentary nephridia are exonephric.
Integumentary and pharyngeal nephridia have no nephrostome. Only septal nephridia collect coelomic fluid through a ciliated funnel.
The earthworm's nerve cord is ventral and solid. The frog's is dorsal and hollow. 'Nerve cord' alone is not a shared structure.
The brain is the supra-pharyngeal ganglia in segment 3, not a swelling of the ventral cord in the clitellum.
keyPoints: Three nephridia: septal, integumentary, pharyngeal.
Septal nephridia from segment 15, with a nephrostome, enteronephric into the intestine.
Integumentary nephridia open on the skin. Pharyngeal tufts in segments 4, 5 and 6 open into the pharynx.
Brain in segment 3, sub-pharyngeal ganglia in segment 4, double ventral cord with segmental ganglia.
A reflex is receptor, sensory fibre, ganglion, motor fibre, muscle.
importantStatements: Enteronephric excretion discharges into the gut and conserves water.
A nephrostome is the ciliated funnel of a septal nephridium only.
The ventral nerve cord is double in origin and ganglionated in every segment.
examples: Coelomic fluid is drawn into a septal nephridium through the nephrostome and eventually reaches the intestine.
Fluid from integumentary nephridia spreads on the skin and supports cutaneous respiration.
A sharp touch on one segment shortens the muscles of that segment before the whole animal changes direction.
universalFacts: Pheretima is mainly ureotelic, which fits a terrestrial life better than dumping ammonia into the soil water.
Strong light drives the worm back into the burrow. The receptors are in the skin. There are no eyes.

exercises.question: Sort these into septal, integumentary or pharyngeal: a ciliated funnel on the septum of segment 20; a duct opening on the skin of segment 30; a tuft in segment 5 opening into the pharynx.
steps: A funnel on a septum behind segment 15 is a septal nephridium. Its duct system ends in the intestine, so it is enteronephric.
A duct that opens on the skin, with no funnel, is an integumentary nephridium. It is exonephric.
A tuft in segment 5 that opens into the pharynx is a pharyngeal nephridium. Segments 4, 5 and 6 are its only range.
Only the first of the three has a nephrostome.
exercises.answer: Septal, integumentary, pharyngeal, in that order. Only the septal nephridium has a nephrostome.

data.summary: Pheretima excretes mainly urea through three kinds of nephridia. Septal nephridia, from segment 15, have a nephrostome and discharge into the intestine, which saves water. Integumentary nephridia open on the skin. Pharyngeal nephridia in segments 4 to 6 open into the pharynx. The nervous system is a brain on the pharynx in segment 3, a sub-pharyngeal ganglion in segment 4, and a double ventral cord with a ganglion in every segment. notes: Male reproductive system: testes (2, kidney-shaped, along the dorsal wall) → vasa deferentia → seminal vesicles → cloaca; no copulatory organ.
Female reproductive system: ovaries (2, lobed, along the dorsal wall) → oviducts (funnel-shaped opening near the kidney) → uterus → cloaca.
Eggs: unfertilised ova are released into the oviducts; the oviduct adds a jelly coat; eggs are deposited in water.
Fertilisation: EXTERNAL; the male mounts the female (amplexus), releases sperm over the eggs as the female releases eggs; fertilisation in water.
Amplexus: male grasps the female behind the ribs (axillary amplexus in Rana) to ensure sperm is released near the eggs.
Development: fertilised egg → zygote → blastula → gastrula → tadpole (larva with gills + tail) → metamorphosis → adult frog.
Economic/ecological importance: pest control (eats insects), indicator of water quality (sensitive to pollution), food in some cultures.

The male has two kidney-shaped testes, vasa deferentia, seminal vesicles, and a cloaca (no copulatory organ). The female has two lobed ovaries, oviducts that add a jelly coat, a uterus, and a cloaca. data.summary:
The frog's reproductive system is adapted for external fertilisation in water. The male has two kidney-shaped testes, vasa deferentia, seminal vesicles, and a cloaca (no copulatory organ). The female has two lobed ovaries, oviducts that add a jelly coat, a uterus, and a cloaca. During amplexus, the male grasps the female and both release gametes into the water, where external fertilisation occurs. Development proceeds from the zygote to the tadpole (gills + tail) to the adult frog (lungs, no tail) via metamorphosis. Frogs are ecologically important as pest controllers and water-quality bio-indicators. visualization.desc: Clitellum on segments 14 to 16, the gland that secretes the cocoon. Male pores lie just behind it, on segment 18.

notes: Pheretima is hermaphrodite. Each worm has a full male system and a full female system. Self-fertilisation is not the normal event. Two worms copulate, exchange sperm, and separate. Fertilisation happens later, outside the body, inside a cocoon. That sequence is the whole reproductive story.

The male organs are crowded into a few front segments. Two pairs of testes lie in segments 10 and 11, inside testis sacs. Sperm mature in two pairs of seminal vesicles in segments 11 and 12. Ciliated spermiducal funnels, also in segments 10 and 11, collect the sperm into vasa deferentia. Each side's duct runs back to segment 18, where it joins a prostate gland. The prostate secretion is the fluid in which the sperm leave. The male genital pores open on segment 18. Accessory glands on segments 17 and 19 serve the genital papillae that help the worms hold together.

The female organs are smaller. One pair of ovaries lies in segment 13. An ovarian funnel under each ovary leads into an oviduct, and the two oviducts meet to open at the single female genital pore on segment 14. Eggs are not stored for a long time. They are shed when a cocoon passes that segment. Four pairs of spermathecae, in segments 6, 7, 8 and 9, receive the partner's sperm during copulation. Each spermatheca has a larger ampulla and a narrow diverticulum, and the received sperm stays there until the cocoon is formed.

During copulation the two worms lie head to tail, ventral surface against ventral surface, so that the male pores of each are opposite the spermathecal pores of the other. Mucus and the setae hold them. Sperm and prostatic fluid pass into the spermathecae. No eggs move across. The worms then separate. A worm that has just copulated is carrying another worm's sperm, not embryos.

The cocoon is a product of the clitellum. Glands in segments 14 to 16 secrete a girdle of membrane and albumen. The worm wriggles backward and slips out of the girdle. As the girdle passes segment 14, eggs enter it. As it passes the spermathecal openings, the stored sperm enters. The ends of the girdle close, and the sealed cocoon is left in damp soil. Fertilisation, the actual fusion, takes place in the albumen inside that cocoon. Development is direct. A small worm emerges. There is no trochophore and no other larva.

The same animal that reproduces this way is useful in soil. Burrows let air and water deeper into the ground. Castings return mineral nutrients to the surface in a form roots can use, and they improve the crumb of the soil. Earthworms are the workforce of vermicompost. They are also bait and food for birds. They are not a crop pest in the sense of an insect that eats leaves. Their economic importance is the soil they leave behind them.

visualization.desc: The gut column: stomach, duodenum and ileum, liver and pancreas, and a cloaca rather than a separate anus. Heart and lungs are the next note.

notes: Rana tigrina is the frog named in the course. It lives where land and standing water meet: pond edges, ditches and flooded fields. The adult can spend long periods on land if the skin stays moist, and it must return to water to breed. The tadpole is aquatic. The adult is a carnivore, taking insects, earthworms and other small animals with a flick of the tongue. In winter it hibernates, and in extreme dry heat it aestivates, buried, with metabolism slowed and gas exchange left largely to the skin.

The body has a head and a trunk and no neck. The adult has no tail. The head is triangular. The eyes are large and placed so that a frog sitting in water can see above the surface. A nictitating membrane crosses the eye under water. Behind each eye is a round tympanum, the eardrum, with no external ear flap. Nostrils are small and dorsal. The mouth is a wide terminal slit. The cloaca opens at the end of the trunk.

The forelimb is short, with four fingers and no web, and it props the body up. The hind limb is long, muscular, and five-toed, with a web between the toes. It is the leaping and swimming limb. Males in the breeding season are told apart by a vocal sac on each side of the throat and by a dark nuptial pad on the inner finger of the forelimb, used to grip the female. Females lack both. Size alone is not the character to use.

The alimentary canal is mouth, buccopharyngeal cavity, short oesophagus, stomach, duodenum, ileum, rectum and cloaca. Teeth are present only on the upper jaw: a maxillary row along the margin and vomerine patches on the roof. They are homodont and acrodont, all alike and fused to the jaw surface, and they hold prey. They do not chew it. The tongue is attached at the front of the mouth and free and forked at the back, so it can be thrown out and retrieved with the prey stuck to it.

Digestive glands empty at two stations. The stomach wall has gastric glands. The liver, large and lobed, stores glycogen and produces bile, which is held in a gall bladder. The pancreas lies in the curve between the stomach and the duodenum. The bile duct and the pancreatic duct meet and enter the duodenum together. Mucus from the mouth lubricates the prey. There is no salivary digestion of starch of the kind a mammal does.

Physiology follows the organs. In the mouth the prey is positioned and swallowed. No chemical digestion happens there. In the stomach, hydrochloric acid and pepsin begin the proteins, and the acid kills many of the organisms swallowed with the prey. In the duodenum, bile emulsifies fat and neutralises the acid chyme, and pancreatic juice supplies protease, amylase and lipase. Intestinal juice finishes the breakdown to amino acids, simple sugars, and fatty acids with glycerol. The ileum, with villi, absorbs those products. What remains enters the rectum and leaves by the cloaca, the same chamber that receives urine and gametes. Calling that opening an anus is the wrong word for a frog.

exercises.question: A frog swallows an insect. State what happens to the insect's proteins and fats, in order of organs, and name the exit.
steps: The mouth grips the insect with maxillary and vomerine teeth and swallows it. No enzyme acts there.
In the stomach, hydrochloric acid and pepsin begin protein digestion.
In the duodenum, bile from the liver emulsifies the fat and neutralises the acid. Pancreatic lipase then splits the fat. Pancreatic protease continues the proteins.
Intestinal enzymes finish both to absorbable products. Amino acids and the fat products are absorbed in the ileum.
Undigested remains pass through the rectum and leave by the cloaca.
exercises.answer: Proteins start in the stomach and finish in the intestine. Fats are emulsified by bile and split by lipase in the duodenum. The exit is the cloaca.

data.summary: Rana tigrina is a pond-edge carnivore that hibernates and aestivates. The adult has no tail and no neck, a tympanum, a nictitating membrane, four fingers and a webbed five-toed hind foot. Breeding males add vocal sacs and a nuptial pad. Prey is gripped by upper teeth and a front-hinged tongue, swallowed without chewing, protein-digested in the stomach, and finished in the duodenum with bile and pancreatic juice. Absorption is in the ileum. Faeces leave through the cloaca.

data.topicTitle: Frog: Blood vascular system (structure and working mechanism of heart); respiratory system (respiratory organs and physiology of respiration)

visualization.desc: Three-chambered heart, with two atria and one ventricle leading into the truncus arteriosus, beside skin and lungs as the respiratory surfaces.

notes: The frog's blood system is a closed system of vessels served by a three-chambered heart, and the circulation is an incomplete double circulation. Blood can be sent to the lungs and skin and returned, and it can be sent to the body and returned, but a single ventricle is the pump for both streams. The respiratory surfaces that refresh that blood are the skin, the lining of the mouth, and the lungs. Gills are the tadpole's organs. An adult frog in air does not use them.

On the dorsal side of the heart is the sinus venosus, a thin sac that receives the two anterior venae cavae and the posterior vena cava, so it holds blood returning from the body. It opens into the right atrium. The right atrium is larger than the left. The left atrium receives the pulmonary vein, which brings blood back from the lungs. Both atria open into one ventricle. The ventricle has thick walls and a spongy interior of muscular strands, the trabeculae, which keep the two incoming streams from mixing freely. From the ventricle a truncus arteriosus runs forward and divides into a left and a right branch. A spiral valve inside it helps aim the blood. Each branch supplies a carotid arch to the head, a systemic arch to the body, and a pulmocutaneous arch to the lung and the skin.

The working cycle follows those chambers. Deoxygenated blood from the body fills the sinus venosus and passes into the right atrium. Blood that has crossed the lungs fills the left atrium. The atria contract together and empty into the ventricle, venous blood lying more on the right side of the cavity and pulmonary blood more on the left, with the trabeculae limiting the blend. The ventricle then contracts. Blood leaves through the truncus. The stream that is poorer in oxygen is directed into the pulmocutaneous arches and therefore back to the lungs and the skin, where it can be refreshed. The stream that is richer in oxygen is directed into the systemic arches and the carotids. Mixing is reduced. It is not prevented. That is the reason the double circulation is called incomplete.

Three surfaces exchange gases in the adult, and which one dominates depends on where the frog is. The skin is thin, glandular and full of capillaries. It works in water, on land, and it is the surface that matters during hibernation, when the animal is still and the lungs are barely ventilated. The lining of the buccopharyngeal cavity exchanges a smaller amount while the floor of the mouth is moving. The lungs are a pair of elastic sacs, only lightly folded, opened from the buccopharyngeal cavity through the glottis. They are the main surface when the frog is active on land.

Lung ventilation has no diaphragm and no expanding ribcage. The floor of the mouth is the pump. For inspiration the glottis is shut, the nostrils are open, and the buccal floor drops, so air is drawn into the mouth. The nostrils then close, the glottis opens, and the buccal floor rises, pressing that air into the lungs. For expiration the lungs recoil, air returns to the mouth, the nostrils open, and the air leaves. Cutaneous exchange needs none of this pumping. Oxygen simply diffuses into the skin capillaries, and carbon dioxide diffuses out, as long as the skin is moist. A dry skin stops that path, which is why a frog in a dry box dies of respiratory failure before it dies of thirst alone.

The two systems meet at different doors of the heart. Blood refreshed in the lungs returns by the pulmonary vein to the left atrium. Blood refreshed in the skin returns with the ordinary body blood, by the venae cavae, to the sinus venosus and the right atrium. Skin respiration therefore does not fill the left atrium. A question that says 'all oxygenated blood enters the left atrium' is wrong for a frog, because cutaneous blood does not.

confusion: The ventricle is single. Two atria do not make a four-chambered heart. The chambers that count are two atria plus one ventricle.
Oxygenated blood from the skin enters the right atrium, via the sinus venosus. Only pulmonary blood enters the left atrium.
The truncus arteriosus is part of the arterial exit. It is not a vein, and it is not a fourth chamber.
Adult frogs do not breathe with gills. Gills are larval. Hibernating adults rely on skin.
keyPoints: Sinus venosus, right atrium, left atrium, one ventricle, truncus arteriosus.
Incomplete double circulation: one ventricle, mixing reduced by trabeculae and the spiral valve.
Pulmocutaneous arch to lung and skin. Systemic arches to the body. Carotids to the head.
Respiratory surfaces: skin, buccal lining, lungs. No diaphragm.
Buccal floor pumps lung air. Skin respiration needs only moisture and blood flow.
importantStatements: The right atrium receives body blood and cutaneous return. The left atrium receives pulmonary return.
Incomplete double circulation means two circuits and one ventricle, not a single circuit like a fish.
The buccal floor, not a diaphragm, ventilates the lungs.
examples: A frog under water closes its glottis and depends on skin capillaries.
A frog leaping on the bank fills its lungs by raising the floor of the mouth with the nostrils shut.
Blood leaving toward the head has been steered into the carotid arch by the spiral valve.
universalFacts: The sinus venosus is dorsal. It is easy to miss on a ventral dissection.
Pulmonary veins are the exception among veins: they carry oxygenated blood, and they enter the left atrium.
formulas: Body to sinus venosus to right atrium. Lungs to pulmonary vein to left atrium. Both to the ventricle. Ventricle to truncus.
Three arches on each side: carotid, systemic, pulmocutaneous.
Inspiration: nostrils open, floor down, then nostrils shut, floor up, air into lungs.
practice: Name the chamber that receives the pulmonary vein and the chamber that receives the venae cavae.
Describe one inspiration and one expiration without using the word diaphragm.
Explain why cutaneous blood and pulmonary blood do not enter the same atrium.
practiceQuestions: What makes the frog's double circulation incomplete?
Which arch carries blood to the lung and the skin?
Why does a dry skin stop cutaneous respiration?
examNotes: The heart answer is a route: venae cavae, sinus venosus, right atrium, pulmonary vein, left atrium, ventricle, truncus, three arches.
The respiration answer must include the buccal pump and a separate sentence on skin. Lungs alone are incomplete.
examShortTricks: Right atrium body, left atrium lungs, one ventricle, truncus out.
Floor down to fill the mouth. Floor up to fill the lungs.
specialNotes: Do not draw four chambers. The spiral valve is inside the truncus, not a wall that divides the ventricle into two.
Hibernation uses skin. Do not write that a hibernating frog breathes with lungs at the summer rate.
importantNotes: Trabeculae reduce mixing. They do not create a left and right ventricle.
The pulmocutaneous artery splits the job: one branch to the lung, one to the skin. Both leave from the same arch.
importantConcepts: Path of blood through one beat
importantTasks: Write the heart route as eight arrows on one line.
Write inspiration as four actions: glottis, nostrils, floor, then the switch.

exercises.question: Trace a volume of blood from the posterior vena cava until part of it reaches the lungs, and say what is oxygenated on the way back.
steps: The posterior vena cava enters the sinus venosus.
The sinus venosus empties into the right atrium.
The right atrium contracts into the single ventricle.
Ventricular contraction sends the less oxygenated blood into the pulmocutaneous arch.
That arch supplies the lung. Blood refreshed in the lung returns by the pulmonary vein to the left atrium, not to the sinus venosus.
exercises.answer: Posterior vena cava to sinus venosus to right atrium to ventricle to pulmocutaneous arch to the lung, and back by the pulmonary vein to the left atrium.

bounds: Digestive organs are the previous note. The reproductive system of the frog is not this topic.
Arch names are limited to carotid, systemic and pulmocutaneous.
data.summary: The frog heart has a sinus venosus, a right atrium for body and skin blood, a left atrium for pulmonary blood, one spongy ventricle, and a truncus arteriosus with a spiral valve. The circulation is an incomplete double circulation because the streams meet in that single ventricle and mixing is only reduced. Gas exchange is by moist skin, the mouth lining, and lungs ventilated by the buccal floor, with no diaphragm. Skin blood returns to the right atrium. Lung blood returns to the left atrium.

notes: Study of animal diversity from protozoa through invertebrates to vertebrates, focusing on classification and morphology.
Ernst Haeckel proposed kingdom Protista; animal diversity spans from unicellular to complex multicellular organisms
Protozoa: unicellular animals; classified by locomotion — flagellates (Euglena), ciliates (Paramecium), amoeboids (Amoeba), sporozoans (Plasmodium)
Plasmodium vivax causes malaria; Plasmodium falciparum causes malignant malaria
Animal body plans: asymmetrical (sponges), radial (jellyfish), bilateral (most animals)
Body cavities: acoelomate (no cavity), pseudocoelomate (false cavity), coelomate (true cavity)
Segmentation: body divided into repeated units (metamerism); seen in annelids and arthropods
Phylum Porifera: sponges; sessile filter feeders; canal system for water flow
Phylum Coelenterata: jellyfish, corals, hydra; radially symmetrical; cnidoblasts for defense

data.topicTitle: Introduction: Three domains of life, binomial nomenclature, five kingdom classification system (Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia)
notes: **Binomial nomenclature.** Carolus Linnaeus gave the two-word naming system: the first word is the capitalised genus and the second the lowercase species, italicised or underlined — for example, Homo sapiens.
**Five-kingdom classification.** R.H. Whittaker grouped life into Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia using cell structure, thallus organisation, nutrition and reproduction as criteria.
**Three domains.** Carl Woese's rRNA studies split living organisms into Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya; Monera falls in the prokaryotic domains while the other kingdoms lie in Eukarya.

**Kingdom criteria.** Prokaryotic cell structure places an organism in Monera, eukaryotic unicellular forms in Protista, absorptive heterotrophs in Fungi, and photosynthetic or ingestive eukaryotes in Plantae and Animalia.
**Taxonomic hierarchy.** Every organism is placed in a sequence of categories — Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species — with species as the basic unit of classification.
Viruses sit outside Whittaker's five kingdoms because they have no cell. A domain answer that forces HIV into Monera has mixed a particle with an organism.

visualization.desc: Domains sit above kingdoms. A binomial is two words, not one.

notes: **Binomial nomenclature.** Carolus Linnaeus gave the two-word naming system: the first word is the capitalised genus and the second the lowercase species, italicised or underlined — for example, Homo sapiens.
**Five-kingdom classification.** R.H. Whittaker grouped life into Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia using cell structure, thallus organisation, nutrition and reproduction as criteria.
**Three domains.** Carl Woese's rRNA studies split living organisms into Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya; Monera falls in the prokaryotic domains while the other kingdoms lie in Eukarya.

**Kingdom criteria.** Prokaryotic cell structure places an organism in Monera, eukaryotic unicellular forms in Protista, absorptive heterotrophs in Fungi, and photosynthetic or ingestive eukaryotes in Plantae and Animalia.
**Taxonomic hierarchy.** Every organism is placed in a sequence of categories — Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species — with species as the basic unit of classification.
Viruses sit outside Whittaker's five kingdoms because they have no cell. A domain answer that forces HIV into Monera has mixed a particle with an organism.

data.title: Three Domains and Classification

mcqs.question: The five-kingdom classification was proposed by:
Fungi are separated from plants in the five-kingdom system because they:
The three-domain system is based on:
In bryophytes, the dominant generation is:

notes: Three-domain system (Woese, 1977): Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya — based on 16S rRNA gene sequences.
Five-kingdom classification (Whittaker, 1969): Monera (prokaryotes), Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia — based on cell type and mode of nutrition.
Binomial nomenclature (Linnaeus, 1753): Genus species (italicised, e.g. Rhododendron arboreum).
Taxonomic hierarchy: Domain > Kingdom > Phylum/Division > Class > Order > Family > Genus > Species.
Plantae: eukaryotic, autotrophic, cell wall (cellulose); includes algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms, angiosperms.
Plant evolution: algae → bryophytes (non-vascular) → pteridophytes (seedless vascular) → gymnosperms (naked seeds) → angiosperms (flowers + enclosed seeds).
Alternation of generations: haploid gametophyte ↔ diploid sporophyte; in bryophytes the gametophyte is dominant; in seed plants the sporophyte is dominant.
confusion: Five-kingdom (Whittaker) separates fungi from plants; the older two-kingdom (Linnaeus) placed fungi under plants.
Three-domain and five-kingdom are complementary: domains refer to genetic/cell structure; kingdoms to ecological role.
In bryophytes, the Gametophyte (n) is the dominant, visible generation; in seed plants the Sporophyte (2n) is dominant.
Pteridophytes have true vascular tissue (xylem + phloem) but no seeds; bryophytes lack true vascular tissue.
Gymnosperms produce "naked" seeds in cones; angiosperms produce seeds enclosed in fruit.

Whittaker's five-kingdom system (1969) is still the most widely used teaching classification.
Nepal's national flower, Rhododendron arboreum, belongs to the family Rhododendraceae (order Ericales).
DNA-based phylogenetics has shown that all eukaryotes share a common ancestor distinct from prokaryotes.

enrichedContent.summary: Modern taxonomy classifies life using two complementary systems: the three-domain system (Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya) based on molecular evidence, and the five-kingdom system (Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia) based on cell structure and nutrition. The taxonomic hierarchy (Domain → Species) and binomial nomenclature (Genus species) provide universal naming. Plant evolution shows a progressive transition from simple algae to complex angiosperms, with alternation of generations as a unifying feature.
specialNotes: NEB expects students to know the five-kingdom system (Whittaker) and the three-domain system (Woese) with their bases of classification.
Taxonomic hierarchy questions are very frequent — memorise all 8 ranks with examples.
Binomial nomenclature: always italicise or underline the full scientific name; only the genus is capitalised.
Alternation of generations is a hallmark of Plantae; the dominant generation (gametophyte vs sporophyte) varies by division.
importantStatements: The three-domain system reorganised all life into three primary lineages based on 16S rRNA sequence analysis.
Whittaker's five-kingdom system remains the most widely used classification in school-level biology.
All land plants undergo alternation of generations between haploid and diploid phases.
The evolution of the flower and seed (angiosperm innovation) made plants the most successful terrestrial group.

data.topicTitle: Status of flora in Nepal and world representation
notes: Nepal occupies under 0.1% of the world's land area but hosts about 2% of its flowering plants — over 7,000 vascular plant species have been recorded from the country.

Altitude drives Nepal's floral belts: tropical sal and chir pine forest in the Terai, oak–rhododendron and temperate conifer belts in the hills, birch–juniper scrub and alpine meadows above the tree line.
Endemism is high for a country of its size: roughly 3% of Nepal's flowering plants are endemic, concentrated in the central Himalaya (for example Himalayan hemlock and spiny berryl).
World pattern: tropical rainforests cover under 10% of the earth's land but hold about two-thirds of all plant species; species richness falls steadily with increasing latitude and altitude.

Threats to flora include habitat loss, over-harvesting, invasive species and climate change; conservation uses in-situ methods (protected areas) together with ex-situ methods (seed banks, botanical gardens).
The timberline, near 4000 m, is where trees stop. The snowline is higher. Alpine herbs live between them, so a sentence that puts Sal above the timberline has left the tropical belt.

notes: Algae: photosynthetic, eukaryotic (mostly), aquatic or damp-environment organisms; no true roots, stems, or leaves.

data.topicTitle: Fungi: General introduction and characteristic features of phycomycetes, ascomycetes, basidiomycetes and deuteromycetes
notes: **General features.** Fungi are achlorophyllous, heterotrophic, eukaryotic organisms whose body is a thallus made of thread-like hyphae (a mycelium); cell walls contain chitin and food is stored as glycogen.
**Phycomycetes.** These lower fungi have aseptate (coenocytic) hyphae and form thick-walled zygospores sexually; examples are Mucor, Rhizopus and the plant pathogen Albugo.
**Ascomycetes.** Sac fungi have septate hyphae and produce ascospores inside sac-like asci; Saccharomyces, Aspergillus, Penicillium and morels belong to this group.
**Basidiomycetes.** Club fungi bear basidiospores on club-shaped basidia; Agaricus (button mushroom), Puccinia (wheat rust) and Ustilago (smut) are common examples.
**Deuteromycetes.** The imperfect fungi show no known sexual stage and are classified by their conidia; Alternaria, Trichoderma and Colletotrichum are important members.
Fungal walls are chitin and the reserve is glycogen, which is why a mushroom is not given a place in Plantae even when it grows in soil like a plant.

notes: DETAILED BRYOPHYTE (Marchantia) STRUCTURE AND LIFE CYCLE.
Thallus: flat, ribbon-like, dichotomously branched; upper surface with air cavities (photorespiration) + photosynthetic chambers; lower surface with rhizoids (anchorage + absorption) + scales.
Gemma cups: dome-shaped, on the upper surface; contain gemmae (asexual, multicellular) that splash out and grow into new thalli.

Sexual organs: antheridia (male, flask-shaped, at the base of the antheridiophore) produce biflagellated sperm; archegonia (female, neck + venter, at the base of the archegoniophore) produce a single egg.
Fertilisation: sperm swim through water to the egg in the archegonium → zygote (2n) in the venter.
Sporophyte: dependent on the thallus; foot (attached) + seta (stalk) + capsule (sporangium) with elaters; meiosis in the spore mother cell → spores (n).
Spores germinate → new protonema → thallus (gametophyte) — the DOMINANT generation.
Life cycle: alternation of generations with gametophyte (n) dominant; sporophyte (2n) short-lived and nutritionally dependent.
Economic/ecological: pioneer on bare rock, soil formation, moisture retention, SO2 bio-indicator, ornamental; peat (from Sphagnum moss) used as fuel + soil conditioner.

notes: **Mucor thallus.** Mucor is a saprophytic mould with branched, aseptate (coenocytic) hyphae that grow on decaying organic matter such as bread and fruit.
**Mucor reproduction.** Asexually it forms sporangiospores inside a globose sporangium; sexually, compatible hyphae fuse to produce a thick-walled zygospore.
**Yeast structure.** Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a unicellular, oval eukaryote with a chitinous wall, a large vacuole and a single nucleus — it has no mycelium.
**Yeast reproduction.** Yeast multiplies by budding and fission; under sexual conditions it forms ascospores inside an ascus, so it is classified with the ascomycetes.

The columella inside a Mucor sporangium is sterile. Spores are cut from the cytoplasm around it. Plus and minus strains are both required for the zygospore in the usual heterothallic account.

notes: **Basidiocarp.** The mushroom is the fleshy fruiting body of a basidiomycete, with a cap (pileus), stalk (stipe) and gills (lamellae) on which basidiospores are produced.
**Edible mushrooms.** Agaricus bisporus (button mushroom) and Pleurotus (oyster mushroom) are cultivated widely and are rich in protein, vitamins and minerals.
**Poisonous mushrooms.** Amanita muscaria (fly agaric) and other toxic species contain deadly toxins; misidentification can cause severe poisoning, so wild mushrooms must never be eaten unverified.
**Ecological role.** Many mushrooms are decomposers, and forest trees depend on mycorrhizal fungal associations for mineral and water absorption.
**Cultivation.** Mushroom farming uses composted substrate spawned with fungal mycelium under humid, shaded conditions — a growing cottage industry in Nepal.
Agaricus is the edible button mushroom of the course. Amanita includes deadly species. Colour and a pleasant smell are not safe tests. Only a known edible species is food.

notes: DETAILED PTERIDOPHYTE (Dryopteris) MORPHOLOGY AND REPRODUCTION.
Rhizome: short, creeping, bearing scales + adventitious roots; the main vegetative organ.
Frond: the leaf-like organ; stipe (stalk) + blade (lamina); blade divided into pinnae, each into pinules.
Sori: clusters of sporangia on the underside of the pinnae; often covered by an indusium (a flap of tissue).
Sporangium: bears an annulus (a row of specialized cells for dehiscence); meiosis in the spore mother cell → spores (n).
Spore: one-celled, motile-free, wind-dispersed; germinates in moist conditions.
Prothallus (gametophyte): small, heart-shaped, free-living; bears antheridia (male) + archegonia (female); produces biflagellated sperm + egg.
Fertilisation: sperm swims through water to the egg → zygote (2n) → young sporophyte (dependent on the prothallus initially).
Young sporophyte: develops a rhizome + fronds; becomes independent; the prothallus withers.
Life cycle: alternation of generations with SPOROPHYTE (2n) dominant; gametophyte (n) small, free-living, and short-lived.
Key difference from bryophytes: true vascular tissue (xylem + phloem) + dominant sporophyte.
Economic importance: medicinal (ferns in traditional medicine), ornamental (garden ferns), soil stabilisation; fossil pteridophytes form coal deposits.
Other pteridophytes: horsetails (Equisetum — jointed, silica), clubmosses (Lycopodium — cones), tree ferns (Cyathea).
NEB focus: detailed Dryopteris frond + rhizome structure, sori/annulus, the prothallus, and the full life cycle.
confusion: The prothallus (gametophyte) is small and heart-shaped; it is NOT the main plant body (that is the frond-bearing sporophyte).
Sori are clusters of sporangia on the frond underside; the indusium covers them (not the sori themselves).
The annulus is the specialized dehiscent structure of the sporangium (a row of cells that snaps the capsule open).
Fertilisation STILL requires water in pteridophytes (flagellated sperm) — a key exam point.
The young sporophyte is initially dependent on the prothallus; it becomes independent as it develops its own rhizome + fronds.
Pteridophytes have TRUE vascular tissue; bryophytes do NOT — the key distinction.

data.summary: A detailed study of Dryopteris (fern) shows a short, creeping, scaled rhizome bearing adventitious roots and fronds. The frond (stipe + blade) has pinnae and pinules, with sori (clusters of sporangia with an annulus and indusium) on the underside. Pteridophytes are seedless vascular plants that represent the evolutionary transition between non-vascular bryophytes and seed-bearing plants. The sporophyte (2n) is the dominant generation; the gametophyte (prothallus) is small and free-living. Ferns like Dryopteris have fronds with sori (spore clusters). Fertilisation still requires water. Pteridophytes are economically important as medicinal herbs, ornamentals, soil stabilisers, and the source of coal deposits.

notes: DETAILED GYMNOSPERM (Pinus) MORPHOLOGY AND REPRODUCTION.
Plant body: woody stem (trunk) + branch system; needle-like (Pinus) or scale-like (Deodar) leaves; no true flowers; reproduction via cones (strobili).
Male cone (microstrobilus): small, clustered at the base of new shoots; microsporangia → microspores (n) → pollen grains (male gametophyte) with an air-sac for wind dispersal.

Female cone (megasporangium / seed cone): larger, at the tip of shoots; megasporangia → megaspores (n) → female gametophyte (archegonia) on the ovule; the ovule is exposed on the cone scale (naked seed).
Pollination: wind (anemophilous); pollen lands on the resinous ovule; pollen tube grows to the archegonium; fertilisation (no water needed).
Seed: embryo + endosperm (n) + seed coat; no fruit (naked); dispersed by wind.
Life cycle: SPOROPHYTE (2n) dominant; gametophyte reduced, non-photosynthetic, and dependent on the sporophyte.
Key differences from angiosperms: no flowers, no fruits, no double fertilisation; seeds exposed on cone scales.
Economic importance: timber (construction, paper), resin (turpentine from Pinus), ornamental (conifers in gardens), soil stabilisation in alpine regions; Deodar is a sacred tree in Nepali tradition.
Other gymnosperms: Ginkgo (living fossil, deciduous), Cycas (cycad, palm-like), Gnetum (angiosperm-like).
NEB focus: detailed Pinus male + female cone structure, pollen, ovule, seed, and the life cycle; economic importance in Nepal.

notes: **Symbiotic association.** A lichen is a partnership between a fungus (mycobiont) and a photosynthetic alga or cyanobacterium (phycobiont); the fungus supplies shelter and minerals while the partner supplies food.
**Thallus types.** Lichens are crustose (crust-like, tightly attached), foliose (leafy, loosely attached) and fruticose (shrubby or pendant).
**Pioneer vegetation.** Lichens colonise bare rock and gradually build soil, so they are pioneer species in primary succession.
**Pollution indicator.** Lichens are extremely sensitive to sulphur dioxide and other air pollutants; their abundance signals clean air and their disappearance signals polluted air.
**Economic importance.** Lichens yield litmus and dyes, provide fodder (reindeer moss), and produce antibiotic compounds such as usnic acid.
Crustose lichens lie flat on rock, foliose ones are leafy, and fruticose ones hang or stand, as Usnea does on temperate branches in Nepal.

notes: **General features.** Algae are simple, autotrophic, thalloid plants containing chlorophyll and other pigments; they occur in fresh water, marine water and moist soil and reproduce by spores and gametes.
**Chlorophyceae (green algae).** They contain chlorophyll a and b, store food as starch in pyrenoids and include Chlamydomonas, Spirogyra and Chlorella.
**Phaeophyceae (brown algae).** Fucoxanthin gives the brown colour; food is stored as mannitol and laminarin, and Fucus and Laminaria are marine examples.

Spirogyra has a spiral chloroplast with pyrenoids. Sexual reproduction is conjugation: a tube joins two filaments and a zygospore results. That is not a seed.

notes: Angiosperms (flowering plants): seeds enclosed in a fruit; include ~90% of all plant species; the most diverse and successful plant group.
Flower structure: perianth (sepals + petals), androecium (stamens: anther + filament), gynoecium/pistil (carpel: ovary + style + stigma).
Root: taproot (dicots) or fibrous (monocots); functions: absorption, anchorage, storage.
Stem: herbaceous (soft) or woody (hard); functions: support, transport (xylem up, phloem down).
Leaf: blade + petiole; venation (pinnate, palmate, parallel); stomata for gas exchange.
Inflorescence: arrangement of flowers on a peduncle (raceme, corymb, umbel, spike, capitulum).
Fruit: mature ovary; types: simple (pea, apple), aggregate (raspberry), multiple (pineapple).
Taxonomic hierarchy: Division > Class > Order > Family > Genus > Species.

NEB families: Brassicaceae (mustard, cabbage — 4 petals, cross shape), Fabaceae (pea, bean — zygomorphic, pod), Solanaceae (tomato, potato — 5 petals, bell shape), Liliaceae (tulip, onion — 6 tepals, monocot).

Classification systems: Artificial (Linnaeus — based on few characters), Natural (De Candolle, Bentham & Hooker — based on many characters), Phylogenetic (Engler, Takhtajan — based on evolutionary relationships).
confusion: Angiosperms produce BOTH seeds AND fruits; gymnosperms produce seeds only (no fruit).
Monocots have parallel venation, fibrous roots, and 3-parted flowers; dicots have net venation, taproots, and 4-or-5-parted flowers.
The carpel (gynoecium) is the female part of the flower; the stamen is the male part.
Brassicaceae flowers have 4 petals in a cross shape (cruciform); Solanaceae have 5 petals (rotate-symmetric).
Fabaceae flowers are zygomorphic (bilaterally symmetric); most other angiosperm flowers are actinomorphic (radially symmetric).
An inflorescence is the arrangement of flowers; it is NOT a single flower.

notes: **Amphibians of the plant kingdom.** Bryophytes live in damp places and need water for fertilisation because the male gametes swim to the egg, yet they lack true vascular tissue.
**Gametophyte dominance.** The leafy or thalloid gametophyte is the persistent phase; the sporophyte is small, short-lived and remains attached to it.
**Sex organs.** Gametes are produced in multicellular antheridia (sperm) and archegonia (egg), both embedded in the gametophyte tissue.
**Examples.** Marchantia is a thalloid liverwort, Anthoceros a hornwort, and Funaria a moss with a leafy gametophyte and a seta–capsule sporophyte.
**Importance.** Sphagnum peat is used as fuel and packing material, bryophytes hold moisture and prevent soil erosion, and they indicate humid habitats.

notes: **First vascular plants.** Pteridophytes possess true roots, stems and leaves with xylem and phloem, which allowed plants to grow tall and colonise land fully.
**Sporophyte dominance.** The conspicuous plant is the diploid sporophyte; the tiny gametophyte (prothallus) is short-lived and requires water for fertilisation.
**Spore-bearing structures.** Spores are produced in sporangia clustered into sori on the undersurface of sporophylls.
**Homosporous vs heterosporous.** Lycopodium, Equisetum and Pteris produce one kind of spore, while Selaginella, Marsilea and Salvinia produce two kinds (microspores and megaspores).
**Importance.** Ferns are ornamentals (Adiantum, Nephrolepis), some pteridophytes serve as food and medicine, and their ancient forms contributed to coal deposits.

Dryopteris holds sori on the underside of fronds, often under an indusium. Young fronds uncoil, which is circinate vernation. The gametophyte is a small green prothallus that still needs water for fertilisation.

notes: **Naked seeds.** Gymnosperms bear seeds that are not enclosed in a fruit; ovules lie exposed on the surface of megasporophylls, usually in cones.
**Plant body.** They are mostly evergreen, woody trees and shrubs with well-developed roots (often with mycorrhizae) and needle-like or scale-like leaves.
**Reproduction.** Male cones release pollen carried by wind to female cones; the ovule contains the female gametophyte and fertilisation gives a seed with a stored food supply.
**Examples.** Cycas, Pinus, Cedrus (deodar), Ginkgo and Ephedra are familiar gymnosperms; Cycas retains fern-like leaflets and coralloid roots with nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria.
**Economic importance.** Gymnosperms give timber, resins, turpentine, ephedrine (medicine) and ornamentals; their pollen can also cause allergies.
Pinus is monoecious: male cones and female cones on one tree. Pollen is winged and carried by wind. Pollination and fertilisation are separated by many months. The seed is winged.

notes: **Root systems.** Roots are taproot (mustard), fibrous (grass) or adventitious (banyan prop roots); they anchor the plant, absorb water and minerals and often store food.
**Stem.** The stem bears nodes, internodes, leaves and buds, and may be modified for storage (potato tuber), support (tendrils) or protection (thorns).
**Leaves.** Leaves show simple or compound lamina, reticulate (dicot) or parallel (monocot) venation, and arrangements called phyllotaxy (alternate, opposite, whorled).
**Inflorescence.** Flowers are arranged as racemose (acropetal succession) or cymose (basipetal succession) inflorescences on the floral axis.
**Flower and fruit.** A complete flower has calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium; after fertilisation the ovary becomes a fruit whose pericarp encloses the seeds.

A potato is a stem tuber because it has buds. A sweet potato is a storage root. A thorn of a citrus-type stem is a modified stem, while a prickle may be superficial. The presence of nodes or buds decides a stem.

notes: **Taxonomy.** Taxonomy is the branch of biology that identifies, describes, classifies and names organisms; systematics additionally studies their evolutionary relationships.
**Hierarchy of categories.** Classification follows the sequence Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species, with species as the fundamental unit.
**Binomial nomenclature.** Each species gets a two-word Latin name (genus + species) in italics or underlined, with the genus capitalised, as in Panthera tigris.

**Systems of classification.** Artificial systems (Linnaeus) use a few visible characters, natural systems (Bentham and Hooker) use many characters, and phylogenetic systems use evolutionary relationships.
**Taxonomic aids.** Herbaria, botanical gardens, museums, keys and manuals help identify and study organisms; a key narrows identity through paired contrasting characters.

Linnaeus's sexual system was artificial: a few floral characters carried the whole classification. Bentham and Hooker built a natural system from many characters at once. A phylogenetic system tries to follow ancestry.

data.title: Angiosperm families with economic importance: Brassicacea…
data.topicTitle: Angiosperm families with economic importance: Brassicaceae, Fabaceae, Solanaceae and Liliaceae
notes: **Brassicaceae (Cruciferae).** Mustard family: flowers with four petals in a cross, six stamens (four long, two short), and silique fruits; mustard oil gives the pungent taste.
**Fabaceae (Papilionoideae).** Pea family: papilionaceous corolla (standard, wings, keel), ten stamens (nine fused), legume fruits, and root nodules housing nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium.
**Solanaceae.** Potato family: five epipetalous stamens with swollen anthers, bicarpellary superior ovary, and berry or capsule fruits; tomato, brinjal and chilli belong here.
**Liliaceae.** Lily family: monocots with parallel-veined leaves, trimerous flowers with six tepals, and superior trilocular ovary; onion, garlic and tulip are examples.
**Economic importance.** These four families supply food crops, spices, medicines (alkaloids), oils and ornamentals — they are among the most useful angiosperm families.

Brassicaceae has a cruciform corolla and tetradynamous stamens, four long and two short, and a siliqua. Fabaceae has a papilionaceous flower, diadelphous stamens in a 9+1 bundle, a legume, and Rhizobium nodules.

In the Field of Health, Disease and Medicine: Biology provides essential knowledge for understanding human health, disease mechanisms, and developing medical treatments.

It helps to maintain health and control epidemic diseases, offering insights into controlling and curing diseases transmitted by parasites like Anopheles (malaria), sandfly (kala-azar), Tse-tse (sleeping sickness), and housefly (typhoid).
Advancements in medical technology often involve testing drugs and vaccines on animals.
In the Field of agriculture: Agriculture is a part of applied biology.

# Introduction to Biology: Scope and fields of biology

## 1. Introduction
**Biology** (Greek *bios* = life, *logos* = study) is the natural science of life — of every living thing, from a virus particle barely 20 nanometres across to a blue whale, and of every level at which life is organised, from molecules inside a cell to the whole biosphere. What makes biology one science rather than many is its single question asked at every level: **how do living systems stay ordered, reproduce and adapt while obeying the laws of chemistry and physics?**

A Nepali student meets this question daily without naming it. The rice in a Jhapa paddy that tillers after transplanting, the *gundruk* fermenting in a clay pot through lactic-acid bacteria, the Rhododendron (*lali gurans*) blooming across a mid-hill forest in Chaitra, the child vaccinated at a health post against measles — each is a biological process a biologist can describe, explain and predict.

**Scope of this topic.** You will learn (i) the definition and meaning of biology and why it is called the science of life; (ii) the scope of biology — what it studies and where its boundaries lie; (iii) the major fields (branches) of biology, pure and applied, each with its subject matter and examples; and (iv) how biology connects with everyday life in Nepal — agriculture, medicine, forestry and food. The next topic shows how biology borrows from and lends to physics, chemistry and the other sciences.

**Learning outcomes.** After this topic you can: define biology and state its scope; list and distinguish at least ten fields of biology with one example each; classify any new branch (e.g., bioinformatics) as pure or applied; and explain two Nepal-context applications of biological knowledge.

## 2. Hierarchy body — what biology is and what it covers

### What biology is
1. **Definition.** Biology is the branch of natural science that studies living organisms — their structure, function, growth, origin, evolution and distribution — and their interactions with each other and the non-living environment.
2. **Why "science of life".** Like physics studies matter-energy and chemistry studies substances, biology studies the one class of natural systems that shows all seven life processes together: organisation, metabolism, homeostasis, growth, reproduction, response and evolution. A flame grows and moves but does not reproduce with heredity; a crystal is ordered but does not metabolise — neither is alive.
3. **Biology is experimental.** Observation (a naturalist watching red panda behaviour in Langtang), comparison (healthy vs diseased paddy), and controlled experiment (vaccine trials) are its methods — the same scientific method as physics and chemistry, applied to living material.

### Scope of biology
1. **Breadth of objects.** Biology ranges over microbes (bacteria, viruses, fungi), plants, animals and humans — including fossils and extinct forms, which is why palaeontology belongs inside biology.
2. **Breadth of levels.** Molecules → cells → tissues → organs → organisms → populations → communities → ecosystems → biosphere. No level is "the" biology; genetics works at the molecular level while ecology works at the population level, and both are fully biology.
3. **Breadth of time.** From the origin of life (~3.5–3.8 billion years ago, evidenced by stromatolite fossils) to present-day evolution (antibiotic resistance appearing within years) — biology covers deep time and real time together.
4. **Breadth of purpose.** Pure inquiry (how does photosynthesis split water?) and applied use (how do we breed drought-tolerant wheat?) are both inside the scope; NEB examines both angles.

### Major fields of biology — pure branches
1. **Botany** — study of plants: e.g., the morphology and life cycle of *Marchantia* (a liverwort you will meet in Floral Diversity).
2. **Zoology** — study of animals: e.g., the organ systems of earthworm and frog (Faunal Diversity).
3. **Microbiology** — study of microbes: e.g., bacterial structure, viruses and bacteriophages.
4. **Genetics** — heredity and variation: e.g., Mendel's laws, DNA replication (Class 12 Heredity & Evolution).
5. **Cell biology (cytology)** — structure and function of cells: e.g., the fluid-mosaic membrane (next unit).
6. **Physiology** — how bodies work: e.g., digestion in humans, transpiration in plants.
7. **Ecology** — organisms and their environment: e.g., pond ecosystem, food chains (Ecology unit).
8. **Evolutionary biology** — origin and diversification of life: e.g., Lamarckism vs Darwinism.
9. **Taxonomy and systematics** — naming and classifying organisms: e.g., the five-kingdom system, binomial nomenclature.
10. **Molecular biology** — life at the molecule level: e.g., transcription and translation of the genetic code.

### Applied (interdisciplinary) branches
1. **Agriculture** — crop and livestock science: e.g., Khumal-4 rice and hybrid maize bred for Nepali hills.
2. **Medicine and health** — disease, treatment, public health: e.g., the national immunisation programme, antibiotics.
3. **Forestry** — forest management and conservation: e.g., community forestry, protected areas (Conservation Biology).
4. **Biotechnology** — using living systems to make products: e.g., fermentation, recombinant insulin (Class 12).
5. **Fisheries and animal husbandry** — e.g., trout farming in Himalayan streams, poultry breeds.
6. **Newer applied fields** — bioinformatics (biology + computing), biomedical engineering, environmental biotechnology. Any new "-omics" or "bio-" field slots into this table by the same rule: name → what it studies → one example.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Major fields of biology at a glance**

| Field | What it studies | Example you will meet | Pure or applied |
|---|---|---|---|
| Botany | Plants | *Marchantia* life cycle | Pure |
| Zoology | Animals | Earthworm digestive system | Pure |
| Microbiology | Microbes | Bacteriophage structure | Pure |
| Genetics | Heredity and variation | Mendel's monohybrid cross | Pure |
| Cell biology | Cells | Fluid-mosaic membrane | Pure |
| Physiology | Body functions | Human digestion | Pure |
| Ecology | Organisms + environment | Pond ecosystem | Pure |
| Evolutionary biology | Origin and diversity of life | Human-evolution timeline | Pure |
| Taxonomy | Naming and classification | Five-kingdom system | Pure |
| Molecular biology | Molecules of life | DNA replication | Pure |
| Agriculture | Crops and livestock | Khumal rice varieties | Applied |
| Biotechnology | Living systems as tools | Fermentation, rDNA insulin | Applied |

**Table 2 — Levels of biological organisation**

| Level | Example | What biologists study there |
|---|---|---|
| Molecule | DNA, protein | Replication, enzyme action |
| Cell | Guard cell, bacterium | Membrane transport, division |
| Tissue | Xylem, muscle | Conduction, contraction |
| Organ | Leaf, heart | Photosynthesis, pumping |
| Organism | Paddy plant, frog | Life cycle, behaviour |
| Population | Deer herd in Chitwan | Growth, competition |
| Community | Forest flora + fauna | Food webs |
| Ecosystem | Pokhara lake | Energy flow, cycles |
| Biosphere | Earth | Global element cycles |

| Definition and meaning of biology | Science of life: structure → function → evolution | 1-mark define + 2-mark explain |

## 5. Worked examples and applications
1. **Rice breeding (agriculture).** Problem: hill farmers need short-duration rice. Biology used: genetics (selecting early-flowering variants) + physiology (matching growth to monsoon). Result: varieties such as Khumal-4 mature before the cold — pure genetics applied to food security.
2. **Gundruk fermentation (microbiology + food).** Mustard leaves + salt + warm anaerobic pot → lactic-acid bacteria (*Lactobacillus*, *Pediococcus*) convert sugars to lactic acid, preserving the vegetable for months. Steps: wilt → shred → pack airtight → ferment 7–10 days → sun-dry.
3. **Antibiotics (microbiology + medicine).** *Penicillium* mould makes penicillin, which blocks bacterial cell-wall synthesis. Human cells have no walls, so the drug kills bacteria, not us — structure explains selectivity.
4. **Rhizobium biofertilizer (microbiology + agriculture).** Root nodules of bean/pea house *Rhizobium*, which fixes atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia the plant can use — applied nitrogen cycle, cutting urea cost.
5. **Community forestry (ecology + forestry).** Nepal's community-forest groups manage local forests for fuel, fodder and timber while protecting habitat — population and ecosystem principles running a national programme.
6. **Immunisation (physiology + public health).** A vaccine trains adaptive immunity (antibodies + memory cells) without the disease — the applied end of the immune-system tree you will draw in Class 12.
7. **Disease diagnosis (cell biology + medicine).** A blood smear under the microscope shows malarial parasites inside red cells — cell biology read directly off a slide in a health post.

## 6. Key terms and statements
- **Biology** — the natural science of living organisms: their structure, function, growth, origin, evolution and distribution.
- **Bios / logos** — Greek roots: life / study or discourse.
- **Scope** — the full range a science covers: objects, levels, time and purposes.
- **Botany / zoology** — study of plants / study of animals; the two classical pure divisions.
- **Microbiology** — study of microorganisms (bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa).
- **Genetics** — study of heredity and variation.
- **Ecology** — study of interactions between organisms and their environment.
- **Physiology** — study of how living bodies function.
- **Taxonomy** — science of naming, describing and classifying organisms.
- **Biotechnology** — technological use of living systems or their products.
- **Pure vs applied branches** — pure seeks understanding (genetics, ecology); applied seeks use (medicine, agriculture, biotechnology).
- **Levels of organisation** — molecule → cell → tissue → organ → organism → population → community → ecosystem → biosphere.

## 7. Exam Zone
**NEB map.** One-markers ask definitions (biology, botany, ecology) and one-example lists. Two-markers ask scope, "botany vs zoology", or two applied branches with examples. Long answers (4–5 marks) ask the fields of biology with examples, or the scope of biology with reference to Nepal.

**Short tricks.** "B-Z-M-G-C-P-E" = Botany, Zoology, Microbiology, Genetics, Cytology, Physiology, Ecology (seven pure branches in syllabus order). "Molecule to Biosphere" ladder: *My Cat Took Our Popcorn, Children Eat Bread* (Molecule, Cell, Tissue, Organ, Population, Community, Ecosystem, Biosphere).

**Sources for the facts above:** OpenStax *Biology 2e* ch. 1 (study of life); Raven Biology §1 (themes of biology); NEB/CDC Grade 11 Biology textbook (scope and branches).

## 8. Summary and self-check
Biology is the science of life — its structure, function, growth, origin, evolution and distribution. Its scope spans all organisms, all levels from molecule to biosphere, deep time to real time, and pure understanding to applied use. Pure branches (botany, zoology, microbiology, genetics, cell biology, physiology, ecology, evolution, taxonomy, molecular biology) build the knowledge; applied branches (agriculture, medicine, forestry, biotechnology, fisheries) spend it — in Nepal, on rice, forests, fermentation and vaccines.

**Self-check.** (1) Define biology and give its two Greek roots. (2) Name the nine levels of organisation with one example each. (3) Classify bioinformatics as pure or applied, with a reason. (4) Give two Nepal-context applications, each naming the pure branch behind it. (5) Why is a flame not alive although it grows and moves?

**Common confusions.** Microbiology ≠ only disease (most microbes are harmless or useful) · biotechnology ≠ genetic engineering only (fermentation is biotechnology too) · scope ≠ branches (scope is the range; branches are the divisions) · ecology ≠ environment alone (it is the *study of interactions*).

notes: Biology is interconnected with other sciences: it relies on and contributes to Chemistry (biochemistry), Physics (biophysics), Mathematics (biostatistics), and Earth Science (geobiology).
Biochemistry: the chemistry of life — metabolism, enzymes, DNA/RNA/protein structures.
Biophysics: physics applied to biology — biophysics of the cell, nerve conduction, muscle mechanics, imaging (MRI, X-ray).
Biostatistics: mathematics used in biology — genetics (Punnett), population models, experimental design.
Geobiology: interaction of life with Earth — evolution (fossils, climate), ecology (biogeochemical cycles), palaeontology.
Interdisciplinary fields: medicine (biology + chemistry + physics), agriculture (biology + ecology), conservation biology (biology + policy), biotechnology (biology + engineering).
NEB focus: how biology connects with chemistry, physics, mathematics, and earth science.
Biology uses scientific tools from other disciplines: microscopes (physics), spectrometers (chemistry), statistical software (mathematics).
confusion: Biochemistry is NOT the same as organic chemistry; it focuses on the chemistry of living systems (metabolism, enzymes, macromolecules).
Biophysics applies physics to biological problems; it is not "physics of life" in a vague sense.
Biostatistics is a branch of statistics, not a branch of biology; it is used BY biologists.
Geobiology (biology + earth science) is different from ecology (biology + environment).
Interdisciplinary fields combine multiple sciences; they are NOT a new "fourth" science.
Biology uses tools from other sciences (microscopes, spectrometers) but has its own methods (experiments, observations, classifications).

The electron microscope (physics) revealed cellular structures that light microscopes could not.
CRISPR-Cas9 (biology) is a gene-editing tool derived from a bacterial immune system.
Biology is the most data-rich science; a single human cell contains ~100,000 proteins.

Geobiology: fossil records (earth science) provide evidence for evolution (biology).
Interdisciplinary: medicine combines biology (anatomy, physiology) with chemistry (pharmacology) and physics (imaging).
