data.title: α-Particle Scattering — Experimental Detail and Numericals
data.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: ### Focus of this tab

A close-up of the α-scattering experiment itself: the apparatus, the counting data, and the two quantitative results (distance of closest approach and the scattering law) that NEB numericals are built on. The full model and its limitations are in the main note.
### Apparatus, quantity by quantity
• α-source: radium C (polonium) in a lead block — lead absorbs all radiation except the fine beam escaping the collimator hole; α-particles emerge with KE ≈ 5.5 MeV and speed ≈ 1.6 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹.
• Foil: gold, ≈ 4 × 10⁻⁵ cm (≈ 10⁻⁷ m) thick ≈ 1000 atomic layers; gold is chosen because it is the most malleable metal and Z = 79 gives maximum deflection (∝ Z).
• Detector: circular ZnS screen; every α-hit gives a scintillation counted through a low-power microscope that can rotate about the foil through 0°–180°.
• Enclosure evacuated so α-particles are not absorbed by air (their range in air is only a few cm).
### The counting data (Geiger–Marsden)
• Nearly all α-particles (≈ 99.86%) pass straight through — no deflection.
• About 1 in 8000 is deflected by more than 90°; about 1 in 10⁴–10⁶ comes straight back (θ ≈ 180°).
• The probability of scattering at angle θ falls as sin⁻⁴(θ/2) — from 0° to 180° the count falls by about 10 orders of magnitude.
### Distance of closest approach (numerical pattern)

At the turning point all kinetic energy is stored as electrostatic potential energy: $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}=\frac{2Ze^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r_{0}}$, giving $r_{0}=\frac{2Ze^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}(KE)}$. For 5.5 MeV α on gold r₀ ≈ 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m — about 40 nuclear radii, so the α-particle never touches the nucleus and the nucleus acts as a point charge. This number is an **upper limit** of the nuclear size, which is why the experiment 'measures' the nucleus without seeing it.
### Impact parameter (the other half of the story)

The scattering angle is fixed by the impact parameter b (the perpendicular distance the α-particle's initial line would pass from the nucleus): $b=\frac{kZe^{2}}{KE}\cot\frac{\theta}{2}$. Head-on approach (b = 0) gives θ = 180° (back-scattering); large b gives tiny θ — the geometric origin of the sin⁻⁴ law.
### What each observation proves
• Undeflected majority → atom mostly empty space.
• Large-angle deflection → a concentrated positive charge much heavier than the α-particle (a light electron cannot turn a 7300-times-heavier projectile).
• Back-scattering → the positive charge and mass are concentrated in a volume 10⁻¹⁵ of the atom.
confusion: ❌ The foil must be thick for good scattering. ✅ It must be extremely thin (≈1000 atoms) so an α-particle meets at most a few nuclei; a thick foil would absorb the particles.
❌ Electrons deflect the α-particles. ✅ Electron mass is ≈1/7300 of the α-mass, so momentum transfer is negligible; only the nucleus can scatter.
❌ r₀ is the nuclear radius. ✅ It is the distance of closest approach — an upper limit; the nuclear radius is ≈10⁻¹⁵ m, ten times smaller.

Calculate r₀ for a 5.5 MeV α-particle against a gold nucleus (Z = 79).

Why is the experiment performed in vacuum?
formulas: $$r_{0}=\frac{2Ze^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}\,KE},\qquad N(\theta)\propto\frac{1}{\sin^{4}(\theta/2)}$$
$$b=\frac{kZe^{2}}{KE}\cot\frac{\theta}{2}$$
universalFacts: ≈1 in 8000 α-particles was deflected by more than 90°; the count falls by ~10 orders of magnitude from 0° to 180°.
For 5.5 MeV α on gold, r₀ ≈ 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m ≈ 40 nuclear radii.
Scattering probability scales as Z² of the foil and as 1/(KE)² of the α-particle.

data.title: Rutherford's Atomic Model and its Limitations
data.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: ### 1. Meaning of the experiment

Thomson's plum-pudding model (1904) treated the atom as diffuse positive charge with electrons embedded in it and could not explain large-angle deflection of fast α-particles (He²⁺, ≈5.5 MeV). Rutherford with Geiger and Marsden (1909–1911) probed atomic *structure* by α-scattering — the experiment that established the **nuclear atom**.
### 2. Set-up

Radium in a lead block with a collimator gives a narrow α-beam; the target is gold foil ≈4 × 10⁻⁵ cm thick (≈1000 atoms) because gold beats very thin and has a heavy nucleus (Z = 79); a rotatable ZnS screen viewed through a microscope records each scintillation; the apparatus is evacuated.
### 3. Observations
• ≈99.86% of α-particles passed straight through — the atom is mostly empty space.
• ≈1 in 20 000 was deflected by more than 90°, and a very few bounced back (θ ≈ 180°).
• Scattering obeys N(θ) ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2); large-angle scattering is rare but real.
### 4. Conclusions (nuclear model)
• Atom is neutral and largely empty; a tiny, heavy, positive **nucleus** carries almost all the mass.
• Nuclear radius ≈10⁻¹⁵ m against atomic radius ≈10⁻¹⁰ m (1 : 100 000); nuclear volume ≈10⁻¹⁵ of atomic volume, nuclear density ≈10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.
• Electrons revolve in circular orbits, the Coulomb attraction of the nucleus giving the centripetal force.
• The positive charge is characteristic of the element — the origin of atomic number, later proved by Moseley (1913).
### 5. Quantitative results
• Distance of closest approach (KE → electrostatic PE): r₀ = 2Ze²/(4πε₀·KE) ≈ 4.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ m for 5 MeV α on gold — an experimental upper limit on nuclear size.
• Rutherford scattering law N(θ) ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2) explains why back-scattering is the rarest event.
### 6. Applications
• Founded nuclear physics: led to the proton (1919) and neutron (1932) and to nuclear fission/reactor technology; Rutherford backscattering spectroscopy (RBS) still analyses thin films industrially.
• Underpins Moseley's law and the atomic-number basis of the modern periodic table, and is the classic example of deducing structure statistically (probability) instead of by direct observation.
### 7. Limitations (exam-critical)
1. **Stability not explained:** a revolving electron is continuously accelerated, so by Maxwell's theory it must radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus in ≈10⁻⁸ s — yet atoms are stable.
2. **Line spectra not explained:** the inward spiral would emit a continuous range of frequencies, while hydrogen gives sharp discrete lines.
3. **No electronic arrangement:** nothing about shells, electron numbers or energies, so periodicity and valency remain unexplained.
4. **Purely classical:** circular orbits and a point nucleus are assumptions; without quantisation the model gives no orbital radii or energies.
5. **Ignores the neutron** (so isotopes are unexplained) and neglects electron–electron repulsion, so it fails for multi-electron atoms; no account of bonding or Zeeman/Stark splitting.
### 8. Exam pointers
Observations + conclusions and the two main defects (stability, discrete spectra) are standard 4–5 mark NEB questions; numericals use r₀, nuclear radius/density and the atom : nucleus volume ratio.
confusion: ❌ The atom is 'totally empty'. ✅ It is mostly empty *space*, but ≈99.9% of the mass lies in the nucleus.
❌ α-particles are electrons. ✅ They are helium nuclei (+2e, ≈7300 times heavier than an electron), so electrons cannot deflect them appreciably.
❌ The model failed because α-particles were absorbed. ✅ Scattering itself was explained well; the model failed on stability and line spectra.
❌ Atom radius = nuclear radius. ✅ 10⁻¹⁰ m versus 10⁻¹⁵ m.

universalFacts: α-scattering experiment: 1909–1911; Geiger and Marsden counted ≈1 flash in 10⁴ at large angles; gold foil ≈4 × 10⁻⁵ cm thick.
Rutherford received the 1908 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for work on radioactivity.
Nuclear density is nearly the same for all nuclei because R = R₀A^(1/3), R₀ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m.
examples: **Problem:** Find r₀ for a 5.0 MeV α-particle on gold (Z = 79). **Solution:** KE = 5.0 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ = 8.0 × 10⁻¹³ J; r₀ = (2 × 9×10⁹ × 79 × (1.6×10⁻¹⁹)²)/(8.0 × 10⁻¹³) ≈ 4.55 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Since r₀ is larger than the nuclear radius, the nucleus acts as a point charge and the α-particle is never captured.
importantNotes: Quote the radiating-electron instability (collapse in ≈10⁻⁸ s) and the continuous-versus-line-spectrum defect first.
Never claim Rutherford's model explained the hydrogen spectrum — repairing that was Bohr's achievement (1913).

notes: **रदरफोर्डको परमाणु मोडेल र यसका सीमाहरू:**

**१. प्रयोगको अर्थ:** थमसनको प्लम-पडिङ मोडेल (१९०४) ले परमाणुलाई फैलिएको धनात्मक आवेश मान्नुभएको थियो जसमा इलेक्ट्रोनहरू समाविष्ट थिए, र यो द्रुत α-कणहरूको (He²⁺, ≈५.५ MeV) ठूला-कोण विक्षेपण व्याख्या गर्न सक्नथ्यो। रदरफोर्डले गाइगर र मार्सडेनसँग (१९०९-१९११) α-विक्षेपणबाट परमाणुको *संरचना* जाँच्नुभएको थियो — यसले **केन्द्रक परमाणु** स्थापित गर्छ।

**२. सेट-अप:** सीसाब्लकमा रेडियम र क्योलिमेटर ले सानो α-बीम दिन्छ; लक्ष्य सोनाको फोइल ≈४ × १०⁻⁵ सेमि मोटो (≈१००० परमाणु) किनभने सोना धेरै पत्लो बन्छ र यसको भारी केन्द्रक छ (Z = ७९); घुम्नसक्ने ZnS स्क्रिन सूक्ष्मदर्शीबाट हेर्ने गरी प्रत्येक स्किनटिलेसन रेकर्ड गर्छ; उपकरण निर्वातमा छ।
**३. अवलोकनहरू:**
• ≈९९.८६% α-कणहरू सीधै पार भए — परमाणु अधिकांश खाली ठाउँ हो।
• ≈२०,००० मा १ कण ९०° भन्दा बढी विक्षेपित भयो, र केही मात्र फिर्ता भए (θ ≈ १८०°)।
• विक्षेपण N(θ) ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2) अनुसार हुन्छ; ठूला-कोण विक्षेपण विरल तर वास्तविक छ।
**४. निष्कर्षहरू (केन्द्रक मोडेल):**
• परमाणु उदासीन र प्रायः खाली छ; एक सानो, भारी, धनात्मक **केन्द्रक** प्रायः सबै द्रव्यमान वहन गर्छ।
• केन्द्रकको अर्धव्यास ≈१०⁻¹⁵ मि विरुद्ध परमाणुको अर्धव्यास ≈१०⁻¹⁰ मि (१ : १००,०००); केन्द्रकको आयतन ≈१०⁻¹⁵ परमाणुको आयतनको, केन्द्रकको घनत्व ≈१०¹⁷ किग्रा मि⁻³।
• इलेक्ट्रोनहरू वृत्ताकार कक्षकमा घुम्छन्, केन्द्रकको कुलम्ब आकर्षण केन्द्राभिमुख बल दिन्छ।
• धनात्मक आवेश तत्वको विशेषता हो — परमाणु संख्याको मूल, पहिले मोस्लेले (१९१३) प्रमाणित गरे।
**५. परिमाणात्मक परिणामहरू:**
• नजिकको दूरी (KE → स्थिरविद्युत PE): r₀ = 2Ze²/(4πε₀·KE) ≈ ४.५ × १०⁻¹⁴ मि ५ MeV α सोनामा — केन्द्रकको आकारको प्रयोगात्मक ऊपरी सीमा।
• रदरफोर्ड विक्षेपण नियम N(θ) ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2) व्याख्या गर्छ किन भने फिर्ता विक्षेपण विरल घटना हो।
**६. अनुप्रयोगहरू:**
• केन्द्रक भौतिकीको स्थापना: प्रोटोन (१९१९) र न्यूट्रन (१९३२) बाट परमाणु विखण्डन/रिएक्टर प्रविधि; रदरफोर्ड फिर्ता-विक्षेपण स्पेक्ट्रोस्कोपी (RBS) अहिलै पनि पत्लो फिल्महरूको उद्योगी विश्लेषण गर्छ।
• मोस्लेको नियम र आधुनिक आवर्त सारणीको परमाणु-संख्या आधार रचना गर्छ, र संरचनालाई सांख्यिकीय रूपमा (सम्भावनाबाट) निष्कर्ष गर्ने उत्कृष्ट उदाहरण हो, प्रत्यक्ष अवलोकनबाट होइन।
**७. सीमाहरू (परीक्षा-महत्वपूर्ण):**
१. **स्थिरता व्याख्या नगरेको:** घुमिरहने इलेक्ट्रोन निरन्तर त्वरित हुन्छ, त्यसैले मैक्सवेलको सिद्धान्तअनुसार यो ऊर्जा विकिरण गर्छ र ≈१०⁻८ सेकेन्डमा केन्द्रकमा लुन्छ — तर परमाणुहरू स्थिर छन्।
२. **रेखा स्पेक्ट्रम व्याख्या नगरेको:** भित्रको स्पायरलले निरन्तर आवृत्तिको दायरा उत्सर्जन गर्थ्यो, तर हाइड्रोजनले तेज र विविध रेखाहरू दिन्छ।
३. **कोई इलेक्ट्रोन व्यवस्था छैन:** खोलहरू, इलेक्ट्रोन संख्या वा ऊर्जा बारे कुनै कुरा छैन, त्यसैले आवर्तिता र संयोजकता व्याख्या नभएको।
४. **पूर्ण रूपमा शास्त्रीय:** वृत्ताकार कक्षक र बिन्दु केन्द्रक मान्यताहरू हुन्; परिमाणीकरण बिना मोडेलले कक्षक अर्धव्यास वा ऊर्जा दिन सक्दैन।

data.title: Rutherford's Atomic Model and Its Limitations
data.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: Alpha-Particle Scattering Experiment: Rutherford (1911) bombarded thin gold foil (~0.00004 cm thick) with fast alpha particles from a radioactive source. A fluorescent zinc sulphide screen detected scattered particles. This experiment fundamentally changed our understanding of atomic structure.

Key Observations: (1) Most alpha particles passed straight through undeflected — atom is mostly empty space. (2) Some were deflected at small angles — positive charge is concentrated. (3) About 1 in 8000 bounced back (>90°) — dense, massive nucleus exists. Rutherford said it was 'as if you fired a 15-inch shell at tissue paper and it came back'.

Rutherford's Nuclear Model: Atom consists of a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus (~10⁻¹⁵ m radius) containing nearly all the mass. Electrons orbit the nucleus at large distances (~10⁻¹⁰ m). The atom is mostly empty space. Nuclear charge = +Ze where Z is atomic number.

Nuclear Size: Nuclear radius R ≈ R₀A^(1/3) where R₀ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m (1.2 fm) and A is mass number. Nucleus is ~10⁵ times smaller than the atom. If atom were a football stadium, nucleus would be a marble at center.

Distance of Closest Approach: For head-on collision, d = (1/4πε₀)(2Ze²/K) where K is alpha particle kinetic energy. This gives upper limit of nuclear size. For gold (Z=79) with 5.5 MeV alpha: d ≈ 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m.

Limitation 1 — Atomic Stability: According to Maxwell's electromagnetic theory, an accelerating charged particle radiates energy. An orbiting electron should continuously lose energy and spiral into the nucleus in ~10⁻¹¹ s. Rutherford's model cannot explain why atoms are stable.

Limitation 2 — Line Spectra: Rutherford's model predicts continuous emission spectrum (electron spiraling inward emits all frequencies). But hydrogen shows discrete line spectrum (Balmer, Lyman series). The model cannot explain quantized energy levels or spectral lines.

Limitation 3 — Chemical Behavior: The model provides no explanation for chemical bonding, valency, or periodic properties. It says nothing about electron arrangement or energy distribution that determines reactivity.
Impact Parameter: b = perpendicular distance of initial velocity vector from nucleus center. Smaller b → larger scattering angle. Relationship: b ∝ cot(θ/2). Head-on collision has b = 0, θ = 180°.

Transition to Bohr Model: Rutherford's limitations directly motivated Bohr (1913) to propose quantized orbits where electrons do not radiate in stationary states, explaining both stability and line spectra.

data.title: Postulates of Bohr's Atomic Model and their Applications
data.topicTitle: Postulates of Bohr's atomic model and its application
notes: ### 1. Meaning — why a new model was needed

Rutherford's nuclear model could not explain (i) why the revolving electron does not fall into the nucleus and (ii) why hydrogen gives discrete spectral lines. In 1913 Niels Bohr combined classical mechanics with Planck's quantum theory for the hydrogen atom and other one-electron species (He⁺, Li²⁺).
### 2. Postulates of Bohr's model (state them in order)
• **Stationary orbits:** the electron revolves only in certain permitted circular orbits (stationary states) of definite energy and does **not** radiate while in such an orbit.
• **Quantisation of angular momentum:** only orbits with mvr = nh/2π are allowed, n = 1, 2, 3, … (n = principal quantum number).
• **Frequency condition:** energy is absorbed or emitted only during a jump between orbits, hν = |E₂ − E₁| (emission on falling, absorption on rising).
• **Force condition:** the Coulomb attraction provides the centripetal force, mv²/r = kZe²/r² — used with the quantisation rule to find r and E.
### 3. Results derived from the postulates
• Orbit radius: $r_{n}=0.529\,\frac{n^{2}}{Z}$ Å; the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen (0.529 Å = 52.9 pm) is the **Bohr radius**.
• Orbital speed: $v_{n}=2.18\times10^{6}\,\frac{Z}{n}$ m s⁻¹ (for H, ground state = c/137, so the motion is non-relativistic).

• Energy: $E_{n}=-13.6\,\frac{Z^{2}}{n^{2}}$ eV = $-2.18\times10^{-18}\frac{Z^{2}}{n^{2}}$ J, with $KE=-E_{n}$ and $PE=2E_{n}$; total energy is **negative** because the zero of energy is at infinite separation.
• Rydberg constant follows from the model: $R=\frac{2\pi^{2}me^{4}}{h^{3}c}=1.097\times10^{7}$ m⁻¹.
### 4. Applications
• **Hydrogen spectrum:** gives the wave number of every line, $\bar{\nu}=RZ^{2}(\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}})$, and identifies the Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett and Pfund series.
• **Ionisation energy/enthalpy:** IE of H = 13.6 eV = 1312 kJ mol⁻¹; for He⁺ (Z = 2) it is 54.4 eV, and so on for Li²⁺, Be³⁺.
• **Atomic size and stability:** explains radii of the order 10⁻¹⁰ m growing as n², and shows why the atom does not collapse — stationary orbits do not radiate.
• **Spectra of hydrogen-like ions** (He⁺, Li²⁺) and energy-level diagrams still used in spectroscopy and astrophysics for highly ionised plasmas.
### 5. Successes and the edge of validity

Successes: atomic stability, hydrogen line spectrum and its series limits, the Rydberg constant, ionisation energy and orbital radii. It stops working for more than one electron and cannot explain fine structure, line intensities or the Zeeman and Stark effects (see 'Defects of Bohr's Theory').
**Fact.** Bohr model: electron in fixed circular orbits; angular momentum mvr = nh/2π; energy En = −13.6 eV·Z²/n² (for H, Z=1).
**Fact.** Rydberg/Balmer series: 1/λ = R(H)(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²). Absorption/emission = ΔE = hν between levels.
**Fact.** Four quantum numbers: n (shell), l (subshell, 0…n−1), mₗ (orientation, −l…+l), mₛ (spin ±½). Orbitals: s (spherical), p (dumbbell).
**Fact.** Filling order (Aufbau, n+l rule): 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d…; Hund's rule: maximise unpaired spin before pairing; Pauli: no two electrons share all four quantum numbers.
### Focus of this tab

The application machinery of Bohr's postulates: how each standard numerical is produced from the formulas, with the n-, Z- and mass-dependences made explicit. Use this tab to drill the calculation patterns.
### The four workhorse formulas
### Dependences to memorise
• r ∝ n²/Z (larger orbit for larger n, smaller for larger Z).
• v ∝ Z/n (fastest in the innermost orbit of the heaviest one-electron ion).
• E ∝ −Z²/n² (energy spacing shrinks as 1/n³ in difference form: ΔE ≈ 2 × 13.6 Z²/n³ for adjacent high levels).
• λ of a line ∝ n³/(Z²) roughly for adjacent-level transitions.
### Standard numerical patterns
• Radius of the nth orbit of a one-electron ion: substitute n and Z (He⁺ Z = 2, Li²⁺ Z = 3).
• Ionisation energy: IE = 13.6 Z²/n² eV (from the level n to ∞). For H ground state 13.6 eV = 1312 kJ mol⁻¹; for He⁺ (n = 1, Z = 2) 54.4 eV.
• Excitation energy: ΔE = 13.6 Z²(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) eV; convert with λ(nm) = 1240/ΔE(eV).
• Velocity ratio: v(n₁, Z₁)/v(n₂, Z₂) = (Z₁/n₁)/(Z₂/n₂).
### Two results worth memorising
• The ground-state speed of the H electron is c/137 ≈ 2.19 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ — non-relativistic, validating the model.
• The energy of the nth level approaches 0 as n → ∞, and the level spacing → 0: that is why spectral lines crowd toward the series limit.

The four postulates, stated cleanly with the physical meaning of each — the fastest way to secure full marks on the 'state the postulates' question. Derivations and applications are in the main note and the companion application tab.
### Postulate 1 — stationary orbits

The electron in a hydrogen atom revolves only in certain fixed circular orbits around the nucleus. While in such an orbit it does **not** emit or absorb energy, although it is accelerating. Each orbit is a *stationary state* with a definite energy. Meaning: this postulate suspends classical electrodynamics inside the atom.
### Postulate 2 — quantisation of angular momentum

Only those orbits are permitted for which the angular momentum is an integral multiple of h/2π: $mvr=\frac{nh}{2\pi}$, n = 1, 2, 3, … The integer n is the principal quantum number. Meaning: the allowed orbits are discrete because the angular momentum comes in packets of ħ.
### Postulate 3 — frequency (energy) condition

Energy is emitted or absorbed only when the electron jumps between orbits: $h\nu=E_{2}-E_{1}$ (emission when it falls to a lower level, absorption when it is raised). Meaning: this is exactly Planck's quantum hypothesis applied to atoms, and it is what produces sharp spectral lines.
### Postulate 4 — force condition

The Coulomb attraction of the nucleus provides the centripetal force for the circular motion: $\frac{mv^{2}}{r}=\frac{kZe^{2}}{r^{2}}$. Meaning: the mechanics is classical; only the *allowed states* are quantum — a hybrid (semi-classical) model.
### Vocabulary attached to the postulates

Ground state: lowest energy orbit (n = 1). Excited state: any higher orbit. Ionisation: complete removal of the electron (n = ∞). Binding energy: −Eₙ, the energy holding the electron. All definitions follow directly from the postulates.

How Bohr's frequency condition produces the two kinds of line spectra, why absorption lines and emission lines fall at the *same* wavelengths, and where each spectrum is used. Complements the main postulates tab.
### Emission spectrum (bright lines)

Atoms are excited — by a flame, discharge tube, or collision — to higher levels n₂. The electron falls back to a lower level n₁ and emits one photon per jump with $h\nu=E_{2}-E_{1}$. The spectrum is a set of bright lines on a dark background: each line = one allowed transition. In a discharge tube both atoms and electrons collide, so many levels are populated and several series appear at once.
### Absorption spectrum (dark lines)

Cool gas (ground-state atoms) is placed in front of a continuous white-light source. The atoms absorb only those photons whose energy exactly equals a level gap from the populated (usually ground) state: the transmitted light is missing those wavelengths — dark lines on a bright continuum. Fraunhofer's solar lines are exactly this: the cool solar atmosphere absorbing against the hot photosphere.
### Why the lines coincide

The same energy difference E₂ − E₁ is involved in both directions, so absorption and emission lines fall at identical wavelengths (Kirchhoff's law). The *pattern* differs, though: absorption requires the lower level to be populated, so absorption lines start mainly from the ground state (only the Lyman series in cold hydrogen gas), while emission can populate every series (Lyman, Balmer, Paschen …).
### Energy-level diagram language

Vertical arrows up = absorption; arrows down = emission. The ground level is the zero-height reference; higher levels crowd together as n grows; the n = ∞ limit is the ionisation continuum. Every allowed jump must obey the selection Δn = any (Bohr) — quantum mechanics later restricts it by Δl = ±1.
### Applications
• Chemical analysis: every element's line pattern is unique → qualitative and quantitative spectroscopy (flame tests, AAS, ICP).
• Astronomy: composition, temperature and Doppler velocity of stars from line positions and shifts; redshift of galaxies.
• Lasers: population inversion and stimulated emission between discrete levels (He–Ne 632.8 nm).
• Neon signs, fireworks and street lamps: line colours of excited atoms (Ne red-orange, Na yellow D-line 589 nm).
Why Bohr energies are negative, what the zero of energy means, and the three energy relations (E, KE, PE) that follow from the force condition.
### Where the negative sign comes from

Bohr takes the zero of energy at infinite separation — the electron just free of the atom, at rest. Any bound orbit is *below* that reference, so all bound-state energies are negative: $E_{n}=-13.6\,Z^{2}/n^{2}$ eV. The magnitude |E| is the binding energy — exactly the energy that must be supplied to free the electron (ionisation).
### The three relations

From the Coulomb force condition, $\frac{mv^{2}}{r}=\frac{kZe^{2}}{r^{2}}$ gives $KE=\frac{kZe^{2}}{2r}$ and $PE=-\frac{kZe^{2}}{r}$. Therefore: **KE = −E** and **PE = 2E = −2|E|**, with E = KE + PE. Check for hydrogen ground state: E = −13.6 eV, KE = +13.6 eV, PE = −27.2 eV. As n grows: E → 0⁻, KE → 0, PE → 0⁻ (a loosely bound, slow electron).
### Reading the numbers
• n = 1: E = −13.6 eV (most tightly bound, v = c/137).
• n = 2: E = −3.4 eV; n = 3: −1.51 eV; n = 4: −0.85 eV — level differences shrink as 1/n², hence the converging spectral series.
• n = ∞: E = 0 — ionisation; the electron is free.
### Why the sign matters in chemistry

Ionisation energy = |Eₙ| (positive number supplied); electron affinity and bond energies follow the same convention (energy *released* on going to a bound state is positive when reported as 'released'). Mixing the two sign conventions is the standard source of error — always state which convention you use.
confusion: ❌ 'Stationary orbit' means the electron is at rest. ✅ The electron moves, but the orbit is stationary *in energy* — it does not radiate.
❌ Bohr orbits and orbitals are the same. ✅ Orbits are fixed 2D circular paths of definite radius/energy; orbitals are 3D probability regions from the Schrödinger equation.
❌ A bound electron has positive energy. ✅ Its energy is negative (zero at infinite separation).
❌ Bohr's model works for all atoms. ✅ Only for one-electron species: H, He⁺, Li²⁺, Be³⁺.
❌ The electron radiates while revolving in an allowed orbit. ✅ Radiation occurs only during a jump.
❌ rₙ ∝ n/Z. ✅ rₙ = 0.529 n²/Z Å — the n-dependence is squared.
❌ Ionisation energy from level n is 13.6 Z²/n² eV multiplied by n. ✅ It is exactly 13.6 Z²/n² eV (removal from that level to ∞).
❌ Speed increases with n. ✅ v decreases as 1/n; outer electrons move slower.
❌ Stationary orbit means the electron is at rest. ✅ It revolves, but the orbit is stationary *in energy* (non-radiating).
❌ Bohr's postulates were derived from classical mechanics. ✅ They were imposed; only the force condition is classical.
❌ The frequency condition applies to the electron's own motion. ✅ It concerns the emitted/absorbed photon only.
❌ Absorption lines are produced when atoms emit energy. ✅ They appear when atoms *remove* matching photons from a continuous beam.
❌ Absorption and emission lines occur at different wavelengths. ✅ They coincide; only the pattern/populated series differ.
❌ A ground-state hydrogen atom can emit any Balmer line. ✅ Emission requires prior excitation; a ground-state atom can only absorb (Lyman lines).
❌ Negative energy means the calculation is wrong. ✅ It is a *bound state* referenced to infinite separation.
❌ KE is also negative. ✅ KE = −E is positive (½mv²); only total E and PE are negative.
❌ The electron loses mass when bound. ✅ Mass–energy differences are negligible here (13.6 eV vs 511 keV rest mass).

data.title: The Stability Crisis of Rutherford's Atom
data.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: ### Focus of this tab
The stability defect worked out quantitatively: how long the classical Rutherford atom would survive, and why that number forces quantisation. The full limitations list is in the main note.
### The classical argument

An electron moving in a circle is in accelerated motion (its velocity vector changes direction continuously). Maxwell's electromagnetic theory requires every accelerated charged body to radiate electromagnetic energy of frequency equal to its revolution frequency. Radiating means losing energy, so the electron must spiral inward.
### The spiral-in time

Using classical electrodynamics for hydrogen (r = 0.529 Å), the energy loss rate gives a collapse time of about $t\approx1.6\times10^{-11}\ \text{s}$ — commonly quoted as ≈10⁻⁸ s or less in textbooks. Either way it is far shorter than any observable lifetime: classical atoms would vanish in a flash.
### Two observable failures follow
• **No stable atoms:** matter could not exist, yet atoms are billions of years old.

• **Continuous spectrum:** as the electron spirals, its revolution frequency (and hence the radiated frequency) changes continuously, so the atom should emit a continuous spectrum. Experiment shows hydrogen emits sharp discrete lines (656.3 nm, 486.1 nm, …).
### Bohr's escape (what had to be assumed)

Bohr (1913) imposed two non-classical rules: (1) electrons move only in certain **stationary orbits** in which they do *not* radiate, and (2) radiation is emitted only during a jump, with $h\nu=E_{2}-E_{1}$. Both rules violate classical electrodynamics — that is precisely the price of saving the atom, and it opened the road to quantum mechanics.
### Why this matters for the exam

The stability crisis is the *reason* Bohr's first postulate exists. A complete answer always links: accelerated charge radiates → energy loss → spiral in → (i) no stability, (ii) continuous spectrum → both contradicted by experiment → quantisation required.
confusion: ❌ An electron radiates because it moves fast. ✅ Uniform motion radiates nothing; it is the *acceleration* (changing direction in a circle) that radiates.
❌ The electron spirals in slowly over years. ✅ Classical theory gives a collapse in ≈10⁻¹¹–10⁻⁸ s — effectively instantaneous.
❌ Bohr removed radiation altogether. ✅ Radiation still occurs during jumps; only radiation *within* a stationary orbit is forbidden.
practice: Use Maxwell's electromagnetic theory to show that Rutherford's atom is unstable.
What two experimental facts does the classical atom fail to explain?
State the two Bohr postulates that resolve the stability crisis and point out where classical physics is violated.
formulas: $$\text{accelerated charge} \Rightarrow \text{radiation},\qquad \nu_{\text{radiated}}=\nu_{\text{revolution}}\ (\text{classical})$$
$$t_{\text{collapse}}\approx10^{-11}-10^{-8}\ \text{s}\ (\text{classical hydrogen})$$
universalFacts: The classical collapse time for the hydrogen ground orbit is about 1.6 × 10⁻¹¹ s.
The discrete 656.3 nm Hα line is the experimental fact the classical atom cannot produce.
Bohr's 1913 postulates were the first successful breach of classical electrodynamics inside the atom.
examples: **Problem:** Why does a spiralling electron give a continuous spectrum? **Solution:** the revolution frequency ν_rev = v/2πr changes continuously as r shrinks; classical radiation copies this frequency, so all frequencies in a range are emitted — contradicting the observed sharp lines.
importantNotes: Always give both consequences (no stability + continuous spectrum); quoting only one loses marks.
State that the postulates are *postulates* — Bohr could not derive them classically.

data.title: Spectrum of the Hydrogen Atom
notes: ### 1. Meaning of 'spectrum'

A spectrum is the ordered display of the wavelengths in a beam of radiation after dispersion by a prism or grating. An **emission** spectrum is bright lines on a dark background (excited atoms emitting); an **absorption** spectrum is dark lines on a continuous background (cool atoms removing their own characteristic wavelengths). Atomic spectra are *line* spectra — band spectra come from molecules, continuous spectra from incandescent solids.
### 2. Origin of the hydrogen spectrum

Each line is one electron transition: the electron falls from n₂ to n₁ and emits one photon, hν = E₂ − E₁ = 13.6(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) eV for hydrogen. Since the levels are discrete, only discrete wavelengths appear — hence a line spectrum rather than a continuous one.
### 3. The spectral series of hydrogen
• **Lyman** (n₁ = 1): to the ground level — ultraviolet; first line 121.6 nm, series limit 91.2 nm.
• **Balmer** (n₁ = 2): the only *visible* series — Hα 656.3 nm (red), Hβ 486.1 nm, Hγ 434.0 nm, Hδ 410.2 nm; limit 364.6 nm.
• **Paschen** (n₁ = 3), **Brackett** (n₁ = 4) and **Pfund** (n₁ = 5): infrared.
• Lines within a series crowd together and converge at the series limit; beyond it the spectrum becomes continuous because the atom is ionised.
### 4. Rydberg equation and the Rydberg constant

$$\bar{\nu}=\frac{1}{\lambda}=RZ^{2}\left(\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}}\right),\qquad n_{2}>n_{1}$$ with R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ = 109 678 cm⁻¹ for hydrogen (Z = 1). Bohr's theory *derived* R = 2π²me⁴/h³c, turning Rydberg's empirical formula into theory — the model's greatest success.
### 5. Applications
• Spectral analysis identifies elements: each element has a unique line pattern, used in chemistry labs, metallurgy, forensics and pollution monitoring.
• Astronomy: composition, temperature and motion (Doppler shift) of stars are read from hydrogen lines; the 21 cm hydrogen line maps interstellar gas.
• Technology: atomic emission/absorption spectroscopy (AAS, ICP), flame tests, He–Ne gas lasers (632.8 nm) and spectrometer calibration all rest on hydrogen-like energy levels.
• Frank–Hertz and discharge-tube experiments confirm discrete energy levels and the Bohr energy expression.
### 6. Limitations of this treatment

The Bohr/Rydberg picture gives series positions but not line *fine structure* (Hα is really a doublet), relative intensities, or splitting in magnetic (Zeeman) and electric (Stark) fields; beyond hydrogen it needs multi-electron and relativistic corrections.
### Focus of this tab
A series-by-series reference table for the hydrogen spectrum, plus the line-counting rule — the data side of the main spectrum note.
### The five series at a glance
• **Lyman** (n₁ = 1): UV. First line 121.6 nm (2→1); series limit 91.2 nm. Discovered by Lyman, 1906.
• **Balmer** (n₁ = 2): visible. Hα 656.3 nm (3→2), Hβ 486.1 nm (4→2), Hγ 434.0 nm (5→2), Hδ 410.2 nm (6→2); limit 364.6 nm. Discovered by Balmer, 1885.
• **Paschen** (n₁ = 3): near IR. First line 1875 nm (4→3); limit 820.4 nm. Discovered 1908.
• **Brackett** (n₁ = 4): IR. First line 4051 nm (5→4); limit 1458 nm. Discovered 1922.
• **Pfund** (n₁ = 5): far IR. First line 7460 nm (6→5); limit 2279 nm. Discovered 1924. (A sixth, Humphreys, n₁ = 6, lies in the far IR.)
### Counting lines
• From a single excited level n: the number of different lines = n(n − 1)/2 (e.g. n = 4 → 6 lines: 3 Lyman + 2 Balmer + 1 Paschen).
• In one series, from level n to fixed n₁: n − n₁ lines (e.g. Balmer lines down from n = 4: two lines).
### Line spacing within a series

Successive lines crowd together and converge at the series limit (n₂ → ∞): $\bar{\nu}_{limit}=R/n_{1}^{2}$. The Balmer limit 364.6 nm marks the end of visible lines; beyond it the atom ionises and the spectrum becomes continuous.
### Wavelength ↔ energy conversions

$\Delta E(\text{eV})=\frac{1240}{\lambda(\text{nm})}$ and $\Delta E=13.6(\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}})$. Every line position follows from these two relations; the wavelength of any hydrogen-like ion scales as 1/Z² (He⁺ lines are 4× more energetic, shifted to ¼ wavelength).
How the Rydberg equation follows from Bohr's theory, what the Rydberg constant means, and the standard numerical patterns built on it.
### Derivation (short form)
### Meaning of R

R is the wave number of the hydrogen series limit (n₁ = 1, n₂ → ∞): $\bar{\nu}_{limit}=R$, λ = 91.2 nm. Because m appears in R, the constant is slightly isotope-dependent (reduced-mass correction): R(²H) ≈ R(¹H) × 1.00027 — the basis of measuring deuterium in heavy water spectroscopically.
### Numerical patterns
• Wavelength of a given line: pick n₁ (series) and n₂ (upper level); compute $\bar{\nu}$, invert for λ.
• Series limit: set n₂ → ∞ → $\bar{\nu}=RZ^{2}/n_{1}^{2}$.
• First line of a series: n₂ = n₁ + 1.
• Identification: given λ and a series, solve for n₂; given two lines, form their difference to get a third line (Ritz combination principle).
• Hydrogen-like ions: multiply by Z² (He⁺ Balmer lines are 4× the wave number of hydrogen's).
### Units trap
R is quoted both as 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ and 109 677 cm⁻¹. Convert before mixing: 1 cm⁻¹ = 100 m⁻¹; λ(nm) = 10⁷/ν̄(cm⁻¹).
confusion: ❌ The Balmer series lies in the ultraviolet. ✅ Balmer (n₁ = 2) is visible; Lyman (n₁ = 1) is UV and Paschen onward are IR.
❌ A ground-state hydrogen atom can emit a line. ✅ Emission needs excitation first; the ground state can only absorb.
❌ Within a series the lines get farther apart. ✅ They crowd together and converge at the series limit.
❌ Absorption lines mean the atom lost energy. ✅ The atom absorbs exactly the photons matching its level gaps, so those wavelengths are missing from the transmitted beam.
❌ Every line requires n₂ − n₁ = 1. ✅ Any n₂ > n₁ gives a line; the number of lines from level n is n(n − 1)/2.
❌ The Balmer series starts from n = 1. ✅ Balmer lines end at n₁ = 2; the lower level defines the series, not the upper one.
❌ The number of lines from level n is n − 1. ✅ That counts one series only; the total is n(n − 1)/2.
❌ The series limit is the strongest line. ✅ It is the *convergence* point where lines merge into the ionisation continuum.
❌ R is an empirical fitted constant with no origin. ✅ Bohr derived it from m, e, h and c — a theoretical prediction confirmed by experiment.
❌ ν̄ is the frequency. ✅ It is the wave number (1/λ); frequency ν = c·ν̄.
❌ The same R applies unchanged to He⁺. ✅ Multiply by Z² (and apply the reduced-mass correction for precision).

data.title: Defects (Limitations) of Bohr's Theory
notes: ### 1. Meaning

Bohr's model is **semi-classical**: it keeps classical circular orbits and Coulomb mechanics but bolts on an unexplained quantum condition (mvr = nh/2π). Its defects are exactly where classical thinking and the single-electron assumption break down.
### 2. Works only for one-electron species

It succeeds for H, He⁺, Li²⁺, Be³⁺ but fails for He, Li and every multi-electron atom: electron–electron repulsion and the screening (shielding) of nuclear charge by inner electrons are ignored, so calculated energies do not match experiment.
### 3. Cannot explain fine structure (line splitting)

High-resolution spectra show that many 'single' lines are doublets or multiplets (sodium D lines at 589.0/589.6 nm; Hα itself is a doublet). Bohr's model contains no relativity and no electron spin, so it cannot explain fine structure; Sommerfeld's elliptical orbits and later Dirac's relativistic theory were needed.
### 4. Cannot explain the Zeeman and Stark effects

Lines split in a magnetic field (Zeeman) and in an electric field (Stark). The model has no orbital magnetic moment or orientation concept and no magnetic quantum number, so it cannot predict these splittings.
### 5. Cannot explain intensities or selection rules
It gives the possible wavelengths but not their relative strengths, nor why many conceivable transitions are never observed. Line intensities need transition probabilities from quantum mechanics.
### 6. Contradicts the uncertainty principle

Bohr's orbit assigns the electron a definite radius **and** a definite speed at the same time — a definite trajectory. Heisenberg's Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π forbids this, so a well-defined orbit is inadmissible in principle.
### 7. Contradicts wave–particle duality

The model treats the electron purely as a particle in a path. de Broglie's matter waves, electron diffraction and the Schrödinger equation replace orbits with **orbitals** (probability distributions).
### 8. Ad hoc postulates and no chemistry

The quantisation condition is imposed rather than derived; the model gives no orbital shapes, no account of chemical bonding, no molecular (band) spectra, and only the crude Bohr–Bury scheme for periodicity.
### 9. No probability interpretation, no subshell structure

It cannot describe electron density ('where the electron is most likely'), degeneracy of subshells, hybridisation or directional bonds — all of which need the four quantum numbers of the quantum-mechanical model.
### 10. Rescue and replacement

Sommerfeld (1916) used elliptical orbits and the azimuthal quantum number for fine structure; de Broglie (1924), Heisenberg (1927) and Schrödinger (1926) produced the quantum-mechanical model, which removes every defect listed above.
**Fact.** Bohr model: electron in fixed circular orbits; angular momentum mvr = nh/2π; energy En = −13.6 eV·Z²/n² (for H, Z=1).
**Fact.** Rydberg/Balmer series: 1/λ = R(H)(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²). Absorption/emission = ΔE = hν between levels.
**Fact.** Four quantum numbers: n (shell), l (subshell, 0…n−1), mₗ (orientation, −l…+l), mₛ (spin ±½). Orbitals: s (spherical), p (dumbbell).
**Fact.** Filling order (Aufbau, n+l rule): 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d…; Hund's rule: maximise unpaired spin before pairing; Pauli: no two electrons share all four quantum numbers.
### Focus of this tab

The Bohr–Bury scheme (1921) — the shell-filling rules that Bohr's model alone could not give. It explains how the periodic table was first built from orbits and where it needed repair (a defect of the Bohr framework).
### The three Bohr–Bury rules
1. **Capacity rule:** the maximum number of electrons in a shell n is 2n² — K 2, L 8, M 18, N 32.
2. **Octet rule (valence shells):** the outermost shell cannot hold more than 8 electrons; when it has 8 (noble-gas configuration: He duplet, Ne octet) the shell is stable and a new shell begins.

3. **Filling order:** shells fill roughly in order of increasing energy; within a shell, electrons enter before a new shell starts — except that 4s begins filling before 3d is complete (the (n + l) order in modern language).
### What the scheme achieved
• Explained chemical inertness of the noble gases (closed shells) and the valency pattern of the main groups.
• Connected atomic number with the periodic law: element 11 (Na) starts the third shell, so period 3 begins — the periodicity of properties follows from shell structure.
• Predicted the electron configurations up to about Z = 20 reliably (K, Ca).
### Where the scheme fails (defects of the Bohr framework)
• No subshell concept: it cannot explain why 4s fills before 3d, the 8/18/32 period lengths beyond period 3, or the s/p/d/f blocks.
• It ignores electron–electron repulsion and exchange energy, so anomalies like Cr ([Ar]3d⁵4s¹) and Cu ([Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹) are impossible for it.
• Orbits are still definite paths — the uncertainty principle and orbital shapes are outside the scheme; 'subshell energy order' needs penetration and shielding, i.e. the quantum-mechanical model.
### Bridge to the modern picture

The 2n² capacity survives in modern form as Σ2(2l + 1) over the subshells of shell n; the octet rule survives as the special stability of filled s + p valence sets; and the filling order is the Madelung (n + l) rule. The Bohr–Bury scheme is thus the correct skeleton with the wrong (orbital-free) flesh.
A compressed revision list of Bohr's defects, each with its one-line reason — the fast recall version. The fully argued list is in the main defects note.
### The eight defects (with one-line reasons)
1. **One-electron only** — electron–electron repulsion and screening (Z_eff) are ignored; fails for He, Li, all multi-electron atoms.
2. **No fine structure** — no relativity, no spin; cannot explain doublets (Na D 589.0/589.6 nm; Hα doublet).
3. **No Zeeman/Stark splitting** — no magnetic quantum number or orbital magnetic moment; cannot explain splitting in magnetic/electric fields.
4. **No line intensities or selection rules** — gives possible wavelengths, not probabilities of transitions.
5. **Contradicts the uncertainty principle** — definite r and p simultaneously is impossible (Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π); orbits cannot be real trajectories.
6. **Ignores wave–particle duality** — treats the electron as a particle in a path; de Broglie/Schrödinger replace orbits by orbitals.
7. **Ad hoc postulates** — mvr = nh/2π is imposed, not derived (de Broglie's standing waves later justified it).
8. **No probability, no chemistry** — cannot give electron density, orbital shapes, subshell structure, bonding or molecular spectra; only the crude Bohr–Bury scheme for periodicity.
### The rescue timeline

1916 Sommerfeld (elliptical orbits, azimuthal quantum number → fine structure) → 1924 de Broglie (matter waves) → 1925 Pauli/Uhlenbeck–Goudsmit (spin) → 1926 Schrödinger (wave equation, orbitals) → 1927 Heisenberg (uncertainty). Each repair targets one defect above.
The single postulate mvr = nh/2π — how Bohr used it, why it was 'ad hoc', and how de Broglie's standing waves turned it into a consequence (this bridge is also where the defects discussion begins).
### Bohr's use of the postulate

Combined with the classical force condition $\frac{mv^{2}}{r}=\frac{kZe^{2}}{r^{2}}$, the quantisation rule fixes the allowed orbits: eliminating v gives $r_{n}=\frac{n^{2}h^{2}\varepsilon_{0}}{\pi m e^{2}Z}$ (numerically 0.529 n²/Z Å) and $v_{n}=\frac{2\pi ke^{2}Z}{nh}$. Without the rule, classical mechanics permits a continuum of orbits and no discrete spectrum.
### Why it was a defect

The rule was *imposed*, not derived — no classical argument forces the angular momentum to come in packets of ħ. Critics (and Bohr himself) treated it as an arbitrary rule that happened to work. This is defect 'ad hoc postulates' in the limitations list.
### de Broglie's rescue (1924)

If the electron is a wave of wavelength λ = h/mv, a stable orbit must be a **standing wave**: the circumference must contain a whole number of wavelengths, nλ = 2πr. Substituting λ gives n(h/mv) = 2πr → mvr = nh/2π — Bohr's condition *derived*, not assumed. For other orbits the wave interferes destructively with itself and the state is forbidden.
### The remaining problem

Even with de Broglie's justification, the orbit picture keeps a definite trajectory (definite r and p), which the uncertainty principle forbids — so the standing-wave argument is the *bridge* from Bohr to Schrödinger, not the destination: the wave must be treated in three dimensions, giving orbitals.
### Check the numbers

n = 1: mvr = h/2π = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. Circumference 2πr₁ = 3.32 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and λ = h/mv = 3.32 × 10⁻¹⁰ m — exactly one wavelength fits the first orbit; n = 2 fits two, and so on. The integer n literally counts the waves around the orbit.
confusion: ❌ Bohr's theory is completely wrong and useless. ✅ It is quantitatively excellent for one-electron species (H, He⁺) and is still used there; the defects appear beyond that scope.
❌ Fine structure arises because of many electrons. ✅ It arises from relativistic effects and electron spin even in a one-electron atom.
❌ The uncertainty principle reflects imperfect instruments. ✅ It is a fundamental limit of nature, not a measurement limitation.
❌ Bohr failed because orbits are not circular. ✅ The fatal objection is that a definite orbit (simultaneous r and p) cannot exist; probability orbitals replace them.
❌ Zeeman splitting is explained by Bohr's model. ✅ It requires the magnetic quantum number and orbital magnetic moment of the quantum-mechanical model.
❌ The M shell can hold 18 electrons before the N shell starts. ✅ The outermost shell is capped at 8; after 8 electrons in M, filling of N begins.
❌ The Bohr–Bury scheme is a quantum-mechanical theory. ✅ It is a shell-filling rule set from the Bohr orbit picture; subshells and orbital shapes are absent.
❌ 2n² applies to the outermost shell. ✅ 2n² is the *capacity*; the octet rule (8) restricts the valence shell's occupancy.
❌ Bohr's theory failed completely. ✅ It is exact for one-electron species (H, He⁺) — defects appear only beyond that scope.
❌ Fine structure needs many electrons. ✅ It comes from spin and relativity even in hydrogen.
❌ Defect 5 means measurements are inaccurate. ✅ It is a fundamental limit of nature, not an instrument problem.
❌ Bohr derived his quantisation from classical mechanics. ✅ He postulated it; de Broglie justified it in 1924.
❌ A non-integer number of waves still gives a stable orbit. ✅ Destructive interference destroys the wave; only nλ = 2πr orbits survive.
❌ Standing waves remove the uncertainty objection. ✅ They justify quantisation but keep the trajectory idea; Schrödinger's orbitals are needed for that.

data.title: Elementary Idea of the Quantum Mechanical Model — de Broglie's Wave Equation
data.topicTitle: Elementary idea of quantum mechanical model: de Broglie's wave equation
notes: ### 1. Meaning — dual nature of matter

Light behaves both as a wave and as a stream of particles (photons). In 1924 Louis de Broglie proposed the converse for matter: every moving material particle has a wave associated with it. These waves are called **matter waves** or de Broglie waves, and the hypothesis is the bridge from Bohr's orbits to the quantum-mechanical model.
### 2. de Broglie's wave equation

For a particle of mass m moving with speed v, wavelength $\lambda=\frac{h}{mv}=\frac{h}{p}$; using kinetic energy, $\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2mKE}}$; for an electron accelerated through a potential difference V volts, $\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}=\sqrt{\frac{150}{V}}\ \text{Å}\approx\frac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}}\ \text{Å}$. Derivation sketch: from $E=mc^{2}$ and $E=h\nu$ for a photon, $\lambda=h/p$ is obtained and applied to matter.
### 3. Meaning of the numbers

λ ∝ 1/m and ∝ 1/v: a 1 g mass moving at 1 m s⁻¹ has λ ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻³¹ m — unobservably small, which is why cricket balls show no wave nature. A 100 V electron has λ ≈ 1.23 Å, comparable with atomic spacings, so crystals diffract electrons. Wave behaviour is therefore a *microscopic* phenomenon.
### 4. Experimental proof

Davisson and Germer (1927) diffracted slow electrons from a nickel crystal and obtained a diffraction pattern whose maxima obey nλ = d sin θ; G. P. Thomson obtained similar patterns with high-speed electrons. Electron diffraction is the direct proof of matter waves.
### 5. How de Broglie's idea repairs Bohr's model

If the electron forms a standing wave round the orbit, the circumference must contain a whole number of wavelengths: nλ = 2πr. Substituting λ = h/mv gives mvr = nh/2π — Bohr's *unexplained* quantisation postulate now has a physical meaning. Modern quantum mechanics (Schrödinger, 1926) replaced the orbit by a wave function ψ, whose square |ψ|² gives the probability density of finding the electron — the **orbital**.
### 6. Applications
• Electron microscopes use the tiny λ of accelerated electrons to resolve objects far smaller than light allows; electron and neutron diffraction determine crystal and molecular structures.
• Explains quantisation of energy levels, the origin of quantum numbers, quantum tunnelling (STM, tunnel diodes, alpha decay) and the whole wave-mechanical picture of the atom.
• Underlies semiconductor physics, quantum dots, lasers and matter-wave interferometry (atom interferometers, BEC experiments).
### 7. Limitations of the elementary treatment

λ = h/mv is non-relativistic (for v close to c use λ = h/√(p² + (mv)²/c²) type corrections); the wave function is a *probability amplitude*, not a mechanical wave in a medium; the simple equation applies to a single free particle and needs the Schrödinger equation in a potential; the wavelength of everyday objects is far too small to detect.
### Focus of this tab
The derivation of λ = h/mv from the photon equations and the experimental proof — the two parts of de Broglie's idea that complete the main note.
### Derivation from the photon picture

For a photon: $E=h\nu$ and $E=mc^{2}$ (equivalence of energy and mass). Equating: $mc^{2}=h\nu=h\frac{c}{\lambda}$ → $\lambda=\frac{h}{mc}=\frac{h}{p}$. de Broglie's 1924 leap: the same relation must hold for **matter**, so a particle of momentum p = mv has wavelength $\lambda=\frac{h}{mv}$. For accelerated electrons, $\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}=\frac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}}\ \text{Å}$ (V in volts).
### Why the wave nature is only microscopic

λ ∝ 1/m: a 1 g body at 1 m s⁻¹ has λ ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻³¹ m (undetectable), while a 100 V electron has λ ≈ 1.23 Å — the size of atomic spacings, so crystals diffract electrons. Wave behaviour is not absent for large bodies; it is unobservable.
### Experimental proof (Davisson–Germer, 1927)

Electrons accelerated through ≈54 V strike a single nickel crystal; the detector records a maximum at φ = 50°. Bragg's law gives the wavelength: nλ = 2d sin θ with d = 0.091 nm → λ ≈ 0.165 nm; the de Broglie value for 54 V is λ = 12.27/√54 ≈ 1.67 Å = 0.167 nm — agreement within experiment. G. P. Thomson's high-energy electron diffraction through thin films confirmed it independently (both shared the 1937 Nobel Prize).
### Consequences that matter for chemistry
• Justifies Bohr's quantisation: nλ = 2πr → mvr = nh/2π.
• Basis of the Schrödinger equation and the orbital concept.
• Electron diffraction and the electron microscope (λ ≈ 0.005 nm at 50 kV → atomic resolution); neutron diffraction for structure determination.
• Quantum tunnelling and matter-wave interferometry (atom interferometers, BEC) are direct technologies of matter waves.
The equation that turned de Broglie's matter waves into the quantum-mechanical model — what ψ means, what solving it gives, and how the four quantum numbers appear.
### The equation (elementary form)

For a particle moving in one dimension: $-\frac{h^{2}}{8\pi^{2}m}\frac{d^{2}\psi}{dx^{2}}+V\psi=E\psi$, i.e. $\hat{H}\psi=E\psi$ — a wave equation in which the 'wave property' comes from de Broglie (through the momentum operator) and the energy from classical mechanics. For the hydrogen atom V is the Coulomb potential, and the equation is solved in spherical coordinates $(r,\theta,\phi)$.
### What ψ and ψ² mean

ψ itself has no direct physical meaning; the measurable quantity is **|ψ|², the probability density** — the chance of finding the electron in a unit volume at that point. Max Born supplied this interpretation. The total probability over all space is normalised to 1 (∫|ψ|²dV = 1). Regions where ψ = 0 are **nodes**.
### What solving the hydrogen atom gives

• A set of allowed wave functions ψₙ,ₗ,ₘ (orbitals) labelled by three quantum numbers — n (size/energy), l (shape), m (orientation) — that arise automatically from the boundary conditions (ψ must be single-valued, finite and vanish at infinity).
• Energies $E_{n}=-13.6/n^{2}$ eV, agreeing with Bohr — but degeneracy appears: for n = 2 the solutions 2s and 2p have the same energy, which Bohr cannot give.
• Probability distributions instead of paths: the electron cloud, radial probability maxima (0.529 Å for 1s), and orbital shapes (spherical s, dumbbell p).
### Why this replaces Bohr

The uncertainty principle forbids definite orbits; Schrödinger's equation never uses a trajectory. It works for multi-electron atoms (approximately, with effective nuclear charge), explains fine structure when spin is added, and predicts molecular bonding — every defect of Bohr's theory is repaired.
confusion: ❌ Matter waves are electromagnetic waves. ✅ They are probability (matter) waves carrying no charge; they are not E–B oscillations.
❌ Heavier bodies have longer wavelengths. ✅ λ = h/mv — larger mass means a *shorter* (unobservable) wavelength.
❌ de Broglie's hypothesis was accepted immediately on publication. ✅ It became convincing only after the Davisson–Germer electron-diffraction experiment (1927).
❌ de Broglie's waves replace Bohr's quantisation with nothing. ✅ They *justify* it through the standing-wave condition nλ = 2πr.
❌ An electron microscope uses electron particles and light waves together. ✅ It uses the electron's short de Broglie wavelength, not visible light.
❌ de Broglie waves travel at the speed of light. ✅ They travel with the particle (v ≪ c); the phase velocity even exceeds c, while the group velocity equals v.
❌ The derivation needs relativistic mass. ✅ For non-relativistic particles λ = h/mv directly; the photon derivation only motivates the form.
❌ Davisson–Germer proved light has particle nature. ✅ It proved *electrons* have wave nature — the converse of the photoelectric effect.
❌ ψ is a measurable wave like a light wave. ✅ ψ is a probability amplitude; only |ψ|² is physically meaningful.
❌ Quantum numbers are put in by hand. ✅ They emerge from solving the equation with boundary conditions.
❌ Solving the equation gives exact paths. ✅ It gives probability distributions; trajectories do not exist.

data.title: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle and the Concept of Probability
data.topicTitle: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle and concept of probability
notes: ### 1. Meaning and statement

Werner Heisenberg (1927) showed that for a microscopic particle it is impossible to determine simultaneously and exactly both its position and its momentum: $\Delta x\cdot\Delta p\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$, or $\Delta x\cdot\Delta v\ge\frac{h}{4\pi m}$. Other conjugate pairs obey the same pattern: $\Delta E\cdot\Delta t\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$ and $\Delta L\cdot\Delta\theta\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$.
### 2. Why it happens

To locate an electron we must 'illuminate' it with radiation of wavelength comparable to its size; such a photon collides with the electron and changes its momentum by an unknown amount, while using longer-wavelength radiation blurs the position. The disturbance is a property of matter, not an experimental defect — the γ-ray microscope is the standard illustration.
### 3. Consequence: the concept of probability

A definite orbit needs exact r and p simultaneously, which the principle forbids. The electron's location can only be described by a wave function ψ, where |ψ|² dV is the **probability** of finding the electron in volume dV — the electron-cloud or **orbital** picture. The radial probability peak for the 1s orbital lies at 0.529 Å: the same number Bohr obtained, now interpreted as a most-probable distance instead of a fixed radius.
### 4. Applications

• **Atomic stability and size:** an electron confined to a nucleus (Δx ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ m) would need Δp ≈ 10⁻¹⁹ kg m s⁻¹, i.e. KE of the order 10¹⁰ eV — impossible; hence electrons cannot sit inside nuclei and atoms are ≈10⁻¹⁰ m across, which also explains why the electron does not fall into the nucleus.
• **Natural line width:** an excited state living Δt ≈ 10⁻⁸ s has ΔE ≥ h/4πΔt, so spectral lines are broadened; the same relation explains tunnelling and virtual-particle processes.

• **Zero-point energy** of confined particles, resolution limits of electron microscopes, quantum-dot behaviour and NMR line widths all follow from the principle, and all quantum-mechanical predictions (average radii, orbital shapes) are probabilistic.
### 5. Limitations and cautions

The relation matters only for microscopic particles — for a 1 g body the product is utterly negligible, so classical mechanics holds. It forbids *simultaneous* exact knowledge, not knowledge of one quantity: perfect momentum knowledge leaves position completely undefined. Interpretations differ (Copenhagen versus measurement-disturbance readings), so it is safest to state it as a property of quantum ensembles; it is not a statement about instrument precision and does not mean measurement is impossible.
**Fact.** P(E) = favourable/total. Additive law: P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). If mutually exclusive, P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B).
**Fact.** Multiplicative: P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B|A); independence: P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B).
**Fact.** Complement: P(A') = 1 − P(A). For discrete: ΣP = 1; expected value E(X) = Σxᵢpᵢ.
### Focus of this tab
The three standard forms of the principle and the two numerical patterns NEB asks (electron in an atom; electron in the nucleus). The probability interpretation is in the main note.
### The three forms
• Position–momentum: $\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$, or with velocity $\Delta x\,\Delta v\ge\frac{h}{4\pi m}$.
• Energy–time: $\Delta E\,\Delta t\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$ — an excited state living Δt has a minimum energy spread ΔE, which broadens spectral lines (natural line width).
• Angular momentum–angle: $\Delta L\,\Delta\theta\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$.
### Numerical pattern 1 — electron localised to atomic size

Δx = 10⁻¹⁰ m: Δv ≥ h/(4πmΔx) = 6.626×10⁻³⁴/(4π × 9.11×10⁻³¹ × 10⁻¹⁰) ≈ 5.8 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. This is comparable with the electron's own speed (2.2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹), so a definite orbit is impossible — the standard argument against Bohr orbits.
### Numerical pattern 2 — electron inside the nucleus

Δx = 10⁻¹⁴ m (nuclear size): Δp ≈ h/(4πΔx) ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ kg m s⁻¹ → KE ≈ (Δp)²/2m ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ J ≈ 10⁹ eV. Nuclear binding energies are ~10⁷ eV, so the electron cannot be confined in the nucleus — proof that electrons are not nuclear constituents (β-particles are created at emission).
### Relation to the probability concept

Because r and p cannot both be sharp, the electron's state is described by ψ with |ψ|² = probability density. The 1s radial probability peaks at 0.529 Å — Bohr's radius reappears as the *most probable* distance. 'Electron cloud', boundary surfaces and atomic radii averages all follow from this probabilistic description.
### Limits of the principle
It matters only for microscopic particles: for a 1 g body at Δx = 10⁻¹⁰ m, Δv ≈ 10⁻²⁴ m s⁻¹ — utterly negligible, so classical mechanics remains valid for everyday objects.
confusion: ❌ The principle is due to clumsy instruments. ✅ It is fundamental; better instruments cannot beat h/4π.
❌ It says nothing about the electron can be known. ✅ Either quantity may be exact; only the *product* of uncertainties is bounded below.
❌ It applies equally to a moving cricket ball. ✅ For macroscopic bodies the uncertainty product is negligible, so classical physics applies.
❌ The principle proves electrons do not exist in atoms. ✅ It replaces fixed orbits by probability distributions (orbitals) described by |ψ|².
❌ ΔE·Δt ≥ h/4π is a different law. ✅ It is the energy–time form of the same principle, explaining natural line broadening.
❌ The principle sets a limit on *both* quantities individually. ✅ Only the *product* of the two uncertainties is bounded; either one alone can be exact.
❌ ΔE·Δt means energy conservation is violated. ✅ It permits transient fluctuations within ΔE for times shorter than Δt — the basis of virtual processes and tunnelling.
❌ A better microscope can beat the limit. ✅ The limit is fundamental, not technical.

data.title: Quantum Numbers
notes: ### 1. Meaning

Solving the Schrödinger equation for the hydrogen atom yields a set of numbers that completely describe the state of an electron. These are the **quantum numbers** — effectively the 'address' of an electron in an atom. Four numbers are needed: principal (n), azimuthal or angular-momentum (l), magnetic (m or mₗ) and spin (s or mₛ).
### 2. Principal quantum number (n)

Determines the **shell** (energy level) and, in effect, the size: r ∝ n². Values n = 1, 2, 3, … ∞; the shell letters are K, L, M, N …; maximum capacity of a shell = 2n² electrons (n = 1 → 2, n = 2 → 8, n = 3 → 18, n = 4 → 32). It corresponds to Bohr's orbit number but is now a quantum label, not a path.
### 3. Azimuthal quantum number (l)

Determines the **subshell** and the *shape* of the orbital. Values l = 0, 1, 2, 3 … (n − 1), i.e. (n − 1) subshells per shell; the letters are s (l = 0), p (1), d (2), f (3). Orbital angular momentum = $\sqrt{l(l+1)}\,\frac{h}{2\pi}$. Within a shell the energies follow the order s < p < d < f, and a subshell holds 2(2l + 1) electrons (s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14).
### 4. Magnetic quantum number (mₗ)

Determines the **orientation** of the orbital in space (equivalently the component of angular momentum along a chosen axis). Values run from −l through 0 to +l, i.e. (2l + 1) values: one s orbital, three p orbitals (px, py, pz), five d orbitals, seven f orbitals. All orbitals of a subshell are degenerate (equal energy) in a free atom and split in a magnetic field — the origin of the Zeeman effect.
### 5. Spin quantum number (mₛ)

Describes the intrinsic spin of the electron; values +1/2 (↑) or −1/2 (↓). Introduced from the Stern–Gerlach experiment and the doublet structure of spectra (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1925). Because of it each orbital holds at most two electrons, giving the total capacities 2, 6, 10, 14 and 2n² per shell.
### 6. Orbitals, subshells and shells at a glance

n = 1: 1s (2e⁻, 1 orbital). n = 2: 2s + 2p (8e⁻, 4 orbitals). n = 3: 3s + 3p + 3d (18e⁻, 9 orbitals). n = 4: 4s + 4p + 4d + 4f (32e⁻, 16 orbitals). In general, orbitals in a shell = n², electrons = 2n², and an orbital is written n l (e.g. 3p).
### 7. Applications
• They define **electronic configuration**, the order of filling, and hence the position of an element in the periodic table and its block (s, p, d, f).
• They predict **magnetic behaviour**: unpaired electrons (Hund's rule follows from spin) give paramagnetism; fully paired species are diamagnetic.
• They explain spectral fine structure, the Zeeman and Stark effects, spin-orbit coupling, MRI/NMR (nuclear spin), lasers and selection rules.
• They let us test validity of a given set (e.g. l = n is forbidden) and count orbitals, unpaired electrons and quantum states in a subshell.
### 8. Limitations

Quantum numbers describe one electron at a time (not a pair or an atom as a whole); they do not give an electron's position, only the probability; the exact energies for multi-electron atoms need Z_eff and electron–electron interaction; mₛ comes from relativistic Dirac theory and is not contained in the simple Schrödinger solution; and spin–orbit coupling requires the total angular-momentum quantum number J, which is beyond Bohr's picture.
### Focus of this tab
Where the quantum numbers come from mathematically and the counting metrics (orbitals, capacities, designations) in one table.
### Origins

• n, l and m arise as **separation constants** when the Schrödinger equation for the hydrogen atom is solved in spherical coordinates — the radial equation gives n, the angular equations give l and m. They are not assumptions; they are forced by the boundary conditions.

• mₛ does **not** come from the Schrödinger equation: it enters through the relativistic Dirac equation (1928) and was inferred earlier (1925, Uhlenbeck–Goudsmit) from the Stern–Gerlach experiment and spectral doublets.
### The metrics table

Shell n: orbitals n², electrons 2n² (K 1/2, L 4/8, M 9/18, N 16/32). Subshell l: orbitals 2l + 1 (s 1, p 3, d 5, f 7), electrons 2(2l + 1) (s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14). Nodes: radial n − l − 1, angular l, total n − 1. Orbital designation nl (1s, 2p, 3d, 4f).
### Energy order within a shell

For hydrogen all subshells of a shell are degenerate (E depends only on n). In multi-electron atoms penetration makes $E_{ns}<E_{np}<E_{nd}<E_{nf}$, and across shells the (n + l) Madelung order governs filling — the two facts the Bohr–Bury scheme could not express.
### Counting patterns (exam drills)
• Electrons with n = 4, l = 2 → 4d: 2(2·2+1) = 10.
• Orbitals with n = 3 → 9 = 3² (1 s + 3 p + 5 d).
• Electrons with n = 3 and m = 0 → 6 (one each in 3s, 3p, 3d, doubled by spin).
• Unpaired electrons in a subshell from Hund's rule → paramagnetism; fully paired → diamagnetism.
How (n, l, m) triples map onto orbital designations, and what the spin quantum number adds — including the box-and-arrow notation used in configuration questions.
### The designation matrix
• l = 0 → s, 1 orbital (m = 0): 1s, 2s, 3s, 4s …
• l = 1 → p, 3 orbitals (m = −1, 0, +1): 2p, 3p, 4p … each written px, py, pz.
• l = 2 → d, 5 orbitals (m = −2 … +2): 3d, 4d … (dxy, dyz, dxz, dx²−y², dz²).
• l = 3 → f, 7 orbitals (m = −3 … +3): 4f, 5f …
The full designation combines n and the subshell letter (3p) or, fully, (n, l, m) — e.g. (3, 1, 0) is the 3pz orbital.
### The spin quantum number

mₛ = +½ (↑) or −½ (↓). Electron spin is an intrinsic angular momentum with magnitude √(3/4)·h/2π = √3/2 ħ — it is not literally a spinning ball, but the name survives. Evidence: Stern–Gerlach (silver atoms split into two beams) and doublet structure of alkali spectra. With spin, each orbital (defined by n, l, m) holds exactly two electrons of opposite spin — Pauli's exclusion principle.
### Box-and-arrow notation (configuration drawing)

Draw one box per orbital; fill per Aufbau/Pauli/Hund. Nitrogen: 2p ↑ ↑ ↑ (three boxes, parallel arrows); oxygen: 2p ↑↓ ↑ ↑. The notation encodes unpaired-electron counts, hence magnetic behaviour: N has 3 unpaired (paramagnetic), Ne has 0 (diamagnetic).
### Magnetic behaviour from the matrix
Count unpaired electrons u: spin-only magnetic moment μ = √(u(u + 2)) BM. Fe³⁺ (3d⁵): u = 5 → μ ≈ 5.92 BM; Cu²⁺ (3d⁹): u = 1 → 1.73 BM; Zn²⁺ (3d¹⁰): u = 0 → diamagnetic.

The four quantum numbers through one concrete example — the 2p electron of carbon — the fastest route to the 'write the quantum numbers' question. Definitions and the full metric table are in the main note and the metrics tab.
### The example worked through

Carbon (Z = 6): 1s² 2s² 2p². Take a 2p electron: n = 2 (L shell, second energy level); l = 1 (p subshell, dumbbell shape); m = −1, 0 or +1 (which of px, py, pz the orbital is); mₛ = +½ or −½ (spin). Hund's rule puts the two 2p electrons in different p orbitals with parallel spins, so a valid full set for the first is n = 2, l = 1, m = −1, mₛ = +½ and for the second n = 2, l = 1, m = 0, mₛ = +½.
### What each number fixes
• **n:** shell, size and energy (r ∝ n²; capacity 2n²).
• **l:** subshell and shape (s spherical, p dumbbell, d clover, f complex); angular momentum √(l(l+1))·h/2π; permitted values 0 … n − 1.
• **m:** orientation in space; 2l + 1 values; explains Zeeman splitting.
• **mₛ:** spin ±½; Pauli exclusion follows — no two electrons share all four numbers.
### The validity ladder (check in this order)
n ≥ 1 → l ≤ n − 1 → |m| ≤ l → mₛ = ±½. So (n = 2, l = 2) is invalid (l = n), (n = 3, l = 2, m = −3) is invalid (|m| > l), and (n = 2, l = 1, m = 0, mₛ = ±½) is valid.
### Degeneracy and pairing

The three p orbitals are degenerate in a free atom; a magnetic field splits them (Zeeman). Filling follows Hund's rule: singly with parallel spins first — the origin of carbon's two unpaired 2p electrons and hence its divalent/paramagnetic behaviour.

data.title: Orbitals and the Shapes of s and p Orbitals
data.topicTitle: Orbitals and shape of s and p orbitals only
notes: ### 1. Meaning of an orbital

An orbital is the three-dimensional region around the nucleus in which the probability of finding the electron is maximum (the ~90–95% boundary-surface region) for a given energy state. It comes from the wave function ψ of the Schrödinger equation, and |ψ|² is the probability density. An orbital has *no sharp boundary* and does not describe a path.
### 2. Orbital vs orbit
• Orbit (Bohr): fixed two-dimensional circular path with definite radius and energy.
• Orbital (quantum mechanics): three-dimensional probability distribution — spherical (s) or directional (p, d) — with no definite path and no sharp edge.
### 3. Shape of s orbitals
• **Spherical** and hence non-directional; present in every shell from n = 1.
• Size and energy increase with n (1s < 2s < 3s); the radial probability distribution shows (n − 1) maxima, the outermost being the most probable distance (0.529 Å for 1s).
• (n − 1) spherical nodes and no nodal plane; 1s has no node.
### 4. Shape of p orbitals
• **Dumbbell (peanut) shaped** — two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus with a nodal plane through the nucleus where probability is zero.
• They appear from n = 2 as three orbitals at 90° to one another: px, py, pz (m = −1, 0, +1).
• The three are **degenerate** in a free atom and split in a magnetic field (Zeeman effect).
• Each p orbital holds 2 electrons, so a p subshell holds 6; the shapes are identical, only the orientation differs.
### 5. Nodes, penetration and degeneracy

Nodes are zero-probability regions: radial = n − l − 1, angular (nodal planes) = l, total = n − 1. Because s orbitals penetrate closer to the nucleus than p orbitals of the same shell, they are less shielded and lower in energy — the reason for the ns < np < nd order in multi-electron atoms.
### 6. Applications
• **Bonding and molecular shape:** the directionality of p orbitals explains the 90° H–S–H angle, the VSEPR shapes, and the σ (end-on) versus π (side-on) classification of bonds.
• **Hybridisation:** mixing s and p orbitals (sp, sp², sp³) explains the linear BeF₂, trigonal-planar BF₃ and tetrahedral CH₄ geometries.
• **Periodic table:** three p orbitals per subshell (capacity 6) explain the six-membered p-block and the period lengths 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32.
• Explains paramagnetism (degenerate orbitals occupied singly per Hund's rule) and the spherical electron cloud of the noble gases.
### 7. Limitations

Orbital pictures are *boundary-surface diagrams* at a chosen probability level — the electron is not confined to the drawn shape and no motion is shown. Exact shapes strictly hold only for one-electron systems; electron correlation and bonding perturb them in real atoms and molecules; d and f orbitals are far more complex (this syllabus limits us to s and p); and orbitals cannot be observed directly — only electron density can.
### Focus of this tab
Spin quantum number and the box-arrow notation, mapped onto the shell structure — the drawing skills needed for configuration and orbital-diagram questions.
### The spin quantum number

mₛ = +½ (↑) or −½ (↓) for every electron, independent of n, l, m. Spin angular momentum is √(3/4)ħ. Consequences: an orbital holds at most 2 electrons (Pauli); a shell holds 2n²; a subshell holds 2(2l + 1).
### Box notation rules
• One box per orbital; label the subshell above (2p: three boxes).
• Aufbau: fill orbitals in increasing (n + l) order.
• Hund: in degenerate boxes, one up-arrow per box before any pairing.
• Pauli: two arrows in one box must be opposite (↑↓).
### Shell mapping (putting orbitals into shells)
### Worked box diagrams
• N (Z = 7): 1s ↑↓ | 2s ↑↓ | 2p ↑ ↑ ↑ → 3 unpaired electrons, paramagnetic.
• O (Z = 8): 2p ↑↓ ↑ ↑ → 2 unpaired.
• Cr (Z = 24): [Ar] 3d ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ with 4s ↑ — the half-filled exception.
### What the diagrams predict

Unpaired electrons → paramagnetism, μ = √(u(u + 2)) BM; paired → diamagnetic. The diagram also shows why carbon forms two covalent bonds after promotion (two half-filled p orbitals) and why the noble gases are inert (all boxes paired).
The orbit–orbital distinction in tabular form plus the s-orbital details (radial probability distribution) that the main note covers briefly.
### Orbit versus orbital (six-row table)
• Origin: Bohr's model / Schrödinger's equation.
• Nature: fixed 2D circular path / 3D probability region.
• Definiteness: exact radius and momentum / neither is definite (Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π).
• Number: one orbit per n / n² orbitals per shell.
• Direction: non-directional concept / s spherical, p directional.
• Status: contradicted by experiment / the accepted modern picture.
### The s orbital in detail
• Shape: sphere — electron density depends only on distance r, not direction (non-directional, hence s orbitals give no directionality in bonding).

• Radial probability distribution: the chance of finding the electron between r and r + dr peaks at the most probable distance — 0.529 Å for 1s. For 2s the curve has two maxima separated by a radial node where probability is exactly zero.
• Nodes: 1s none; 2s one spherical node at r = 2a₀ ≈ 1.06 Å; 3s two; in general (n − 1) spherical nodes. There are no nodal planes for s.
• Size and energy: both increase with n (1s < 2s < 3s), and higher s orbitals penetrate closer to the nucleus than p of the same shell — the origin of the ns < np energy order.
### Why s orbitals matter chemically

Spherical symmetry makes s orbitals the 'all-direction' bond formers (H uses 1s in every bond), the mixing component of every hybrid (sp, sp², sp³), and the reason the noble-gas electron clouds (filled s and p) are spherically symmetric — the chemical basis of their inertness.
confusion: ❌ Orbit and orbital mean the same thing. ✅ Orbit = fixed 2D path; orbital = 3D probability region.
❌ A p orbital has two lobes, so it holds two electrons in each lobe. ✅ The lobes together form one orbital, which holds a pair of electrons of opposite spin.
❌ s orbitals become dumbbell-shaped in higher shells. ✅ All s orbitals stay spherical; only size and nodes change with n.
❌ px, py and pz have different energies in an isolated atom. ✅ They are degenerate; a magnetic or ligand field is needed to split them.
❌ The electron stays inside the drawn boundary. ✅ The surface is a probability contour; there is a small chance of finding it outside.
❌ Arrows in the same box may point the same way. ✅ Pauli forbids it — opposite spins only.
❌ Pairing starts in the first p box. ✅ Hund's rule: each degenerate box gets one electron first.
❌ Spin affects the shape of orbitals. ✅ Spin changes capacity and magnetism, not the shape given by l.
❌ 2s is just a bigger 1s. ✅ 2s also has an inner radial node and a second probability maximum — qualitatively different.
❌ The electron sits on the surface of the drawn sphere. ✅ The sphere is a probability boundary; the density decays continuously outward.
❌ s orbitals can be directional after hybridisation. ✅ Pure s is spherical; directionality appears only in hybrid orbitals (sp, sp², sp³).

data.title: Aufbau Principle, Pauli's Exclusion Principle, Hund's Rule and Electronic Configurations (up to Z = 30)
data.topicTitle: Aufbau principle, Pauli's exclusion principle, Hund's rule and electronic configurations of atoms and ions (up to atomic no. 30)
notes: ### 1. Meaning

These three rules distribute electrons among the orbitals of an atom in its ground state: Aufbau fixes the *order* of filling, Pauli fixes the *capacity* of an orbital, and Hund fixes *how degenerate orbitals are filled*.
### 2. Aufbau principle and the (n + l) rule

Electrons fill the available orbital of lowest energy first. Order is given by the **Madelung (n + l) rule**: smaller (n + l) first; for equal (n + l), smaller n first. Thus 4s (n + l = 4) fills before 3d (n + l = 5), giving 1s < 2s < 2p < 3s < 3p < 4s < 3d < 4p < 5s < 4d < 5p < 6s < 4f < 5d < 6p < 7s < 5f < 6d < 7p.
### 3. Pauli's exclusion principle

No two electrons in an atom can have all four quantum numbers identical; equivalently an orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins (↑↓). Consequences: subshell capacities 2, 6, 10, 14; shell capacity 2n².
### 4. Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity

Electrons enter degenerate orbitals (same n and l, e.g. the three 2p) singly with parallel spins before pairing; pairing starts only after every degenerate orbital has one electron. Reason: pairing costs Coulomb repulsion energy while parallel spins gain exchange energy. Example: N 2p³ = ↑ ↑ ↑ (three unpaired); O 2p⁴ = ↑↓ ↑ ↑ (two unpaired).
### 5. Extra stability of half-filled and fully-filled subshells

d⁵, d¹⁰, p³ and p⁶ arrangements gain exchange energy and symmetry, which explains the anomalies at Z = 24 and 29: Cr = [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ (not 3d⁴4s²) and Cu = [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ (not 3d⁹4s²). Similar anomalies occur at Nb, Mo, Ru, Rh, Pd, Ag, Pt and Au.
### 6. Electronic configurations, Z = 1–30 (noble-gas shorthand)

H 1s¹ · He 1s² · Li [He]2s¹ · Be [He]2s² · B [He]2s²2p¹ · C 2p² · N 2p³ · O 2p⁴ · F 2p⁵ · Ne 2p⁶ · Na [Ne]3s¹ · Mg 3s² · Al 3s²3p¹ · Si 3p² · P 3p³ · S 3p⁴ · Cl 3p⁵ · Ar 3p⁶ · K [Ar]4s¹ · Ca 4s² · Sc 3d¹4s² · Ti 3d²4s² · V 3d³4s² · Cr 3d⁵4s¹ · Mn 3d⁵4s² · Fe 3d⁶4s² · Co 3d⁷4s² · Ni 3d⁸4s² · Cu 3d¹⁰4s¹ · Zn 3d¹⁰4s².
### 7. Configurations of ions

Electrons are removed from the highest-n (outermost) shell first even though 4s filled before 3d: Fe ([Ar]3d⁶4s²) → Fe²⁺ ([Ar]3d⁶) → Fe³⁺ ([Ar]3d⁵, half-filled and extra stable); Cu ([Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹) → Cu⁺ ([Ar]3d¹⁰); Mn → Mn²⁺ ([Ar]3d⁵). This explains why Fe³⁺ and Mn²⁺ are the commonest oxidation states of those metals.
### 8. Applications
• Predicts valency, oxidation states and magnetic behaviour (Fe³⁺: 5 unpaired → paramagnetic; Zn²⁺: 3d¹⁰ → diamagnetic; Cu²⁺: 1 unpaired) and the colours of transition-metal ions.
• Explains the structure of the periodic table — s, p, d, f blocks and period lengths 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32 — and is the basis of hybridisation and complex chemistry.
### 9. Limitations

The (n + l) rule is only approximate — the many anomalous configurations of Cr, Cu, Nb, Mo, Ru, Rh, Pd, Ag, Pt, Au and of the lanthanides/actinides show that electron repulsion, exchange energy and relativistic effects decide the real order; the orbital energy order changes with Z and inside ions or ligand fields; Hund's rule has exceptions in excited states; Aufbau fails for heavy elements; and none of the rules predicts reactivity or reaction rates.
confusion: ❌ 4s is always lower in energy than 3d. ✅ It fills first in neutral atoms, but in ions the 4s electrons are removed first (Fe²⁺ = 3d⁶).
❌ Pauli's principle forbids two electrons in one orbital. ✅ They may share an orbital if their spins are opposite (different mₛ).
❌ Hund's rule says electrons pair as soon as possible. ✅ Pairing begins only after every degenerate orbital holds one electron.
❌ Cr is [Ar]3d⁴4s². ✅ It is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ because the half-filled d subshell wins on exchange energy.
