data.title: Liquid State: Physical Properties of Liquids
data.topicTitle: Liquid state: physical properties of liquids — evaporation and condensation, vapour pressure and boiling point, surface tension and viscosity (qualitative idea only)
notes: ### 1. Meaning of the liquid state

A liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape: molecules are close together (short intermolecular distances) and slide over one another, so a liquid can flow, is practically incompressible and shows short-range order only. Intermolecular forces are strong enough to hold the molecules together but not strong enough to fix them in a lattice, as in a solid.
### 2. Evaporation and condensation

**Evaporation** is the escape of high-energy molecules from the *surface* of a liquid into the vapour phase at any temperature below the boiling point. It is endothermic (the liquid cools — earthen pots, sweating, petrichor), and its rate increases with temperature, surface area, wind/movement and dryness of the air, and decreases with humidity. **Condensation** is the reverse change of vapour to liquid, releasing the same latent heat; when the rates become equal a dynamic equilibrium is established and the vapour is said to be saturated (dew point for atmospheric condensation).
### 3. Vapour pressure and boiling point

Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by the vapour when it is in dynamic equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature. It depends only on the nature of the liquid and the temperature — **not** on the amount of liquid or the size of the container. Volatile liquids have high vapour pressure (ether, acetone, alcohol); water has 23.8 mm Hg at 25 °C and 760 mm Hg at 100 °C. Vapour pressure rises steeply with temperature; the quantitative relation is the Clausius–Clapeyron equation.

**Boiling** occurs when the vapour pressure of the liquid becomes equal to the external (atmospheric) pressure; the temperature at that point is the boiling point, and heat supplied thereafter goes into converting liquid to vapour (latent heat of vaporisation) so the temperature stays constant. Consequences: boiling point rises with external pressure (pressure cooker) and falls in the mountains/vacuum (water boils below 100 °C at high altitude; vacuum distillation for heat-sensitive liquids).
### 4. Surface tension

Molecules in the bulk are pulled equally in all directions, but a surface molecule experiences a net inward pull, so the surface behaves like a stretched membrane and tends to minimise its area. Surface tension γ is the force per unit length acting along the surface (γ = F/l), with units N m⁻¹ or J m⁻². It decreases as temperature rises (becoming zero at the critical temperature) and is lowered by soaps and detergents. Consequences: spherical drops, capillary rise in narrow tubes (used by plants and blotting paper), meniscus shapes (water concave, mercury convex), flotation of light insects and needles, and the functioning of detergents and wetting agents.
### 5. Viscosity

Viscosity is the internal friction (resistance to flow) between adjacent layers of a liquid moving with different speeds; the coefficient of viscosity η has units N s m⁻² (Pa s) or poise (P), with 1 P = 0.1 Pa s. Viscosity arises from intermolecular attraction and decreases rapidly as temperature rises (for gases it increases). Examples: honey and glycerol flow slowly (high η), water and ether flow easily; engine oils are graded by SAE numbers according to their viscosity, and lubricating oil must be chosen for the operating temperature.
### 6. Other physical properties (brief)

Liquids are practically incompressible (very high bulk modulus), diffuse slowly compared with gases, conduct heat but not electricity (except molten salts/metals), and expand slightly on heating. Their thermal conductivity makes them useful as coolants (water, oil) and their low compressibility is the basis of hydraulic brakes and hydraulic lifts.
### 7. Applications

• **Vapour pressure and boiling:** distillation and fractional distillation, steam distillation, vacuum distillation of heat-sensitive liquids (petroleum fractions, glycerine), autoclaves and pressure cookers, and the working of refrigerants.
• **Evaporation:** cooling by evaporation (earthen pots, desert coolers, sweating), drying of paints and wet clothes, and evaporative humidifiers.

• **Surface tension:** detergents and soaps (lowering γ improves wetting and emulsification), waterproofing agents, flotation of insects, capillary rise in xylem and blotting paper, and mercury barometers where the convex meniscus must be corrected.

• **Viscosity:** selection of lubricating oils and greases for machines, engine-oil grades (SAE 30 etc.), flow of blood in vessels and the effect of temperature on it, pipeline transport of oil, and viscosity measurements to determine molar mass of polymers.
### 8. Limitations

There is no simple equation of state for liquids — the kinetic model that works for gases fails because liquids show short-range order and strong interactions; surface tension and viscosity are interpreted qualitatively (values depend on the measurement method and on impurities); vapour pressure is reduced by non-volatile solutes (Raoult's law), so impure samples give wrong boiling points, and the Clausius–Clapeyron treatment assumes that ΔH_vap is constant over the range (an approximation). Many real liquids are non-Newtonian (blood, paint, ketchup), so a single viscosity value is misleading, and near the critical temperature all these properties change drastically, which no simple description covers.
confusion: ❌ Evaporation happens only at the boiling point. ✅ It occurs at every temperature from the liquid surface; boiling is evaporation throughout the bulk at the boiling point.
❌ Vapour pressure depends on how much liquid is present. ✅ It depends only on the liquid's nature and the temperature (and on the presence of solutes).
❌ Surface tension makes the surface a real skin. ✅ It is an inward pull on surface molecules that makes the surface behave like a stretched membrane.
❌ Glycerine is more viscous than water because it is denser. ✅ Viscosity comes from stronger intermolecular (H-bonding) attraction, not from density.
❌ A liquid boils when the vapour pressure exceeds the atmospheric pressure. ✅ Boiling starts when vapour pressure *equals* the external pressure (an overshoot just makes it boil faster).

formulas: $$\gamma=\frac{F}{l}\ (\text{N m}^{-1});\qquad \eta\ \text{in Pa s}\ (1\ \text{poise}=0.1\ \text{Pa s})$$
$$\text{Clausius–Clapeyron: }\ln\frac{P_{2}}{P_{1}}=\frac{\Delta H_{\text{vap}}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_{1}}-\frac{1}{T_{2}}\right)$$
$$\text{Capillary rise: }h=\frac{2\gamma\cos\theta}{r\rho g}$$
universalFacts: Vapour pressure of water: 23.8 mm Hg at 25 °C, 760 mm Hg at 100 °C (normal boiling point).
Surface tension of water ≈ 72 mN m⁻¹ at 25 °C, falling to zero at the critical temperature (374 °C).
Viscosity of water ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s at 20 °C; glycerol ≈ 1.5 Pa s — about a thousand times greater.
answer pattern for "Liquid state: physical properties of liquids — evaporatio…": define → method → result. Structure earns the marks on 6–10 mark questions.
examples: **Problem:** Why does a wet cloth dry faster on a windy day? **Solution:** wind removes the vapour layer above the surface, keeping the vapour pressure below saturation so the net evaporation rate stays high; higher temperature and larger exposed area act in the same direction.

**Problem:** Estimate the boiling point of water at 8000 m where the pressure is about 0.36 atm. **Solution:** the boiling temperature is reached when vapour pressure equals 0.36 atm ≈ 274 mm Hg; from vapour-pressure tables this corresponds to about 72 °C — hence cooking takes much longer at altitude.
importantNotes: Remember the three marks-carrying definitions: vapour pressure (equilibrium), boiling point (vapour pressure = external pressure), surface tension (force per unit length).
For liquids, viscosity *decreases* with temperature, whereas for gases it increases — a standard one-mark comparison.
Syllabus asks for qualitative treatment only: describe causes, trends and applications, not derivations.

data.title: Solid State: Types of Solids, Amorphous and Crystalline Solids
data.topicTitle: Solid state: types of solids, amorphous and crystalline solids
notes: ### 1. Meaning of the solid state

A solid has a definite shape and volume because its constituent particles are held in fixed mean positions by strong intermolecular (or interatomic/ionic) forces. The particles can only vibrate about their positions, so solids are rigid, practically incompressible and diffuse extremely slowly. Solids are classified by the *arrangement* of particles (crystalline vs amorphous) and by the *nature of the binding force* (ionic, covalent, molecular, metallic, hydrogen-bonded).
### 2. Crystalline solids

The particles are arranged in a regular, repeating three-dimensional pattern called a **crystal lattice**, which extends over a long range (long-range order). Properties: definite geometrical shape (crystal habit), sharp melting point, cleavage along definite planes, anisotropic physical properties (refractive index, thermal expansion, conductivity differ along different directions) and a characteristic X-ray diffraction pattern. Examples: NaCl, KCl, sugar, quartz, diamond, ice, alum, copper.
### 3. Types of crystalline solids (by binding force)
• **Ionic:** ions held by strong electrostatic forces (NaCl, CaF₂) — hard, brittle, high melting point, non-conducting as solids but conducting when molten or in solution, soluble in polar solvents.

• **Covalent (network/atomic):** atoms joined by a continuous network of covalent bonds (diamond, graphite, SiC, quartz) — extremely hard, very high melting point, usually insulators or semiconductors (graphite conducts).
• **Molecular:** molecules held by weak van der Waals forces or hydrogen bonds (iodine, dry ice, naphthalene, sugar, ice) — soft, low melting point, volatile, poor conductors.

• **Metallic:** positive ion cores in a sea of delocalised electrons (Na, Cu, Fe) — lustrous, malleable, ductile, good conductors of heat and electricity, melting points from very low (Hg, Ga) to very high (W).
### 4. Amorphous solids

Amorphous solids have only short-range order — the particles are randomly arranged over long distances, so there is no definite lattice. Properties: no definite geometrical shape, no sharp melting point (they soften gradually over a temperature range and have a glass-transition temperature Tg), isotropic properties, irregular cleavage and a broad diffuse X-ray pattern. They are described as pseudo-solids or **supercooled liquids** because their particles can flow very slowly. Examples: glass, rubber, plastics, amorphous sulfur and selenium, cellophane.
### 5. Crystalline versus amorphous (comparison points)

Melting point: sharp vs gradual; order: long-range vs short-range; shape: definite geometry vs irregular; cleavage: definite planes vs irregular; physical properties: anisotropic vs isotropic; X-ray diffraction: sharp lines vs broad halos; thermodynamic stability: stable vs metastable; examples: NaCl, diamond vs glass, rubber.
### 6. Isotropy and anisotropy

A substance is isotropic when a physical property has the same value in all directions (amorphous solids, liquids, gases) and anisotropic when the property depends on direction (single crystals). For example the refractive index of quartz differs along different crystallographic axes, and graphite conducts electricity along its layers but not across them.
### 7. Applications

• **Single crystals** are grown for technology — Czochralski-pulled silicon and germanium for semiconductors, quartz for oscillators and watches, sapphire for optical windows, and organic crystals for lasers and detectors.

• Ionic and molecular crystals are the basis of the salt, sugar, fertiliser and pharmaceutical industries (recrystallisation is the standard purification method; crystal polymorphism controls drug dissolution).

• Amorphous solids find wide use precisely because of their isotropic, easy-to-shape nature — window and container glass, optical fibres, plastics, rubber, amorphous silicon solar cells and metallic glasses.
• Diamond, SiC and quartz illustrate structure-property relations: giant covalent lattices give extreme hardness and high melting points used in abrasives, cutting tools and refractories.
### 8. Limitations

The crystalline/amorphous division is not sharp: most materials are polycrystalline or semi-crystalline (plastics, silk, cotton, metals) with both ordered and disordered regions, so the perfect crystal is an idealisation. Anisotropy appears only in single crystals — a polycrystalline aggregate usually behaves isotropically in bulk. The classification by binding force is itself approximate, since many crystals show mixed bonding (graphite: covalent + van der Waals; ice: covalent + hydrogen bonding), and amorphous solids are **metastable**, so their properties drift with time (glass devitrification) and depend on thermal history rather than on composition alone.
confusion: ❌ Amorphous solids are true solids with a very high viscosity. ✅ They are regarded as pseudo-solids or supercooled liquids because they lack long-range order and flow over long times.
❌ All solids have sharp melting points. ✅ Amorphous solids soften over a range (glass-transition temperature); only crystalline solids melt sharply.
❌ Isotropy means the same as anisotropy. ✅ Isotropic = same property in all directions (amorphous); anisotropic = direction-dependent (single crystals).
❌ Graphite is a molecular solid. ✅ Graphite is a covalent network with strong covalent layers held by weak van der Waals forces — which explains its lubricity and conductivity.
❌ Metals melt at high temperature because they are covalently bonded. ✅ Metallic bonding strength varies widely; Hg melts at −39 °C while W melts at 3422 °C.

universalFacts: Quartz, diamond and graphite are allotropic forms of giant covalent crystals; graphite is anisotropic (conducts along layers).
Glass is a supercooled liquid — very old window glass is measurably thicker at the bottom because of slow flow.
Amorphous silicon is used in thin-film solar cells and LCD backplanes, where its cheaper deposition outweighs its lower efficiency.

examples: **Problem:** Why does glass not show a sharp melting point on heating? **Solution:** amorphous solids lack a periodic lattice, so bonds break over a range of energies — the material softens gradually between the glass-transition and melting regions instead of melting at one temperature.

**Problem:** Graphite conducts electricity while diamond does not, though both are carbon. **Solution:** in graphite each carbon uses three of four valence electrons in σ bonds; the fourth electron is delocalised between layers enabling conduction, whereas in diamond all four electrons are localised in σ bonds.

data.title: Boyle's Law in Detail — Isotherms, Numericals and Limitations
notes: ### Focus of this tab
The first gas law in full: statement, graphs, molecular explanation, numericals and where it breaks — the pattern to reproduce for Charles' and Avogadro's laws.
### Statement (1662, Robert Boyle)

At constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure: V ∝ 1/P, i.e. PV = constant, or P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. Conditions: fixed mass, constant T, ideal behaviour (low P).
### Graphical forms (all three are examinable)
• P versus V: rectangular hyperbola (each temperature gives one hyperbola — an isotherm; higher T curves lie farther from the origin).
• P versus 1/V: straight line through the origin, slope = nRT.
• PV versus P: horizontal straight line for an ideal gas; real gases show a dip (attraction) then a rise (volume effect) — the first visible sign of non-ideality.
### Molecular explanation

Halving the volume doubles the number density of molecules, so wall collisions per unit area per second double, doubling the pressure — the inverse relation is pure collision statistics at fixed average molecular speed (fixed T).
### Numericals
• V₂ = P₁V₁/P₂: 500 cm³ at 700 mm Hg → at 1400 mm Hg: 250 cm³.
• Density application: since m fixed, d ∝ P at constant T — a compressed gas is proportionally denser.
• Bubble problem: an air bubble rising from depth doubles its volume as pressure halves (plus water-column corrections with 10 m water ≈ 1 atm).
### Limitations
• Ideal-gas law: fails at high pressure (PV rises above nRT) and near liquefaction; gases with strong attraction (CO₂, SO₂, NH₃) deviate most; H₂ and He deviate least.
• Requires fixed mass and constant temperature — a temperature change during compression invalidates it.
• Cannot be extrapolated to the liquid state; below the critical temperature compression produces condensation, not further Boyle-law shrinkage.
confusion: ❌ PV = constant for any gas under any conditions. ✅ Only for fixed mass at constant temperature and ideal behaviour.
❌ Doubling pressure halves the temperature. ✅ Boyle's law holds T constant; the P–T relation is Gay-Lussac's law.
❌ The P–V graph is a straight line. ✅ It is a hyperbola; the straight line appears for P versus 1/V.

Explain Boyle's law using the kinetic theory.

formulas: $$P_{1}V_{1}=P_{2}V_{2}\ (\text{fixed mass, constant }T);\qquad d\propto P\ (\text{constant }T)$$
universalFacts: Boyle published the law in 1662 — the first quantitative gas law.
At constant T the product PV equals nRT for every ideal gas; its graph versus P is flat.
Real-gas Boyle plots dip below the ideal line at moderate pressure — evidence of intermolecular attraction.
examples: **Problem:** A diver's air bubble of 5 mL forms at 4 atm (depth ≈30 m). What volume at the surface (1 atm), ignoring temperature change? **Solution:** V₂ = P₁V₁/P₂ = 4 × 5/1 = 20 mL — a fourfold expansion, the classic Boyle's law safety example.
importantNotes: State the two conditions (fixed mass, constant T) every time the law is quoted.
Draw the PV-vs-P horizontal line with the real-gas dip to show mastery beyond the ideal law.

data.title: The Gaseous State — Characteristics and Measurable Properties
notes: ### Focus of this tab
What defines a gas and the four measurable variables (P, V, T, n) whose relationships the gas laws and kinetic theory explain — the orientation before the postulates.
### Defining characteristics of the gaseous state
• No fixed shape or volume — a gas fills its container completely.
• Very low density compared with liquids/solids (air ≈ 1.3 kg m⁻³ vs water 1000 kg m⁻³); highly compressible; diffuse rapidly.
• Molecules are far apart (intermolecular distances ≈ 10 molecular diameters at STP) with negligible attraction — hence expansion and compressibility.
• Exerts pressure uniformly in all directions (momentum transfer on wall collisions).
• Mixes completely and homogeneously (diffusion, effusion through pinholes).
### The four state variables
• **Pressure (P):** force per unit area; units Pa (N m⁻²), atm (1 atm = 101325 Pa = 760 mm Hg), bar (1 bar = 10⁵ Pa); measured with barometers/manometers.
• **Volume (V):** space occupied; 1 m³ = 1000 L = 10⁶ cm³ (mL).
• **Temperature (T):** kelvin only in gas laws; T(K) = t(°C) + 273.15.
• **Amount (n):** moles; links to mass via molar mass and to particles via N_A.
### What the gas laws connect

Boyle (P–V at fixed T), Charles (V–T at fixed P), Gay-Lussac (P–T at fixed V), Avogadro (V–n at fixed P, T), combined equation and PV = nRT. Each law fixes two variables and studies the other two — the 'constant-holding' logic of all gas-law experiments.
### Why gases need a molecular model

The measured regularities (PV = nRT for all gases at low P) are too universal to be accidental: they point to a common microscopic structure. The kinetic theory supplies it — postulates → PV = ⅓mnc̄² → PV = nRT — and its idealisations (point molecules, no attraction) mark exactly where real gases deviate.

The postulate → consequence mapping: each idealisation of the kinetic theory, what it explains, and which real-gas failure it causes. A different cut through the material from the main postulates note.
### Postulate → consequence → failure table
• 'Molecules are point masses (negligible volume)' → explains compressibility and large empty space → fails at high pressure (free volume < container volume, real PV > nRT).

• 'No intermolecular attraction except during collision' → explains indefinite expansion and Dalton's partial pressures → fails near liquefaction (attraction lowers observed pressure, real Z < 1) and is the reason gases condense at all.

• 'Collisions perfectly elastic' → kinetic energy redistributed, not lost; gas temperature stays constant in a rigid container → fails slightly (real collisions excite vibrations; polyatomic gases need internal degrees of freedom for their specific heats).

• 'Random straight-line motion, huge numbers' → statistics (Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution) explains steady macroscopic pressure from microscopic chaos → fails for very low densities where molecule counts fluctuate.
• 'KE ∝ T' → defines absolute temperature microscopically: KE = (3/2)kT per molecule, (3/2)RT per mole → explains why T must be kelvin and why all gases share the same R.
### The central derivation chain

$PV=\frac{1}{3}mn\bar{c}^{2}$ (pressure from momentum transfer) + KE ∝ T (postulate) → $PV=nRT$ → Boyle's, Charles' and Avogadro's laws fall out immediately. One set of postulates explains *all* the gas laws at once — the model's greatest virtue.
### What the model explains beyond the laws

Graham's diffusion/effusion (r ∝ 1/√M), Dalton's partial pressures (independent molecules), Graham's law of effusion, viscosity (momentum transfer between layers) and Brownian-motion style randomness of molecular speeds.
### Where the idealisations bite (recap for exams)

High P: molecular volume matters. Low T / near Tc: attraction matters. Polyatomic gases: rotation/vibration. Very light gases at low T: quantum effects. Liquid state: attraction and volume together — outside the model entirely.
confusion: ❌ Gases have negligible mass. ✅ They have small but definite mass — 22.4 L of air weighs about 29 g at STP.
❌ Temperature in gas laws may be taken in °C. ✅ Absolute (kelvin) temperature only; 0 °C is 273.15 K.
❌ A gas exerts pressure only downward. ✅ Pressure is isotropic — equal in every direction.
❌ 'Negligible molecular volume' is a minor technicality. ✅ It is one of the two postulates whose failure defines all real-gas deviation (the other is no attraction).
❌ Kinetic theory explains why gases liquefy. ✅ It cannot — liquefaction comes from the attractive forces it assumes away; that requires the van der Waals model.
❌ Elastic collisions mean molecules never exchange energy. ✅ They exchange freely but the *total* KE is conserved.

$$PV=\tfrac{1}{3}mn\bar{c}^{2},\qquad KE=\tfrac{3}{2}kT\ (\text{molecule})=\tfrac{3}{2}RT\ (\text{mole})$$

One mole of any gas at STP occupies 22.4 L and, for air, weighs ≈28.97 g (average molar mass).

**Problem:** Which postulate fails when a gas is compressed to 200 atm? **Solution:** 'molecular volume is negligible' — the molecules' own volume is no longer negligible against the container volume, so the free space shrinks and observed pressure exceeds the ideal prediction (Z > 1).

data.title: Dalton's Atomic Theory and its Postulates
data.topicTitle: Dalton's atomic theory and its postulates
notes: ### 1. Meaning and background

John Dalton (1803–1808, *A New System of Chemical Philosophy*) proposed the first quantitative atomic theory. Its purpose was to explain the experimentally discovered laws of chemical combination (conservation of mass, definite proportions, multiple proportions) by assuming that matter is made of discrete, indestructible particles called **atoms**. The theory marks the birth of modern chemistry because it turned qualitative ideas about matter into a testable, quantitative model.
### 2. Postulates (state them in order)
• Matter is composed of extremely small, indivisible particles called atoms.
• Atoms of the same element are identical in mass, size and chemical properties; atoms of different elements have different masses and properties.
• Atoms cannot be created, destroyed or divided by chemical reactions — a chemical change only rearranges atoms (this explains the conservation of mass).
• Atoms of different elements combine in fixed, simple whole-number ratios to form compounds (this explains the law of definite proportions and the law of multiple proportions).
• The atom is the smallest particle that can take part in a chemical reaction; in a compound, atoms are held together by chemical attraction.
• Atoms of one element cannot be converted into atoms of another element by ordinary chemical means.
### 3. Successes (why it was accepted)

It explained the law of conservation of mass, the law of definite (constant) proportions and the law of multiple proportions by pure logic, provided the basis for balancing equations and hence for all stoichiometric calculation, introduced the idea of atomic (relative) masses, and prepared the ground for the mole concept and Avogadro's molecular hypothesis.
### 4. Applications
• Quantitative chemistry: balanced equations, mole calculations, limiting-reactant and yield problems all rest on atoms being conserved and combining in fixed ratios.
• Determination of atomic and molecular masses; formulation of the atomic mass unit and relative atomic mass scale.
• Basis of the modern atomic model (with the modifications listed below), of stoichiometry-based industry (fertilisers, metallurgy, cement, pharmaceuticals) and of chemical analysis by mass balance.
### 5. Limitations and modifications (exam-critical)
1. **Atoms are divisible:** the discovery of the electron (Thomson, 1897), proton (Rutherford, 1919) and neutron (Chadwick, 1932) showed that atoms contain subatomic particles and can be split.
2. **Not all atoms of an element are identical:** isotopes (¹²C, ¹³C, ¹⁴C; ³⁵Cl, ³⁷Cl) have the same chemical properties but different masses.
3. **Atoms of different elements can have the same mass:** isobars such as ⁴⁰Ar and ⁴⁰Ca.
4. **Atoms of one element can be changed into another:** nuclear reactions and transmutation (¹⁴N + α → ¹⁷O + p; radioactivity, fission and fusion) achieve exactly what Dalton denied.

5. **Mass is not strictly conserved** in nuclear processes — the mass defect appears as energy according to E = mc², so the conservation-of-mass postulate is only valid for ordinary chemical reactions.

6. **It did not explain** the nature of the force holding atoms together (chemical bonding), the structure of the atom, the law of gaseous volumes and the law of reciprocal proportions; it also could not account for allotropes, giant molecules or the existence of diatomic element molecules (H₂, O₂, N₂) until Avogadro's molecular concept.

**Summing up:** Dalton's core idea — that matter is atomic and that reactions rearrange atoms — is still valid; his absolute statements about indivisibility, identical masses and non-convertibility are the parts that modern chemistry and physics have modified.
confusion: ❌ Dalton's atomic theory is completely wrong today. ✅ Its core (matter is atomic and reactions only rearrange atoms) is fully valid; only its absolute claims about indivisibility, identical masses and non-convertibility have been modified.
❌ Atoms of the same element always have the same mass. ✅ Isotopes such as ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl differ in mass while remaining chemically similar.
❌ Dalton explained the law of gaseous volumes. ✅ That was Gay-Lussac (1809), and Avogadro's hypothesis was needed to interpret it — Dalton's theory by itself could not accommodate it.
❌ Nuclear reactions obey Dalton's postulates. ✅ They violate them: atoms are split, elements change and mass is converted into energy.
❌ Dalton's theory explained chemical bonding. ✅ It assumed atoms are held together by 'chemical attraction' without explaining its nature.

$$\text{Mass defect (nuclear): }\ \Delta m=\frac{E}{c^{2}}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{chemical mass is not strictly conserved in nuclear change}$$

**Problem:** Why does the mass of a sealed tube containing AgNO₃ and NaCl solutions remain constant after mixing and precipitation? **Solution:** the reacting atoms are only rearranged into AgCl and NaNO₃, so the total mass is unchanged — a direct verification of the law of conservation of mass.

Remember that Dalton's theory, not Lavoisier's, is the one that *predicted* multiple proportions.

data.title: Law of Conservation of Mass — Statement, Verification and Applications
notes: ### Focus of this tab
The first law of chemical combination in depth — statement, historical verification, microscopic explanation and its one important limitation.
### Statement and history

'In a chemical reaction, matter can neither be created nor destroyed; the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products.' Established by Antoine Lavoisier (1774) from careful weighings — e.g. mercury calx (HgO) heated in a sealed retort gave mercury and oxygen with no loss of mass — the work that made chemistry quantitative.
### Experimental verification (Landolt, 1893)

Landolt placed two reacting solutions (AgNO₃ and NaCl) in separate limbs of an H-shaped sealed tube, weighed it, inverted to mix, waited for complete precipitation (AgCl), and reweighed — mass unchanged within 1 part in 10⁷. Modern verification uses any precipitation, neutralisation or redox reaction carried out in a sealed system.
### Microscopic explanation

A reaction only rearranges atoms: bonds break and form, but no atom disappears or appears (Dalton's third postulate). The equation must therefore be balanced — atom counts, and hence masses, are equal on both sides. This is why balancing is the first step of every stoichiometric calculation.
### What must be included in the weighing

All gaseous reactants/products (CO₂ escaping an open flask breaks the balance), the solvent, the precipitate, and the container. The classic school error: burning magnesium on an open balance shows a mass *gain* — oxygen has entered; in a sealed flask the mass is constant.
### Limitation (important)

The law holds for **chemical** reactions only. In nuclear reactions (fission, fusion, radioactivity) a measurable mass defect converts to energy: E = Δmc² — mass and energy are jointly conserved. Even in chemistry the energy change has a mass equivalent, but it is ≈10⁻¹⁰ of the reacting mass, far below weighing precision.
### Applications

Balancing equations; material balances in industry (input = output accounting for ammonia, cement, steel plants); gravimetric analysis; detecting loss of product (leaks, volatilisation); and every 'how much product' calculation in stoichiometry.
confusion: ❌ Magnesium burning in air contradicts the law because the ash is heavier. ✅ The extra mass is the oxygen that combined; in a closed system the total is constant.
❌ The law applies to nuclear reactions. ✅ It is limited to chemical reactions; nuclear processes show mass–energy equivalence.
❌ A balanced equation conserves molecules. ✅ It conserves atoms and mass; molecular counts may change (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃: 4 molecules → 2).

Explain the law using Dalton's atomic theory.

formulas: $$\sum m_{\text{reactants}}=\sum m_{\text{products}};\qquad E=\Delta mc^{2}\ (\text{nuclear limit})$$
universalFacts: Landolt's sealed-tube experiments confirmed conservation to 1 part in 10⁷.
Lavoisier's mercury(II) oxide decomposition was the founding quantitative experiment of chemistry.
In the burning of 12 g of carbon, exactly 44 g of CO₂ is formed — conservation in one line.
examples: **Problem:** 2.16 g of Ag₂O is completely decomposed; 2.00 g of silver remains. Find the mass of oxygen evolved. **Solution:** m(O₂) = 2.16 − 2.00 = 0.16 g — the mass balance of the law applied directly.
importantNotes: Use 'total mass of reactants = total mass of products' verbatim in the statement.
Quote Landolt's sealed tube as the verification and E = Δmc² as the limitation.

data.title: Law of Definite (Constant) Proportions — Statement, Examples and Limitations
notes: ### Focus of this tab
The second law of chemical combination: Proust's law of definite proportions with its classic percentage data, the calculations it supports, and the compounds that break it.
### Statement and history

'A chemical compound always contains the same elements combined in the same fixed proportion by mass, regardless of its source or method of preparation.' Established by Joseph Proust (1799) against Berthollet, who believed composition could vary continuously with conditions.
### The classic data
• Water: from river, sea, rain or synthesised from H₂ + O₂ — H : O = 1 : 8 by mass (11.1% H, 88.9% O).
• Carbon dioxide: 27.27% C, 72.73% O (C : O = 3 : 8) whether from burning carbon, respiration or limestone decomposition.
• Copper oxide: 79.9% Cu, 20.1% O whether prepared by heating copper in air or reducing CuO in hydrogen.
### Why it holds

A pure compound has a fixed formula (H₂O, CO₂, CuO): fixed atom counts and fixed atomic masses give a fixed mass ratio — a direct consequence of Dalton's theory (the law was actually strong evidence *for* atoms).
### Calculations it supports
• Percentage composition: % element = (mass of element in formula ÷ molar mass) × 100.
• Mass of element in a given sample: sample mass × (%/100) — e.g. oxygen in 90 g of water = 90 × (8/9) = 80 g.
• Purity analysis: a brass sample or an ore is assayed by comparing its metal percentage with the theoretical value for the pure compound.
### Limitations (where the law fails)
1. **Non-stoichiometric (berthollide) compounds:** Fe₀.₉₃O, FeS₁₋ₓ, Cu₂₋ₓO — composition varies within a small range; the law needs a true formula compound.
2. **Isotopic variation:** D₂O (heavy water) has H : O = 2 : 8, not 1 : 8 — the same 'compound' differs when isotopes change.
3. **Mixtures, solutions and alloys** vary continuously in composition — the law is for pure compounds only.
4. Polymers and associated molecules with variable chain length have no single fixed composition.
confusion: ❌ The law means elements always combine in the same proportion. ✅ It applies to a given *compound*; the same two elements may form several compounds (CO, CO₂) with different ratios — that is multiple proportions.
❌ Heavy water is a counterexample to chemistry being consistent. ✅ It shows the law depends on the isotope chosen — D₂O and H₂O are different compounds.
❌ The law applies to brass or steel. ✅ Alloys are mixtures with variable composition; only pure compounds are covered.

Calculate the percentage of nitrogen in NH₃ and the mass of nitrogen in 100 g of it.
Explain how non-stoichiometric compounds limit the law.
Distinguish the law of definite proportions from the law of multiple proportions with CO and CO₂.
formulas: $$\%\text{element}=\frac{\text{mass of element in one mole}}{\text{molar mass}}\times100;\qquad \text{H:O in water}=1:8$$
universalFacts: Proust's law was contested by Berthollet until careful analysis of artificial and natural carbonates settled it.
CuO is always 79.9% copper by mass, whatever its origin.
The 1 : 8 hydrogen–oxygen mass ratio reappears in every electrolysis and combustion calculation.
examples: **Problem:** 1.0 g of a metal oxide contains 0.72 g of metal. If the metal's equivalent behaviour repeats, find the % oxygen. **Solution:** O = 0.28 g → 28% oxygen — a fixed composition the law predicts for this oxide.
importantNotes: Say 'proportion *by mass*' — volume ratios belong to Gay-Lussac's law.
Always name the source-independence (natural or synthetic) when stating the law.

Law of Conservation of Mass (Lavoisier): Total mass of reactants equals total mass of products in a chemical reaction.
Law of Definite Proportions (Proust): A pure compound always contains the same elements in fixed proportion by mass.
Law of Multiple Proportions (Dalton): When two elements form more than one compound, masses of one element combining with fixed mass of other are in simple whole-number ratios.

Gay-Lussac's Law of Gaseous Volumes: Gases react in simple whole-number volume ratios at same temperature and pressure.
Avogadro's Law: Equal volumes of all gases at same temperature and pressure contain equal number of molecules.

data.title: Laws of Stoichiometry
notes: ### 1. Meaning

Stoichiometry is the study of the quantitative relations between the amounts of reactants and products in a chemical reaction, derived from the balance of atoms. The **laws of chemical combination** (laws of stoichiometry) are the experimental generalisations on which those calculations rest: conservation of mass, definite proportions, multiple proportions, reciprocal proportions and gaseous volumes (with Avogadro's law completing the set).
### 2. Law of conservation of mass (Lavoisier, 1774)

In a chemical reaction matter is neither created nor destroyed: the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products. Verified by Landolt in sealed tubes (and by many reactions, e.g. AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO₃). It follows from atoms being merely rearranged; gases, precipitates and the mass of the container must all be accounted for. This law is the reason every chemical equation must be balanced.
### 3. Law of definite (constant) proportions (Proust, 1799)

A given chemical compound always contains the same elements combined in the same fixed ratio by mass, no matter how it was prepared, its source or its purity. Water obtained from any source has H : O = 1 : 8 by mass; CO₂ always has C : O = 3 : 8. It is a consequence of a fixed number of atoms in the formula unit.
### 4. Law of multiple proportions (Dalton, 1803)

If two elements combine to form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in the ratio of small whole numbers. Examples: CO and CO₂ (fixed 12 g C combines with 16 g and 32 g O → 1 : 2); H₂O and H₂O₂ (fixed 2 g H with 16 g and 32 g O → 1 : 2); NO, N₂O, NO₂, N₂O₅ with a fixed mass of N give oxygen masses in 1 : 2 : 4 : 5. This law gave the strongest support for the atomic theory.
### 5. Law of reciprocal (equivalent) proportions (Richter, 1792)

The masses of two elements that combine separately with a fixed mass of a third element are in a simple ratio to the masses in which they combine with each other. Example with hydrogen as the reference: H : O = 1 : 8 in water and H : C = 1 : 3 in methane; therefore in carbon dioxide C : O = 3 : 8, exactly the simple ratio predicted — the law that led to the concept of equivalent mass.
### 6. Law of gaseous volumes (Gay-Lussac, 1809)

When gases react, they do so in volumes that bear a simple whole-number ratio to one another and to the volumes of gaseous products, at the same temperature and pressure: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl (1 : 1 : 2); N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ (1 : 3 : 2). This law inspired Avogadro's hypothesis — equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules — and is used for all volume–volume stoichiometry.
### 7. Meaning and applications

The laws convert qualitative chemistry into arithmetic: balancing equations (conservation of mass and atoms), finding percentage composition (definite proportions), deciding formulas of oxides and hydrides (multiple and reciprocal proportions), and performing gas-volume calculations in reactions (gaseous volumes with Avogadro's law). Practical uses: industrial material balances for ammonia, sulphuric acid and cement plants, analysis of ores and alloys, calculation of reactant quantities and costs, fuel combustion and pollution control, and every titration or gravimetric analysis performed in a laboratory.
### 8. Limitations
• The law of conservation of mass fails in nuclear reactions, where a small mass defect appears as energy (E = mc²); even chemically it needs all gaseous products to be captured.

• The law of definite proportions does not hold for non-stoichiometric (berthollide) compounds such as Fe₀.₉₃O or the iron sulphides, where composition varies within a range; isotopic substitution (D₂O vs H₂O) also changes the mass ratio.
• These laws apply to pure compounds and chemical reactions, never to mixtures, solutions or alloys, whose composition can be varied continuously.
• The law of multiple proportions requires very accurate analysis — small errors in percentage composition hide or create apparent ratios; it is a description, not an explanation of atomic structure.

• Reciprocal proportions and gaseous-volume laws demand accurate measurement; the volume law is strictly valid only for gases behaving ideally at the same T and P, and it fails for dissociating or associating vapours (PCl₅, NH₄Cl).
• None of the laws says anything about reaction rate, mechanism, equilibrium or side reactions — they give only the mass/volume bookkeeping of a completed reaction.
confusion: ❌ The laws of stoichiometry explain why reactions occur. ✅ They describe the quantitative relationships; the reason lies in atomic structure and bonding.
❌ Definite proportions holds for every compound. ✅ Non-stoichiometric compounds (Fe₀.₉₃O, FeS₁₊ₓ) violate it, and isotopic variants change the mass ratio.

❌ Multiple proportions and reciprocal proportions are the same law. ✅ Multiple proportions compares two compounds of the same two elements; reciprocal proportions compares two compounds sharing a third element.
❌ Gay-Lussac's volume law needs no conditions. ✅ Volumes must be measured at the same temperature and pressure, and the gases must behave ideally.
❌ Conservation of mass means mass is always conserved everywhere. ✅ It holds for chemical reactions but not for nuclear reactions (mass–energy equivalence).

$$\text{Gaseous volumes: }\frac{V_{1}}{n_{1}}=\frac{V_{2}}{n_{2}}\ \text{(same }T,P\text{)},\quad 2H_{2}+O_{2}\rightarrow2H_{2}O\ (2:1:2)$$
$$\%\text{element}=\frac{n\times A_{\text{element}}}{M_{\text{compound}}}\times100$$
universalFacts: Lavoisier (1774) established conservation of mass; Proust (1799) definite proportions; Dalton (1803) multiple proportions; Richter (1792) reciprocal proportions; Gay-Lussac (1809) gaseous volumes.
CO₂ always contains 27.3% carbon and 72.7% oxygen by mass, whatever its source.
Beryllium oxide, BeO, obeys the law of definite proportions, while iron(II) oxide Fe₁₋ₓO does not.
examples: **Problem:** Two oxides of nitrogen contain 46.7% and 30.4% oxygen. Show that the data obey the law of multiple proportions. **Solution:** with a fixed mass of nitrogen (53.3 g and 69.6 g nitrogen per unit), the oxygen masses are 46.7 and 30.4 → ratio 46.7/30.4 ≈ 1.54 ≈ 3 : 2, a simple whole-number ratio (these correspond to NO₂ and NO type oxides).

**Problem:** 10 mL of a hydrocarbon burns in 50 mL of oxygen to give 30 mL CO₂ and 40 mL H₂O vapour (same conditions). Find its formula. **Solution:** volume ratio = mole ratio → C : H = 30 : 80 → 3 : 8, hence C₃H₈; the result is obtained purely from the law of gaseous volumes.
importantNotes: In long answers, pair each law with the name and year: Lavoisier 1774, Proust 1799, Dalton 1803, Richter 1792, Gay-Lussac 1809.
Always mention that the volume law requires the same T and P and that the laws are idealisations with the stated exceptions.
For 'limitations' questions, quote at least one counter-example: non-stoichiometric Fe₀.₉₃O and nuclear mass defect.

data.title: Avogadro's Law and its Deductions (Molecular Mass, Vapour Density, Volume and Number of Particles)
data.topicTitle: Avogadro's law and some deductions: molecular mass and vapour density, molecular mass and volume of gas, molecular mass and number of particles
notes: ### 1. Meaning and statement

Avogadro's law (Amedeo Avogadro, 1811, published as a hypothesis) states: equal volumes of all gases, under the same conditions of temperature and pressure, contain equal numbers of molecules. Hence for a gas $V\propto n$ at constant T and P, and volume ratio = mole ratio. One mole of any gas contains the Avogadro number N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ molecules and occupies a molar volume of 22.4 dm³ (22.4 L) at STP (273.15 K, 1 atm) or ≈24 L at RTP. The law resolved the confusion between atoms and molecules that had blocked Dalton's theory and Gay-Lussac's volume results.
### 2. Deduction 1 — molecular mass and vapour density

**Vapour density (VD)** of a gas is the ratio of the mass of a certain volume of the gas to the mass of the same volume of hydrogen under identical conditions. Because equal volumes contain equal numbers of molecules, masses are in the ratio of molecular masses, and with hydrogen as the standard (M = 2): $VD=\frac{M}{2}$, so **molecular mass = 2 × vapour density**. Example: VD of CO₂ = 22 → M = 44 g mol⁻¹. (With air as reference, M = 28.94 × relative density.)
### 3. Deduction 2 — molecular mass and volume of gas

Since 1 mol of any gas occupies 22.4 L at STP, the mass of 22.4 L of a gas at STP equals its molar mass in grams. Hence $n=\frac{V\ (\text{at STP})}{22.4\ \text{L mol}^{-1}}$ and $M=\frac{\text{mass of the gas}}{\text{volume at STP}}\times22.4$. Conversely, the volume occupied by a known mass m is $V=\frac{m}{M}\times22.4$ L at STP. This is the basis of all gas-volume stoichiometry.
### 4. Deduction 3 — molecular mass and number of particles

One mole contains N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ particles, so $n=\frac{N}{N_{A}}$, the mass of one molecule $=\frac{M}{N_{A}}$ (e.g. 3.0 × 10⁻²³ g for water), and the volume of one molecule follows from the molar volume. Gram-molecular mass is the mass in grams numerically equal to the molecular mass, and it always contains 6.022 × 10²³ molecules (gram-atomic mass contains the same number of atoms).
### 5. Applications

• **Atomicity of gases:** comparing volumes of a gas with the volumes of its elements (e.g. 2 volumes H₂ + 1 volume O₂ → 2 volumes H₂O vapour) shows that H₂, O₂ and N₂ are diatomic while O₃ and P₄ are polyatomic.
• **Molecular mass of gases and volatile liquids:** by vapour density (M = 2 × VD) or by Victor Meyer's and Dumas' methods, and by the limiting-density/effusion methods.
• **Molar-volume stoichiometry:** volume–volume and mass–volume calculations for gases at STP; determination of the molar volume of a gas and of Avogadro's constant.
• **Establishing formulas:** Avogadro's law plus Gay-Lussac's volume law fixed the formulas H₂O, NH₃, CO₂ and HCl (which Dalton's theory alone could not).
### 6. Limitations
• Avogadro's law applies to **gases only** — it says nothing about the volume of liquids or solids, whose molar volumes differ greatly.

• It assumes ideal behaviour; real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature, so the simple 22.4 L molar volume is approximate except near STP (for NH₃ or CO₂ it can be in error by a few per cent).

• It fails for gases that **dissociate or associate** in the vapour state: PCl₅, N₂O₄ and NH₄Cl give anomalously high or low vapour densities, and a correction factor (degree of dissociation/association) is needed.
• It provides no information about the size, shape or mass of individual molecules; 'equal numbers of molecules' says nothing about molecular structure.

• The law was ignored for nearly half a century because Berzelius and Dalton did not accept the atom–molecule distinction — a reminder that it depends on the concept of a molecule, not merely on measurement.
• The molar volume figures are defined at specified T and P (22.4 L at STP, 24 L at RTP), so results must always state the conditions.

data.title: Law of Multiple Proportions — Dalton's Law with Worked Data
notes: ### Focus of this tab
Dalton's own law: the full statement, the standard data sets (CO/CO₂, H₂O/H₂O₂, nitrogen oxides) and the method of showing whole-number ratios — the NEB calculation pattern.
### Statement and history

'When two elements combine to form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in the ratio of small whole numbers.' Proposed by John Dalton (1803) — in fact the law is the strongest historical evidence for his atomic theory, since whole-number ratios are what whole atoms give.
### Standard data sets
• **Carbon oxides:** in CO, 12 g C combines with 16 g O; in CO₂, 12 g C with 32 g O. Fixed carbon → oxygen ratio 16 : 32 = 1 : 2.
• **Hydrogen oxides:** H₂O (2 g H : 16 g O) and H₂O₂ (2 g H : 32 g O) → 1 : 2.
• **Sulphur oxides:** SO₂ (32 g S : 32 g O) and SO₃ (32 g S : 48 g O) → 2 : 3.
• **Nitrogen oxides:** N₂O, NO, N₂O₃, NO₂, N₂O₅ — with a fixed mass of nitrogen, oxygen masses stand in 1 : 2 : 3 : 4 : 5.
• **Iron chlorides:** FeCl₂ and FeCl₃ — chlorine ratio 2 : 3 for fixed iron.
### The calculation method (do it in this order)

(1) Choose a fixed mass of one element (usually 1 g or the atomic mass). (2) Compute the mass of the other element combined with that fixed mass in each compound (divide/multiply proportionally). (3) Divide the masses by the smallest to get the simple ratio; multiply up if fractions appear.
### Why it works and where it stops

Atoms combine as whole units: one C with one or two O atoms — hence 1 : 2. The law needs accurate analysis (small errors destroy the whole-number pattern), applies to *pure* compounds of the same two elements, and says nothing about structure or bonding.
confusion: ❌ The law compares masses of both elements. ✅ One element's mass is held fixed; the other's varies in whole-number ratios.
❌ CO and CO₂ show definite proportions. ✅ Each compound separately follows definite proportions; the *pair* demonstrates multiple proportions.
❌ Any ratio qualifies as 'small whole number'. ✅ It must be genuinely integral (1 : 2, 2 : 3); 1 : 1.49 signals analytical error.
practice: State the law of multiple proportions and verify it with CO and CO₂ data.
Two oxides of a metal contain 50% and 40% oxygen. Show that the data obey the law.
Explain how the law supports Dalton's atomic theory.
Why does the law fail for non-stoichiometric compounds?
formulas: $$\frac{m_{O}\ (\text{in oxide 2})}{m_{O}\ (\text{in oxide 1})}=\frac{\text{simple integer}}{1}\ (\text{fixed mass of the other element})$$
universalFacts: The law was published in Dalton's 'New System of Chemical Philosophy' (1808).
Nitrogen's five oxides give the textbook 1 : 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 ladder.
The law historically convinced chemists that atoms combine in whole numbers.
examples: **Problem:** Two oxides of metal M contain 50% and 40% oxygen respectively. Show multiple proportions. **Solution:** per 100 g: oxide 1 has 50 g M : 50 g O → per 1 g M, 1 g O; oxide 2 has 60 g M : 40 g O → per 1 g M, 0.667 g O. Ratio of oxygen masses = 1 : 0.667 = 3 : 2 — a simple whole-number ratio.
importantNotes: Fix the mass of one element before comparing — the most common methodological mark.
Present the final ratio in smallest whole numbers (3 : 2, not 1.5 : 1).

data.title: Law of Reciprocal (Equivalent) Proportions — Richter's Law
notes: ### Focus of this tab
The law of reciprocal proportions (Richter, 1792; also called the law of equivalent proportions) — statement, the reference-element method, worked verification and its link to equivalent masses.
### Statement

'The masses of two elements which combine separately with a fixed mass of a third element are either the same as, or simple multiples of, the masses in which they combine with each other.' It is the law that connects compounds sharing a common third element.
### The standard verification (H as reference)
• Water H₂O: H : O = 1 : 8.
• Methane CH₄: H : C = 1 : 3, i.e. C : H = 3 : 1 — 3 g C combines with 1 g H.
• Carbon dioxide CO₂: C : O = 12 : 32 = 3 : 8.
Check: with a fixed mass of H (1 g), the masses of C and O that combine are 3 g and 8 g. The ratio C : O = 3 : 8 — exactly the ratio in which C and O combine in CO₂. The law is verified.
### Second pattern (oxygen as reference)

In SO₂, S : O = 32 : 32 = 1 : 1; in H₂O, H : O = 1 : 8. With a fixed mass of O (say 8 g), H = 1 g and S = 8 g combine. In H₂S the actual ratio is H : S = 1 : 16 = 1 : 16, which is a simple multiple (×2) of the predicted 8 : 1 → the law holds in 'simple multiple' form.
### Connection to equivalent masses

The 'masses combining with a fixed mass of the reference element' are precisely the **equivalent masses** (H = 1.008, O = 8, C = 3 when valency 4 is chosen...). The law is the logical basis of the equivalent-mass concept and of the classical method of determining equivalent masses by analysis.
### Limitations

It applies to pure compounds and exact analyses; like multiple proportions it fails for berthollides; and it requires the three elements actually to form the relevant binary compounds (e.g. some noble gases form none). It is also the hardest of the laws to verify experimentally because the data must be very accurate.
confusion: ❌ This law compares two compounds of the same two elements. ✅ That is multiple proportions; reciprocal proportions links three elements through two compounds.
❌ The ratio must be identical. ✅ It may be the same or a *simple multiple* — the 'simple multiple' clause is part of the statement.
❌ The reference element must be hydrogen. ✅ Any common third element works; hydrogen and oxygen are just the textbook choices.
practice: State the law of reciprocal proportions and verify it with H₂O, CH₄ and CO₂.
How is the law related to the concept of equivalent mass?
Verify the law using H₂O, SO₂ and H₂S.
State the limitations of the law of reciprocal proportions.
formulas: $$\frac{m_{C}\ (\text{with fixed H})}{m_{O}\ (\text{with fixed H})}=\frac{m_{C}}{m_{O}}\ (\text{in }CO_{2})\quad\text{or a simple multiple}$$
$$\text{equivalent mass}=\frac{\text{atomic mass}}{\text{valency}}$$
universalFacts: Richter published the law in 1792 — before Dalton's atomic theory (1803).
Equivalent masses derived from this law underpin the classical titration and electrochemical (Faraday) calculations.
The law is also called the law of equivalent proportions for this reason.
examples: **Problem:** Given C : H = 3 : 1 in CH₄ and H : O = 1 : 8 in H₂O, predict C : O in carbon's oxide. **Solution:** fix H = 1 g → C = 3 g, O = 8 g → predicted C : O = 3 : 8. Experiment gives 3 : 8 in CO₂ — verified (and 3 : 4 would be a simple multiple form, as in CO).
importantNotes: Keep the three compounds clearly identified: two with the reference element, one with the pair being compared.
Remember the 'simple multiple' clause — verification need not be equality.

data.title: Mole and its Relation with Mass, Volume and Number of Particles
data.topicTitle: Mole and its relation with mass, volume and number of particles
notes: ### 1. Meaning of the mole

A mole is the SI unit of amount of substance. It is the amount of substance that contains exactly the same number of elementary entities (atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, formula units) as there are atoms in 12 g of carbon-12, that is **6.022 × 10²³** entities — the Avogadro number N_A. The mole is simply a counting unit, like 'dozen' or 'score', but on a scale suited to atoms and molecules: it links the invisible particle world with weighable masses.
### 2. Relation with mass

$n=\frac{m}{M}$, where m is the mass in grams and M the molar mass (g mol⁻¹). Molar mass = relative atomic/molecular mass expressed in g mol⁻¹: 1 atom of carbon has a mass of 12 u (1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 1/12 the mass of one ¹²C atom), while 1 mole of carbon atoms has a mass of 12 g. Gram-atomic mass and gram-molecular mass are the mass of one mole of atoms and of molecules respectively. Example: 44 g of CO₂ = 1 mol = 6.022 × 10²³ molecules.
### 3. Relation with number of particles

$n=\frac{N}{N_{A}}$; N = n × N_A. The number of *atoms* must be counted with care: 1 mol of H₂SO₄ contains 2 mol H atoms, 1 mol S, 4 mol O (7 mol of atoms in total, 6.022 × 10²³ H₂SO₄ molecules), while 1 mol of H₂ contains 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ atoms. Ions, electrons and formula units can also be counted in moles (1 mol of NaCl gives 1 mol Na⁺ + 1 mol Cl⁻).
### 4. Relation with volume (gases)

For gases the mole relates to volume through Avogadro's law: 1 mol of any gas at STP (273.15 K, 1 atm) occupies 22.4 L, so $n=\frac{V\ (\text{at STP})}{22.4}$; at RTP (25 °C, 1 bar) the molar volume is ≈24.0 L. For any other conditions the ideal gas equation is used: $n=\frac{PV}{RT}$. Concentration extends the idea to solutions: $n=M_{\text{conc}}\times V_{\text{L}}$ (molarity × volume in litres).
### 5. Applications
• Core of every stoichiometric calculation: converting masses, gas volumes and numbers of particles into moles and back, so that the mole ratio of a balanced equation can be applied.
• Determination of relative atomic and molecular masses, molar volumes, vapour densities and Avogadro's constant; standardisation of solutions and titrations.

• Industry and pharmacy: calculating exact reactant quantities and costs for ammonia, sulphuric acid, cement or drug manufacture; agriculture: fertiliser dosage; environment: calculating CO₂ (44 g mol⁻¹) and pollutant emissions per tonne of fuel; medicine: expressing doses and concentrations in moles.
### 6. Limitations
• The mole counts *specified entities*: '1 mol of oxygen' is ambiguous (O atoms or O₂ molecules?), so the entity must always be named; the mole is meaningless without it.
• Since the 2019 SI revision N_A is a defined number (6.02214076 × 10²³) rather than being tied to 12 g of ¹²C, so the earlier 'gram-atom' style definitions are outdated.

• Molar masses are based on **standard atomic weights**, which are average values for the natural isotopic composition and therefore carry an uncertainty (and vary slightly for elements such as boron, lithium and lead whose isotopic abundances differ with source). Exact work needs isotope-specific molar masses.

• The relation n = V/22.4 L holds only for gases at STP that behave ideally; for real gases and for other conditions PV = nRT must be used, and for associating gases the particle count differs from the formula count.

• The mole expresses *amount*, not concentration — molarity, molality and mole fraction are different measures; molarity in particular is temperature-dependent because volume changes with temperature.
• Mole-based stoichiometry cannot predict how fast a reaction goes, in which direction it proceeds, or what yield it gives; those come from kinetics, thermodynamics and equilibrium.
**Fact.** 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ entities (Avogadro constant, Nₐ). Molar mass (M) is g·mol⁻¹; for a compound M = Σ(atomic masses).
**Fact.** n (mol) = mass/M = volume(ideal gas, STP)/22.4 L = N/Nₐ.
**Fact.** Limiting reactant is the one consumed first; % yield = (experimental/theoretical)×100.
confusion: ❌ One mole of oxygen means 6.022 × 10²³ oxygen atoms always. ✅ It depends on the entity: 1 mol O atoms = 16 g, but 1 mol O₂ molecules = 32 g and contains 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ atoms.
❌ Molar mass and molecular mass are the same thing. ✅ Molecular mass is a relative number in u; molar mass is the mass of one mole in g mol⁻¹ (numerically equal for most purposes).
❌ One mole of a gas always occupies 22.4 L. ✅ Only at STP and only for an ideal gas.
❌ The mole is a mass unit. ✅ It is the SI unit of *amount of substance*; it is converted to mass through the molar mass.
❌ Avogadro's number can be measured to any precision. ✅ It is now a defined constant exactly equal to 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

data.title: Calculations Based on Mole Concept
notes: Mole Concept Foundation: One mole contains exactly 6.022 × 10²³ entities (Avogadro's number Nₐ). The molar mass M (g/mol) of any substance equals its atomic or molecular mass numerically. This bridges the microscopic (atoms/molecules) and macroscopic (grams) worlds.

Mass-to-Moles Conversion: n = m/M where n = moles, m = mass in grams, M = molar mass in g/mol. Example: 36 g water (M = 18 g/mol) → n = 36/18 = 2 mol. This is the most fundamental stoichiometric calculation.
Moles-to-Particles Conversion: Number of particles N = n × Nₐ. Example: 0.5 mol CO₂ contains 0.5 × 6.022×10²³ = 3.011×10²³ molecules. Reverse: n = N/Nₐ when given particle count.

Molar Volume at STP: One mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 L at STP (0°C, 1 atm). n = V/22.4 for gases at STP. Example: 5.6 L O₂ at STP → n = 5.6/22.4 = 0.25 mol. Non-STP conditions require PV = nRT.

Percentage Composition: % of element = (mass of element in 1 mol compound / molar mass of compound) × 100. Example: In H₂O, %H = (2×1.008/18.015)×100 = 11.19%, %O = (16.00/18.015)×100 = 88.81%. Used to determine empirical formulas from experimental data.

Empirical Formula Determination: Step 1: Convert % composition to grams (assume 100 g sample). Step 2: Convert grams to moles for each element. Step 3: Divide all mole values by smallest mole value. Step 4: Multiply by integer if ratios are not whole numbers. Result gives simplest whole-number ratio of atoms.

Molecular Formula from Empirical: Molecular formula = (empirical formula)ₙ where n = molecular mass / empirical formula mass. Example: Empirical CH₂O (mass 30), molecular mass 180 → n = 180/30 = 6 → molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose).

Stoichiometric Calculations from Balanced Equations: Coefficients give mole ratios. For 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O: 2 mol H₂ reacts with 1 mol O₂ to produce 2 mol H₂O. Convert given quantity to moles → use ratio → convert back to desired units.

Mass-Mass Stoichiometry: Given mass of reactant A, find mass of product B. Steps: mass A → moles A (÷M_A) → moles B (×ratio) → mass B (×M_B). Example: How much CO₂ from 100 g CaCO₃? CaCO₃→CaO+CO₂. n(CaCO₃)=100/100=1 mol → n(CO₂)=1 mol → m=44 g.
Mass-Volume Stoichiometry (Gases): For reactions involving gases, use molar volume. Example: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. From 6.5 g Zn (0.1 mol), H₂ produced = 0.1 mol = 0.1×22.4 = 2.24 L at STP.

Solution Stoichiometry: Molarity M = n/V(L). n = M × V. Use in titration calculations: M₁V₁/n₁ = M₂V₂/n₂ where n₁,n₂ are coefficients. Example: 25 mL 0.1M NaOH neutralizes how many mL of 0.05M H₂SO₄? Ratio 2:1 → V = (0.1×25×1)/(0.05×2) = 25 mL.

Limiting Reagent Identification: Calculate moles of each reactant. Divide by coefficient in balanced equation. Smallest value identifies limiting reagent. All product calculations based on limiting reagent only. Excess reagent remains partially unreacted.

Theoretical Yield Calculation: Maximum possible product based on limiting reagent and stoichiometry. Actual yield is always less due to incomplete reactions, side reactions, and losses during purification.

Percentage Yield: % yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100. Industrial processes aim for >90%. Low yields indicate inefficiency, side reactions, or equilibrium limitations. NEB frequently asks numerical problems combining limiting reagent and % yield.

Percentage Purity: % purity = (mass of pure substance / mass of impure sample) × 100. Impure samples require correction before stoichiometric calculations. Example: 80% pure limestone means only 80 g CaCO₃ per 100 g sample participates in reaction.

data.title: Limiting Reactant and Excess Reactant
notes: ### 1. Meaning

The **limiting reactant (limiting reagent)** is the reactant completely consumed in a reaction, and it therefore determines the maximum amount of product that can form (the theoretical yield). The other reactant, part of which is left over when the reaction stops, is the **excess reactant**. The idea is needed whenever the reactants are not mixed in exactly the stoichiometric ratio of the balanced equation.
### 2. How to identify the limiting reactant

Method 1 (standard): convert the given masses/volumes of all reactants into moles, divide each by its stoichiometric coefficient, and the smallest quotient identifies the limiting reactant. Method 2: compare the moles *required* (from the mole ratio) with the moles *available*; the reactant for which the requirement exceeds the supply is limiting.
### 3. Worked example — ammonia synthesis

N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. With 2 mol N₂ and 3 mol H₂: for N₂ the quotient is 2/1 = 2, for H₂ it is 3/3 = 1 → **H₂ is limiting**. Hydrogen needs only 1 mol N₂, so 1 mol N₂ stays unused (excess), and NH₃ formed = (2/3) × 3 = 2 mol = 34 g.
### 4. Worked example — combustion (mass basis)

CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, with 8 g CH₄ (0.5 mol) and 24 g O₂ (0.75 mol): quotients 0.5 for CH₄ and 0.75/2 = 0.375 for O₂ → **O₂ is limiting**. It consumes 0.375 mol CH₄, so 0.125 mol CH₄ (2 g) remains excess and 0.375 mol CO₂ (16.5 g) is formed.
### 5. Applications

• Laboratory and industry: fixing reactant quantities for a target product mass, material balances in the Haber process, contact process and lime kiln, and choosing which reactant to use in excess on the basis of cost, hazards and equilibrium considerations.
• Combustion engineering: excess air is supplied to burn fuel completely (avoiding CO and soot), while excessive excess air wastes heat and promotes NOₓ formation.

• Pharmaceutical and fine-chemical synthesis: the cheaper or more easily handled reagent is taken in excess to drive the expensive intermediate to completion, and by-product amounts are predicted from the limiting reagent.
• Analytical and environmental work: computing the maximum pollutant that can be produced, and in titrations, where the equivalence point marks the stoichiometric balance of acid and base.
### 6. Meaning of 'extent of reaction'

The limiting reactant fixes how far the reaction can proceed: while it remains, the reaction continues; once it is consumed, a simple irreversible reaction stops. This is why the theoretical yield is always calculated from the limiting reactant, and why excess reactant is added deliberately in practice.
### 7. Limitations

• The concept requires a known single reaction with fixed stoichiometry; with side reactions, reversibility or equilibrium the idea must be replaced by the equilibrium constant, conversion and selectivity.
• Comparison must be made in **moles**; comparing masses directly (5 g H₂ with 5 g O₂) leads to wrong conclusions.

• In a kinetically controlled reaction the slowest step may govern the rate even though the reagent is stoichiometrically in excess — the limiting reagent is not automatically the rate-determining species.
• When a reactant acts as the solvent or medium (water, large excess of acid), the concept loses meaning.
• The yield computed from the limiting reactant is an upper limit only; actual yields are lower because of incomplete reaction, side products and handling losses.
Theoretical yield is always calculated from the limiting reactant, never from the excess reactant.
Percentage yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100; actual yield is always less than theoretical.
In industrial processes, the cheaper reactant is usually taken in excess to maximize conversion of the expensive reactant.
confusion: ❌ The reactant present in the smallest mass is limiting. ✅ The limiting reactant is found in *moles* divided by the stoichiometric coefficient, not by mass.
❌ The limiting reactant is the one that runs out last. ✅ It is used up first and stops the reaction; the other reactant is in excess.
❌ Excess reactant also becomes product. ✅ Only the consumed part reacts; the remainder is unreacted excess.
❌ Every reaction has a limiting reactant. ✅ Only when the reactants are not in the exact stoichiometric mole ratio.
❌ Limiting-reactant reasoning gives the actual yield of a reversible reaction. ✅ It gives the maximum possible yield; the equilibrium position decides the actual extent.
❌ Assume 100% yield in calculations → ✅ Theoretical yield is the maximum possible; actual yield accounts for losses and incomplete reactions.

data.title: Verifying Whole-Number Ratios from Experimental Data
notes: ### Focus of this tab

The computational skill behind all the combination laws: converting raw percentage/mass data into whole-number ratios — the shared method of definite, multiple and reciprocal proportions, and of empirical-formula work.
### The standard five-step method

(1) Take the percentage of each element as mass in 100 g (or use the given masses). (2) Divide each mass by the atomic mass of that element → moles. (3) Divide all values by the smallest. (4) If the ratios are still fractional (e.g. 1 : 1.5, 1 : 1.33, 1 : 1.67), multiply the whole set by 2, 3 or 4 respectively to clear fractions. (5) Interpret: the whole-number ratio is the atomic ratio in the compound.
### Worked pattern 1 — a binary oxide

An oxide contains 60% metal and 40% oxygen (atomic mass of metal = 48). Metal = 60/48 = 1.25; O = 40/16 = 2.5. Divide by 1.25 → M : O = 1 : 2 → formula MO₂. (With 70% metal it would be 1.46 : 1.875 → 1 : 1.28… → careful: re-check data, since real ratios must resolve.)
### Worked pattern 2 — two oxides checked against multiple proportions

Oxide A: 46.7% N; oxide B: 30.4% N. Per gram of nitrogen: A has 46.7/53.3 = 0.876 g O; B has 30.4/69.6 = 0.437 g O. Ratio 0.876 : 0.437 = 2 : 1 — a whole-number ratio, so the data obey the law of multiple proportions (NO₂-type and NO-type oxides).
### Recognising the intended multiplier
### Error awareness (limitations of the method)

Real analytical data carry errors, so ratios like 1 : 1.48 may 'want' to be 1 : 1.5 while 1 : 1.35 may be measurement noise around 1 : 1.33. Judgement (and significant figures) decide; non-stoichiometric compounds (Fe₀.₉₃O) will never resolve exactly, and the method assumes the compound is a true formula compound.
confusion: ❌ Any near-integer ratio may be rounded freely. ✅ Round only with analytical justification; 1 : 1.9 is not 1 : 2 in a berthollide.
❌ The ratio is of masses. ✅ After dividing by atomic masses, the ratio is of *atoms* (moles), not grams.
❌ Multiplying changes the formula. ✅ Scaling the whole ratio set preserves it (2 : 4 is the same as 1 : 2).

formulas: $$n=\frac{\%\text{ element}}{100\times A_{\text{element}}};\qquad \text{divide all by the smallest, then clear fractions}$$
universalFacts: This is exactly the arithmetic that produces empirical formulas from combustion data.
Cannizzaro used whole-number ratios of molecular weights to sort atomic masses in 1858.
The 'divide by smallest' step is the single most-omitted step in exam scripts.

importantNotes: Always divide by atomic masses before comparing — comparing raw masses is the classic wrong method.
State the multiplier used when clearing fractions (×2, ×3, ×4).

data.title: Theoretical Yield, Experimental Yield and Percentage Yield
data.topicTitle: Theoretical yield, experimental yield and % yield
notes: ### 1. Meaning of the three quantities

**Theoretical yield** is the maximum amount of product calculated from the balanced equation using the limiting reactant (assuming complete reaction and no losses). **Experimental (actual) yield** is the amount of pure product actually isolated in the experiment. **Percentage yield** compares them: $\%\text{yield}=\frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}}\times100$. Related terms: conversion (fraction of reactant consumed), selectivity (fraction converted to the desired product) and atom economy (mass of desired product ÷ mass of all reactants × 100).
### 2. Why the actual yield is lower than the theoretical yield
• The reaction is **incomplete** — the limiting reactant is not fully consumed in the time allowed.
• The reaction is **reversible**, so it stops at an equilibrium position (this is exactly the case in the Haber process).
• **Side reactions** produce by-products (organic syntheses especially).
• **Mechanical losses** during filtration, decantation, transfer, crystallisation, evaporation and drying, plus product remaining dissolved in the mother liquor (solubility loss).
• Product may be **volatile, thermally unstable or hygroscopic**, and impurities may interfere with the reaction.
• Weighing, reading and calculation errors of the experimenter.
A yield greater than 100% always indicates experimental error: the product is wet or impure, or unreacted starting material has been weighed as product.
### 3. Worked examples
**Example 1:** CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. From 100 g CaCO₃ the theoretical yield of CaO is 56 g; if 47.6 g is obtained, % yield = 47.6/56 × 100 = 85%.
**Example 2:** C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH. 7.0 g of ethene (0.25 mol) should give 0.25 mol = 11.5 g of ethanol; an actual yield of 9.2 g gives 80%.
**Example 3:** Aspirin synthesis: 5.0 g of salicylic acid (M = 138) gives a theoretical 6.5 g of aspirin (M = 180, 1:1 mole ratio); a student isolating 5.2 g reports (5.2/6.5) × 100 = 80%.
### 4. Meaning and use of atom economy

Percentage yield measures how much of the *intended* product is recovered, whereas atom economy measures how much of the *reactant mass* ends up in the desired product (substitution and elimination reactions with by-products have poor atom economy). Green chemistry prefers high atom economy because it minimises waste, an idea quantified by the E-factor (mass of waste ÷ mass of product). Both concepts are needed to judge whether a process is efficient and environmentally acceptable.
### 5. Applications

• Industrial economics: yield determines raw-material cost, plant capacity and profitability. In the Haber process only about 15% of the gas reacts per pass, so unreacted gas is recycled to raise the overall yield; the contact process similarly recycles SO₂.
• Laboratory synthesis (aspirin, soap, esters, dyes, polymers): the percentage yield is the standard measure of how successful a procedure was, and it is compared with literature values.
• Green chemistry: atom economy and the E-factor (waste ÷ product) supplement % yield to judge environmental performance — a high-yield reaction with a poor atom economy still generates much waste.

• Pharmaceutical and food quality control: yield data with assays (purity) are used for batch release, cost estimation and process optimisation, and yield losses indicate equipment or procedural faults.
### 6. Limitations
• Percentage yield does not measure **purity** — a 100% yield can be an impure or wet product; a separate assay (%, melting point, chromatography) is needed.
• The theoretical value is only as good as its assumptions: the correct limiting reactant, the correct balanced equation and a single principal reaction must all be established first.
• A value greater than 100% is always an error (impure/wet product, unreacted starting material, weighing mistake) and should never be reported as a good result.

• For reversible reactions the theoretical yield calculated from stoichiometry is not attainable at all; the equilibrium yield depends on K, temperature, pressure and recycling — the practical yield must be measured.

• Percentage yield says nothing about energy consumption, solvent use, hazards or waste, so it cannot by itself establish that a process is efficient or green; and it cannot be predicted theoretically — it must be determined experimentally.
confusion: ❌ A 100% yield means a pure product. ✅ Purity is a separate property; yields above 100% are the usual sign of an impure or wet product.
❌ Percentage yield is calculated from the reactant taken in excess. ✅ It is calculated from the limiting reactant, which fixes the theoretical yield.
❌ The theoretical yield is what you actually get. ✅ It is the maximum possible amount; the actual yield is always lower for practical reasons.
❌ Yield and atom economy measure the same thing. ✅ Yield is about recovery of product; atom economy is about how much of the reactant mass ends up in the desired product.
❌ Yield can be predicted by stoichiometry alone. ✅ Stoichiometry gives only the theoretical maximum; the actual yield depends on kinetics, equilibrium and technique.

$$\text{atom economy}=\frac{M_{\text{desired product}}}{\sum M_{\text{all reactants}}}\times100,\qquad \%\text{purity}=\frac{\text{mass of pure substance}}{\text{total mass of sample}}\times100$$
