A flywheel spinning at 300 RPM accelerates uniformly to 900 RPM in 10 seconds. Find the angular acceleration and total angular displacement. Solution: $\omega_0 = 300 \times 2\pi/60 = 10\pi$ rad/s, $\omega = 900 \times 2\pi/60 = 30\pi$ rad/s. $\alpha = (30\pi - 10\pi)/10 = 2\pi$ rad/s$^2$. $\theta = \omega_0 t + \frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2 = 10\pi \times 10 + \frac{1}{2} \times 2\pi \times 100 = 100\pi + 100\pi = 200\pi$ rad $\approx 628$ rad.

A wheel of radius 0.5 m rotates with $\omega = 10$ rad/s and $\alpha = 4$ rad/s$^2$. Find the tangential speed, centripetal acceleration, and tangential acceleration. Solution: $v = r\omega = 0.5 \times 10 = 5$ m/s. $a_c = r\omega^2 = 0.5 \times 100 = 50$ m/s$^2$. $a_t = r\alpha = 0.5 \times 4 = 2$ m/s$^2$.
The period of a rotating fan is 0.25 s. Find its angular velocity and frequency. Solution: $\omega = 2\pi/T = 2\pi/0.25 = 8\pi \approx 25.13$ rad/s. $f = 1/T = 4$ Hz.

A disc starts from rest and reaches 1200 RPM in 4 s with uniform angular acceleration. Find $\alpha$ and the number of revolutions. Solution: $\omega = 1200 \times 2\pi/60 = 40\pi$ rad/s. $\alpha = 40\pi/4 = 10\pi$ rad/s$^2$. $\theta = \frac{1}{2} \times 10\pi \times 16 = 80\pi$ rad $= 40$ revolutions.
A point on a rim is at radius 0.3 m from the axis. After rotating through $6\pi$ radians, how far has this point traveled? Solution: $s = r\theta = 0.3 \times 6\pi = 1.8\pi \approx 5.65$ m.
universalFacts: Angular velocity is a vector along the axis of rotation — its direction is given by the right-hand rule.
The kinematic equations for constant angular acceleration are identical in form to those for linear motion.
v = rω links linear speed to angular speed — this is why the outside of a rotating disc moves faster than the inside.
Angular acceleration is caused by torque (rotational analogue of force): τ = Iα, where I is the moment of inertia.
The number of revolutions is θ/(2π) — always divide angular displacement in radians by 2π to get revolutions.
The radian is the natural unit for angular measurements in physics because it directly relates arc length to radius: $s = r\theta$. Using degrees in formulas would introduce extra conversion factors.
Angular velocity is a vector directed along the rotation axis by the right-hand rule. Two gears meshing in opposite directions have angular velocities of opposite signs.
In uniform circular motion, angular velocity is constant ($\alpha = 0$) but the object still has centripetal acceleration because the direction of velocity continuously changes.
The period $T$ and frequency $f$ are inversely related: $f = 1/T$. The SI unit of frequency is the hertz (Hz), where $1\,\text{Hz} = 1\,\text{s}^{-1}$.
Rotational kinematic equations have exact analogs to translational kinematics: replace $x$ with $\theta$, $v$ with $\omega$, and $a$ with $\alpha$.

data.title: Centripetal Acceleration and Force
notes: **Centripetal acceleration (a_c):** the acceleration directed toward the centre of a circular path that keeps a body moving in a circle. Magnitude: a_c = v²/r = rω². Direction: always toward the centre (hence 'centripetal' = 'centre-seeking'). It changes the direction of velocity, not its magnitude.

**Centripetal force (F_c):** the net force required to produce centripetal acceleration: F_c = mv²/r = mrω². It is NOT a new force — it is the RESULTANT of real forces (tension, gravity, friction, normal) pointing toward the centre.

**Why centripetal force is not a separate force:** the centripetal force is always provided by one or more real forces. For a car turning on a flat road, friction provides F_c. For a planet orbiting the Sun, gravity provides F_c. For a ball on a string, tension provides F_c.

**Derivation of a_c = v²/r:** consider a body moving at constant speed v in a circle of radius r. In a small time Δt, it moves from A to B. The change in velocity Δv points toward the centre. From similar triangles: Δv/v = Δs/r → Δv = vΔs/r. Acceleration a = Δv/Δt = v²/r (since Δs/Δt = v).

**Worked example — car turning:** a 1000 kg car turns a flat curve of radius 50 m at 20 m/s. Required friction: F_c = mv²/r = 1000 × 400/50 = 8000 N. If μ_s = 0.6, max friction = 0.6 × 1000 × 9.8 = 5880 N — the car skids (8000 > 5880).
**Worked example — ball on a string:** a 0.5 kg ball on a 1.5 m string rotates at 4 m/s. Tension = mv²/r = 0.5 × 16/1.5 = 5.33 N. If the string breaks at 10 N, max speed = √(10 × 1.5/0.5) = 5.48 m/s.

**Worked example — planet orbit:** Earth orbits the Sun at 30 km/s at a distance of 1.5 × 10¹¹ m. Centripetal acceleration = v²/r = (3×10⁴)²/(1.5×10¹¹) = 6 × 10⁻³ m/s². This is provided by the Sun's gravity.
**NEB exam focus:** calculating centripetal force/acceleration; identifying which real force provides F_c; maximum speed problems (string breaking, car skidding); linking v, ω, r, and a_c.

**Centripetal force is not a force — it is a role:** the term 'centripetal force' describes the NET force pointing toward the center. It is always provided by some real force or combination of forces: tension (string), gravity (planets), friction (car on road), normal force (banked road), magnetic force (charged particle). Always draw an FBD and identify WHICH real force plays this role.

**Centrifugal force in rotating frames:** in a reference frame attached to the rotating body (e.g., a car turning), passengers feel pushed outward. This is called centrifugal force. It is a pseudo-force — it arises from the inertia of the body wanting to move in a straight line. In an inertial (non-accelerating) frame, there is NO outward force — only the inward centripetal force.

**Derivation via vector diagram:** consider a particle moving at constant speed v around a circle of radius r. After a small time Δt, it moves through angle Δθ = vΔt/r. The velocity vectors change direction by Δθ. From the similar triangles formed by position vectors and velocity vectors: |Δv|/v = |Δr|/r = Δs/r = vΔt/r. Therefore a = |Δv|/Δt = v²/r.

**Worked example — satellite orbit:** a satellite orbits Earth at altitude 400 km (r = 6771 km) with speed 7.67 km/s. Centripetal acceleration: a_c = v²/r = (7670)²/6771000 = 8.69 m/s². This equals the local gravitational acceleration at that altitude, confirming that gravity provides the centripetal force.

**Common NEB trap — direction of acceleration:** students often confuse the direction of centripetal acceleration (toward center) with the direction of velocity (tangential). Remember: a_c changes the DIRECTION of v, not its magnitude. If speed is changing too, there is also a tangential component a_t.
confusion: ❌ 'Centrifugal force pulls the body outward.' ✅ Centrifugal force is a pseudo-force that appears only in a rotating reference frame. In an inertial frame, there is only centripetal force toward the centre.
❌ 'Centripetal force is a new type of force.' ✅ Centripetal force is the RESULTANT of real forces (tension, gravity, friction). It is not a separate force you add to the FBD.
❌ 'The body in circular motion is in equilibrium.' ✅ The body accelerates toward the centre (a_c = v²/r). It is NOT in equilibrium — the net force is mv²/r toward the centre.
❌ 'Centripetal acceleration changes the speed.' ✅ Centripetal acceleration changes only the DIRECTION of velocity. Tangential acceleration (if present) changes the speed.
❌ 'Centripetal force acts outward.' ✅ Centripetal force acts INWARD, toward the centre. The tendency to move outward is inertia, not a force.
❌ 'If the string breaks, the body moves radially outward.' ✅ If the string breaks, the body moves TANGENT to the circle (in the direction of its velocity at that instant), not radially.

data.title: Relation Between Angular and Linear Velocity and Acceleration
data.topicTitle: Relation between angular and linear velocity and acceleration
notes: **Angular displacement (Δθ):** the angle through which a body rotates about a fixed axis. Measured in radians (rad). 1 rad = 57.3°, 2π rad = 360°. Angular displacement is a vector along the axis (right-hand rule): positive for anticlockwise rotation.

**Angular velocity (ω):** the rate of change of angular displacement: ω = dθ/dt (instantaneous), ω = Δθ/t (average). Unit: rad/s. Direction: along the axis (right-hand rule). For uniform circular motion, ω is constant.
**Angular acceleration (α):** the rate of change of angular velocity: α = dω/dt = d²θ/dt². Unit: rad/s². When α is constant, the kinematic equations mirror linear motion.

**Relationship between linear and angular quantities (for circular motion):** v = rω (linear speed = radius × angular speed), a_t = rα (tangential acceleration), a_c = v²/r = rω² (centripetal acceleration). These links connect rotational and translational motion.

**Kinematic equations for constant angular acceleration (mirror linear v = u + at, etc.):** ω = ω₀ + αt; θ = ω₀t + ½αt²; ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ; θ = (ω + ω₀)t/2. The structure is identical to linear motion — just swap x→θ, v→ω, a→α.

**Worked example — spinning wheel:** a wheel starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 rad/s² for 5 s. Angular displacement: θ = 0 + ½ × 2 × 25 = 25 rad. Final angular velocity: ω = 0 + 2 × 5 = 10 rad/s. Number of revolutions: 25/(2π) ≈ 3.98 rev.

**Worked example — decelerating fan:** a fan blade rotating at 120 rpm (120 × 2π/60 = 12.57 rad/s) comes to rest in 8 s. Angular acceleration: α = (0 − 12.57)/8 = −1.57 rad/s². Angular displacement: θ = 12.57 × 8/2 = 50.27 rad ≈ 8 rev.

**NEB exam focus:** converting between rpm and rad/s; applying the kinematic equations for constant angular acceleration; linking linear and angular quantities (v = rω, a = rω²); finding number of revolutions from angular displacement.

**Right-hand rule for angular quantities:** curl the fingers of your right hand in the direction of rotation; your thumb points along the angular velocity/acceleration vector. For anticlockwise rotation (as viewed from above), the vector points upward; for clockwise, it points downward.

**Angular displacement is NOT a simple angle:** while measured in radians, angular displacement has direction (along the axis). For rotations greater than 2π, the magnitude keeps increasing — unlike a simple angle which resets after 360°. This is why angular displacement is a true vector quantity.

**Non-uniform circular motion:** when angular acceleration α ≠ 0, both tangential acceleration (a_t = rα) and centripetal acceleration (a_c = rω²) are present. The total acceleration is the vector sum: a = √(a_t² + a_c²). The direction of total acceleration is at angle φ = arctan(a_c/a_t) from the tangential direction.

**Small angle approximation:** for oscillatory motion (pendulums, springs), when θ is small (θ < 0.1 rad ≈ 6°), we can approximate sin θ ≈ θ and cos θ ≈ 1. This linearizes the equations and makes them solvable analytically.

**Angular quantities as vectors — addition is NOT commutative for large angles:** while infinitesimal angular displacements dθ are vectors (they commute), finite angular displacements do NOT commute. Rotating 90° about x then 90° about y gives a different result than rotating 90° about y then 90° about x. This is why angular velocity is a true vector but finite angular displacement is not.
**Linear to angular:** $\omega = v/r$. A point at the rim of a wheel moves faster in linear speed but has the same angular velocity as a point near the centre.
**Angular to linear:** $v = r\omega$. If $\omega$ is constant, linear speed increases with radius — which is why the outer edge of a spinning disc has higher speed.
**Tangential acceleration:** $a_t = r\alpha$. This is the acceleration tangent to the circle, changing the speed along the path.
**Centripetal acceleration:** $a_c = v^2/r = r\omega^2$. This is the inward acceleration required to keep the object moving in a circle.
**Total acceleration:** when both speed and direction change, $\vec{a} = \vec{a}_t + \vec{a}_c$. The two components are perpendicular.
**Direction of $\vec{v}$:** the linear velocity is always tangential to the circular path. The direction changes continuously even when speed is constant.
**Instantaneous vs average:** $v = r\omega$ relates instantaneous values. For average values, $\bar{v} = r\bar{\omega}$ holds only if angular acceleration is constant.
**Vector form:** $\vec{v} = \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r}$. This cross product automatically gives the correct direction (tangential) and magnitude ($r\omega$).

**Multiple radii on one body:** all points on a rigid rotating body share the same $\omega$ and $\alpha$, but their tangential speed and tangential acceleration differ proportionally to their distance from the axis.

**Practical example:** a grinding wheel at 3000 RPM with diameter 0.2 m: $\omega = 3000 \times 2\pi/60 = 100\pi \approx 314$ rad/s. Rim speed $v = 0.1 \times 314 = 31.4$ m/s, fast enough to be dangerous.

confusion: ❌ 'Angular displacement and angle are the same.' ✅ Angular displacement is a vector (along the axis), while angle is a scalar. For a full revolution, angular displacement = 2π rad, but the body returns to its starting position.
❌ 'Angular velocity is always constant in circular motion.' ✅ Only in UNIFORM circular motion is ω constant. In non-uniform circular motion, ω changes and there is angular acceleration.

❌ 'The direction of angular velocity is tangential.' ❌ The direction of angular velocity is ALONG THE AXIS of rotation (right-hand rule), not tangential. Tangential velocity is v = rω, but ω itself points along the axis.

❌ 'Angular acceleration means the body is speeding up.' ✅ Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity. If α and ω have the same sign, the body speeds up; if opposite signs, it slows down.
❌ 'The kinematic equations for rotation are different from linear motion.' ✅ They are IDENTICAL in form: just replace x with θ, v with ω, and a with α. The same problem-solving approach works.
❌ 'rpm and rad/s are the same.' ✅ 1 rpm = 2π/60 rad/s ≈ 0.105 rad/s. Always convert rpm to rad/s before using formulas.

All points on a rigid body have the same angular velocity $\omega$, but points farther from the axis have greater linear speed $v = r\omega$. The relation $v = r\omega$ does not mean larger radius means larger $\omega$.

Centripetal acceleration $a_c = v^2/r$ depends on $v$ at that radius. Since $v = r\omega$, substituting gives $a_c = r\omega^2$, which increases with $r$. Do not confuse with $v^2/r$ appearing to decrease with $r$ — that is for fixed $v$, not fixed $\omega$.

Tangential acceleration $a_t = r\alpha$ changes the speed. Centripetal acceleration $a_c = r\omega^2$ changes the direction. They are perpendicular and independent — you can have one without the other.
The formula $\vec{v} = \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r}$ is the vector relationship. In one dimension, it simplifies to $v = r\omega$. But the vector form is essential for 3D problems.
For a rolling wheel, the velocity of the top is $v + r\omega$ (which equals $2v$) and the bottom is $v - r\omega = 0$ (instantaneous rest for rolling without slipping).

A point on a disc of radius 0.1 m is at 5 m/s tangential speed. Find the angular velocity and the centripetal acceleration. Solution: $\omega = v/r = 5/0.1 = 50$ rad/s. $a_c = v^2/r = 25/0.1 = 250$ m/s$^2$. Alternatively $a_c = r\omega^2 = 0.1 \times 2500 = 250$ m/s$^2$.

A spinning disc has angular acceleration $\alpha = 10$ rad/s$^2$ and angular velocity $\omega = 20$ rad/s at a point 0.15 m from the axis. Find the total acceleration. Solution: $a_t = r\alpha = 0.15 \times 10 = 1.5$ m/s$^2$. $a_c = r\omega^2 = 0.15 \times 400 = 60$ m/s$^2$. $a = \sqrt{1.5^2 + 60^2} \approx 60.02$ m/s$^2$. Direction: $\theta = \tan^{-1}(1.5/60) = 1.43^{\circ}$ from the radial direction.

A merry-go-round rotates at 20 RPM. Two children sit at 1 m and 2 m from the centre. Find their linear speeds and the difference. Solution: $\omega = 20 \times 2\pi/60 = 2\pi/3$ rad/s. $v_1 = 1 \times 2\pi/3 = 2.09$ m/s. $v_2 = 2 \times 2\pi/3 = 4.19$ m/s. Difference $= 2.10$ m/s.

data.title: Conical Pendulum
notes: **Conical pendulum:** a small bob of mass m attached to a string of length L, moving in a horizontal circle at constant speed such that the string traces out a cone. The string makes angle θ with the vertical and the bob moves in a circle of radius r = L sin θ.

**Forces and geometry:** two forces act on the bob: tension T along the string, and weight mg downward. The tension has vertical component T cos θ (balances weight) and horizontal component T sin θ (provides centripetal force).

**Key equations:** T cos θ = mg (vertical equilibrium) ... (1); T sin θ = mω²r = mω²L sin θ (centripetal) ... (2). From (2): T = mω²L. Substituting into (1): mω²L cos θ = mg → cos θ = g/(ω²L). Also: ω = √(g/L cos θ) and T_period = 2π√(L cos θ/g).

**Key insight — period depends only on L cos θ:** the period T = 2π√(L cos θ/g) is independent of the mass of the bob. A taller cone (larger θ, smaller cos θ) has a shorter period (faster rotation). The minimum period is when θ → 0: T_min = 2π√(L/g) (same as a simple pendulum of length L).

**Worked example:** a 0.2 kg bob on a 2 m string rotates with θ = 30°. cos 30° = 0.866. Angular speed: ω = √(9.8/(2 × 0.866)) = √5.66 = 2.38 rad/s. Period: T = 2π/2.38 = 2.64 s. Tension: T = mω²L = 0.2 × 5.66 × 2 = 2.26 N. Radius: r = 2 × sin 30° = 1 m.

**Comparison with simple pendulum:** both have period T = 2π√(L_eff/g). For a simple pendulum, L_eff = L. For a conical pendulum, L_eff = L cos θ (the vertical height of the cone). So a conical pendulum swings slower than a simple pendulum of the same string length.
**NEB exam focus:** deriving the relation cos θ = g/(ω²L); finding the period, angular speed, or tension; showing that the period is independent of mass; comparing conical and simple pendulums.
**Practical examples:** a tethered aeroplane model, a ball on a string swung in a horizontal circle, vehicles banking on a curved road (same geometry — the road provides the 'tension' component).

**Deriving the key result step by step:** from vertical equilibrium: T cos θ = mg → T = mg/cos θ. From horizontal force: T sin θ = mω²r = mω²L sin θ. Canceling sin θ (assuming θ ≠ 0): T = mω²L. Equating: mω²L = mg/cos θ → ω² = g/(L cos θ) → ω = √(g/L cos θ). This derivation is the standard NEB proof question.

**Period formula insight:** T_period = 2π/ω = 2π√(L cos θ/g). Note that L cos θ is the VERTICAL HEIGHT h of the cone. So T = 2π√(h/g) — the period depends only on the vertical height, not on the radius or the mass. A cone with height 1 m has the same period regardless of how wide it is.

**Relation to simple pendulum:** a simple pendulum of length L has period T = 2π√(L/g). A conical pendulum of string length L has period T = 2π√(L cos θ/g) = 2π√(h/g). Since cos θ < 1, the conical pendulum's period is LONGER than a simple pendulum of the same string length — it swings more slowly.

**Connection to banking of roads:** the conical pendulum and a banked road share identical force geometry. In the pendulum, tension provides both vertical support and centripetal force. In a banked road, the normal force plays the same dual role. The equation tan θ = v²/(rg) for banking is equivalent to the conical pendulum's geometry.

**Watt's governor:** the conical pendulum is the basis of the centrifugal governor used in steam engines. As the engine speeds up, the bobs rise (θ increases), which mechanically reduces the steam supply. This is a real-world application that NEB sometimes references.

**Conical pendulum:** a small bob of mass $m$ attached to a string of length $L$, moving in a horizontal circle at constant speed such that the string traces out a cone. The string makes angle $\theta$ with the vertical and the bob moves in a circle of radius $r = L \sin\theta$.

**Forces and geometry:** two forces act on the bob: tension $T$ along the string, and weight $mg$ downward. The tension has vertical component $T \cos\theta$ (balances weight) and horizontal component $T \sin\theta$ (provides centripetal force).

**Key equations:** $T \cos\theta = mg$ (vertical equilibrium) ... (1); $T \sin\theta = m\omega^2 r = m\omega^2 L \sin\theta$ (centripetal) ... (2). From (2): $T = m\omega^2 L$. Substituting into (1): $m\omega^2 L \cos\theta = mg$ → $T \cos\theta = mg$. Also: $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{g}{L \cos\theta}}$ and $T_{period} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L \cos\theta}{g}}$.

**Key insight — period depends only on $L \cos\theta$:** the period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L \cos\theta}{g}}$ is independent of the mass of the bob. A taller cone (larger $\theta$, smaller $\cos\theta$) has a shorter period (faster rotation). The minimum period is when $\theta \to 0$: $T_{min} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$ (same as a simple pendulum of length $L$).

**Worked example:** a $0.2\text{ kg}$ bob on a $2\text{ m}$ string rotates with $\theta = 30^\circ$. $\cos 30^\circ = 0.866$. Angular speed: $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{9.8}{2 \times 0.866}} = \sqrt{5.66} = 2.38\text{ rad/s}$. Period: $T = 2\pi/2.38 = 2.64\text{ s}$. Tension: $T = m\omega^2 L = 0.2 \times 5.66 \times 2 = 2.26\text{ N}$. Radius: $r = 2 \times \sin 30^\circ = 1\text{ m}$.

**Comparison with simple pendulum:** both have period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L_{\mathrm{eff}}/g}$. For a simple pendulum, $L_{\mathrm{eff}} = L$. For a conical pendulum, $L_{\mathrm{eff}} = L \cos\theta$ (the vertical height of the cone). So a conical pendulum swings slower than a simple pendulum of the same string length.

**NEB exam focus:** deriving the relation $\cos\theta = \frac{g}{\omega^2 L}$; finding the period, angular speed, or tension; showing that the period is independent of mass; comparing conical and simple pendulums.

**Deriving the key result step by step:** from vertical equilibrium: $T \cos\theta = mg \implies T = \frac{mg}{\cos\theta}$. From horizontal force: $T \sin\theta = m\omega^2 r = m\omega^2 L \sin\theta$. Canceling $\sin\theta$ (assuming $\theta \neq 0$): $T = m\omega^2 L$. Equating: $m\omega^2 L = \frac{mg}{\cos\theta} \implies \omega^2 = \frac{g}{L \cos\theta} \implies \omega = \sqrt{\frac{g}{L \cos\theta}}$. This derivation is the standard NEB proof question.

**Period formula insight:** $T_{period} = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L \cos\theta}{g}}$. Note that $L \cos\theta$ is the VERTICAL HEIGHT $h$ of the cone. So $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{h}{g}}$ — the period depends only on the vertical height, not on the radius or the mass. A cone with height $1\text{ m}$ has the same period regardless of how wide it is.

**Relation to simple pendulum:** a simple pendulum of length $L$ has period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$. A conical pendulum of string length $L$ has period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L \cos\theta}{g}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{h}{g}}$. Since $\cos\theta < 1$, the conical pendulum's period is LONGER than a simple pendulum of the same string length — it swings more slowly.

**Connection to banking of roads:** the conical pendulum and a banked road share identical force geometry. In the pendulum, tension provides both vertical support and centripetal force. In a banked road, the normal force plays the same dual role. The equation $\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg}$ for banking is equivalent to the conical pendulum's geometry.
**Setup:** a mass $m$ attached to a string of length $l$ rotates in a horizontal circle, making a constant angle $\theta$ with the vertical.
**Forces:** tension $T$ has components $T\cos\theta$ upward balancing weight $mg$, and $T\sin\theta$ inward providing centripetal force.
**Period:** $T_{period} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l\cos\theta}{g}}$. The period depends on the string length, the angle, and gravity.
**Special case — small angles:** when $\theta$ is small, $\cos\theta \approx 1$, so $T_{period} \approx 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$, the same as a simple pendulum.
**Speed:** $v = \sqrt{gr\tan\theta}$, where $r = l\sin\theta$ is the radius of the horizontal circle. Faster spin means a larger angle $\theta$.
**Height of the pendulum:** the vertical distance from the suspension point to the mass is $h = l\cos\theta$. The period depends only on this height: $T_{period} = 2\pi\sqrt{h/g}$.
**Angular velocity:** $\omega = \sqrt{g/(l\cos\theta)} = \sqrt{g/h}$. As the mass spins faster, $\theta$ increases, $h$ decreases, and the period decreases.
**Tension:** from $T\cos\theta = mg$, we get $T = mg/\cos\theta$. As $\theta$ increases, tension increases without bound. At $\theta = 90^{\circ}$, tension would be infinite — physically impossible.

**Maximum angle limit:** as $\omega \to \infty$, $\theta \to 90^{\circ}$ but never reaches it. The mass rises toward the horizontal but cannot get there because the required tension would be infinite.

**Analogy with a spinning conical top:** the path swept by the string traces a cone, hence the name. The path on a horizontal plane is circular, but the full trajectory in 3D is the surface of a cone.
**Relation to simple pendulum:** a conical pendulum with very small $\theta$ behaves like a simple pendulum of the same length, oscillating back and forth rather than spinning around.
confusion: ❌ 'The tension in the string equals mg.' ✅ The vertical component of tension equals mg. The total tension is greater: T = mg/cos θ (since cos θ < 1, T > mg).
❌ 'The bob is in equilibrium.' ✅ The bob is in vertical equilibrium (T cos θ = mg) but NOT horizontal equilibrium — it accelerates toward the centre (centripetal acceleration).
❌ 'The period depends on the mass of the bob.' ✅ The period T = 2π√(L cos θ/g) is independent of mass. A heavier bob rotates at the same period (for the same θ).
❌ 'A faster rotation gives a smaller θ.' ✅ A FASTER rotation gives a LARGER θ (the cone becomes flatter). From cos θ = g/(ω²L), as ω increases, cos θ decreases, so θ increases.
❌ 'The radius of the circle is L.' ✅ The radius is r = L sin θ, which is LESS than L. Only if θ = 90° would r = L (but then cos θ = 0 and the equations break down).
❌ 'The centripetal force is a new force to add to the FBD.' ✅ The centripetal force IS the horizontal component of tension: T sin θ = mω²r. No new force is added.
❌ 'The tension in the string equals mg.' ✅ The vertical component of tension equals mg. The total tension is greater: $T = \frac{mg}{\cos\theta}$ (since $\cos\theta < 1$, $T > mg$).
❌ 'The bob is in equilibrium.' ✅ The bob is in vertical equilibrium ($T \cos\theta = mg$) but NOT horizontal equilibrium — it accelerates toward the centre (centripetal acceleration).
❌ 'The period depends on the mass of the bob.' ✅ The period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L \cos\theta}{g}}$ is independent of mass. A heavier bob rotates at the same period (for the same $\theta$).

❌ 'A faster rotation gives a smaller θ.' ✅ A FASTER rotation gives a LARGER θ (the cone becomes flatter). From $\cos\theta = \frac{g}{\omega^2 L}$, as $\omega$ increases, $\cos\theta$ decreases, so $\theta$ increases.
❌ 'The radius of the circle is L.' ✅ The radius is $r = L \sin\theta$, which is LESS than $L$. Only if $\theta = 90^\circ$ would $r = L$ (but then $\cos\theta = 0$ and the equations break down).
❌ 'The centripetal force is a new force to add to the FBD.' ✅ The centripetal force IS the horizontal component of tension: $T \sin\theta = m\omega^2 r$. No new force is added.
The period of a conical pendulum $T_{period} = 2\pi\sqrt{l\cos\theta/g}$ is always less than that of a simple pendulum of the same length ($2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$) because $\cos\theta < 1$.
Tension in a conical pendulum is always greater than $mg$ because $T = mg/\cos\theta$ and $\cos\theta < 1$. The faster the rotation, the greater the tension.
The period of a conical pendulum decreases as it spins faster (larger $\theta$), unlike a simple pendulum where period depends only on length and $g$.
The period depends on the vertical height $h = l\cos\theta$, not on the radius of the circle. Two conical pendulums with the same $h$ have the same period regardless of their lengths.
The conical pendulum is not a 2D problem. The mass moves in a horizontal circle, but the string sweeps out a cone in 3D space.

A 0.5 kg ball is attached to a 1 m string and swings in a conical pendulum at $\theta = 45^{\circ}$. Find the period, tension, and speed. Solution: $T_{period} = 2\pi\sqrt{l\cos\theta/g} = 2\pi\sqrt{1 \times 0.707/9.8} = 2\pi\sqrt{0.0721} = 2\pi \times 0.269 = 1.69$ s. $T = mg/\cos\theta = 0.5 \times 9.8/0.707 = 6.93$ N. $r = l\sin\theta = 0.707$ m. $v = \sqrt{gr\tan\theta} = \sqrt{9.8 \times 0.707 \times 1} = 2.63$ m/s.

A conical pendulum has a period of 2 s and a string length of 1 m. Find the angle $\theta$ and the radius of the circle. Solution: $T_{period} = 2\pi\sqrt{l\cos\theta/g}$, so $2 = 2\pi\sqrt{\cos\theta/9.8}$. $(2/(2\pi))^2 = \cos\theta/9.8$. $\cos\theta = 9.8/(\pi^2) = 0.993$. $\theta = 6.8^{\circ}$. $r = 1 \times \sin 6.8^{\circ} = 0.119$ m.

A 0.2 kg mass on a 0.5 m string rotates in a horizontal circle at 3 rad/s. Find the angle, tension, and height. Solution: $\omega = \sqrt{g/(l\cos\theta)}$, so $\cos\theta = g/(l\omega^2) = 9.8/(0.5 \times 9) = 2.18$. Since this exceeds 1, the pendulum cannot maintain this angular velocity — the required angle would exceed 90 degrees. The maximum $\omega = \sqrt{g/l} = \sqrt{9.8/0.5} = 4.43$ rad/s.

Two conical pendulums: Pendulum A has length 0.8 m at $\theta = 30^{\circ}$, Pendulum B has length 0.5 m at $\theta = 45^{\circ}$. Which has the shorter period? Solution: $h_A = 0.8\cos 30^{\circ} = 0.693$ m, $h_B = 0.5\cos 45^{\circ} = 0.354$ m. $T_A = 2\pi\sqrt{0.693/9.8} = 1.67$ s, $T_B = 2\pi\sqrt{0.354/9.8} = 1.19$ s. Pendulum B has the shorter period.

Solution: $T_{period} = 2\pi\sqrt{l\cos\theta/g}$, so $\cos\theta = gT^2/(4\pi^2 l) = 9.8 \times 2.25/(4\pi^2 \times 0.6) = 22.05/23.69 = 0.931$. $\theta = 21.4^{\circ}$. $T = mg/\cos\theta = 0.1 \times 9.8/0.931 = 1.05$ N. $r = 0.6\sin 21.4^{\circ} = 0.217$ m. $v = 2\pi r/T = 2\pi \times 0.217/1.5 = 0.91$ m/s.

specificConditions: **Vertical Angle Limit:** For the conical pendulum to exist ($\cos	heta \le 1$), the angular velocity must satisfy $\omega \ge \sqrt{g/L}$. Below this speed, the bob cannot maintain a horizontal circular path and will simply hang at the bottom.

**String Tension Constraint:** The tension in the string is *always* greater than the weight of the bob ($T = mg/\cos	heta > mg$) because it must support the weight *and* provide the centripetal force.

**Small Angle Assumption:** The formulas rely on the string remaining taut. If the bob rotates too slowly, the string goes slack, and the motion ceases to be a horizontal circle (conical pendulum) and becomes a vertical oscillation.

data.title: Motion in a Vertical Circle
notes: **Motion in a vertical circle:** a body of mass m attached to a string moves in a vertical plane under gravity. Unlike horizontal circular motion, the speed varies with height — fastest at the bottom, slowest at the top.

**Why speed varies:** gravity does work on the body as it moves vertically. Kinetic energy is converted to gravitational PE on the way up, and back to KE on the way down. Total mechanical energy is conserved (ignoring air resistance).

**Critical distinction — string vs rigid rod:** a string can only pull (tension ≥ 0), so the body must have enough speed at the top to keep the string taut. A rigid rod can push or pull, so the body can reach the top with zero speed.

**Minimum speed at the top (string):** at the top, both tension T and weight mg point downward: T + mg = mv²/r. The minimum speed occurs when T → 0: mg = mv_min²/r → v_top(min) = √(gr). Below this, the string goes slack.

**Minimum speed at the bottom (string):** using energy conservation from bottom to top: ½mv_bottom² = ½mv_top² + mg(2r). With v_top = √(gr): ½v_bottom² = ½(gr) + 2gr → v_bottom² = 5gr → v_bottom(min) = √(5gr). This is the critical NEB result.

**Minimum speed at the bottom (rod):** since the rod can push, the body can reach the top with v_top = 0. Energy conservation: ½v_bottom² = 0 + 2gr → v_bottom(min) = √(2gr). This is lower than the string case.
**Tension at the bottom:** T_bottom − mg = mv_bottom²/r → T_bottom = mg + mv_bottom²/r. For the minimum case (string): T_bottom = mg + 5mg = 6mg. The tension at the bottom is 6 times the weight.
**Tension at the top:** T_top + mg = mv_top²/r → T_top = mv_top²/r − mg. For the minimum case (string): T_top = 0.
**Worked example:** a 0.5 kg bob on a 1.5 m string. v_top(min) = √(9.8 × 1.5) = 3.83 m/s. v_bottom(min) = √(5 × 9.8 × 1.5) = 8.57 m/s. T_bottom = 6 × 0.5 × 9.8 = 29.4 N.
**NEB exam focus:** deriving v_top(min) = √(gr) and v_bottom(min) = √(5gr); comparing string vs rod; finding tension at top and bottom; energy conservation between positions.

**Energy diagram for vertical circle:** plot KE, PE, and total E vs. height. KE is maximum at the bottom (½mv_b²), minimum at the top (½mv_t²). PE is minimum (0) at the bottom and maximum (mg·2r) at the top. Total energy E = ½mv_b² = ½mv_t² + 2mgr — a horizontal line on the diagram.

**Tension variation around the circle:** at any angle θ from the bottom, T = mv²/r + mg cos θ. At the bottom (θ = 0°): T = mg + mv²/r (maximum). At the top (θ = 180°): T = mv²/r − mg (minimum). The tension difference between bottom and top is always 6mg when the minimum-speed condition holds.

**Worked example — tension at arbitrary point:** a 0.2 kg bob on a 0.8 m string has speed 6 m/s at the bottom. At the top: ½v_t² = ½ × 36 − 9.8 × 1.6 = 18 − 15.68 = 2.32 → v_t = 2.15 m/s. T_top = 0.2 × 4.62/0.8 − 1.96 = 1.16 − 1.96 = −0.80 N. Since T < 0, the string goes slack before reaching the top. The bob cannot complete the circle.

**Rod vs. string — key differences:** a rod can support compression, so the bob can reach the top with v = 0. The rod pushes upward with force mg at the top. Minimum bottom speed for a rod: √(2gr). For a string: √(5gr). The factor 5 versus 2 is the critical distinction tested in NEB.

**Complete-the-circle condition:** for a string, the condition is v_bottom ≥ √(5gr). For a rod, it is v_bottom ≥ √(2gr). If v_bottom is between √(2gr) and √(5gr), the bob completes the circle with a rod but not with a string.
confusion: ❌ 'The speed is constant in vertical circular motion.' ✅ The speed VARIES — gravity speeds up the body on the way down and slows it on the way up. Only energy is conserved.
❌ 'The minimum speed at the top is zero.' ✅ For a STRING, the minimum speed at the top is √(gr). For a ROD, it is indeed zero.
❌ 'The tension is the same at all points.' ✅ The tension varies — maximum at the bottom (T = mg + mv²/r) and minimum at the top (T = mv²/r − mg).
❌ 'The minimum speed at the bottom is √(2gr).' ✅ That is for a ROD. For a STRING, it is √(5gr) — the body must have enough energy to reach the top with speed √(gr).
❌ 'If the string goes slack, the body stops.' ✅ If the string goes slack, the body becomes a projectile — it follows a parabolic path under gravity.
❌ 'The centripetal force is constant.' ✅ The centripetal force (mv²/r) varies because v varies. At the bottom, it is maximum; at the top, it is minimum.

data.title: Applications of Banking
notes: **Banking of roads:** the practice of raising the outer edge of a curved road above the inner edge so that the normal reaction from the road surface provides part or all of the centripetal force needed to turn. This reduces reliance on friction and prevents skidding.

**Why banking is needed:** on a flat road, the entire centripetal force must come from friction: F_c = μmg. At high speeds or on slippery roads, friction may be insufficient and the vehicle skids outward. Banking tilts the road so the normal force has a horizontal component pointing toward the center.

**Forces on a banked road:** the road is tilted at angle θ. The normal reaction N acts perpendicular to the road surface. Resolving N: vertical component N cos θ balances weight (N cos θ = mg); horizontal component N sin θ provides centripetal force (N sin θ = mv²/r).

**Key equation — ideal banking angle (no friction needed):** dividing the two equations: tan θ = v²/(rg). For a given radius r and design speed v, the road should be banked at angle θ = arctan(v²/(rg)). At this angle, no friction is required.

**Friction on a banked road:** if the vehicle moves faster than the design speed, friction acts DOWN the slope (preventing outward skid). If slower, friction acts UP the slope (preventing inward sliding). The general formula: tan(θ + φ) = v²/(rg), where φ = arctan(μ).
**Maximum speed on a banked road with friction:** v_max = √[rg(tan θ + μ)/(1 − μ tan θ)]. When μ = 0 (no friction), this reduces to v = √(rg tan θ). When θ = 0 (flat road), it reduces to v = √(μrg).
**Worked example — car on banked curve:** a road of radius 100 m is banked at θ = 15°. Design speed (no friction): v = √(100 × 9.8 × tan 15°) = √(100 × 9.8 × 0.268) = √262.6 = 16.2 m/s (≈ 58 km/h).

**Railway banking (superelevation):** railways use the same principle. The outer rail is raised by height h above the inner rail. For track gauge w and banking angle θ: tan θ ≈ h/w. This prevents wear on rails and ensures passenger comfort.
**NEB exam focus:** deriving tan θ = v²/(rg); finding the design speed for a given banking angle; maximum speed with friction; railway superelevation problems.

**Force resolution on a banked road — detailed derivation:** draw the FBD with N perpendicular to the road and mg vertically down. Resolve N into: vertical component N cos θ (balances weight) and horizontal component N sin θ (provides centripetal force). From N cos θ = mg: N = mg/cos θ. From N sin θ = mv²/r: (mg/cos θ) sin θ = mv²/r → mg tan θ = mv²/r → tan θ = v²/(rg). This derivation is the standard NEB proof.

**Friction on a banked road — general case:** when friction is present, there are two limiting cases. Case 1 (going too fast): friction acts DOWN the slope, adding to the centripetal force. Case 2 (going too slow): friction acts UP the slope, preventing inward sliding. The general equation combining both: N sin θ ± f cos θ = mv²/r (horizontal) and N cos θ ∓ f sin θ = mg (vertical), where f = μN.

**Worked example — finding banking angle:** a curve of radius 150 m is designed for 90 km/h (25 m/s). Required banking angle: tan θ = v²/(rg) = 625/(150 × 9.8) = 0.425 → θ = 23.0°. At this angle, a car can negotiate the curve without any friction.

**Worked example — height of outer rail:** a railway track of gauge 1.5 m is banked at 5°. The height by which the outer rail is raised: h = w tan θ = 1.5 × tan 5° = 1.5 × 0.0875 = 0.131 m ≈ 13.1 cm. This is a typical NEB numerical problem.

**Why banking reduces tire wear:** on a flat road, friction must provide all centripetal force, causing lateral tire stress. On a banked road at the design speed, the normal force provides the centripetal component — no lateral friction needed. This dramatically reduces tire wear and fuel consumption.
confusion: ❌ 'Banking eliminates friction entirely.' ✅ Banking REDUCES friction requirement. At the design speed (tan θ = v²/(rg)), friction is zero. At other speeds, friction is still needed.
❌ 'A steeper bank angle is always better.' ✅ Too steep a bank angle causes problems at low speeds — the vehicle may slide inward. The ideal angle depends on the design speed.
❌ 'The normal force equals mg on a banked road.' ✅ The normal force is N = mg/cos θ, which is GREATER than mg because the road is tilted.
❌ 'Banking angle depends on the mass of the vehicle.' ✅ The ideal banking angle tan θ = v²/(rg) is independent of mass — it depends only on speed and radius.
❌ 'On a banked road, friction always acts up the slope.' ✅ Friction direction depends on speed: if v > design speed, friction acts DOWN the slope; if v < design speed, friction acts UP.
❌ 'A higher banking angle means a lower maximum speed.' ✅ A HIGHER banking angle INCREASES the maximum speed — more of the normal force contributes to centripetal force.

data.title: Circular Motion Mindmap
notes: Circular motion: motion of a body along a circular path. Key quantities: angular displacement (θ), angular velocity (ω), angular acceleration (α), centripetal acceleration (a_c = v²/r = rω²).
Angular displacement: θ = s/r (radians); 2π rad = 360° = 1 revolution; vector along axis (right-hand rule).
Angular velocity: ω = dθ/dt; uniform circular motion has constant ω; unit: rad/s; rpm conversion: × 2π/60.
Angular acceleration: α = dω/dt; constant α gives kinematic equations mirroring linear motion.
Centripetal acceleration: a_c = v²/r = rω² — always directed toward the center; changes direction of velocity, not speed.
Centripetal force: F_c = mv²/r — not a new force; provided by tension, gravity, friction, or normal force.
Conical pendulum: bob moves in horizontal circle; string traces cone; period T = 2π√(L cos θ/g), independent of mass.
Vertical circle: speed varies with height; minimum top speed (string) = √(gr); minimum bottom speed = √(5gr).
Banking of roads: tan θ = v²/(rg) for ideal angle; reduces friction requirement; railway superelevation h = w tan θ.
NEB exam focus: converting rpm to rad/s; centripetal force identification; conical pendulum derivation; vertical circle min speeds; banking angle calculations.

data.title: Current-Voltage Relations and Ohmic/Non-Ohmic Resistance
data.topicTitle: Current-voltage relations; ohmic and non-ohmic resistance
notes: **Ohmic conductor:** obeys Ohm's law. The $I$-$V$ graph is a straight line through the origin. Resistance is constant.
**Non-ohmic conductor:** does not obey Ohm's law. The $I$-$V$ graph is curved. Resistance changes with voltage or current.

**Examples of non-ohmic:** diode (conducts easily in one direction only), filament lamp (resistance increases with temperature as current increases), thermistor (resistance decreases with temperature).
**Why filament lamp is non-ohmic:** as current increases, the filament heats up, increasing its resistivity. The $I$-$V$ curve bends because $R$ is not constant.
**Dynamic resistance:** $R_d = dV/dI$ at a point on the $I$-$V$ curve. For non-ohmic devices, this is the useful measure of resistance at a specific operating point.
**Forward bias diode:** current flows easily once the voltage exceeds the threshold ($\\\\approx 0.7$ V for silicon, $\\\\approx 0.3$ V for germanium). Below threshold, very little current flows.
**Reverse bias diode:** almost no current flows (except a tiny leakage current). At the breakdown voltage, current increases sharply and the diode may be damaged.
**Thermistor:** a semiconductor device whose resistance decreases sharply with temperature (NTC type). Used as temperature sensors and inrush current limiters.
**Zener diode:** operates in reverse breakdown at a precise voltage. It maintains a nearly constant voltage across it, used as a voltage regulator.

**Filament lamp $I$-$V$ curve:** starts linearly at low voltage (cool filament, low resistance). At higher voltages, the curve bends toward the voltage axis as the filament heats and resistance increases.

**Temperature coefficient of filament:** tungsten has $\\\\alpha \\\\approx 0.0045$ $^{\\\\circ}$C$^{-1}$. A 100 W, 230 V bulb has cold resistance of about $50\\\\,\\\\Omega$ but hot resistance of $529\\\\,\\\\Omega$.
confusion: Ohm's law $V = IR$ is a definition of resistance, not a law that all materials obey. Only ohmic conductors have a linear $I$-$V$ relationship. For non-ohmic devices, $R = V/I$ is still defined but varies.

A filament lamp becomes a better conductor (lower resistance) when cold. This is why bulbs often burn out at the moment they are switched on - the initial current surge is 10 times the steady-state current.

The dynamic resistance $dV/dI$ is different from the static resistance $V/I$. For a non-ohmic device, the static resistance is $V/I$ while the dynamic resistance is the slope of the $I$-$V$ curve at that point.

A diode is not simply a 'one-way valve' for current. In reverse bias, a tiny leakage current (nA to $\\\mu$A range) still flows. In forward bias, the current is exponentially related to voltage, not linearly.

Thermistors are not simply temperature-dependent resistors. Their resistance changes exponentially with temperature: $R = R_0 e^{\ eta(1/T - 1/T_0)}$, which makes them highly sensitive to small temperature changes.
practice: A filament lamp has a resistance of $20\\\\,\\\\Omega$ when cold and $240\\\\,\\\\Omega$ when glowing at full brightness. If connected to a 12 V supply, find the current when cold and when glowing. Solution: Cold: $I = V/R = 12/20 = 0.6$ A. Glowing: $I = V/R = 12/240 = 0.05$ A. The inrush current is 12 times the steady-state current.

A silicon diode has a forward voltage drop of 0.7 V at a current of 10 mA. It is connected in series with a 500 $\\\Omega$ resistor and a 5 V battery. Find the current. Solution: The diode drops 0.7 V, so the resistor sees $5 - 0.7 = 4.3$ V. $I = 4.3/500 = 8.6$ mA.

A thermistor has resistance $R_0 = 10\\\\,\	ext{k}\\\\Omega$ at 25$^{\\\\circ}$C and $R = 2\\\\,\	ext{k}\\\\Omega$ at 50$^{\\\\circ}$C. Find the resistance at 0$^{\\\\circ}$C assuming a linear temperature coefficient. Solution: $\\\\alpha = (R_0 - R)/(R \\\\cdot \\\\Delta T) = (10000 - 2000)/(2000 \	imes 25) = 0.16$ $^{\\\\circ}$C$^{-1}$. At 0$^{\\\\circ}$C: $R = R_0/(1 + \\\\alpha \\\\cdot 25) = 10000/(1 + 4) = 2000\\\\,\\\\Omega$.

A $I$-$V$ graph of a device shows that at $V = 3$ V, the current is 0.15 A, and the tangent at that point has slope $dI/dV = 0.02$ A/V. Find the static resistance and dynamic resistance. Solution: Static resistance $R_s = V/I = 3/0.15 = 20\\\\,\\\\Omega$. Dynamic resistance $R_d = 1/(dI/dV) = 1/0.02 = 50\\\\,\\\\Omega$.

A Zener diode with breakdown voltage 6 V is connected in parallel with a load resistor of 1 k$\\\Omega$ across a 10 V battery with series resistor of 500 $\\\Omega$. Find the current through the Zener diode. Solution: Voltage across load: 6 V (clamped by Zener). Current through 500 $\\\Omega$: $I = (10 - 6)/500 = 8$ mA. Current through load: $I_L = 6/1000 = 6$ mA. Current through Zener: $I_Z = 8 - 6 = 2$ mA.
universalFacts: A tungsten filament lamp has a resistance that changes by a factor of 10-15 between cold and hot, making it a classic example of non-ohmic behavior due to temperature-dependent resistivity.

The threshold voltage of a silicon diode is approximately 0.7 V because this is the energy needed to overcome the potential barrier of the p-n junction, corresponding to the band gap energy of silicon.
Semiconductors have a negative temperature coefficient of resistance (NTC thermistors) because more charge carriers are thermally excited across the band gap, increasing conductivity.
Ohmic materials include most metals at constant temperature. Non-ohmic materials include all semiconductors, electrolytes, and any device where temperature or other conditions change with current.
The $I$-$V$ characteristic of a diode is exponential: $I = I_0(e^{eV/kT} - 1)$, where $I_0$ is the reverse saturation current, $k$ is Boltzmann's constant, and $T$ is temperature.
specificConditions: **Ohmic Behavior Constraint:** A device is ohmic only if $I \propto V$ *and* the temperature is constant. Metals at constant temperature are ohmic; semiconductors, electrolytes, and gas discharges are inherently non-ohmic.

**Dynamic vs. Static Resistance:** For non-ohmic devices, the static resistance $R_s = V/I$ depends on the operating point, while the dynamic (small-signal) resistance $r_d = dV/dI$ describes the response to small AC signals superimposed on the DC bias.

**Temperature as Hidden Variable:** In filament lamps and thermistors, the non-ohmic behavior arises because the current heats the device, changing its resistivity. The $I$-$V$ curve actually represents a parametric plot where temperature varies with current.

data.title: Current-Voltage Relations: Ohmic and Non-Ohmic Resistance
data.topicTitle: Current-voltage relations; ohmic and non-ohmic resistance
notes: Ohm's Law: For an ohmic conductor at constant physical conditions (especially temperature), the current $I$ flowing through it is directly proportional to the potential difference $V$ across its ends: $V = IR$, where $R$ is the resistance. The graph of $V$ vs $I$ is a straight line through the origin.

Resistance Definition: Resistance $R$ of a conductor is defined as the ratio of potential difference across it to the current through it: $R = V/I$. SI unit: ohm ($\Omega = 	ext{V/A} = 	ext{V}^2/	ext{W}$). Dimensions: $[M L^2 T^{-3} I^{-2}]$.

Resistivity: The resistance of a uniform conductor depends on its geometry and material: $R = \rho L/A$, where $\rho$ is resistivity (material property), $L$ is length, and $A$ is cross-sectional area. SI unit of $\rho$: $\Omega\cdot	ext{m}$. Conductivity $\sigma = 1/\rho$.

Ohmic Conductors: Conductors that obey Ohm's law ($V$-$I$ graph is linear) are called ohmic. Examples: metals at constant temperature, electrolytes, carbon resistors. Their resistance is independent of $V$ and $I$ (within limits).

Non-Ohmic Conductors: Conductors that do NOT obey Ohm's law ($V$-$I$ graph is non-linear). Examples: diode, transistor, thermistor, filament lamp, vacuum tube, electrolyte at high voltage. Their resistance varies with $V$ or $I$ (dynamic resistance $r_d = dV/dI$).

Temperature Dependence: For metals, resistance increases with temperature: $R_T = R_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$, where $\alpha$ is temperature coefficient of resistance (positive for metals). For semiconductors, $\alpha$ is negative (resistance decreases with temperature).
Filament Lamp: A filament lamp is non-ohmic because its temperature rises as current increases, changing its resistance. Cold resistance is lower than hot resistance.
Diode: A p-n junction diode conducts easily in forward bias (small resistance) and blocks in reverse bias (large resistance). Its $V$-$I$ characteristic is highly non-linear.

Superconductors: Below a critical temperature $T_c$, certain materials exhibit zero electrical resistance ($R = 0$) and expel magnetic fields (Meissner effect). Examples: mercury ($T_c \approx 4.2\text{ K}$), niobium-titanium alloys.

specificConditions: Ohm's Law Validity: Ohm's law $V = IR$ holds only for ohmic materials at constant temperature and other physical conditions. It is NOT a fundamental law of nature but an empirical observation valid for many conductors.

The temperature coefficient of resistance is positive for metals (lattice scattering increases) but negative for semiconductors (more carriers generated).

confusion: Confusing ohmic with linear: Ohm's law requires linearity AND constant temperature; a heated metal is not ohmic even if its V-I graph looks linear at low currents.

Assuming all metals obey Ohm's law perfectly: At very low temperatures or high fields, even metals deviate.
Confusing resistance with resistivity: Resistance depends on geometry; resistivity does not.

data.title: EMF and Internal Resistance
notes: **EMF ($\\\\mathcal{E}$):** the open-circuit voltage of a source. It is the work done per unit charge in moving charge around the complete circuit.
**Internal resistance $r$:** the resistance inside the cell due to electrolyte and electrodes. It causes the terminal voltage to drop when current flows.
**Terminal voltage:** $V = \\\\mathcal{E} - Ir$. When no current flows ($I=0$), $V = \\\\mathcal{E}$. Under load, $V < \\\\mathcal{E}$.
**Cells in series:** $\\\\mathcal{E}_{total} = \\\\mathcal{E}_1 + \\\\mathcal{E}_2 + \\\\ldots$, $r_{total} = r_1 + r_2 + \\\\ldots$. Series adds both EMF and internal resistance.
**Cells in parallel:** $\\\\mathcal{E}_{total} = \\\\mathcal{E}$ (if all equal), $r_{total} = r/n$ for $n$ identical cells. Parallel reduces internal resistance, allowing higher current delivery.
**Maximum power transfer:** the power delivered to an external load $R$ is maximum when $R = r$. The maximum power is $P_{max} = \\\\mathcal{E}^2/(4r)$.
**Current in a simple circuit:** $I = \\\\mathcal{E}/(R + r)$, where $R$ is the external resistance and $r$ is the internal resistance.
**Efficiency:** the efficiency of power transfer is $\\\\eta = R/(R + r)$. Maximum efficiency approaches 100% when $R \\\\gg r$, but maximum power requires $R = r$.
**Short circuit current:** when $R = 0$, $I_{sc} = \\\\mathcal{E}/r$. This can be very large and dangerous, causing heating and damage.
**Cells with different EMFs:** when cells with different EMFs are connected in parallel, circulating currents flow between them. This can damage cells and should be avoided.
**Real cell behavior:** as a cell discharges, its EMF slowly decreases and its internal resistance increases. An old battery reads lower than its rated voltage even when not loaded.
**Emf.** The emf E of a cell is the work done by the cell in moving unit charge once around the whole circuit; it is measured with a voltmeter across the open terminals and is not a force.
**Terminal potential difference.** With current flowing, internal resistance drops Ir inside the cell, so the terminal voltage is V = E − I·r while discharging (V = E + I·r while charging).
**Internal resistance.** r depends on the electrolyte (r = ρl/a), electrode area and separation; a fresh cell has small r which grows with use.
**V–I characteristic.** A plot of V against I is a straight line whose slope gives r and whose intercept on the V axis gives E — the standard graph question.
**Practical limits.** Short-circuit current I_s = E/r; the external load receives maximum power when its resistance equals r, which is also why terminal voltage falls under heavy load.
confusion: EMF is not a force - it is a voltage (energy per unit charge). The name is historical. EMF is measured in volts, not newtons.

Terminal voltage $V = \\\\mathcal{E} - Ir$ is less than EMF when current flows out of the cell. But when charging the cell, current flows into the positive terminal, so $V = \\\\mathcal{E} + Ir$ - the terminal voltage is greater than EMF.
In series, both EMF and internal resistance add. In parallel, the equivalent EMF is the same as one cell, but the equivalent internal resistance is reduced, allowing more current.
Maximum power transfer ($R = r$) occurs at 50% efficiency. For efficient power delivery, you want $R \\\\gg r$ (high efficiency, low power). For maximum power, you sacrifice efficiency.
A fresh battery has a high open-circuit voltage (close to its EMF) but drops significantly under load if its internal resistance has increased with age. That is why old batteries seem weak.
Carefully distinguish between similar-looking concepts in emf and internal resistance.
Pay attention to the conditions under which formulas and theorems apply.
Practice with multiple examples to solidify your understanding.
practice: A cell with EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 $\\\Omega$ is connected to a 7 $\\\Omega$ resistor. Find the current, terminal voltage, and power delivered to the resistor. Solution: $I = 1.5/(7+0.5) = 0.2$ A. $V = 1.5 - 0.2 \	imes 0.5 = 1.4$ V. $P = I^2 R = 0.04 \	imes 7 = 0.28$ W.

A cell gives 2.0 V when no current flows and 1.8 V when delivering 1 A. Find the EMF and internal resistance. Solution: EMF $\\\\mathcal{E} = 2.0$ V (open circuit). Under load: $1.8 = 2.0 - 1 \	imes r$, so $r = 0.2\\\\,\\\\Omega$.

Three identical cells of EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.3 $\\\Omega$ each are connected in series across a 6 $\\\Omega$ load. Find the current. Solution: $\\\\mathcal{E}_{total} = 4.5$ V, $r_{total} = 0.9\\\\,\\\\Omega$. $I = 4.5/(6+0.9) = 0.652$ A.

The same three cells above are connected in parallel across the same 6 $\\\Omega$ load. Find the current. Solution: $\\\\mathcal{E}_{total} = 1.5$ V, $r_{total} = 0.3/3 = 0.1\\\\,\\\\Omega$. $I = 1.5/(6+0.1) = 0.246$ A.

Find the external resistance for maximum power transfer to a cell with EMF 12 V and internal resistance 2 $\\\Omega$. Find the maximum power. Solution: $R = r = 2\\\\,\\\\Omega$. $I = 12/(2+2) = 3$ A. $P_{max} = I^2 R = 9 \	imes 2 = 18$ W. Alternatively $P_{max} = \\\\mathcal{E}^2/(4r) = 144/8 = 18$ W.

universalFacts: The internal resistance of a typical AA alkaline cell is about 0.15 $\\\Omega$ when fresh, but increases to 0.5 $\\\Omega$ or more as it discharges.
Connecting cells in series increases the available voltage while keeping the same current capacity. Connecting in parallel increases the current capacity while keeping the same voltage.
A short-circuited 12 V car battery with internal resistance 0.01 $\\\Omega$ can deliver 1200 A, which is why it can melt tools and cause severe burns.
The maximum power transfer theorem ($R = r$) is a fundamental design principle for matching loads to sources, but it is inefficient for power distribution systems where $R \\\\gg r$ is desired.
In a battery pack, series strings are often used to increase voltage, and parallel strings within each series group are used to increase capacity and reduce internal resistance.
This topic is a cornerstone of the physics curriculum and appears consistently in examinations.
Understanding emf and internal resistance builds the foundation for more advanced topics in mathematics.
Real-world applications of emf and internal resistance span engineering, physics, economics, and computer science.
specificConditions: **EMF vs Terminal Voltage:** EMF ($\mathcal{E}$) is the open-circuit voltage (no current). Terminal voltage $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$ under discharge; $V = \mathcal{E} + Ir$ during charging. The sign of the $Ir$ term depends on current direction.

**Series/Parallel Cell Rules:** In series: $\mathcal{E}_{total} = \sum \mathcal{E}_i$, $r_{total} = \sum r_i$. In parallel (identical cells): $\mathcal{E}_{total} = \mathcal{E}$, $r_{total} = r/n$. These assume no circulating currents between mismatched cells.

**Maximum Power Transfer Theorem:** Maximum power to load $R$ occurs at $R = r$, giving $P_{max} = \mathcal{E}^2/(4r)$. At this point, efficiency is 50%. For efficiency $>50\%$, need $R > r$; for $>90\%$, need $R > 9r$.

data.topicTitle: Electromotive force of a source, internal resistance
notes: EMF Definition: Electromotive force (EMF, $\mathcal{E}$) is the energy supplied by a source per unit charge to move charge through the complete circuit. It is NOT a force but a potential difference measured in volts. $\mathcal{E} = W/q$ where $W$ is work done by the source and $q$ is charge moved.

Terminal Potential Difference: When current $I$ flows, the terminal voltage $V$ across the source terminals is $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$, where $r$ is internal resistance. The voltage drop $Ir$ inside the source is called lost volts.

Internal Resistance: Every real source (cell, battery, generator) has internal resistance $r$ due to electrolyte resistance, electrode resistance, and chemical factors. It causes the terminal voltage to drop below EMF when current is drawn.
Open Circuit: When $I = 0$ (open circuit), $V = \mathcal{E}$ — the terminal voltage equals the EMF since there is no internal voltage drop.
Short Circuit: When terminals are shorted ($R = 0$), $I = \mathcal{E}/r$ — maximum current flows, limited only by internal resistance. This can damage the source.

Cells in Series: For $n$ identical cells each of EMF $\mathcal{E}$ and internal resistance $r$ in series: total EMF $= n\mathcal{E}$, total internal resistance $= nr$, equivalent $V = n\mathcal{E} - Inr$.

Cells in Parallel: For $n$ identical cells each of EMF $\mathcal{E}$ and internal resistance $r$ in parallel: equivalent EMF $= \mathcal{E}$, equivalent internal resistance $= r/n$ (current capacity increases).
Mixed Grouping: Cells in series-parallel combinations balance voltage and current requirements for specific applications.

Determination of EMF and Internal Resistance: Measure terminal voltage $V$ for different currents $I$. Plot $V$ vs $I$: y-intercept $= \mathcal{E}$, slope $= -r$. Alternatively use a potentiometer for accurate EMF measurement.
Power Delivered: Power delivered to external load $R$ is $P = I^2R = (\mathcal{E}/(R+r))^2 R$. Maximum power transfer occurs when $R = r$, with $P_\text{max} = \mathcal{E}^2/4r$.

Internal resistance increases as a cell ages or discharges — old batteries have higher $r$ and lower terminal voltage under load.
Short-circuit current $I = \mathcal{E}/r$ can be very large and damage the source — never short a battery.
EMF is not a force despite the name — it is energy per unit charge (volts).

data.title: EMF, Internal Resistance and Cells in Combination
data.topicTitle: Electromotive force of a source, internal resistance
notes: **EMF ($\mathcal{E}$):** the open-circuit voltage of a source. It is the work done per unit charge in moving charge around the complete circuit.
**Internal resistance $r$:** the resistance inside the cell due to electrolyte and electrodes. It causes the terminal voltage to drop when current flows.
**Terminal voltage:** $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$. When no current flows ($I=0$), $V = \mathcal{E}$. Under load, $V < \mathcal{E}$.
**Cells in series:** $\mathcal{E}_{total} = \mathcal{E}_1 + \mathcal{E}_2 + \ldots$, $r_{total} = r_1 + r_2 + \ldots$. Series adds both EMF and internal resistance.
**Cells in parallel:** $\mathcal{E}_{total} = \mathcal{E}$ (if all equal), $r_{total} = r/n$ for $n$ identical cells. Parallel reduces internal resistance, allowing higher current delivery.
**Maximum power transfer:** the power delivered to an external load $R$ is maximum when $R = r$. The maximum power is $P_{max} = \mathcal{E}^2/(4r)$.
**Current in a simple circuit:** $I = \mathcal{E}/(R + r)$, where $R$ is the external resistance and $r$ is the internal resistance.
**Efficiency:** the efficiency of power transfer is $\eta = R/(R + r)$. Maximum efficiency approaches 100% when $R \gg r$, but maximum power requires $R = r$.
**Short circuit current:** when $R = 0$, $I_{sc} = \\\\mathcal{E}/r$. This can be very large and dangerous, causing heating and damage.
**Cells with different EMFs:** when cells with different EMFs are connected in parallel, circulating currents flow between them. This can damage cells and should be avoided.
**Real cell behavior:** as a cell discharges, its EMF slowly decreases and its internal resistance increases. An old battery reads lower than its rated voltage even when not loaded.
confusion: EMF is not a force - it is a voltage (energy per unit charge). The name is historical. EMF is measured in volts, not newtons.

Terminal voltage $V = \\\\mathcal{E} - Ir$ is less than EMF when current flows out of the cell. But when charging the cell, current flows into the positive terminal, so $V = \\\\mathcal{E} + Ir$ - the terminal voltage is greater than EMF.
In series, both EMF and internal resistance add. In parallel, the equivalent EMF is the same as one cell, but the equivalent internal resistance is reduced, allowing more current.
Maximum power transfer ($R = r$) occurs at 50% efficiency. For efficient power delivery, you want $R \\\\gg r$ (high efficiency, low power). For maximum power, you sacrifice efficiency.
A fresh battery has a high open-circuit voltage (close to its EMF) but drops significantly under load if its internal resistance has increased with age. That is why old batteries seem weak.
practice: A cell with EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 $\\\Omega$ is connected to a 7 $\\\Omega$ resistor. Find the current, terminal voltage, and power delivered to the resistor. Solution: $I = 1.5/(7+0.5) = 0.2$ A. $V = 1.5 - 0.2 \	imes 0.5 = 1.4$ V. $P = I^2 R = 0.04 \	imes 7 = 0.28$ W.

A cell gives 2.0 V when no current flows and 1.8 V when delivering 1 A. Find the EMF and internal resistance. Solution: EMF $\mathcal{E} = 2.0$ V (open circuit). Under load: $1.8 = 2.0 - 1 \	imes r$, so $r = 0.2\\\\,$\Omega$.

Three identical cells of EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.3 $\\\Omega$ each are connected in series across a 6 $\\\Omega$ load. Find the current. Solution: $\mathcal{E}_{total} = 4.5$ V, $r_{total} = 0.9\\\\,$\Omega$. $I = 4.5/(6+0.9) = 0.652$ A.

The same three cells above are connected in parallel across the same 6 $\\\Omega$ load. Find the current. Solution: $\mathcal{E}_{total} = 1.5$ V, $r_{total} = 0.3/3 = 0.1\\\\,$\Omega$. $I = 1.5/(6+0.1) = 0.246$ A.

Find the external resistance for maximum power transfer to a cell with EMF 12 V and internal resistance 2 $\\\Omega$. Find the maximum power. Solution: $R = r = 2\\\\,$\Omega$. $I = 12/(2+2) = 3$ A. $P_{max} = I^2 R = 9 \	imes 2 = 18$ W. Alternatively $P_{max} = \\\\mathcal{E}^2/(4r) = 144/8 = 18$ W.
universalFacts: The internal resistance of a typical AA alkaline cell is about 0.15 $\\\Omega$ when fresh, but increases to 0.5 $\\\Omega$ or more as it discharges.
Connecting cells in series increases the available voltage while keeping the same current capacity. Connecting in parallel increases the current capacity while keeping the same voltage.
A short-circuited 12 V car battery with internal resistance 0.01 $\\\Omega$ can deliver 1200 A, which is why it can melt tools and cause severe burns.
The maximum power transfer theorem ($R = r$) is a fundamental design principle for matching loads to sources, but it is inefficient for power distribution systems where $R \\\\gg r$ is desired.
In a battery pack, series strings are often used to increase voltage, and parallel strings within each series group are used to increase capacity and reduce internal resistance.
specificConditions: **EMF vs Terminal Voltage:** EMF ($\mathcal{E}$) is the open-circuit voltage (no current). Terminal voltage $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$ under discharge; $V = \mathcal{E} + Ir$ during charging. The sign of the $Ir$ term depends on current direction.

**Series/Parallel Cell Rules:** In series: $\mathcal{E}_{total} = \sum \mathcal{E}_i$, $r_{total} = \sum r_i$. In parallel (identical cells): $\mathcal{E}_{total} = \mathcal{E}$, $r_{total} = r/n$. These assume no circulating currents between mismatched cells.

**Maximum Power Transfer Theorem:** Maximum power to load $R$ occurs at $R = r$, giving $P_{max} = \mathcal{E}^2/(4r)$. At this point, efficiency is 50%. For efficiency $>50\%$, need $R > r$; for $>90\%$, need $R > 9r$.

data.title: Work and Power in Electrical Circuits
data.topicTitle: Work and power in electrical circuits
notes: **Electrical work:** $W = VIt = I^2Rt = V^2t/R$. Work done by a current is the energy transferred.
**Electrical power:** $P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R$. Power is the rate of energy transfer.
**Joule heating:** $P = I^2R$ is the power dissipated as heat in a resistor. This is also called $I^2R$ loss.
**Kilowatt-hour:** unit of electrical energy. $1\\\\,\	ext{kWh} = 3.6 \	imes 10^6\\\\,\	ext{J}$. This is what electricity meters measure.
**Efficiency:** useful power output divided by total power input. Transmission lines use high voltage to reduce $I^2R$ losses because $P_{loss} \\\\propto I^2$.

**Power in different elements:** in a resistor, all electrical energy is converted to heat: $P = I^2R$. In a motor, electrical energy converts to mechanical work plus heat: $P_{input} = VI = I^2R + P_{mech}$. In a battery being charged, electrical energy is stored as chemical energy: $P_{input} = \\\\mathcal{E}I + I^2r$.

**Energy conservation in circuits:** the total electrical energy supplied equals the sum of energy dissipated as heat and energy converted to other forms: $V_{source} \\\\cdot I \\\\cdot t = I^2Rt + \	ext{other forms}$.
**Power rating of resistors:** resistors are rated by the maximum power they can dissipate without damage. Common ratings are 0.25 W, 0.5 W, and 1 W. Exceeding this causes overheating and failure.
**Domestic electrical cost:** the cost of running an appliance is $\	ext{Cost} = P(\	ext{kW}) \	imes t(\	ext{h}) \	imes \	ext{rate (per kWh)}$. A 100 W bulb running for 5 hours uses 0.5 kWh.
**Power factor:** for AC circuits, $P = VI\\\\cos\\\\phi$, where $\\\\cos\\\\phi$ is the power factor. For DC circuits, $\\\\cos\\\\phi = 1$, so $P = VI$ always.
**Heat energy in calories:** $H = 0.24 I^2 R t$ calories (mechanical equivalent of heat). In SI units, $H = I^2 R t$ joules.

confusion: Power $P = I^2R$ and $P = V^2/R$ are both correct but apply in different contexts. Use $I^2R$ when current is known (series circuits). Use $V^2/R$ when voltage is known (parallel circuits). Using the wrong one gives a wrong answer because $V$ and $I$ are not independent.
Electrical energy is measured in joules (J) or kilowatt-hours (kWh), NOT in watts (W). Watt is a unit of power (energy per time). $1\\\\,\	ext{kWh} = 3.6 \	imes 10^6$ J.

A 100 W bulb connected to 230 V draws less current than a 60 W bulb (because $I = P/V$, so the 100 W bulb has $I = 0.43$ A vs $I = 0.26$ A for the 60 W bulb). The 100 W bulb actually has LOWER resistance.

In a series circuit, the higher-wattage bulb glows dimmer because it has lower resistance, and in series the same current flows through both: $P = I^2R$, so the higher resistance (60 W bulb) gets more power.
Power dissipated in internal resistance ($I^2r$) is wasted energy. This is why battery-powered devices get warm - the internal resistance converts some chemical energy to heat instead of useful work.
practice: A 60 W, 230 V bulb is connected to a 230 V supply. Find the current, resistance, and energy consumed in 5 hours. Solution: $I = P/V = 60/230 = 0.261$ A. $R = V/I = 230/0.261 = 881\\\\,\\\\Omega$. $W = Pt = 60 \	imes 5 = 300\\\\,\	ext{Wh} = 0.3\\\\,\	ext{kWh} = 1.08 \	imes 10^6$ J.

A 12 V car headlamp draws 5 A. Find the power, resistance, and cost of running it for 4 hours at 8 pence per kWh. Solution: $P = VI = 12 \	imes 5 = 60$ W. $R = V/I = 12/5 = 2.4\\\\,\\\\Omega$. Energy $= 60 \	imes 4/1000 = 0.24\\\\,\	ext{kWh}$. Cost $= 0.24 \	imes 8 = 1.92$ pence.

A 100 $\\\Omega$ resistor carries a current of 2 A for 5 minutes. Find the heat produced in joules and calories. Solution: $H = I^2Rt = 4 \	imes 100 \	imes 300 = 120000$ J. In calories: $H = 120000/4.184 = 28681$ cal $\\\\approx 28.7$ kcal.

A transmission line carries 100 A at 11 kV over a total resistance of 5 $\\\Omega$. Find the power loss and the percentage of power lost. Solution: $P_{loss} = I^2R = 10000 \	imes 5 = 50000$ W $= 50$ kW. Power transmitted $= VI = 11000 \	imes 100 = 1.1 \	imes 10^6$ W $= 1100$ kW. Percentage loss $= 50/1100 = 4.5\\\\%$.

A 1.5 V cell with internal resistance 0.5 $\\\Omega$ is connected to a variable resistor. Find the resistance for maximum power transfer and the power delivered. Solution: $R = r = 0.5\\\\,\\\\Omega$. $I = 1.5/(0.5+0.5) = 1.5$ A. $P_{max} = I^2R = 2.25 \	imes 0.5 = 1.125$ W.
universalFacts: A 100 W incandescent bulb is only about 5% efficient - most electrical energy is converted to heat rather than visible light. LEDs are about 15-20% efficient but produce far more lumens per watt.

Electric transmission lines carry power at very high voltages (up to 765 kV) to minimize $I^2R$ losses. Halving the voltage doubles the current and quadruples the power loss, which is why high-voltage transmission is essential.
The unit of electrical energy consumption, the kilowatt-hour, is not an SI unit. The SI unit of energy is the joule: $1\\\\,\	ext{kWh} = 3.6 \	imes 10^6$ J.
A typical household circuit breaker is rated for 15-20 A at 120-240 V, giving a maximum power of 1.8-4.8 kW. Connecting too many high-power appliances can trip the breaker or cause a fire.
The heating effect of current was discovered by James Prescott Joule in 1841. His law $H = I^2Rt$ is a fundamental result of energy conservation in electrical circuits.
specificConditions: **Power Formula Context:** $P = I^2R$ is used when current is known (series circuits). $P = V^2/R$ is used when voltage is known (parallel circuits). Both are derived from $P = VI$ and Ohm's law; using the wrong one gives incorrect results because $V$ and $I$ are coupled through $R$.

**Joule Heating is Irreversible:** The power $P = I^2R$ dissipated in a resistor represents an irreversible conversion of electrical energy to heat. It cannot be recovered within the circuit. This is distinct from energy stored in inductors/capacitors or converted to mechanical work.

**Energy Units:** Electrical energy is measured in joules (SI) or kilowatt-hours (practical). $1 	ext{ kWh} = 3.6 	imes 10^6 	ext{ J}$. Power (watts) is the *rate* of energy transfer, not energy itself.

data.title: Pure Spectrum and Dispersive Power
notes: A prism forms a spectrum because refractive index varies with wavelength. In normal dispersion, violet has a larger index and deviation than red. A pure spectrum has narrow, well-separated colour images with little overlap.
For a thin prism, angular dispersion is Δδ=(nv−nr)A and yellow mean deviation is δy=(ny−1)A. Their ratio is ω=Δδ/δy=(nv−nr)/(ny−1).
Worked example: if δy=3° and ω=0.06, the red–violet spread is Δδ=0.18°. A material with twice the dispersive power gives twice the spread at the same mean deviation.
To obtain a purer spectrum, use a narrow slit, collimate the incident beam and focus the dispersed rays with a lens. A wide slit broadens each colour image and causes neighbouring bands to overlap.
A spectrometer uses a collimator slit and telescope to form and inspect a sharp spectrum. Resolution improves when the source image is narrow and the optical alignment is correct.

A pure spectrum is formed when each colour is brought to its own sharp image and those images do not overlap. A slit at the focus of a collimating lens sends parallel light into the prism, and a telescope then focuses each colour separately.

data.title: Chromatic and Spherical Aberration
notes: Chromatic aberration is colour fringing caused by a lens having different focal lengths for different wavelengths. In ordinary glass, blue/violet light is refracted more strongly than red, so their images do not share one focus.

Longitudinal chromatic aberration is the axial separation Δf=|fv−fr| of two colour foci. Transverse chromatic aberration is a wavelength-dependent lateral image displacement, often visible at the edge of a wide field.

Spherical aberration has a different cause: marginal and paraxial rays of the same colour focus at different points because the surface is spherical. It can be reduced with an aperture stop or aspheric surfaces.
Worked comparison: if red focuses at 50.0 cm and blue at 49.0 cm, longitudinal chromatic aberration is 1.0 cm. This is axial focus separation, not a 1 cm sideways image shift.
An achromatic doublet pairs converging crown glass with diverging flint glass so two selected colours focus together. Stopping down reduces marginal-ray error but does not remove material dispersion.

A single lens focuses violet closer to the lens than red, because violet has the higher index and a shorter focal length. The gap between those foci along the axis is the longitudinal chromatic aberration, about ω times the mean focal length.

data.title: Achromatism
notes: An optical pair is achromatic for two chosen colours when their wavelength-dependent deviations cancel and both colours share a final focus. The lenses remain dispersive individually; their effects compensate.

For two thin lenses in contact with signed focal lengths f1,f2 and dispersive powers ω1,ω2, primary achromatism requires ω1/f1+ω2/f2=0. A crown converging lens is commonly paired with a more dispersive flint diverging lens.
Worked design: f1=+20 cm, ω1=0.02 and ω2=0.04 require 0.02/20+0.04/f2=0, giving f2=−40 cm. The negative sign identifies a diverging flint element.
The net power is 1/F=1/f1+1/f2, so the doublet can remain converging while cancelling colour spread. Camera, telescope and microscope objectives use achromatic groups to reduce coloured fringes.
Primary achromatism corrects two selected wavelengths; other colours may still form a secondary spectrum. More elaborate apochromatic systems correct additional wavelengths.

The contact condition uses powers, so the dispersive powers are divided by the focal lengths. If the two lenses are separated by a distance, the condition changes and a Huygens eyepiece uses that separated arrangement. Quoting the contact rule for a separated pair gives the wrong flint lens.
