data.title: Linear Momentum and Impulse

notes: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version emphasises the momentum form of Newton's second law and the impulse–momentum theorem with force–time graphs — the framing NEB theory questions use.

**Impulsive Force:** A force that acts for a very short time but produces a finite change in momentum. Examples: hammer hitting a nail, bat hitting a ball, foot kicking a football. The force is extremely large, often thousands of Newtons, but the duration is milliseconds. The impulse is the area under the force-time curve, $J = \int F dt$.

**Linear momentum:** $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$ — mass in motion, SI unit kg·m/s. It is a VECTOR along the velocity. A 1 kg ball at 10 m/s and a 10 kg cart at 1 m/s carry equal momentum but very different kinetic energies ($\frac{1}{2}mv^2$: 50 J vs 5 J). Momentum is a measure of the 'difficulty' to stop an object. It is the 'inertia of motion'.

**Physical Significance:** Momentum is fundamentally linked to the translational symmetry of space (Noether's theorem). In quantum mechanics, momentum is related to the wave vector $k$ by $p = \hbar k$.
**Conservation:** Momentum is conserved in any system where the net external force is zero. This is a universal law, holding from subatomic particles to galactic collisions.

**Newton's second law in momentum form:** $\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \dfrac{d(m\vec{v})}{dt}$. For constant mass this reduces to $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$ — but the momentum form is the GENERAL law and is the version that stays valid for variable-mass systems (rockets).

**Impulse:** $\vec{J} = \vec{F}\,\Delta t$ for a constant force, and $\vec{J} = \int \vec{F}\,dt$ in general — the AREA under a force–time graph. Impulse has units N·s = kg·m/s, the same as momentum — by design.

**Impulse–momentum theorem:** $\vec{J} = \Delta\vec{p} = m\vec{v}_f - m\vec{v}_i$. Any desired momentum change can be had with a LARGE force for a short time or a SMALL force for a long time — the product is what matters.

**Why airbags/crumple zones work:** to stop a passenger, $\Delta p$ is fixed by the crash; extending the collision time $\Delta t$ cuts the average force $F_{avg} = \Delta p/\Delta t$. Bending your knees on landing, catching a cricket ball with draw-back hands, and jumping with flexed legs are all the same physics.

**Worked example:** a 0.15 kg cricket ball at 30 m/s is stopped in 0.1 s. $\Delta p = 0.15 \times 30 = 4.5$ kg·m/s → $F_{avg} = 45$ N. If caught in 0.02 s: 225 N — five times the force from the same momentum change.

**Variable force:** when $F(t)$ is a curve, impulse is the area under it; for $F = F_0 e^{-t/\tau}$-style impacts, $J = F_0\tau$. NEB usually gives triangular or rectangular force–time pulses — count the areas.

**NEB exam focus:** define momentum and impulse with units; state and use $F = dp/dt$; compute impulse from force–time graphs; apply $J = \Delta p$ to catches, kicks and landings; explain safety devices via the force–time argument.
confusion: ❌ 'Momentum and kinetic energy are interchangeable measures of motion.' ✅ Momentum $mv$ is a vector conserved in ALL collisions; kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ is a scalar conserved only in elastic ones. Both grow with speed but differently.
❌ 'Impulse equals force.' ✅ Impulse = force × time (or the area under $F$–$t$). A small force acting long can deliver a huge impulse.

❌ 'The ball exerts no force on the bat while being hit because the bat is harder.' ✅ Newton's third law: contact forces are equal and opposite during the collision — the ball's velocity change comes from the contact force acting on IT.
❌ 'A heavy object always has more momentum.' ✅ Momentum = mass × VELOCITY — a light fast bullet can out-momentum a heavy slow trolley; direction matters too.
❌ Using $F = ma$ for a rocket ejecting fuel. ✅ Mass changes with time, so $F = ma$ fails; the momentum form $F = dp/dt$ handles it and yields the rocket equation.
❌ Impulse has units of newtons. ✅ N·s (= kg·m/s) — momentum units. Dimensionally $[MLT^{-1}]$.
practice: A 60 kg runner at 8 m/s is stopped in 0.5 s. Find the impulse and the average force. — $J = 480$ kg·m/s; $F = 960$ N.
A 0.5 kg ball hits a wall at 12 m/s and rebounds at 8 m/s. Find the impulse. — $\Delta p = 0.5(8+12) = 10$ kg·m/s BACKWARD (note the sign reversal!).
From a triangular $F$–$t$ pulse peaking at 400 N over 0.02 s, find the impulse delivered to a 0.2 kg ball at rest. — Area $= \frac{1}{2}(0.02)(400) = 4$ N·s → $v = 20$ m/s.
A 1000 kg car at 20 m/s crashes into a barrier that stops it in 0.4 s. Find the average force, and compare with a crumple-zone stop in 1.0 s. — 50 kN vs 20 kN.
A machine-gun fires 30 g bullets at 400 m/s, 10 per second. Find the average recoil force. — $F = n\,mv = 10 \times 12 = 120$ N.
universalFacts: Airbags, crumple zones, helmets and safety nets are all impulse engineering: stretch the stopping time, cut the peak force, keep $\Delta p$ fixed.
The impulse–momentum theorem explains why follow-through matters in sports — prolonging contact time increases delivered impulse and exit speed.
Rocketry is continuous impulse: each second, expelling mass $dm$ at exhaust speed $v_e$ gives thrust $v_e\,dm/dt$ — momentum conservation making spaceflight possible.
Karate masters break boards by maximising $\Delta p$ in minimum $\Delta t$: peak contact forces of thousands of newtons in a few milliseconds.
The concept of 'impulse' is crucial in collision theory, where the duration of contact is often too short to measure the force directly, but the change in momentum is easily observed.
In relativistic mechanics, momentum is defined as $\vec{p} = \gamma m\vec{v}$, where $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}$. At low speeds, $\gamma \approx 1$, and it reduces to the classical $m\vec{v}$.
**Fluid Impulse:** A jet of water hitting a wall exerts a force $F = \dot{m} v$, where $\dot{m}$ is the mass flow rate (kg/s). This is the principle behind Pelton wheels and jet engines.

**Impulse-Momentum Theorem:** $\vec{J} = \Delta \vec{p}$. This theorem is the foundation for analyzing collisions, explosions, and recoil. It allows us to relate the force-time history of a collision to the change in velocity of the objects involved.
examples: Example 1 (recoil): a 5 kg rifle fires a 20 g bullet at 300 m/s — recoil speed $= \frac{0.02 \times 300}{5} = 1.2$ m/s backward.
Example 2 (kicking): a footballer gives a 0.45 kg ball at rest a speed of 20 m/s in 0.05 s — impulse 9 N·s, average force 180 N.
Example 3 (graph): a rectangular $F$–$t$ pulse of 250 N lasting 0.04 s delivers $J = 10$ N·s — a 2 kg cart leaves at 5 m/s.
Example 4 (safety): the same 4000 kg·m/s car momentum change stopped in 0.1 s (rigid wall) means 40 kN; in 0.5 s (crumple zone) only 8 kN — five times gentler.
Example 5 (jump landing): a 60 kg jumper hitting the ground at 6 m/s stops in 0.3 s with stiff legs (1200 N extra) vs 0.9 s with bent knees (400 N extra).
practiceQuestions: Q1. Define linear momentum and impulse, and state the relation between them.
Q2. Show that Newton's second law can be written as $F = dp/dt$ and state when this reduces to $F = ma$.
Q3. A 0.3 kg ball moving at 15 m/s is hit back along the same path at 25 m/s. Find the impulse delivered.
Q4. Explain, using the impulse–momentum theorem, why a crumple zone reduces injury in a crash.
Q5. From a given force–time graph (triangle), determine the final velocity of the struck body.
Q6. A 2 kg object is subjected to a force $F = 10t$ N. Find the change in momentum in 3 seconds.
Q7. Compare the impulse delivered by a constant force of 10 N for 5 s and a force $F = 2t$ for 5 s.
formulas: Momentum: $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$  [kg·m/s]
Second law (general): $\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$; constant mass: $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$
Impulse (constant force): $\vec{J} = \vec{F}\Delta t$; general: $\vec{J} = \int \vec{F}\,dt$ (area under $F$–$t$)
Impulse–momentum theorem: $\vec{J} = \Delta\vec{p} = m\vec{v}_f - m\vec{v}_i$
Average force: $F_{avg} = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$
keyPoints: Momentum is a vector — always assign signs/directions before computing $\Delta p$.
Impulse and momentum share units (N·s = kg·m/s); impulse is the area under the force–time graph.
For a FIXED momentum change, force and time trade off: $F_{avg} = \Delta p/\Delta t$.
$F = dp/dt$ is the general second law — essential for variable-mass (rocket) problems.
Momentum conservation holds in all collisions; kinetic energy only in elastic ones.
Recoil problems are momentum bookkeeping: $M V + m v = 0$ from rest.
enrichedContent.summary: Linear momentum $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$ measures 'quantity of motion'. Newton's second law in its general form is $\vec{F} = d\vec{p}/dt$, and integrating it over a collision interval gives the impulse–momentum theorem $\vec{J} = \int F\,dt = \Delta\vec{p}$ — impulse is the area under the force–time graph. Because a given momentum change can come from a big force briefly or a small force slowly, safety design (airbags, crumple zones, bent knees) is the art of stretching $\Delta t$. Recoil, ball games and rocket thrust are all direct applications.
specialNotes: Note 1: In rebound problems the velocity CHANGES SIGN — $\Delta p = m(v_f + v_i)$, not the difference. The commonest numerical error.
Note 2: Quote impulse in N·s and momentum in kg·m/s — numerically identical, and examiners check units.
Note 3: For force–time graphs, rectangular pulses are $F\Delta t$; triangular pulses are $\frac{1}{2}F_{max}\Delta t$.
Note 4: When a question says 'average force', it means $\Delta p/\Delta t$ — the constant force delivering the same impulse.
importantStatements: Statement 1: The linear momentum of a body is the product of its mass and velocity — a vector along the velocity.
Statement 2: The rate of change of momentum of a body equals the net force acting on it (general form of Newton's second law).
Statement 3: Impulse of a force is the product of the force and the time for which it acts, equal to the change in momentum produced.
Statement 4: For a fixed momentum change, the average force is inversely proportional to the collision time.
importantNotes: Note 1: Impulse units (N·s) and momentum units (kg·m/s) are identical — that is the theorem speaking.
Note 2: Momentum is directional: a rebound doubles the magnitude change versus a stop at the same speeds.
Note 3: The momentum form $F = dp/dt$ remains valid when mass varies (rockets, leaking trucks) where $F = ma$ fails.
Note 4: Force–time graph areas: rectangle = $F\Delta t$; triangle = $\frac{1}{2}F_{max}\Delta t$.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: Rebounds: add the speeds in $\Delta p = m(v_f + v_i)$ — sign flip doubles the effect.
Trick 2: 'Soft landing' MCQs: longer $\Delta t$ ⇒ smaller $F$ ⇒ pick the option that stretches the time.
Trick 3: Recoil from rest: $V = mv/M$ instantly, with $V$ opposite the bullet.
Trick 4: Machine-gun/stream problems: average force = mass flow rate × exit speed ($n\,mv$).
Trick 5: If a force–time curve has no nice shape, the answer is still its AREA — estimate with boxes if needed.
Trick 6: Impulsive force problems: always look for the 'short time' keyword — it implies $F_{avg} = \Delta p/\Delta t$ is the intended approach.
examNotes: Exam Tip 1: Theory answers should state BOTH $J = F\Delta t$ and $J = \Delta p$ and connect them — one-line answers lose marks.
Exam Tip 2: In numericals, convert grams to kg and quote directions ('opposite to initial motion') with magnitudes.
Exam Tip 3: Graph-reading impulse questions: label the base and height you used to compute the area.
Exam Tip 4: Safety-device explanations score full marks only with the chain: fixed $\Delta p$ → longer $\Delta t$ → smaller $F_{avg}$.

**Impulse–momentum theorem:** $\vec{J} = \Delta\vec{p} = m\vec{v}_f - m\vec{v}_i$. Any desired momentum change can be had with a LARGE force for a short time or a SMALL force for a long time — the product is what matters.

**Why airbags/crumple zones work:** to stop a passenger, $\Delta p$ is fixed by the crash; extending the collision time $\Delta t$ cuts the average force $F_{avg} = \Delta p/\Delta t$. **Worked example:** a 0.15 kg cricket ball at 30 m/s is stopped in 0.1 s. $\Delta p = 0.15 \times 30 = 4.5$ kg·m/s → $F_{avg} = 45$ N. If caught in 0.02 s: 225 N — five times the force from the same momentum change.

**Variable force:** when $F(t)$ is a curve, impulse is the area under it; for $F = F_0 e^{-t/\tau}$-style impacts, $J = F_0\tau$. NEB usually gives triangular or rectangular force–time pulses — count the areas.

data.title: Conservation of Linear Momentum

notes: **Law of Conservation of Linear Momentum:** In an isolated system (no external net force), the total linear momentum remains constant: $\sum \vec{p}_i = \sum \vec{p}_f$. This is a fundamental law derived from the homogeneity of space (Noether's theorem). It is a direct consequence of the fact that the laws of physics are the same at all points in space.

**Isolated System:** A system where the net external force is zero. Internal forces (like collision forces) do not change the total momentum because they act in equal and opposite pairs (Newton's 3rd law). The system can be as small as two colliding particles or as large as the entire universe.

**Coefficient of Restitution (e):** A measure of elasticity in collisions: $e = (v_2 - v_1) / (u_1 - u_2)$. $e=1$ (perfectly elastic), $0 < e < 1$ (inelastic), $e=0$ (perfectly inelastic). This coefficient depends on the materials of the colliding objects and their surface properties.
**Collisions:** Events where momentum is conserved. Elastic collisions also conserve kinetic energy; inelastic collisions do not (energy is lost to heat, sound, deformation).
**Explosions:** A reverse collision where an object breaks apart. Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy increases (internal energy is converted to motion).
**Recoil:** A classic application. A gun firing a bullet: $M_g V_g + m_b v_b = 0$ (initially at rest).
**NEB exam focus:** State the law; apply it to 1D and 2D collisions; distinguish between elastic and inelastic collisions; solve recoil and explosion problems.
confusion: ❌ 'Momentum is conserved only in elastic collisions.' ✅ Momentum is conserved in ALL collisions (elastic or inelastic) as long as the system is isolated.
❌ 'Kinetic energy is always conserved in collisions.' ✅ Only in perfectly elastic collisions. In inelastic collisions, KE is lost.
❌ 'Internal forces change the total momentum.' ✅ Internal forces (like collision forces) cancel out in pairs (Newton's 3rd law) and do not change the total momentum of the system.
❌ 'Conservation of momentum applies to individual objects.' ✅ It applies to the SYSTEM of objects.

A 5 kg rifle fires a 20 g bullet at 400 m/s. Find the recoil velocity. — $v = 1.6$ m/s.
A 1000 kg car at 10 m/s hits a 2000 kg truck at rest. If they stick, find the final speed. — $v = 3.33$ m/s.
universalFacts: The law of conservation of momentum is one of the fundamental laws of physics, derived from the homogeneity of space (Noether's theorem).

specificConditions: **Isolated System Requirement:** Momentum conservation ($\sum \vec{p}_i = \sum \vec{p}_f$) holds strictly only when the net *external* force on the system is zero. External forces like gravity, friction, or applied pushes must be absent or balanced.

**Collisions vs. Continuous Interaction:** In a collision, the interaction is brief and impulsive; internal forces dominate. In continuous interactions (e.g., rocket propulsion), momentum is conserved at each instant, but mass changes must be tracked using the variable-mass form $F = dp/dt$.

**Kinetic Energy Distinction:** Momentum is conserved in *all* isolated collisions (elastic or inelastic). Kinetic energy is conserved *only* in perfectly elastic collisions. In inelastic collisions, some KE is converted to heat, sound, or deformation energy.

notes: **Law of Conservation of Linear Momentum:** In an isolated system (no external net force), the total linear momentum remains constant: $\sum \vec{p}_i = \sum \vec{p}_f$. This is a fundamental law derived from the homogeneity of space (Noether's theorem). It is a direct consequence of the fact that the laws of physics are the same at all points in space.

**Isolated System:** A system where the net external force is zero. Internal forces (like collision forces) do not change the total momentum because they act in equal and opposite pairs (Newton's 3rd law). The system can be as small as two colliding particles or as large as the entire universe.

**Coefficient of Restitution (e):** A measure of elasticity in collisions: $e = (v_2 - v_1) / (u_1 - u_2)$. $e=1$ (perfectly elastic), $0 < e < 1$ (inelastic), $e=0$ (perfectly inelastic). This coefficient depends on the materials of the colliding objects and their surface properties.
**Collisions:** Events where momentum is conserved. Elastic collisions also conserve kinetic energy; inelastic collisions do not (energy is lost to heat, sound, deformation).
**Explosions:** A reverse collision where an object breaks apart. Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy increases (internal energy is converted to motion).
**Recoil:** A classic application. A gun firing a bullet: $M_g V_g + m_b v_b = 0$ (initially at rest).
**NEB exam focus:** State the law; apply it to 1D and 2D collisions; distinguish between elastic and inelastic collisions; solve recoil and explosion problems.

**Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version derives the conservation law from Newton's third law and the impulse picture, then applies it to recoil, explosions and two-body systems — the application chain NEB numericals follow.

**The law:** if the net EXTERNAL force on a system is zero, its total linear momentum stays constant: $m_1\vec{u}_1 + m_2\vec{u}_2 = m_1\vec{v}_1 + m_2\vec{v}_2$. Internal forces (the pair between the two bodies) can change individual momenta but never the total.

**Why it holds (third-law derivation):** during contact, body 1 pushes body 2 with $\vec{F}_{12}$ and body 2 pushes back $\vec{F}_{21} = -\vec{F}_{12}$ for the SAME time $\Delta t$. Impulses: $\Delta\vec{p}_1 = \vec{F}_{21}\Delta t$ and $\Delta\vec{p}_2 = \vec{F}_{12}\Delta t$; adding gives $\Delta(\vec{p}_1 + \vec{p}_2) = (\vec{F}_{21} + \vec{F}_{12})\Delta t = 0$ — the total momentum cannot change.

**When it applies:** always for INTERNAL interactions; for the whole system even during explosions and collisions (internal forces are huge compared to external ones over the short interaction). Gravity/friction are external — momentum is conserved only along directions with zero net external force.

**Recoil (from rest):** initial momentum zero → $M\vec{V} + m\vec{v} = 0$, so $\vec{V} = -\dfrac{m}{M}\vec{v}$. Cannon–ball, rifle–bullet, rocket–exhaust, boat–passenger: the lighter body carries proportionally more speed.

**Explosions and separations:** a body of mass $(m_1 + m_2)$ at rest splits into pieces moving in opposite directions: $m_1 v_1 = m_2 v_2$. Kinetic energy is NOT conserved here (chemical energy converts to motion) — momentum alone is the reliable bookkeeper.

**Worked example:** a 60 kg skater at rest throws a 3 kg ball at 8 m/s. Recoil: $V = \frac{3 \times 8}{60} = 0.4$ m/s backward. If thrown at 30° above horizontal, only the horizontal component ($8\cos30°$) enters the horizontal recoil balance.

**Collision bookkeeping:** in ANY collision (elastic or not) total momentum is conserved: $m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = m_1v_1 + m_2v_2$ (1-D). Two unknowns need a second equation — kinetic energy (elastic) or the coefficient of restitution $e = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{u_1 - u_2}$.

**NEB exam focus:** state the law with its condition (no net external force); derive it from the third law; solve recoil and explosion numericals; explain rocket propulsion and the gun recoil by momentum conservation.

data.title: Conservation of Linear Momentum

notes: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version emphasises the momentum form of Newton's second law and the impulse–momentum theorem with force–time graphs — the framing NEB theory questions use.

**Linear momentum:** $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$ — mass in motion, SI unit kg·m/s. It is a VECTOR along the velocity. A 1 kg ball at 10 m/s and a 10 kg cart at 1 m/s carry equal momentum but very different kinetic energies ($\frac{1}{2}mv^2$: 50 J vs 5 J).

**Newton's second law in momentum form:** $\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \dfrac{d(m\vec{v})}{dt}$. For constant mass this reduces to $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$ — but the momentum form is the GENERAL law and is the version that stays valid for variable-mass systems (rockets).

**Impulse:** $\vec{J} = \vec{F}\,\Delta t$ for a constant force, and $\vec{J} = \int \vec{F}\,dt$ in general — the AREA under a force–time graph. Impulse has units N·s = kg·m/s, the same as momentum — by design.

**Impulse–momentum theorem:** $\vec{J} = \Delta\vec{p} = m\vec{v}_f - m\vec{v}_i$. Any desired momentum change can be had with a LARGE force for a short time or a SMALL force for a long time — the product is what matters.

**Why airbags/crumple zones work:** to stop a passenger, $\Delta p$ is fixed by the crash; extending the collision time $\Delta t$ cuts the average force $F_{avg} = \Delta p/\Delta t$. Bending your knees on landing, catching a cricket ball with draw-back hands, and jumping with flexed legs are all the same physics.

**Worked example:** a 0.15 kg cricket ball at 30 m/s is stopped in 0.1 s. $\Delta p = 0.15 \times 30 = 4.5$ kg·m/s → $F_{avg} = 45$ N. If caught in 0.02 s: 225 N — five times the force from the same momentum change.

**Variable force:** when $F(t)$ is a curve, impulse is the area under it; for $F = F_0 e^{-t/\tau}$-style impacts, $J = F_0\tau$. NEB usually gives triangular or rectangular force–time pulses — count the areas.

**NEB exam focus:** define momentum and impulse with units; state and use $F = dp/dt$; compute impulse from force–time graphs; apply $J = \Delta p$ to catches, kicks and landings; explain safety devices via the force–time argument.
confusion: ❌ 'Momentum and kinetic energy are interchangeable measures of motion.' ✅ Momentum $mv$ is a vector conserved in ALL collisions; kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ is a scalar conserved only in elastic ones. Both grow with speed but differently.
❌ 'Impulse equals force.' ✅ Impulse = force × time (or the area under $F$–$t$). A small force acting long can deliver a huge impulse.

❌ 'The ball exerts no force on the bat while being hit because the bat is harder.' ✅ Newton's third law: contact forces are equal and opposite during the collision — the ball's velocity change comes from the contact force acting on IT.
❌ 'A heavy object always has more momentum.' ✅ Momentum = mass × VELOCITY — a light fast bullet can out-momentum a heavy slow trolley; direction matters too.
❌ Using $F = ma$ for a rocket ejecting fuel. ✅ Mass changes with time, so $F = ma$ fails; the momentum form $F = dp/dt$ handles it and yields the rocket equation.
❌ Impulse has units of newtons. ✅ N·s (= kg·m/s) — momentum units. Dimensionally $[MLT^{-1}]$.
practice: A 60 kg runner at 8 m/s is stopped in 0.5 s. Find the impulse and the average force. — $J = 480$ kg·m/s; $F = 960$ N.
A 0.5 kg ball hits a wall at 12 m/s and rebounds at 8 m/s. Find the impulse. — $\Delta p = 0.5(8+12) = 10$ kg·m/s BACKWARD (note the sign reversal!).
From a triangular $F$–$t$ pulse peaking at 400 N over 0.02 s, find the impulse delivered to a 0.2 kg ball at rest. — Area $= \frac{1}{2}(0.02)(400) = 4$ N·s → $v = 20$ m/s.
A 1000 kg car at 20 m/s crashes into a barrier that stops it in 0.4 s. Find the average force, and compare with a crumple-zone stop in 1.0 s. — 50 kN vs 20 kN.
A machine-gun fires 30 g bullets at 400 m/s, 10 per second. Find the average recoil force. — $F = n\,mv = 10 \times 12 = 120$ N.
universalFacts: Airbags, crumple zones, helmets and safety nets are all impulse engineering: stretch the stopping time, cut the peak force, keep $\Delta p$ fixed.
The impulse–momentum theorem explains why follow-through matters in sports — prolonging contact time increases delivered impulse and exit speed.
Rocketry is continuous impulse: each second, expelling mass $dm$ at exhaust speed $v_e$ gives thrust $v_e\,dm/dt$ — momentum conservation making spaceflight possible.
Karate masters break boards by maximising $\Delta p$ in minimum $\Delta t$: peak contact forces of thousands of newtons in a few milliseconds.
examples: Example 1 (recoil): a 5 kg rifle fires a 20 g bullet at 300 m/s — recoil speed $= \frac{0.02 \times 300}{5} = 1.2$ m/s backward.
Example 2 (kicking): a footballer gives a 0.45 kg ball at rest a speed of 20 m/s in 0.05 s — impulse 9 N·s, average force 180 N.
Example 3 (graph): a rectangular $F$–$t$ pulse of 250 N lasting 0.04 s delivers $J = 10$ N·s — a 2 kg cart leaves at 5 m/s.
Example 4 (safety): the same 4000 kg·m/s car momentum change stopped in 0.1 s (rigid wall) means 40 kN; in 0.5 s (crumple zone) only 8 kN — five times gentler.
Example 5 (jump landing): a 60 kg jumper hitting the ground at 6 m/s stops in 0.3 s with stiff legs (1200 N extra) vs 0.9 s with bent knees (400 N extra).

notes: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version emphasises the momentum form of Newton's second law and the impulse–momentum theorem with force–time graphs — the framing NEB theory questions use.

**Linear momentum:** $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$ — mass in motion, SI unit kg·m/s. It is a VECTOR along the velocity. A 1 kg ball at 10 m/s and a 10 kg cart at 1 m/s carry equal momentum but very different kinetic energies ($\frac{1}{2}mv^2$: 50 J vs 5 J).

**Newton's second law in momentum form:** $\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \dfrac{d(m\vec{v})}{dt}$. For constant mass this reduces to $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$ — but the momentum form is the GENERAL law and is the version that stays valid for variable-mass systems (rockets).

**Impulse:** $\vec{J} = \vec{F}\,\Delta t$ for a constant force, and $\vec{J} = \int \vec{F}\,dt$ in general — the AREA under a force–time graph. Impulse has units N·s = kg·m/s, the same as momentum — by design.

**Impulse–momentum theorem:** $\vec{J} = \Delta\vec{p} = m\vec{v}_f - m\vec{v}_i$. Any desired momentum change can be had with a LARGE force for a short time or a SMALL force for a long time — the product is what matters.

**Why airbags/crumple zones work:** to stop a passenger, $\Delta p$ is fixed by the crash; extending the collision time $\Delta t$ cuts the average force $F_{avg} = \Delta p/\Delta t$. Bending your knees on landing, catching a cricket ball with draw-back hands, and jumping with flexed legs are all the same physics.

**Worked example:** a 0.15 kg cricket ball at 30 m/s is stopped in 0.1 s. $\Delta p = 0.15 \times 30 = 4.5$ kg·m/s → $F_{avg} = 45$ N. If caught in 0.02 s: 225 N — five times the force from the same momentum change.

**Variable force:** when $F(t)$ is a curve, impulse is the area under it; for $F = F_0 e^{-t/\tau}$-style impacts, $J = F_0\tau$. NEB usually gives triangular or rectangular force–time pulses — count the areas.

**NEB exam focus:** define momentum and impulse with units; state and use $F = dp/dt$; compute impulse from force–time graphs; apply $J = \Delta p$ to catches, kicks and landings; explain safety devices via the force–time argument.

❌ 'Impulse equals force.' ✅ Impulse = force × time (or the area under $F$–$t$). A small force acting long can deliver a huge impulse.

specificConditions: **Isolated System Requirement:** Momentum conservation ($\sum \vec{p}_i = \sum \vec{p}_f$) holds strictly only when the net *external* force on the system is zero. External forces like gravity, friction, or applied pushes must be absent or balanced.

**Collisions vs. Continuous Interaction:** In a collision, the interaction is brief and impulsive; internal forces dominate. In continuous interactions (e.g., rocket propulsion), momentum is conserved at each instant, but mass changes must be tracked using the variable-mass form $F = dp/dt$.

**Kinetic Energy Distinction:** Momentum is conserved in *all* isolated collisions (elastic or inelastic). Kinetic energy is conserved *only* in perfectly elastic collisions. In inelastic collisions, some KE is converted to heat, sound, or deformation energy.

Because a given momentum change can come from a big force briefly or a small force slowly, safety design (airbags, crumple zones, bent knees) is the art of stretching $\Delta t$. Recoil, ball games and rocket thrust are all direct applications.

data.title: Application of Newton's Laws

notes: **The problem-solving framework (the 'FBD method'):** (1) isolate the body, (2) draw ALL forces acting ON it (weight, normal, friction, tension, applied), (3) choose axes (one along acceleration), (4) write $ΣF = ma$ for each axis, (5) solve. Every single NEB numerical follows this pattern.

**Elevator weight paradox:** in an accelerating upward elevator, the normal force $N = m(g + a)$ — you feel heavier. Accelerating downward: $N = m(g - a)$ — you feel lighter. Free fall ($a = g$): $N = 0$ (weightlessness). The weight $mg$ never changes; what changes is the apparent weight (the normal force).

**Atwood's machine (two masses on a pulley):** acceleration $a = \frac{(m_1 - m_2)g}{m_1 + m_2}$; tension $T = \frac{2m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2}$. The string is massless and inextensible; the pulley is frictionless — if not, extra terms appear.

**Connected bodies (push and pull):** a single force F applied to a system of masses (m₁, m₂, m₃) gives $a = \frac{F}{m_1 + m_2 + m_3}$. The contact force between $m_1$ and $m_2$ is the force needed to accelerate the trailing masses: $N = (m_2 + m_3) \times a$.

**Inclined plane:** weight components: mg sin θ down the slope, mg cos θ into the plane. Normal N = mg cos θ. With friction: net force down slope = $mg \sin\theta - \mu mg \cos\theta$. The body slides when $\sin\theta > \mu \cos\theta$, i.e., $\tan\theta > \mu$ — the critical angle depends only on $\mu$, NOT on mass.

**Non-inertial frames and pseudo-forces:** When analyzing motion from an accelerating frame (e.g., inside an accelerating car), Newton's laws require the addition of a 'pseudo-force' $F_p = -ma_{frame}$ to account for the frame's acceleration. This force is not real (no agent), but it makes the math work.
**Static vs. Kinetic Friction:** Static friction $f_s \le \mu_s N$ acts when there is no relative motion; kinetic friction $f_k = \mu_k N$ acts when sliding occurs. Always \mu_s > \mu_k.
**Worked example:** a 5 kg block on a 30° rough slope (μ = 0.3) — does it slide? tan 30° = 0.577 > 0.3 → yes. Acceleration: a = g(sin 30° − 0.3 cos 30°) = 9.8(0.5 − 0.26) = 2.35 m/s² down the slope.

**Apparent weight in fluids:** an object submerged in a liquid appears lighter by the buoyant force (Archimedes): apparent weight = mg − ρVg. This is still a Newton's second law application: ΣF = mg − ρVg = ma.

**NEB exam focus:** elevator problems, Atwood's machine, connected bodies on horizontal surfaces, inclined plane with/without friction, apparent weight in accelerating systems — all use the same FBD → ΣF = ma framework.
confusion: ❌ 'The normal force is always mg.' ✅ N = mg only on a horizontal surface with no vertical acceleration. On a slope N = mg cos θ; in an accelerating elevator N = m(g ± a).

❌ 'Friction always opposes motion.' ✅ Friction opposes RELATIVE motion (or its tendency). Static friction can act in the direction of motion — e.g., the static friction on your feet pushes you forward when walking.
❌ 'The tension in a string equals the weight of the hanging mass.' ✅ Only if the system is in equilibrium. In an accelerating Atwood's machine, T ≠ mg — use ΣF = ma on each mass to find T.
❌ 'Action and reaction forces cancel each other.' ✅ They act on DIFFERENT bodies, so they never cancel in a single FBD. Include only forces acting ON the body you are analyzing.
❌ 'Heavier bodies slide slower down a slope.' ✅ a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ) has no mass term — all bodies slide at the same rate (if μ is the same), just like free fall.
❌ 'A body at rest has no forces acting on it.' ✅ Static equilibrium means ΣF = 0, not zero forces — weight and normal (and possibly friction and tension) all act, they just balance.

**NEB exam focus:** elevator problems, Atwood's machine, connected bodies on horizontal surfaces, inclined plane with/without friction, apparent weight in accelerating systems — all use the same FBD → ΣF = ma framework.

**Newton's First Law (Inertia):** a body remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by an external force. Inertia is the resistance to change in motion, quantified by mass. Mass is the measure of inertia — more massive objects are harder to accelerate.

**Newton's Second Law:** $\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$. The acceleration of a body is directly proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to its mass. In the form $\vec{F} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$, it is valid even when mass changes (e.g., rockets).

**Newton's Third Law:** for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. $\vec{F}_{AB} = -\vec{F}_{BA}$. Action and reaction forces act on DIFFERENT bodies, so they never cancel each other in a free-body diagram of a single body.

**Free-body diagrams:** the key tool for applying Newton's laws. Draw the body of interest and show ALL forces acting ON it (not forces it exerts on others). Common forces: weight $mg$, normal reaction $N$, tension $T$, friction $f$.

**Tension in a string:** for a massless, inextensible string, tension is the same throughout. For a massive string, tension varies along its length. At a pulley, the tension is the same on both sides if the pulley is massless and frictionless.

**Normal reaction:** the force perpendicular to a surface. On an inclined plane at angle $\theta$, $N = mg\cos\theta$ (if no other vertical forces act). The normal force adjusts to prevent penetration of the surface.

**Pseudo force:** in a non-inertial frame accelerating with $\vec{a}$, a fictitious force $-m\vec{a}$ appears on every mass. For example, in an accelerating car, passengers feel pushed backward — this is the pseudo force. It has no reaction pair.

**Connected masses:** when two bodies are connected by a string over a pulley (Atwood machine), they share the same acceleration magnitude. Write $F = ma$ for each body separately and solve the system of equations.

**Friction in Newton's laws:** static friction $f_s \leq \mu_s N$ adjusts to prevent slipping; kinetic friction $f_k = \mu_k N$ opposes motion. Always include friction as a force in the free-body diagram when surfaces are rough.

**Apparent weight:** the normal force experienced by a person in an accelerating elevator. When accelerating upward, apparent weight $= m(g + a) > mg$. When accelerating downward, apparent weight $= m(g - a) < mg$. In free fall ($a = g$), apparent weight is zero — weightlessness.

**Atwood machine:** two masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ ($m_2 > m_1$) connected by a string over a frictionless pulley. Acceleration: $a = \frac{(m_2 - m_1)g}{m_1 + m_2}$. Tension: $T = \frac{2m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2}$. This is a standard problem type in NEB exams.

**Inclined plane:** a block of mass $m$ on a plane inclined at angle $\theta$. Resolve weight into components: $mg\sin\theta$ down the plane and $mg\cos\theta$ perpendicular to the plane. Normal reaction $N = mg\cos\theta$.

**System approach:** for connected bodies, you can sometimes treat the system as a whole. The net external force on the system equals total mass times acceleration: $F_{net, ext} = M_{total} \cdot a$. Internal forces (tension between connected bodies) cancel.

**Limiting friction:** the maximum static friction just before motion begins: $f_{s,max} = \mu_s N$. If the applied force exceeds this, the object starts moving and kinetic friction takes over: $f_k = \mu_k N < f_{s,max}$.

**Friction on an incline:** a block on an inclined plane begins to slide when $mg\sin\theta > \mu_s mg\cos\theta$, i.e., when $\tan\theta > \mu_s$. The critical angle is $\theta_c = \tan^{-1}\mu_s$, called the angle of repose.

**Pulley systems:** in a simple pulley, the tension is the same on both sides. In a block-and-tackle system with $n$ supporting strands, the mechanical advantage is $n$ — the force needed is $\frac{1}{n}$ of the weight (neglecting friction and pulley mass).

**Contact force between blocks:** when two blocks are pushed together on a frictionless surface, the contact force depends on how the external force is applied. If force $F$ pushes block $m_1$ which contacts $m_2$, the contact force on $m_2$ is $F \cdot \frac{m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$.

**Newton's laws in everyday life:** walking (friction pushes you forward), swimming (water pushes you forward as you push water backward), driving (friction between tyres and road provides forward force), jumping (ground pushes you up). All illustrate Newton's third law.

**Weightlessness in orbit:** astronauts in orbit are not weightless because gravity is absent — they are in continuous free fall around Earth. The normal force from the spacecraft floor is zero, giving the sensation of weightlessness.

**Non-inertial frames:** in an accelerating frame, Newton's second law must be modified: $\vec{F}_{net} + \vec{F}_{pseudo} = m\vec{a}_{rel}$. The pseudo force is $-m\vec{a}_{frame}$, where $\vec{a}_{frame}$ is the acceleration of the reference frame.

confusion: ❌ 'The normal force is always mg.' ✅ N = mg only on a horizontal surface with no vertical acceleration. On a slope N = mg cos θ; in an accelerating elevator N = m(g ± a).

❌ 'Friction always opposes motion.' ✅ Friction opposes RELATIVE motion (or its tendency). Static friction can act in the direction of motion — e.g., the static friction on your feet pushes you forward when walking.
❌ 'The tension in a string equals the weight of the hanging mass.' ✅ Only if the system is in equilibrium. In an accelerating Atwood's machine, T ≠ mg — use ΣF = ma on each mass to find T.
❌ 'Action and reaction forces cancel each other.' ✅ They act on DIFFERENT bodies, so they never cancel in a single FBD. Include only forces acting ON the body you are analyzing.
❌ 'Heavier bodies slide slower down a slope.' ✅ a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ) has no mass term — all bodies slide at the same rate (if μ is the same), just like free fall.
❌ 'A body at rest has no forces acting on it.' ✅ Static equilibrium means ΣF = 0, not zero forces — weight and normal (and possibly friction and tension) all act, they just balance.

Action-reaction pairs NEVER act on the same body — they act on two different bodies. A common mistake is to say "the book pushes down on the table and the table pushes up on the book, so they cancel" — these forces act on different bodies and never cancel for a single body's analysis.
Newton's second law is $\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$, not $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$ for any single force. You must sum ALL forces acting on the body before setting them equal to $m\vec{a}$.
The normal reaction is NOT always equal to $mg$. On an inclined plane, $N = mg\cos\theta$. If an additional vertical force acts, $N$ changes. Always determine $N$ from the specific situation.

Tension is NOT a force that "saves" energy — it does no work on a system of connected masses because the displacements at both ends are equal (for an inextensible string), so the net work by tension is zero.

In an accelerating reference frame, pseudo forces are NOT real forces — they have no reaction pair and do not arise from any physical interaction. They are introduced only to make Newton's second law work in non-inertial frames.

A body moving at constant velocity has zero net force on it, but it can still have forces acting on it. The forces simply balance. A car moving at constant speed on a level road has engine force balancing friction and air resistance.
The tension in a string is NOT always equal to the weight of a hanging mass. If the mass is accelerating, $T = m(g \pm a)$. Only when the mass is at rest or moving at constant velocity does $T = mg$.

When two bodies of different masses are dropped from the same height, they fall with the same acceleration $g$ (neglecting air resistance). The gravitational force is larger on the heavier body, but its greater inertia exactly compensates.

A 5 kg block rests on a smooth horizontal table. A horizontal force of 20 N is applied. Find the acceleration and the tension in a string connecting it to a 3 kg hanging mass over a frictionless pulley. Solution: For the system: $F_{net} = (5+3)a$, so $20 = 8a$, $a = 2.5$ m/s$^2$. For the 5 kg block: $T = 5 \times 2.5 = 12.5$ N. For the 3 kg mass: $3g - T = 3 \times 2.5$, so $T = 30 - 7.5 = 22.5$ N. Wait — recheck: the applied force is 20 N on the 5 kg block, and the hanging mass provides additional tension. Let me solve the system properly: $20 + 3g - T_{internal} = 8a$... Actually, with the 20 N force on the 5 kg block and the 3 kg hanging: equations are (1) $20 - T = 5a$ and (2) $T - 3g = 3a$ — no, the hanging mass pulls down: $3g - T = 3a$ is wrong if 20 N pulls the other way. Correct: $20 - T = 5a$ and $T - 3g = 3a$ (if upward is positive for hanging mass). Adding: $20 - 3g = 8a$, $20 - 29.4 = 8a$, $a = -1.175$ m/s$^2$. The system accelerates with the 3 kg mass falling, so $a = 1.175$ m/s$^2$ downward for the 3 kg mass. Tension: $T = 20 - 5(1.175) = 14.125$ N.

A 10 kg body is pulled up a smooth incline of angle 30° by a force of 80 N parallel to the incline. Find the acceleration. Solution: Forces along the incline: $F - mg\sin\theta = ma$. $80 - 10 \times 9.8 \times \sin 30° = 10a$. $80 - 49 = 10a$, so $a = 3.1$ m/s$^2$ up the incline.

An elevator of mass 500 kg is suspended by a cable. Find the tension when the elevator (a) accelerates upward at 2 m/s$^2$, (b) moves at constant velocity, (c) accelerates downward at 2 m/s$^2$. Solution: (a) $T - mg = ma$, $T = m(g+a) = 500(9.8+2) = 5900$ N. (b) $a = 0$, $T = mg = 500 \times 9.8 = 4900$ N. (c) $mg - T = ma$, $T = m(g-a) = 500(9.8-2) = 3900$ N.

Two masses $m_1 = 4$ kg and $m_2 = 6$ kg are connected by a string over a frictionless pulley (Atwood machine). Find the acceleration and tension. Solution: $a = \frac{(m_2 - m_1)g}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{(6-4) \times 9.8}{10} = 1.96$ m/s$^2$. $T = \frac{2m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{2 \times 4 \times 6 \times 9.8}{10} = 47.04$ N.

A 2 kg block rests on a rough horizontal surface ($\mu_s = 0.5$, $\mu_k = 0.4$). A horizontal force of 8 N is applied. Find the friction force and acceleration. Solution: Maximum static friction $f_{s,max} = \mu_s N = 0.5 \times 2 \times 9.8 = 9.8$ N. Since applied force (8 N) < $f_{s,max}$ (9.8 N), the block does not move. Friction force = 8 N (equal and opposite to the applied force). Acceleration = 0.

A 4 kg block is pulled up a rough incline of angle 20° by a force of 30 N parallel to the incline. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.2. Find the acceleration. Solution: Normal force $N = mg\cos 20° = 4 \times 9.8 \times 0.9397 = 36.85$ N. Friction $f_k = 0.2 \times 36.85 = 7.37$ N. Net force up the incline: $F - mg\sin 20° - f_k = 30 - 4 \times 9.8 \times 0.3420 - 7.37 = 30 - 13.42 - 7.37 = 9.21$ N. Acceleration: $a = \frac{9.21}{4} = 2.30$ m/s$^2$.

A 10 kg box is pushed across a horizontal floor with a force of 50 N at an angle of 30° below the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.3. Find the acceleration. Solution: Vertical forces: $N = mg + F\sin 30° = 10 \times 9.8 + 50 \times 0.5 = 98 + 25 = 123$ N. Friction: $f_k = 0.3 \times 123 = 36.9$ N. Horizontal force: $F\cos 30° = 50 \times 0.866 = 43.3$ N. Net force: $43.3 - 36.9 = 6.4$ N. Acceleration: $a = \frac{6.4}{10} = 0.64$ m/s$^2$.

Three blocks of masses 2 kg, 3 kg, and 5 kg are connected in a line on a frictionless surface. A force of 20 N pulls the 5 kg block. Find the tension between each pair. Solution: Total mass = 10 kg, acceleration $a = \frac{20}{10} = 2$ m/s$^2$. Tension between 2 kg and 3 kg: $T_1 = 2 \times 2 = 4$ N. Tension between 3 kg and 5 kg: $T_2 = (2+3) \times 2 = 10$ N. Check: $T_2 - T_1 = 10 - 4 = 6$ N on the 3 kg block, giving $a = 6/3 = 2$ m/s$^2$. ✓
universalFacts: Newton's second law (ΣF = ma) is the master equation of mechanics — it connects forces to motion.
Every mechanics problem in the NEB exam can be solved by drawing a correct FBD and applying ΣF = ma.
The apparent weight of a body depends on the acceleration of its support — the basis of weightlessness in orbit.
In the absence of friction, all bodies slide down a slope at the same rate regardless of mass — a parallel to Galileo's free-fall result.
The tension in a string transmits force between bodies — it is the mechanism by which connected bodies influence each other's motion.
Pseudo-forces are a mathematical convenience for analyzing motion in non-inertial reference frames.
Newton's laws were published in his Principia Mathematica in 1687 and remain the foundation of classical mechanics.
Newton's second law in the form $\vec{F} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$ is more general than $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$ — it correctly describes systems with changing mass, such as rockets.
The concept of pseudo force is essential for solving problems in accelerating frames like elevators, rotating platforms, and accelerating vehicles.
Newton's third law implies conservation of momentum for an isolated system — the two laws are deeply connected.
In real-world applications, Newton's laws are supplemented by empirical force laws: friction ($f = \mu N$), spring force ($F = -kx$), and drag force ($F \propto v$ or $v^2$).
The normal force is a constraint force — it adjusts to whatever value is needed to prevent interpenetration of surfaces. It is not a fixed value but responds to the specific situation.
In a frictionless Atwood machine, the acceleration is always less than $g$ (unless one mass is zero). The tension is always between the two weights: $m_1g < T < m_2g$ (assuming $m_2 > m_1$).
A person standing on a scale in an elevator reads different values depending on the elevator's acceleration. This reading is the apparent weight, equal to the normal force from the scale.

data.title: Application of Newton's Laws

notes: **The problem-solving framework (the 'FBD method'):** (1) isolate the body, (2) draw ALL forces acting ON it (weight, normal, friction, tension, applied), (3) choose axes (one along acceleration), (4) write ΣF = ma for each axis, (5) solve. Every single NEB numerical follows this pattern.

**Elevator weight paradox:** in an accelerating upward elevator, the normal force N = m(g + a) — you feel heavier. Accelerating downward: N = m(g − a) — you feel lighter. Free fall (a = g): N = 0 (weightlessness). The weight mg never changes; what changes is the apparent weight (the normal force).

**Atwood's machine (two masses on a pulley):** acceleration a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂); tension T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂). The string is massless and inextensible; the pulley is frictionless — if not, extra terms appear.

**Connected bodies (push and pull):** a single force F applied to a system of masses (m₁, m₂, m₃) gives a = F/(m₁ + m₂ + m₃). The contact force between m₁ and m₂ is the force needed to accelerate the trailing masses: N = (m₂ + m₃) × a.

**Inclined plane:** weight components: mg sin θ down the slope, mg cos θ into the plane. Normal N = mg cos θ. With friction: net force down slope = mg sin θ − μmg cos θ. The body slides when sin θ > μ cos θ, i.e., tan θ > μ — the critical angle depends only on μ, NOT on mass.
**Worked example:** a 5 kg block on a 30° rough slope (μ = 0.3) — does it slide? tan 30° = 0.577 > 0.3 → yes. Acceleration: a = g(sin 30° − 0.3 cos 30°) = 9.8(0.5 − 0.26) = 2.35 m/s² down the slope.

**Apparent weight in fluids:** an object submerged in a liquid appears lighter by the buoyant force (Archimedes): apparent weight = mg − ρVg. This is still a Newton's second law application: ΣF = mg − ρVg = ma.

**NEB exam focus:** elevator problems, Atwood's machine, connected bodies on horizontal surfaces, inclined plane with/without friction, apparent weight in accelerating systems — all use the same FBD → ΣF = ma framework.

❌ 'Friction always opposes motion.' ✅ Friction opposes RELATIVE motion (or its tendency). Static friction can act in the direction of motion — e.g., the static friction on your feet pushes you forward when walking.

notes: **Torque (moment of a force):** $\tau = rF \sin \theta$, where r is the distance from the pivot to the point of application, F is the force, and $\theta$ is the angle between r and F. The SI unit is Nm. Torque is positive for anticlockwise rotation, negative for clockwise.

**Equilibrium of a rigid body:** two conditions must BOTH hold: (1) translational equilibrium: $\sum F = 0$ (no net force → no linear acceleration); (2) rotational equilibrium: $\sum \tau = 0$ (no net torque → no angular acceleration). A body at rest or rotating at constant angular velocity satisfies both.

**Couple:** two equal and opposite forces separated by a distance d produce a pure torque (independent of pivot): $\tau = F \times d$. The net force is zero, so there is no linear acceleration — only rotation. The turning effect is the same about ANY point.

**Centre of gravity (CG):** the single point where the entire weight of a body may be considered to act. For regular uniform bodies, the CG is at the geometric centre. For irregular bodies, it can be found by balancing or suspension.

**Worked example — seesaw:** a 40 kg child sits 2 m from the fulcrum. Where must a 50 kg child sit to balance? Torque balance: $40 \times 9.8 \times 2 = 50 \times 9.8 \times x ightarrow x = 1.6 \text{ m}$. The heavier child sits closer to the fulcrum.

**Worked example — ladder:** a uniform ladder of length L leans against a smooth wall at angle $\theta$. The wall reaction is horizontal (smooth), the ground reaction has both normal and friction components. Torque about the base eliminates the unknown ground reaction: $N_{\text{wall}} \times L \sin \theta = mg \times (L/2) \cos \theta$.

**Equilibrium in the NEB exam:** the standard problem is a beam/ladder/plank with multiple forces — apply $\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$, and $\sum \tau = 0$ (choosing the pivot wisely to eliminate unknowns). Three equations for up to three unknowns.

**Practical examples:** opening a door (push at the handle, not near the hinge — larger r gives more $\tau$), using a spanner (longer handle = more torque for the same force), a wheelbarrow (load CG near the wheel reduces the lifting torque).

❌ 'A body with zero net force is in equilibrium.' ✅ It must ALSO have zero net torque. A couple (equal and opposite forces) produces zero net force but a non-zero torque — the body rotates.
❌ 'The torque depends on the pivot chosen.' ✅ The torque of a single force depends on the pivot, but the NET torque in equilibrium is zero about ANY pivot. Choose the pivot to eliminate unknowns.
❌ 'Heavier bodies always produce more torque.' ✅ Torque depends on BOTH force and distance. A small force far from the pivot can produce more torque than a large force close to it.

**Centre of gravity (CG):** the single point where the entire weight of a body may be considered to act. For regular uniform bodies, the CG is at the geometric centre. For irregular bodies, it can be found by balancing or suspension.

**Equilibrium in the NEB exam:** the standard problem is a beam/ladder/plank with multiple forces — apply $\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$, and $\sum \tau = 0$ (choosing the pivot wisely to eliminate unknowns). Three equations for up to three unknowns.

**Practical examples:** opening a door (push at the handle, not near the hinge — larger r gives more $\tau$), using a spanner (longer handle = more torque for the same force), a wheelbarrow (load CG near the wheel reduces the lifting torque).

**Moment of a force (torque):** $\tau = rF\sin\theta$, where $r$ is the distance from the pivot to the point of application and $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{r}$ and $\vec{F}$. The perpendicular distance $d = r\sin\theta$ is called the moment arm or lever arm.

**Vector form:** $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$. Torque is a vector perpendicular to the plane containing $\vec{r}$ and $\vec{F}$, following the right-hand rule. Its magnitude is $\tau = rF\sin\theta$.
**Units:** torque has units of N·m. Note: while dimensionally equivalent to joules, torque is NOT energy and is never expressed in joules. Torque is a vector; energy is a scalar.
**Couple:** two equal and opposite forces whose lines of action do not coincide. A couple produces pure rotation with zero net force, so it causes angular acceleration without translation.

**Moment of a couple:** $\tau = F \cdot d$, where $d$ is the perpendicular distance between the lines of action. The moment of a couple is the same about ANY point — it is a free vector, independent of the reference point.

**Equilibrium conditions:** for a rigid body to be in static equilibrium: (1) $\sum\vec{F} = 0$ (translational equilibrium) and (2) $\sum\vec{\tau} = 0$ about any point (rotational equilibrium). Both conditions must be satisfied simultaneously.

**Types of equilibrium:** (1) Stable — body returns to equilibrium when displaced slightly (centre of gravity rises). (2) Unstable — body moves further from equilibrium when displaced (centre of gravity falls). (3) Neutral — body stays in new position (centre of gravity at same height).

**Center of gravity:** the point where the entire weight of the body may be considered to act. For a uniform body, it coincides with the geometrical center. For irregular bodies, it can be found experimentally by suspension.

**Principle of moments:** for a body in equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about that point. This is a direct consequence of $\sum\vec{\tau} = 0$.

**Lever classes:** (1) Class 1: fulcrum between effort and load (seesaw). (2) Class 2: load between fulcrum and effort (wheelbarrow). (3) Class 3: effort between fulcrum and load (tweezers, human forearm). Mechanical advantage differs for each class.

**Calculating torque about a point:** choose a pivot point and calculate the torque of each force about that point. A force whose line of action passes through the pivot produces zero torque. Choose the pivot to eliminate unknown forces from the torque equation.

**Stability and center of gravity:** a body is stable when its center of gravity is low and its base of support is wide. Tipping occurs when the vertical line through the CG falls outside the base. This principle explains why racing cars have wide wheelbases and low centers of gravity.

**Torque and angular acceleration:** just as $F = ma$ governs translational motion, $\tau = I\alpha$ governs rotational motion, where $I$ is the moment of inertia and $\alpha$ is the angular acceleration.

**Static vs dynamic equilibrium:** static equilibrium means the body is at rest ($\vec{v} = 0$, $\vec{\omega} = 0$). Dynamic equilibrium means the body moves with constant velocity and constant angular velocity ($\vec{a} = 0$, $\vec{\alpha} = 0$). Both require $\sum\vec{F} = 0$ and $\sum\vec{\tau} = 0$.

**Finding the center of gravity experimentally:** suspend the body from two different points. The CG lies at the intersection of the vertical lines through each suspension point. This method works for any irregular shape.

**Torque balance in biological systems:** the human body uses lever systems extensively. The biceps muscle exerts a large force at a short distance from the elbow joint to lift a smaller weight at a longer distance — a class 3 lever with mechanical advantage less than 1.

**Torque and power:** rotational power is $P = \tau\omega$. For a given power, a larger torque produces slower rotation and vice versa. This is why bicycles use gear ratios — changing the effective torque at the wheel.

**Resultant of concurrent forces:** if multiple forces act on a body and their lines of action intersect at a point, you can find the resultant by vector addition. The body is in translational equilibrium if the resultant is zero.

**Non-concurrent forces:** when forces do not intersect at a single point, you must check both force equilibrium and torque equilibrium. A body can have zero net force but non-zero net torque (pure couple), causing rotation without translation.

confusion: ❌ 'Torque and moment are different.' ✅ In physics problems, they are the same quantity: $\tau = rF \sin \theta$. Engineers sometimes distinguish 'moment' (bending) from 'torque' (twisting), but here they are interchangeable.
❌ 'A body with zero net force is in equilibrium.' ✅ It must ALSO have zero net torque. A couple (equal and opposite forces) produces zero net force but a non-zero torque — the body rotates.
❌ 'The torque depends on the pivot chosen.' ✅ The torque of a single force depends on the pivot, but the NET torque in equilibrium is zero about ANY pivot. Choose the pivot to eliminate unknowns.
❌ 'Heavier bodies always produce more torque.' ✅ Torque depends on BOTH force and distance. A small force far from the pivot can produce more torque than a large force close to it.
❌ 'The centre of gravity is always inside the body.' ✅ For a ring, the CG is at the centre (in empty space). For an L-shaped body, it lies outside the material.

❌ 'A ladder leaning against a wall is safe if $\sum F = 0$.' ✅ You also need $\sum \tau = 0$ AND friction at the ground to be $\le \mu N$. The ladder slips when the required friction exceeds $\mu N_{\text{ground}}$.
Torque depends on the choice of pivot point, but the moment of a couple does NOT — it is the same about any point. This is because a couple produces pure rotation with no net force.
Zero net force does not imply zero net torque, and zero net torque does not imply zero net force. A body can be in rotational equilibrium but accelerating translationally, or vice versa.
The N·m unit for torque is NOT the same as the joule (energy), even though they are dimensionally equivalent. Torque is a vector (or pseudovector); energy is a scalar.

The point about which you calculate torque is arbitrary for equilibrium problems — if the body is in equilibrium, the net torque is zero about ANY point. Choose the point that minimizes the number of unknowns.
A body can have zero acceleration but non-zero torque if it is rotating with constant angular velocity — this is dynamic equilibrium, not static equilibrium.

In a class 3 lever (like a seesaw where the fulcrum is in the middle), the effort and load are on opposite sides. The mechanical advantage is less than 1, meaning you need more effort force than the load, but the load moves farther.
When calculating torque, only the component of force perpendicular to the position vector contributes. The parallel component ($F\cos\theta$) produces no torque about the pivot.
A body in stable equilibrium has its center of gravity at a minimum height. When displaced, the CG rises, and gravity provides a restoring torque that returns the body to equilibrium.

A uniform beam of length 4 m and weight 100 N is supported at its ends. A 200 N weight is placed 1.5 m from the left end. Find the reactions at the supports. Solution: Let $R_L$ and $R_R$ be the left and right reactions. Force equilibrium: $R_L + R_R = 100 + 200 = 300$ N. Taking moments about the left end: $200 \times 1.5 + 100 \times 2 = R_R \times 4$. $300 + 200 = 4R_R$, so $R_R = 125$ N and $R_L = 175$ N.

A couple consists of two forces of 50 N each, acting at the ends of a 0.4 m rod. Find the torque of the couple. Solution: $\tau = F \times d = 50 \times 0.4 = 20$ N·m. This torque is the same about any point on or off the rod.

A ladder of length 5 m and weight 200 N leans against a smooth vertical wall with its foot 3 m from the wall. Find the friction force at the ground. Solution: The ladder forms a 3-4-5 triangle, so the height on the wall is 4 m. Taking moments about the foot: $200 \times 1.5 = N_{wall} \times 4$, so $N_{wall} = 75$ N. Since the wall is smooth, friction at the ground balances the wall reaction: $f = 75$ N. Force equilibrium gives $N_{ground} = 200$ N. Coefficient of friction: $\mu = \frac{f}{N} = \frac{75}{200} = 0.375$.

A see-saw 4 m long is pivoted at its centre. A 30 kg child sits 1.5 m from the pivot. Where must a 20 kg child sit to balance the see-saw? Solution: For rotational equilibrium: $30 \times g \times 1.5 = 20 \times g \times d$. $45 = 20d$, so $d = 2.25$ m from the pivot.

A horizontal cantilever beam of length 2 m projects from a wall. A load of 500 N is applied at the free end. Find the torque about the wall support. Solution: $\tau = F \times r = 500 \times 2 = 1000$ N·m. The wall must exert an equal and opposite torque to maintain equilibrium.

A uniform meter rule of weight 1.2 N is pivoted at the 40 cm mark. Where must a 0.8 N weight be placed to balance the rule? Solution: The weight of the rule acts at the 50 cm mark, 10 cm from the pivot. Taking moments about the pivot: $0.8 \times d = 1.2 \times 10$, so $d = 15$ cm. The 0.8 N weight must be placed at the 25 cm mark (15 cm to the left of the pivot).

A horizontal boom of length 3 m and weight 200 N is hinged at a wall and supported by a cable making 30° with the horizontal at the far end. A 500 N weight hangs from the far end. Find the tension in the cable and the hinge reaction. Solution: Taking moments about the hinge: $500 \times 3 + 200 \times 1.5 = T\sin 30° \times 3$. $1500 + 300 = 1.5T$, so $T = 1200$ N. Vertical forces: $R_y + T\sin 30° = 500 + 200$, so $R_y = 700 - 600 = 100$ N. Horizontal forces: $R_x = T\cos 30° = 1200 \times 0.866 = 1039$ N. Hinge reaction: $R = \sqrt{100^2 + 1039^2} \approx 1044$ N.

A uniform ladder of weight $W$ and length $L$ rests against a smooth wall with its foot on rough ground ($\mu = 0.4$). Find the minimum angle with the horizontal for the ladder not to slip. Solution: Taking moments about the foot: $W \cdot \frac{L}{2}\cos\theta = N_{wall} \cdot L\sin\theta$, so $N_{wall} = \frac{W\cos\theta}{2\sin\theta} = \frac{W}{2\tan\theta}$. Horizontal equilibrium: $f = N_{wall}$. At limiting friction: $f = \mu W = 0.4W$. So $\frac{W}{2\tan\theta} = 0.4W$, giving $\tan\theta = \frac{1}{0.8} = 1.25$, so $\theta = 51.3°$.

data.title: Moment, Torque and Equilibrium

notes: **Torque (moment of a force):** τ = rF sin θ, where r is the distance from the pivot to the point of application, F is the force, and θ is the angle between r and F. The SI unit is Nm. Torque is positive for anticlockwise rotation, negative for clockwise.

**Equilibrium of a rigid body:** two conditions must BOTH hold: (1) translational equilibrium: ΣF = 0 (no net force → no linear acceleration); (2) rotational equilibrium: Στ = 0 (no net torque → no angular acceleration). A body at rest or rotating at constant angular velocity satisfies both.

**Couple:** two equal and opposite forces separated by a distance d produce a pure torque (independent of pivot): τ = F × d. The net force is zero, so there is no linear acceleration — only rotation. The turning effect is the same about ANY point.

**Centre of gravity (CG):** the single point where the entire weight of a body may be considered to act. For regular uniform bodies, the CG is at the geometric centre. For irregular bodies, it can be found by balancing or suspension.

**Worked example — seesaw:** a 40 kg child sits 2 m from the fulcrum. Where must a 50 kg child sit to balance? Torque balance: 40×9.8×2 = 50×9.8×x → x = 1.6 m. The heavier child sits closer to the fulcrum.

**Worked example — ladder:** a uniform ladder of length L leans against a smooth wall at angle θ. The wall reaction is horizontal (smooth), the ground reaction has both normal and friction components. Torque about the base eliminates the unknown ground reaction: N_wall × L sin θ = mg × (L/2) cos θ.

**Equilibrium in the NEB exam:** the standard problem is a beam/ladder/plank with multiple forces — apply ΣF_x = 0, ΣF_y = 0, and Στ = 0 (choosing the pivot wisely to eliminate unknowns). Three equations for up to three unknowns.

**Practical examples:** opening a door (push at the handle, not near the hinge — larger r gives more τ), using a spanner (longer handle = more torque for the same force), a wheelbarrow (load CG near the wheel reduces the lifting torque).

data.title: Solid Friction

notes: **What friction is:** a contact force that opposes relative motion (or its tendency) between two surfaces in contact. It acts parallel to the contact surface. Static friction (no sliding) and kinetic friction (sliding) are the two main types.

**Laws of friction:** (1) Friction is independent of the apparent area of contact (to a good approximation). (2) Maximum static friction and kinetic friction are both proportional to the normal reaction: f_s(max) = μ_sN, f_k = μ_kN. (3) μ_k < μ_s — it is harder to start sliding than to keep sliding.

**Static friction is a variable force:** it matches the applied force up to a maximum: f_s ≤ μ_sN. If you push with 30 N and the object doesn't move, f_s = 30 N (not μ_sN). Only at the point of slipping does f_s = μ_sN.

**Angle of friction (λ):** the angle between the normal reaction and the resultant reaction (normal + friction) when slipping is about to occur. tan λ = μ_s. The resultant reaction makes angle λ with the normal.

**Angle of repose (θ_r):** the steepest angle of a slope at which a body just remains at rest. At this angle, mg sin θ_r = μ_s mg cos θ_r → tan θ_r = μ_s. So θ_r = λ — the angle of repose equals the angle of friction.

**Worked example — body on a slope:** a 10 kg block on a 25° slope (μ_s = 0.5). Does it slide? tan 25° = 0.466 < 0.5 → no, it stays. Static friction = mg sin 25° = 41.5 N (less than μ_sN = 0.5 × 92.4 = 46.2 N).

**Worked example — pulling a block:** a 5 kg block on a horizontal surface (μ_k = 0.3). Pulled by a 20 N force at 30° above horizontal. Normal N = mg − F sin 30° = 49 − 10 = 39 N. Friction = 0.3 × 39 = 11.7 N. Net force = 20 cos 30° − 11.7 = 5.6 N. a = 5.6/5 = 1.12 m/s².

**NEB exam focus:** distinguish static vs kinetic friction; solve slope problems (does it slide? find acceleration); angle of repose and its equality with angle of friction; pulling/pushing at an angle (changes the normal, hence friction).
confusion: ❌ 'Friction always opposes motion.' ✅ Friction opposes RELATIVE motion (or its tendency). Static friction can act IN the direction of motion — e.g., the static friction on your feet pushes you forward when walking.

❌ 'Friction depends on the area of contact.' ✅ For a given normal force, friction is (approximately) independent of area. A wide tyre and a narrow tyre with the same load have the same maximum friction (in the simple model).
❌ 'Static friction is always μ_sN.' ✅ Static friction is VARIABLE: it matches the applied force up to μ_sN. Only at the point of slipping does f_s = μ_sN.
❌ 'μ_k > μ_s because sliding is faster.' ✅ μ_k < μ_s — it is harder to start sliding than to keep sliding. This is why a heavy box jerks when you first push it.
❌ 'The angle of repose depends on the mass of the body.' ✅ tan θ_r = μ_s — mass cancels out. All bodies with the same μ_s have the same angle of repose.

❌ 'Pulling a block at an angle reduces friction because the force is smaller.' ✅ Pulling upward reduces the normal (N = mg − F sin θ), which reduces friction. Pushing downward increases the normal and friction.

universalFacts: Friction is independent of the apparent area of contact — a counterintuitive but experimentally verified law.
μ_k < μ_s for most surface pairs — this is why objects jerk when starting to slide.
The angle of repose equals the angle of friction: θ_r = λ = tan⁻¹μ_s — a beautiful geometric connection.
Friction can act in the direction of motion — static friction is the force that accelerates you forward when walking.
Pulling a block at an angle reduces friction (by reducing N); pushing at an angle increases it (by increasing N).
examples: Slope: A 5 kg block on a 30° slope (μ_s = 0.4). tan 30° = 0.577 > 0.4 → slides. a = g(sin30° − μ_k cos30°) = 9.8(0.5 − 0.4×0.866) = 1.51 m/s².
Horizontal pull: A 10 kg block (μ_k = 0.25) pulled by 40 N at 20° above horizontal. N = 98 − 40sin20° = 84.3 N; f = 21.1 N; F_net = 40cos20° − 21.1 = 16.5 N; a = 1.65 m/s².
Angle of repose: A block slides at constant speed down a 35° slope. μ_k = tan 35° = 0.70. μ_s is slightly higher (≈ 0.75).
Static friction variable: A 20 kg box (μ_s = 0.5). Push with 40 N — box doesn't move, f_s = 40 N. Push with 120 N — box moves (max f_s = 98 N).
Pulling vs pushing: A 15 kg block (μ_k = 0.3). Pull at 25°: N = 147 − Fsin25°. Push at 25°: N = 147 + Fsin25°. Pulling gives less friction.

notes: **What friction is:** a contact force that opposes relative motion (or its tendency) between two surfaces in contact. It acts parallel to the contact surface. Static friction (no sliding) and kinetic friction (sliding) are the two main types.

**Laws of friction:** (1) Friction is independent of the apparent area of contact (to a good approximation). (2) Maximum static friction and kinetic friction are both proportional to the normal reaction: f_s(max) = μ_sN, f_k = μ_kN. (3) μ_k < μ_s — it is harder to start sliding than to keep sliding.

**Static friction is a variable force:** it matches the applied force up to a maximum: f_s ≤ μ_sN. If you push with 30 N and the object doesn't move, f_s = 30 N (not μ_sN). Only at the point of slipping does f_s = μ_sN.

**Angle of friction (λ):** the angle between the normal reaction and the resultant reaction (normal + friction) when slipping is about to occur. tan λ = μ_s. The resultant reaction makes angle λ with the normal.

**Angle of repose (θ_r):** the steepest angle of a slope at which a body just remains at rest. At this angle, mg sin θ_r = μ_s mg cos θ_r → tan θ_r = μ_s. So θ_r = λ — the angle of repose equals the angle of friction.

**Worked example — body on a slope:** a 10 kg block on a 25° slope (μ_s = 0.5). Does it slide? tan 25° = 0.466 < 0.5 → no, it stays. Static friction = mg sin 25° = 41.5 N (less than μ_sN = 0.5 × 92.4 = 46.2 N).

**Worked example — pulling a block:** a 5 kg block on a horizontal surface (μ_k = 0.3). Pulled by a 20 N force at 30° above horizontal. Normal N = mg − F sin 30° = 49 − 10 = 39 N. Friction = 0.3 × 39 = 11.7 N. Net force = 20 cos 30° − 11.7 = 5.6 N. a = 5.6/5 = 1.12 m/s².

specificConditions: **Static vs. Kinetic Threshold:** The maximum static friction $f_s^{\max} = \mu_s N$ is the *upper bound* for static friction. Static friction is a *variable* force that matches the applied force up to this limit. Kinetic friction $f_k = \mu_k N$ applies *only* when sliding occurs, with $\mu_k < \mu_s$.

**Normal Force Dependency:** Friction is proportional to the *normal reaction*, not the weight. Any vertical force component (pulling up, pushing down, incline) changes $N$, which directly changes the friction force. Always compute $N$ first.

**Area Independence (Ideal Model):** The laws of friction assume friction is independent of the apparent contact area (Coulomb's model). This holds well for dry, rigid surfaces but breaks down for soft materials, lubricated contacts, or adhesive forces where real contact area matters.

**Friction:** the force that opposes relative motion (or impending motion) between two surfaces in contact. It arises from microscopic irregularities and molecular adhesion between surfaces.
**Coefficient of friction $\mu$:** $\mu = \frac{F}{R}$, where $F$ is the limiting frictional force and $R$ is the normal reaction. $\mu$ is dimensionless — it is a ratio of two forces.

**Laws of friction:** (1) Friction acts opposite to the direction of impending motion. (2) Limiting friction $F_s = \mu_s R$, proportional to the normal reaction. (3) Friction is independent of the apparent area of contact (for a given normal force). (4) Friction depends on the nature and condition of the surfaces in contact.

**Static vs kinetic friction:** static friction adjusts up to a maximum $F_{s,max} = \mu_s R$; kinetic friction is approximately constant at $F_k = \mu_k R$, where typically $\mu_s > \mu_k$. This is why it is harder to start moving an object than to keep it moving.

**Angle of friction $\lambda$:** the angle between the resultant contact force and the normal reaction when limiting friction is reached. $\tan\lambda = \mu_s$. When the incline angle equals the angle of friction, the body is on the point of sliding.
**Angle of repose:** the maximum angle of an incline at which a body just rests on the plane without sliding. It equals the angle of friction: $\theta_{repose} = \lambda = \tan^{-1}\mu_s$.

**Verification of area independence:** experiments show that for a given normal force, doubling the contact area halves the pressure but leaves the frictional force unchanged because the increased number of molecular interactions compensates.
**Rolling friction:** much smaller than sliding friction because rolling deforms surfaces less and the contact time per point is shorter. Ball bearings use this principle to reduce friction.
**Units check:** $\mu = F/R$ — both numerator and denominator are forces, so $\mu$ is dimensionless. Friction force $F = \mu R$ has units of newtons.
confusion: ❌ 'Friction always opposes motion.' ✅ Friction opposes RELATIVE motion (or its tendency). Static friction can act IN the direction of motion — e.g., the static friction on your feet pushes you forward when walking.

❌ 'Friction depends on the area of contact.' ✅ For a given normal force, friction is (approximately) independent of area. A wide tyre and a narrow tyre with the same load have the same maximum friction (in the simple model).
❌ 'Static friction is always μ_sN.' ✅ Static friction is VARIABLE: it matches the applied force up to μ_sN. Only at the point of slipping does f_s = μ_sN.
❌ 'μ_k > μ_s because sliding is faster.' ✅ μ_k < μ_s — it is harder to start sliding than to keep sliding. This is why a heavy box jerks when you first push it.
❌ 'The angle of repose depends on the mass of the body.' ✅ tan θ_r = μ_s — mass cancels out. All bodies with the same μ_s have the same angle of repose.

❌ 'Pulling a block at an angle reduces friction because the force is smaller.' ✅ Pulling upward reduces the normal (N = mg − F sin θ), which reduces friction. Pushing downward increases the normal and friction.

Friction is NOT always opposite to the direction of motion — it is opposite to the direction of relative motion (or impending relative motion) between the two surfaces. For example, when you walk, friction on your foot points forward (in the direction of motion), preventing your foot from slipping backward.

The friction force is NOT always $\mu R$. This formula gives the LIMITING (maximum static) friction. For static friction, $f_s \leq \mu_s R$, and the actual value adjusts to match the applied force up to the maximum.

Friction being independent of area is an approximation that holds for rigid bodies with moderate contact pressures. For very soft materials (like rubber tyres) or very high pressures, the relationship becomes more complex.

$\mu_s > \mu_k$ is generally true but not universal. Some materials (like Teflon on Teflon) have nearly equal coefficients, and certain combinations can even have $\mu_k > \mu_s$ under specific conditions.

The normal reaction $R$ is NOT always equal to $mg$. On an inclined plane, $R = mg\cos\theta$. If an additional vertical force is applied, $R$ changes accordingly. Always determine $R$ from force equilibrium in the direction perpendicular to the surface.

A 10 kg box rests on a horizontal floor. The coefficient of static friction is 0.5. Find the minimum horizontal force needed to start the box moving. Solution: $R = mg = 10 \times 9.8 = 98$ N. Limiting friction $F_s = \mu_s R = 0.5 \times 98 = 49$ N. Minimum force to start motion = 49 N.

A 5 kg block slides down an incline of angle 30° at constant velocity. Find the coefficient of kinetic friction. Solution: At constant velocity, acceleration is zero, so forces are balanced: $mg\sin\theta = \mu_k mg\cos\theta$. $\mu_k = \tan\theta = \tan 30° = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 0.577$.

A 20 kg crate is pushed across a floor with a coefficient of kinetic friction of 0.3. If the crate moves at constant speed, find the applied force. Solution: $R = mg = 20 \times 9.8 = 196$ N. $F_k = \mu_k R = 0.3 \times 196 = 58.8$ N. Since velocity is constant, applied force = friction force = 58.8 N.

An inclined plane is raised until a block just begins to slide at angle 35°. Find the coefficient of static friction and the angle of friction. Solution: At the point of sliding, $\mu_s = \tan\theta = \tan 35° \approx 0.700$. The angle of friction $\lambda = \tan^{-1}(\mu_s) = 35°$. The angle of repose equals the angle of friction.

A 8 kg block is on a horizontal surface ($\mu_s = 0.6$, $\mu_k = 0.4$). A horizontal force of 30 N is applied. Find the friction force and acceleration. Solution: $R = mg = 8 \times 9.8 = 78.4$ N. $F_{s,max} = 0.6 \times 78.4 = 47.04$ N. Since applied force (30 N) < $F_{s,max}$ (47.04 N), the block does not move. Friction force = 30 N (equal and opposite to applied force). Acceleration = 0.

The laws of friction were first systematically studied by Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519), but they were rediscovered and formalized by Guillaume Amontons in 1699 and further refined by Charles-Augustin de Coulomb in 1785.
The coefficient of friction for rubber on dry concrete is about 1.0, while for ice on steel it is only about 0.03 — a factor of 33 difference, explaining why ice skating is possible.
Friction generates heat: the work done against friction is converted into thermal energy. This is why brakes get hot and why meteoroids burn up in the atmosphere.

In ideal mathematical models, friction is treated as independent of contact area and sliding speed. In reality, both factors can affect friction, especially for rubber, polymers, and at very high or very low speeds.

The friction force can do positive, negative, or zero work depending on the reference frame. In the frame of the surface, friction on a sliding object does negative work; in the frame of a moving conveyor belt, friction can do positive work on an object placed on it.
