data.title: Newton's Law of Gravitation

notes: **Law statement:** every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force that is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres: $F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$.

**The universal constant G:** $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2/\text{kg}^2$. It is the same everywhere in the universe (hence 'universal') and was first measured by Cavendish (1798) using a torsion balance. G is very small, which is why the gravitational attraction between everyday objects is imperceptible.

**Vector form & direction:** the force on mass m₁ due to m₂ is $F_{12} = -G\frac{m_1m_2}{r^2} \hat{r}_{12}$, directed along the line joining the centres, always attractive. Newton's third law applies: $F_{12} = -F_{21}$.

**Superposition:** when several masses act on one particle, the net force is the vector sum of the individual forces: $F_{\text{net}} = \sum F_i$. Each pair obeys the inverse-square law independently.

**Worked example — Earth and Moon:** $m_{\text{Earth}} = 6\times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$, $m_{\text{Moon}} = 7.4\times 10^{22} \text{ kg}$, $r = 3.84\times 10^8 \text{ m}$. $F = \frac{6.67\times 10^{-11} \times 6\times 10^{24} \times 7.4\times 10^{22}}{(3.84\times 10^8)^2} = 2.0\times 10^{20} \text{ N}$ — enough to hold the Moon in orbit.

**Gravitational field strength:** $g = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{GM}{r^2}$, the force per unit mass at a distance r from mass M. On Earth's surface $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$, which gives Earth's mass: $M = \frac{gR^2}{G} \approx 5.97\times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$.

**Why G is used in orbits:** equating gravitational force to centripetal force ($\frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{mv^2}{r}$) gives orbital velocity $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$ and period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}$ — Kepler's third law follows directly.

**Important comparisons:** gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces — between two protons the gravitational force is $\sim 10^{-36}$ times the electric force — yet it dominates cosmology because mass adds up while electric charges cancel.
confusion: ❌ 'There is a force of gravity only near Earth.' ✅ Gravity acts between ANY two masses anywhere in the universe — it never switches off, it only weakens with the square of distance.
❌ 'G can change with temperature or medium.' ✅ G is a universal constant — independent of temperature, pressure, medium, or the objects involved.
❌ 'The force depends on the square of the distance — it dies quickly.' ✅ It dies as 1/r² but never reaches zero; at double distance the force is a quarter, at ten times it is one-hundredth.

❌ 'Heavier objects fall faster because gravity pulls them harder.' ✅ Gravity pulls harder on heavier objects ($F = mg$), but their acceleration is the same: $a = F/m = g$, hence all bodies in free fall accelerate equally (ignoring air resistance).

❌ 'Earth pulls the Moon but the Moon does not pull Earth.' ✅ The forces are equal and opposite (Newton's third law). Earth and Moon pull on each other with equal forces — the Moon's acceleration is larger because its mass is smaller.
❌ 'Inside Earth gravity stops.' ✅ Inside a uniform sphere, g decreases linearly with distance from the centre, reaching zero at the centre — it is not zero except exactly at the centre.

The modern value of $G = 6.674\times 10^{-11}$ is still the least precisely known fundamental constant because gravity is so weak.

specificConditions: **Universal Scope:** Newton's law ($F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$) applies to *all* masses in the universe, at all distances. It is exact for point masses or spherically symmetric bodies (Shell Theorem). For non-spherical objects, integration or numerical methods are required.

**Inverse-Square Nature:** The $1/r^2$ dependence means the force has infinite range but drops rapidly. It never reaches zero at any finite distance. This inverse-square law is equivalent to saying gravitational flux through a closed surface is proportional to enclosed mass (Gauss's law for gravity).

**G vs g Distinction:** $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ is a *universal constant*. $g = GM/r^2$ is the *local gravitational field strength*, varying with location. On Earth's surface $g \approx 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$; at height $h$, $g' = g(R/(R+h))^2$.

notes: **Law statement:** every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force that is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres: $F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$.

**The universal constant G:** $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2/\text{kg}^2$. It is the same everywhere in the universe (hence 'universal') and was first measured by Cavendish (1798) using a torsion balance. G is very small, which is why the gravitational attraction between everyday objects is imperceptible.

**Vector form & direction:** the force on mass m₁ due to m₂ is $F_{12} = -G\frac{m_1m_2}{r^2} \hat{r}_{12}$, directed along the line joining the centres, always attractive. Newton's third law applies: $F_{12} = -F_{21}$.

**Superposition:** when several masses act on one particle, the net force is the vector sum of the individual forces: $F_{\text{net}} = \sum F_i$. Each pair obeys the inverse-square law independently.

**Worked example — Earth and Moon:** $m_{\text{Earth}} = 6\times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$, $m_{\text{Moon}} = 7.4\times 10^{22} \text{ kg}$, $r = 3.84\times 10^8 \text{ m}$. $F = \frac{6.67\times 10^{-11} \times 6\times 10^{24} \times 7.4\times 10^{22}}{(3.84\times 10^8)^2} = 2.0\times 10^{20} \text{ N}$ — enough to hold the Moon in orbit.

**Gravitational field strength:** $g = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{GM}{r^2}$, the force per unit mass at a distance r from mass M. On Earth's surface $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$, which gives Earth's mass: $M = \frac{gR^2}{G} \approx 5.97\times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$.

**Why G is used in orbits:** equating gravitational force to centripetal force ($\frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{mv^2}{r}$) gives orbital velocity $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$ and period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}$ — Kepler's third law follows directly.

**Important comparisons:** gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces — between two protons the gravitational force is $\sim 10^{-36}$ times the electric force — yet it dominates cosmology because mass adds up while electric charges cancel.

confusion: ❌ 'There is a force of gravity only near Earth.' ✅ Gravity acts between ANY two masses anywhere in the universe — it never switches off, it only weakens with the square of distance.

notes: **Law statement:** every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force that is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres: $F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$.

**The universal constant G:** $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2/\text{kg}^2$. It is the same everywhere in the universe (hence 'universal') and was first measured by Cavendish (1798) using a torsion balance. G is very small, which is why the gravitational attraction between everyday objects is imperceptible.

**Vector form & direction:** the force on mass m₁ due to m₂ is $F_{12} = -G\frac{m_1m_2}{r^2} \hat{r}_{12}$, directed along the line joining the centres, always attractive. Newton's third law applies: $F_{12} = -F_{21}$.

**Superposition:** when several masses act on one particle, the net force is the vector sum of the individual forces: $F_{\text{net}} = \sum F_i$. Each pair obeys the inverse-square law independently.

**Worked example — Earth and Moon:** $m_{\text{Earth}} = 6\times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$, $m_{\text{Moon}} = 7.4\times 10^{22} \text{ kg}$, $r = 3.84\times 10^8 \text{ m}$. $F = \frac{6.67\times 10^{-11} \times 6\times 10^{24} \times 7.4\times 10^{22}}{(3.84\times 10^8)^2} = 2.0\times 10^{20} \text{ N}$ — enough to hold the Moon in orbit.

**Gravitational field strength:** $g = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{GM}{r^2}$, the force per unit mass at a distance r from mass M. On Earth's surface $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$, which gives Earth's mass: $M = \frac{gR^2}{G} \approx 5.97\times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$.

**Why G is used in orbits:** equating gravitational force to centripetal force ($\frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{mv^2}{r}$) gives orbital velocity $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$ and period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}$ — Kepler's third law follows directly.

**Important comparisons:** gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces — between two protons the gravitational force is $\sim 10^{-36}$ times the electric force — yet it dominates cosmology because mass adds up while electric charges cancel.

❌ 'The force depends on the square of the distance — it dies quickly.' ✅ It dies as 1/r² but never reaches zero; at double distance the force is a quarter, at ten times it is one-hundredth.

❌ 'Heavier objects fall faster because gravity pulls them harder.' ✅ Gravity pulls harder on heavier objects ($F = mg$), but their acceleration is the same: $a = F/m = g$, hence all bodies in free fall accelerate equally (ignoring air resistance).

❌ 'Earth pulls the Moon but the Moon does not pull Earth.' ✅ The forces are equal and opposite (Newton's third law). Earth and Moon pull on each other with equal forces — the Moon's acceleration is larger because its mass is smaller.
❌ 'Inside Earth gravity stops.' ✅ Inside a uniform sphere, g decreases linearly with distance from the centre, reaching zero at the centre — it is not zero except exactly at the centre.

data.title: Gravitational Potential and Potential Energy

notes: **Gravitational potential V:** the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to a point, without acceleration. For a point mass M: $V = -\frac{GM}{r}$. At infinity $V = 0$, and everywhere else V is negative because gravity does positive work as the mass approaches — the field does the work, so potential decreases.

**Gravitational potential energy U:** the work done against gravity in assembling a system; for two masses separated by r: $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$. It is the energy of the whole system, not of one mass alone. U is negative because the system is bound — you must supply $GMm/r$ of energy to separate the masses to infinity.

**Why the minus sign matters:** potential energy is defined with zero at infinity. Since the force is attractive, energy is released (and PE decreases) as masses come together. A satellite in orbit at radius r has $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ — its total mechanical energy is $E = K + U = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$, which is negative, confirming a bound orbit.

**Near Earth's surface:** for small heights h above the surface, $U = mgh$. This is the constant-g approximation of $-\frac{GMm}{r}$: since $\Delta(1/r) \approx -h/R^2$, the change matches $mgh$. Use $mgh$ only for $h \ll R$; use $-\frac{GMm}{r}$ for large altitudes (satellites, rockets).

**Worked example — escape energy:** to launch a mass m from Earth's surface (R) to infinity you must supply $GMm/R$. Numerically for m = 1 kg: $\frac{6.67\times 10^{-11}\times 5.97\times 10^{24}}{6.37\times 10^6} \approx 6.25\times 10^{7} \text{ J} \approx 62.5 \text{ MJ}$ per kg. This energy corresponds to the escape speed 11.2 km/s.

**Potential vs potential energy vs field:** field $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ (the force per unit mass, a vector); potential V is a scalar (J/kg); potential energy $U = mV$. The field is the negative gradient of the potential: $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ radially.

**Equipotential surfaces:** surfaces of constant V. Moving along an equipotential surface requires zero work; the field is always perpendicular to these surfaces. For a point mass, equipotentials are concentric spheres.

**Superposition:** for multiple masses, $V = \sum\left(-\frac{GM_i}{r_i}\right)$ and $U = \sum\left(-\frac{GM_i m}{r_i}\right)$ — potentials add as scalars, which is much simpler than adding force vectors.
confusion: ❌ 'Potential and potential energy are the same.' ✅ Potential V is work per unit mass (J/kg); potential energy $U = mV$ (J). V belongs to a point in the field; U belongs to the mass–field system.
❌ 'Negative energy is unphysical.' ✅ Negative potential energy simply means the system is BOUND — energy must be added to separate it. It is a matter of the reference at infinity.

notes: **Gravitational potential V:** the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to a point, without acceleration. For a point mass M: $V = -\frac{GM}{r}$. At infinity $V = 0$, and everywhere else V is negative because gravity does positive work as the mass approaches — the field does the work, so potential decreases.

**Gravitational potential energy U:** the work done against gravity in assembling a system; for two masses separated by r: $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$. It is the energy of the whole system, not of one mass alone. U is negative because the system is bound — you must supply $GMm/r$ of energy to separate the masses to infinity.

**Why the minus sign matters:** potential energy is defined with zero at infinity. Since the force is attractive, energy is released (and PE decreases) as masses come together. A satellite in orbit at radius r has $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ — its total mechanical energy is $E = K + U = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$, which is negative, confirming a bound orbit.

**Near Earth's surface:** for small heights h above the surface, $U = mgh$. This is the constant-g approximation of $-\frac{GMm}{r}$: since $\Delta(1/r) \approx -h/R^2$, the change matches $mgh$. Use $mgh$ only for $h \ll R$; use $-\frac{GMm}{r}$ for large altitudes (satellites, rockets).

**Worked example — escape energy:** to launch a mass m from Earth's surface (R) to infinity you must supply $GMm/R$. Numerically for m = 1 kg: $\frac{6.67\times 10^{-11}\times 5.97\times 10^{24}}{6.37\times 10^6} \approx 6.25\times 10^{7} \text{ J} \approx 62.5 \text{ MJ}$ per kg. This energy corresponds to the escape speed 11.2 km/s.

**Potential vs potential energy vs field:** field $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ (the force per unit mass, a vector); potential V is a scalar (J/kg); potential energy $U = mV$. The field is the negative gradient of the potential: $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ radially.

**Equipotential surfaces:** surfaces of constant V. Moving along an equipotential surface requires zero work; the field is always perpendicular to these surfaces. For a point mass, equipotentials are concentric spheres.

**Superposition:** for multiple masses, $V = \sum\left(-\frac{GM_i}{r_i}\right)$ and $U = \sum\left(-\frac{GM_i m}{r_i}\right)$ — potentials add as scalars, which is much simpler than adding force vectors.

data.title: Gravitational Potential; Gravitational Potential Energy
notes: Gravitational Potential: Gravitational potential $V$ at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to that point: $V = W/m = -GM/r$. It is a scalar quantity with SI unit J/kg. Potential is zero at infinity (reference) and negative everywhere else.

Gravitational Potential Energy: Potential energy $U$ of mass $m$ at a point where potential is $V$: $U = mV = -GMm/r$. Near Earth's surface ($h \ll R$): $U = mgh$ (relative to surface). Change in PE: $\Delta U = mg\Delta h$.
Work Done by Gravitational Force: Work done in moving mass $m$ from $r_1$ to $r_2$: $W = -\Delta U = GMm(1/r_2 - 1/r_1)$. Work is path-independent (conservative force).
Gravitational Field and Potential Relation: $\vec{g} = -\nabla V$ or $g = -dV/dr$ for radial field. Field points in direction of decreasing potential.
Potential Due to Spherical Shell: Outside ($r > R$): $V = -GM/r$. Inside ($r < R$): $V = -GM/R$ (constant, equal to surface value). Field inside is zero but potential is not zero.
Potential Due to Solid Sphere: Outside ($r > R$): $V = -GM/r$. Inside ($r \le R$): $V = -\frac{GM}{2R^3}(3R^2 - r^2)$. At center: $V = -3GM/2R$.

Escape Velocity: Minimum speed to escape to infinity from surface: $v_\text{esc} = \sqrt{2GM/R} = \sqrt{2gR}$. For Earth: $\approx 11.2\text{ km/s}$. Derived from energy conservation: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 - GMm/R = 0$.
Gravitational Potential is Scalar: Unlike field (vector), potential adds algebraically. Potential at a point due to multiple masses: $V = -\sum Gm_i/r_i$.

data.title: Variation in g due to Altitude and Depth
data.topicTitle: Variation in g due to Altitude and Depth

notes: **g above the surface (altitude):** at height h above Earth's surface, $g' = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2} = g\left(\frac{R}{R+h}\right)^2$. As h increases, g decreases. For small h ($h \ll R$), a binomial expansion gives $g' \approx g\left(1 - \frac{2h}{R}\right)$ — a useful approximation.

**g below the surface (depth):** at depth d, only the mass inside the concentric sphere of radius ($R-d$) contributes: $g' = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)$ — gravity DECREASES linearly with depth. At the centre ($d = R$), $g' = 0$.

**Why they differ:** above the surface, whole-earth mass acts from a larger distance ($1/r^2$ law); below the surface, the shell above the point exerts zero net force (shell theorem) and only the inner sphere matters, whose mass scales as ($R-d$)^3 while distance scales as ($R-d$) — giving linear decrease.

**Worked example — altitude:** at $h = R$ (one Earth radius up), $g' = g\left(\frac{R}{2R}\right)^2 = g/4 = 2.45 \text{ m/s}^2$. At $h = 100$ km, using the small-h formula, the fractional decrease is $2h/R = 2\times 100/6400 = 0.031$, so $g' \approx 9.5 \text{ m/s}^2$.
**Worked example — depth:** at $d = R/2$ (3200 km deep), $g' = g(1 - 1/2) = g/2 = 4.9 \text{ m/s}^2$. At $d = R$ (centre) → $g' = 0$ (weightlessness, though pressure is immense).
**Graphs (NEB favourite):** $g$ vs $r$ rises linearly from 0 at the centre to g at the surface, then falls as $1/r^2$ beyond the surface. The maximum value of g on Earth is at the surface.

**Other causes of variation:** (1) rotation of Earth: g reduced by $\omega^2 R \cos^2 \lambda$ ($\lambda$ = latitude), maximum at the equator; (2) shape: Earth is an oblate spheroid — g is larger at the poles ($\approx 9.832$) than the equator ($\approx 9.78$); (3) local density anomalies (mountains, mineral deposits) cause tiny local changes used in geophysics.

**Altitude formula for satellites:** for an orbit at height h, effective $r = R + h$: $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{R+h}}$ and the orbital g is $g' = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2}$ — the same g formula used at that radius.
confusion: ❌ 'g increases with altitude.' ✅ Above the surface g DEcreases as $\frac{1}{(R+h)^2}$; below the surface it also decreases (linearly). g is max at the surface.
❌ 'From height h, g falls by $h/R$.' ✅ The small-h approximation is $2h/R$ (from the square), not $h/R$. At $h = 100$ km, that is ≈ 3%.
❌ 'Deep inside Earth, g keeps growing.' ✅ It decreases linearly: $g' = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)$, zero at the centre. The shell above you pulls equally in all directions (zero net).
❌ 'g is the same at poles and equator.' ✅ Rotation and the oblate shape make g slightly larger at the poles (~0.5% difference).
❌ 'At altitude 6400 km, g is half of surface.' ✅ At $h = R$, $g' = g/4$ — the height doubles the distance, so the square halves twice.
❌ 'Weightlessness in orbit means no gravity.' ✅ Astronauts at 400 km still feel ~88% of surface gravity — they float because they are in free fall around Earth.

specificConditions: **Altitude Formula:** Above the surface ($h \ge 0$), $g' = g(R/(R+h))^2$ follows the inverse-square law exactly. For $h \ll R$, the binomial approximation gives $g' \approx g(1 - 2h/R)$ — the factor of 2 comes from the square in the denominator.

**Depth Formula:** Below the surface ($d \le R$), only the mass interior to radius $R-d$ contributes (Shell Theorem). Since mass $\propto (R-d)^3$ and distance $\propto (R-d)$, $g' = g(1 - d/R)$ — a linear decrease to zero at the center.

**Surface Maximum:** $g$ reaches its maximum at Earth's surface. It decreases in both directions: $1/r^2$ outside, linear inside. The graph of $g$ vs $r$ is triangular-like: linear rise from center to surface, then inverse-square fall.

notes: **g above the surface (altitude):** at height h above Earth's surface, $g' = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2} = g\left(\frac{R}{R+h}\right)^2$. As h increases, g decreases. For small h ($h \ll R$), a binomial expansion gives $g' \approx g\left(1 - \frac{2h}{R}\right)$ — a useful approximation.

**g below the surface (depth):** at depth d, only the mass inside the concentric sphere of radius ($R-d$) contributes: $g' = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)$ — gravity DECREASES linearly with depth. At the centre ($d = R$), $g' = 0$.

**Why they differ:** above the surface, whole-earth mass acts from a larger distance ($1/r^2$ law); below the surface, the shell above the point exerts zero net force (shell theorem) and only the inner sphere matters, whose mass scales as ($R-d$)^3 while distance scales as ($R-d$) — giving linear decrease.

**Worked example — altitude:** at $h = R$ (one Earth radius up), $g' = g\left(\frac{R}{2R}\right)^2 = g/4 = 2.45 \text{ m/s}^2$. At $h = 100$ km, using the small-h formula, the fractional decrease is $2h/R = 2\times 100/6400 = 0.031$, so $g' \approx 9.5 \text{ m/s}^2$.
**Worked example — depth:** at $d = R/2$ (3200 km deep), $g' = g(1 - 1/2) = g/2 = 4.9 \text{ m/s}^2$. At $d = R$ (centre) → $g' = 0$ (weightlessness, though pressure is immense).
**Graphs (NEB favourite):** $g$ vs $r$ rises linearly from 0 at the centre to g at the surface, then falls as $1/r^2$ beyond the surface. The maximum value of g on Earth is at the surface.

**Other causes of variation:** (1) rotation of Earth: g reduced by $\omega^2 R \cos^2 \lambda$ ($\lambda$ = latitude), maximum at the equator; (2) shape: Earth is an oblate spheroid — g is larger at the poles ($\approx 9.832$) than the equator ($\approx 9.78$); (3) local density anomalies (mountains, mineral deposits) cause tiny local changes used in geophysics.

**Altitude formula for satellites:** for an orbit at height h, effective $r = R + h$: $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{R+h}}$ and the orbital g is $g' = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2}$ — the same g formula used at that radius.

**g above the surface (altitude):** at height h above Earth's surface, g' = GM/(R+h)² = g(R/(R+h))². As h increases, g decreases. For small h (h ≪ R), a binomial expansion gives g' ≈ g(1 − 2h/R) — a useful approximation.

**g below the surface (depth):** at depth d, only the mass inside the concentric sphere of radius (R−d) contributes: g' = g(1 − d/R) — gravity DECREASES linearly with depth. At the centre (d = R), g' = 0.

**Why they differ:** above the surface, whole-earth mass acts from a larger distance (1/r² law); below the surface, the shell above the point exerts zero net force (shell theorem) and only the inner sphere matters, whose mass scales as (R−d)³ while distance scales as (R−d) — giving linear decrease.

confusion: ❌ 'g increases with altitude.' ✅ Above the surface g DEcreases as $\frac{1}{(R+h)^2}$; below the surface it also decreases (linearly). g is max at the surface.
❌ 'From height h, g falls by $h/R$.' ✅ The small-h approximation is $2h/R$ (from the square), not $h/R$. At $h = 100$ km, that is ≈ 3%.
❌ 'Deep inside Earth, g keeps growing.' ✅ It decreases linearly: $g' = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)$, zero at the centre. The shell above you pulls equally in all directions (zero net).
❌ 'g is the same at poles and equator.' ✅ Rotation and the oblate shape make g slightly larger at the poles (~0.5% difference).
❌ 'At altitude 6400 km, g is half of surface.' ✅ At $h = R$, $g' = g/4$ — the height doubles the distance, so the square halves twice.
❌ 'Weightlessness in orbit means no gravity.' ✅ Astronauts at 400 km still feel ~88% of surface gravity — they float because they are in free fall around Earth.

data.topicTitle: Variation in value of 'g' due to altitude and depth
notes: Acceleration Due to Gravity: At Earth's surface, $g = GM/R^2 \approx 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$. It varies with location due to altitude, depth, Earth's rotation, and shape.
Variation with Altitude: At height $h$ above surface: $g_h = GM/(R+h)^2 = g(1+h/R)^{-2} \approx g(1 - 2h/R)$ for $h \ll R$. Gravity decreases with altitude — inverse square law.
Variation with Depth: At depth $d$ below surface (assuming uniform density): $g_d = g(1 - d/R) = g(R-d)/R$. Gravity decreases linearly with depth, becoming zero at Earth's center.
Comparison: For small $h$ and $d$, decrease at height $h$ ($\Delta g \approx -2gh/R$) is twice the decrease at depth $d$ ($\Delta g = -gd/R$). Gravity decreases faster with altitude than with depth.

Earth's Rotation: Effective gravity at latitude $\lambda$: $g' = g - \omega^2 R \cos^2\lambda$. Maximum at poles ($\lambda = 90^\circ$, no rotation effect), minimum at equator ($\lambda = 0^\circ$, maximum centrifugal reduction).
Earth's Shape: Earth is oblate (equatorial radius > polar radius). Since $g \propto 1/R^2$, $g$ is higher at poles (closer to center) and lower at equator.
Combined Effects: The measured $g$ varies from about $9.78\text{ m/s}^2$ at equator to $9.83\text{ m/s}^2$ at poles due to rotation + shape + altitude.

mcs.explanation: Assuming uniform density, $g_d = g(1 - d/R)$ — decreases linearly with depth.

mcs.explanation: At center, mass is symmetrically distributed — net gravitational pull is zero.

mcs.explanation: Height: Δg ≈ -2gh/R; Depth: Δg = -gd/R. Height decrease is twice depth decrease.

data.topicTitle: Centre of Mass and Centre of Gravity

notes: **Centre of mass (COM):** the point where the entire mass of a body (or system) may be considered to be concentrated for translational (linear) motion analysis. Position: $R_{cm} = \frac{\Sigma m_i r_i}{\Sigma m_i}$. For continuous bodies: $R_{cm} = \frac{\int r dm}{M}$.

**Centre of gravity (CG):** the point where the entire weight of a body may be considered to act. In a uniform gravitational field, the CG coincides exactly with the COM. If the field is non-uniform (very large bodies, varying g), the CG may shift slightly relative to the COM.

**Why CG equals COM in uniform g:** weight $W = mg$ at each point, and since $g$ is the same everywhere, the torque balance condition that defines the CG reduces to the same weighted average that defines the COM. The two centres coincide.
**Solved example — two masses:** masses 2 kg at x = 0 and 8 kg at x = 3 m. COM: $x_{cm} = \frac{2 \times 0 + 8 \times 3}{2+8} = \frac{24}{10} = 2.4 \text{ m}$. The COM is closer to the heavier mass.

**Solved example — system of three:** 1 kg at (0,0), 2 kg at (2,0), 3 kg at (0,4). $x_{cm} = \frac{1 \times 0 + 2 \times 2 + 3 \times 0}{6} = \frac{4}{6} = 0.67 \text{ m}$; $y_{cm} = \frac{1 \times 0 + 2 \times 0 + 3 \times 4}{6} = \frac{12}{6} = 2 \text{ m}$. COM at (0.67, 2) m.

**Properties:** (1) The COM of a uniform, symmetric body lies at its geometric centre. (2) The COM of two bodies lies on the line joining them. (3) For irregular bodies the COM can lie OUTSIDE the material (e.g., a ring, a boomerang, a bent L-shape). (4) The total linear momentum of a system equals $M \cdot V_{cm}$ — external forces alone can change $V_{cm}$.

**Finding CG experimentally (NEB practical):** suspend the body from two different points; the two vertical lines through the suspension points intersect at the centre of gravity. Plumb lines are used — the intersection of the two suspension lines locates the CG.

**Applications:** designing stable structures (ships, cars, tables) keeps the CG low and inside the base; balancing acts use alignment of the CG above the support; in projectiles, the COM follows a smooth parabola even if the object rotates; spacecraft alignment uses the COM.

❌ 'COM is a force point.' ✅ COM is a mass-weighted average position — a geometric point for translational dynamics, not a force.
❌ 'To find the COM, only the largest mass matters.' ✅ All masses contribute proportionally: $R_{cm} = \frac{\Sigma m_i r_i}{\Sigma m_i}$.
❌ 'The COM moves when the body spins.' ✅ The COM of an isolated system moves uniformly (or stays still); spinning happens about the COM.

notes: **Fact.** Newton: F = G m₁m₂/r²; g = GM/r²; at Earth's surface g = GM/R² ≈ 9.8 m/s².
**Fact.** Orbital velocity v = √(GM/r); time period T = 2π√(r³/GM); escape velocity v_esc = √(2GM/r) = √2·v_orbital (at same r).
**Fact.** For a uniform sphere, g ∝ r inside and g = 0 at the centre; g decreases as 1/r² outside.

**Orbital velocity (v₀):** a satellite stays in a circular orbit when the gravitational pull GMm/r² provides the required centripetal force mv²/r. Equating: GMm/r² = mv₀²/r → v₀ = √(GM/r). Near Earth's surface, v₀ = √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km/s.

**Why v₀ matters:** too slow → the satellite spirals in; too fast → it escapes to a higher ellipse. The orbital speed depends only on the radius (GM/r), not on the satellite's mass — heavy and light satellites share the same orbit speed.

**Time period (T):** T = circumference/velocity = 2πr/v₀ = 2π√(r³/GM) — Kepler's third law. Squaring: T² ∝ r³. A higher orbit has a longer period: the Moon (r ≈ 3.84×10⁸ m) takes ~27.3 days; the ISS (r ≈ 6.8×10⁶ m) takes ~92 minutes.

**Energy of an orbiting satellite:** K = ½mv₀² = GMm/2r, U = −GMm/r, so E_total = −GMm/2r. Notice K = −U/2 and E = U/2 — a signature of circular orbits. To raise a satellite to a higher orbit you must ADD energy, but the KE actually decreases (higher orbit = slower speed).
**Worked example — geostationary orbit:** for T = 24 h, r = (GMT²/4π²)^(1/3) ≈ 4.22×10⁷ m ≈ 35,800 km above the equator with v₀ ≈ 3.08 km/s.

**Low Earth vs geostationary comparison:** LEO (200–2000 km): v ≈ 7.8 km/s, T ≈ 90 min, covers Earth rapidly (imaging, ISS). Geostationary (35,800 km): v ≈ 3.07 km/s, T = 24 h, appears fixed over one spot (communications, weather).

**Orbit changes:** to transfer between circular orbits, a Hohmann ellipse uses two engine burns; near perigee/apogee speeds change by Δv = v₂ − v₁. Firing thrust ahead slows the satellite and lowers the orbit; firing backward raises it.

❌ 'A satellite must be above the atmosphere to feel no gravity.' ✅ A satellite feels gravity at every altitude — it is in continuous free fall. It never falls to Earth because its forward speed curves its fall into an orbit.

data.title: Motion of a Satellite

notes: **Orbital velocity (v₀):** a satellite stays in a circular orbit when the gravitational pull $GMm/r^2$ provides the required centripetal force $mv^2/r$. Equating: $GMm/r^2 = mv_0^2/r \rightarrow v_0 = \sqrt{GM/r}$. Near Earth's surface, $v_0 = \sqrt{gR} \approx 7.9 \text{ km/s}$.

**Why v₀ matters:** too slow → the satellite spirals in; too fast → it escapes to a higher ellipse. The orbital speed depends only on the radius (GM/r), not on the satellite's mass — heavy and light satellites share the same orbit speed.

**Time period (T):** $T = \frac{2\pi r}{v_0} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}$ — Kepler's third law. Squaring: $T^2 \propto r^3$. A higher orbit has a longer period: the Moon (r ≈ 3.84×10⁸ m) takes ~27.3 days; the ISS (r ≈ 6.8×10⁶ m) takes ~92 minutes.

**Energy of an orbiting satellite:** $K = \frac{1}{2}mv_0^2 = \frac{GMm}{2r}$, $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$, so $E_{total} = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$. Notice $K = -U/2$ and $E = U/2$ — a signature of circular orbits. To raise a satellite to a higher orbit you must ADD energy, but the KE actually decreases (higher orbit = slower speed).

**Worked example — ISS orbit:** at height 400 km, r = 6.8×10⁶ m. $v_0 = \sqrt{\frac{6.67\times10^{-11} \times 5.97\times10^{24}}{6.8\times10^6}} = \sqrt{5.86\times10^7} \approx 7.66 \text{ km/s}$. $T = \frac{2\pi \times 6.8\times10^6}{7.66\times10^3} \approx 5570 \text{ s} \approx 93 \text{ min}$.

**Worked example — geostationary orbit:** for T = 24 h, $r = \left(\frac{GMT^2}{4\pi^2}\right)^{1/3} \approx 4.22\times10^7 \text{ m} \approx 35,800 \text{ km}$ above the equator with $v_0 \approx 3.08 \text{ km/s}$.

**Low Earth vs geostationary comparison:** LEO (200–2000 km): v ≈ 7.8 km/s, T ≈ 90 min, covers Earth rapidly (imaging, ISS). Geostationary (35,800 km): v ≈ 3.07 km/s, T = 24 h, appears fixed over one spot (communications, weather).

**Orbit changes:** to transfer between circular orbits, a Hohmann ellipse uses two engine burns; near perigee/apogee speeds change by $\Delta v = v_2 - v_1$. Firing thrust ahead slows the satellite and lowers the orbit; firing backward raises it.
confusion: ❌ 'A satellite must be above the atmosphere to feel no gravity.' ✅ A satellite feels gravity at every altitude — it is in continuous free fall. It never falls to Earth because its forward speed curves its fall into an orbit.
❌ 'Weightlessness means g = 0 on the ISS.' ✅ g at 400 km is ≈ 8.7 m/s² (89% of surface). Astronauts float because both they and the station accelerate toward Earth together (free fall).
❌ 'Heavier satellites orbit slower.' ✅ Orbital speed is independent of the satellite's mass: $v_0 = \sqrt{GM/r}$.

❌ 'Higher orbit → faster speed.' ✅ Higher orbit means SLOWER speed ($v_0 = \sqrt{GM/r}$) but a LONGER period. To reach a higher orbit you must speed up at launch; once there, the circular speed is lower.
❌ 'T is proportional to r.' ✅ $T \propto r^{3/2}$ — the period grows faster than the radius.

❌ 'A satellite's kinetic energy increases as it moves to a higher orbit.' ✅ $KE = \frac{GMm}{2r}$ DECREASES with height; the added energy is stored as potential energy ($+GmM\cdot\Delta(1/r)$) making the total $E = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$ less negative.

**Worked example — ISS orbit:** at height 400 km, r = 6.8×10⁶ m. $v_0 = \sqrt{\frac{6.67\times10^{-11} \times 5.97\times10^{24}}{6.8\times10^6}} = \sqrt{5.86\times10^7} \approx 7.66 \text{ km/s}$. $T = \frac{2\pi \times 6.8\times10^6}{7.66\times10^3} \approx 5570 \text{ s} \approx 93 \text{ min}$.

**Worked example — geostationary orbit:** for T = 24 h, $r = \left(\frac{GMT^2}{4\pi^2}\right)^{1/3} \approx 4.22\times10^7 \text{ m} \approx 35,800 \text{ km}$ above the equator with $v_0 \approx 3.08 \text{ km/s}$.

**Low Earth vs geostationary comparison:** LEO (200–2000 km): v ≈ 7.8 km/s, T ≈ 90 min, covers Earth rapidly (imaging, ISS). Geostationary (35,800 km): v ≈ 3.07 km/s, T = 24 h, appears fixed over one spot (communications, weather).

**Orbit changes:** to transfer between circular orbits, a Hohmann ellipse uses two engine burns; near perigee/apogee speeds change by $\Delta v = v_2 - v_1$. Firing thrust ahead slows the satellite and lowers the orbit; firing backward raises it.
confusion: ❌ 'A satellite must be above the atmosphere to feel no gravity.' ✅ A satellite feels gravity at every altitude — it is in continuous free fall. It never falls to Earth because its forward speed curves its fall into an orbit.
❌ 'Weightlessness means g = 0 on the ISS.' ✅ g at 400 km is ≈ 8.7 m/s² (89% of surface). Astronauts float because both they and the station accelerate toward Earth together (free fall).
❌ 'Heavier satellites orbit slower.' ✅ Orbital speed is independent of the satellite's mass: $v_0 = \sqrt{GM/r}$.

❌ 'Higher orbit → faster speed.' ✅ Higher orbit means SLOWER speed ($v_0 = \sqrt{GM/r}$) but a LONGER period. To reach a higher orbit you must speed up at launch; once there, the circular speed is lower.
❌ 'T is proportional to r.' ✅ $T \propto r^{3/2}$ — the period grows faster than the radius.

❌ 'A satellite's kinetic energy increases as it moves to a higher orbit.' ✅ $KE = \frac{GMm}{2r}$ DECREASES with height; the added energy is stored as potential energy ($+GmM\cdot\Delta(1/r)$) making the total $E = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$ less negative.

data.title: Escape Velocity
notes: Escape velocity is the minimum speed at radius r that lets an object reach infinity with zero final speed when no further thrust or drag acts. With gravitational potential energy zero at infinity, energy conservation gives (1/2)mv²−GMm/r=0.
Solving gives ve=√(2GM/r). At the surface r=R, g=GM/R², so ve=√(2gR). The escaping object’s mass cancels, so the ideal threshold is independent of its mass.
Worked Earth estimate: g=9.81 m s⁻² and R=6.37×10⁶ m give ve=√(2gR)≈1.12×10⁴ m s⁻¹=11.2 km s⁻¹.
At altitude h, use r=R+h: ve(h)/ve(0)=√[R/(R+h)]. At h=R, local escape speed is 1/√2 of its surface value.
Circular orbital speed at the same radius is vc=√(GM/r), so ve=√2 vc. This is an ideal energy threshold; real launches must account for atmosphere, rotation, gravity losses and propulsion.

Escape velocity is the speed that lets a projectile coast to infinity, where the gravitational potential is taken as zero. It does not depend on the mass of the projectile. From the Earth's surface it is about 11 km/s, which is √2 times the speed of a low circular orbit.

**No Atmosphere Assumption:** The formula assumes no air resistance. In reality, atmospheric drag requires higher initial speed for Earth; for the Moon (no atmosphere), the formula is exact. Also assumes a spherically symmetric, non-rotating body.

data.title: Geostationary Satellite

notes: **Geostationary satellite:** a satellite that appears stationary relative to a point on the Earth's equator. It must satisfy three conditions: (1) orbit in the plane of the equator (equatorial plane), (2) orbit in the same direction as Earth's rotation (west → east), and (3) have a period exactly equal to Earth's rotation period (T = 24 hours).
**Height above Earth:** using T = 2π√(r³/GM) with T = 86400 s → r ≈ 4.22×10⁷ m from the centre → altitude h = r − R ≈ 35,800 km above the surface. This is about 5.6 Earth radii.
**Orbital speed:** v₀ = 2πr/T = 2π×4.22×10⁷/86400 ≈ 3.07 km/s. It matches Earth's angular speed: the satellite and the point below rotate together, so the satellite hangs over the same longitude.

**Only the equator works:** a satellite over the equator is the only way the orbit plane can contain both the satellite and Earth's rotation axis while keeping the satellite fixed over one point. An inclined orbit would carry the satellite north and south each day.
**Why 24 h is exact:** for T = T_Earth, the angular speeds match: ω_sat = ω_Earth. From r³ = GMT²/4π² the altitude is fixed (~35,800 km) — there is a unique geostationary height.

**Applications:** communications satellites (broadcast, TV, internet), weather satellites (HIMAWARI, INSAT type), and some navigation augmentation systems. Their fixed position means ground dishes never need to move.

**Geostationary vs geosynchronous:** a geosynchronous satellite has a 24-h period but may have an inclined or elliptical orbit, so it drifts north/south in the sky. A geostationary satellite is a special geosynchronous satellite confined to the equatorial plane at fixed longitude.

**Energy at geostationary orbit:** for m = 1000 kg, U = −GMm/r ≈ −9.4×10⁹ J, E_total = −GMm/2r ≈ −4.7×10⁹ J. Launching to this height needs a large boost — the standard launch uses a geostationary transfer orbit (GTO) followed by an apogee burn.
confusion: ❌ 'Any 24-hour satellite is geostationary.' ✅ A geostationary satellite must ALSO be equatorial, circular, and west-to-east. A geosynchronous one just matches the 24-h period.
❌ 'Geostationary orbit can be at any height above the equator.' ✅ There is exactly ONE geostationary altitude: ≈ 35,800 km. It is set by Earth's rotation period.
❌ 'A geostationary satellite stays above one spot because it has no gravity.' ✅ It stays because its orbital period exactly equals Earth's rotation; gravity still holds it in orbit at v ≈ 3.07 km/s.
❌ 'The satellite is stationary in space.' ✅ It moves at 3.07 km/s; it is stationary only relative to the rotating Earth.
❌ 'At high latitudes people see it overhead.' ✅ A geostationary satellite is always over the equator — at high latitudes it appears low on the horizon, and near the poles it is not visible at all.
❌ 'The Moon is a geostationary satellite.' ✅ The Moon has a 27.3-day period and an inclined orbit — it is not geostationary.

notes: **Geostationary satellite:** a satellite that appears stationary relative to a point on the Earth's equator. It must satisfy three conditions: (1) orbit in the plane of the equator (equatorial plane), (2) orbit in the same direction as Earth's rotation (west → east), and (3) have a period exactly equal to Earth's rotation period (T = 24 hours).
**Height above Earth:** using T = 2π√(r³/GM) with T = 86400 s → r ≈ 4.22×10⁷ m from the centre → altitude h = r − R ≈ 35,800 km above the surface. This is about 5.6 Earth radii.
**Orbital speed:** v₀ = 2πr/T = 2π×4.22×10⁷/86400 ≈ 3.07 km/s. It matches Earth's angular speed: the satellite and the point below rotate together, so the satellite hangs over the same longitude.

**Only the equator works:** a satellite over the equator is the only way the orbit plane can contain both the satellite and Earth's rotation axis while keeping the satellite fixed over one point. An inclined orbit would carry the satellite north and south each day.
**Why 24 h is exact:** for T = T_Earth, the angular speeds match: ω_sat = ω_Earth. From r³ = GMT²/4π² the altitude is fixed (~35,800 km) — there is a unique geostationary height.

**Applications:** communications satellites (broadcast, TV, internet), weather satellites (HIMAWARI, INSAT type), and some navigation augmentation systems. Their fixed position means ground dishes never need to move.

**Geostationary vs geosynchronous:** a geosynchronous satellite has a 24-h period but may have an inclined or elliptical orbit, so it drifts north/south in the sky. A geostationary satellite is a special geosynchronous satellite confined to the equatorial plane at fixed longitude.

**Energy at geostationary orbit:** for m = 1000 kg, U = −GMm/r ≈ −9.4×10⁹ J, E_total = −GMm/2r ≈ −4.7×10⁹ J. Launching to this height needs a large boost — the standard launch uses a geostationary transfer orbit (GTO) followed by an apogee burn.

data.title: Potential and Kinetic Energy of the Satellite
data.topicTitle: Potential and kinetic energy of the satellite

notes: **Gravitational potential V:** the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to a point, without acceleration. For a point mass M: V = −GM/r. At infinity V = 0, and everywhere else V is negative because gravity does positive work as the mass approaches — the field does the work, so potential decreases.

**Gravitational potential energy U:** the work done against gravity in assembling a system; for two masses separated by r: U = −GMm/r. It is the energy of the whole system, not of one mass alone. U is negative because the system is bound — you must supply GMm/r of energy to separate the masses to infinity.

**Why the minus sign matters:** potential energy is defined with zero at infinity. Since the force is attractive, energy is released (and PE decreases) as masses come together. A satellite in orbit at radius r has U = −GMm/r — its total mechanical energy is E = K + U = −GMm/2r, which is negative, confirming a bound orbit.

**Near Earth's surface:** for small heights h above the surface, U = mgh. This is the constant-g approximation of −GMm/r: since Δ(1/r) ≈ −h/R², the change matches mgh. Use mgh only for h ≪ R; use −GMm/r for large altitudes (satellites, rockets).

**Worked example — escape energy:** to launch a mass m from Earth's surface (R) to infinity you must supply GMm/R. Numerically for m = 1 kg: (6.67×10⁻¹¹)(5.97×10²⁴)/6.37×10⁶ ≈ 6.25×10⁷ J ≈ 62.5 MJ per kg. This energy corresponds to the escape speed 11.2 km/s.

**Potential vs potential energy vs field:** field g = −dV/dr (the force per unit mass, a vector); potential V is a scalar (J/kg); potential energy U = mV. The field is the negative gradient of the potential: g = −dV/dr radially.

**Equipotential surfaces:** surfaces of constant V. Moving along an equipotential surface requires zero work; the field is always perpendicular to these surfaces. For a point mass, equipotentials are concentric spheres.
**Superposition:** for multiple masses, V = Σ(−GMᵢ/rᵢ) and U = Σ(−GMᵢm/rᵢ) — potentials add as scalars, which is much simpler than adding force vectors.
confusion: ❌ 'Potential and potential energy are the same.' ✅ Potential V is work per unit mass (J/kg); potential energy U = mV (J). V belongs to a point in the field; U belongs to the mass–field system.
❌ 'Negative energy is unphysical.' ✅ Negative potential energy simply means the system is BOUND — energy must be added to separate it. It is a matter of the reference at infinity.
❌ 'U = mgh and U = −GMm/r disagree.' ✅ They agree for small heights: mgh is the CHANGE in −GMm/r near the surface. Use the right one for the régime.
❌ 'Potential is maximum at Earth's surface.' ✅ Potential is most negative at the surface (−GM/R) and rises toward zero with altitude — at infinity it reaches the (higher) value 0.
❌ 'Doubling the distance doubles the potential energy.' ✅ U = −GMm/r — doubling r halves the magnitude, so U becomes −GMm/2r (less negative).

❌ 'A satellite far away has lots of potential energy.' ✅ A far-away satellite has potential energy near ZERO (least negative, but U ≈ 0). It needs enormous kinetic energy (orbital speed) that comes from the launch energy.

universalFacts: Gravitational potential energy is exactly the 'missing' energy that binds systems — this is why the binding energy of Earth + satellite equals |U|.
The concept of potential is useful because it is scalar: complex many-body problems reduce to addition rather than vector resolution.
Near a black hole, gravitational potential becomes so deep (−GM/r) that even light cannot escape — the origin of the event horizon.
Gravitational potential determines whether planets retain atmospheres: gas molecules with thermal speeds above the local escape speed leak away.
The Voyager probes were launched using the escape-energy budget — their final trajectory traced the potential wells of the Sun and giant planets.

U of 1000 kg satellite at r = 6.8×10⁶ m: U = −GMm/r = −5.9×10¹⁰ J.
Escape energy per kg: GM/R = 6.25×10⁷ J ≈ 17 kWh per kg.

Total energy of circular orbit: E = −GMm/2r — negative, so the orbit is bound.

notes: **Gravitational potential V:** the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to a point, without acceleration. For a point mass M: V = −GM/r. At infinity V = 0, and everywhere else V is negative because gravity does positive work as the mass approaches — the field does the work, so potential decreases.

**Gravitational potential energy U:** the work done against gravity in assembling a system; for two masses separated by r: U = −GMm/r. It is the energy of the whole system, not of one mass alone. U is negative because the system is bound — you must supply GMm/r of energy to separate the masses to infinity.

**Why the minus sign matters:** potential energy is defined with zero at infinity. Since the force is attractive, energy is released (and PE decreases) as masses come together. A satellite in orbit at radius r has U = −GMm/r — its total mechanical energy is E = K + U = −GMm/2r, which is negative, confirming a bound orbit.

**Near Earth's surface:** for small heights h above the surface, U = mgh. This is the constant-g approximation of −GMm/r: since Δ(1/r) ≈ −h/R², the change matches mgh. Use mgh only for h ≪ R; use −GMm/r for large altitudes (satellites, rockets).

**Worked example — escape energy:** to launch a mass m from Earth's surface (R) to infinity you must supply GMm/R. Numerically for m = 1 kg: (6.67×10⁻¹¹)(5.97×10²⁴)/6.37×10⁶ ≈ 6.25×10⁷ J ≈ 62.5 MJ per kg. This energy corresponds to the escape speed 11.2 km/s.

**Potential vs potential energy vs field:** field g = −dV/dr (the force per unit mass, a vector); potential V is a scalar (J/kg); potential energy U = mV. The field is the negative gradient of the potential: g = −dV/dr radially.

**Equipotential surfaces:** surfaces of constant V. Moving along an equipotential surface requires zero work; the field is always perpendicular to these surfaces. For a point mass, equipotentials are concentric spheres.
**Superposition:** for multiple masses, V = Σ(−GMᵢ/rᵢ) and U = Σ(−GMᵢm/rᵢ) — potentials add as scalars, which is much simpler than adding force vectors.
confusion: ❌ 'Potential and potential energy are the same.' ✅ Potential V is work per unit mass (J/kg); potential energy U = mV (J). V belongs to a point in the field; U belongs to the mass–field system.
❌ 'Negative energy is unphysical.' ✅ Negative potential energy simply means the system is BOUND — energy must be added to separate it. It is a matter of the reference at infinity.
❌ 'U = mgh and U = −GMm/r disagree.' ✅ They agree for small heights: mgh is the CHANGE in −GMm/r near the surface. Use the right one for the régime.
❌ 'Potential is maximum at Earth's surface.' ✅ Potential is most negative at the surface (−GM/R) and rises toward zero with altitude — at infinity it reaches the (higher) value 0.
❌ 'Doubling the distance doubles the potential energy.' ✅ U = −GMm/r — doubling r halves the magnitude, so U becomes −GMm/2r (less negative).

❌ 'A satellite far away has lots of potential energy.' ✅ A far-away satellite has potential energy near ZERO (least negative, but U ≈ 0). It needs enormous kinetic energy (orbital speed) that comes from the launch energy.

data.title: GPS

notes: **What GPS is:** the Global Positioning System is a satellite-based navigation system that tells a receiver its exact 3D position on Earth. It uses the same gravitational/orbital physics as any satellite, which is why it lives in the gravitation chapter.

**Principle of position fixing:** each GPS satellite broadcasts a radio signal stamped with its position and precise transmission time. The receiver measures the travel time of signals from at least four satellites and solves for (x, y, z, t) — the fourth equation corrects the receiver clock offset.

**How distance is measured:** distance = speed of light × time delay. Since the receiver's clock is not atomic-precise, a fourth satellite provides the clock-error term, giving accuracy of a few metres.

**Satellite constellation:** 24+ satellites orbit at ≈ 20,200 km altitude (medium Earth orbit) in six planes inclined 55° to the equator. Each satellite has a period of ≈ 11 h 58 min (half a sidereal day) and speed ≈ 3.87 km/s — from T = 2π√(r³/GM).

**Why the orbits are chosen:** six planes × four satellites each guarantee that at least 4–6 satellites are above the horizon at any place and time. The 55° inclination covers up to the poles, unlike a geostationary belt.

**Relativity in GPS:** satellite clocks run faster than ground clocks by ~38 µs/day (7 µs from special relativity + 45 µs from general relativity). This systematic shift must be compensated, otherwise GPS positions would drift by ~10 km per day — a practical proof of relativity.

**Accuracy and sources of error:** ionospheric delays, multipath reflections, satellite clocks, and geometry (DOP). With corrections (differential GPS / WAAS / dual-frequency) accuracy reaches centimetre level for surveying.

**Applications:** navigation (cars, ships, aircraft), mapping, timing synchronisation for power grids and financial networks, agriculture, disaster relief, and scientific studies (tectonic plate motion). GPS is a direct practical payoff of satellite motion physics.
confusion: ❌ 'GPS signal carries your position from the satellite.' ✅ The satellite only sends its OWN position + time. YOUR receiver computes your position by triangulating delays.
❌ 'Three satellites suffice for full 3D positioning.' ✅ Three give (x,y,z) only if the clock is perfect; a fourth is required for a practical unknown clock offset.
❌ 'GPS works by measuring signal strength.' ✅ It measures signal TRAVEL TIME (c × Δt), not strength.
❌ 'GPS satellites are geostationary.' ✅ They orbit at ≈ 20,200 km in inclined MEO orbits with ≈ 12 h periods — not geostationary.
❌ 'Relativistic corrections are too tiny to matter.' ✅ Without them GPS would be off by ~10 km/day. The effect is 38 µs/day — essential.
❌ 'Position accuracy is limited by the number of satellites visible.' ✅ With ≥ 4 satellites you can fix position; more satellites reduce error statistics but don't change the basic math.

universalFacts: GPS was developed by the US Department of Defense and declared fully operational in 1995; it is freely available worldwide.
The constellation was designed by military engineers using Newton's law and Kepler's equations — a textbook application of gravitational physics.
The GPS satellites transmit on L1 (1575.42 MHz) and L2 (1227.60 MHz); dual-frequency receivers cancel ionospheric delay.
GPS timing synchronises global telecom networks and power grids — a 1 µs clock error maps to ~300 m of position error.
India's NAVIC and other regional systems use the same principles as GPS.

notes: **What GPS is:** the Global Positioning System is a satellite-based navigation system that tells a receiver its exact 3D position on Earth. It uses the same gravitational/orbital physics as any satellite, which is why it lives in the gravitation chapter.

**Principle of position fixing:** each GPS satellite broadcasts a radio signal stamped with its position and precise transmission time. The receiver measures the travel time of signals from at least four satellites and solves for (x, y, z, t) — the fourth equation corrects the receiver clock offset.

**How distance is measured:** distance = speed of light × time delay. Since the receiver's clock is not atomic-precise, a fourth satellite provides the clock-error term, giving accuracy of a few metres.

**Satellite constellation:** 24+ satellites orbit at ≈ 20,200 km altitude (medium Earth orbit) in six planes inclined 55° to the equator. Each satellite has a period of ≈ 11 h 58 min (half a sidereal day) and speed ≈ 3.87 km/s — from T = 2π√(r³/GM).

**Why the orbits are chosen:** six planes × four satellites each guarantee that at least 4–6 satellites are above the horizon at any place and time. The 55° inclination covers up to the poles, unlike a geostationary belt.

**Relativity in GPS:** satellite clocks run faster than ground clocks by ~38 µs/day (7 µs from special relativity + 45 µs from general relativity). This systematic shift must be compensated, otherwise GPS positions would drift by ~10 km per day — a practical proof of relativity.

**Accuracy and sources of error:** ionospheric delays, multipath reflections, satellite clocks, and geometry (DOP). With corrections (differential GPS / WAAS / dual-frequency) accuracy reaches centimetre level for surveying.

**Applications:** navigation (cars, ships, aircraft), mapping, timing synchronisation for power grids and financial networks, agriculture, disaster relief, and scientific studies (tectonic plate motion). GPS is a direct practical payoff of satellite motion physics.

data.topicTitle: Molecular concept of thermal energy, heat and temperature; cause and direction of heat flow
notes: Matter is made of molecules in motion. In a solid they vibrate about fixed positions. In a liquid they move through the liquid. In a gas they move almost freely and collide. The energy of this motion, and of the molecular forces, is the internal energy of the body.

Temperature is the quantity that indicates how hot a body is. For an ideal gas it is proportional to the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules. A higher temperature means faster molecular motion, not a larger object.

Heat is energy that flows from one body to another because their temperatures differ. It is not a substance stored in a tank. Once the energy has entered a body it is part of that body's internal energy, and it is no longer called heat.

The direction of the flow is from the higher temperature to the lower temperature. The flow stops, in the sense that net transfer ends, when the two bodies reach the same temperature. That shared state is thermal equilibrium.

A large mass at a moderate temperature can hold more internal energy than a small mass at a higher temperature. Heat flow does not follow the amount of energy stored. It follows the temperature difference.
Putting a warm hand on a metal rail feels colder than putting it on wood at the same temperature because the metal conducts heat away faster. The temperatures were equal. The rates of flow were not.

data.title: Thermal Energy, Heat and Temperature
notes: **Definition:** A temperature scale is created by identifying two easily reproducible fixed points (usually the freezing and boiling points of water at standard atmospheric pressure), then dividing the interval between them into equal divisions.

**Celsius scale (°C):** Introduced by Anders Celsius in 1742. Freezing point of water = 0°C, boiling point = 100°C at 1 atm. Has 100 equal divisions between the fixed points. The SI unit for temperature intervals is the degree Celsius.
**Fahrenheit scale (°F):** Introduced by Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit in 1720. Freezing point = 32°F, boiling point = 212°F at 1 atm. Has 180 equal divisions. Widely used in the United States.

**Kelvin scale (K):** The SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature, named after Lord Kelvin. It is an absolute scale with zero at absolute zero (0 K = −273.15°C). Freezing point of water = 273.15 K, boiling point = 373.15 K. The Kelvin has the same magnitude as the Celsius degree, so ΔT(K) = ΔT(°C).

**Absolute zero:** 0 K = −273.15°C = −459.67°F. The theoretical temperature at which all molecular motion ceases (classical picture). It is unreachable in practice due to quantum zero-point energy. Modern definition: 0 K is the temperature at which the triple point of water occurs at exactly 273.16 K.

**Triple point of water:** The unique temperature and pressure at which solid, liquid, and vapor phases of water coexist in equilibrium: 273.16 K (0.01°C) at 611.657 Pa. This is the defining fixed point of the Kelvin scale.
**Reaumur scale (°R or °Ré):** Freezing point = 0°Ré, boiling point = 80°Ré. Rarely used today, except historically in some European countries.
**Rankine scale (°Ra):** The absolute version of Fahrenheit. 0°Ra = 0 K = −459.67°F. Freezing point of water = 491.67°Ra, boiling point = 671.67°Ra.

**Why use Kelvin?** In gas laws (PV = nRT), temperature must be in Kelvin because the relationship P ∝ T is linear only with absolute temperature. At 0 K, the extrapolated volume of an ideal gas would be zero, making physical sense. In Celsius, this would be −273.15°C - a non-zero volume at "zero" temperature.

**Gas thermometer:** The most accurate temperature measurement uses a constant-volume gas thermometer. It measures pressure of a fixed volume of gas, which is proportional to absolute temperature. The ideal gas law PV = nRT allows extrapolation to zero pressure for perfect accuracy.

**Platinum resistance thermometer:** Uses the fact that electrical resistance of metals increases nearly linearly with temperature. R = R₀(1 + αT), where α is the temperature coefficient of resistance. Platinum is used due to its stability and near-linear behavior.
**Thermal Energy, Heat and Temperature:** This topic covers the fundamental concepts of thermal energy, heat and temperature in the physics curriculum.
Understanding thermal energy, heat and temperature is essential for solving problems and building higher-level mathematical skills.
Key definitions and theorems related to thermal energy, heat and temperature should be memorized and practiced regularly.
confusion: Temperature and heat are NOT the same. Temperature is an intensive property (per unit mass); heat is energy transferred (extensive). A bathtub of 30°C water has more heat than a cup of 80°C water, but lower temperature.
A temperature difference of 1°C is NOT the same as 1°F. ΔT(°C) = (5/9)ΔT(°F). A 10°C change equals an 18°F change, so 5°C ≠ 5°F.
Kelvin is NOT written as '°K' - it is simply 'K' (e.g., 300 K, not 300°K). There is no 'degree Kelvin.' The word 'kelvin' is not capitalized when spelled out.

Absolute zero is NOT just 'really cold' - it is the state where classical thermal motion ceases entirely. At 0 K, only quantum zero-point energy remains, and all real substances have condensed to their ground states.
The triple point of water (273.16 K) and the freezing point of water (273.15 K) differ by exactly 0.01 K. Confusing these is a common source of error in metrology.
Carefully distinguish between similar-looking concepts in thermal energy, heat and temperature.

practice: Convert 300 K to Celsius and Fahrenheit. Solution: T(°C) = 300 − 273.15 = 26.85°C. T(°F) = (9/5)(26.85) + 32 = 80.33°F.

At what temperature do Celsius and Fahrenheit scales read the same? Solution: Set C = F in the conversion F = (9/5)C + 32. C = (9/5)C + 32 → C − (9/5)C = 32 → −(4/5)C = 32 → C = −40. Both read −40° at −40° (the same temperature!).

A faulty thermometer reads the freezing point of water as 5° (on its scale) and the boiling point as 95°. The temperature difference between these on the real Celsius scale is 100°C, and on the faulty scale is 90°. If the faulty thermometer reads 59°, what is the true Celsius temperature? Solution: Each faulty degree = 100/90 = 1.111°C. Offset from freezing = 59 − 5 = 54 faulty degrees. True temperature = 54 × (100/90) + 0 = 60°C.

An ideal gas at 0°C is heated at constant pressure until its volume doubles. Find the new temperature in °C and K. Solution: Charles's law: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂. T₁ = 273.15 K. V₂/V₁ = 2 → T₂ = 2T₁ = 546.3 K. In °C: 546.3 − 273.15 = 273.15°C.
The Sun's core temperature is about 1.5 × 10⁷ K. Express this in (a) °C, (b) °F. Solution: (a) T(°C) = 1.5×10⁷ − 273.15 ≈ 1.497×10⁷°C. (b) T(°F) = (9/5)(1.497×10⁷) + 32 ≈ 2.695×10⁷°F.

universalFacts: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles: ⟨KE⟩ = (3/2)kT, where k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K is Boltzmann's constant. This is why temperature must be in Kelvin - kinetic energy cannot be negative.

There is no upper limit to temperature - particle speeds can increase without bound. The Planck temperature (1.417 × 10³² K) is a theoretical limit where quantum gravity effects become important, not a physical maximum.
The Kelvin scale was originally defined by the triple point of water (273.16 K) and absolute zero (0 K). Since 2019, it is defined by fixing the Boltzmann constant k to exactly 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J/K.

Different thermometric substances give slightly different scales because their expansion is not perfectly linear with temperature. Gas thermometers are most accurate because ideal gases have perfectly linear behavior in the limit of zero pressure.
The Rankine scale (°R) is to Fahrenheit as Kelvin is to Celsius - it is the absolute temperature scale. NASA uses Rankine in some engineering calculations alongside SI.

data.title: Thermal Equilibrium and Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
data.topicTitle: Meaning of thermal equilibrium and Zeroth law of thermodynamics
data.summary: Thermal equilibrium occurs when two bodies in contact have no net heat flow — they share the same temperature. The Zeroth Law states that if A is in thermal equilibrium with B, and B with C, then A is in equilibrium with C. This transitive property justifies temperature as a measurable state variable and validates thermometer use.
notes: Thermal Contact: Two systems are in thermal contact when heat can flow between them through a diathermal (heat-conducting) wall. An adiabatic wall prevents heat transfer.

Thermal Equilibrium Definition: Two systems in thermal contact are in thermal equilibrium when there is no net flow of heat between them. Their macroscopic properties (pressure, volume, temperature) remain constant over time. This implies they have the same temperature.

Zeroth Law Statement: If system A is in thermal equilibrium with system B, and system B is in thermal equilibrium with system C, then system A is in thermal equilibrium with system C. This is the transitive property of thermal equilibrium.

Significance of Zeroth Law: It establishes temperature as a fundamental, measurable property of matter. Without this law, we could not define a universal temperature scale or trust thermometer readings across different systems.
Temperature as State Variable: The Zeroth Law allows us to assign a numerical value (temperature) to every system in equilibrium. All systems in mutual equilibrium share the same temperature value.

Thermometer Principle: A thermometer is system B. When placed in contact with system A, it reaches equilibrium and displays a reading. If two systems give the same reading on the same thermometer, they are in equilibrium with each other — guaranteed by the Zeroth Law.

Historical Context: Though logically prior to the First and Second Laws, the Zeroth Law was formulated last (Fowler, 1931). It was named 'Zeroth' because it underpins all thermodynamics but was recognized after the other laws were established.

Equilibrium vs Steady State: Thermal equilibrium requires NO net heat flow AND uniform temperature throughout. A metal rod with ends at different temperatures may have steady-state heat flow but is NOT in thermal equilibrium.
Practical Applications: Calibration of thermometers, defining fixed points (ice point, steam point), ensuring consistent temperature measurements across laboratories worldwide.

specificConditions: Diathermal Wall Required: Systems must be able to exchange heat to reach equilibrium. Adiabatic isolation prevents equilibrium establishment.
Time to Reach Equilibrium: Equilibrium is not instantaneous. Poor conductors take longer. The Zeroth Law applies only AFTER equilibrium is achieved.

Empirical temperature scales: Linear interpolation between fixed points, e.g., $t = \frac{X - X_{ice}}{X_{steam} - X_{ice}} \times 100°C$

data.title: Thermal Equilibrium — Mercury Thermometer
data.topicTitle: Thermal Equilibrium as a Working Principle of a Mercury Thermometer
data.summary: A mercury thermometer works on the principle of thermal equilibrium and thermal expansion. When the thermometer bulb contacts a body, heat flows until both reach the same temperature (thermal equilibrium). Mercury expands uniformly and the level in the capillary tube indicates temperature.
notes: Thermal Equilibrium: Two bodies in thermal contact are in thermal equilibrium when they are at the same temperature and no net heat flows between them.

Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics: If bodies A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with body C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This establishes temperature as a measurable property.

Mercury Thermometer Working: The bulb contains mercury. When placed in contact with a body, mercury absorbs heat and expands. The expansion moves the mercury column up the capillary tube. The height is calibrated to read temperature.
Why Mercury: Mercury has uniform thermal expansion, high boiling point (357°C), low freezing point (-39°C), does not wet glass, and is easily visible due to its shiny surface.
Thermometer Calibration: Two fixed points are used — lower fixed point (ice point, 0°C) and upper fixed point (steam point, 100°C). The interval is divided into 100 equal parts (Celsius scale).
Temperature Reading: Temperature T = ((L_t - L_0)/(L_100 - L_0)) × 100°C, where L_t is length at temperature T, L_0 at ice point, L_100 at steam point.

data.title: Heat and Temperature
notes: **Definition:** A temperature scale is created by identifying two easily reproducible fixed points (usually the freezing and boiling points of water at standard atmospheric pressure), then dividing the interval between them into equal divisions.

**Celsius scale (°C):** Introduced by Anders Celsius in 1742. Freezing point of water = 0°C, boiling point = 100°C at 1 atm. Has 100 equal divisions between the fixed points. The SI unit for temperature intervals is the degree Celsius.
**Fahrenheit scale (°F):** Introduced by Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit in 1720. Freezing point = 32°F, boiling point = 212°F at 1 atm. Has 180 equal divisions. Widely used in the United States.

**Kelvin scale (K):** The SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature, named after Lord Kelvin. It is an absolute scale with zero at absolute zero (0 K = −273.15°C). Freezing point of water = 273.15 K, boiling point = 373.15 K. The Kelvin has the same magnitude as the Celsius degree, so ΔT(K) = ΔT(°C).

**Absolute zero:** 0 K = −273.15°C = −459.67°F. The theoretical temperature at which all molecular motion ceases (classical picture). It is unreachable in practice due to quantum zero-point energy. Modern definition: 0 K is the temperature at which the triple point of water occurs at exactly 273.16 K.

**Triple point of water:** The unique temperature and pressure at which solid, liquid, and vapor phases of water coexist in equilibrium: 273.16 K (0.01°C) at 611.657 Pa. This is the defining fixed point of the Kelvin scale.
**Reaumur scale (°R or °Ré):** Freezing point = 0°Ré, boiling point = 80°Ré. Rarely used today, except historically in some European countries.
**Rankine scale (°Ra):** The absolute version of Fahrenheit. 0°Ra = 0 K = −459.67°F. Freezing point of water = 491.67°Ra, boiling point = 671.67°Ra.

**Why use Kelvin?** In gas laws (PV = nRT), temperature must be in Kelvin because the relationship P ∝ T is linear only with absolute temperature. At 0 K, the extrapolated volume of an ideal gas would be zero, making physical sense. In Celsius, this would be −273.15°C - a non-zero volume at "zero" temperature.

**Gas thermometer:** The most accurate temperature measurement uses a constant-volume gas thermometer. It measures pressure of a fixed volume of gas, which is proportional to absolute temperature. The ideal gas law PV = nRT allows extrapolation to zero pressure for perfect accuracy.

**Platinum resistance thermometer:** Uses the fact that electrical resistance of metals increases nearly linearly with temperature. R = R₀(1 + αT), where α is the temperature coefficient of resistance. Platinum is used due to its stability and near-linear behavior.
confusion: Temperature and heat are NOT the same. Temperature is an intensive property (per unit mass); heat is energy transferred (extensive). A bathtub of 30°C water has more heat than a cup of 80°C water, but lower temperature.
A temperature difference of 1°C is NOT the same as 1°F. ΔT(°C) = (5/9)ΔT(°F). A 10°C change equals an 18°F change, so 5°C ≠ 5°F.
Kelvin is NOT written as '°K' - it is simply 'K' (e.g., 300 K, not 300°K). There is no 'degree Kelvin.' The word 'kelvin' is not capitalized when spelled out.

Absolute zero is NOT just 'really cold' - it is the state where classical thermal motion ceases entirely. At 0 K, only quantum zero-point energy remains, and all real substances have condensed to their ground states.
The triple point of water (273.16 K) and the freezing point of water (273.15 K) differ by exactly 0.01 K. Confusing these is a common source of error in metrology.
practice: Convert 300 K to Celsius and Fahrenheit. Solution: T(°C) = 300 − 273.15 = 26.85°C. T(°F) = (9/5)(26.85) + 32 = 80.33°F.

At what temperature do Celsius and Fahrenheit scales read the same? Solution: Set C = F in the conversion F = (9/5)C + 32. C = (9/5)C + 32 → C − (9/5)C = 32 → −(4/5)C = 32 → C = −40. Both read −40° at −40° (the same temperature!).

A faulty thermometer reads the freezing point of water as 5° (on its scale) and the boiling point as 95°. The temperature difference between these on the real Celsius scale is 100°C, and on the faulty scale is 90°. If the faulty thermometer reads 59°, what is the true Celsius temperature? Solution: Each faulty degree = 100/90 = 1.111°C. Offset from freezing = 59 − 5 = 54 faulty degrees. True temperature = 54 × (100/90) + 0 = 60°C.

An ideal gas at 0°C is heated at constant pressure until its volume doubles. Find the new temperature in °C and K. Solution: Charles's law: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂. T₁ = 273.15 K. V₂/V₁ = 2 → T₂ = 2T₁ = 546.3 K. In °C: 546.3 − 273.15 = 273.15°C.
The Sun's core temperature is about 1.5 × 10⁷ K. Express this in (a) °C, (b) °F. Solution: (a) T(°C) = 1.5×10⁷ − 273.15 ≈ 1.497×10⁷°C. (b) T(°F) = (9/5)(1.497×10⁷) + 32 ≈ 2.695×10⁷°F.
universalFacts: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles: ⟨KE⟩ = (3/2)kT, where k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K is Boltzmann's constant. This is why temperature must be in Kelvin - kinetic energy cannot be negative.

There is no upper limit to temperature - particle speeds can increase without bound. The Planck temperature (1.417 × 10³² K) is a theoretical limit where quantum gravity effects become important, not a physical maximum.
The Kelvin scale was originally defined by the triple point of water (273.16 K) and absolute zero (0 K). Since 2019, it is defined by fixing the Boltzmann constant k to exactly 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J/K.

Different thermometric substances give slightly different scales because their expansion is not perfectly linear with temperature. Gas thermometers are most accurate because ideal gases have perfectly linear behavior in the limit of zero pressure.
The Rankine scale (°R) is to Fahrenheit as Kelvin is to Celsius - it is the absolute temperature scale. NASA uses Rankine in some engineering calculations alongside SI.
specificConditions: **Temperature vs Heat Distinction:** Temperature is an *intensive* property (average kinetic energy per particle, measured in K). Heat is *extensive* energy transferred due to temperature difference (measured in J). A bathtub of 30°C water has more heat energy than a cup of 80°C water despite lower temperature.

**Absolute Temperature Requirement:** In kinetic theory and gas laws ($PV = nRT$, $\langle KE angle =  rac{3}{2}kT$), temperature must be in Kelvin (absolute scale). The linear relationship $P \propto T$ and $V \propto T$ only holds with $T$ in Kelvin, where $T=0$ corresponds to zero kinetic energy.

**Triple Point Defines Kelvin:** Since 2019, the Kelvin is defined by fixing Boltzmann's constant $k = 1.380649 	imes 10^{-23}$ J/K exactly. The triple point of water (273.16 K) is a reproducible reference, not the definition.

data.title: Quantity of Heat
data.summary: Quantity of heat is the energy transferred due to temperature difference. Specific heat capacity, heat capacity, latent heat, and calorimetry principle govern heat transfer calculations. Q = mcΔT for temperature change and Q = mL for phase change.
notes: Heat: Energy transferred between bodies due to temperature difference. SI unit: joule (J). Heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature.
Heat Capacity: C = Q/ΔT is the heat required to raise the temperature of a body by 1 K (or 1°C). Unit: J/K. Depends on mass and material of the body.
Specific Heat Capacity: c = C/m = Q/(mΔT) is the heat required to raise unit mass of a substance by 1 K. Unit: J/(kg·K). Characteristic property of the material.
Molar Heat Capacity: Cₘ = C/n = Q/(nΔT) is heat per mole. Unit: J/(mol·K). Used in thermodynamics and kinetic theory.
Calorimetry Principle: In an isolated system, heat lost by hot bodies equals heat gained by cold bodies. Assumes no heat loss to surroundings.
Latent Heat: Heat absorbed or released during phase change at constant temperature. Q = mL. L_f = latent heat of fusion (solid↔liquid), L_v = latent heat of vaporization (liquid↔gas).
Specific Latent Heat: L = Q/m is latent heat per unit mass. Unit: J/kg. Different for each substance and each phase change.
specificConditions: Heat Capacity Definition: Heat capacity C = ΔQ/ΔT is the heat required to raise temperature by 1 K. Specific heat capacity c = C/m is per unit mass (J/kg·K). Molar heat capacity Cₘ = C/n is per mole (J/mol·K).

Phase Change Latent Heat: During phase change (melting, boiling), temperature is constant while heat is absorbed/released as latent heat: Q = mL. Latent heat of fusion L_f (solid↔liquid) and vaporization L_v (liquid↔gas) are material properties.

Calorimetry Principle: In an isolated system, heat lost by hot bodies = heat gained by cold bodies. This assumes no heat loss to surroundings and no phase changes unless accounted for. The final equilibrium temperature is found by equating m₁c₁(T_f - T₁) = m₂c₂(T₂ - T_f).
formulas: Heat transfer: Q = mcΔT
Heat capacity: C = Q/ΔT
Specific heat capacity: c = Q/(mΔT)
Molar heat capacity: Cₘ = Q/(nΔT)
Latent heat: Q = mL
Specific latent heat: L = Q/m
Calorimetry: m₁c₁(T_f - T₁) = m₂c₂(T₂ - T_f) (heat lost = heat gained)
keyPoints: Heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature.
Specific heat capacity c = Q/(mΔT) is a characteristic property of material.
Water has high specific heat (4186 J/kg·K) — moderates climate.
During phase change, temperature remains constant despite heat absorption.
Calorimetry: heat lost = heat gained in an isolated system.
Latent heat of fusion L_f for melting; latent heat of vaporization L_v for boiling.
importantStatements: Statement 1: Heat is energy transferred due to temperature difference; SI unit is joule.
Statement 2: Specific heat capacity c = Q/(mΔT) is the heat per unit mass per degree temperature rise.
Statement 3: Latent heat Q = mL is heat absorbed/released during phase change at constant temperature.
Statement 4: Calorimetry principle states heat lost by hot body = heat gained by cold body in an isolated system.
Statement 5: Water's high specific heat (4186 J/kg·K) makes it an effective coolant.

notes: A temperature scale is a system for measuring temperature based on fixed reference points and equal divisions between them.
