data.title: HEAT AND TEMPERATURE â€” Chapter 9, Class 11 Physics (Concepts, All 5 Scales & Step-by-Step Numericals)
notes: ðŸ“˜ TOPIC OUTLINE: Temperature vs Heat | Effects of Heat | Thermal Equilibrium & Zeroth Law | Thermometry | The 5 Temperature Scales & Fundamental Interval | General Conversion Formula | Numericals (Direct Conversion, Coincidence/Double-Reading Problems, Faulty Thermometer Problems, Arbitrary/Offset Scale Problems, Rate/Error Problems)

ðŸŒ¡ï¸ TEMPERATURE â€” DEFINITION: Temperature is the average kinetic energy of all molecules present in a body. It tells you the DIRECTION heat will flow (hot â†’ cold). Measured using a thermometer. SI unit: kelvin (K).

ðŸ”¥ HEAT â€” DEFINITION: Heat is the SUM (total) of the kinetic energy of all molecules of a substance. It is a form of energy, measured in joules. Heat flows from a body at higher temperature to one at lower temperature until equilibrium is reached.

ðŸ’¡ KEY CONCEPTUAL DIFFERENCE (exam favorite): Temperature is an AVERAGE (intensive property â€” doesn't depend on amount of substance). Heat is a TOTAL/SUM (extensive property â€” depends on mass/amount). This is why a bucket of lukewarm water can contain MORE heat than a cup of boiling tea, even though its temperature is lower â€” more molecules means a bigger total, even if each molecule individually has less average energy.

âš¡ EFFECTS OF HEAT: When heat is applied to a body, it can bring: (i) Change in temperature (ii) Change in volume (iii) Change of state of matter (iv) Electric effect (v) Generation of light energy (vi) Change in resistance.
âš–ï¸ THERMAL EQUILIBRIUM: Two bodies are in thermal equilibrium when NO heat flows from one to the other after being brought into contact â€” meaning they are at the same temperature.

ðŸ“ ZEROTH LAW OF THERMODYNAMICS: If two systems are separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then they must also be in thermal equilibrium with each other. (This law is what actually justifies using a thermometer â€” the thermometer is the 'third system'.)
ðŸ§ª THERMODYNAMIC SYSTEM: A system that can be described using thermodynamic parameters â€” Temperature, Pressure, Volume, and Heat exchange.
ðŸ”¬ THERMOMETRY: The science of temperature and its measurement. THREE MAIN STEPS: (i) Construction (ii) Calibration (iii) Sensitiveness.
â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â• SECTION A: THE 5 TEMPERATURE SCALES & FUNDAMENTAL INTERVAL â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•

ðŸ’¡ WHAT IS 'FUNDAMENTAL INTERVAL'? It is simply the NUMBER OF DIVISIONS between the Lower Fixed Point (LFP â€” ice/melting point) and Upper Fixed Point (UFP â€” steam/boiling point) on a scale. This single number is the KEY to comparing any two scales, because it tells you how 'coarse' or 'fine' each degree-step is. A bigger fundamental interval = smaller, finer degree-steps.
ðŸ“ TABLE A1 â€” ALL 5 TEMPERATURE SCALES

| Scale | Symbol | LFP (Ice Point) | UFP (Steam Point) | Fundamental Interval (UFPâˆ’LFP) | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Celsius | Â°C | 0 | 100 | 100 | Relative (0 = ice point) |
| Fahrenheit | Â°F | 32 | 212 | 180 | Relative (0 â‰  ice point) |
| Kelvin | K | 273 | 373 | 100 | Absolute (0 = absolute zero) |
| RÃ©aumur | Â°R (RÃ©) | 0 | 80 | 80 | Relative (0 = ice point) |
| Rankine | Â°Ra | 491.67 | 671.67 | 180 | Absolute (0 = absolute zero) |

ðŸ”‘ FEEL IT, DON'T MEMORIZE: Kelvin is just Celsius SHIFTED so 0 lands on absolute zero (same degree-SIZE as Celsius, fundamental interval 100). Rankine is just Fahrenheit SHIFTED so 0 lands on absolute zero (same degree-SIZE as Fahrenheit, fundamental interval 180). So Celsiusâ†”Kelvin is a pure SHIFT (add 273), and Fahrenheitâ†”Rankine is also a pure SHIFT (add 459.67). But Celsiusâ†”Fahrenheit needs both a SHIFT and a SCALE change (Ã—9/5) because their degree-sizes differ.

ðŸ“ GENERAL CONVERSION FORMULA (works for ANY two scales, including Rankine): (Reading âˆ’ LFP)/(Fundamental Interval) is the SAME fraction on every scale, because all scales measure the identical physical range between ice point and steam point.

âš ï¸ COMMON MISTAKE: Students often try converting Rankine using the Celsius-style formula (Raâˆ’0)/x. WRONG â€” Rankine's zero is absolute zero, NOT the ice point, so you MUST use (Raâˆ’491.67)/180, matching Fahrenheit's fundamental interval of 180, not Kelvin's 100.
â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â• SECTION B: DIRECT CONVERSION NUMERICALS â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•
ðŸ“ NUMERICAL B1: Convert 30Â°C into Fahrenheit scale.
Step 2: Substitute C = 30: 30/100 = (Fâˆ’32)/180
Step 3: Cross-multiply: 30Ã—180/100 = Fâˆ’32 â†’ 54 = Fâˆ’32
âœ… ANSWER: 30Â°C = 86Â°F
ðŸ“ NUMERICAL B2: Convert 98.6Â°F (normal body temperature) into Kelvin and Rankine.
Step 1: Find Celsius first: (Câˆ’0)/100=(Fâˆ’32)/180 â†’ C = (98.6âˆ’32)Ã—100/180 = 37Â°C
Step 2: Convert to Kelvin: K = C+273 = 37+273 = 310 K
Step 3: Convert to Rankine directly from Fahrenheit: Ra = F+459.67 = 98.6+459.67 = 558.27
âœ… ANSWER: 98.6Â°F = 310 K = 558.27 Â°Ra

ðŸ’¡ TIP: Kelvin was obtained from Celsius by pure ADDITION (+273), Rankine from Fahrenheit by pure ADDITION (+459.67) â€” no multiplication needed, since each absolute scale shares its degree-size with its 'parent' relative scale.
â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â• SECTION C: 'DOUBLE READING' & 'COINCIDING SCALE' NUMERICALS (Concept-Challenging) â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•

ðŸ“ METHOD: These problems give a RELATIONSHIP between two scale readings (e.g. 'one is double the other' or 'both are equal') instead of a direct value. Assign a variable to the unknown common temperature, express both readings in terms of it using the given relationship, plug into the master equation, and solve.
ðŸ“ NUMERICAL C1: At what temperature will the Kelvin reading double the Fahrenheit reading?
Step 1: Let K = 2F
Step 3: Cross-multiply: 100(Fâˆ’32) = 180(2Fâˆ’273) â†’ 100Fâˆ’3200 = 360Fâˆ’49140
âœ… ANSWER: At 176.69Â°F (353.38 K), Kelvin reading is double Fahrenheit reading.
ðŸ“ NUMERICAL C2: At what temperature will the Celsius reading double the Fahrenheit reading?
Step 1: Let F = x, so C = 2x
Step 4: x = âˆ’12.307
âœ… ANSWER: At âˆ’12.307Â°F, Celsius reading is double Fahrenheit reading.
ðŸ“ NUMERICAL C3: At what point does the Kelvin reading coincide with (equal) the Fahrenheit reading?
Step 1: Let both = x
âœ… ANSWER: At 574.25 K = 574.25Â°F, the readings coincide.
ðŸ“ NUMERICAL C4 (Concept-challenging â€” physically impossible case): At what temperature would the Rankine reading equal the Celsius reading numerically?
Step 1: Let both = x. Using Ra = 1.8(C+273): x = 1.8(x+273)
Step 3: Check against absolute zero (âˆ’273Â°C): âˆ’614.25Â°C is colder than absolute zero, so it cannot exist.

ðŸ’¡ TIP: ALWAYS sanity-check your final answer against absolute zero (âˆ’273Â°C / 0 K) when an absolute scale is involved â€” algebra can give you a number, but physics can reject it.
ðŸ“ NUMERICAL C5: At what temperature will the RÃ©aumur reading be numerically equal to the Fahrenheit reading?
Step 1: Let both = x. x/80 = (xâˆ’32)/180
Step 3: x = âˆ’25.6
âœ… ANSWER: At âˆ’25.6Â°RÃ© = âˆ’25.6Â°F, the readings coincide.
â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â• SECTION D: FAULTY / MISCALIBRATED THERMOMETER NUMERICALS â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•

ðŸ“ METHOD: A faulty thermometer has WRONG numbers marked at its LFP and UFP, but still divides the space between them proportionally. Use: (Faulty reading âˆ’ Faulty LFP)/(Faulty UFP âˆ’ Faulty LFP) = (Correct reading âˆ’ Correct LFP)/(Correct UFP âˆ’ Correct LFP)
ðŸ“ NUMERICAL D1: A faulty thermometer has fixed points marked at 2 and 98 (instead of 0 and 100). What is the correct Celsius temperature when it reads 20Â°C?
âœ… ANSWER: 18.75Â°C.
ðŸ“ NUMERICAL D2: A thermometer reads the melting point of ice as âˆ’10Â°C, and reads 60Â°C in place of the correct 50Â°C. Find its reading at the actual boiling point of water (100Â°C).
âœ… ANSWER: The faulty thermometer reads 130Â°C at the true boiling point.
ðŸ“ NUMERICAL D3: The distance between LFP and UFP on a thermometer is 80 cm. Find the Celsius temperature when mercury has risen 10.4 cm above the LFP.
Step 1: 80 cm = 100Â°C, so 1 cm = 100/80 parts
âœ… ANSWER: 13Â°C.
ðŸ’¡ TIP: This is the same ratio logic as the faulty-thermometer formula â€” physical stem length is just another 'scale' being converted into Celsius.
â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â• SECTION E: ARBITRARY / OFFSET SCALE NUMERICALS (Concept-Challenging) â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•
ðŸ“ METHOD: These invent a new scale with its own LFP/UFP. Treat it exactly like Celsius vs Fahrenheit â€” set up the ratio, don't panic just because the scale is unfamiliar.
ðŸ“ NUMERICAL E1: In an arbitrary scale, water freezes at 40Â° and boils at 290Â°. Find the reading on this scale corresponding to 62Â°C.
Step 1: Arbitrary fundamental interval = 290âˆ’40 = 250
âœ… ANSWER: 62Â°C corresponds to 195Â° on the arbitrary scale.
ðŸ“ NUMERICAL E2: A new scale 'X' has its ice point at âˆ’20Â°X and steam point at 130Â°X. Find the reading on X when Celsius reads 50Â°C.
Step 1: Fundamental interval of X = 130âˆ’(âˆ’20) = 150
âœ… ANSWER: X = 55Â°X
ðŸ“ NUMERICAL E3 (two unknown scales, no Celsius needed): Thermometer P has LFP=10, UFP=160. Thermometer Q has LFP=20, UFP=120. When P reads 70, what does Q read?
Step 3: Qâˆ’20 = 40 â†’ Q = 60
âœ… ANSWER: Q reads 60.
ðŸ’¡ TIP: Celsius is not mandatory as a 'bridge' â€” the ratio method works between ANY two linear scales directly.
ðŸ“ NUMERICAL E4: Scale 'Y' has the SAME fundamental interval as Celsius (100 divisions) but its ice point is marked at 50Â°Y. If Y reads 68Â°Y, find the Celsius equivalent.
Step 1: Equal fundamental intervals â†’ pure shift relationship: C = Yâˆ’50
âœ… ANSWER: 18Â°C.

ðŸ’¡ TIP: When two scales share the SAME fundamental interval, conversion is always pure addition/subtraction (like Celsiusâ†”Kelvin) â€” no multiplication needed. Different fundamental intervals force a scaling step.
â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â• SECTION F: RATE / ERROR / CHANGE NUMERICALS â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•

Step 1: True Fahrenheit equivalent of 37Â°C: 37/100 = (Fâˆ’32)/180 â†’ 6660 = 100Fâˆ’3200 â†’ F = 98.6
Step 2: Error = 99âˆ’98.6 = 0.4
âœ… ANSWER: 0.4Â°F.
ðŸ“ NUMERICAL F2: A lab thermometer reads only in Â°F. Initial sample temperature is 68.2Â°F, and it must be increased by 40Â°C. Find the final temperature in Â°F.
Step 1: For a CHANGE (not absolute reading), use only the scaling ratio: 100 parts in Â°C = 180 parts in Â°F
Step 2: 40Â°C change = (180/100)Ã—40 = 72Â°F change
âœ… ANSWER: 140.2Â°F.

âš ï¸ COMMON MISTAKE: Never apply the full C-to-F formula (Ã—9/5, +32) to a temperature CHANGE â€” the '+32' offset applies only to absolute readings. For a change, only the scaling factor (180/100) applies. This is the single most common error in this topic.
ðŸ“ NUMERICAL F3: A Celsius scale reads 30Â°C when a standard Kelvin scale reads 300 K. Find the error in the Celsius reading.
Step 1: True Celsius equivalent of 300 K: C = 300âˆ’273 = 27
Step 2: Error = 30âˆ’27 = 3

âœ… ANSWER: C = âˆ’30.48Â°C, F = âˆ’22.86Â°F.
ðŸ“ NUMERICAL F5 (Rankine, concept-challenging): A gas thermometer shows a temperature change from 500Â°Ra to 680Â°Ra. Express this change in Celsius degrees.

Step 2: Since Rankine shares fundamental interval 180 with Fahrenheit, and Fahrenheit-to-Celsius scaling ratio is 100/180: Celsius change = 180Ã—(100/180) = 100

data.title: Ideal Gas Equation
notes: The ideal-gas equation combines Boyle’s, Charles’s and Avogadro’s laws: PV=nRT. P is absolute pressure, V volume, n amount in moles, T absolute temperature and R=8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Always convert Celsius using T(K)=t(°C)+273.15 and use consistent units. For 1.00 mol at 300 K in 24.6 L, P≈(8.314×300)/0.0246=1.01×10⁵ Pa.
For fixed amount n, PV/T stays constant between equilibrium states: P1V1/T1=P2V2/T2. In a sealed rigid vessel heated from 300 K to 450 K, pressure rises by the factor 450/300=1.5.

The model assumes molecules have negligible volume and exert no long-range intermolecular forces except during elastic collisions. Real gases approach ideal behaviour at low pressure and high temperature.
Use absolute rather than gauge pressure in the equation. If a gauge pressure is given, add atmospheric pressure before substituting.

The ideal-gas equation links pressure, volume, amount and temperature. The temperature must be in kelvin. A celsius value used in P V = n R T is the usual error, and it matters most near the ice point where 0°C is 273 K, not a small correction.

data.title: Molecular Properties of Matter
notes: **Kinetic theory of matter:** All matter is composed of tiny particles (atoms or molecules) that are in constant, random motion. The motion is thermal motion - faster at higher temperatures.

**States of matter and molecular spacing:** In gases, intermolecular spacing is much larger than molecular diameter (10Ã— or more), so molecules move freely. In liquids, spacing is about 1 molecular diameter. In solids, molecules are tightly packed in a regular arrangement.

**Intermolecular forces:** Attractive forces between molecules (van der Waals, hydrogen bonding, dipole-dipole). These forces are strongest in solids (holding molecules in fixed positions), moderate in liquids, and very weak in gases at ordinary conditions.

**Kinetic energy vs potential energy in matter:** In gases, kinetic energy dominates (molecules move freely). In solids, potential energy dominates (molecules held in fixed positions by strong intermolecular forces). At the melting/boiling point, energy input goes into breaking bonds (increasing PE) without changing temperature.

**Brownian motion:** Random zigzag motion of microscopic particles suspended in a fluid, first observed by Robert Brown (1827). Explained by Einstein (1905) as the result of unequal bombardment by fluid molecules - strong evidence for the kinetic theory.

**Diffusion:** The spontaneous mixing of particles due to random molecular motion. Occurs in all states but fastest in gases and slowest in solids. Fick's law: diffusion rate $\propto$ concentration gradient. At higher temperature, diffusion is faster (faster molecules).

**Thermal expansion:** Matter expands when heated (generally). In gases, expansion is large (Charles's law). In liquids, expansion is moderate. In solids, expansion is small but measurable. Due to increased molecular vibration amplitudes at higher temperatures.

**Mean free path:** The average distance a molecule travels between collisions. $\lambda = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2} n \sigma}$, where $n$ is the number density and $\sigma$ is the collision cross-section. At STP, the mean free path of air molecules is about 68 nm.

**Degrees of freedom:** The number of independent ways a molecule can store energy. Monatomic gas: 3 translational DOF. Diatomic: 5 (3 translational + 2 rotational). Polyatomic: 6 (3 translational + 3 rotational) at room temperature.

**Equipartition theorem:** Each quadratic degree of freedom contributes $\frac{1}{2}k_BT$ of energy per molecule, or $\frac{1}{2}RT$ per mole. For monatomic gas ($f=3$): $U = \frac{3}{2}nRT$. For diatomic ($f=5$): $U = \frac{5}{2}nRT$.

**Phase transitions and energy:** During melting or boiling, temperature stays constant even though heat is added. The energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds (increasing PE), not increasing KE. This is latent heat: $Q = mL$ where $L$ is latent heat.

**Surface tension:** A consequence of intermolecular attractive forces. Molecules at the surface experience a net inward pull, creating a 'skin' effect. Surface tension $\gamma$ has units of N/m or J/m$^2$. Water has high surface tension (72 mN/m at 25Â°C) due to hydrogen bonding.

**Viscosity:** A measure of a fluid's resistance to flow. Caused by intermolecular forces and molecular momentum transfer. Gases become more viscous at higher temperature (faster molecules, more momentum transfer). Liquids become less viscous at higher temperature (bonds break more easily).

confusion: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of molecules, NOT the total energy. A hot object has higher average KE per molecule, but a large cold object may have more total thermal energy (more molecules).

Heat and temperature are NOT the same. Temperature is a measure of average molecular KE (intensive property). Heat is the transfer of thermal energy between objects due to temperature difference (extensive property). You can add heat without changing temperature (phase change).

Intermolecular forces are NOT the same as intramolecular (chemical) forces. Intermolecular forces hold molecules together in condensed phases (weak, ~1-100 kJ/mol). Intramolecular forces hold atoms together within a molecule (strong, ~100-1000 kJ/mol).
Diffusion in liquids is faster than in solids, but much slower than in gases. This is often confused with the rate of dissolving, which also involves convection and stirring.

A gas molecule at high altitude has LESS kinetic energy if it has risen (energy converts to gravitational PE). But temperature is a statistical property - individual molecules have a range of speeds given by the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, not a single speed.
practice: Estimate the average distance between molecules in air at STP. Solution: Number density $n = N_A/V_m = 6.022 \times 10^{23} / 0.0224 = 2.69 \times 10^{25}$ molecules/m$^3$. Average spacing $d \approx n^{-1/3} = (2.69 \times 10^{25})^{-1/3} = 3.3 \times 10^{-9}$ m $= 3.3$ nm. This is about 10 molecular diameters.

Calculate the root-mean-square speed of O$_2$ at 300 K. $M_{O_2} = 0.032$ kg/mol. Solution: $v_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M} = \sqrt{3 \times 8.314 \times 300 / 0.032} = \sqrt{7482.6 / 0.032} = \sqrt{233,831} = 483.6$ m/s. About 1741 km/h!

A 100 g block of ice at 0Â°C melts to water at 0Â°C. How much energy is required? ($L_f = 334$ kJ/kg). Solution: $Q = mL = 0.1 \times 334,000 = 33,400$ J = 33.4 kJ. Temperature doesn't change - all energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds (increasing PE).

Compare the mean free path of gas molecules at STP (68 nm) vs at 1/10th the pressure. Solution: $\lambda \propto 1/P$. At $P/10$, $\lambda = 680$ nm = 0.68 $\mu$m. At very low pressure (vacuum), mean free path can be kilometers long.

Using equipartition, calculate the molar internal energy of CO$_2$ at room temperature (assume linear molecule with 4 active DOF: 3 translational + 1 rotational... wait, CO$_2$ is linear so 3 trans + 2 rot = 5 DOF). Solution: $U = \frac{5}{2}RT = \frac{5}{2} \times 8.314 \times 300 = 6235.5$ J/mol $= 6.24$ kJ/mol.
universalFacts: Einstein's 1905 paper on Brownian motion provided the first quantitative evidence for the existence of atoms and molecules. Jean Perrin experimentally confirmed Einstein's predictions in 1908, earning the Nobel Prize in 1926.

The kinetic theory was developed by Daniel Bernoulli in 1738 (in his Hydrodynamica), but was ignored until revived by Clausius, Maxwell, and Boltzmann in the 19th century. Bernoulli proposed that gas pressure comes from molecular collisions - centuries before it was accepted.

At room temperature, gas molecules move at hundreds of meters per second (sound speed!). But gas smells take time to travel across a room because molecules undergo billions of collisions per second (mean free path ~70 nm), resulting in a random walk.

The equipartition theorem fails at low temperatures, where quantum effects 'freeze out' certain degrees of freedom. This was one of the early successes of quantum mechanics - Planck's quantization explained why solids' heat capacity drops at low $T$ (Einstein model, 1907).
Water's high surface tension (due to hydrogen bonding) allows insects to walk on water, allows needles to float, and drives capillary action in plants - all critical for life on Earth.
specificConditions: **State-Dependent Molecular Spacing:** In gases, intermolecular spacing $\gg$ molecular diameter ($\sim 10\times$); in liquids, spacing $\approx$ molecular diameter; in solids, molecules are locked in a lattice. This spacing determines the dominant energy (KE in gases, PE in solids) and compressibility.

**Intermolecular vs Intramolecular Forces:** Intermolecular forces (van der Waals, H-bonding, dipole-dipole) are weak ($\sim 1-100$ kJ/mol) and govern phase changes. Intramolecular (chemical) bonds are strong ($\sim 100-1000$ kJ/mol) and govern molecular structure. Phase transitions break intermolecular bonds, not intramolecular ones.

**Mean Free Path $\lambda \propto 1/(n\sigma)$:** The average distance between collisions $\lambda = 1/(\sqrt{2}n\sigma)$ decreases with number density $n$ and collision cross-section $\sigma$. At STP for air, $\lambda \approx 68$ nm; at low pressure (vacuum), $\lambda$ can reach kilometers, enabling ballistic transport.

data.title: Average Translational Kinetic Energy of Gas Molecule
data.topicTitle: Average translational kinetic energy of gas molecule
notes: Kinetic theory relates pressure to molecular motion: pV=(1/3)Nm⟨c²⟩. Combining this with pV=NkBT gives (1/2)m⟨c²⟩=(3/2)kBT, the average translational kinetic energy per molecule.

At fixed absolute temperature, different ideal-gas molecules have equal mean translational kinetic energy. Their speeds differ because a lighter molecule needs greater speed to have the same kinetic energy.
Per mole, the mean translational kinetic energy is (3/2)RT. At 300 K this is about (3/2)(8.314)(300)=3.74 kJ mol⁻¹, or 6.21×10⁻²¹ J per molecule.
The result is for translation only. In a monatomic ideal gas it accounts for all classical internal energy; diatomic and polyatomic gases can also store energy in rotation and vibration.
The root-mean-square speed follows from the same result: vrms=√(3kBT/m)=√(3RT/M). Use molecular mass with kB or molar mass with R.

The average translational kinetic energy of one ideal-gas molecule is (3/2) k T. It depends on the temperature and not on the mass. A hydrogen molecule and an oxygen molecule at the same temperature have the same average translational energy, and the hydrogen molecule is faster.

data.title: Boltzmann Constant, Root Mean Square Speed and Heat Capacities
data.topicTitle: Boltzmann constant, root mean square speed
notes: **Boltzmann constant:** $k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}$ J/K. It connects microscopic and macroscopic thermodynamics. Named after Ludwig Boltzmann (1844-1906).
**RMS speed:** $v_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M}$, where $M$ is molar mass in kg/mol. At STP (273 K), $v_{rms}$ for air is about 479 m/s. At 300 K, about 484 m/s. Lighter gases move faster on average.
**Most probable speed:** $v_p = \sqrt{2RT/M}$. This is the speed at which the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution peaks. At 300 K for air: $v_p \approx 364$ m/s. At 300 K for Hâ‚‚: $v_p \approx 1650$ m/s.
**Mean speed:** $v_{mean} = \sqrt{8RT/\pi M}$. The average of all molecular speeds. At 300 K for air: $v_{mean} \approx 464$ m/s. At 300 K for Hâ‚‚: $v_{mean} \approx 1760$ m/s.

**Heat capacities - monatomic gases:** $C_V = \frac{3}{2}R$, $C_P = \frac{5}{2}R$. The ratio $\gamma = C_P/C_V = 5/3 \approx 1.67$. Monatomic gases (He, Ne, Ar) only have translational degrees of freedom.

**Heat capacities - diatomic gases:** $C_V = \frac{5}{2}R$, $C_P = \frac{7}{2}R$ at ordinary temperatures ($\gamma = 7/5 = 1.4$). Includes 3 translational + 2 rotational DOF. At high temperature, vibration adds more, so $C_V \rightarrow 4R$, $C_P \rightarrow 5R$, $\gamma \rightarrow 9/7 \approx 1.29$.

**Dulong-Petit law for solids:** Molar heat capacity of most solid elements at room temperature $\approx 3R \approx 25$ J/(molÂ·K). This comes from 3 quadratic degrees of freedom per atom (one for each spatial axis), each contributing $R$ per mole of atoms.

**Why heat capacities differ:** The ratio $C_P/C_V = \gamma$ matters for adiabatic processes ($PV^\gamma = \text{const}$). This affects everything from engine cycles to atmospheric science. $\gamma \approx 1.4$ for air is crucial in meteorology.

**Experimental verification:** Heat capacities were measured by Regnault and others in the 19th century. The agreement with kinetic theory predictions was one of the great successes of molecular physics.
**Units:** $k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}$ J/K. $C_P, C_V$ have units J/(molÂ·K). Gas constant R has the same units.
**Connection to energy:** Each degree of freedom contributes $\frac{1}{2}R$ per mole or $\frac{1}{2}k_B$ per molecule. 3 translational DOF $ightarrow 3 \times \frac{1}{2}R = \frac{3}{2}R$ for $C_V$

confusion: The ratio $\gamma = C_P/C_V$ is NOT always 5/3 or 7/5. It depends on temperature and molecular structure. At very high temperatures, vibrational modes activate, changing $\gamma$.
The formula $C_V = \frac{3}{2}R$ applies ONLY to monatomic ideal gases. For diatomic or polyatomic gases, rotational (and sometimes vibrational) modes contribute.

Dulong's law ($C \approx 3R$) for solids works well at room temperature but fails at very low temperatures (quantum effects freeze out degrees of freedom). Einstein and Debye developed low-temperature models.
The Boltzmann constant $k_B$ is NOT the same as the gas constant R. $k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}$ J/K per molecule. R = 8.314 J/(molÂ·K) per mole. $R = N_A k_B$.

Most probable speed is NOT the average speed. For the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution: $v_p \cdot \sqrt{2} < v_{mean} < v_{rms}$. The order is always $v_p < v_{mean} < v_{rms}$ at the same temperature.
practice: Calculate the root-mean-square speed of nitrogen molecules (Nâ‚‚, M = 0.028 kg/mol) at 350 K. Solution: $v_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M} = \sqrt{3 \times 8.314 \times 350 / 0.028} = \sqrt{3471.8 / 0.028} = \sqrt{123,993} = 352$ m/s.

Find the most probable speed of helium atoms (He, M = 0.004 kg/mol) at 400 K. Solution: $v_p = \sqrt{2RT/M} = \sqrt{2 \times 8.314 \times 400 / 0.004} = \sqrt{6651.2 / 0.004} = \sqrt{1662800} = 1290$ m/s.

Calculate the mean speed of oxygen molecules (Oâ‚‚, M = 0.032 kg/mol) at 273 K. Solution: $v_{mean} = \sqrt{8RT/\pi M} = \sqrt{8 \times 8.314 \times 273 / (\pi \times 0.032)} = \sqrt{18136 / 0.1005} = \sqrt{180,458} = 425$ m/s.

If the rms speed of helium at 300 K is 1250 m/s, what is the rms speed at 600 K? Solution: $v_{rms} \propto \sqrt{T}$. $v_{rms}(600) = v_{rms}(300) \times \sqrt{600/300} = 1250 \times \sqrt{2} = 1768$ m/s.
A container has 1 mol of gas at 300 K. What is the total internal energy for (a) monatomic gas? Solution: $U = \frac{3}{2}nRT = \frac{3}{2} \times 1 \times 8.314 \times 300 = 3741$ J.
Find the heat capacity ratio $\gamma$ for a diatomic gas at room temperature. Solution: $\gamma = C_P/C_V = (7/2R)/(5/2R) = 7/5 = 1.4$.
universalFacts: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution was first derived by James Clerk Maxwell in 1860 and later generalized by Ludwig Boltzmann. It describes the distribution of speeds in an ideal gas and is one of the most important results of kinetic theory.

At 300 K, the three speed measures for nitrogen (M=28 g/mol) are: most probable $v_p \approx 422$ m/s, mean speed $v_{mean} \approx 477$ m/s, and rms speed $v_{rms} \approx 517$ m/s. The ratios are always $v_p : v_{mean} : v_{rms} = \sqrt{2} : \sqrt{8/\pi} : \sqrt{3} \approx 1.414 : 1.596 : 1.732$.

The Boltzmann constant $k_B$ was first introduced by Max Planck in his derivation of the blackbody radiation formula (1900). He used it to connect the energy of oscillators to temperature: $E = k_BT$.

Dulong and Petit's law ($C \approx 3R$ for solids) was discovered in 1819. It took nearly 150 years to understand why it works - the kinetic theory's 3 degrees of freedom per atom (1859-1870s) provided the explanation.

The ratio $\gamma = C_P/C_V$ determines whether sound speed is faster in an adiabatic process: $v_{sound} = \sqrt{\gamma RT/M}$. For air ($\gamma \approx 1.4$), $v_{sound} \approx 343$ m/s at 300 K. For helium ($\gamma = 5/3 \approx 1.67$), $v_{sound} \approx 965$ m/s at 300 K.

**Speed Hierarchy:** For the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution: $v_p = \sqrt{2RT/M}$, $ ar{v} = \sqrt{8RT/\pi M}$, $v_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M}$. The order is always $v_p <  ar{v} < v_{rms}$ with ratios $\sqrt{2} : \sqrt{8/\pi} : \sqrt{3} \approx 1.414 : 1.596 : 1.732$.

**Heat capacities - diatomic gases:** $C_V = \ rac{5}{2}R$, $C_P = \ rac{7}{2}R$ at ordinary temperatures ($\\\\gamma = 7/5 = 1.4$). Includes 3 translational + 2 rotational DOF. At high temperature, vibration adds more, so $C_V \ightarrow 4R$, $C_P \ightarrow 5R$, $\\\\gamma \ightarrow 9/7 \\\approx 1.29$.

**Dulong-Petit law for solids:** Molar heat capacity of most solid elements at room temperature $\\\approx 3R \\\\approx 25$ J/(mol·K). This comes from 3 quadratic degrees of freedom per atom (one for each spatial axis), each contributing $R$ per mole of atoms.

**Why heat capacities differ:** The ratio $C_P/C_V = \\\\gamma$ matters for adiabatic processes ($PV^\\\gamma = \	ext{const}$). This affects everything from engine cycles to atmospheric science. $\\\gamma \\\\approx 1.4$ for air is crucial in meteorology.

**Experimental verification:** Heat capacities were measured by Regnault and others in the 19th century. The agreement with kinetic theory predictions was one of the great successes of molecular physics.
**Units:** $k_B = 1.38 \	imes 10^{-23}$ J/K. $C_P, C_V$ have units J/(mol·K). Gas constant R has the same units.
**Connection to energy:** Each degree of freedom contributes $\ rac{1}{2}R$ per mole or $\ rac{1}{2}k_B$ per molecule. 3 translational DOF $ightarrow 3 \	imes \ rac{1}{2}R = \ rac{3}{2}R$ for $C_V$

**Heat capacity definition:** The amount of heat required to raise the temperature of a substance by 1 K (or 1°C). It depends on the amount of substance and the conditions (constant volume or constant pressure).
**Specific heat capacity (c):** Heat required to raise 1 kg of substance by 1 K. Units: J/(kg·K). Water has c = 4186 J/(kg·K) at 20°C. This is the highest of any common substance.
**Molar heat capacity (C):** Heat required to raise 1 mole by 1 K. Units: J/(mol·K). For water (M = 0.018 kg/mol): $C = 4186 \times 0.018 = 75.3$ J/(mol·K).

**Constant volume molar heat capacity $C_V$:** For an ideal gas, $C_V = \frac{f}{2}R$, where $f$ is the number of active degrees of freedom. Monatomic: $C_V = \frac{3}{2}R = 12.5$ J/(mol·K). Diatomic: $C_V = \frac{5}{2}R = 20.8$ J/(mol·K).

**Constant pressure molar heat capacity $C_P$:** $C_P = C_V + R$. This extra $R$ is the work the gas does expanding against external pressure when heated at constant pressure. Monatomic: $C_P = \frac{5}{2}R = 20.8$ J/(mol·K). Diatomic: $C_P = \frac{7}{2}R = 29.1$ J/(mol·K).
**Mayer's relation:** $C_P - C_V = R$. This fundamental relation holds for all ideal gases, independent of molecular structure. Derived from the first law of thermodynamics and the ideal gas law.

**Heat capacity ratio $\gamma = C_P/C_V$:** For monatomic ideal gas: $\gamma = 5/3 \approx 1.67$. For diatomic (room temp): $\gamma = 7/5 = 1.4$. For triatomic (nonlinear): $\gamma = 8/6 = 4/3 \approx 1.33$.

**Degrees of freedom and $C_V$:** Each quadratic degree of freedom contributes $\frac{1}{2}R$ to $C_V$. Monatomic (3 trans): $C_V = 3 \times \frac{1}{2}R = \frac{3}{2}R$. Linear diatomic (3 trans + 2 rot): $C_V = 5 \times \frac{1}{2}R = \frac{5}{2}R$. Non-linear triatomic (3 trans + 3 rot): $C_V = 6 \times \frac{1}{2}R = 3R$.

**Vibrational modes at high temperature:** Each vibrational mode contributes 2 degrees of freedom (kinetic + potential), so $2 \times \frac{1}{2}R = R$ per mode. At room temperature, vibration is usually frozen out. At high T, $C_V$ increases further.

**Dulong-Petit law for solids:** At room temperature, the molar heat capacity of most solid elements is approximately $C = 3R \approx 25$ J/(mol·K). This comes from 3 quadratic DOF per atom: $\frac{3}{2}k_B$ per atom $\times N_A = \frac{3}{2}R$ per mole, but since each atom can vibrate in 3D (kinetic + potential), total is $3R$.

**Why Dulong-Petit law works:** At high temperature, all degrees of freedom are excited according to equipartition. Each atom has 3 vibrational modes (x, y, z), each with kinetic + potential, giving 6 DOF. So $C = 6 \times \frac{1}{2}R = 3R$.

**Failure of Dulong-Petit at low T:** At low temperatures, heat capacity drops toward zero. This was explained by Einstein (1907) using quantum mechanics: vibrational energy is quantized, and at low T, most oscillators are in the ground state, so they don't contribute to heat capacity.

**Debye model:** Peter Debye (1912) refined Einstein's model by considering the spectrum of vibrational frequencies (phonons) in a solid. The Debye model gives $C \propto T^3$ at very low temperatures, which matches experiment much better than Einstein's model.

**Applications:** Heat capacities determine how much a gas heats up for a given heat input. In isochoric heating ($V$ constant): $Q = n C_V \Delta T$. In isobaric heating ($P$ constant): $Q = n C_P \Delta T$. The difference is important for engines operating at constant pressure.

confusion: The ratio $\\\\gamma = C_P/C_V$ is NOT always 5/3 or 7/5. It depends on temperature and molecular structure. At very high temperatures, vibrational modes activate, changing $\\\\gamma$.
The formula $C_V = \ rac{3}{2}R$ applies ONLY to monatomic ideal gases. For diatomic or polyatomic gases, rotational (and sometimes vibrational) modes contribute.

Dulong's law ($C \\\\approx 3R$) for solids works well at room temperature but fails at very low temperatures (quantum effects freeze out degrees of freedom). Einstein and Debye developed low-temperature models.
The Boltzmann constant $k_B$ is NOT the same as the gas constant R. $k_B = 1.38 \	imes 10^{-23}$ J/K per molecule. R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) per mole. $R = N_A k_B$.

Most probable speed is NOT the average speed. For the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution: $v_p \\\\cdot \\\\sqrt{2} < v_{mean} < v_{rms}$. The order is always $v_p < v_{mean} < v_{rms}$ at the same temperature.

Heat capacity is NOT the same as specific heat. Heat capacity $C$ is for the whole object; specific heat $c$ is per unit mass. Molar heat capacity $C_m$ is per mole. They are related: $C = mc$ for uniform objects.

$C_P \neq C_V$. Many students think the heat capacity is the same regardless of conditions. At constant pressure, the gas expands and does work, requiring more heat input to achieve the same temperature rise. $C_P > C_V$ always.

The Dulong-Petit law ($C \approx 3R$) works only at sufficiently high temperatures (well above Debye temperature). Below that, quantum effects dominate and heat capacity drops. For diamond, this 'high temperature' is over 2000 K!

Degrees of freedom 'freeze out' at different temperatures. At room temperature: translational (always active), rotational (active for most molecules), vibrational (usually frozen). The textbook $C_V$ values assume rotational but not vibrational modes are active.

Heat capacity depends on temperature for real substances. The values $C_V = \frac{5}{2}R$ for diatomic gases are approximate room-temperature values. Over a wide temperature range, $C_V$ can change significantly.
practice: Calculate the root-mean-square speed of nitrogen molecules (N₂, M = 0.028 kg/mol) at 350 K. Solution: $v_{rms} = \\\\sqrt{3RT/M} = \\\\sqrt{3 \	imes 8.314 \	imes 350 / 0.028} = \\\\sqrt{3471.8 / 0.028} = \\\\sqrt{123,993} = 352$ m/s.

Find the most probable speed of helium atoms (He, M = 0.004 kg/mol) at 400 K. Solution: $v_p = \\\\sqrt{2RT/M} = \\\\sqrt{2 \	imes 8.314 \	imes 400 / 0.004} = \\\\sqrt{6651.2 / 0.004} = \\\\sqrt{1662800} = 1290$ m/s.

Calculate the mean speed of oxygen molecules (O₂, M = 0.032 kg/mol) at 273 K. Solution: $v_{mean} = \\\\sqrt{8RT/\\\\pi M} = \\\\sqrt{8 \	imes 8.314 \	imes 273 / (\\\\pi \	imes 0.032)} = \\\\sqrt{18136 / 0.1005} = \\\\sqrt{180,458} = 425$ m/s.

If the rms speed of helium at 300 K is 1250 m/s, what is the rms speed at 600 K? Solution: $v_{rms} \\\\propto \\\\sqrt{T}$. $v_{rms}(600) = v_{rms}(300) \	imes \\\\sqrt{600/300} = 1250 \	imes \\\\sqrt{2} = 1768$ m/s.
A container has 1 mol of gas at 300 K. What is the total internal energy for (a) monatomic gas? Solution: $U = \ rac{3}{2}nRT = \ rac{3}{2} \	imes 1 \	imes 8.314 \	imes 300 = 3741$ J.
Find the heat capacity ratio $\\\\gamma$ for a diatomic gas at room temperature. Solution: $\\\\gamma = C_P/C_V = (7/2R)/(5/2R) = 7/5 = 1.4$.

Calculate the heat required to raise the temperature of 2 mol of helium (monatomic) by 50 K at (a) constant volume, (b) constant pressure. Solution: (a) $Q = n C_V \Delta T = 2 \times (3/2 \times 8.314) \times 50 = 2 \times 12.47 \times 50 = 1247$ J. (b) $Q = n C_P \Delta T = 2 \times (5/2 \times 8.314) \times 50 = 2 \times 20.79 \times 50 = 2079$ J. Note: extra heat goes into expansion work.

Find the molar heat capacity at constant volume for CO₂ (linear triatomic). At room temperature, ignore vibration. Solution: Linear molecule has 3 translational + 2 rotational = 5 DOF. $C_V = \frac{5}{2}R = 20.8$ J/(mol·K). $C_P = C_V + R = 29.1$ J/(mol·K). $\gamma = 29.1/20.8 = 1.4$.
A 1 kg iron block (c = 449 J/(kg·K)) is heated from 20°C to 80°C. Find the heat absorbed. Solution: $Q = mc\Delta T = 1 \times 449 \times (80-20) = 449 \times 60 = 26,940$ J $\approx 27$ kJ.

Show that for an ideal gas, $C_P - C_V = R$. Solution: At constant volume: $Q_V = n C_V \Delta T = \Delta U$ (no $PV$ work). At constant pressure: $Q_P = n C_P \Delta T = \Delta U + P\Delta V$. For ideal gas: $P\Delta V = nR\Delta T$. So $n C_P \Delta T = n C_V \Delta T + nR\Delta T \rightarrow C_P - C_V = R$.

Compare the heat required to raise 1 mol of H₂ vs 1 mol of Xe by 10 K at constant volume. Solution: Both are diatomic (H₂) or monatomic (Xe). For H₂ (diatomic, $C_V = 5/2 R$): $Q = 1 \times 20.8 \times 10 = 208$ J. For Xe (monatomic, $C_V = 3/2 R$): $Q = 1 \times 12.5 \times 10 = 125$ J. More complex molecules require more heat.
universalFacts: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution was first derived by James Clerk Maxwell in 1860 and later generalized by Ludwig Boltzmann. It describes the distribution of speeds in an ideal gas and is one of the most important results of kinetic theory.

At 300 K, the three speed measures for nitrogen (M=28 g/mol) are: most probable $v_p \\\\approx 422$ m/s, mean speed $v_{mean} \\\\approx 477$ m/s, and rms speed $v_{rms} \\\\approx 517$ m/s. The ratios are always $v_p : v_{mean} : v_{rms} = \\\\sqrt{2} : \\\\sqrt{8/\\\\pi} : \\\\sqrt{3} \\\\approx 1.414 : 1.596 : 1.732$.

The Boltzmann constant $k_B$ was first introduced by Max Planck in his derivation of the blackbody radiation formula (1900). He used it to connect the energy of oscillators to temperature: $E = k_BT$.

Dulong and Petit's law ($C \\\\approx 3R$ for solids) was discovered in 1819. It took nearly 150 years to understand why it works - the kinetic theory's 3 degrees of freedom per atom (1859-1870s) provided the explanation.

The ratio $\\\\gamma = C_P/C_V$ determines whether sound speed is faster in an adiabatic process: $v_{sound} = \\\\sqrt{\\\\gamma RT/M}$. For air ($\\\gamma \\\\approx 1.4$), $v_{sound} \\\\approx 343$ m/s at 300 K. For helium ($\\\gamma = 5/3 \\\\approx 1.67$), $v_{sound} \\\\approx 965$ m/s at 300 K.
The law of Dulong and Petit (1819) states that the specific heat of solids is inversely proportional to atomic weight. This was an important empirical law before atomic theory was fully accepted.

Maxwell's equipartition theorem (1860s) explained why heat capacity should be proportional to the number of degrees of freedom. Each quadratic term in the energy contributes $\frac{1}{2}k_BT$ per molecule.

The failure of classical equipartition at low temperatures was one of the first major problems solved by quantum mechanics. Einstein's 1907 paper on specific heats was one of the first successful applications of Planck's quantum hypothesis.

The Debye model (1912) treated vibrations in a solid as sound waves (phonons) with a range of frequencies. It correctly predicted $C \propto T^3$ at very low temperatures, for which Debye received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1936.

In calorimetry, water's high specific heat (4186 J/(kg·K)) makes it an excellent coolant and heat storage medium. This is why coastal areas have milder climates than inland — the ocean absorbs/releases enormous amounts of heat with small temperature changes.

data.title: Instantaneous Velocity and Acceleration
notes: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version complements the original note with the limit-definition approach, calculus forms and graphical slope reasoning for instantaneous velocity and acceleration.

**Average quantities first:** average velocity $v_{avg} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$ uses the whole interval; average acceleration $a_{avg} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$ likewise. They smooth out everything that happened in between — a car doing 100 km in 2 h has $v_{avg} = 50$ km/h regardless of traffic.

**The limit idea:** instantaneous velocity is the average velocity as $\Delta t \to 0$: $v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{dx}{dt}$. It answers 'how fast RIGHT NOW' — exactly what a speedometer reads.
**Instantaneous acceleration:** $a = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}$. Acceleration is the derivative of velocity — the 'slope of the slope'.

**Graphical meaning:** on an $x$–$t$ graph, velocity = slope of the tangent at the instant (not the chord); on a $v$–$t$ graph, acceleration = slope of the tangent, and the AREA under the curve between two times gives the displacement.

**Sign reasoning:** $v > 0$ → moving forward; $v < 0$ → moving backward; $a > 0$ with $v > 0$ → speeding up; $a > 0$ with $v < 0$ → slowing down (a negative velocity becoming more negative). 'Slowing down' means $v$ and $a$ have OPPOSITE signs — the classic exam trap.

**Worked calculus example:** $x(t) = 5t^2 - 3t$. Then $v = dx/dt = 10t - 3$ and $a = dv/dt = 10\,\text{m/s}^2$ (constant). At $t = 2$ s: $v = 17$ m/s; the particle is momentarily at rest when $t = 0.3$ s.

**Uniform vs non-uniform acceleration:** if $a$ is constant the SUVAT equations apply; if $a$ varies with time, position or velocity, only the calculus definitions (or graphs) work. This is why the derivative definition is the more general and more fundamental one.

**NEB exam focus:** define instantaneous velocity/acceleration as limits; differentiate a given $x(t)$; find when a particle is at rest or reverses; convert between $x$–$t$, $v$–$t$ and $a$–$t$ graphs (slopes and areas).
confusion: ❌ 'Instantaneous velocity equals average velocity.' ✅ Only when motion is uniform. In general $v_{inst} = dx/dt$ while $v_{avg} = \Delta x/\Delta t$; they coincide only if the $x$–$t$ graph is a straight line.

❌ 'Negative acceleration always means slowing down.' ✅ Slowing means $v$ and $a$ have OPPOSITE signs. A ball thrown upward (up = positive) has $v > 0$ with $a = -g$ — it slows going up and speeds up coming down, with the SAME downward acceleration throughout.
❌ 'The area under an $x$–$t$ graph gives velocity.' ✅ The SLOPE of $x$–$t$ gives velocity; the AREA under a $v$–$t$ graph gives displacement. Mixing these up is the classic graph-question error.
❌ 'At the turning point, acceleration is zero.' ✅ At a reversal, $v = 0$ but $a$ is NOT zero (e.g. a ball at the top of its flight has $v = 0$, $a = g$ downward). Zero velocity ≠ zero acceleration.
❌ 'Speed can be negative.' ✅ Speed is $|v|$, always non-negative; velocity carries the sign (direction).
❌ 'If $v = 0$ at an instant, the particle has stopped permanently.' ✅ $v = 0$ can be a momentary pause (top of a throw) — check the acceleration to know what happens next.
practice: Given $x(t) = 4t^3 - 2t^2 + 5$ (m): find $v(t)$ and $a(t)$; evaluate at $t = 1$ s. — $v = 12t^2 - 4t = 8$ m/s; $a = 24t - 4 = 20$ m/s².
A particle's velocity is $v(t) = 6t - 3t^2$ (m/s). When is it instantaneously at rest, and what is its acceleration then? — $t = 0$ or $2$ s; at $t = 2$: $a = 6 - 6t = -6$ m/s².
From a $v$–$t$ graph consisting of a straight line from (0, 4) to (4, 12) m/s, find the acceleration and the displacement in 4 s. — $a = 2$ m/s²; displacement = area $= \frac{4+12}{2}\times4 = 32$ m.
A stone is thrown up at 20 m/s ($g = 10$ m/s²). Find its velocity and acceleration at the highest point. — $v = 0$; $a = 10$ m/s² downward — zero velocity, non-zero acceleration.
The position of two trains is $x_1 = 20t$ and $x_2 = 5t^2$ (m). When are their instantaneous velocities equal, and where? — $20 = 10t$ → $t = 2$ s at $x = 40$ m.
universalFacts: Calculus was invented (Newton and Leibniz, 1660s–70s) precisely to handle instantaneous quantities — physics and calculus were born together, and Newton's name for the derivative was the 'fluxion'.
Car speedometers show instantaneous speed, while trip computers computing distance ÷ time show average speed — the two can differ enormously in city traffic.

Radar guns and GPS speed trackers estimate instantaneous velocity by measuring position over very small time windows — a physical implementation of the limit $\Delta x/\Delta t$ with $\Delta t \to 0$.
In relativity and quantum mechanics, instantaneous velocity remains fundamental: particle accelerators track beam particles through billions of instantaneous velocity updates per second.

formulas: Instantaneous velocity: $v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{dx}{dt}$
Instantaneous acceleration: $a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}$
Displacement from velocity: $x_2 - x_1 = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} v\,dt$ (area under $v$–$t$ curve)
Velocity from acceleration: $v_2 - v_1 = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} a\,dt$
Rest condition: $v = \frac{dx}{dt} = 0$; reversal check: sign change of $v$ around that instant
keyPoints: Instantaneous velocity is the slope of the tangent of the $x$–$t$ graph; instantaneous acceleration is the slope of the $v$–$t$ graph.
Displacement is the area under the $v$–$t$ graph; change in velocity is the area under the $a$–$t$ graph.
$v = 0$ does not imply $a = 0$ — turning points have zero velocity but non-zero acceleration.
Speeding up ⟺ $v$ and $a$ share the same sign; slowing down ⟺ opposite signs.
Derivatives go down the chain $x \to v \to a$; integrals go up $a \to v \to x$, using initial conditions.
The limit definition is valid for ANY motion — SUVAT equations are special cases of constant acceleration only.

data.summary: Instantaneous velocity and acceleration are defined as limits: $v = dx/dt$ and $a = dv/dt = d^2x/dt^2$. Graphically, $v$ is the tangent slope of the $x$–$t$ curve and $a$ the tangent slope of the $v$–$t$ curve, while areas under $v$–$t$ and $a$–$t$ curves give displacement and velocity change. These definitions work for all motion — uniform or not — making them more fundamental than the constant-acceleration equations. Key exam skills: differentiating given $x(t)$, locating rest/reversal instants, and reading slopes and areas correctly with attention to signs. Instantaneous Velocity & Instantaneous Acceleration covers essential principles and applications.

specificConditions: **Limit Definition Universality:** Instantaneous velocity $v = dx/dt$ and acceleration $a = dv/dt$ are defined as limits ($\Delta t 	o 0$). They apply to *any* motion — uniform or non-uniform, constant or variable acceleration. The SUVAT equations ($v = u + at$, etc.) are special cases valid *only* for constant $a$.

**Graph Duality — Slopes vs Areas:** On $x$-$t$ graph: slope of tangent = $v$. On $v$-$t$ graph: slope of tangent = $a$; area under curve = displacement. On $a$-$t$ graph: area under curve = change in velocity. Mixing up slope/area is the most common graph error.

**Sign Logic for Speeding/Slowing:** Speeding up $\Leftrightarrow$ $v$ and $a$ have *same* sign. Slowing down $\Leftrightarrow$ $v$ and $a$ have *opposite* signs. This is true regardless of coordinate choice. At a turning point ($v=0$), $a 
eq 0$ (e.g., ball at top of flight: $v=0$, $a=g$).
examples: Example 1: $x(t) = 3t^2$ m → $v = 6t$ m/s; at $t = 2$ s the instantaneous velocity is 12 m/s, while the average velocity over 0–2 s is $\frac{12-0}{2} = 6$ m/s — different because the motion speeds up.
Example 2: A metro train's $v$–$t$ graph: trapezoid of acceleration, cruise, braking. Displacement = area of trapezoid; acceleration = slope in each segment.
Example 3: $v(t) = 8 - 4t$: the particle reverses at $t = 2$ s where $v = 0$ but $a = -4$ m/s² throughout — illustrating reversal with constant acceleration.
Example 4: Two instants with equal speeds but different velocities: $v = +10$ m/s at $t_1$ and $v = -10$ m/s at $t_2$ — same speed, opposite direction of motion.
Example 5: From $a = 6t$ and $v(0) = 2$ m/s: integrate to $v = 3t^2 + 2$ and, with $x(0) = 0$, $x = t^3 + 2t$ — showing how derivatives run downward ($x \to v \to a$) and integrals run upward.

data.title: Relative Velocity
notes: **Definition of relative velocity:** The velocity of an object B as measured from the reference frame of another moving object A. It is the velocity of B relative to A.

**Same direction (one-dimensional):** If car A moves at velocity v_A and car B at v_B in the same direction, the velocity of B relative to A is v_{B/A} = v_B - v_A. If v_B > v_A, B moves ahead relative to A; if v_B < v_A, B falls behind.

**Opposite directions (one-dimensional):** If A and B move toward each other with speeds v_A and v_B, the relative speed (magnitude of relative velocity) is v_{rel} = v_A + v_B. The direction of v_{B/A} is toward A if B is moving toward A.

**Vector form (two/three dimensions):** \vec{v}_{B/A} = \vec{v}_B - \vec{v}_A. This is the velocity of B in the ground frame minus the velocity of A in the ground frame. In components: (v_{B/A})_x = v_{Bx} - v_{Ax}, etc.

**Relative velocity in 2D — Rain example:** If rain falls vertically downward at speed v_r and a person runs horizontally at speed v_p, the rain appears to come at the person at an angle 	heta where tan	heta = v_p / v_r. The apparent speed is \sqrt{v_r^2 + v_p^2}.

**River crossing (boat relative to water vs. ground):** Let \vec{v}_{bw} be the boat's velocity relative to the water (its heading and speed), and \vec{v}_{wg} be the water's velocity relative to ground (current). Then the boat's ground velocity is \vec{v}_{bg} = \vec{v}_{bw} + \vec{v}_{wg}. To reach a point directly across, the boat must angle upstream.

**Relative velocity of approach/separation:** For two objects approaching, the rate at which their separation decreases is v_{rel} = v_A + v_B (if opposite directions) or |v_B - v_A| (if same direction). For collision problems, relative velocity is crucial.

**Frame of reference transformation:** To transform from frame A to frame B, subtract the velocity of frame A: \vec{v}' = \vec{v} - \vec{v}_A. The laws of physics (Newton's laws) are the same in all inertial frames (Galilean relativity).

**Galilean velocity addition:** In classical mechanics, velocities add vectorially: \vec{v}_{B/C} = \vec{v}_{B/A} + \vec{v}_{A/C}. This chain rule allows finding velocity of B relative to C via an intermediate frame A.

**Relative motion on an incline:** If a block slides down an incline at speed v relative to the incline, and the incline itself moves (e.g., on a truck), the block's ground velocity is the vector sum of its velocity relative to the incline and the incline's velocity relative to ground.

**Closing speed vs. relative velocity:** Closing speed is the rate at which the distance between two objects decreases. For objects moving directly toward each other, closing speed = |v_A| + |v_B|. This is the magnitude of the relative velocity only if they are on a collision course.

confusion: Relative velocity is NOT the same as the difference in speeds. For two cars moving at 60 km/h and 40 km/h in the SAME direction, the relative speed is 20 km/h, NOT 100 km/h. For opposite directions, the relative speed is the SUM (100 km/h).

When subtracting vectors, the ORDER MATTERS: \vec{v}_{B/A} = \vec{v}_B - \vec{v}_A. This is the velocity of B AS SEEN BY A. \vec{v}_{A/B} = \vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_B = -\vec{v}_{B/A}. They are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction.

A common mistake in river problems: students add the boat's speed to the current speed as scalars. You must add them as VECTORS: the boat's velocity relative to water PLUS water's velocity relative to ground. The angle matters!

In the rain problem, the rain does NOT change its actual velocity — it still falls vertically. Only the APPARENT velocity (relative to the moving person) is angled. The person tilts their umbrella forward to block the apparent rain.

Galilean relativity breaks down at speeds close to the speed of light (c). Einstein's special relativity replaces it with the Lorentz velocity addition formula: v = (v1 + v2)/(1 + v1v2/c^2). For everyday speeds (<< c), this reduces to Galilean addition.
practice: Two trains A and B are moving on parallel tracks. Train A moves east at 60 km/h. Train B moves east at 80 km/h. Find the velocity of B relative to A, and the velocity of A relative to B. Solution: v_{B/A} = 80 - 60 = 20 km/h east (B moves ahead of A at 20 km/h). v_{A/B} = 60 - 80 = -20 km/h (20 km/h west, meaning A falls behind B).

Rain is falling vertically at 30 m/s. A man runs horizontally at 10 m/s. At what angle from vertical does the rain appear to fall? What is the apparent speed? Solution: tan	heta = v_man/v_rain = 10/30 = 1/3. 	heta = 	an^{-1}(1/3) = 18.4° from vertical. Apparent speed = \sqrt{30^2 + 10^2} = \sqrt{1000} = 31.6 m/s.

A boat's speed in still water is 5 m/s. The river flows at 3 m/s east. The boat wants to reach a point directly across the river (north). (a) At what angle must the boat head? (b) What is its ground speed? (c) Time to cross a 100 m wide river? Solution: (a) Boat must cancel eastward current: 5 sin	heta = 3 → 	heta = 36.9° west of north. (b) v_ground = 5 cos	heta = 5 × 0.8 = 4 m/s north. (c) t = width/v_ground = 100/4 = 25 s.

Two particles move on the x-axis. Particle A: x_A(t) = 2t + 1. Particle B: x_B(t) = -3t + 10. Find their relative velocity at t = 2 s. Solution: v_A = dx_A/dt = 2 m/s. v_B = dx_B/dt = -3 m/s. v_{B/A} = v_B - v_A = -3 - 2 = -5 m/s. The distance between them decreases at 5 m/s.

An airplane flies at 400 km/h relative to air. The wind blows at 100 km/h from the west (toward east). What is the plane's ground speed and direction if it heads (a) north? (b) northeast? Solution: (a) v_ground = \sqrt{400^2 + 100^2} = 412 km/h. Direction: tan	heta = 100/400 = 1/4 → 	heta = 14° east of north. (b) v_plane = 400/\sqrt{2} north + 400/\sqrt{2} east. v_wind = 100 east. v_ground = (400/\sqrt{2}) north + (400/\sqrt{2} + 100) east = 283 north + 383 east. Speed = \sqrt{283^2 + 383^2} = 476 km/h.
universalFacts: Galilean relativity (velocity addition v' = v - u) was the standard until Einstein's special relativity (1905) showed it is only an approximation valid for v ≪ c. At everyday speeds, the error is completely negligible.
Relative velocity is a fundamental concept in all of physics — from classical mechanics to electromagnetism (magnetic fields are electric fields viewed from a moving frame) to special relativity.

The principle of Galilean relativity: the laws of motion are identical in all inertial frames. If you toss a ball up in a moving train (constant velocity), it lands back in your hand — the ball has the train's forward velocity added to its motion.

In collision problems, the relative velocity of approach is often more useful than individual velocities. For elastic collisions, the relative velocity of separation equals the relative velocity of approach (in magnitude).

The concept of relative velocity explains why we don't feel Earth's orbital speed (30 km/s) or rotation speed (0.46 km/s at equator) — we move with the Earth, so our velocity relative to Earth is zero. Only in non-inertial frames (acceleration) do we feel fictitious forces.
specificConditions: **Vector Subtraction Rule:** $\vec{v}_{B/A} = \vec{v}_B - \vec{v}_A$ is the velocity of B as measured in A's rest frame. The order matters: $\vec{v}_{A/B} = -\vec{v}_{B/A}$. This is a vector equation — subtract components, not speeds.

**Galilean Relativity Limit:** Velocity addition $\vec{v} = \vec{v}' + \vec{u}$ (where $\vec{u}$ is frame velocity) is valid only for speeds $\ll c$. At relativistic speeds, Einstein's velocity addition $v = (v' + u)/(1 + v'u/c^2)$ must be used. For everyday kinematics, Galilean addition is exact.

**Apparent vs Real Motion:** In the rain/river problems, the actual velocity of the rain/boat is unchanged; only the *observed* (relative) velocity changes when the observer moves. The rain still falls vertically; the umbrella is tilted to match the apparent velocity.

data.title: Equations of Motion — Graphical Treatment
notes: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version derives all three equations of motion graphically (from the velocity–time graph) — the derivation style NEB asks for 'using a graphical method'.

**Setup:** a body starts with initial velocity $u$ and accelerates uniformly at $a$; after time $t$ its velocity is $v$. On a $v$–$t$ graph this is a straight line from $(0, u)$ to $(t, v)$ — the straightness is exactly the meaning of uniform acceleration.
**First equation (from the slope):** slope of the line = acceleration $a = \frac{v - u}{t}$. Rearranging: $v = u + at$ — 'final velocity = initial velocity + rate of change of velocity × time'.

**Second equation (from the area):** displacement = area under the $v$–$t$ line = area of the trapezoid = area of rectangle $ut$ + area of triangle $\frac{1}{2} \times t \times (v - u)$. Since $v - u = at$: $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$.

**Second equation, alternate area view:** average velocity $\times$ time: $s = \left(\frac{u + v}{2}\right)t$ — the trapezoid's mean-height form. Both views give the same result and both are accepted in exams.

**Third equation (eliminating $t$):** from $t = \frac{v-u}{a}$ substitute into $s = \left(\frac{u+v}{2}\right)t$: $s = \frac{(u+v)(v-u)}{2a} = \frac{v^2 - u^2}{2a}$, giving $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ — the time-free equation, ideal when $t$ is neither given nor asked.

**Reading the other graphs:** on an $x$–$t$ graph, constant $a$ appears as a parabola (curvature fixed); the tangent slope at any point is $v$. On an $a$–$t$ graph, constant $a$ is a horizontal line and the area under it ($a \times t$) gives the change in velocity $v - u$.

**Displacement in the $n$-th second:** $s_n = u + \tfrac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$ — obtained from areas: distance covered between $t = n-1$ and $t = n$. For free fall from rest this gives the odd-numbers rule 1 : 3 : 5 : 7 (Galileo).

**NEB exam focus:** derive $v = u + at$ and $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ with a labelled $v$–$t$ graph; derive $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$; state which equation to choose from what is given/asked; apply to braking, free fall and projected bodies.

confusion: ❌ 'The area under the $v$–$t$ graph gives acceleration.' ✅ Area gives DISPLACEMENT; the SLOPE gives acceleration. Swap-proof: slope of $v$–$t$ = $a$ (m/s²), area of $v$–$t$ = $s$ (m).

❌ Using $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ for the distance in the $n$-th second directly with $t = n$. ✅ That gives the total distance in $n$ seconds. The $n$-th SECOND distance is $s_n = u + \tfrac{a}{2}(2n-1)$, i.e. $s(n) - s(n-1)$.

❌ Applying $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with sign errors during braking. ✅ Take one positive direction and keep it: braking at 20 m/s with $a = -5$ m/s² gives $0 = 400 + 2(-5)s \Rightarrow s = 40$ m — the minus sign is essential.
❌ 'The equations work if acceleration changes gradually.' ✅ All three equations REQUIRE constant acceleration; if $a$ varies, use graphs/areas or calculus.
❌ Treating $u$ and $v$ as interchangeable. ✅ $u$ is the velocity at $t = 0$; $v$ is at time $t$. A body dropped from rest has $u = 0$; a body thrown up has $u = +20$ m/s while $a = -10$ m/s².

❌ Confusing distance with displacement when the body reverses. ✅ The equations give displacement (vector). For total path length through a reversal, split the motion at the $v = 0$ instant and add the two parts.
practice: Derive $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ from the trapezoid area, stating every step and labelling the $v$–$t$ graph.
A car brakes from 30 m/s to rest in 6 s. Using a $v$–$t$ graph find the acceleration and stopping distance. — $a = -5$ m/s²; $s = \frac{30 \times 6}{2} = 90$ m (triangle area).
A body starting at 4 m/s accelerates at 2 m/s². Find (a) $v$ at 5 s, (b) $s$ in 5 s, (c) $s$ in the 5th second. — (a) 14 m/s; (b) 45 m; (c) $4 + 1(9) = 13$ m.
A stone dropped from a cliff hits the ground at 40 m/s ($g = 10$ m/s²). Find the cliff height using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ and the fall time. — $s = 80$ m; $t = 4$ s.
A train travelling at 72 km/h applies brakes producing $-0.5$ m/s². How far does it travel before stopping, and how long does it take? — $u = 20$ m/s; $s = 400$ m; $t = 40$ s.
universalFacts: The velocity–time 'trapezoid' derivation appears in Galileo's reasoning (via inclined planes and odd-number distances) two centuries before formal calculus existed.
Air-force and driving-school 'stopping distance' charts are exactly the $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ equation with $v = 0$ — doubling speed quadruples braking distance.
Crash investigators reconstruct vehicle speeds from skid marks using $u = \sqrt{2\mu g s}$ — the same third equation rearranged with friction as the deceleration.
Physics simulators (games, driving sims) integrate $v$–$t$ areas every frame — the trapezoid rule your textbook uses graphically is the numerical engine behind them.
examples: Example 1 (slope): a cyclist's $v$–$t$ line rises from 2 m/s to 10 m/s in 4 s → $a = \frac{10-2}{4} = 2$ m/s², read straight off the graph.
Example 2 (area): the same cyclist covers $s = \frac{2+10}{2} \times 4 = 24$ m — the trapezoid area, no equation needed.
Example 3 (third equation): a car at 25 m/s needs to stop within 50 m. Required deceleration: $0 = 25^2 + 2a(50) \Rightarrow a = -6.25$ m/s² — time never enters, which is why this equation fits.
Example 4 (two-stage motion): a train accelerates at 1 m/s² for 20 s then brakes at 2 m/s² to stop. Draw the $v$–$t$ trapezoid; peak speed 20 m/s; total distance = area = 300 m.
Example 5 (drop with initial speed): a stone thrown down a well at 2 m/s strikes water 3 s later: $s = 2(3) + \tfrac{1}{2}(10)(9) = 51$ m — the rectangle-plus-triangle areas directly.

keyPoints: Slope of $v$–$t$ = acceleration; area under $v$–$t$ = displacement.
The three equations hold ONLY for constant acceleration.
$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ is the equation of choice when time is unknown.
$s = \left(\frac{u+v}{2}\right)t$ is the graphical 'average velocity × time' form.

data.summary: All three equations of motion follow from the straight-line $v$–$t$ graph of uniform acceleration: the slope gives $v = u + at$; the area (rectangle + triangle, or the trapezoid mean-height $\frac{u+v}{2}t$) gives $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$; eliminating $t$ yields $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$. The $a$–$t$ graph (area = change in velocity) and the $x$–$t$ parabola complete the graphical picture. These derivations are standard NEB questions, and the equations themselves — with careful sign conventions — solve braking, free-fall and multi-stage motion numericals.

specificConditions: **Constant Acceleration Requirement:** The three equations $v = u + at$, $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$, $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ are valid *only* when acceleration is constant. **Graphical Derivation Logic:** The $v$-$t$ graph for constant $a$ is a straight line. Slope = $a$ gives $v = u + at$. Area (trapezoid) = $s = \frac{u+v}{2}t = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$. Eliminating $t$ gives $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$. These derivations are NEB favorites.

data.title: Motion of a Freely Falling Body
data.topicTitle: Motion of a Freely Falling Body
notes: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version works free fall entirely through the equations of motion with sign conventions and the up-and-down symmetry argument — the pattern NEB numericals follow.

**Definition:** a freely falling body moves under gravity ALONE — no air resistance, no push after release. All bodies fall with the same acceleration $g \approx 9.8$ m/s² (take 10 m/s² in numericals) independent of mass — Galileo's famous result.

**Sign convention method:** choose upward positive. Then for a body projected up at $u$: $v = u - gt$, $h = ut - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, $v^2 = u^2 - 2gh$. The SAME equations with $u = 0$ describe a dropped body; with the throw downward, $u$ enters negative.

**Up–down symmetry:** a body thrown up with speed $u$ returns to the launch point with the same speed (downward); time up = time down $= u/g$; total flight $T = 2u/g$. Air resistance would break this symmetry — its absence is the point of 'free' fall.

**Key instants for a body thrown up:** at the top, $v = 0$ but $a = g$ downward (never zero); height reached $h_{max} = u^2/2g$; velocities at equal heights going up and down are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
**Dropped from a height $h$:** $v = gt$, $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, $v = \sqrt{2gh}$. Time to fall: $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$. Falling 1:3:5:7 distances each second (Galileo's odd-number rule).

**Bodies with initial downward or upward motion from a height** (e.g. a ball thrown down at 5 m/s): $v^2 = u^2 + 2gh$ with BOTH terms positive when down is the direction of travel — the third equation handles every case once signs are set.

**Relative fall problems:** a ball dropped from a descending/ascending lift, or two balls released with a time gap — write each body's position $y_i(t)$ with the same origin, then use their difference. E.g. separation between a dropped ball and one thrown down 1 s later grows as $\Delta y = \tfrac{1}{2}g + (u)t$.

**NEB exam focus:** state that $g$ is mass-independent (with the Galileo/feather-coin argument); compute maximum height, time of flight, velocity on impact; apply up–down symmetry; solve dropped/thrown-from-lift problems with one consistent sign convention.
confusion: ❌ 'Heavier bodies fall faster.' ✅ In free fall ALL bodies have the same acceleration $g$; observed differences come from air resistance — demonstrated by the Apollo 15 hammer–feather drop on the Moon.
❌ 'At the top of the flight, acceleration is zero because the body stops.' ✅ $v = 0$ but $a = g$ downward at ALL points of the flight. If $a$ were zero at the top, the body would stay there!

❌ Using $g = -10$ m/s² AND taking $h$ positive upward in $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$. ✅ Put the sign in ONCE: either $g$ negative with up positive, or down positive with $g$ positive — never both conventions mixed.
❌ 'A body thrown up takes longer to rise than to fall.' ✅ Without air resistance the times are EXACTLY equal ($u/g$ each way); with air resistance the fall takes LONGER, not the rise.
❌ 'Velocity on returning to the thrower is less than the launch speed.' ✅ Equal in magnitude (symmetry). Only air resistance or bounce changes it.
❌ Treating 'dropped' and 'thrown down' identically. ✅ Dropped means $u = 0$; thrown down means $u \ne 0$ downward — the equations differ by that initial term.
practice: A stone is thrown up at 29.4 m/s. Find (a) max height, (b) time to top, (c) total flight time ($g = 9.8$). — (a) 44.1 m; (b) 3 s; (c) 6 s.
A ball dropped from a tower takes 2.5 s to land. Find the tower height and impact speed ($g = 10$). — $h = 31.25$ m; $v = 25$ m/s.
A body is thrown down at 4 m/s from a 50 m building. When does it land and at what speed? — $50 = 4t + 5t^2 \Rightarrow t = 2.78$ s; $v = 4 + 10(2.78) \approx 31.8$ m/s.
A ball thrown up passes a window at 10 m/s going up. When does it pass the window again (same speed downward)? — By symmetry it returns with 10 m/s; time gap $= 2u/g = 2$ s.

From a lift descending at 4 m/s, a coin is dropped. Relative to the lift floor, describe its motion; relative to the ground, find its acceleration. — Relative to lift: falls with $g$ from rest; relative to ground: $u = 4$ m/s down, $a = g$ down.
universalFacts: Apollo 15 commander David Scott dropped a hammer and falcon feather on the Moon (1971): both hit the dust together — the most-watched verification that $g$ is mass-independent.
Vacuum-tube 'Guinea and feather' demonstrations in classrooms reproduce the same result; air resistance, not gravity, distinguishes everyday falls.
$g$ varies over Earth: about 9.78 m/s² at the equator and 9.83 m/s² at the poles — precise free-fall experiments are used by geophysicists to survey underground density (gravimetry).
Skydivers reach terminal velocity (~55 m/s belly-down) only because air resistance grows with speed; in free fall proper, speed would grow by 9.8 m/s every second without limit.
examples: Example 1 (dropped): a mango falls from a 20 m tree — $t = \sqrt{2h/g} = \sqrt{4} = 2$ s; strikes at $v = \sqrt{2(10)(20)} = 20$ m/s.
Example 2 (thrown up): a ball goes up at 15 m/s — top after 1.5 s, $h_{max} = 11.25$ m, back in hand after 3 s at 15 m/s (symmetry).
Example 3 (through a window): a ball dropped past a 2 m window takes 0.1 s — speed at window top $\approx \frac{2}{0.1} - \tfrac{1}{2}(10)(0.1) \approx 19.5$ m/s, hence fall height $\approx 19$ m.
Example 4 (two balls): one dropped and one thrown down at 10 m/s from the same tower stay $10t$ apart — both gain speed at $g$; the throw only adds a constant offset.
Example 5 (lift): a lift falls freely — objects inside float relative to the cabin because both cabin and objects have $a = g$ (weightlessness in free fall).

Q2. A stone dropped from a bridge strikes the water in 3 s. Find the bridge height and the striking velocity ($g = 10$).
Q3. A ball is thrown upward and rises 45 m. Find its initial speed and total time of flight.
Q4. Show that a body thrown up returns to the starting point with the same speed, using $v^2 = u^2 - 2gh$.
Q5. A coin is dropped from a lift moving up at constant velocity 6 m/s. Find its acceleration relative to (a) the lift, (b) the ground.
formulas: Dropped from rest: $v = gt$, $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, $v = \sqrt{2gh}$
Thrown up (up positive): $v = u - gt$, $h = ut - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, $v^2 = u^2 - 2gh$
Maximum height: $h_{max} = \dfrac{u^2}{2g}$ (at $v = 0$)
Times: $t_{up} = t_{down} = \dfrac{u}{g}$, total flight $T = \dfrac{2u}{g}$
$n$-th second fall distance: $s_n = \tfrac{g}{2}(2n - 1)$ — ratio $1:3:5:7\ldots$
keyPoints: Free fall acceleration $g$ is independent of mass, size and material.
At every instant of the flight, $a = g$ downward — including the top ($v = 0$, $a \ne 0$).
Up–down symmetry: equal speeds at equal heights, equal times up and down.
Use ONE sign convention throughout a problem; put $g$'s sign in consistently.
'Dropped' = $u = 0$; 'thrown' = $u \ne 0$ — the equations differ by the $ut$ term.
Air resistance is neglected in free fall; it is what produces terminal velocity in reality.

data.summary: Free fall is uniform acceleration $g$ with no air resistance: all bodies fall alike. The up–down symmetry (equal times and speeds) is the key structural insight, and $v = 0$ with $a = g$ at the top is the classic conceptual test point. data.title: Projectile Motion
notes: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version builds projectile motion from the independence of the two components and derives all standard results step by step — the derivation chain NEB expects.

**The governing idea:** horizontal and vertical motions are INDEPENDENT. Gravity acts only vertically, so the horizontal velocity stays constant ($v_x = u\cos\theta$) while the vertical motion is free fall with initial speed $u\sin\theta$. The path is the combination — a parabola.

**Component equations (up positive, launch at angle $\theta$ with speed $u$):** horizontal: $x = (u\cos\theta)t$, $v_x = u\cos\theta$; vertical: $y = (u\sin\theta)t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, $v_y = u\sin\theta - gt$.
**Time of flight:** set $y = 0$ on landing: $T = \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$ — twice the time to the top ($u\sin\theta/g$).
**Maximum height:** at the top $v_y = 0$: $H = \dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$ — vertical throw with initial speed $u\sin\theta$.

**Horizontal range:** $R = v_x T = \dfrac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$. Since $\sin 2\theta$ peaks at $2\theta = 90°$, **maximum range at $\theta = 45°$**, and complementary angles ($30°$ & $60°$, $15°$ & $75°$) give the SAME range.

**Velocity at any instant:** $v = \sqrt{(u\cos\theta)^2 + (u\sin\theta - gt)^2}$ at angle $\phi = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{u\sin\theta - gt}{u\cos\theta}\right)$ below/above horizontal. On landing, magnitude equals $u$ (symmetry) with direction $-\theta$.
**Trajectory equation:** eliminate $t$: $y = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{g x^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$ — a parabola. Also useful: $R = 4H\cot\theta$ connecting range and height.

**Applications to quote:** cannon/artillery ranges, projectile games (javelin, football), water-fountain arcs, bombing-release problems (bomb keeps the plane's horizontal velocity), and projectile on an inclined plane (extension: $R = \frac{2u^2\cos\theta\sin(\theta-\alpha)}{g\cos^2\alpha}$ for incline angle $\alpha$ — beyond syllabus but good insight).

**NEB exam focus:** state independence of motions; derive $T$, $H$, $R$; prove max range at 45°; show complementary angles share range; compute velocity (magnitude and direction) at a given time or height; draw the labelled trajectory.
confusion: ❌ 'A projectile's horizontal velocity decreases during flight.' ✅ $v_x = u\cos\theta$ is CONSTANT (no horizontal force in the ideal model); only $v_y$ changes.
❌ 'At the top of the trajectory the velocity is zero.' ✅ Only $v_y = 0$; the horizontal component $u\cos\theta$ persists — speed at the top is $u\cos\theta$, the MINIMUM of the flight.
❌ 'The path is part of a circle / straight line decaying.' ✅ The trajectory is a PARABOLA — the graph of $y = x\tan\theta - gx^2/(2u^2\cos^2\theta)$.
❌ Using $\sin\theta$ instead of $\sin 2\theta$ in the range. ✅ $R = u^2\sin 2\theta/g$; and $\sin 2\theta$ is maximal at $\theta = 45°$, not $90°$.
❌ 'Complementary angles give different ranges.' ✅ $\sin 2(90°-\theta) = \sin(180°-2\theta) = \sin 2\theta$ — $30°$ and $60°$ land at the SAME spot (the 60° shot flies higher).
❌ Doubling $u$ doubles the range. ✅ $R \propto u^2$ — doubling launch speed QUADRUPLES range (and quadruples max height too).

Prove that the speed on landing equals the launch speed, using components at $t = T$.
A projectile has range 100 m and time of flight 4 s. Find its horizontal velocity and launch angle. — $v_x = 25$ m/s; $u_y = gt/2 = 20$ m/s → $\theta = \tan^{-1}(20/25) = 38.7°$.

universalFacts: Galileo's *Dialogues* (1638) first showed projectile motion is a parabola by superposing uniform horizontal motion with vertical fall — the first known composition of motions.
Artillery fire above ~30 km (Paris Gun, WWI) deviates from the parabola: thin air changes drag and $g$'s direction varies — ideal parabolic flight is a near-Earth, no-air model.
Long-jump athletes take off near 21°, not 45°, because take-off speed itself drops with steeper angles — the real optimum balances range angle against speed loss.
Basketball free throws exploit the high-arc (complementary-angle) region: a steep entry angle enlarges the effective hoop target, even though the flatter shot travels the same distance.
examples: Example 1 (horizontal launch): a stone thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from a 20 m tower: $t = \sqrt{2 \times 20/10} = 2$ s; lands 30 m out — vertical fall sets the TIME, horizontal speed sets the DISTANCE.
Example 2 (full trajectory): $u = 25$ m/s at $\theta = 37°$ ($\sin 37° = 0.6$, $\cos 37° = 0.8$): $T = 3$ s, $H = 11.25$ m, $R = 60$ m — the classic 3-4-5 projectile.
Example 3 (velocity at top): speed at the top $= u\cos\theta = 20$ m/s for the previous shot — the projectile is never at rest.
Example 4 (45° range): maximum range with $u = 30$ m/s is $R_{max} = u^2/g = 90$ m at 45°, with $H = R/4 = 22.5$ m — note $R_{max} = 4H$.
Example 5 (bomb release): a plane at 500 m flying level at 100 m/s releases a bomb — it lands after $t = 10$ s, $500$ m ahead of the release point (it keeps the plane's horizontal velocity).

specificConditions: **Independence of Components:** Horizontal motion (constant $v_x = u\cos	heta$) and vertical motion (free fall $v_y = u\sin	heta - gt$) are completely independent. They share only the time variable $t$. This is the foundational principle — no horizontal force means $v_x$ is constant.

**Trajectory is a Parabola:** Eliminating $t$ gives $y = x	an	heta -  rac{g x^2}{2u^2\cos^2	heta}$, a downward-opening parabola. This assumes no air resistance, constant $g$, and flat ground. With drag, the trajectory is not a parabola and range decreases.

**Symmetry and Range Maxima:** Time of flight $T =  rac{2u\sin	heta}{g}$, max height $H =  rac{u^2\sin^2	heta}{2g}$, range $R =  rac{u^2\sin 2	heta}{g}$. Maximum range at $	heta = 45^\circ$. Complementary angles ($	heta$ and $90^\circ-	heta$) give identical ranges because $\sin 2	heta = \sin(180^\circ-2	heta)$. Speed at launch = speed at landing (symmetry).

data.title: Lens Maker's Formula
notes: The lens-maker relation predicts focal length from material and curvature. For a thin lens in air, 1/f=(n−1)(1/R1−1/R2), where n is lens refractive index and R1,R2 are signed radii in a stated convention.

For light travelling left to right, a biconvex lens commonly has R1>0 and R2<0, so the curvature contributions add to positive converging power. Do not substitute unsigned radii into a signed formula.
Worked example: n=1.50, R1=+20 cm and R2=−20 cm give 1/f=0.50(1/20+1/20)=0.05 cm⁻¹, hence f=+20 cm.
In a surrounding medium use relative index nrel=nlens/nmedium. As nrel approaches 1, the lens bends light less and |f| increases; a lens can change sign if the surrounding medium has a larger index.
The formula assumes a thin lens and paraxial rays. Thick lenses require principal-plane treatment, and very wide ray bundles show aberrations.

The lens-maker formula builds the focal length from the glass index and the two radii. For a double-convex lens used with light travelling left to right, the first centre is to the right of its surface and the second centre is to the left, so the two contributions add.

specificConditions: **Thin Lens Approximation:** The lens maker's formula $\frac{1}{f} = (n-1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$ assumes a *thin* lens (thickness $\ll$ radii of curvature). For thick lenses, the full Gullstrand formula with principal planes must be used.

**Sign Convention for Radii:** Using the Cartesian sign convention (light travels left to right): $R$ is positive if the center of curvature is to the *right* of the surface (convex toward incident light), negative if to the *left* (concave). This is opposite to some older conventions.

**Material and Medium Dependence:** The formula uses relative refractive index $n = n_{lens}/n_{medium}$. For a lens in air, $n_{medium} \approx 1$. If immersed in water ($n \approx 1.33$), the focal length increases by factor $n_{lens}/n_{water}$ relative to air.
