data.title: Spherical Lenses and Angular Magnification
notes: A spherical lens has two refracting surfaces that are portions of spheres. A convex lens is usually converging in air; a concave lens is usually diverging. Immersion in a medium with a different refractive index can alter this behaviour.
Linear magnification m=hi/ho=v/u in the Cartesian lens convention compares image and object heights. Its magnitude gives size ratio; its sign indicates orientation.
Angular magnification M=β/α compares the angle subtended at the eye with the instrument to that without it. For a simple magnifier with near point D, M≈1+D/f; for relaxed viewing at infinity, M≈D/f.
Worked example: a magnifier with f=5.0 cm used at the conventional near point D=25 cm gives M≈1+25/5=6. A shorter focal length gives greater angular magnification.
The near point is a convention (often 25 cm for a normal eye). Real comfortable viewing distance varies; a magnifier also has a limited field of view and depth of focus.

Angular magnification compares the angle subtended by the image with the angle subtended by the object at the near point. For a relaxed eye the object sits at the focus of the magnifier and the magnification is about D/f. A shorter focal length is a stronger magnifier.

data.title: Spherical Lenses, Angular Magnification
notes: Spherical Lens: A lens is a transparent medium bounded by two spherical surfaces (or one plane and one spherical). Convex lens (converging) is thicker at center; concave lens (diverging) is thinner at center.

Lens Maker's Formula: $\frac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$ where $\mu$ is refractive index of lens material relative to medium, $R_1$ and $R_2$ are radii of curvature (Cartesian sign convention).
Lens Formula: $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$ using sign convention (u negative for object on left). Magnification $m = v/u = h_i/h_o$.
Power of Lens: $P = 1/f$ (f in metres). Unit: dioptre (D). Convex lens has positive power; concave has negative power. Lenses in contact: $P = P_1 + P_2$.
Combination of Lenses: Two lenses separated by distance d: equivalent focal length $\frac{1}{F} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2} - \frac{d}{f_1 f_2}$. Power: $P = P_1 + P_2 - d P_1 P_2$.

Angular Magnification: For a simple magnifier, angular magnification $M = \theta_i/\theta_o$. When image at near point: $M = 1 + D/f$; when image at infinity: $M = D/f$, where $D = 25\text{ cm}$ (least distance of distinct vision).
Compound Microscope: Total magnification $M = m_o \times m_e = (v_o/u_o)(1 + D/f_e)$ (final image at near point) or $(v_o/u_o)(D/f_e)$ (at infinity).
Astronomical Telescope: Angular magnification $M = f_o/f_e$ (normal adjustment, final at infinity) or $M = (f_o/f_e)(1 + f_e/D)$ (final at near point). Length $L = f_o + f_e$.

data.title: Power of a Lens
notes: Lens power measures convergence or divergence: P=1/f when f is in metres. Its SI-derived unit is the dioptre, 1 D=1 m⁻¹. A converging lens has positive power and a diverging lens negative power in air.
Worked example: f=+25 cm=+0.25 m gives P=+4 D. A diverging lens with f=−50 cm=−0.50 m has P=−2 D.
Thin lenses in contact have additive powers. A +4 D lens and −1.5 D lens make Peq=+2.5 D, so feq=1/2.5=0.40 m.
Power is not magnification: focal length determines power, while image size and orientation also depend on object distance through the lens equation.
For separated lenses the equivalent power includes separation; the simple algebraic sum applies only when thin lenses are in contact or separation is negligible.

The power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length in metres. Opticians add powers because two thin lenses in contact really do add. A +2.0 D lens and a −0.50 D lens in contact give +1.5 D, a weaker converging pair.

specificConditions: **Lens Power Definition:** Power $P = 1/f$ (in meters) measured in diopters (D). A converging lens has $P > 0$, a diverging lens has $P < 0$. Power is additive for thin lenses in contact: $P_{total} = \sum P_i$.

**Combination of Thin Lenses:** For thin lenses in contact, the total focal length is given by $1/f_{total} = \sum 1/f_i$, or equivalently $P_{total} = \sum P_i$. This assumes negligible separation between lenses. For separated lenses, use the equivalent focal length formula including the separation $d$.

**Power vs Magnification:** Lens power $P = 1/f$ relates to focal length, not directly to magnification. Magnification $m = v/u = f/(f-u)$ depends on object distance. A high-power lens (short $f$) gives larger magnification for a given object distance, but $m$ is not simply proportional to $P$.

notes: Worked Example: Density Calculation with Significant Figures
Mass of an object is measured to be 4.237 kg (four significant figures) and its volume is measured to be 2.51 mÂ³ (three significant figures), then its density is given by
$$\text{Density} = \frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Volume}} = \frac{4.237}{2.51} = 1.6880 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$$
Here 1.6880 kg mâ»Â³ has five significant figures but according to rule it should be expressed to only three significant figures i.e. 1.69 kg mâ»Â³.
One must remember that in general, the final result should not have more significant figures than the original data from which it was obtained.

Area of an object is measured to be (2.51 mÂ³) as five significant figures but the least precise measurement must also be expressed to the 0.1 decimal place so our final result should be expressed to the 0.1 decimal place, giving us 106.3 kg.
But the least precise measurement is 103.9. This measurement is expressed to the 0.1 decimal place. Thus, the answer is rounded to the tenths place, giving us 106.319 kg = 106.3 kg.

data.title: Nucleus: Discovery, Density and Composition
data.topicTitle: Nucleus: discovery of nucleus; nuclear density; mass number; atomic number
data.motionGraphics: Animated nucleon assembly showing mass defect release; spinning isotope models with particle highlights; mass spectrometer ion separation visualization
notes: **Atomic mass unit (u):** $1\\\\,\	ext{u} = 1.660539\	imes 10^{-27}\\\\,\	ext{kg}$. Defined as exactly $1/12$ the mass of a neutral carbon-12 atom in its ground state. All nuclear masses are expressed in u for convenience.

**Exact mass vs mass number:** The mass number $A$ is the integer count of nucleons. The exact mass in u differs slightly from $A$ due to mass defect. For example, $^{12}\	ext{C}$ has exact mass $12\\\\,\	ext{u}$ by definition, but $^{1}\	ext{H}$ has exact mass $1.007825\\\\,\	ext{u}$, not $1\\\\,\	ext{u}$.

**Isotopes:** atoms of the same element ($Z$ same) with different mass numbers ($A$ different). They have identical chemical properties (same electron configuration) but different nuclear masses, stabilities, and decay modes. Example: $^{35}\	ext{Cl}$ ($75.78\\\\%$) and $^{37}\	ext{Cl}$ ($24.22\\\\%$) are chlorine isotopes.

**Mass defect $\\\\Delta m$:** $\\\\Delta m = Zm_p + Nm_n - M_{\	ext{nucleus}}$, where $m_p \\\\approx 1.007276\\\\,\	ext{u}$ is the proton mass, $m_n \\\\approx 1.008665\\\\,\	ext{u}$ is the neutron mass, and $M_{\	ext{nucleus}}$ is the nuclear mass in u. The mass defect is always positive - the nucleus is lighter than its separated parts.

**Packing fraction:** $f = (M - A)/A$, where $M$ is the exact atomic mass in u and $A$ is the mass number. $f$ measures the fractional deviation from $A$. Negative $f$ (mass less than mass number) indicates strong binding; positive $f$ indicates weaker binding. $^{56}\	ext{Fe}$ has the most negative $f$, making it the most stable nuclide.

**Binding energy:** $BE = \\\\Delta m c^2$. The energy equivalent of the mass defect. In MeV, $BE\	ext{(MeV)} \\\\approx 931.494 \	imes \\\\Delta m\	ext{(u)}$. For $^{56}\	ext{Fe}$, $BE/A \\\\approx 8.8\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$, the peak of the binding-energy curve.

**Binding energy per nucleon:** $BE/A$. Rises from $\\\\sim 1\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$ for light hydrogen to $\\\\sim 8.8\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$ near iron ($A \\\\approx 56$), then slowly declines to $\\\\sim 7.6\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$ for uranium. This curve explains why light nuclei release energy via fusion and heavy nuclei via fission.

**Carbon-14 dating:** $^{14}\	ext{C}$ is a radioactive isotope with half-life $5730\\\\,\	ext{years}$. While alive, living organisms maintain $^{14}\	ext{C}/^{12}\	ext{C} \\\\approx 1.1\	imes 10^{-12}$. After death, $^{14}\	ext{C}$ decays via $\ eta^-$; measuring the remaining $^{14}\	ext{C}$ gives the time since death (archaeological dating up to $\\\\sim 50\\\\,\	ext{kyr}$).

**Isotopic abundance:** The natural abundance of each isotope (given as a percentage) determines the standard atomic weight listed in the periodic table. For chlorine, $\ ar{A} = 0.7578 \	imes 34.96885 + 0.2422 \	imes 36.96590 \\\\approx 35.45\\\\,\	ext{u}$, matching the tabulated value.

**Mass spectrometry:** A device that separates ions by their mass-to-charge ratio ($m/z$). Ions are accelerated through electric fields and deflected by magnetic fields; lighter ions deflect more. The resulting spectrum shows peaks at different $m/z$ values corresponding to different isotopes, with peak heights proportional to abundance.

**Stable vs. radioactive isotopes:** Only $\\\\sim 254$ isotopes are stable; over 3000 are known to be radioactive. Stable isotopes have balanced neutron-proton ratios; too many or too few neutrons leads to instability and radioactive decay.

**Nuclide notation:** A nuclide is written as $^{A}_{Z}\	ext{X}$, where $A$ is the mass number (protons + neutrons), $Z$ is the atomic number (protons), and $\	ext{X}$ is the element symbol. Example: $^{238}_{92}\	ext{U}$ has 92 protons and $238 - 92 = 146$ neutrons.

**Rutherford's gold foil experiment (1911):** α particles (⁴He²⁺) were fired at a thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, but some were scattered at large angles. Rutherford concluded atoms have a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at the center.

**Unexpected result:** Rutherford expected, based on J.J. Thomson's 'plum pudding' model, that α particles would experience only slight deflection. The large-angle scattering (some α particles bounced back nearly 180°) proved the positive charge (and most of the mass) was concentrated in a tiny, dense region — the nucleus.

**Size of nucleus:** The nucleus is roughly 10⁴ times smaller in radius than the atom. For a gold atom (radius ∼125 pm), the nucleus radius is ∼7 fm (femtometers = 10⁻¹⁵ m). The nucleus occupies a volume of about 10⁻¹² of the atom's volume.

**Nuclear density:** The density of nuclear matter is nearly constant for all nuclei. This can be derived from R = R₀A^(1/3), where A is the mass number. Since m_nucleus ≈ Am_u (atomic mass unit), density ρ = M_nucleus/V_nucleus = Am_u / (4/3 π R₀³A) = 3m_u/(4πR₀³). The A's cancel out!

**Nuclear density value:** Using R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm and m_u ≈ 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, the nuclear density ρ_nuc ≈ 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg/m³. This is about 2.3 × 10¹⁴ times denser than ordinary matter — a sugar-cube-sized amount of neutron star material would weigh about 100 million tons on Earth.

**Mass number (A):** A = Z + N, the total number of protons (Z) plus neutrons (N) in the nucleus. Written as a superscript before the element name: ⁵⁶Fe, ²³⁵U. It approximates the atomic mass in atomic mass units (though the actual mass is slightly less due to mass defect).

**Atomic number (Z):** The number of protons in the nucleus, which determines the chemical element. All atoms of hydrogen have Z = 1, all helium atoms have Z = 2, all carbon atoms have Z = 6. Z also equals the number of orbiting electrons in a neutral atom.

**Neutron number (N):** N = A − Z, the number of neutrons in the nucleus. Neutrons contribute to the strong nuclear force that holds the nucleus together but do not affect the chemical properties of the element. They also add mass without adding Coulomb repulsion.

**Isotopes:** Atoms of the same element (same Z) but different neutron numbers (different N, different A). Example: hydrogen has three isotopes — protium (¹H, N=0), deuterium (²H, N=1), and tritium (³H, N=2). They have the same chemistry but different nuclear properties.

**Nuclear radius formula:** R = R₀A^(1/3), where R₀ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m is a constant. This shows that nuclear radius scales as the cube root of mass number — a consequence of the constant density. The nuclear force is short-range (1-2 fm), so adding a nucleon adds it to the surface.

**Rutherford scattering formula:** The number of α particles scattered at angle θ is proportional to 1/sin⁴(θ/2). This sharp angular dependence confirmed the concentrated-charge, small-radius nature of the nucleus. The formula matched Rutherford's theoretical predictions precisely.

**Discovery of neutron (1932):** James Chadwick discovered the neutron by bombarding beryllium with α particles. The neutral, massive particles (neutrons) could knock out protons from paraffin wax. This confirmed the proton-neutron model of the nucleus.

**Nuclear composition:** Nuclei contain Z protons (positively charged) and N neutrons (neutral), held together by the strong nuclear force. The strong force is short-range (fewer than 2-3 fm) but extremely powerful — overcoming the electrostatic repulsion between protons.

**Density calculation example:** For a carbon-12 nucleus (A = 12): R = 1.2 × 12^(1/3) = 1.2 × 2.29 = 2.75 fm. Mass = 12 × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 1.99 × 10⁻²⁶ kg. Volume = 4/3 π(2.75 × 10⁻¹⁵)³ = 8.72 × 10⁻⁴⁴ m³. Density = 1.99×10⁻²⁶/8.72×10⁻⁴⁴ = 2.28 × 10¹⁷ kg/m³. Same as uranium — confirming constant density.
confusion: Misconception - Mass number $A$ is an integer count of nucleons; exact atomic mass in u is not exactly $A$. The difference is the mass defect, which is small but measurable. Mass spectrometry separates isotopes by their exact masses, not their mass numbers.

Misconception - Packing fraction $f = (M - A)/A$ can be negative because the bound nucleus weighs less than its constituent nucleons. Students expect $M > A$ by adding individual proton and neutron masses, but binding energy release makes $M < Zm_p + Nm_n$.

Misconception - Isotopes share the same $Z$ but have different $A$; isobars share the same $A$ but have different $Z$; isotones share the same $N$ but have different $A$. These three distinctions are common exam distractors.

Misconception - Standard atomic weight (the periodic table value) is the weighted-average of all naturally occurring isotopic masses, not the mass of any single atom. A single chlorine atom has mass $\\\sim 35\\\,	ext{u}$ or $\\\sim 37\\\,	ext{u}$, never $35.45\\\,	ext{u}$.

Misconception - Binding energy per nucleon $BE/A$ peaks at iron ($A \\\\sim 56$) at $\\\sim 8.8\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$, while uranium has $BE/A \\\\approx 7.6\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$. Fission energy release depends on the difference between parent and daughter nuclei, not a fixed value.

Misconception - $1\\\\,\	ext{u}$ of mass defect is equivalent to $931.5\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$ of energy. This conversion factor is essential for all nuclear binding-energy calculations; omitting it produces results that are off by a factor of $\\\sim 10^8$.

Misconception - In $ eta^-$ decay, a neutron converts to a proton, electron, and antineutrino: $n \ightarrow p + e^- + \ ar{\
u}_e$. The emitted electron originates from the nucleus, not from the orbital electron cloud.
Misconception - Half-life is the time required for a radioactive sample to decay to half its original amount. After $n$ half-lives, the fraction remaining is $(1/2)^n$, not $1/(2n)$.

The nucleus is NOT the same as the atom — the nucleus is the tiny dense central part (protons and neutrons), while the atom includes the orbiting electrons. A nucleus is about 10,000 times smaller in radius than the atom it belongs to.

Nuclear density is NOT the same as atomic density. Atomic density (mass/volume of the entire atom) is about 10³ kg/m³ (like water or solid materials). Nuclear density (mass/volume of just the nucleus) is about 10¹⁷ kg/m³ — unimaginably denser.

Mass number A approximates atomic mass in atomic mass units, but is NOT exactly equal. For example, ¹²C has A = 12 and atomic mass exactly 12 u (by definition), but most nuclei have actual mass slightly less than A due to binding energy (mass defect).

The nuclear radius formula R = R₀A^(1/3) shows that doubling the mass number (e.g., from helium A=4 to beryllium A=8) does NOT double the radius — it increases it by 2^(1/3) ≈ 1.26. This cubic-root scaling confirms the constant density hypothesis.

Atomic number Z determines the element, but ISOTOPES of the same element have the same Z but different A. You cannot tell isotopes apart chemically, but they differ greatly in their nuclear stability (e.g., ¹H is stable; ³H is radioactive with a 12-year half-life).
practice: Problem: Chlorine has two isotopes: $^{35}\	ext{Cl}$ (75.78%, exact mass $34.96885\\\\,\	ext{u}$) and $^{37}\	ext{Cl}$ (24.22%, exact mass $36.96590\\\\,\	ext{u}$). Calculate the standard atomic weight of chlorine in u. [Solution: $ ar{A} = 0.7578 \	imes 34.96885 + 0.2422 \	imes 36.96590 = 26.495 + 8.953 = 35.448 \\\\approx 35.45\\\\,\	ext{u}$, matching the periodic table value.]

Problem: The mass of a $^{4}\	ext{He}$ nucleus is $4.002603\\\\,\	ext{u}$. Given $m_p = 1.007276\\\\,\	ext{u}$ and $m_n = 1.008665\\\\,\	ext{u}$, find the mass defect and binding energy in MeV. [Solution: $\\\Delta m = 2(1.007276) + 2(1.008665) - 4.002603 = 4.031882 - 4.002603 = 0.029279\\\\,\	ext{u}$; $BE = 0.029279 \	imes 931.494 \\\\approx 27.27\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$; $BE/A = 27.27/4 \\\\approx 6.82\\\\,\	ext{MeV/nucleon}$.]

Problem: A $^{238}\	ext{U}$ sample contains $2.5\\\\,\	ext{mg}$ of uranium. How many $^{238}\	ext{U}$ atoms are present? (Molar mass $\\\approx 238\\\\,\	ext{g/mol}$.) [Solution: $n = 2.5\	imes 10^{-3}\\\\,\	ext{g} / 238\\\\,\	ext{g/mol} = 1.050 \	imes 10^{-5}\\\\,\	ext{mol}$; $N = 1.050\	imes 10^{-5} \	imes 6.022\	imes 10^{23} \\\\approx 6.32\	imes 10^{18}$ atoms.]

Problem: A $^{14}\	ext{C}$ sample decays to $12.5\\\\%$ of its original activity in $17{,}190\\\\,\	ext{years}$. Calculate the half-life of $^{14}\	ext{C}$ and verify it against the known value of $5730\\\\,\	ext{years}$. [Solution: $12.5\\\\% = (1/2)^3$, so 3 half-lives have elapsed. $T_{1/2} = 17{,}190 / 3 = 5730\\\\,\	ext{years}$, which exactly matches the known value.]

Problem: For the reaction $^{14}\	ext{N} + n \ightarrow ^{14}\	ext{C} + p$, use masses $m(^{14}\	ext{N}) = 14.003074\\\\,\	ext{u}$, $m(^{14}\	ext{C}) = 14.003242\\\\,\	ext{u}$, $m_n = 1.008665\\\\,\	ext{u}$, $m_p = 1.007276\\\\,\	ext{u}$ to determine if the reaction is exothermic or endothermic, and calculate the Q-value. [Solution: Initial mass $= 14.003074 + 1.008665 = 15.011739\\\\,\	ext{u}$; final mass $= 14.003242 + 1.007276 = 15.010518\\\\,\	ext{u}$; $\\\Delta m = 15.011739 - 15.010518 = 0.001221\\\\,\	ext{u} > 0$, so energy is released. $Q = 0.001221 \	imes 931.494 \\\\approx 1.14\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$; exothermic.]

Calculate the radius, diameter, and density of a carbon-12 nucleus (A = 12). Use R₀ = 1.2 fm. Solution: R = 1.2 × 12^(1/3) = 1.2 × 2.289 = 2.747 fm. Diameter = 2R = 5.494 fm. Mass = 12 × 1.66×10⁻²⁷ = 1.993×10⁻²⁶ kg. Volume = 4/3 πR³ = 4/3 π(2.747×10⁻¹⁵)³ = 8.67×10⁻⁴⁴ m³. Density = 1.993×10⁻²⁶/8.67×10⁻⁴⁴ = 2.30×10¹⁷ kg/m³.

A uranium-238 nucleus (A = 238, radius ≈ 7.4 fm) has density equal to a carbon-12 nucleus (A = 12, radius ≈ 2.7 fm). Prove this mathematically using R = R₀A^(1/3). Solution: ρ_C = M_C/V_C = (12m_u)/(4/3 π( R₀12^(1/3))³) = 12m_u/(4/3 π R₀³ × 12) = m_u/(4/3 π R₀³). ρ_U = 238m_u/(4/3 π( R₀238^(1/3))³) = 238m_u/(4/3 π R₀³ × 238) = m_u/(4/3 π R₀³). They are EQUAL — confirming constant density.

The radius of a gold nucleus (A = 197) is measured at 7.4 fm. What is the value of R₀? Solution: R = R₀A^(1/3) → R₀ = R/A^(1/3) = 7.4/197^(1/3). 197^(1/3) = 5.82. R₀ = 7.4/5.82 = 1.27 fm. This is close to the standard value of 1.2 fm, with differences due to experimental measurement uncertainties.

A copper sample contains two stable isotopes: ⁶³Cu (69.3% abundant, A=63) and ⁶⁵Cu (30.7% abundant, A=65). Find the average atomic mass in u and the average nuclear radius. Solution: Average mass = 0.693×63 + 0.307×65 = 43.66 + 20.0 = 63.7 u. Average radius = 1.2 × 63.7^(1/3) = 1.2 × 3.99 = 4.79 fm. (Note: isotopes have same Z=29 but slightly different nuclear radii due to different neutron count.)

If a nucleus has 50 protons and 75 neutrons, what is its isotope, and what is its radius? Use R₀ = 1.2 fm. Solution: Z = 50 → element is tin (Sn). A = 50 + 75 = 125 → isotope is ¹²⁵Sn. Radius R = 1.2 × 125^(1/3) = 1.2 × 5.0 = 6.0 fm. Density = 125m_u/(4/3 π R³) ≈ 2.3×10¹⁷ kg/m³ (same for all nuclei).
universalFacts: Fact (Historical): Frederick Soddy proposed the concept of isotopes in 1913, discovering that different radioactive elements could occupy the same position in the periodic table. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1921 for this work.

Fact (Application): Mass spectrometry is used in forensic science to analyze trace evidence, in environmental science to track pollution sources, in pharmacology to verify drug composition, and in astronomy to determine stellar composition.

Fact (Exam tip): Remember the conversion $1\\\\,\	ext{u} = 931.5\\\\,\	ext{MeV}/c^2$. For mass defect problems, always compute $\\\Delta m$ first in u, then multiply by $931.5$ to get binding energy in MeV. This avoids errors from using SI units.

Fact (Connection): The periodic table atomic weight of an element varies slightly depending on geographic source. For example, boron from different mines has different isotopic compositions, giving atomic weights between 10.81 and 10.82.

Fact (Everyday): Carbon-14 dating is used to verify the age of ancient manuscripts, authenticate artwork, date archaeological artifacts, and even verify the vintage of wine and spirits by measuring $^{14}\	ext{C}$ levels.

Fact (Conservation): In all nuclear reactions, both mass number $A$ (total nucleons) and atomic number $Z$ (total charge) are conserved. These two conservation laws are the first checks students should perform when balancing nuclear equations.

Fact (Scale): Converting $1\\\\,\	ext{g}$ of matter entirely to energy releases $E = mc^2 = 1\	imes 10^{-3} \	imes (3\	imes 10^8)^2 = 9\	imes 10^{13}\\\\,\	ext{J}$, equivalent to about $21\\\\,\	ext{kilotons}$ of TNT-the yield of the Hiroshima bomb.

Fact (Nuclear stability): The most stable nuclide is $^{56}\	ext{Fe}$ with a binding energy per nucleon of $8.79\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$. Nuclides lighter than iron release energy through fusion; those heavier than iron release energy through fission.

The density of nuclear matter (∼2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg/m³) is so extreme that a single teaspoon of it would weigh about 6 billion tons on Earth. This is the density of neutron stars — objects with the mass of the Sun compressed into a city-sized sphere.

Rutherford's gold foil experiment took place in Geiger and Marsden's lab at the University of Manchester in 1909. Only about 1 in 8000 α particles was scattered at angles greater than 90° — but that one in 8000 was the key evidence.

The nuclear radius scales as A^(1/3) — this is a key piece of evidence that the strong nuclear force has a short range (about 1-2 femtometers). If the force were longer range, nuclei would be smaller and denser.

Atomic number Z determines all chemical properties (because chemistry is governed by electron configuration), while the number of neutrons N affects only nuclear stability and decay modes (isotopes differ in this).

All atoms of an element have identically sized nuclei only if they are the same isotope. Isotopes of the same element have slightly different nuclear radii because the additional neutrons increase A and thus R = R₀A^(1/3).
specificConditions: **Rutherford Scattering Experiment:** Alpha particles were fired at a thin gold foil. Most passed through with little deflection, but a few scattered at large angles (>90°). This disproved the Thomson plum-pudding model and established the nuclear model: a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus containing most of the atom's mass.

**Nuclear Size vs Atom Size:** The nucleus is ~10⁻¹⁵ m (1-10 fm) while the atom is ~10⁻¹⁰ m (1 Å). The nucleus occupies ~10⁻¹⁵ of the atomic volume but contains >99.9% of the mass. The rest is empty space where electrons orbit.

**Nuclear Density:** Nearly constant for all nuclei: ρ = mass/volume ≈ A·1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg / (4/3 π (1.2×10⁻¹⁵ A¹ᐟ³)³) ≈ 2.3×10¹⁷ kg/m³. This constancy supports the liquid-drop model and the idea that nucleons are closely packed.

notes: Atomic Models Timeline: Dalton's solid sphere (1808) → Thomson's plum pudding (1897) → Rutherford's nuclear model (1911) → Bohr's quantum model (1913). Each model addressed limitations of the previous.
Thomson's Plum Pudding Model: Atom as positively charged pudding with electrons embedded like plums. Could not explain alpha scattering results.

Rutherford's Alpha Scattering Experiment: Alpha particles from radioactive source directed at thin gold foil (~0.00004 cm). Most passed straight, some deflected at small angles, very few (~1 in 8000) bounced back at angles >90°.

Rutherford's Nuclear Model: Atom has tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus (~10⁻¹⁴ m) containing nearly all mass. Electrons revolve around nucleus at large distance (~10⁻¹⁰ m). Most of atom is empty space.
Nuclear Size: Nuclear radius R ≈ R₀A^(1/3) where R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm (10⁻¹⁵ m) and A is mass number. Nucleus is ~10⁴ times smaller than atom.
Nuclear Composition: Nucleus contains protons (Z = atomic number) and neutrons (N = neutron number). Mass number A = Z + N. Nucleus charge = +Ze.
Limitations of Rutherford Model: Could not explain atomic stability (accelerating electrons should radiate energy and spiral into nucleus) or line spectra.

universalFacts: Rutherford's gold foil experiment (1911) is considered one of the most important experiments in physics history.
The term 'nucleus' was coined by Rutherford in 1912.

Thinking nucleus contains electrons: Nucleus contains only protons and neutrons (neutrons discovered later by Chadwick, 1932).
Believing all alpha particles bounce back: Only ~1/8000 scatter >90°; most pass through.
Confusing nuclear size with atomic size: Nucleus ~10⁻¹⁴ m, atom ~10⁻¹⁰ m — factor of 10⁴ difference.
Thinking Rutherford model explains spectra: It cannot explain line spectra or atomic stability.

data.summary: Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment revealed a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus (~10⁻¹⁴ m) containing nearly all atomic mass. Most of the atom is empty space. Nuclear radius R = R₀A^(1/3). Rutherford's model could not explain stability or spectra — leading to Bohr's quantum model.

data.title: Atomic Mass, Isotopes and Mass Defect
data.motionGraphics: Animated nucleon assembly showing mass defect release; spinning isotope models with particle highlights; mass spectrometer ion separation visualization
notes: **Atomic mass unit (u):** $1\\\\,\	ext{u} = 1.660539\	imes 10^{-27}\\\\,\	ext{kg}$. Defined as exactly $1/12$ the mass of a neutral carbon-12 atom in its ground state. All nuclear masses are expressed in u for convenience.

**Exact mass vs mass number:** The mass number $A$ is the integer count of nucleons. The exact mass in u differs slightly from $A$ due to mass defect. For example, $^{12}\	ext{C}$ has exact mass $12\\\\,\	ext{u}$ by definition, but $^{1}\	ext{H}$ has exact mass $1.007825\\\\,\	ext{u}$, not $1\\\\,\	ext{u}$.

**Isotopes:** atoms of the same element ($Z$ same) with different mass numbers ($A$ different). They have identical chemical properties (same electron configuration) but different nuclear masses, stabilities, and decay modes. Example: $^{35}\	ext{Cl}$ ($75.78\\\\%$) and $^{37}\	ext{Cl}$ ($24.22\\\\%$) are chlorine isotopes.

**Mass defect $\\\\Delta m$:** $\\\\Delta m = Zm_p + Nm_n - M_{\	ext{nucleus}}$, where $m_p \\\\approx 1.007276\\\\,\	ext{u}$ is the proton mass, $m_n \\\\approx 1.008665\\\\,\	ext{u}$ is the neutron mass, and $M_{\	ext{nucleus}}$ is the nuclear mass in u. The mass defect is always positive - the nucleus is lighter than its separated parts.

**Packing fraction:** $f = (M - A)/A$, where $M$ is the exact atomic mass in u and $A$ is the mass number. $f$ measures the fractional deviation from $A$. Negative $f$ (mass less than mass number) indicates strong binding; positive $f$ indicates weaker binding. $^{56}\	ext{Fe}$ has the most negative $f$, making it the most stable nuclide.

**Binding energy:** $BE = \\\\Delta m c^2$. The energy equivalent of the mass defect. In MeV, $BE\	ext{(MeV)} \\\\approx 931.494 \	imes \\\\Delta m\	ext{(u)}$. For $^{56}\	ext{Fe}$, $BE/A \\\\approx 8.8\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$, the peak of the binding-energy curve.

**Binding energy per nucleon:** $BE/A$. Rises from $\\\\sim 1\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$ for light hydrogen to $\\\\sim 8.8\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$ near iron ($A \\\\approx 56$), then slowly declines to $\\\\sim 7.6\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$ for uranium. This curve explains why light nuclei release energy via fusion and heavy nuclei via fission.

**Carbon-14 dating:** $^{14}\	ext{C}$ is a radioactive isotope with half-life $5730\\\\,\	ext{years}$. While alive, living organisms maintain $^{14}\	ext{C}/^{12}\	ext{C} \\\\approx 1.1\	imes 10^{-12}$. After death, $^{14}\	ext{C}$ decays via $\ eta^-$; measuring the remaining $^{14}\	ext{C}$ gives the time since death (archaeological dating up to $\\\\sim 50\\\\,\	ext{kyr}$).

**Isotopic abundance:** The natural abundance of each isotope (given as a percentage) determines the standard atomic weight listed in the periodic table. For chlorine, $\ ar{A} = 0.7578 \	imes 34.96885 + 0.2422 \	imes 36.96590 \\\\approx 35.45\\\\,\	ext{u}$, matching the tabulated value.

**Mass spectrometry:** A device that separates ions by their mass-to-charge ratio ($m/z$). Ions are accelerated through electric fields and deflected by magnetic fields; lighter ions deflect more. The resulting spectrum shows peaks at different $m/z$ values corresponding to different isotopes, with peak heights proportional to abundance.

**Stable vs. radioactive isotopes:** Only $\\\\sim 254$ isotopes are stable; over 3000 are known to be radioactive. Stable isotopes have balanced neutron-proton ratios; too many or too few neutrons leads to instability and radioactive decay.

**Nuclide notation:** A nuclide is written as $^{A}_{Z}\	ext{X}$, where $A$ is the mass number (protons + neutrons), $Z$ is the atomic number (protons), and $\	ext{X}$ is the element symbol. Example: $^{238}_{92}\	ext{U}$ has 92 protons and $238 - 92 = 146$ neutrons.
confusion: Misconception - Mass number $A$ is an integer count of nucleons; exact atomic mass in u is not exactly $A$. The difference is the mass defect, which is small but measurable. Mass spectrometry separates isotopes by their exact masses, not their mass numbers.

Misconception - Packing fraction $f = (M - A)/A$ can be negative because the bound nucleus weighs less than its constituent nucleons. Students expect $M > A$ by adding individual proton and neutron masses, but binding energy release makes $M < Zm_p + Nm_n$.

Misconception - Isotopes share the same $Z$ but have different $A$; isobars share the same $A$ but have different $Z$; isotones share the same $N$ but have different $A$. These three distinctions are common exam distractors.

Misconception - Standard atomic weight (the periodic table value) is the weighted-average of all naturally occurring isotopic masses, not the mass of any single atom. A single chlorine atom has mass $\\\sim 35\\\,	ext{u}$ or $\\\sim 37\\\,	ext{u}$, never $35.45\\\,	ext{u}$.

Misconception - Binding energy per nucleon $BE/A$ peaks at iron ($A \\\\sim 56$) at $\\\sim 8.8\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$, while uranium has $BE/A \\\\approx 7.6\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$. Fission energy release depends on the difference between parent and daughter nuclei, not a fixed value.

Misconception - $1\\\\,\	ext{u}$ of mass defect is equivalent to $931.5\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$ of energy. This conversion factor is essential for all nuclear binding-energy calculations; omitting it produces results that are off by a factor of $\\\sim 10^8$.

Misconception - In $ eta^-$ decay, a neutron converts to a proton, electron, and antineutrino: $n \ightarrow p + e^- + \ ar{\
u}_e$. The emitted electron originates from the nucleus, not from the orbital electron cloud.
Misconception - Half-life is the time required for a radioactive sample to decay to half its original amount. After $n$ half-lives, the fraction remaining is $(1/2)^n$, not $1/(2n)$.
practice: Problem: Chlorine has two isotopes: $^{35}\	ext{Cl}$ (75.78%, exact mass $34.96885\\\\,\	ext{u}$) and $^{37}\	ext{Cl}$ (24.22%, exact mass $36.96590\\\\,\	ext{u}$). Calculate the standard atomic weight of chlorine in u. [Solution: $ ar{A} = 0.7578 \	imes 34.96885 + 0.2422 \	imes 36.96590 = 26.495 + 8.953 = 35.448 \\\\approx 35.45\\\\,\	ext{u}$, matching the periodic table value.]

Problem: The mass of a $^{4}\	ext{He}$ nucleus is $4.002603\\\\,\	ext{u}$. Given $m_p = 1.007276\\\\,\	ext{u}$ and $m_n = 1.008665\\\\,\	ext{u}$, find the mass defect and binding energy in MeV. [Solution: $\\\Delta m = 2(1.007276) + 2(1.008665) - 4.002603 = 4.031882 - 4.002603 = 0.029279\\\\,\	ext{u}$; $BE = 0.029279 \	imes 931.494 \\\\approx 27.27\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$; $BE/A = 27.27/4 \\\\approx 6.82\\\\,\	ext{MeV/nucleon}$.]

Problem: A $^{238}\	ext{U}$ sample contains $2.5\\\\,\	ext{mg}$ of uranium. How many $^{238}\	ext{U}$ atoms are present? (Molar mass $\\\approx 238\\\\,\	ext{g/mol}$.) [Solution: $n = 2.5\	imes 10^{-3}\\\\,\	ext{g} / 238\\\\,\	ext{g/mol} = 1.050 \	imes 10^{-5}\\\\,\	ext{mol}$; $N = 1.050\	imes 10^{-5} \	imes 6.022\	imes 10^{23} \\\\approx 6.32\	imes 10^{18}$ atoms.]

Problem: A $^{14}\	ext{C}$ sample decays to $12.5\\\\%$ of its original activity in $17{,}190\\\\,\	ext{years}$. Calculate the half-life of $^{14}\	ext{C}$ and verify it against the known value of $5730\\\\,\	ext{years}$. [Solution: $12.5\\\\% = (1/2)^3$, so 3 half-lives have elapsed. $T_{1/2} = 17{,}190 / 3 = 5730\\\\,\	ext{years}$, which exactly matches the known value.]

Problem: For the reaction $^{14}\	ext{N} + n \ightarrow ^{14}\	ext{C} + p$, use masses $m(^{14}\	ext{N}) = 14.003074\\\\,\	ext{u}$, $m(^{14}\	ext{C}) = 14.003242\\\\,\	ext{u}$, $m_n = 1.008665\\\\,\	ext{u}$, $m_p = 1.007276\\\\,\	ext{u}$ to determine if the reaction is exothermic or endothermic, and calculate the Q-value. [Solution: Initial mass $= 14.003074 + 1.008665 = 15.011739\\\\,\	ext{u}$; final mass $= 14.003242 + 1.007276 = 15.010518\\\\,\	ext{u}$; $\\\Delta m = 15.011739 - 15.010518 = 0.001221\\\\,\	ext{u} > 0$, so energy is released. $Q = 0.001221 \	imes 931.494 \\\\approx 1.14\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$; exothermic.]

universalFacts: Fact (Historical): Frederick Soddy proposed the concept of isotopes in 1913, discovering that different radioactive elements could occupy the same position in the periodic table. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1921 for this work.

Fact (Application): Mass spectrometry is used in forensic science to analyze trace evidence, in environmental science to track pollution sources, in pharmacology to verify drug composition, and in astronomy to determine stellar composition.

Fact (Exam tip): Remember the conversion $1\\\\,\	ext{u} = 931.5\\\\,\	ext{MeV}/c^2$. For mass defect problems, always compute $\\\Delta m$ first in u, then multiply by $931.5$ to get binding energy in MeV. This avoids errors from using SI units.

Fact (Connection): The periodic table atomic weight of an element varies slightly depending on geographic source. For example, boron from different mines has different isotopic compositions, giving atomic weights between 10.81 and 10.82.

Fact (Everyday): Carbon-14 dating is used to verify the age of ancient manuscripts, authenticate artwork, date archaeological artifacts, and even verify the vintage of wine and spirits by measuring $^{14}\	ext{C}$ levels.

Fact (Conservation): In all nuclear reactions, both mass number $A$ (total nucleons) and atomic number $Z$ (total charge) are conserved. These two conservation laws are the first checks students should perform when balancing nuclear equations.

Fact (Scale): Converting $1\\\\,\	ext{g}$ of matter entirely to energy releases $E = mc^2 = 1\	imes 10^{-3} \	imes (3\	imes 10^8)^2 = 9\	imes 10^{13}\\\\,\	ext{J}$, equivalent to about $21\\\\,\	ext{kilotons}$ of TNT-the yield of the Hiroshima bomb.

Fact (Nuclear stability): The most stable nuclide is $^{56}\	ext{Fe}$ with a binding energy per nucleon of $8.79\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$. Nuclides lighter than iron release energy through fusion; those heavier than iron release energy through fission.

**Binding Energy Conversion:** $BE = \Delta m \cdot c^2 = \Delta m \times 931.494$ MeV. The binding energy is the energy needed to separate the nucleus into free nucleons. It is positive for bound nuclei.

**Isotope Chemistry vs Nuclear Properties:** Isotopes (same Z, different A) have identical chemical properties (electron configuration) but different nuclear masses, stabilities, and half-lives. Chemical separation is impossible; nuclear methods (centrifugation, diffusion, laser) are required.

data.topicTitle: Nuclear density; mass number; atomic number
notes: Mass Number (A): Total number of nucleons (protons + neutrons) in nucleus. A = Z + N. Dimensionless integer. Nuclei with same A but different Z are isobars.
Atomic Number (Z): Number of protons in nucleus = number of electrons in neutral atom. Determines element identity and chemical properties. Nuclei with same Z but different N are isotopes.
Neutron Number (N): Number of neutrons = A - Z. Nuclei with same N but different Z are isotones.

Nuclear Density: Density ρ = mass/volume. Nuclear mass ≈ A × m_p (m_p ≈ 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg). Volume = (4/3)πR³ = (4/3)π(R₀A^(1/3))³ = (4/3)πR₀³A. Density ρ = A·m_p / ((4/3)πR₀³A) = 3m_p/(4πR₀³) — INDEPENDENT of A!
Nuclear Density Value: ρ ≈ 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg/m³ — about 10¹⁴ times denser than ordinary matter. Comparable to neutron star density.
Nuclear Size: Radius R = R₀A^(1/3), R₀ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. Volume ∝ A — nucleus grows linearly with nucleon count, explaining constant density.
Isobars, Isotopes, Isotones: Isobars: same A, different Z. Isotopes: same Z, different A (same element). Isotones: same N, different Z.
Nuclear Mass vs Atomic Mass: Nuclear mass = atomic mass - mass of Z electrons + binding energy of electrons/c² (electron binding negligible, ~eV scale vs MeV nuclear).

data.topicTitle: Einstein's mass-energy relation; mass defect, packing fraction, binding energy per nucleon
data.motionGraphics: Animated nucleon assembly showing mass defect release; spinning isotope models with particle highlights; mass spectrometer ion separation visualization
notes: **Atomic mass unit (u):** $1\\\\,\	ext{u} = 1.660539\	imes 10^{-27}\\\\,\	ext{kg}$. Defined as exactly $1/12$ the mass of a neutral carbon-12 atom in its ground state. All nuclear masses are expressed in u for convenience.

**Exact mass vs mass number:** The mass number $A$ is the integer count of nucleons. The exact mass in u differs slightly from $A$ due to mass defect. For example, $^{12}\	ext{C}$ has exact mass $12\\\\,\	ext{u}$ by definition, but $^{1}\	ext{H}$ has exact mass $1.007825\\\\,\	ext{u}$, not $1\\\\,\	ext{u}$.

**Isotopes:** atoms of the same element ($Z$ same) with different mass numbers ($A$ different). They have identical chemical properties (same electron configuration) but different nuclear masses, stabilities, and decay modes. Example: $^{35}\	ext{Cl}$ ($75.78\\\\%$) and $^{37}\	ext{Cl}$ ($24.22\\\\%$) are chlorine isotopes.

**Mass defect $\\\\Delta m$:** $\\\\Delta m = Zm_p + Nm_n - M_{\	ext{nucleus}}$, where $m_p \\\\approx 1.007276\\\\,\	ext{u}$ is the proton mass, $m_n \\\\approx 1.008665\\\\,\	ext{u}$ is the neutron mass, and $M_{\	ext{nucleus}}$ is the nuclear mass in u. The mass defect is always positive - the nucleus is lighter than its separated parts.

**Packing fraction:** $f = (M - A)/A$, where $M$ is the exact atomic mass in u and $A$ is the mass number. $f$ measures the fractional deviation from $A$. Negative $f$ (mass less than mass number) indicates strong binding; positive $f$ indicates weaker binding. $^{56}\	ext{Fe}$ has the most negative $f$, making it the most stable nuclide.

**Binding energy:** $BE = \\\\Delta m c^2$. The energy equivalent of the mass defect. In MeV, $BE\	ext{(MeV)} \\\\approx 931.494 \	imes \\\\Delta m\	ext{(u)}$. For $^{56}\	ext{Fe}$, $BE/A \\\\approx 8.8\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$, the peak of the binding-energy curve.

**Binding energy per nucleon:** $BE/A$. Rises from $\\\\sim 1\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$ for light hydrogen to $\\\\sim 8.8\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$ near iron ($A \\\\approx 56$), then slowly declines to $\\\\sim 7.6\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$ for uranium. This curve explains why light nuclei release energy via fusion and heavy nuclei via fission.

**Carbon-14 dating:** $^{14}\	ext{C}$ is a radioactive isotope with half-life $5730\\\\,\	ext{years}$. While alive, living organisms maintain $^{14}\	ext{C}/^{12}\	ext{C} \\\\approx 1.1\	imes 10^{-12}$. After death, $^{14}\	ext{C}$ decays via $\ eta^-$; measuring the remaining $^{14}\	ext{C}$ gives the time since death (archaeological dating up to $\\\\sim 50\\\\,\	ext{kyr}$).

**Isotopic abundance:** The natural abundance of each isotope (given as a percentage) determines the standard atomic weight listed in the periodic table. For chlorine, $\ ar{A} = 0.7578 \	imes 34.96885 + 0.2422 \	imes 36.96590 \\\\approx 35.45\\\\,\	ext{u}$, matching the tabulated value.

**Mass spectrometry:** A device that separates ions by their mass-to-charge ratio ($m/z$). Ions are accelerated through electric fields and deflected by magnetic fields; lighter ions deflect more. The resulting spectrum shows peaks at different $m/z$ values corresponding to different isotopes, with peak heights proportional to abundance.

**Stable vs. radioactive isotopes:** Only $\\\\sim 254$ isotopes are stable; over 3000 are known to be radioactive. Stable isotopes have balanced neutron-proton ratios; too many or too few neutrons leads to instability and radioactive decay.

**Nuclide notation:** A nuclide is written as $^{A}_{Z}\	ext{X}$, where $A$ is the mass number (protons + neutrons), $Z$ is the atomic number (protons), and $\	ext{X}$ is the element symbol. Example: $^{238}_{92}\	ext{U}$ has 92 protons and $238 - 92 = 146$ neutrons.

**Einstein's mass-energy relation (1905):** E = mc². Mass and energy are equivalent — a change in mass corresponds to a change in energy by ΔE = Δmc². The speed of light c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s, so c² ≈ 9 × 10¹⁶ m²/s².
**Rest energy:** The energy associated with an object's mass at rest is E_0 = m_0c². This is the minimum energy the mass can have. Even stationary mass has this enormous energy content.

**Mass defect:** When nucleons (protons and neutrons) form a nucleus, the measured nuclear mass M_A is slightly less than the sum of the individual nucleon masses: (Zm_p + Nm_n). The difference Δm = (Zm_p + Nm_n) − M_A is called the mass defect. It is always positive.

**Origin of mass defect:** The missing mass Δm converts to binding energy via E = Δmc². The nucleus is formed in an exothermic process, releasing energy. This energy holds the nucleus together — it is the binding energy.

**Binding energy (BE):** BE = Δm × c². It is the energy required to completely disassemble a nucleus into its individual protons and neutrons at rest. Also equals the energy released when the nucleus forms from its constituent nucleons.

**Binding energy per nucleon (BE/A):** BE divided by mass number A. This normalizes for nucleus size. The BE/A curve peaks at iron-56 (≈ 8.8 MeV per nucleon). For nuclei lighter than iron, fusion increases BE/A (releases energy). For nuclei heavier than iron, fission increases BE/A (releases energy).

**Packing fraction:** f = (M - A)/A, where M is the actual atomic mass (in u) and A is the mass number. Introduced by Aston. Negative packing fraction means the nucleus is more stable than the average for that mass number. Positive means less stable. This led to the discovery of isotopes and mass defects.

**Mass-energy equivalence in chemical reactions:** Chemical bonds have binding energies too, but they are much smaller (a few eV per bond) compared to nuclear binding (∼10⁶ eV). The mass defect in chemical bonds is negligible but measurable with precision instruments.

**Energy units in nuclear physics:** 1 eV (electron volt) = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. The binding energy of nucleons is typically 1-8 MeV per nucleon, while chemical bond energies are 1-10 eV per atom — nuclear energies are ∼10⁶ times larger.

**Q-value of nuclear reactions:** Q = (mass of reactants - mass of products) × c². If Q > 0, the reaction is exothermic (releases energy). If Q < 0, it is endothermic (absorbs energy). Q equals the kinetic energy released or absorbed.

**Stability and binding:** The most stable nuclides have the highest binding energy per nucleon. Iron-56, nickel-62, and iron-58 are the most tightly bound. Very light and very heavy nuclei are less stable.

**Einstein's famous equation derivation:** From the special theory of relativity, the relativistic energy-momentum relation E² = (mc²)² + (pc)² simplifies to E = mc² when p = 0 (particle at rest). This holds for ALL particles, not just nuclear ones.
confusion: Misconception - Mass number $A$ is an integer count of nucleons; exact atomic mass in u is not exactly $A$. The difference is the mass defect, which is small but measurable. Mass spectrometry separates isotopes by their exact masses, not their mass numbers.

Misconception - Packing fraction $f = (M - A)/A$ can be negative because the bound nucleus weighs less than its constituent nucleons. Students expect $M > A$ by adding individual proton and neutron masses, but binding energy release makes $M < Zm_p + Nm_n$.

Misconception - Isotopes share the same $Z$ but have different $A$; isobars share the same $A$ but have different $Z$; isotones share the same $N$ but have different $A$. These three distinctions are common exam distractors.

Misconception - Standard atomic weight (the periodic table value) is the weighted-average of all naturally occurring isotopic masses, not the mass of any single atom. A single chlorine atom has mass $\\\sim 35\\\,	ext{u}$ or $\\\sim 37\\\,	ext{u}$, never $35.45\\\,	ext{u}$.

Misconception - Binding energy per nucleon $BE/A$ peaks at iron ($A \\\\sim 56$) at $\\\sim 8.8\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$, while uranium has $BE/A \\\\approx 7.6\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$. Fission energy release depends on the difference between parent and daughter nuclei, not a fixed value.

Misconception - $1\\\\,\	ext{u}$ of mass defect is equivalent to $931.5\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$ of energy. This conversion factor is essential for all nuclear binding-energy calculations; omitting it produces results that are off by a factor of $\\\sim 10^8$.

Misconception - In $ eta^-$ decay, a neutron converts to a proton, electron, and antineutrino: $n \ightarrow p + e^- + \ ar{\
u}_e$. The emitted electron originates from the nucleus, not from the orbital electron cloud.
Misconception - Half-life is the time required for a radioactive sample to decay to half its original amount. After $n$ half-lives, the fraction remaining is $(1/2)^n$, not $1/(2n)$.

E = mc² means mass and energy are CONSERVATED TOGETHER, not that mass can be freely converted to energy in any process. The mass-energy of the entire system is conserved. In nuclear reactions, the total mass-energy of all particles before equals after.
The mass defect is NOT the binding energy — it is the mass DEFICIT that, when multiplied by c², gives the binding energy. Δm = BE/c², not BE = Δm. BE = Δm × c².

Mass defect arises because binding energy is negative potential energy. When nucleons come together, potential energy decreases (becomes more negative), so mass decreases (since energy decreased). The system is more stable at lower mass-energy.

Binding energy per nucleon is NOT the same as binding energy. BE/A peaks at iron. Even though a heavy nucleus has a large total BE (it is very bound), BE/A can be low. This is why heavy nuclei can undergo fission to release energy.

The formula E = Δmc² does NOT mean you can convert any arbitrary mass m into energy. Only the mass associated with the binding energy (the 'defect') can be released in nuclear reactions. The rest mass of a stable nucleus cannot be converted to energy without destroying the nucleus.

Chemical energy does NOT involve mass-energy equivalence — chemical reactions involve rearrangement of electrons, and the mass changes are too tiny to measure. Nuclear physics deals with changes in the nucleus itself.
practice: Problem: Chlorine has two isotopes: $^{35}\	ext{Cl}$ (75.78%, exact mass $34.96885\\\\,\	ext{u}$) and $^{37}\	ext{Cl}$ (24.22%, exact mass $36.96590\\\\,\	ext{u}$). Calculate the standard atomic weight of chlorine in u. [Solution: $ ar{A} = 0.7578 \	imes 34.96885 + 0.2422 \	imes 36.96590 = 26.495 + 8.953 = 35.448 \\\\approx 35.45\\\\,\	ext{u}$, matching the periodic table value.]

Problem: The mass of a $^{4}\	ext{He}$ nucleus is $4.002603\\\\,\	ext{u}$. Given $m_p = 1.007276\\\\,\	ext{u}$ and $m_n = 1.008665\\\\,\	ext{u}$, find the mass defect and binding energy in MeV. [Solution: $\\\Delta m = 2(1.007276) + 2(1.008665) - 4.002603 = 4.031882 - 4.002603 = 0.029279\\\\,\	ext{u}$; $BE = 0.029279 \	imes 931.494 \\\\approx 27.27\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$; $BE/A = 27.27/4 \\\\approx 6.82\\\\,\	ext{MeV/nucleon}$.]

Problem: A $^{238}\	ext{U}$ sample contains $2.5\\\\,\	ext{mg}$ of uranium. How many $^{238}\	ext{U}$ atoms are present? (Molar mass $\\\approx 238\\\\,\	ext{g/mol}$.) [Solution: $n = 2.5\	imes 10^{-3}\\\\,\	ext{g} / 238\\\\,\	ext{g/mol} = 1.050 \	imes 10^{-5}\\\\,\	ext{mol}$; $N = 1.050\	imes 10^{-5} \	imes 6.022\	imes 10^{23} \\\\approx 6.32\	imes 10^{18}$ atoms.]

Problem: A $^{14}\	ext{C}$ sample decays to $12.5\\\\%$ of its original activity in $17{,}190\\\\,\	ext{years}$. Calculate the half-life of $^{14}\	ext{C}$ and verify it against the known value of $5730\\\\,\	ext{years}$. [Solution: $12.5\\\\% = (1/2)^3$, so 3 half-lives have elapsed. $T_{1/2} = 17{,}190 / 3 = 5730\\\\,\	ext{years}$, which exactly matches the known value.]

Problem: For the reaction $^{14}\	ext{N} + n \ightarrow ^{14}\	ext{C} + p$, use masses $m(^{14}\	ext{N}) = 14.003074\\\\,\	ext{u}$, $m(^{14}\	ext{C}) = 14.003242\\\\,\	ext{u}$, $m_n = 1.008665\\\\,\	ext{u}$, $m_p = 1.007276\\\\,\	ext{u}$ to determine if the reaction is exothermic or endothermic, and calculate the Q-value. [Solution: Initial mass $= 14.003074 + 1.008665 = 15.011739\\\\,\	ext{u}$; final mass $= 14.003242 + 1.007276 = 15.010518\\\\,\	ext{u}$; $\\\Delta m = 15.011739 - 15.010518 = 0.001221\\\\,\	ext{u} > 0$, so energy is released. $Q = 0.001221 \	imes 931.494 \\\\approx 1.14\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$; exothermic.]

The binding energy of a helium-4 nucleus is 28.2 MeV. If the masses of protons and neutrons that form it have a total mass of 4.03282 u, find (a) the mass of the ⁴He nucleus, (b) the mass defect, (c) the binding energy per nucleon. (1 u = 931.5 MeV/c²). Solution: (a) Mass of He-4 = sum of constituents minus mass equivalent of BE. BE = 28.2 MeV, Δm = BE/c² = 28.2/931.5 = 0.03027 u. Mass of He-4 = 4.03282 - 0.03027 = 4.00255 u. (b) Mass defect = 0.03027 u. (c) BE/A = 28.2/4 = 7.05 MeV/nucleon.

Calculate the binding energy per nucleon for lithium-7. Given: m(7Li) = 7.01600 u, m(p) = 1.00783 u, m(n) = 1.00867 u. Solution: 3 protons + 4 neutrons. Mass of constituents = 3×1.00783 + 4×1.00867 = 3.02349 + 4.03468 = 7.05817 u. Mass defect = 7.05817 - 7.01600 = 0.04217 u. BE = 0.04217 × 931.5 = 39.28 MeV. BE/A = 39.28/7 = 5.61 MeV/nucleon.

In a nuclear reaction: ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n. Given masses: 2.01410 u, 3.01605 u, 4.00260 u, 1.00867 u. Find Q-value. Solution: Mass of reactants = 2.01410 + 3.01605 = 5.03015 u. Mass of products = 4.00260 + 1.00867 = 5.01127 u. Δm = 5.03015 - 5.01127 = 0.01888 u. Q = 0.01888 × 931.5 = 17.59 MeV. Positive Q means energy is released (fusion).

How much mass is converted to energy per year by a 1000 MW coal power plant if it operates 80% of the time, assuming 35% efficiency? Solution: Annual output energy = 1000×10⁶ W × 0.8 × 365 × 24 × 3600 = 2.52 × 10¹⁶ J. This is 35% of the thermal energy. Thermal energy = 2.52×10¹⁶/0.35 = 7.2 × 10¹⁶ J. Δm = E/c² = 7.2×10¹⁶/(3×10⁸)² = 8.0 × 10⁻¹ kg = 0.8 kg per year.

Using the semi-empirical mass formula (Weizsäcker), the binding energy per nucleon for uranium-238 is about 7.5 MeV and for krypton-92 is 8.7 MeV. If uranium-238 fissions into krypton-92 + barium-141 + 3 neutrons, estimate Q-value. Solution: BE of U-238 = 7.5 × 238 = 1785 MeV. BE of products = 8.7(92) + 8.5(141) + 2(3) = 786.4 + 1200 + 6 = 1992 MeV. Q = 1992 - 1785 = 207 MeV (energy released).
universalFacts: Fact (Historical): Frederick Soddy proposed the concept of isotopes in 1913, discovering that different radioactive elements could occupy the same position in the periodic table. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1921 for this work.

Fact (Application): Mass spectrometry is used in forensic science to analyze trace evidence, in environmental science to track pollution sources, in pharmacology to verify drug composition, and in astronomy to determine stellar composition.

Fact (Exam tip): Remember the conversion $1\\\\,\	ext{u} = 931.5\\\\,\	ext{MeV}/c^2$. For mass defect problems, always compute $\\\Delta m$ first in u, then multiply by $931.5$ to get binding energy in MeV. This avoids errors from using SI units.

Fact (Connection): The periodic table atomic weight of an element varies slightly depending on geographic source. For example, boron from different mines has different isotopic compositions, giving atomic weights between 10.81 and 10.82.

Fact (Everyday): Carbon-14 dating is used to verify the age of ancient manuscripts, authenticate artwork, date archaeological artifacts, and even verify the vintage of wine and spirits by measuring $^{14}\	ext{C}$ levels.

Fact (Conservation): In all nuclear reactions, both mass number $A$ (total nucleons) and atomic number $Z$ (total charge) are conserved. These two conservation laws are the first checks students should perform when balancing nuclear equations.

Fact (Scale): Converting $1\\\\,\	ext{g}$ of matter entirely to energy releases $E = mc^2 = 1\	imes 10^{-3} \	imes (3\	imes 10^8)^2 = 9\	imes 10^{13}\\\\,\	ext{J}$, equivalent to about $21\\\\,\	ext{kilotons}$ of TNT-the yield of the Hiroshima bomb.

Fact (Nuclear stability): The most stable nuclide is $^{56}\	ext{Fe}$ with a binding energy per nucleon of $8.79\\\\,\	ext{MeV}$. Nuclides lighter than iron release energy through fusion; those heavier than iron release energy through fission.

E = mc² is valid for ALL energy, not just nuclear — chemical, electrical, even mechanical. However, the mass changes are usually too small to detect (e.g., a compressed spring gains mass by about 10⁻¹⁶ kg).

The binding energy curve explains why fusion releases energy for elements lighter than iron and fission releases energy for elements heavier than iron. Iron is the most stable nucleus — its formation (in stars) is the end of fusion as an energy source.

The mass of a proton or neutron (about 1.008 u) is not exactly the sum of quark masses — most of the nucleon's mass comes from the strong interaction energy (E = mc² applied to the binding within the nucleon itself).

Annihilation (particle + antiparticle → photons) converts ALL rest mass to energy: E = 2m_p c² for electron-positron annihilation. But matter-antimatter annihilation is not used as an energy source because antimatter is extremely rare and difficult to produce.

The packing fraction method discovered the mass defect and led to the development of the Liquid Drop Model (Bethe-Weizsäcker formula) which quantitatively predicts nuclear binding energies, crucial for understanding fission and fusion.
specificConditions: **E=mc² and Binding Energy:** Einstein's relation $E = mc^2$ underpins nuclear binding energy. The mass defect $\Delta m$ corresponds to binding energy $BE = \Delta m \cdot c^2$. In nuclear reactions, the total mass-energy (rest mass + kinetic) is conserved.

**Packing Fraction Significance:** Packing fraction $f = (M - A)/A$ measures how much the actual atomic mass $M$ deviates from the mass number $A$. Negative $f$ means the nucleus is bound (mass less than sum of parts). Most stable nuclei have the most negative $f$ (e.g., $^{56}$Fe).

**Binding Energy Curve and Stability:** $BE/A$ peaks at ~8.8 MeV for $^{56}$Fe. Nuclei lighter than iron gain stability through fusion (increasing $BE/A$). Nuclei heavier than iron gain stability through fission (increasing $BE/A$). This curve is the master key to nuclear energy release.

notes: Annihilation occurs when a particle meets its antiparticle; rest mass may convert to photons while energy, momentum and charge remain conserved. For an electron and positron initially at rest, two photons travel in opposite directions so total momentum is zero.
An electron rest energy is mec²=0.511 MeV. An at-rest electron–positron pair can produce two 0.511 MeV photons, total energy 1.022 MeV.

Creation/annihilation of particle–antiparticle pairs is distinct from nuclear fission and fusion, although all processes obey mass-energy conservation.

specificConditions: **Particle-Antiparticle Annihilation:** When a particle meets its antiparticle (e.g., $e^- + e^+$), they annihilate into pure energy (photons). Total mass-energy is conserved: $2m_e c^2 = 2 \times 0.511$ MeV = 1.022 MeV of gamma rays. Charge, lepton number, and momentum are also conserved.

**Pair Production (Creation):** The reverse of annihilation: a high-energy photon ($E > 1.022$ MeV) creates an $e^- e^+$ pair near a nucleus (to conserve momentum). The photon must have $E \ge 2m_e c^2$. Excess energy becomes kinetic energy of the pair.

**Fission vs Fusion in $BE/A$ Context:** Both processes release energy by moving toward the iron peak ($^{56}$Fe, $BE/A \approx 8.8$ MeV). Fission splits heavy nuclei ($A > 56$); fusion combines light nuclei ($A < 56$). Both increase the average binding energy per nucleon of the final products compared to initial reactants.

data.title: Einstein's Mass-Energy Relation
notes: Mass-Energy Equivalence: Einstein's special relativity (1905) established that mass and energy are equivalent: E = mc². A mass m at rest possesses rest energy E₀ = mc². This is the most famous equation in physics.
Rest Energy: Every particle has rest energy E₀ = m₀c² even when not moving. For electron: E₀ = 0.511 MeV; for proton: E₀ = 938 MeV; for 1 kg: E₀ = 9 × 10¹⁶ J (enough to power a city for years).

Mass Defect and Binding Energy: In nuclear reactions, the mass of products differs from reactants. The mass difference Δm appears as energy: ΔE = Δmc². This is the basis of nuclear fission and fusion energy.
Atomic Mass Unit Energy: 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c². A mass defect of 1 u releases 931.5 MeV — a convenient unit for nuclear calculations.
Pair Production and Annihilation: Energy can create matter (pair production: γ → e⁻ + e⁺, requires E ≥ 2m_ec² = 1.022 MeV) and matter can become energy (annihilation: e⁻ + e⁺ → 2γ).

Nuclear Binding Energy per Nucleon: Typical values ~8 MeV per nucleon. Iron-56 has maximum binding energy (~8.8 MeV/nucleon) — most stable nucleus. Fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei both release energy by moving toward Fe-56.
Correspondence Principle: E = mc² reduces to Newtonian mechanics at v ≪ c. The kinetic energy correction: KE = (γ - 1)m₀c² ≈ ½m₀v² for small v.

data.title: Mass Defect, Packing Fraction, Binding Energy per Nucleon
data.topicTitle: Mass defect, packing fraction, binding energy per nucleon
notes: Mass Defect: The mass defect Δm is the difference between the sum of individual nucleon masses and the actual nuclear mass: Δm = Z·m_p + N·m_n - M_nucleus. This "missing mass" is converted to binding energy when the nucleus forms.

Binding Energy: The energy required to completely separate a nucleus into its constituent nucleons: BE = Δm·c². It is also the energy released when the nucleus forms from separate nucleons. MEV scale: BE ≈ Δm(u) × 931.5 MeV.

Binding Energy per Nucleon: BE/A — average energy holding each nucleon in the nucleus. Values range from ~1 MeV (light nuclei) to ~8.8 MeV (Fe-56) to ~7.6 MeV (uranium). Higher BE/A = more stable nucleus.

Packing Fraction: f = (M - A)/A × 10⁴ where M is atomic mass in u and A is mass number. Can be positive or negative. Related to stability — lower (more negative) packing fraction generally means more stable.
BE/A Curve: Rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks at Fe-56 (~8.8 MeV), then slowly decreases for heavy nuclei. Explains why fusion (light → medium) and fission (heavy → medium) both release energy.
Nuclear Stability: Nuclei with BE/A near maximum (Fe-56 region) are most stable. Very light and very heavy nuclei are less stable and can undergo fusion/fission respectively.
Semi-Empirical Mass Formula: BE = a_v·A - a_s·A^(2/3) - a_c·Z²/A^(1/3) - a_a·(A-2Z)²/A + pairing term. Volume, surface, Coulomb, asymmetry, pairing contributions.

data.title: Creation and Annihilation
notes: Pair Production: A high-energy photon (gamma ray) converts into an electron-positron pair near a nucleus: γ + nucleus → e⁻ + e⁺ + nucleus. The nucleus recoils to conserve momentum. Threshold energy: E_γ ≥ 2m_ec² = 1.022 MeV.

Pair Annihilation: An electron and positron collide and convert to photons: e⁻ + e⁺ → 2γ. Each photon has energy m_ec² = 0.511 MeV (if at rest), emitted in opposite directions (180° apart) to conserve momentum.
Energy Conservation: In pair production, photon energy = 2m_ec² + kinetic energies of pair + recoil of nucleus. In annihilation, total energy (rest + kinetic) converts to photon energy.
Momentum Conservation: A photon cannot produce an e⁻e⁺ pair in empty space — momentum cannot be conserved. A nearby nucleus (or electron) absorbs recoil momentum.
Charge Conservation: Pair production creates net charge 0 (−e + +e = 0); annihilation starts with net charge 0. Charge is conserved.

Applications: PET scans (positron emission tomography) use annihilation photons (511 keV each, back-to-back) for medical imaging. Positrons from radioactive tracers annihilate with electrons in tissue.
Matter-Antimatter Asymmetry: Universe appears dominated by matter with very little antimatter — one of the great unsolved problems in physics (baryon asymmetry).

data.title: Nuclear Fission and Fusion
notes: Nuclear Fission: Splitting of a heavy nucleus (A > 230) into two lighter nuclei (fission fragments) plus neutrons and energy. Example: ²³⁵U + n → ²³⁵U* → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n + ~200 MeV. Triggered by thermal (slow) neutron capture.

Chain Reaction: Fission releases neutrons (2-3 per event) that trigger more fissions. Critical mass: minimum mass for self-sustaining chain reaction. Subcritical: reaction dies; critical: steady; supercritical: exponential growth (explosion).

Nuclear Reactor: Controlled chain reaction. Components: fuel (²³⁵U/²³⁹Pu), moderator (heavy water, graphite) slows neutrons, control rods (boron, cadmium) absorb neutrons, coolant removes heat, concrete shield.

Nuclear Fusion: Joining of light nuclei (A < 20) into heavier nucleus, releasing energy. Example: ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n + 17.6 MeV. Requires extreme temperature (~10⁸ K) and pressure to overcome Coulomb repulsion.
Thermonuclear Fusion: Fusion occurring at high temperatures (stars, hydrogen bombs). In sun: proton-proton chain converts 4H → ⁴He + 2e⁺ + 2ν + γ (~26.7 MeV).
Energy Comparison: Fission: ~200 MeV per nucleus (~0.1% mass converted). Fusion: ~17.6 MeV per D-T reaction (~0.4% mass converted). Fusion releases more energy per unit mass.
Fission Fragments: Typically A ≈ 90-140, radioactive, undergo beta decay. Neutrons emitted: prompt (immediate) and delayed (from fission fragments, important for reactor control).
Fusion Fuel: Deuterium (²H from seawater) and tritium (³H from lithium). Deuterium is abundant — fusion fuel is virtually unlimited.

data.title: Optics — Introduction
data.summary: Geometrical (ray) optics and wave optics: light obeys reflection and refraction (Snell's law) derived from Fermat's principle; interference, diffraction and polarization demand the wave picture. Ray optics is valid while object sizes and apertures are much greater than the wavelength.
notes: Nature of Light: Light is an electromagnetic wave that exhibits both wave and particle (photon) behavior. Speed of light in vacuum c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

Ray Optics (Geometrical Optics): Light travels in straight lines in a homogeneous medium. Valid when object sizes and apertures are much larger than the wavelength λ. Deals with reflection, refraction, and image formation by mirrors and lenses.
Wave Optics (Physical Optics): Explains interference, diffraction, and polarization — phenomena that cannot be explained by ray optics alone. Required when apertures or obstacles are comparable to λ.
Fermat's Principle of Least Time: Light travels between two points along the path that takes the least time. This principle derives both the law of reflection and Snell's law of refraction.
Reflection: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection (i = r). The incident ray, reflected ray, and normal all lie in the same plane.
Refraction: When light passes from one medium to another, it bends. Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, where n is the refractive index of the medium.
Refractive Index: n = c/v, where v is the speed of light in the medium. Absolute refractive index is relative to vacuum. Relative refractive index ⁿ₂n₁ = v₁/v₂ = n₂/n₁.
specificConditions: Optical Principles: The behavior of light is governed by the laws of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection) and refraction (Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂). These laws derive from Fermat's principle of least time.

Wave Nature of Light: Light exhibits wave phenomena including interference, diffraction, and polarization. These cannot be explained by ray optics alone and require wave optics. The wavelength λ and frequency f are related by c = λf.

Approximations and Validity: Ray optics (geometrical optics) is valid when object sizes are much greater than wavelength λ. Wave optics is required when apertures or obstacles are comparable to λ. Quantum optics is needed for single-photon phenomena.
formulas: Speed of light: c = λf, where c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum
Refractive index: n = c/v, where v is speed of light in the medium
Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂
Law of reflection: angle of incidence i = angle of reflection r
Relative refractive index: ⁿ₂n₁ = v₁/v₂ = n₂/n₁
keyPoints: Light exhibits both wave and particle (photon) dual nature.
Ray optics is valid when object sizes ≫ wavelength λ.
Wave optics explains interference, diffraction, and polarization.
Fermat's principle of least time derives reflection and refraction laws.
Refractive index n = c/v measures how much light slows in a medium.

Statement 2: Snell's law states n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ for refraction at an interface.
Statement 3: The law of reflection states angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.
Statement 4: Fermat's principle of least time is the foundation of geometrical optics.
Statement 5: Wave optics is needed when apertures are comparable to the wavelength.
importantNotes: Refractive index is dimensionless and has no units.
When light enters a denser medium, it bends towards the normal.
When light enters a rarer medium, it bends away from the normal.
The frequency of light remains unchanged during refraction; wavelength and speed change.
Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from denser to rarer medium beyond the critical angle.
examShortTricks: n = c/v — higher n means slower light in medium.
Denser to rarer → bends away from normal.
Rarer to denser → bends towards normal.
i = r for reflection — always measure from normal.
c = λf — frequency stays constant across media.
examNotes: NEB frequently asks to state and explain Snell's law and the laws of reflection.
Refractive index numericals: n = c/v, real depth/apparent depth = n.
Fermat's principle is often asked as a theoretical derivation question.
Distinguish between ray optics (images, mirrors, lenses) and wave optics (interference, diffraction).
examples: Light travels from air (n ≈ 1) into glass (n = 1.5). Speed in glass: v = c/n = (3 × 10⁸)/1.5 = 2 × 10⁸ m/s.
A ray strikes a plane mirror at 30° to the surface. Angle of incidence = 60° (from normal), angle of reflection = 60°.
Light passes from water (n = 1.33) to air (n = 1.00) at 45° incidence. Using Snell's law: 1.33 sin 45° = 1.00 sin θ₂ → sin θ₂ = 0.94 → θ₂ ≈ 70°.

universalFacts: The speed of light in vacuum (c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s) is a fundamental constant of nature.
Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) is considered the father of optics for his work on reflection and refraction.
Willebrord Snellius discovered the law of refraction in 1621, though it was published by Descartes.

Thinking speed changes during reflection: Speed remains the same in the same medium during reflection.

Confusing refractive index with optical density: Higher n means optically denser, not necessarily physically denser.

data.title: Mirrors and Lenses
data.summary: Mirrors and lenses form images by reflection and refraction. Plane mirrors form virtual images; spherical mirrors (concave/convex) and lenses use the mirror/lens formula with sign conventions to determine image position, size, and nature.
notes: Plane Mirror: Forms a virtual, erect, same-sized image behind the mirror. Image distance equals object distance. Lateral inversion occurs (left-right reversed).
Spherical Mirrors: Concave (converging) and convex (diverging) mirrors. Key terms: pole (P), center of curvature (C), radius of curvature (R), focus (F), focal length (f = R/2), principal axis.
Mirror Formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u, where u = object distance, v = image distance, f = focal length. Sign convention: distances measured from pole; positive in direction of incident light.
Magnification: m = -v/u = h_i/h_o, where h_i is image height and h_o is object height. Negative m means inverted image.
Convex Lens: Converging lens. Thicker at center. Forms real inverted images (except when object within focal length). Lens formula: 1/f = 1/v - 1/u.
Concave Lens: Diverging lens. Thinner at center. Always forms virtual, erect, diminished images.
Power of Lens: P = 1/f (f in meters), unit: diopter (D). Convex lens: P > 0. Concave lens: P < 0. Lenses in contact: P = P₁ + P₂ + ...
Spherical Aberration: Marginal rays focus at different points than paraxial rays. Minimized by using small apertures or parabolic mirrors.
specificConditions: Thin Lens/Mirror Approximation: The mirror equation (1/f = 1/u + 1/v) and lens formula (1/f = 1/v - 1/u) assume thin optics where thickness is negligible. For thick lenses, principal planes must be used. Sign convention (Cartesian): distances measured from pole/lens center; positive in direction of incident light for u, opposite for v/f.

Spherical Aberration: Paraxial rays (close to axis) follow the simple formulas. Non-paraxial rays focus at different points, causing spherical aberration. The formulas assume paraxial approximation (small angles, sin θ ≈ θ).

Lens/Mirror Power: Power P = 1/f (meters) in diopters. Converging (convex lens, concave mirror): P > 0. Diverging (concave lens, convex mirror): P < 0. Powers add for thin lenses in contact: P_total = Σ P_i.
formulas: Mirror formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u
Lens formula: 1/f = 1/v - 1/u
Magnification: m = -v/u = h_i/h_o
Focal length and radius: f = R/2
Power of lens: P = 1/f (f in meters), unit: diopter
Lenses in contact: P = P₁ + P₂ + ...
keyPoints: Plane mirror: virtual, erect, same-size image, image distance = object distance.
