universalFacts: The cross product was independently developed by Josiah Willard Gibbs and Oliver Heaviside in the 1880s as part of their effort to simplify vector calculus for physics applications.
The cross product is unique to three dimensions (and seven dimensions with a special construction). In 3D, it is essential for describing rotation, angular momentum, and magnetic forces.

In computer graphics, the cross product is used to compute surface normals for lighting calculations. The normal vector determines how light reflects off a 3D surface, creating the illusion of depth and texture.
The scalar triple product $\vec{A} \cdot (\vec{B} \times \vec{C})$ is used to determine if three vectors are coplanar — if the volume they enclose is zero, the vectors lie in the same plane.
In quantum mechanics, the commutation relation $[x, p_x] = i\hbar$ is analogous to the cross product's anti-commutative property — order matters, and swapping changes the sign.
This topic is a cornerstone of the physics curriculum and appears consistently in examinations.
Understanding resolution of vectors and unit vectors builds the foundation for more advanced topics in mathematics.
Real-world applications of resolution of vectors and unit vectors span engineering, physics, economics, and computer science.

Find the unit vector perpendicular to both $\vec{A} = \hat{i} + \hat{j}$ and $\vec{B} = \hat{j} + \hat{k}$. $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(1) - \hat{j}(1) + \hat{k}(1) = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$. Magnitude: $\sqrt{1 + 1 + 1} = \sqrt{3}$. Unit vector: $\hat{n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k})$.

Calculate the torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$ where $\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}$ m and $\vec{F} = 4\hat{i} - 5\hat{j}$ N. $\vec{\tau} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 4 & -5 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{k}(-10 - 12) = -22\hat{k}$ N·m. The torque is 22 N·m clockwise (into the page).

Find the area of the triangle with vertices at $A(1,0,0)$, $B(0,2,0)$, and $C(0,0,3)$. Vectors: $\vec{AB} = -\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}$, $\vec{AC} = -\hat{i} + 3\hat{k}$. $\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ -1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(6) - \hat{j}(-3) + \hat{k}(2) = 6\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$. Area = $\frac{1}{2}|\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}| = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{36 + 9 + 4} = \frac{\sqrt{49}}{2} = 3.5$ square units.

If $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 6\hat{k}$ and $|\vec{A}| = 3$, $|\vec{B}| = 4$, find the angle between $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$. $|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}| = AB\sin\theta$. $6 = 3 \times 4 \times \sin\theta$. $\sin\theta = 6/12 = 0.5$. $\theta = 30°$ or $150°$. Since the result is $+6\hat{k}$, using the right-hand rule, the angle from $\vec{A}$ to $\vec{B}$ is 30° (counterclockwise looking down the +z axis).

universalFacts: The cross product was independently developed by Josiah Willard Gibbs and Oliver Heaviside in the 1880s as part of their effort to simplify vector calculus for physics applications.
The cross product is unique to three dimensions (and seven dimensions with a special construction). In 3D, it is essential for describing rotation, angular momentum, and magnetic forces.

In computer graphics, the cross product is used to compute surface normals for lighting calculations. The normal vector determines how light reflects off a 3D surface, creating the illusion of depth and texture.
The scalar triple product $\vec{A} \cdot (\vec{B} \times \vec{C})$ is used to determine if three vectors are coplanar — if the volume they enclose is zero, the vectors lie in the same plane.
In quantum mechanics, the commutation relation $[x, p_x] = i\hbar$ is analogous to the cross product's anti-commutative property — order matters, and swapping changes the sign.
Vectors have magnitude + direction; a = aî + bĵ + c k̂. |a| = √(a²+b²+c²).
Dot: a·b = |a||b|cosθ = a₁b₁+a₂b₂+a₃b₃ (scalar; =0 ⟂). Cross: a×b (vector, ⟂ to both; |a×b| = |a||b|sinθ; area = ½|a×b|).
Triangle/parallelogram/polygon laws: vector sum is independent of order (commutative).

data.topicTitle: Work done by a constant force and a variable force
notes: Work by Constant Force: W = F·d·cosθ = Fd cosθ where F is force magnitude, d is displacement, θ is angle between force and displacement vectors. SI unit: joule (J = N·m). Scalar quantity — can be positive, negative, or zero.
Work by Variable Force: When force varies with position, W = ∫F(x)·dx from x₁ to x₂. Graphically, W = area under F-x curve between limits. For F = kx (spring): W = ½kx².
Positive Work: Force component in direction of displacement (0° ≤ θ < 90°). Example: gravity on falling object, applied force pushing object forward.
Negative Work: Force component opposite to displacement (90° < θ ≤ 180°). Example: friction on sliding object, gravity on object thrown upward.
Zero Work: θ = 90° (force perpendicular to displacement) or d = 0 or F = 0. Example: centripetal force in circular motion, carrying object while walking horizontally.
Work-Energy Theorem: Net work on object equals change in kinetic energy: W_net = ΔK = ½mv_f² - ½mv_i². Valid for constant and variable forces, conservative and non-conservative.
Units: 1 J = 1 N·m = 1 kg·m²/s². Erg (CGS): 1 erg = 10⁻⁷ J. Electronvolt: 1 eV = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ J.

data.title: Work Done by a Constant Force and a Variable Force
data.topicTitle: Work done by a constant force and a variable force
notes: **Definition of work (constant force):** $W = F s \\\\cos\	heta$, where $F$ is the magnitude of the constant force, $s$ is the displacement, and $\	heta$ is the angle between the force vector and displacement vector. Work is a scalar quantity - it has magnitude but no direction.

**Sign of work:** Work is POSITIVE when $0^\\\\circ \\\\le \	heta < 90^\\\\circ$ (force component along displacement). Work is ZERO when $\	heta = 90^\\\\circ$ (force perpendicular to displacement, e.g., centripetal force, normal force on horizontal surface). Work is NEGATIVE when $90^\\\\circ < \	heta \\\\le 180^\\\\circ$ (force opposes displacement, e.g., kinetic friction, gravity when lifting).

**Work by multiple forces:** Total work is the sum of works by individual forces: $W_{\	ext{net}} = \\\\sum W_i = \\\\sum F_i s \\\\cos\	heta_i$. This is equivalent to the work done by the net force: $W_{\	ext{net}} = F_{\	ext{net}} s \\\\cos\	heta_{\	ext{net}}$.

**Variable force definition:** When force varies with position, work is the integral of force over the displacement: $W = \\\\int_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x) \\\\, dx$ (for 1D motion). Graphically, this is the area under the $F$ vs $x$ curve between the initial and final positions.

**Work by a spring force (Hooke's law):** For an ideal spring, $F = -kx$. Work done BY the spring when moving from $x_i$ to $x_f$: $W_{\	ext{spring}} = \\\\int_{x_i}^{x_f} (-kx) dx = \ rac{1}{2}k x_i^2 - \ rac{1}{2}k x_f^2$. Work done ON the spring (by external agent) is the negative of this.

**Work by gravity (near Earth):** Gravity is a constant force $F_g = mg$ downward. If an object moves vertically by $\\\\Delta y$ (up positive), $W_g = -mg \\\\Delta y$. If it moves horizontally, $W_g = 0$. For a path with vertical drop $h$, $W_g = +mgh$ (gravity does positive work).

**Work by a constant force in 2D/3D:** $W = \\\\vec{F} \\\\cdot \\\\vec{s} = F_x s_x + F_y s_y + F_z s_z$. Only the component of force parallel to displacement contributes. This dot product form is frame-independent.

**Work-energy connection (preview):** The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: $W_{\	ext{net}} = \\\\Delta K = \ rac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \ rac{1}{2}mv_i^2$. This is the work-energy theorem, derived from Newton's second law.

**Path dependence for variable forces:** For a variable force, work depends on the path taken. For conservative forces (gravity, spring), work is path-independent and equals $-\\\\Delta U$. For non-conservative forces (friction), work depends on the actual path length.

**Graphical interpretation:** The area under the $F$-$x$ curve (with sign) gives the work. Positive area = positive work; negative area = negative work. For a spring, the $F$-$x$ graph is a straight line through origin with slope $k$, and the area is a triangle $\ rac{1}{2}kx^2$.

**Work by a varying force in 2D:** $W = \\\\int_C \\\\vec{F} \\\\cdot d\\\\vec{r} = \\\\int_C (F_x dx + F_y dy)$. This is a line integral. For a force $\\\\vec{F}(x,y)$, the work along path C depends on the specific curve C unless $\\\\vec{F}$ is conservative ($\
abla \	imes \\\\vec{F} = 0$).

**Constant force vs variable force summary:** Constant force: $W = F s \\\\cos\	heta$ (simple product). Variable force: $W = \\\\int F(x) dx$ (area under curve). Both are special cases of the general definition $W = \\\\int \\\\vec{F} \\\\cdot d\\\\vec{r}$.

**Example - work by gravity on an incline:** Block slides down incline of angle $\	heta$, length $L$. Vertical drop $h = L \\\\sin\	heta$. Work by gravity: $W_g = mgh = mgL \\\\sin\	heta$. This equals force component parallel to incline ($mg\\\\sin\	heta$) times distance $L$.

**Example - work by external agent stretching a spring:** Slowly stretch spring from 0 to $x$ (quasi-static, acceleration $\\\\approx 0$). Applied force $F_{\	ext{app}} = +kx$ (matches spring force). Work done: $W = \\\\int_0^x kx dx = \ rac{1}{2}kx^2$. This energy is STORED as elastic potential energy in the spring.
confusion: Work is NOT force times distance in general - it is force component in the direction of displacement times distance. $W = F s$ only when force and displacement are parallel ($	heta = 0$). Many students forget the $\\\cos\	heta$ factor.

Work done BY a force vs work done ON an object: $W_{\	ext{by}} = -W_{\	ext{on}}$. The work-energy theorem uses $W_{\	ext{net}}$ (work done BY all forces ON the object). Work done BY the object on something else is the negative.

Holding a heavy object stationary: You exert a force, but displacement is zero, so $W = 0$! You get tired because your muscles do internal biochemical work (energy conversion), not mechanical work on the object. This is a classic misconception.

Centripetal force does NO work: $F_c$ is always perpendicular to velocity (displacement), so $\\\\cos 90^\\\\circ = 0$. It changes direction, not speed. A planet in circular orbit around the Sun has zero work done by gravity.

For a variable force, you CANNOT just multiply 'average force' by distance unless you know the average is the integral average. The correct method is always integration or graphical area. A common error: averaging endpoints $\ rac{F_i + F_f}{2}$ only works for linear forces.
practice: A 5 kg block is pulled 10 m across a horizontal floor by a force of 20 N at an angle of 30° above the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.2. Find (a) work done by the applied force, (b) work done by friction, (c) net work, (d) final speed if it started from rest. Solution: (a) $W_F = F s \\\\cos 30^\\\\circ = 20 \	imes 10 \	imes 0.866 = 173.2$ J. (b) Normal force $N = mg - F\\\\sin 30^\\\\circ = 5\	imes9.8 - 20\	imes0.5 = 49 - 10 = 39$ N. universalFacts: The concept of work was formalized by Gaspard-Gustave Coriolis in 1829. He defined 'work' as the product of force and distance - the word 'work' in physics has a precise mathematical meaning different from everyday usage.

Work is a SCALAR, not a vector. It has no direction, only magnitude and sign. Energy (which work changes) is also a scalar. This is why we can add works from different forces as simple numbers: $W_{\	ext{net}} = W_1 + W_2 + \\\\dots$

The work-energy theorem $W_{\	ext{net}} = \\\\Delta K$ is mathematically equivalent to Newton's second law $F = ma$. It's not a new law - it's a reformulation that is often easier to use when forces vary or the path is complex.

One joule (1 J) is the work done by a force of 1 newton moving an object 1 meter in the direction of the force. It's a small amount: lifting a 100 g apple by 1 m does about 1 J of work against gravity.

In thermodynamics, work is energy transfer across a system boundary due to macroscopic forces. The same definition $W = \\\\int F dx$ applies, but the 'system' and 'surroundings' must be clearly defined. The sign convention often differs: work done BY the system on surroundings is POSITIVE in thermodynamics (opposite to mechanics convention for the system).

notes: **कार्य (Work) को परिभाषा (स्थिर बल):** $W = F s \cos\theta$, जहाँ $F$ स्थिर बलको परिमाण हो, $s$ विस्थापन हो, र $\theta$ बल र विस्थापन वेक्टर बिचको कोण हो। कार्य एक अदिश (scalar) मात्रा हो - यसमा परिमाण छ तर दिशा छैन।

**कार्यको चिन्ह (Sign):** कार्य **सकारात्मक (positive)** हुन्छ जब $0^\circ \le \theta < 90^\circ$ (बलको घटक विस्थापनको दिशामा)। कार्य **शून्य (zero)** हुन्छ जब $\theta = 90^\circ$ (बल विस्थापनको लम्बको, जस्तै: केन्द्राभिमुख बल, समतल सतहमा सामान्य बल)। कार्य **नकारात्मक (negative)** हुन्छ जब $90^\circ < \theta \le 180^\circ$ (बल विस्थापनको विपरीत, जस्तै: गतिज घर्षण, उठाउदा गुरुत्वाकर्षण)।

data.title: Power
notes: Power is the rate of energy transfer: average P=ΔW/Δt and instantaneous P=dW/dt. Its SI unit is watt, 1 W=1 J s⁻¹.
For translation, dW=F⃗·dr⃗ gives P=F⃗·v⃗=Fv cosθ. Only the force component parallel to velocity transfers energy; a perpendicular centripetal force does no work in uniform circular motion.

Worked example: a 200 kg load rises steadily at 0.50 m s⁻¹. The lifting force is mg=1960 N for g=9.8 m s⁻², so useful power is Fv=980 W. In 10 s the load rises 5 m and gains 9800 J, confirming P=W/t=980 W.
At constant speed, net power is zero because engine power balances resistive forces. For rotation, P=τ⃗·ω⃗; efficiency η=Pout/Pin distinguishes useful output from input.
A 50 N force at 60° to a crate moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ transfers energy at P=50×3×cos60°=75 W, not 150 W.

Power is the rate of doing work. When a force stays along the velocity, power is the force times the speed. A larger engine can do the same work in less time, which is a larger power, not a larger store of energy.

data.title: Conservation of Energy
notes: **Law of conservation of energy:** Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transformed from one form to another or transferred between systems. The total energy of an isolated system remains constant over time.

**Mechanical energy conservation:** When only conservative forces (gravity, spring force, electrostatic force) act on a system, mechanical energy E = K + U is conserved: ΔK + ΔU = 0, or K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f.

**Potential energy types:** Gravitational PE near Earth: U_g = mgh (h = height above reference). Elastic PE of a spring: U_s = ½kx² (x = compression/extension from natural length). For a universal gravitational field: U = -GMm/r.

**Non-conservative forces and energy loss:** Friction, air resistance, and viscous drag are non-conservative. They convert mechanical energy into thermal energy (heat). Work done by non-conservative forces: W_nc = ΔE_mech = E_final - E_initial.

**Total energy conservation including heat:** Even with friction, total energy is conserved if you include thermal energy: ΔK + ΔU + ΔE_thermal = 0. The first law of thermodynamics: ΔU_internal = Q - W, where Q is heat added, W is work done BY the system.

**Pendulum energy conservation:** For a simple pendulum (mass m, length L, angle θ): At the bottom, K = ½mv², U = 0. At the extremes, v = 0, K = 0, U = mgL(1-cosθ). With no air resistance: ½mv² + mgL(1-cosθ) = constant.
**Spring-mass system:** For a mass m on a spring with constant k: At equilibrium, K = ½mv², U = 0. At max extension x = A, v = 0, K = 0, U = ½kA². Energy oscillates: ½mv² + ½kx² = ½kA² = constant.

**Roller coaster physics:** At the top of a hill, the car has maximum PE (mgh) and minimum KE. At the bottom, maximum KE and minimum PE. Total energy constant (neglecting friction). Minimum speed at top of vertical loop: v ≥ √(gr) to stay on track.

**Energy in collisions:** In elastic collisions, both momentum and KE are conserved. In inelastic collisions, momentum is conserved but KE is not (some converts to heat/sound). In perfectly inelastic collisions, objects stick together and KE loss is maximum.

**Conservation of energy in nuclear reactions:** Mass-energy equivalence E = mc² shows mass is another form of energy. In nuclear fission/fusion, the total mass of products is less than reactants — the mass defect Δm appears as kinetic energy of products: ΔE = Δmc².
**Power and energy relationship:** Power is the rate of energy transfer: P = dE/dt. If power is constant, E = Pt. If power varies, E = ∫P dt. Energy delivered is the area under the P-t curve.

**Real-world energy transformations:** Chemical energy (fuel) → thermal (burning) → mechanical (engine) → electrical (generator) → electromagnetic (light) → thermal (absorber). At each step, some energy becomes heat (second law).

**Reference point for potential energy:** Gravitational PE is defined relative to a chosen zero level. The choice is arbitrary — only differences in PE matter. Usually we set U = 0 at the lowest point in the problem or at ground level.

confusion: Energy is NOT created or destroyed — it only transforms. When a pendulum stops swinging due to friction, the energy doesn't 'disappear'; it becomes thermal energy in the air and the pivot. The FIRST law of thermodynamics says energy is conserved in all processes.

Conservation of mechanical energy (K + U = constant) ONLY holds when ALL forces are conservative. If there is ANY friction, air resistance, or non-conservative force, mechanical energy is NOT conserved. You must include W_nc or track thermal energy.

Potential energy is NOT absolute — it is defined relative to an arbitrary zero point. A ball on a table has U = mgh relative to the floor, but U = mg(h+H) relative to the basement. Only PE differences matter physically.

In a collision, momentum is ALWAYS conserved (if no external forces). Kinetic energy is ONLY conserved in perfectly ELASTIC collisions. Many students think KE is always conserved in collisions — it is NOT. Real collisions are usually somewhat inelastic.

The work-energy theorem (W_net = ΔK) and energy conservation (ΔK + ΔU = -W_nc) are DIFFERENT. The first is about NET work changing kinetic energy. The second is about total mechanical energy. With conservative forces, W_net = -ΔU, so W_net + ΔU = ΔK, which is the work-energy theorem.
practice: A 2 kg block slides down a frictionless incline of height 5 m. Find its speed at the bottom. Solution: U_i = mgh = 2 × 9.8 × 5 = 98 J. K_i = 0. At bottom: U_f = 0. K_f = U_i → ½mv² = 98 → v² = 196/2 = 98 → v = √98 = 9.9 m/s.

A 0.5 kg block on a spring (k = 200 N/m) is compressed 0.1 m and released. Find max speed. Solution: U_s = ½kx² = ½×200×0.01 = 1 J. At equilibrium, all U_s → K. ½mv² = 1 → v² = 4 → v = 2 m/s. Amplitude of oscillation = 0.1 m.

A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s brakes to a stop. The brakes heat up with 80% of the KE going to thermal energy in the brakes. How much heat is generated? Solution: KE_initial = ½×1000×400 = 200,000 J = 200 kJ. Heat = 0.8 × 200 kJ = 160 kJ.

A ball is dropped from height h = 10 m and bounces back to height 7.5 m. Find the coefficient of restitution e and the fraction of energy lost. Solution: Speed before impact = √(2gh) = √(196) = 14 m/s. Speed after = √(2g×7.5) = √(147) = 12.1 m/s. e = v_after/v_before = 12.1/14 = 0.86. Energy lost = 1 - e² = 1 - 0.74 = 26%.

A 5 kg block slides down a rough 30° incline of length 4 m with μ = 0.2. Find its speed at the bottom. Solution: Height drop = 4 sin 30° = 2 m. U_i = mgh = 5×9.8×2 = 98 J. Work by friction: W_f = -μmg cosθ × s = -0.2×5×9.8×cos30°×4 = -0.2×5×9.8×0.866×4 = -34 J. ΔK = U_i + W_f = 98 - 34 = 64 J. v = √(2×64/5) = √(128/5) = 5.06 m/s.
universalFacts: The law of conservation of energy is the first law of thermodynamics and applies to ALL physical processes — mechanics, electromagnetism, thermodynamics, quantum mechanics, general relativity. It is the most fundamental and universal law in physics.

Emmy Noether proved (1918) that conservation of energy is a consequence of time translation symmetry: the laws of physics are the same at all times. This is Noether's theorem — every continuous symmetry implies a conserved quantity.
Perpetual motion machines of the first kind (producing energy without input) are IMPOSSIBLE because they violate energy conservation. No known process in the universe creates net energy from nothing.

The total energy of the universe is a subtle concept in cosmology. In an expanding universe, energy conservation is not globally well-defined in the same way. However, in local physics, energy conservation is exact and tested to incredible precision.

Energy exists in many forms: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, chemical, nuclear, electromagnetic, thermal, rest mass energy (mc²), etc. All can be converted into each other, subject to the laws of physics.
examples: Pendulum: A 2 kg bob is released from 0.5 m above the lowest point. Speed at bottom: mgh = ½mv² → v = √(2×9.8×0.5) = 3.13 m/s.
Spring-mass: A 0.5 kg mass on a spring (k = 200 N/m) compressed 0.1 m. Max speed: ½kA² = ½mv² → v = √(200×0.01/0.5) = 2 m/s.
Roller coaster: A 500 kg car starts at 20 m height. Speed at bottom: v = √(2×9.8×20) = 19.8 m/s.
Free fall: A 1 kg stone dropped from 45 m. Speed at ground: v = √(2×9.8×45) = 29.7 m/s.
Inclined plane: A 3 kg block slides down a smooth 30° slope of length 10 m. Speed at bottom: v = √(2×9.8×5) = 9.9 m/s (h = 10 sin 30° = 5 m).

data.title: Conservative and Non-Conservative Forces
notes: **Conservative force definition:** A force is conservative if the work done by it depends ONLY on the initial and final positions, not on the path taken. Equivalently, the work done around any closed loop is zero: ∮F·dr = 0.

**Path independence:** For a conservative force, W = U_i - U_f = -(U_f - U_i) = -ΔU. The work is the negative of the change in potential energy. This means we can define a potential energy function U(r) such that F = -∇U (force is the negative gradient of potential).
**Examples of conservative forces:** Gravity (near Earth: F = -mg, U = mgh), spring force (F = -kx, U = ½kx²), electrostatic force (F = kQq/r², U = kQq/r), uniform electric field (F = qE, U = qEy).

**Non-conservative force definition:** A force is non-conservative if the work done depends on the path taken. The work around a closed loop is NOT zero: ∮F·dr ≠ 0. Energy is dissipated as heat or sound.

**Examples of non-conservative forces:** Kinetic friction (F_f = μN, work = -μN × distance traveled — depends on path length!), air resistance/viscous drag (proportional to v or v², opposes motion), rolling friction, human muscle force (metabolic energy not recoverable).

**Potential energy association:** Conservative forces ALLOW the definition of potential energy because the work done against them is stored and recoverable. Non-conservative forces do NOT have an associated potential energy — the energy is lost from the mechanical system.

**Closed loop test:** Take any closed path. For gravity: lift a mass up height h (W = -mgh), lower it down (W = +mgh). Net work = 0. For friction: slide a block around a closed square (perimeter = 4L). Each side does work = -μmgL. Net work = -4μmgL ≠ 0.

**Mixed force systems:** When both conservative and non-conservative forces act, use: W_nc = ΔE_mech = (K_f + U_f) - (K_i + U_i). This is the most general energy equation for mechanical systems. If W_nc = 0, mechanical energy is conserved.

**Energy dissipated by friction:** For a block sliding distance d with kinetic friction μ_k, the thermal energy generated is Q = μ_k N d. This comes from the work done BY friction: W_f = -μ_k N d. The mechanical energy lost equals the heat generated.

**Conservative force and curl:** In 3D, a force F is conservative iff its curl is zero: ∇ × F = 0 (everywhere in a simply connected region). This is a mathematical test — if the force field has no circulation, it is conservative.

**Electrostatic force is conservative:** The work done by an electrostatic field depends only on endpoints. This allows defining electric potential V = U/q and voltage differences. The electric field is the negative gradient: E = -∇V.

**Why it matters for problem solving:** If all forces are conservative, use K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f (simple). If non-conservative forces are present, use W_nc = ΔE_mech. Always identify which forces are conservative and which are not.

confusion: Friction does NOT have a potential energy. Many students try to write U_friction = μmgx or something similar. This is WRONG — friction is non-conservative, and the energy it 'removes' from the mechanical system becomes heat, not stored potential energy.

A force being 'conservative' does NOT mean the total energy of the system is conserved. It means mechanical energy can be conserved IF that force is the ONLY force doing work. If you have conservative forces PLUS non-conservative forces, mechanical energy is not conserved even though some forces are conservative.

Normal force and tension are NOT conservative forces — they are constraint forces that do zero work (they are perpendicular to displacement). They don't appear in the energy equation because W = 0, not because they have potential energy.

The term 'non-conservative' does NOT mean 'energy is destroyed.' It means mechanical energy is converted to other forms (heat, sound) that are NOT tracked by potential energy. Total energy is ALWAYS conserved (first law).
Air resistance (drag) is non-conservative. The work done by drag depends on the path (speed profile). You CANNOT define a 'drag potential energy.' The energy lost to drag becomes heat in the air.
practice: A 10 kg block slides on a rough horizontal surface (μ_k = 0.3) from x=0 to x=5 m, then returns to x=0. Find total work done by friction. Solution: W_going = -μmgd = -0.3×10×9.8×5 = -147 J. W_returning = -147 J. Total W = -294 J ≠ 0. Friction is non-conservative. The energy is dissipated as heat.

A 2 kg mass falls 10 m in air with air resistance. Its speed at the bottom is 12 m/s (instead of 14 m/s without air resistance). Find the work done by air resistance. Solution: Without drag: v = √(2gh) = √(196) = 14 m/s, KE = 196 J. With drag: KE = ½×2×144 = 144 J. Work by drag = ΔKE - W_gravity = 144 - 196 = -52 J. 52 J lost to air resistance.

Is the force F(x) = 3x² i + 4y j conservative? Find its potential function if it is. Solution: Check ∇ × F = 0. In 2D: ∂F_y/∂x - ∂F_x/∂y = 0 - 0 = 0. Conservative. Find U: F_x = -dU/dx = 3x² → U = -x³ + f(y). F_y = -dU/dy = 4y → -df/dy = 4y → f = -2y². U = -x³ - 2y² + C.

A spring (k = 500 N/m) launches a 0.5 kg block up a 30° incline with μ = 0.2. The spring is compressed 0.2 m. How far up the incline does the block go? Solution: Initial spring U = ½kx² = ½×500×0.04 = 10 J. Final state: v = 0 at distance d up incline. Height gain = d sin 30° = d/2. U_g = mg(d/2) = 0.5×9.8×d/2 = 2.45d J. Work by friction = -μmg cos30° d = -0.2×0.5×9.8×0.866d = -0.85d. Energy: 10 = 2.45d + 0.85d = 3.3d → d = 10/3.3 = 3.03 m.

A particle moves in a circle of radius r under a force F = -kr (directed toward center). Is this force conservative? Find the work done over one complete circle. Solution: F = -k(xi + yj) is a central force toward origin. Curl = 0, so conservative. Work over closed circle: ∮F·dr = 0 (conservative forces do zero work over closed paths).
universalFacts: The fundamental forces of nature (gravity, electromagnetism, strong, weak) are all conservative at the fundamental level. Non-conservative forces like friction are emergent — they arise from many conservative interactions at the microscopic level, with energy going into microscopic degrees of freedom (heat).

Noether's theorem: Conservation of energy is linked to time translation symmetry. Conservative forces are those derived from a potential that is time-independent. Time-dependent forces (like a time-varying field) can be non-conservative even if they are fundamental.

The electrostatic force is conservative, but the magnetic force is NOT conservative in the usual sense (it does no work because F = qv×B is perpendicular to v, so W = 0). However, in electromagnetic induction, the induced electric field is non-conservative (∇×E = -∂B/∂t).

In quantum mechanics, all forces are fundamentally conservative. The apparent non-conservation in decoherence comes from entanglement with the environment — the system's energy is not conserved, but the total universe energy is.

The work done by a conservative force is the negative of the change in its potential energy: W = -ΔU. This means if you move against a conservative force (lifting a weight), you INCREASE its potential energy (positive ΔU, negative W).

data.title: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions
notes: **Elastic collision:** A collision in which both total momentum AND total kinetic energy are conserved. The bodies rebound without permanent deformation, no sound/heat is produced. The relative velocity of approach equals the relative velocity of separation: v₂ - v₁ = u₁ - u₂.

**Inelastic collision:** A collision in which momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is NOT conserved. Some kinetic energy is converted to internal energy (heat, sound, deformation). The coefficient of restitution e < 1.

**Perfectly inelastic collision:** The extreme case where the colliding bodies stick together after collision and move with a common velocity. Momentum is conserved; KE loss is maximum (but not 100% because momentum must be conserved, so some KE remains as center-of-mass motion).

**One-dimensional elastic collision formulas:** For masses m₁, m₂ with initial velocities u₁, u₂: v₁ = (m₁-m₂)u₁/(m₁+m₂) + 2m₂u₂/(m₁+m₂), v₂ = (m₂-m₁)u₂/(m₁+m₂) + 2m₁u₁/(m₁+m₂). These come from conservation of momentum + conservation of KE.

**Special case — equal masses (m₁ = m₂) in elastic collision:** The masses exchange velocities! v₁ = u₂, v₂ = u₁. If m₂ was initially at rest (u₂ = 0), then v₁ = 0 (first mass stops) and v₂ = u₁ (second mass moves off with the first mass's original speed).

**Special case — very massive m₁, stationary m₂ (m₁ ≫ m₂, u₂ = 0):** m₁ barely slows: v₁ ≈ u₁. m₂ shoots forward at v₂ ≈ 2u₁ (twice the initial speed). This is how a golf club hits a ball, or a bat hits a baseball.

**Coefficient of restitution (e):** e = (relative speed of separation) / (relative speed of approach) = (v₂ - v₁)/(u₁ - u₂). For perfectly elastic: e = 1. For perfectly inelastic: e = 0. For inelastic: 0 < e < 1. e depends on the materials (e.g., tennis ball on concrete: e ≈ 0.75; steel on steel: e ≈ 0.9; putty: e ≈ 0).

**Energy loss in inelastic collisions:** ΔK = K_f - K_i = -½ μ v_rel² (1 - e²), where μ = m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂) is the reduced mass and v_rel = u₁ - u₂ is the relative velocity. The energy lost goes to heat, sound, and permanent deformation.

**Two-dimensional collisions:** Momentum is conserved as a vector: p_x and p_y separately. For elastic collisions, KE is also conserved. The scattering angles depend on the impact parameter. Center-of-mass frame analysis often simplifies 2D collisions.

**Center-of-mass frame:** In the CM frame, total momentum is zero. In an elastic collision, the speeds of particles don't change, only their directions change. The scattering is isotropic for identical particles in the CM frame.

**Real-world applications:** Car crash safety (crumple zones increase collision time, reduce force — KE is dissipated controllably). Billiards (nearly elastic). Newton's cradle (demonstrates momentum and energy transfer through elastic collisions). Sports (baseball, tennis, golf — coefficient of restitution of ball/racket/club matters).

**Explosion — reverse collision:** An object at rest splits into fragments with kinetic energy. Momentum is conserved (total momentum before = 0, after = 0). KE after > KE before — the energy comes from internal chemical/nuclear energy stored in the object. This is a 'reverse' inelastic collision.

confusion: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the objects DO NOT lose ALL their kinetic energy. They lose the MAXIMUM possible KE consistent with momentum conservation. The center-of-mass kinetic energy (½Mv_cm²) MUST remain because momentum is conserved. Only the KE relative to the center of mass can be lost.

The coefficient of restitution e is NOT the ratio of final to initial KE. e = (v₂ - v₁)/(u₁ - u₂) is the ratio of relative speeds. The fraction of KE retained is e² (for equal masses) or a more complex formula for unequal masses. Many students confuse e with KE ratio.

Momentum is ALWAYS conserved in an isolated system (no external forces). Kinetic energy is ONLY conserved in perfectly elastic collisions. Students often think KE is always conserved in collisions — it is NOT. Real collisions are usually somewhat inelastic (0 < e < 1).

For a ball bouncing on the floor: The floor/earth is so massive it doesn't move. The ball's speed before and after impact relates by e = v_after/v_before. The ball loses (1-e²) of its KE each bounce. The floor provides the impulse to change momentum; the earth's recoil is negligible.

A collision where kinetic energy is 'gained' (superelastic) is possible if internal energy is released (explosion, chemical reaction, spring release). These are NOT standard collisions and require tracking internal energy changes.
practice: A 5 kg ball moving at 4 m/s collides elastically with a 3 kg ball at rest. Find their velocities after collision. Solution: m₁=5, m₂=3, u₁=4, u₂=0. v₁ = (5-3)/(5+3)×4 = 2/8×4 = 1 m/s. v₂ = 2×5/(5+3)×4 = 10/8×4 = 5 m/s. Check: KE_i = ½×5×16 = 40 J. KE_f = ½×5×1 + ½×3×25 = 2.5 + 37.5 = 40 J. Momentum: 5×4 = 5×1 + 3×5 = 20.

A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s rear-ends a stationary 1500 kg car. They stick together. Find (a) final velocity, (b) KE lost. Solution: (a) m₁u₁ = (m₁+m₂)v → 1000×20 = 2500v → v = 8 m/s. (b) KE_i = ½×1000×400 = 200,000 J. KE_f = ½×2500×64 = 80,000 J. Lost = 120,000 J = 60% of initial KE. Heat/sound/crushing.

A ball of mass m is dropped from height h onto a massive floor with coefficient of restitution e. To what height does it rebound? How many bounces until height < h/10? Solution: Rebound height h₁ = e²h. After n bounces: h_n = e^(2n)h. For h_n < h/10: e^(2n) < 0.1 → 2n ln e < ln 0.1 → n > ln(0.1)/(2 ln e). If e = 0.8: n > -2.3/(-0.44) = 5.2 → 6 bounces.

Two particles of mass m approach each other with equal speeds u in a perfectly elastic collision. One is deflected by 60° from its original direction. Find the final speeds. Solution: In CM frame, total momentum = 0. Elastic collision: speeds unchanged, only directions change. Initial CM speed = u. After: each has speed u. Angle between final velocities = 180° in CM frame. In lab frame, the deflection angle depends on initial configuration.

A golf club (m = 0.2 kg) moving at 50 m/s strikes a ball (m = 0.046 kg) at rest. e = 0.8. Find ball speed after impact. Solution: u₁ = 50, u₂ = 0. v₂ = (1+e)m₁u₁/(m₁+m₂) = 1.8×0.2×50/0.246 = 18/0.246 = 73.2 m/s. The ball travels faster than the club! This is why golf balls go so fast. v₁ = m₁u₁/m₁+m₂ × (1 - e×m₂/m₁) ≈ 40 m/s.
universalFacts: The coefficient of restitution e was introduced by Newton in the Principia. For elastic collisions, e = 1, and the relative velocity of separation equals the relative velocity of approach. This is a consequence of both momentum and kinetic energy conservation.

In any isolated system, total momentum is ALWAYS conserved (if no external forces). Kinetic energy is NOT always conserved. The only perfectly elastic collisions in nature are between fundamental particles (or at the atomic/molecular level where quantum mechanics makes collisions elastic).

In a perfectly inelastic collision, the maximum possible kinetic energy loss is ΔK_max = -½ μ v_rel², where μ = m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂) is the reduced mass. This is the kinetic energy in the center-of-mass frame, which is entirely lost as heat.

Newton's cradle works because the collisions between identical spheres are nearly elastic, and the equal-mass exchange property (v₁ = u₂, v₂ = u₁) transfers momentum and energy cleanly from one end to the other.

The classification of collisions (elastic, inelastic, perfectly inelastic) is an idealization. Real collisions have 0 < e < 1. The value of e depends on the materials: rubber on concrete e ≈ 0.8, steel on steel e ≈ 0.9, glass on glass e ≈ 0.6, putty e ≈ 0.

Perfectly inelastic: A 3 kg ball at 4 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg ball. They stick together. Common velocity = (3×4 + 0)/(3+1) = 3 m/s. KE lost = ½×3×16 − ½×4×9 = 24 − 18 = 6 J.
Coefficient of restitution: A ball dropped from 5 m rebounds to 3.2 m. e = √(3.2/5) = 0.8.
Golf club: A 0.2 kg club at 50 m/s hits a 0.046 kg ball at rest (e = 0.8). Ball speed = 73.2 m/s (faster than the club!).
Newton's cradle: Pull one ball, release — one ball flies out the other end at the same speed. Pull two balls, two fly out.

data.topicTitle: Work Done by Constant and Variable Force

notes: **Work done by a constant force:** W = F·d·cos θ = Fd cos θ, where F is the magnitude of the force, d is the displacement, and θ is the angle between the force and displacement vectors. Work is a scalar quantity (SI unit: joule, J = N·m). Work is positive when the force has a component in the direction of displacement (θ < 90°), negative when opposite (θ > 90°), and zero when perpendicular (θ = 90°).

**Work done by a variable force:** when force varies with position, work is the area under the F-x graph, or mathematically, W = ∫ F(x) dx from x₁ to x₂. For a spring force F = −kx, the work done by the spring when stretched from x₁ to x₂ is W = ½k(x₁² − x₂²).

**Work-energy theorem:** the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy: W_net = ΔK = ½mv² − ½mu². This is one of the most powerful results in mechanics — it connects forces (through work) to motion (through kinetic energy).

**Work done by gravity:** W_g = mgΔh = mg(h_i − h_f), where Δh is the change in height. Gravity does positive work when the body falls (h decreases) and negative work when it rises (h increases). The work done by gravity is independent of the path — only the vertical displacement matters.

**Work done by a spring:** W_s = ½kx² (work done ON the spring to stretch/compress it by x). The spring does work W = ½k(x_i² − x_f²) when it returns from x_i to x_f. At the natural length (x = 0), the spring does maximum work.

**Work done by friction:** W_f = −f_k·d = −μ_k·N·d. Friction always does negative work (it opposes motion), converting mechanical energy into heat. The work depends on the path length d, not just the displacement — friction is non-conservative.

**Zero work situations:** (1) Force perpendicular to displacement (e.g., normal force on a horizontal surface, centripetal force in circular motion). (2) No displacement (pushing a wall). (3) Force applied to a body that doesn't move.

**NEB exam focus:** work done by constant force (W = Fd cos θ), work done by a spring (W = ½kx²), work-energy theorem (W_net = ΔK), area under F-x graph for variable forces, and identifying zero-work situations.
confusion: ❌ 'Work and energy are different concepts.' ✅ Work is a TRANSFER of energy. When you do work on a body, you transfer energy to it. The work-energy theorem (W_net = ΔK) makes this precise.
❌ 'Work is a vector because force and displacement are vectors.' ✅ Work is a SCALAR — it is the dot product of force and displacement (W = F·d·cos θ). It has magnitude but no direction.

❌ 'If a body moves, work must be done.' ✅ Work is done only if the force has a component along the displacement. Centripetal force does zero work in circular motion (always perpendicular to velocity).
❌ 'Work done by gravity depends on the path.' ✅ Gravity is a conservative force — work depends only on the vertical displacement (mgΔh), not on the path taken.
❌ 'A spring does work W = ½kx² when stretched by x.' ✅ The work done ON the spring to stretch it is ½kx². The work done BY the spring when it returns is also ½kx² (energy is recovered).
❌ 'Friction always does negative work.' ✅ Static friction can do positive work — e.g., the static friction on your feet pushes you forward when walking. Kinetic friction always does negative work.

**Zero work situations:** (1) Force perpendicular to displacement (e.g., normal force on a horizontal surface, centripetal force in circular motion). (2) No displacement (pushing a wall). (3) Force applied to a body that doesn't move.

data.title: Power
notes: Power is the rate of energy transfer: average P=ΔW/Δt and instantaneous P=dW/dt. Its SI unit is watt, 1 W=1 J s⁻¹.
For translation, dW=F⃗·dr⃗ gives P=F⃗·v⃗=Fv cosθ. Only the force component parallel to velocity transfers energy; a perpendicular centripetal force does no work in uniform circular motion.

Worked example: a 200 kg load rises steadily at 0.50 m s⁻¹. The lifting force is mg=1960 N for g=9.8 m s⁻², so useful power is Fv=980 W. In 10 s the load rises 5 m and gains 9800 J, confirming P=W/t=980 W.
At constant speed, net power is zero because engine power balances resistive forces. For rotation, P=τ⃗·ω⃗; efficiency η=Pout/Pin distinguishes useful output from input.
A 50 N force at 60° to a crate moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ transfers energy at P=50×3×cos60°=75 W, not 150 W.

Power is the rate of doing work. When a force stays along the velocity, power is the force times the speed. A larger engine can do the same work in less time, which is a larger power, not a larger store of energy.

data.title: Work-Energy Theorem

notes: **Work done by a constant force:** $W = Fd \cos \theta$, where $F$ is the magnitude of the force, $d$ is the displacement, and $\theta$ is the angle between the force and displacement vectors. Work is a scalar quantity (SI unit: joule, $J = N\cdot m$). Work is positive when the force has a component in the direction of displacement ($\theta < 90^\circ$), negative when opposite ($\theta > 90^\circ$), and zero when perpendicular ($\theta = 90^\circ$).

**Work done by a variable force:** when force varies with position, work is the area under the $F-x$ graph, or mathematically, $W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F(x) \, dx$. For a spring force $F = -kx$, the work done by the spring when stretched from $x_1$ to $x_2$ is $W = \frac{1}{2}k(x_1^2 - x_2^2)$.

**Work-energy theorem:** the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy: $W_{net} = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{1}{2}mu^2$. This is one of the most powerful results in mechanics — it connects forces (through work) to motion (through kinetic energy).

**Work done by gravity:** $W_g = mg\Delta h = mg(h_i - h_f)$, where $\Delta h$ is the change in height. Gravity does positive work when the body falls ($h$ decreases) and negative work when it rises ($h$ increases). The work done by gravity is independent of the path — only the vertical displacement matters.

**Work done by a spring:** $W_s = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$ (work done ON the spring to stretch/compress it by $x$). The spring does work $W = \frac{1}{2}k(x_i^2 - x_f^2)$ when it returns from $x_i$ to $x_f$. At the natural length ($x = 0$), the spring does maximum work.

**Work done by friction:** $W_f = -f_k\cdot d = -\mu_k\cdot N\cdot d$. Friction always does negative work (it opposes motion), converting mechanical energy into heat. The work depends on the path length $d$, not just the displacement — friction is non-conservative.

**Zero work situations:** (1) Force perpendicular to displacement (e.g., normal force on a horizontal surface, centripetal force in circular motion). (2) No displacement (pushing a wall). (3) Force applied to a body that doesn't move.

notes: **Work done by a constant force:** $W = Fd \cos \theta$, where $F$ is the magnitude of the force, $d$ is the displacement, and $\theta$ is the angle between the force and displacement vectors. Work is a scalar quantity (SI unit: joule, $J = N\cdot m$). Work is positive when the force has a component in the direction of displacement ($\theta < 90^\circ$), negative when opposite ($\theta > 90^\circ$), and zero when perpendicular ($\theta = 90^\circ$).

**Work done by a variable force:** when force varies with position, work is the area under the $F-x$ graph, or mathematically, $W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F(x) \, dx$. For a spring force $F = -kx$, the work done by the spring when stretched from $x_1$ to $x_2$ is $W = \frac{1}{2}k(x_1^2 - x_2^2)$.

**Work-energy theorem:** the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy: $W_{net} = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{1}{2}mu^2$. This is one of the most powerful results in mechanics — it connects forces (through work) to motion (through kinetic energy).

**Work done by gravity:** $W_g = mg\Delta h = mg(h_i - h_f)$, where $\Delta h$ is the change in height. Gravity does positive work when the body falls ($h$ decreases) and negative work when it rises ($h$ increases). The work done by gravity is independent of the path — only the vertical displacement matters.

**Work done by a spring:** $W_s = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$ (work done ON the spring to stretch/compress it by $x$). The spring does work $W = \frac{1}{2}k(x_i^2 - x_f^2)$ when it returns from $x_i$ to $x_f$. At the natural length ($x = 0$), the spring does maximum work.

**Work done by friction:** $W_f = -f_k\cdot d = -\mu_k\cdot N\cdot d$. Friction always does negative work (it opposes motion), converting mechanical energy into heat. The work depends on the path length $d$, not just the displacement — friction is non-conservative.

**Zero work situations:** (1) Force perpendicular to displacement (e.g., normal force on a horizontal surface, centripetal force in circular motion). (2) No displacement (pushing a wall). (3) Force applied to a body that doesn't move.

**NEB exam focus:** work done by constant force ($W = Fd \cos \theta$), work done by a spring ($W = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$), work-energy theorem ($W_{net} = \Delta K$), area under $F-x$ graph for variable forces, and identifying zero-work situations.

data.title: Cell Biology & Biomolecules
notes: **Cell theory:** all living organisms are composed of cells; the cell is the structural and functional unit of life; all cells arise from pre-existing cells (Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow).
**Prokaryotic vs eukaryotic cells:** prokaryotes lack a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles (bacteria); eukaryotes have a nucleus and organelles such as mitochondria, ER, Golgi bodies.
**Mitochondrion:** powerhouse of the cell — site of aerobic respiration and ATP synthesis; has its own circular DNA (semi-autonomous organelle).

**Biomolecules:** carbohydrates (energy source; glucose C₆H₁₂O₆), proteins (made of amino acids joined by peptide bonds), lipids (fats/oils; concentrated energy store), nucleic acids (DNA/RNA carry hereditary information).
**Enzymes** are globular protein catalysts that speed up biochemical reactions by lowering activation energy; they are substrate-specific and work best at optimum temperature and pH.
confusion: ❌ 'Prokaryotes lack all organelles.' ✅ They lack *membrane-bound* organelles (nucleus, mitochondria), but possess non-membrane-bound organelles like ribosomes.
❌ 'Nucleotide and nucleoside are the same.' ✅ Nucleotide = Nucleoside (sugar + base) + Phosphate. Nucleoside lacks the phosphate group.
❌ 'Enzymes are consumed in the reaction.' ✅ Enzymes are catalysts; they speed up reactions by lowering activation energy but are NOT consumed (they are regenerated).
❌ 'Mitochondria are purely eukaryotic.' ✅ While found in eukaryotes, their circular DNA and structure suggest an endosymbiotic origin related to prokaryotes.

data.title: Faunal Diversity, Evolution & Environment
notes: **Porifera (sponges):** pore-bearing aquatic animals with canal system; skeleton of spicules.
**Arthropoda:** largest phylum — jointed legs, chitinous exoskeleton, open circulatory system (insects, crabs).
**Chordata characters:** notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits and post-anal tail at some stage of life.

**Oparin–Haldane theory:** life originated from non-living organic molecules in the primitive reducing atmosphere ('primordial soup'); Miller–Urey experiment (1953) supported it by producing amino acids from CH₄, NH₃, H₂, H₂O with electric discharge.
**Darwinism:** natural selection — survival of the fittest; variations that help survival are inherited.

**Ecology levels:** organism → population → community → ecosystem → biome. Food chain shows energy flow; ~10% energy transfers to each trophic level. **Conservation:** in-situ (national parks) and ex-situ (zoos, seed banks).
confusion: ❌ 'Natural selection means the physically strongest survive.' ✅ Natural selection means the 'fittest'—those best *adapted* to the current environment—survive and reproduce.
❌ 'Energy in a food chain is destroyed at each step.' ✅ Energy is *transformed* (largely into heat) per the 10% law, not destroyed (conservation of energy applies).
❌ 'Humans evolved directly from monkeys seen today.' ✅ Humans and modern monkeys share a common ancestor; humans did not evolve from the monkeys seen today.

data.title: Floral Diversity & Microbiology
notes: **Binomial nomenclature** was introduced by Carolus Linnaeus — every organism gets two names: generic name + specific epithet (e.g. Mangifera indica).
**Five kingdom classification (Whittaker):** Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia — based on cell structure, body organisation and nutrition.

**Algae:** chlorophyll-bearing, aquatic thalloid organisms; green algae (Spirogyra) have ribbon-shaped spiral chloroplasts; brown algae (Laminaria) have fucoxanthin; red algae (Polysiphonia) contain r-phycoerythrin.
**Bryophytes:** amphibians of the plant kingdom; need water for fertilisation; e.g. mosses and liverworts.
**Bacteria:** prokaryotic, reproduce by binary fission; useful forms fix nitrogen (Rhizobium) and ferment milk into curd (Lactobacillus).
**Virus:** acellular obligate parasite with DNA or RNA core and protein coat (capsid); e.g. TMV, HIV.
**Fungi:** heterotrophic, cell wall of chitin; yeast is unicellular and used in fermentation; Penicillium gives the antibiotic penicillin.
confusion: ❌ 'All bacteria are harmful.' ✅ Many (e.g., Rhizobium, Lactobacillus) are essential for nitrogen fixation, food fermentation, and gut/health functions.
❌ 'Fungi are plants.' ✅ Fungi are heterotrophic, have cell walls made of *chitin* (not cellulose like plants), and lack chlorophyll.
❌ 'Viruses are living cells.' ✅ They are acellular, obligate parasites that only show life characteristics (like replication) *inside* a host cell.
❌ 'Bryophytes are ferns.' ✅ Bryophytes (mosses) are *non-vascular* (lack xylem/phloem) and reproduce by spores; ferns are *vascular* plants.

data.title: Atomic Structure
notes: **Dalton's atomic theory:** matter consists of indivisible atoms; atoms of an element are identical in mass and properties; compounds form by combination of atoms in fixed ratios.

**Sub-atomic particles:** electron (e⁻, discovered by J.J. Thomson, charge −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mass ≈ 1/1837 u); proton (p⁺, Goldstein/Rutherford, +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 1 u); neutron (n, Chadwick, neutral, 1 u).

**Bohr's model:** electrons revolve in fixed circular orbits (stationary states) with quantised angular momentum mvr = nh/2π; energy is emitted/absorbed only when an electron jumps between orbits: ΔE = hν. Radius rₙ = 0.529 n²/Z Å; energy E_n = −13.6 Z²/n² eV.

**Defects of Bohr's model:** cannot explain spectra of multi-electron atoms, fine structure (splitting of spectral lines), Zeeman and Stark effects, and the dual nature/wave character of the electron (de Broglie) or Heisenberg's uncertainty principle.

**Quantum numbers:** principal (n), azimuthal (l = 0 … n−1: s, p, d, f), magnetic (m_l = −l … +l) and spin (m_s = ±½). **Pauli exclusion:** no two electrons in an atom have identical sets of four quantum numbers. **Hund's rule** and Aufbau principle govern filling order.
confusion: ❌ 'Bohr orbits are the same as orbitals.' ✅ Orbits are 2D fixed circular paths; orbitals are 3D regions in space where electron finding probability is high.
❌ 'Only s-orbitals are spherical.' ✅ Yes, s-orbitals are spherical; p-orbitals are dumbbell-shaped; d-orbitals have complex double-dumbbell shapes.
❌ 'An electron in an atom jumps orbits without emitting/absorbing energy.' ✅ Bohr's model states energy change (ΔE = hν) *must* occur for any orbital jump.
❌ 'Principal quantum number n tells about energy only.' ✅ n primarily dictates size and energy, while l dictates shape.

data.title: Chemical Bonding & Shapes of Molecules (VSEPR)
notes: **Ionic bond:** electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed by transfer of electrons (e.g. NaCl). High melting point, conducts electricity in molten/solution state.
**Covalent bond:** mutual sharing of electron pairs (e.g. H₂, CH₄). Directional; low melting/boiling point compared with ionic solids.
**Coordinate (dative) bond:** shared pair donated by one atom only (e.g. NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺).

**VSEPR theory:** electron pairs around the central atom repel each other and arrange to be as far apart as possible. Repulsion order: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair.

Shapes: AX₂ linear (BeCl₂), AX₃ trigonal planar (BF₃), AX₄ tetrahedral (CH₄), AX₃E pyramidal (NH₃, 107°), AX₂E₂ bent (H₂O, 104.5°), AX₅ trigonal bipyramidal (PCl₅), AX₆ octahedral (SF₆).

**Hybridisation:** intermixing of orbitals of comparable energy to form equivalent hybrid orbitals — sp (linear, 180°), sp² (trigonal planar, 120°), sp³ (tetrahedral, 109.5°), sp³d (trigonal bipyramidal), sp³d² (octahedral).
confusion: ❌ 'Ionic bonds are always stronger than covalent bonds.' ✅ Ionic bonds are strong in crystal lattices, but covalent bonds can be stronger in individual molecules (e.g., C≡C triple bond is very strong).
❌ 'VSEPR considers all electron pairs equally.' ✅ VSEPR accounts for different repulsion strengths: lp-lp > lp-bp > bp-bp, which distorts bond angles from ideal values.
❌ 'NH₃ is trigonal planar because it has 3 bond pairs.' ✅ NH₃ has 3 bp + 1 lp → tetrahedral electron geometry, but molecular shape is PYRAMIDAL (not planar) due to the lone pair.
❌ 'Hybridisation determines geometry; geometry determines hybridisation.' ✅ Hybridisation is a model used to *explain* observed geometries; it is not a physical process that happens before bonding.

data.title: Chemical Equilibrium & Organic Fundamentals
notes: **Chemical equilibrium:** the stage at which rate of forward reaction equals rate of backward reaction; concentrations remain constant. Dynamic in nature.
**Le Chatelier's principle:** if a system at equilibrium is disturbed by changing concentration, pressure or temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that opposes the change.
**Equilibrium constant K_c** = [products]^coeff / [reactants]^coeff. For gas reactions K_p = K_c(RT)^Δn.
**Acids & bases (Bronsted-Lowry):** acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor. pH = −log[H⁺]; pH + pOH = 14.

**Organic chemistry basics:** catenation, tetravalency of carbon, homologous series, functional groups, isomerism (chain, position, functional), IUPAC nomenclature rules for alkanes/alkenes/alkynes and simple derivatives.
confusion: ❌ 'Equilibrium means equal amounts of reactants and products.' ✅ Equilibrium means *constant* concentrations, not equal ones. The position of equilibrium depends on K, which can heavily favour either side.
❌ 'Le Chatelier's principle shifts equilibrium to re-establish old rates.' ✅ It shifts to oppose the *change in conditions* (concentration, pressure, temperature), not to restore old rates.
❌ 'K changes when concentration or pressure changes.' ✅ K is constant at a given temperature. Only temperature changes alter the value of K.
❌ 'Catenation is unique to carbon.' ✅ Carbon shows the *greatest* catenation, but silicon and sulfur also exhibit it to lesser degrees.

data.title: Oxidation, Reduction & Redox Reactions
notes: **Oxidation:** loss of electrons / gain of oxygen / increase in oxidation number. **Reduction:** gain of electrons / loss of oxygen / decrease in oxidation number.
**Oxidising agent** accepts electrons (is reduced); **reducing agent** donates electrons (is oxidised).

**Oxidation number rules:** free element = 0; monatomic ion = its charge; O is usually −2 (−1 in peroxides); H is +1 with non-metals and −1 with metals; the sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral molecule is 0.
**Balancing redox equations** — ion-electron (half-reaction) method or oxidation-number method; in acidic medium balance O with H₂O and H with H⁺.
**Applications:** electrochemical cells, electrolysis, corrosion, bleaching and titrations (redox titrations of KMnO₄/K₂Cr₂O₇).
confusion: ❌ 'Oxidation always involves oxygen.' ✅ Modern definition: oxidation is loss of electrons or increase in oxidation number — oxygen need not be involved.
❌ 'The oxidising agent gets oxidised.' ✅ The oxidising agent accepts electrons and is therefore REDUCED. The reducing agent is oxidised.
❌ 'Oxygen always has oxidation number −2.' ✅ Almost always −2, but −1 in peroxides (H₂O₂), +2 in OF₂, and 0 in O₂.

❌ 'A reaction with no visible colour change cannot be redox.' ✅ Many redox reactions are colourless (e.g., Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu has visible change, but H⁺ + OH⁻ is not redox — check oxidation numbers, not appearance).

data.title: Periodic Table
notes: Modern periodic law: properties are periodic functions of atomic number.
s-block: groups 1-2; p-block: groups 13-18; d-block: groups 3-12.
Trends: atomic radius decreases across a period, increases down a group.
Ionization energy increases across a period; electronegativity follows the same pattern.

data.title: States of Matter (Gaseous State)
notes: **Boyle's law:** at constant T, V ∝ 1/P. **Charles' law:** at constant P, V ∝ T. **Avogadro's law:** equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules at same T and P.
**Ideal gas equation:** PV = nRT, R = 0.0821 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

**Kinetic theory of gases:** molecules are in continuous random motion; collisions are perfectly elastic; volume of molecules is negligible compared with the container; no intermolecular attraction; average KE ∝ absolute temperature.
**Graham's law of diffusion:** rate of diffusion ∝ 1/√(molar mass).
**Real gases** deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressure and low temperature; van der Waals equation corrects for molecular volume and attraction.
confusion: ❌ 'Ideal gases exist in reality.' ✅ Ideal gas is a theoretical model. Real gases approximate ideal behaviour at high temperature and low pressure where intermolecular forces are negligible.

❌ 'Boyle's law and Charles' law apply to real gases under all conditions.' ✅ They are exact only for ideal gases. Real gases deviate at high pressure/low temperature (described by van der Waals equation).

❌ 'Graham's law applies to rate of effusion but not diffusion.' ✅ Graham's law applies to both effusion (through a pinhole) and diffusion, though diffusion is more complex due to molecular collisions.
❌ 'At 0 K, all molecular motion stops completely.' ✅ At absolute zero, translational motion ceases but zero-point quantum energy remains. Also, no real gas reaches 0 K.

data.title: Basic Concepts of Chemistry & Stoichiometry
notes: **Mole:** the amount of substance containing as many particles (atoms, molecules, ions) as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12. One mole = **6.022 × 10²³** particles (Avogadro's number, N_A).
**Molar mass:** mass of one mole of a substance in grams; numerically equal to its molecular/atomic weight. n = given mass / molar mass.
**Laws of chemical combination:** law of conservation of mass, law of definite (constant) proportions, law of multiple proportions and Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes.
**Empirical formula** gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; **molecular formula** = n × empirical formula where n = molecular mass / empirical formula mass.
**Limiting reagent:** the reactant that is completely consumed first and therefore limits the amount of product formed.
**Percentage yield:** (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100.
confusion: ❌ 'One mole of any substance has the same mass.' ✅ One mole has the same NUMBER of particles (6.022 × 10²³), but different masses depending on molar mass (e.g., 1 mol H₂ = 2 g, 1 mol O₂ = 32 g).

❌ 'Empirical and molecular formulas are always the same.' ✅ Empirical formula is the simplest ratio; molecular formula is the actual count. They differ when n > 1 (e.g., empirical CH₂, molecular C₆H₁₂).

❌ 'The limiting reagent determines the mass of all products equally.' ✅ The limiting reagent determines the maximum amount of *each* product formed, but different products have different molar ratios from the balanced equation.
❌ 'Percentage yield can exceed 100%.' ✅ Theoretical yield is the maximum possible. Yield > 100% indicates impure product or incomplete drying, not an error in calculation.

data.title: Q: 12 g of carbon reacts with 32 g of hydrogen to produce 44 g of methane — which chemical law do these data illustrate?
notes: Reactants: carbon (12 g) + hydrogen (32 g)
Total mass of reactants = 12 + 32 = 44 g
Total mass of product (methane) = 44 g
Since the mass before the reaction (44 g) equals the mass after (44 g), mass is neither created nor destroyed
**Answer: this illustrates the Law of Conservation of Mass**

data.title: Q: 20 g of CaCO₃ is heated and produces 11.2 g of CaO — calculate the weight of CO₂ produced
notes: Reaction: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂
By the Law of Conservation of Mass: mass of CaCO₃ = mass of CaO + mass of CO₂
20 g = 11.2 g + mass of CO₂
**Answer: mass of CO₂ = 20 − 11.2 = 8.8 g**

data.title: Q: 6.3 g of NaHCO₃ added to 10 g of HCl solution leaves a 12 g residue — what is the mass of CO₂ released?
notes: Reaction: NaHCO₃ + HCl → Residue + CO₂↑
Total mass of reactants: 6.3 g (NaHCO₃) + 10 g (HCl) = 16.3 g
By the Law of Conservation of Mass: total mass of reactants = total mass of products
16.3 g = 12 g + mass of CO₂
**Answer: mass of CO₂ = 16.3 − 12 = 4.3 g**

data.title: Q: Two samples of common salt contain different masses of chlorine — show these results agree with the law of constant proportion
notes: **Data:** 0.25 g of sample 1 contains 0.1518 g of chlorine; 0.24 g of sample 2 contains 0.1458 g of chlorine
Since the percentage of chlorine is nearly identical in both samples (≈ 60.7%), regardless of sample size, this confirms the **Law of Constant (Definite) Proportion**

data.title: Q: Two copper oxide reduction experiments — show they illustrate the law of definite proportions
notes: **Experiment 1:** 1.375 g of CuO is reduced to 1.098 g of copper by dry hydrogen gas
**Experiment 2:** 1.179 g of metallic copper is formed from 1.476 g of copper oxide
The percentage of copper is essentially constant (≈ 79.9%) across both experiments, verifying the **Law of Definite Proportions**

data.title: Q: Determine the weight of oxide formed by heating 1 g of a carbonate (using the law of definite proportions)
notes: **Data:** 0.36 g of a metal burnt in oxygen yields 0.60 g of oxide; the carbonate of that metal contains 28.57% of the metal
From the oxide experiment: mass of metal = 0.36 g, mass of oxide = 0.60 g → ratio (mass of metal)/(mass of oxide) = 0.36/0.60 = **0.6**
From the carbonate experiment: 1 g of carbonate contains 28.57% metal → mass of metal in 1 g carbonate = 0.2857 g
By the Law of Definite Proportions, the metal-to-oxide ratio stays fixed at 0.6, so: 0.2857 / (mass of oxide) = 0.6
Mass of oxide = 0.2857 / 0.6
**Answer: mass of oxide = 0.4762 g**

data.title: Q: Hydrogen and oxygen react separately to give H₂O₂ and H₂O — what law of stoichiometry is illustrated?
notes: Two elements (hydrogen and oxygen) combine to form more than one compound: H₂O and H₂O₂
For a fixed mass of hydrogen (2 g), the masses of oxygen that combine are 16 g (in H₂O) and 32 g (in H₂O₂)
Ratio of oxygen masses = 16 : 32 = **1 : 2** — a simple whole-number ratio
**Answer: this illustrates the Law of Multiple Proportions**

data.title: Q: A metal forms two oxides (11.9% and 21.2% oxygen) — show these data illustrate the law of multiple proportions
notes: Oxide 1: oxygen = 11.9%, metal = 100 − 11.9 = 88.1% → mass of oxygen combined with 1 g of metal = 11.9/88.1 = **0.135 g**
Oxide 2: oxygen = 21.2%, metal = 100 − 21.2 = 78.8% → mass of oxygen combined with 1 g of metal = 21.2/78.8 = **0.269 g**
Ratio of oxygen combining with a fixed mass (1 g) of metal: 0.135 : 0.269 ≈ **1 : 2**
Since 1:2 is a simple whole-number ratio, this confirms the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

data.title: Q: Element X forms three binary compounds with chlorine (50.08%, 66.73%, 74.95% Cl) — show how these illustrate the law of multiple proportions
notes: Compound 1: Cl = 50.08%, X = 49.92% → mass of Cl per gram of X = 50.08/49.92 = **1.003 g**
Compound 2: Cl = 66.73%, X = 33.27% → mass of Cl per gram of X = 66.73/33.27 = **2.006 g**
Compound 3: Cl = 74.95%, X = 25.05% → mass of Cl per gram of X = 74.95/25.05 = **2.992 g**
Ratio of chlorine masses combining with a fixed mass of X: 1.003 : 2.006 : 2.992 ≈ **1 : 2 : 3**
The simple whole-number ratio confirms the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

data.title: Q: Four hydrocarbons with % compositions (C 75%/H 25%, C 80%/H 20%, C 85.7%/H 14.3%, C 92.3%/H 7.7%) — prove the law of multiple proportions
notes: Find the mass of hydrogen combining with a fixed mass (1 g) of carbon in each: (a) 25/75 = 0.333 g; (b) 20/80 = 0.250 g; (c) 14.3/85.7 = 0.167 g; (d) 7.7/92.3 = 0.083 g
**Ratio of hydrogen masses = 4 : 3 : 2 : 1**
This simple whole-number ratio proves the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

data.title: Q: Three oxides of lead reduced in hydrogen — show this illustrates the law of multiple proportions
notes: **Data:** (i) 1.393 g of litharge gave 1.293 g of lead; (ii) 2.173 g of lead peroxide gave 1.882 g of lead; (iii) 1.712 g of red lead gave 1.552 g of lead
Find the mass of oxygen in each oxide by subtracting the lead mass from the total oxide mass: (i) 1.393 − 1.293 = 0.100 g; (ii) 2.173 − 1.882 = 0.291 g; (iii) 1.712 − 1.552 = 0.160 g
Find the mass of Pb combining with 1 g of O in each: (i) 1.293/0.100 = 12.93 g; (ii) 1.882/0.291 = 6.467 g; (iii) 1.552/0.160 = 9.700 g
Ratio: 12.93 : 6.467 : 9.700 — dividing all terms by 6.467 gives 2 : 1 : 1.5
Clearing the decimal by multiplying by 2: **4 : 2 : 3**
This simple whole-number ratio validates the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

data.title: Q: Nitrogen forms five oxides with oxygen (0.572 g, 1.14 g, 1.73 g, 2.28 g, 2.85 g of O per 1.09 g of N) — show how these illustrate the law of multiple proportions
notes: Fixed mass of nitrogen = 1.09 g in all five oxides
**Ratio of oxygen masses = 1 : 2 : 3 : 4 : 5**
This simple whole-number ratio illustrates the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

data.title: Q: State the observations and conclusions of Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment
notes: **Observation 1:** most α-particles passed straight through the gold foil undeflected → most of the atom's volume is empty space

**Observation 2:** a small fraction were deflected at large angles, and a very small fraction bounced almost straight back → these particles must have encountered something small, dense, and positively charged
**Conclusion:** the atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre, with electrons occupying the mostly empty space around it

data.title: Q: Why does Rutherford's nuclear model fail to explain the stability of an atom?
notes: Maxwell's theory states that any accelerating charge radiates electromagnetic energy
An electron orbiting the nucleus is constantly changing direction, so it is constantly accelerating, and by Maxwell's theory it should continuously lose energy as radiation

Losing energy means the electron's orbital radius should shrink, causing it to spiral inward and collapse into the nucleus within a fraction of a second — but real atoms are stable, which Rutherford's model cannot account for

data.title: Q: How exactly did Bohr's model resolve the stability crisis left unsolved by Rutherford?
notes: Bohr proposed that electrons can only exist in specific 'stationary' orbits where they do NOT radiate energy, regardless of their acceleration — this postulate directly overrides the classical prediction that orbiting charges must radiate
Energy changes only happen in discrete jumps between these fixed orbits (ΔE = hν), not continuously, so there's no mechanism for a gradual energy loss and inward spiral

data.title: Q: Bohr's model works well for hydrogen but fails for helium — why does adding one more electron break the model?
notes: Bohr's postulates and resulting equations were derived by balancing the electrostatic attraction between a single electron and the nucleus against the centripetal force needed for circular motion — a clean two-body problem

With two or more electrons, electron–electron repulsion enters the picture, making it a multi-body problem that Bohr's simple circular-orbit model has no mechanism to account for — this is why it accurately predicts the spectra of H, He⁺, and Li²⁺ (all single-electron species) but not neutral He or heavier atoms

data.title: Q: What do the Zeeman and Stark effects reveal about the limits of Bohr's model?
notes: **Zeeman Effect:** spectral lines split into multiple closely spaced lines when the atom is placed in a magnetic field
**Stark Effect:** spectral lines split when the atom is placed in an electric field

Bohr's model treats each orbit as having a single fixed energy, so it cannot explain why a magnetic or electric field would split a single spectral line into several — this splitting requires additional quantum numbers (like the magnetic quantum number) that only came with the more advanced quantum mechanical model of the atom

data.title: Q: State the three main observations of Rutherford's gold foil experiment and their corresponding conclusions
notes: **Observation 1:** most α-particles passed straight through the foil undeflected → **Conclusion:** atoms are mostly empty space

**Observation 2:** a small fraction were deflected through small-to-moderate angles → **Conclusion:** there is a concentration of positive charge somewhere in the atom that repels the positively charged α-particles

**Observation 3:** a very small fraction (about 1 in 8000) bounced back at large angles, close to 180° → **Conclusion:** this positive charge, along with almost all of the atom's mass, is concentrated in an extremely small volume — the nucleus

data.title: Q (worked example): Calculate the radius of the electron in the 2nd orbit of a Li²⁺ ion
notes: Bohr radius formula: r_n = (0.529 Å)·n²/Z, where n = orbit number and Z = atomic number
For Li²⁺: Z = 3, n = 2
**Answer: r₂ ≈ 0.705 Å**

data.title: Q (worked example): Calculate the wavelength of the series limit of the Lyman series for hydrogen
notes: The series limit occurs as n₂ → ∞, so 1/λ = R_H(1/n₁² − 0) = R_H/n₁²
For the Lyman series, n₁ = 1: 1/λ = 1.097 × 10⁷ × 1 = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹
**Answer: λ ≈ 91.15 nm** — deep ultraviolet, consistent with the Lyman series being a UV series

data.title: Q: Which hydrogen spectral series falls entirely within the visible region of light, and why is it the only one?
notes: The **Balmer series** (n₁ = 2) is the only series entirely visible to the human eye
Its emitted wavelengths (transitions from n₂ = 3, 4, 5... down to n₁ = 2) happen to fall in the roughly 400–700 nm range that human eyes detect

The Lyman series (n₁ = 1) is higher-energy and shorter-wavelength (ultraviolet), while Paschen, Brackett, and Pfund (n₁ = 3, 4, 5) are lower-energy and longer-wavelength (infrared) — both fall outside the visible window

data.title: Self-Practice Checkpoint — Negative Energy & Bohr Critique (Page 108)
notes: **Q1. Why is the energy of an electron in a Bohr orbit taken as negative?** Because the electron is bound to the nucleus; energy must be supplied to remove it. The most negative energy corresponds to the most stable (lowest) orbit, n = 1.

**Q2. State two major defects of Bohr's atomic model.** (1) It could not explain why only certain orbits are allowed (quantization was assumed, not derived). (2) It could not explain the spectra of atoms with more than one electron (e.g. helium), nor the fine structure of spectral lines.

**Q3. What is the significance of E = mc² in the development of quantum mechanics?** It links mass and energy, and combined with Planck's E = hν it leads to the de Broglie relation λ = h/(mv), showing that matter has wave-like properties.

**Q4. How did Schrödinger's 1926 work shift the atomic model?** Schrödinger replaced Bohr's definite circular orbits with a wave equation whose solutions (wave functions ψ) describe the electron's behaviour in three dimensions, giving rise to the probabilistic orbital concept.

data.title: Self-Practice Checkpoint — Duality & Principle Deflections (Page 111)
notes: **Q1. Distinguish between an orbit and an orbital.** An orbit is a definite circular path of the electron (Bohr model), planar and described by one quantum number n. An orbital is a three-dimensional region of high probability of finding the electron (quantum mechanics), described by three quantum numbers (n, l, m) and obeying the uncertainty principle.

**Q2. What is the physical significance of the wave function ψ and of ψ²?** ψ itself has no direct physical meaning; ψ² gives the probability density of finding the electron in a small volume around a point, which is used to map the electron cloud.

**Q3. Why did the wave-mechanical model replace Bohr's definite orbits?** Because the uncertainty principle forbids knowing position and momentum simultaneously, a definite orbit is impossible; the electron must instead be described by a probability distribution (orbital).

data.title: Self-Practice Checkpoint — Numerical Verifications & Degeneracy Mappings (Page 114)
notes: **Q1. How many orbitals are present in the subshell with l = 2? What is its maximum electron capacity?** Number of orbitals = 2l + 1 = 2(2) + 1 = 5. Maximum electron capacity = 2(2l + 1) = 10. So the d subshell has 5 orbitals and holds up to 10 electrons.

**Q2. Write the four quantum numbers that completely describe an electron in the 3p orbital.** Principal n = 3, azimuthal l = 1, magnetic m = −1, 0 or +1 (three possible values), spin s = +½ or −½. Any one of the six possible combinations (3 values of m × 2 spins) describes an electron in 3p.

**Q3. How many degenerate orbitals are there in a p subshell, and why are they called degenerate?** There are three (pₓ, pᵧ, p_z). They have the same energy (they are degenerate) in the absence of an applied magnetic field.

**Q4. For the d subshell, verify the degeneracy mapping.** With l = 2, m takes the values +2, +1, 0, −1, −2, giving 2l + 1 = 5 degenerate orbitals; each holds 2 electrons, so the d subshell accommodates 10 electrons in total.

data.title: Q (worked examples): de Broglie Wavelength & Uncertainty Principle
notes: **Q1. Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving with a velocity of 6.6 × 10⁶ m/s.** Using λ = h/(mv) with h = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg and v = 6.6 × 10⁶ m/s: λ = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 6.6 × 10⁶) = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / 6.006 × 10⁻²⁴ ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.

**Q2. Why is the wave nature of a moving cricket ball (mass ≈ 0.15 kg) not observable?** Using λ = h/(mv), for even a small ball travelling at 30 m/s the wavelength is λ = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / (0.15 × 30) ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻³⁴ m — far smaller than the size of a nucleus and completely unobservable; the wavelength is negligible for macroscopic objects (λ ∝ 1/m).

**Q3. If the uncertainty in the position of an electron is 10⁻¹⁰ m, what is the minimum uncertainty in its velocity?** Using Δx · Δv ≥ h/(4πm): Δv = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / (4 × 3.14 × 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 10⁻¹⁰) = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / 1.143 × 10⁻³⁹ ≈ 5.8 × 10⁵ m/s.

**Q4. Explain why Bohr's definite orbits contradict the uncertainty principle.** A definite orbit requires both position and momentum to be exactly known at every instant, but Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π forbids simultaneous exact knowledge — so the electron cannot follow a sharply defined circular path.

data.title: Q (worked examples): Atomic Number, Mass Number & Isotopes
notes: **Q1. For the atom ₁₂Mg²⁴, find the number of protons, electrons and neutrons.** Atomic number Z = 12, so protons = 12 and electrons = 12 (neutral atom). Mass number A = 24, so neutrons = A − Z = 24 − 12 = 12.

**Q2. The magnesium ion Mg²⁺ has atomic number 12. How many protons and electrons does it contain?** Protons = Z = 12 (unchanged). Since the ion has lost 2 electrons, electrons = 12 − 2 = 10. Its atomic number remains 12.

**Q3. Protium (₁H¹), deuterium (₁H²) and tritium (₁H³) are isotopes. How do they differ?** All three have the same atomic number Z = 1 (one proton and one electron) but different mass numbers. Protium has 0 neutrons, deuterium has 1 neutron, and tritium has 2 neutrons. Protium is most abundant (99.98%), deuterium about 0.015%, and tritium only 10⁻¹⁵ % (radioactive).

**Q4. Show that ₁₈Ar⁴⁰, ₁₉K⁴⁰ and ₂₀Ca⁴⁰ are isobars.** All three atoms have the same mass number A = 40 but different atomic numbers (18, 19, 20). Hence they are isobars — atoms of different elements with the same mass number.

**Q5. Show that ₆C¹⁴, ₇N¹⁵ and ₈O¹⁶ are isotones.** For ₆C¹⁴: neutrons = 14 − 6 = 8. For ₇N¹⁵: neutrons = 15 − 7 = 8. For ₈O¹⁶: neutrons = 16 − 8 = 8. All have the same number of neutrons (8) but different atomic and mass numbers, hence they are isotones.

**Q6. Verify that ₁₉K³⁹ and ₉F¹⁹ are isodiaphers.** For ₁₉K³⁹: neutrons − protons = (39 − 19) − 19 = 20 − 19 = 1. For ₉F¹⁹: neutrons − protons = (19 − 9) − 9 = 10 − 9 = 1. Both have the same isotopic excess (1), hence they are isodiaphers.

data.title: Self-Practice — Rutherford's Model Diagnostic Questions (Page 102)
notes: **Q1. What experimental evidence led Rutherford to conclude that the nucleus of an atom contains the entire mass of the atom?** The fact that a minute fraction of alpha particles (about 1 in 20,000) were reflected back suffering a deflection of 180° shows that the nucleus must possess considerable mass — only a massive, dense centre could reflect alpha particles of considerable mass.

**Q2. What experimental evidence led Rutherford to conclude that the central part (nucleus) of an atom is positively charged?** Some alpha particles (about 1 in 10,000) were deflected by as much as 90° or even larger angles. Since alpha particles are positively charged, they could only be repelled by a positively charged centre — proving the nucleus is positively charged.

**Q3. What experimental evidence led Rutherford to conclude that the atom consists mostly of hollow or empty space?** The vast majority of alpha particles (about 99%) passed straight through the gold foil completely undeflected, showing that most of the space inside the atom is empty.

**Q4. What experimental evidence led Rutherford to conclude that the volume occupied by the nucleus is very small compared to the total volume of the atom?** Only a very small number of alpha particles (about 1 in 10,000) were deflected through 90° or larger angles, indicating that the positively charged centre (nucleus of radius 10⁻¹³ cm) occupies a tiny volume compared to the whole atom (radius 10⁻⁸ cm).

**Q5. Why did Rutherford select gold foil for the α-particle scattering experiment?** Gold can be beaten into an extremely thin sheet (0.00006 cm thickness), thin enough for alpha particles to pass through and interact with individual atoms; gold is also a heavy element with a highly charged nucleus, producing measurable deflections.

data.title: English Grammar & Composition Essentials
