data.title: Recombinant DNA Technology

visualization.desc: Recombinant DNA is two DNA molecules joined into one helix, then copied inside a host.

notes: Recombinant DNA is a DNA molecule made by joining DNA from two different sources. A useful gene is cut out of one molecule and sealed into a vector that can replicate in a host cell.

Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at short palindromic sites. EcoRI recognises 5'-GAATTC-3' and cuts between G and A, leaving 5'-AATT overhangs. Those overhangs are sticky ends. The same enzyme is used on the vector and on the foreign DNA so the ends match.

The host's own DNA is protected because those same sites are methylated. The enzyme's natural job is to cut unprotected DNA, such as a phage genome. In the lab that specificity is what makes the cut reproducible.

DNA ligase seals the nicks by forming phosphodiester bonds. Sticky-end joining is efficient. Blunt ends can be joined too, but much less readily. Ligase is the seal, and the restriction enzyme is the cut. They are not interchangeable.

The vector is usually a plasmid: circular, extra-chromosomal bacterial DNA with its own origin of replication. A cloning vector also needs a selectable marker, such as antibiotic resistance, and a site where the foreign DNA can be inserted. pBR322 carries ampicillin and tetracycline resistance genes and is the classic teaching plasmid.

The recombinant plasmid is taken up by a competent cell. Competence is arranged with cold calcium chloride or by electroporation. Cells that took up the plasmid are selected on the antibiotic. Cells without the plasmid die. That living colony is the clone that multiplies the insert.

data.title: Processes: PCR, Gel Electrophoresis

visualization.desc: PCR copies a chosen stretch of the double helix. Gel electrophoresis then sorts the copies by size.

notes: PCR makes many copies of one chosen stretch of DNA. It does not copy the whole genome unless the primers are aimed at the whole genome. Two primers mark the ends of the target.

Each cycle has three temperature steps. Near 94 °C the two strands separate. The heat replaces a helicase. Near 50 to 65 °C, depending on the primer, the primers bind. At 72 °C a thermostable polymerase extends the primers. Taq polymerase, from Thermus aquaticus, survives the hot step that would destroy an ordinary polymerase.
The tube must contain template DNA, two primers, dNTPs, Taq polymerase and magnesium ions. Miss any one and the reaction stops. Magnesium is a cofactor for the polymerase.

If every molecule is copied, the count follows N = N0 × 2^n. Ten cycles give 2^10 = 1024 copies from one molecule. Twenty cycles give about a million. Thirty cycles give about a billion. Real reactions slow down once primers or dNTPs run low.

Gel electrophoresis sorts the products by size. DNA is negatively charged, so it moves toward the anode in an agarose gel. Smaller fragments slip through the gel faster and travel farther. A lane of known sizes, the ladder, turns distance into a length.

A linear DNA with n restriction sites gives n + 1 bands if every site is cut. A circular plasmid with n sites gives n bands. The pattern of bands is a restriction map you can read. The DNA is seen after a stain that fluoresces under ultraviolet light.

data.topicTitle: Biotechnological applications in agriculture: Bt cotton, nematode-resistant tobacco

visualization.desc: Bt cotton and nematode-resistant tobacco both depend on a gene added to the plant's DNA.

notes: Bt cotton carries cry genes from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. The plant makes the Cry protein in its own tissues. Bollworm larvae that eat the leaf or the boll take the protein in with the meal.

Inside the bacterium the Cry protein is an inactive crystal. In the alkaline gut of a susceptible larva it dissolves and is cut into an active toxin. The toxin forms pores in the midgut lining and the larva dies. cryIAc and cryIIAb are the genes used against cotton bollworms.

The toxin is not a general insect killer. It needs that alkaline gut. Pollinators that do not eat the tissue, and insects whose guts do not activate the crystal, are not the target. The human stomach is acidic, and people do not have the insect midgut receptor the toxin uses.

A field of only Bt plants selects for larvae that survive the toxin. A refuge of non-Bt cotton, about a fifth of the area, lets susceptible insects survive and mate with resistant survivors. That mating dilutes resistance.

Nematode-resistant tobacco uses RNA interference against the root-knot nematode Meloidogyne incognita. Agrobacterium is used to put into the plant a DNA sequence that produces double-stranded RNA matching a gene the nematode needs.

When the nematode feeds on the root it takes up that RNA. The matching mRNA in the worm is silenced, so the nematode cannot develop properly in the root. The protection is gene silencing, not a protein crystal. Bt and this RNAi crop solve pest problems by different molecules.

Bt cotton carries cry genes from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. The plant makes the Cry protein in its own tissues. Bollworm larvae that eat the leaf or the boll take the protein in with the meal.

Inside the bacterium the Cry protein is an inactive crystal. In the alkaline gut of a susceptible larva it dissolves and is cut into an active toxin. The toxin forms pores in the midgut lining and the larva dies. cryIAc and cryIIAb are the genes used against cotton bollworms.

The toxin is not a general insect killer. It needs that alkaline gut. Pollinators that do not eat the tissue, and insects whose guts do not activate the crystal, are not the target. The human stomach is acidic, and people do not have the insect midgut receptor the toxin uses.

A field of only Bt plants selects for larvae that survive the toxin. A refuge of non-Bt cotton, about a fifth of the area, lets susceptible insects survive and mate with resistant survivors. That mating dilutes resistance.

Nematode-resistant tobacco uses RNA interference against the root-knot nematode Meloidogyne incognita. Agrobacterium is used to put into the plant a DNA sequence that produces double-stranded RNA matching a gene the nematode needs.

When the nematode feeds on the root it takes up that RNA. The matching mRNA in the worm is silenced, so the nematode cannot develop properly in the root. The protection is gene silencing, not a protein crystal. Bt and this RNAi crop solve pest problems by different molecules.

data.title: Transgenic animals

visualization.desc: The foreign gene in a transgenic animal is a stretch of the same DNA double helix the host transcribes.

notes: Transgenic animals are used because a chosen gene can be added and then watched in a living body. The course expects five uses: normal development, models of disease, biological products, vaccine safety, and chemical safety.
To study normal physiology, an extra copy or an altered copy of a gene such as a growth-factor gene is introduced. The change in growth or development shows what that gene was doing.

Disease models carry a gene that contributes to a human illness, for example genes studied in cancer or in Alzheimer's disease. The mouse then shows features of the illness, and treatments can be tried before they are tried in people.

Biological products can be made in the animal's milk. Rosie, the first transgenic cow, reported in 1997, produced milk with human alpha-lactalbumin at about 2.4 grams per litre. The milk was more like human milk in that protein. Other projects put human proteins such as alpha-1-antitrypsin into the milk of livestock.

Vaccine safety can be checked in transgenic animals before a batch is widely used, by asking whether the vaccine causes the harm it is supposed to avoid. Chemical safety testing uses the animals to see how toxic a substance is, more quickly than some older assays.

The ethical objections are part of the answer. The animal may suffer. Patenting a sentient animal raises the question of who owns a line. The decision to create the animal has to be justified by the medical or scientific gain, and welfare rules apply.

data.title: Biopiracy and patent issues
notes: A biopatent is a legal right granted over an invention: a new process, a modified organism, or a product. It lasts for a set time and stops others from using that invention commercially without permission. The right is given by a patent office after a claim is examined.

Biopiracy is the use of a community's biological resource or traditional knowledge for profit without permission, without naming the source, and without sharing the benefit. It is a taking. A patent is a grant. The two words are not synonyms.

Turmeric has been used in India for wound healing for a very long time. A US patent was nonetheless issued on that use. India's Council of Scientific and Industrial Research showed the use was already documented traditional knowledge, and the patent was revoked.

Neem was the subject of patents on fungicidal and other uses that farmers already practised. Campaigns against those patents argued that the knowledge was not new. A patent requires novelty. Traditional use is evidence that the claim was not new.

Basmati is a traditional aromatic rice of the Indian subcontinent. RiceTec obtained a US patent on rice lines and grains it marketed in connection with basmati. India challenged the patent because the name and the traits were tied to farmers' varieties, not to a new invention from outside that tradition.

Defences now include writing traditional knowledge down in a form patent examiners will search, such as India's Traditional Knowledge Digital Library, and requiring permission plus a share of profits before a foreign company uses a local resource. Benefit-sharing is the opposite of biopiracy.

Basmati was not invented in a US laboratory. It is a traditional variety. That is the point of the dispute.
Documenting traditional knowledge is not the same as patenting it. The library is there so examiners can see that a claim is old.
keyPoints: Biopatent: a legal right over an invention.
Biopiracy: commercial use without permission or benefit-sharing.

Basmati: RiceTec's patent was challenged by India.
importantStatements: Novelty fails when the knowledge was already public in a traditional form.
The country and the community that kept the resource are entitled to consent and a share.
A searchable record of traditional knowledge is a defence against bad patents.
examples: The turmeric wound patent fell because Ayurvedic and other written use already existed.
Neem extracts used as traditional fungicides were claimed in patents that opponents said lacked novelty.
India objected to a US patent that tied the basmati name and its grain traits to a company's lines.
universalFacts: A patent is refused or revoked when the claimed invention was already known.
Biological resources are not ownerless just because they grow wild or were bred by farmers.
formulas: Biopiracy = resource or traditional knowledge + commercial use + no consent + no share of the benefit.
Prior art (old public knowledge) → novelty fails → patent revoked or refused.

Name the community or the country as the party that was left out. Biopiracy is about people, not only about plants.
importantNotes: CSIR India led the turmeric challenge.

visualization.desc: Genetic engineering rewrites DNA. The helix is the molecule those principles act on.

notes: Biotechnology in this chapter rests on two ideas used together. Genetic engineering changes the genetic material so a cell can make something it did not make before. Bioprocess engineering grows that cell in large, clean cultures and recovers the product.

A changed gene in a test tube is not yet a medicine. The host has to be multiplied without contamination, and the protein has to be separated from thousands of other molecules. Sterile culture is part of the principle, not a side comment. One unwanted microbe can outgrow the production strain.

The genetic-engineering sequence is: isolate the DNA, cut out the wanted piece with a restriction enzyme, join it to a vector with ligase, put the recombinant vector into a host, and select the cells that received it. Each step fails for a different reason, so each has its own check.

The host must be competent, able to take DNA in. For a product that needs human-like sugar chains, a bacterial host may be the wrong choice even if it grows fast. Insulin can be made in E. coli. Some other human proteins need mammalian cells. The host is chosen for the product, not from habit.

Downstream processing is the recovery half of bioprocess engineering. Cells are separated from the broth, the product is extracted, and it is purified until it is safe to use. A culture that made the protein but was never purified has not finished the process.

The same recombinant molecule can be copied only because the vector has an origin of replication and the culture is kept free of competitors. Genetic engineering supplies the instruction. Bioprocess engineering supplies the mass of cells and the clean product. Neither idea alone is the technology.

data.title: Applications of recombinant DNA technology

visualization.desc: Applications of recombinant DNA all start from a gene carried on a double helix the host can copy.

notes: Recombinant DNA is used wherever a cell can be instructed to make a molecule that is hard to collect from its natural source. The applications sit in medicine, farming, industry and the cleanup of pollutants.

In medicine the landmark product is human insulin made in E. coli, approved as Humulin in 1982. The amino-acid sequence is the human one, so the immune reactions that came with some animal insulins became less of a problem. The same logic produces other proteins: human growth hormone, and vaccines such as the hepatitis B surface antigen made in yeast.

Diagnosis uses the same toolkit. PCR amplifies a pathogen's DNA until a test can see it. ELISA detects an antigen or an antibody with an enzyme-linked reaction. One finds nucleic acid. The other finds protein. They answer different clinical questions.

Gene therapy delivers a working copy of a defective gene into a patient's somatic cells. The correction is for that person. It is not passed to children, because the germline is not the target of the permitted treatments. The first approved attempt, in 1990, was for ADA deficiency.

In agriculture the same technology produces Bt crops and other modified plants. In the environment, microbes have been designed or selected to break down oil and other pollutants, which is bioremediation. The microbe eats the waste. It does not make the waste vanish by a physical filter alone.

Every application still depends on the pipeline: a correct gene, a host that can express it, and a product that has been checked. A recombinant protein is not automatically safe or correctly folded. Purification and testing are part of the application, not paperwork after the science.

data.title: Air and Water Pollution
notes: Air pollution is the addition of gases and particles that harm health, crops or buildings. The main primary pollutants in this course are sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, unburnt hydrocarbons and particulate matter. Vehicles, coal, industry and, in many Nepali towns, brick kilns are the sources to name.

Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin as carboxyhaemoglobin and so blocks oxygen transport. Fine particles, especially those small enough to reach the alveoli, damage lungs. Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides irritate the airway and, dissolved in cloud water, become acid rain. Nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons in sunlight also make ground-level ozone, which is a smog pollutant, not the stratospheric shield.

Control follows the pollutant. An electrostatic precipitator charges dust and collects it on plates, so it suits particulates from a chimney. A scrubber sprays liquid through the gas and takes out sulphur dioxide. A catalytic converter, using platinum, palladium and rhodium, turns carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and unburnt hydrocarbons into carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water. Lead in petrol poisons that catalyst, which is why the fuel has to be unleaded. Compressed natural gas burns with less smoke than petrol or diesel and has been used to clean city bus fleets.

Water pollution is the addition of sewage, industrial chemicals, detergents, farm runoff or heat until the water can no longer support its normal life. Organic sewage is measured by biochemical oxygen demand: the oxygen microbes need to oxidise the organic matter in a litre of water, usually over five days at 20 °C. A high BOD means the waste will strip dissolved oxygen from the river.

Nitrates and phosphates from fertiliser and detergents drive eutrophication. Algae bloom, die, and bacteria decay them. Dissolved oxygen collapses and fish die. Non-biodegradable poisons take a different path. DDT and mercury build up in tissues and become more concentrated at each higher trophic level, which is biomagnification. The Minamata mercury poisoning is the human example of that concentration.

Sewage is treated in stages. Primary treatment settles solids. Secondary treatment uses microbes to lower the BOD. Tertiary treatment, where it exists, strips nutrients that would otherwise feed an algal bloom. None of that works if untreated sewage is still discharged beside the plant. Using less phosphate in detergents and less excess fertiliser cuts the problem before the pipe.
confusion: Ground-level ozone in smog is a pollutant. It is not the ozone layer.
A high BOD means the water is more polluted with organic matter, not that the water is richer in oxygen.
Biomagnification is not the same as a large spill. It is the rise in concentration along a food chain.
A catalytic converter does not remove carbon dioxide as its job. It makes carbon dioxide from carbon monoxide.
keyPoints: Air: SO2, NOx, CO, hydrocarbons, particulates.
CO → carboxyhaemoglobin. Fine particles → alveoli. SO2 and NOx → acid rain.
Controls: precipitator, scrubber, catalytic converter, CNG.
BOD measures organic pollution. High BOD, low oxygen left for fish.
Eutrophication is nutrient bloom then oxygen collapse. Biomagnification is DDT or mercury up the food chain.
importantStatements: Lead petrol cannot be used with a catalytic converter.
Secondary sewage treatment is the biological step that cuts BOD.
Top carnivores carry the highest load of a biomagnified poison.
examples: Brick-kiln smoke and diesel exhaust are particulate sources in a Nepali valley.

Mercury at Minamata reached people through contaminated fish, not through a single gulp of bay water.
formulas: Nutrient excess → algal bloom → decay → oxygen collapse → fish kill.
DDT or mercury concentration rises toward the top of the food chain.
Catalytic converter: CO, NOx and hydrocarbons → CO2, N2 and water, on unleaded fuel.

Primary, secondary and tertiary treatment are easy to swap. Settling, then microbes, then nutrients.

data.title: Solid Waste Management
notes: This note is about what to do with solid waste after it exists. The health risk and the treatment method depend on whether the waste can rot, whether it can be recycled, or whether it is infectious or full of metals. A single pit for everything fails all three.

Biodegradable waste is food, garden cuttings and paper that microbes can break down. If it is kept clean of plastic and glass it becomes compost, or it can go into a biogas digester where air-free decay produces methane that is burned as fuel and a slurry that can fertilise a field. That is recovery, not dumping.

Non-biodegradable waste does not join the compost. Glass, metal and many plastics are recycled only when they are dry and sorted. A plastic bottle in a compost heap does not become soil. It has to be collected as plastic. Contaminated recyclables, soaked in food, are often rejected and end up buried anyway, which is why the wet bin and the dry bin are separated at home.

Disposal of what cannot be recycled uses a sanitary landfill or a controlled incinerator. The landfill is lined, the leachate is taken out, the waste is covered, and the gas is managed. Incineration shrinks the volume and can heat water for electricity, but only if the temperature is high and the smoke is cleaned. Incomplete burning makes poisonous organic products and leaves a toxic ash that still needs a landfill.

Two streams injure people if they are treated as ordinary rubbish. Biomedical waste carries pathogens. It is autoclaved or burned in a dedicated incinerator, and sharps are contained so nobody is stuck by a needle. Electronic waste carries lead, mercury and cadmium. Informal open burning, which has been common where repair shops dump boards, puts those metals into the air and the ash. Recovery has to be a controlled process.

The public-health chain from a bad dump is short. Flies and rats move between waste and kitchens. Leachate reaches wells. Methane collects in pockets and can burn. Plastic blocks drains, so the next rain floods the lane with the same dirty water. Integrated management is just the decision to use compost, recycling, a proper landfill and special streams together, instead of one smoking pile.
confusion: Biogas is not compost. Biogas is methane from air-free decay. Compost is aerobic rotting that makes a soil conditioner.
Incineration does not make waste vanish. It makes ash, and bad incineration makes toxic smoke.
Paper can be recycled or composted. Soft plastic film is a different material and often is not composted.
Autoclaving hospital waste sterilises it. It does not recycle it into compost for vegetable beds.
keyPoints: Biodegradable → compost or biogas.
Dry recyclables → recycling, only if they were kept clean.
Sanitary landfill: liner, leachate collection, cover, gas control.
Incineration needs high temperature and smoke cleaning, and it still leaves ash.
Biomedical waste is sterilised or incinerated. E-waste metals are recovered, not openly burned.
importantStatements: The treatment is chosen from the kind of waste, not from whichever truck arrived.
Methane is a useful fuel inside a digester and a hazard inside a dump.
Ash from an incinerator is still waste.
examples: A household wet bin of vegetable peels feeds a community compost pit.
A capped sanitary landfill pipes its gas away instead of letting it seep into nearby basements.
A broken phone sent to an open fire releases lead and plastic fumes. The same phone in a recovery line yields metals and a smaller residue.

Autoclave conditions used to sterilise infectious waste are moist heat under pressure, classically 121 °C.
formulas: Organic waste + air → compost. Organic waste without air → biogas (methane) + slurry.
Integrated route: segregate → compost or biogas, recycle, sanitary landfill or controlled incineration, separate biomedical and e-waste.

data.title: Climate Change and Greenhouse Effect

visualization.desc: This topic is the left panel: greenhouse gases and warming. The ozone panel is a different chapter.

notes: Climate change in this chapter means the warming and the shifted rainfall that follow an enhanced greenhouse effect. The effect itself is natural. Carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, water vapour and CFCs absorb infrared radiation leaving the Earth, so the surface is warmer than it would be. Without them the mean temperature would be about −18 °C rather than about +15 °C.

People have thickened that blanket. Carbon dioxide has risen from about 280 ppm before industry to a little above 420 ppm, which is about 0.04 percent of air. The added carbon dioxide comes from coal, oil, gas and from forests that were cut and burned. Methane comes from livestock, flooded rice fields and rotting waste. Nitrous oxide comes from fertilised soils. These are the gases to write down. Water vapour amplifies warming, but it is not the gas the policies are aimed at.

The results are not only a higher thermometer reading. Ice melts and sea level rises. Heatwaves and heavy rain become more likely. Crop zones move. Disease vectors move with the temperature. In the Himalaya, glaciers retreat and glacial lakes can burst. That is the Nepali form of the same global change, and it is about water and slopes, not about a hole in the ozone layer.

Mitigation means cutting the cause. Burn less fossil fuel, waste less energy, stop clearing forests, and store carbon in vegetation and soil. A landfill that captures methane, or a herd and a rice system that emit less of it, is mitigation of a greenhouse gas. Adaptation means living with the change that is already arriving: crop varieties that tolerate heat or a late monsoon, flood protection, and settlements that are not sitting under an unstable glacial lake.

International targets are part of the answer. The Paris Agreement asks countries to hold warming well below 2 °C and to pursue 1.5 °C above the pre-industrial temperature. A target is not a fall in carbon dioxide by itself. The fall comes from the fuels and the forests.

Ozone depletion is the trap answer. It is caused mainly by chlorine and bromine compounds, it is measured in Dobson units, and it increases ultraviolet-B. Some CFCs do warm the climate and also destroy ozone, but carbon dioxide does not punch the ozone hole, and chlorine is not the reason glaciers retreat. Write them as neighbours, not as synonyms.

Climate change and the ozone hole are not the same measurement and not the same gases.
Mitigation is not adaptation. One cuts emissions. The other copes with impacts.
Water vapour is a greenhouse gas, but listing only water vapour misses the gases people have increased.

CO2: about 280 ppm pre-industrial, a little above 420 ppm now.
Main added gases: CO2, methane, nitrous oxide.
Mitigation cuts emissions. Adaptation reduces harm.
Paris range: pursue 1.5 °C and hold warming well below 2 °C.
importantStatements: Infrared is what the greenhouse gases trap. Sunlight mostly gets in.

examples: Coal-fired electricity raises CO2. Methane from a landfill raises a more potent greenhouse gas in smaller amounts.

examShortTricks: 280 then about 420. 1.5 and 2. −18 and +15.

specialNotes: Do not quote a single 'exact' current ppm as if it never moves. 'A little above 420 ppm' matches the course figure.
Glacial-lake outburst floods are a consequence to name. They are not a greenhouse gas.
importantNotes: Deforestation raises atmospheric CO2 both by burning and by losing a sink.

data.title: Solid waste management
notes: Solid waste is the solid material a household, shop, farm, hospital or factory throws away. Managing it means collecting it, keeping the dangerous fractions apart, and only then burying, burning or recycling what is left. A roadside heap is not management.

The useful split is by what the waste is. Wet organic waste, such as food scraps, can rot. Dry recyclable waste includes paper, glass, metal and many plastics. Biomedical waste from clinics carries infection. Electronic waste carries lead, mercury and cadmium. Industrial hazardous waste may be corrosive or toxic. Mixing these in one bag makes every later step worse.

An open dump breeds flies and rats, blows plastic into drains, and leaks a dirty liquid called leachate into soil and groundwater. Buried organic waste without air control also makes methane, which is flammable and a strong greenhouse gas. The smell is the least of the damage.

A sanitary landfill is a different structure. The base is lined so leachate can be collected rather than soaked away. Waste is compacted and covered. Gas is vented or burned. It still uses land, and it still needs watching, but it is not a hole in the ground.

The order that cuts the problem is reduce, then reuse, then recycle, and only then recover energy or dispose. Segregation at the house is what makes composting, recycling and safe medical disposal possible. A mixed truckload cannot be unsorted cheaply at the dump.

Hospitals must not send dressings, needles and cultures out with kitchen waste. Those items are incinerated at high temperature or sterilised. Electronic goods should go to a recovery workshop that captures the metals. Burning phones and cables in the open releases the metals and the plastic fumes together.

data.title: Ozone layer depletion

visualization.desc: The right-hand panel is this topic: stratospheric ozone, Dobson units, and chlorine from CFCs. Warming is the other panel.

notes: Ozone in the stratosphere, about 15 to 35 km above the surface, absorbs ultraviolet-B that would otherwise reach living tissue. The amount in a vertical column is measured in Dobson units. One DU is a layer 0.01 mm thick at standard temperature and pressure. A normal column is about 300 DU.

Ozone is made and destroyed all the time. Ultraviolet light splits O2 into oxygen atoms, and an atom joining another O2 makes O3. Left alone, formation and breakdown stay in balance. The layer is not a fixed shell of gas that never changes. It is a balance.

CFCs upset that balance. They are stable near the ground and drift upward for years. High in the stratosphere, ultraviolet light breaks a chlorine atom off. Chlorine reacts with ozone to make chlorine monoxide and oxygen, then chlorine monoxide reacts with a free oxygen atom and releases the chlorine again. The chlorine is a catalyst. One atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules. Halons, carbon tetrachloride, methyl bromide and nitrogen oxides do related damage. Halons are harsher per molecule than CFCs.

The Antarctic hole appears in spring. Winter cold forms polar stratospheric clouds. On those icy surfaces, chlorine compounds are converted into forms that sunlight can activate. When the sun returns, ozone falls quickly. A column below about 220 DU is called a hole. The Arctic can thin too, but the classic hole is Antarctic.

More ultraviolet-B means more skin cancer and cataracts, a weaker immune response, and damage to phytoplankton, which are the producers of the sea. Crops can be injured as well. None of this is the same process as the greenhouse effect. Carbon dioxide warms the lower air. Chlorine thins the high ozone. A CFC happens to do both jobs, which is why the two stories get mixed.

The Montreal Protocol, agreed in 1987, cut and then phased out the main ozone-depleting chemicals. Substitutes have their own problems, including a greenhouse effect for some of them, but the protocol is the reason stratospheric chlorine has started to decline. Ground-level ozone, made in smog, is still a pollutant. It does not replace the shield 15 km up.

data.title: Rainwater harvesting and wasteland development
notes: Rainwater harvesting is the deliberate collection of rain before it runs off into a drain and is lost. The water is stored in a tank or guided underground so a well or a spring can use it later. It is a way of keeping a local water supply, not a new source of river water from far away.

A common design catches rain on a roof, sends it through a first-flush or a simple filter that drops leaves and grit, and then either fills a tank or leads the water into a recharge pit, a trench or an abandoned well. Check dams and percolation ponds do the same job for a slope: they slow the runoff so it soaks in instead of racing away.

The gains are practical. The local water table rises, wells last longer into the dry months, and a sudden storm is less likely to flood the street because some of the water was held. In dry districts, traditional tanks and ponds did this long before the modern name. Rooftop collection has also been made compulsory in places such as Tamil Nadu. In Nepal the same idea appears as community ponds and as rooftop tanks.

Wasteland, in this chapter, is land so degraded that it no longer supports the use it once had. Gullied hills, salinity from bad irrigation, mining spoil, waterlogged soil and heavily overgrazed slopes are typical. It is not a wilderness that was always bare. It is land people damaged.

The causes sit in how the land was used. Trees cut from a slope let rain tear the soil. Too many animals remove the cover. Irrigation water that cannot drain leaves salt at the surface. A mine leaves a pile that plants cannot root in. Each cause points at a repair, not at a single universal machine.

Development of that land means putting cover and water control back. Trees and grasses are planted. Contour bunds and check dams slow runoff. Waterlogged ground is drained. Salty ground is leached only where drainage exists, or it is given salt-tolerant plants. Grazing is held off until the cover returns. The aim is a soil that holds water and a plant community that holds the soil.

data.title: Plant Breeding

visualization.desc: Five steps in order: collect germplasm, choose parents, cross them, keep the best progeny, then test and release the variety.

notes: Plant breeding is the deliberate production of a crop that is more useful than its parents. The usefulness is a stated target: more grain, a shorter plant that does not lodge, resistance to a named disease, a duration that fits the monsoon, or a seed with more protein. Simply keeping the heaviest heads from a field is selection. Breeding adds a controlled cross so that characters from two parents finish in one line.

The work has five steps, and the order is the answer. First the variability is collected. That collection is the germplasm: local varieties, old farmer seed, and wild relatives that still carry disease resistance the crop has lost. Second, the collection is evaluated and the parents are chosen, one of them usually the adapted crop, the other the donor of the missing character. Third, those parents are cross-pollinated. The flower that will be the female is emasculated before its own pollen is shed, dusted with the chosen pollen, and bagged so stray pollen cannot land. Fourth, the progeny are grown on and only the plants that actually combined the characters are kept. That selection is repeated down the generations until the line is stable. Fifth, the line is tested in more than one place and more than one season, released under a name, and the seed is multiplied for farmers.

The green-revolution cereals are the examples to attach to those steps. Semi-dwarf wheat, from programmes associated with Norman Borlaug, yielded heavily and stayed short enough not to fall over. Sonalika and Kalyan Sona are the wheat names used in this course. Semi-dwarf rice did the same for paddy: IR-8, Jaya and Ratna. Sugarcane shows a cross made for a region rather than for a single gene. Saccharum officinarum has thick stems and high sugar. Saccharum barberi grows in the north of the subcontinent. The hybrid was bred to keep the sugar and the thick stem and still grow in the north.

Disease resistance uses the same five steps with a resistant parent, often a wild relative. Himgiri wheat was produced against leaf rust, stripe rust and hill bunt. If no parent has the character, mutation breeding is the other door. Seeds or buds are treated with a chemical mutagen or with radiation, and a large number of plants are screened. Most are useless. A few carry a new resistant allele. Mung bean varieties resistant to yellow mosaic virus and powdery mildew were recovered that way. The mutagen does not aim the mutation. The screen does the choosing.

Biofortification aims the same method at nutritional quality instead of tonnes alone: more protein, a better amino-acid balance, more oil, more vitamins, or more iron and zinc. Atlas 66 is the high-protein wheat quoted for this. The plant is still bred by collection, choice of parents, crossing, selection and release. A transgenic line such as vitamin-A rice is a biotechnology product. It is worth knowing as a contrast, and it is not required to explain conventional breeding.

The steps fail in known ways. If the female flower is not emasculated in time, the seed is a self-pollination and the donor character never enters. If the two parents flower weeks apart, the cross cannot be made unless pollen is stored or the sowing dates are staggered. A line that tops the trial in one district can collapse in another because the rust race or the day length is different. The multi-location trial exists to catch that before the variety is named and sold.

data.title: Single Cell Protein

visualization.desc: Three single-cell protein sources side by side: Spirulina, Methylophilus methylotrophus, and mushrooms.

notes: Single cell protein is microbial biomass grown to be eaten, by people or by livestock, because the cells are rich in protein. The product is the cell mass itself, dried or processed. It is not a purified enzyme and not a single amino acid. The point of the method is that microbes multiply in hours in a tank, so protein can be produced without waiting for a crop season or dedicating a large field.

The organisms in the course are a cyanobacterium, a bacterium, and fungi that people already accept as food. Spirulina grows by photosynthesis and is produced as a supplement. It can be cultured on starch, molasses, and waste water from processing plants, so the same tank that grows food also uses a waste. Methylophilus methylotrophus grows on methanol. The comparison used in class is that a culture of about 250 grams of this bacterium can be expected to produce about 25 tonnes of protein, because the cells grow so fast and so much of their dry mass is protein. Mushrooms are fungi. They are SCP in the technical sense, and they are the form that has already become an ordinary food.

Yeasts, including Saccharomyces, are used in the same way, often for animal feed. Other bacterial and algal biomasses have been tried on whey, molasses, and sewage. The shared advantage is the feedstock. Materials that would otherwise be dumped become the carbon source. A fermenter on a small plot can outproduce a field of pulses in kilograms of protein per day, which is the calculation that made SCP attractive as a food strategy.

The biomass supplies protein as the main nutrient, with some fat, minerals and B vitamins depending on the species. It can be mixed into food or fed to animals whose meat, milk or eggs then carry the protein onward. In either use it is a supplement to crops, not a replacement for plant breeding. Breeding changes a plant. SCP adds a different organism.

The limits are practical and chemical. Bacterial cells contain a large amount of nucleic acid. In a human diet that load has to be reduced by processing, because purines from nucleic acids are not wanted in high amounts. The product also has to be free of toxins and of contaminating microbes, and it has to be something people will actually swallow. Mushrooms passed that test. A pale bacterial powder often did not, which is why much of the industrial output is discussed as feed. Cost matters as well: the protein is only useful if it is cheaper than the pulse or the fish meal it is meant to spare.

Set beside plant breeding, SCP skips land, season and rainfall, and it can run on waste. It fails when the biomass is unsafe, too high in nucleic acid, or rejected as food. Breeding fails when the new variety does not suit the district. A food system can use both: a better rice in the field, and a fermenter turning a waste stream into protein beside it.

It can be mixed into food or fed to animals whose meat, milk or eggs then carry the protein onward. In either use it is a supplement to crops, not a replacement for plant breeding. Breeding changes a plant. SCP adds a different organism.

The limits are practical and chemical. Bacterial cells contain a large amount of nucleic acid. In a human diet that load has to be reduced by processing, because purines from nucleic acids are not wanted in high amounts. The product also has to be free of toxins and of contaminating microbes, and it has to be something people will actually swallow. Mushrooms passed that test. A pale bacterial powder often did not, which is why much of the industrial output is discussed as feed. Cost matters as well: the protein is only useful if it is cheaper than the pulse or the fish meal it is meant to spare.

Set beside plant breeding, SCP skips land, season and rainfall, and it can run on waste. It fails when the biomass is unsafe, too high in nucleic acid, or rejected as food. Breeding fails when the new variety does not suit the district. A food system can use both: a better rice in the field, and a fermenter turning a waste stream into protein beside it.
confusion: SCP is the cells, not a protein extracted and bottled as a pure chemical. The cell mass is what is dried.
Mushrooms count. 'Single cell' in the name is historical. The course includes fungal biomass.
The 25-tonne figure belongs to Methylophilus methylotrophus, not to Spirulina and not to a hectare of wheat.
Sewage and waste water are feedstocks only after the process is controlled. The note does not say raw sewage is a food.
keyPoints: SCP is protein-rich microbial biomass used as food or feed.
Spirulina on starch, molasses or processing waste. Methylophilus on methanol.
About 250 g of Methylophilus is the course comparison for about 25 tonnes of protein.
Mushrooms are the SCP already eaten as a normal food. Yeasts go largely to feed.
Nucleic acids, taste, safety and cost are the limits.
importantStatements: The advantage is speed and a feedstock that can be a waste, not a magical amino-acid profile.
Nucleic acid content is the chemical reason bacterial SCP is processed before it becomes a large part of a human diet.
SCP does not replace a breeding programme. It adds a protein source that does not need a field.
examples: Spirulina grown on potato-processing water turns an effluent into a protein supplement.
A methanol-grown culture of Methylophilus is the standard high-yield bacterial example.
Oyster mushrooms on straw are SCP that a household already knows how to cook.
universalFacts: Microbial biomass can double in hours. A cereal cannot.
Photosynthetic SCP such as Spirulina needs light. Methylophilus does not. It oxidises methanol.
formulas: Spirulina: light and waste water. Methylophilus: methanol. Mushroom: straw or compost.

exercises.question: A factory has a methanol supply and a pile of straw. Which SCP organisms fit, and what limit still applies if the product is meant for people?
steps: Methylophilus methylotrophus can be grown on methanol. That is the bacterial match.
Straw suits mushroom cultivation. The fungus, not Methylophilus, uses that pile.
Spirulina is not the match for either feedstock. It wants light and a watery medium such as processing effluent.
If people are going to eat the bacterial biomass, nucleic acids have to be reduced and the product has to be shown to be free of toxins.
Mushrooms avoid most of the acceptability problem because they are already a food. They do not remove the need to keep the culture free of contaminants.
exercises.answer: Methanol for Methylophilus, straw for mushrooms. Bacterial SCP for people must be processed to lower nucleic acids and kept free of toxins.

bounds: Biofertilisers and biogas belong to other topics. Here the microbe is the food.
The yield figure is the course comparison for Methylophilus only.
data.summary: Single cell protein is microbial biomass eaten for its protein. Spirulina is grown in the light on wastes such as processing water, Methylophilus methylotrophus is grown on methanol and is the organism in the 250 gram to 25 tonne comparison, and mushrooms are the fungal form people already eat. The method is fast and can use waste, and it does not need a field. Bacterial products are limited by nucleic acids, safety and whether anyone will eat them.

data.title: Animal Husbandry

visualization.desc: Four managed products: dairy for milk, poultry for eggs and meat, fishery for capture or culture, and apiculture for honey.

notes: Animal husbandry is the managed breeding, feeding and health care of animals so that they yield milk, meat, eggs, fibre, honey or work. The population is a herd, a flock, a stocked pond or a hive. It is not a wild population that happens to be hunted. Management matters as much as the breed. A good genotype with dirty water and no vaccination does not give the yield the breed was chosen for.

Dairying keeps cattle and buffaloes for milk. Milch breeds are selected for milk, draught breeds for pulling, and dual-purpose breeds for both. Sahiwal and Red Sindhi are the milch cattle named in the course. Murrah is the buffalo example with a high milk yield. In Nepal most milk comes from buffaloes. Lime and Parkote are the indigenous buffalo breeds, and in the high mountains the chauri, a yak-cattle hybrid, supplies milk and also carries loads. Housing has to be clean and ventilated, water has to be clean, and the ration needs both roughage and a concentrate. Vaccination and quick treatment of mastitis and foot problems protect the yield. Breed choice without that care does not.

Poultry splits by product. Layers are kept for eggs. Broilers are kept for meat and are marketed young. White Leghorn is the layer example to remember. Chicks need heat, dry litter and a feed that changes with age. Respiratory disease moves quickly through a crowded house, so the management points are space, dry flooring, and removal of sick birds, not only the name of the strain. The same farm can keep both types. It should not feed them as if they were the same animal.

Fishery is either capture, taking fish from rivers and lakes, or culture, growing them in a managed pond. Composite carp culture stocks species that feed at different levels so the same pond yields more than one species without them all competing for one food. Catla feeds near the surface, Rohu in the water column, and Mrigal on the bottom. That vertical split is the reason the combination works. Cold, oxygen-rich hill water is a different culture, used for trout, and it should not be described as a carp pond. Apiculture keeps Apis cerana, the local honey bee, or Apis mellifera, the introduced one. Honey and wax are the products, and the flowers within flight range, the pasturage, decide how much honey arrives. The bees also pollinate nearby crops, which is an agricultural benefit even in a week when little honey is taken.

Breeding methods change the herd on purpose. Inbreeding, the mating of close relatives, makes the offspring more homozygous and can fix a desired character. It also produces inbreeding depression: fertility and general vigour fall. The remedy is an outcross, a mating with an unrelated superior animal of the same breed. Outbreeding covers that outcross, cross-breeding between two breeds, and crosses between species. Hisardale sheep were produced by crossing Merino rams with Bikaneri ewes. A mule, from a male donkey and a female horse, is the interspecific example, and it is sterile because the chromosomes do not pair at meiosis. Artificial insemination lets semen from one selected male serve many females, so the male does not have to be moved and the gain from his genotype spreads in one season.

MOET, multiple ovulation embryo transfer, speeds the female side in the same spirit. A chosen cow is treated with hormones that act like FSH, so she sheds several eggs instead of one. Those eggs are fertilised, commonly with semen from a proven bull. The young embryos are flushed out and transferred into surrogate cows of ordinary merit. The genetic mother does not have to carry each calf, and she can be superovulated again. One elite female thus contributes many more offspring than a single calf a year. Selection then keeps working on a larger set of progeny.

confusion: Inbreeding depression is the loss of vigour from inbreeding. It is not a disease brought in by a vaccine.
A mule is male donkey by female horse. Reversing the parents is a different cross. The mule is sterile.
Catla, Rohu and Mrigal are stocked together because they feed at different depths, not because they are three names for one carp.
Hisardale is a sheep from a Merino and Bikaneri cross. It is not a cattle breed.
keyPoints: Husbandry is breeding plus feeding plus health care for a useful product.
Milch examples: Sahiwal, Red Sindhi, Murrah. Nepal: Lime and Parkote buffalo, chauri in the high mountains.
Layers for eggs, broilers for meat. White Leghorn is a layer.
Composite carp culture: Catla surface, Rohu column, Mrigal bottom. Bees: Apis cerana and Apis mellifera.
Inbreeding fixes genes and can depress vigour. Hisardale is Merino by Bikaneri. MOET multiplies embryos from one cow.
importantStatements: Outcrossing to an unrelated animal of the same breed is the remedy for inbreeding depression.
Composite fish culture works because the species do not eat the same layer of the pond.
MOET uses superovulation and surrogate mothers so one genetic mother yields many calves.
examples: A Murrah buffalo still needs clean water and a proper ration. The breed name does not replace either.
A pond stocked with Catla, Rohu and Mrigal uses surface, middle and bottom foods.
Semen from one proven bull is used by artificial insemination across many farms in a district.
universalFacts: Pasturage, the flowers the bees can reach, sets the honey harvest more strictly than the colour of the hive.
A mule's sterility is a chromosome-pairing failure. It is not cured by better feeding.
formulas: Inbreeding raises homozygosity. Outcrossing restores vigour.
Catla top, Rohu middle, Mrigal bottom.
MOET: superovulate, fertilise, recover embryos, transfer to surrogates.
practice: Distinguish milch, draught and dual-purpose with one use each.
Explain composite culture in three lines, one per fish.
Give the parents of a Hisardale sheep and of a mule.
practiceQuestions: What is inbreeding depression, and how is it corrected?
Why are Catla, Rohu and Mrigal compatible in one pond?
What does the surrogate cow contribute in MOET, and what does she not contribute?
examNotes: A dairy answer needs breed examples plus three management conditions: housing, ration, disease control.
MOET is four verbs: superovulate, fertilise, recover, transfer. The surrogate is not the genetic mother.
examShortTricks: Top Catla, middle Rohu, bottom Mrigal.
Merino with Bikaneri gives Hisardale. Donkey with mare gives a sterile mule.
specialNotes: Lime and Parkote are buffaloes. Do not list them as cattle. Chauri is the yak hybrid of the high mountains.
Apis dorsata is the rock bee and is not the usual hive species. Cerana and mellifera are the managed ones.
importantNotes: Artificial insemination spreads a male genotype. MOET spreads a female genotype. They are not two names for one technique.
Capture fishery does not restock a pond. Culture fishery does. Say which one you are describing.
importantTasks: Tabulate four enterprises: animal, product, one breed or species, one management condition.
Write MOET as four numbered steps and mark which animal is the genetic mother.

exercises.question: A herd has become weak after several generations of mating close relatives. State the name of the problem and one breeding action that corrects it. Then say how MOET would be used if one cow in the herd is still outstanding.
steps: The weakness and loss of fertility after repeated mating of relatives is inbreeding depression.
The correction is an outcross: mate the animals to an unrelated, superior member of the same breed.
The outstanding cow is the genetic mother for MOET. She is treated so that she superovulates.
Her eggs are fertilised with semen from a selected bull, and the embryos are recovered.
Those embryos are transferred into surrogate cows. The surrogates carry the calves. They do not supply the elite genotype.
exercises.answer: Inbreeding depression, corrected by outcrossing. MOET then superovulates the outstanding cow and transfers her embryos to surrogates.

bounds: Plant breeding and single cell protein are the neighbouring notes. This note is animals, fish and bees.
Breed lists are the course examples plus the Nepali buffalo and chauri cases. It is not a national herd book.
data.summary: Animal husbandry manages breeding, feed and health for milk, meat, eggs, fish or honey. Sahiwal, Red Sindhi and Murrah are the dairy examples, with Lime and Parkote buffaloes and the high-mountain chauri in Nepal. Layers such as White Leghorn give eggs, broilers give meat, and a carp pond splits the feeding zones among Catla, Rohu and Mrigal. Inbreeding can fix a trait and can also depress vigour, which outcrossing repairs. Hisardale sheep and the sterile mule are the cross-breeding examples. Artificial insemination multiplies a bull's progeny, and MOET multiplies a cow's, by transferring her embryos into surrogates.

data.title: Integrated Rate Equations
notes: **Indefinite integral:** ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + C where F'(x) = f(x). C is the constant of integration.
**Basic integrals:** ∫xⁿdx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)+C (n≠-1), ∫1/x dx = ln|x|+C, ∫eˣdx = eˣ+C, ∫sin x dx = -cos x+C.
**Integration by substitution:** ∫f(g(x))g'(x)dx = ∫f(u)du where u=g(x).
**Integration by parts:** ∫u dv = uv - ∫v du.
**Definite integral:** ∫[a to b] f(x)dx = F(b)-F(a) where F'=f (Fundamental Theorem of Calculus).
**Properties:** ∫[a to b] f(x)dx = -∫[b to a] f(x)dx, ∫[a to a] f(x)dx = 0, ∫[a to b] f(x)dx = ∫[a to c] + ∫[c to b].

data.topicTitle: Essay writing — argumentative, descriptive, narrative, expository
notes: **What it is:** an essay argues, describes, narrates or explains a topic in organised paragraphs. The examiner marks STANCE + STRUCTURE + evidence, not length.

**Universal skeleton:** Introduction (hook + thesis) → Body paragraphs (ONE reason each: topic sentence → explanation → example) → optional counter-argument (acknowledge, then rebut) → Conclusion (restate thesis + consequence).

**Four types:** *Argumentative* (clear side, reasons, admit the other side), *Descriptive* (5 senses, spatial order, show-don't-tell), *Narrative* (one incident: setup → conflict → climax → reflection), *Expository* (explain causes/process in numbered factors, no opinion).
**Tense logic:** essays live in PRESENT for general truths; past only inside narrative examples; predictions use will/would.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Letter writing — formal and informal
notes: **What it is:** a letter to someone you do NOT know (editor, manager, office). Half the marks are the fixed BLOCK LAYOUT; the other half is polite business tone.

**Block order:** Sender's address → Date → Recipient's designation + address → Subject line → Salutation ('Dear Sir/Madam') → Body (3 short paragraphs: who you are + purpose / details / polite request) → Complimentary close → Signature + full name in capitals.
**The pairing rule that trips everyone:** 'Dear Sir/Madam' → end **Yours faithfully**; 'Dear Mr/Ms Sharma' (real name) → end **Yours sincerely**.
**Tone grammar:** no contractions (*do not*, *I am*); polite modals (*would*, *could*, *may*); passive voice for formality ('the matter is being investigated').

**Variants:** *Editor* (public issue + call for action), *Job application* (post + skills + 'Enclosure: CV'), *Complaint* (what, when, defect + remedy + deadline), *Inquiry/Order* (price/availability/terms).
Class 12 twist: expect combined tasks (application + CV, editor + solutions). Keep the SAME block layout; extend the body with a second developed paragraph rather than a new layout.
CV essentials (when asked): Name & contact → Career objective → Academic qualifications (table: exam, board, year, marks) → Skills → Experience → References. Noun phrases, no full sentences.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Email writing
notes: **What it is:** a letter sent digitally — block format plus To/Subject fields. The examiner mainly checks the SUBJECT line and whether tone matches the receiver.

**Structure:** To → Subject (short phrase, not a sentence) → Salutation matched to receiver ('Dear Principal,' vs 'Hi Anisha,') → 1–2 short paragraphs (purpose → details → courteous close) → Sign-off (formal: Yours faithfully + full name; informal: Best wishes + first name).
**Register decides grammar:** the same message shifts — 'could you please' vs 'can you', 'I require' vs 'I need'. Present perfect introduces news ('I have prepared…').
**Never write a lazy subject** ('Queries') — a precise subject is itself worth marks.

data.title: Report writing and summarisation
notes: **What it is:** factual, third-person, past-tense reporting of an event (sports day, blood donation camp) — not a story, not an opinion.

**Structure:** Headline (short, factual) → Byline ('By a Staff Reporter') + dateline ('Kathmandu, 12 May:') → Lead paragraph answering WHO did WHAT, WHERE, WHEN, WHY in 2–3 sentences → Body in chronological order → a short quotation from the chief guest → closing outcome.
**Tense/voice grammar:** past simple for every event; passive voice is standard for ceremony facts ('trophies were distributed'); reported speech for quotes; third person only — never 'I'.
**Summarisation partner skill:** compress any passage into its core idea in your own words within the word limit — keep the author's viewpoint, drop examples and repetition.

data.title: Note-making and summary
notes: **Summary:** read for gist → underline key ideas → draft (author's main idea first, then 2–4 key supports) → cut modifiers/examples to fit the word limit → verify meaning is unchanged and nothing is copied.

**Summary grammar:** four paraphrase moves — synonym swap (threat→danger), word-class change (pollute→pollution), voice change (active↔passive), sentence merge; report verbs frame it ('the passage argues…'). Never add your own opinion.

**Note-making:** TITLE in caps → numbered sub-headings (1, 2, 3 — noun phrases, one per paragraph) → compact key-phrase points (a, b, c) → abbreviations (&, →, e.g.) with an 'Abbreviations used' note.
**Note grammar:** nominalise verbs for headings ('agricultural expansion'); drop articles/auxiliaries in points; every point under 7 words.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Story writing
notes: **What it is:** a COMPLETE narrative arc judged on plot — situation → problem → turning point → resolution → (often) a quiet moral.

**Structure:** Opening (if the prompt gives a first line, USE it verbatim and continue) → Complication → Rising action → Climax (the decisive moment — slow down here) → Resolution + realisation/moral.

**Tense machinery:** past simple drives the plot; past continuous paints background ('I was dawdling home'); past perfect marks earlier events ('which she had lost'); direct speech at the climax adds life.
**Keep ONE tense zone and ONE narrator** — drifting between present and past, or I/he, breaks the story.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Speech and dialogue writing
notes: **What it is:** writing meant to be SPOKEN — short sentences, rhythm, direct address. The examiner checks 'speakability'.

**Structure:** Salutation in order of seniority ('Respected Chairperson, judges, teachers, and my dear friends —') → Self-intro (if required) → Hook (question/fact/quotation) → 2–3 clear points ('First… Second… Finally…') → Persuasive devices (triads, repetition, rhetorical questions) → Strong closing appeal + 'Thank you.'
**Grammar for the ear:** imperatives command action ('Let us pledge…'); rhetorical questions make the audience answer mentally; triads create rhythm.
**Test:** read your draft aloud — where you gasp, rewrite. Repeat your core phrase 2–3 times.
Dialogue pairing (Class 12 often bundles both): keep turns short and purposeful; use speaker names + colons; contractions, fillers and question tags for naturalness; resolve the exchange explicitly.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Review writing — book and film
notes: **What it is:** a balanced critical evaluation — what the work is, what it does well, what falls short, and whether it is worth the reader's time.

**Structure:** Title + basic details (title, author/director, year, genre) → Brief SPOILER-FREE summary (2–3 sentences) → Strengths (one concrete example/quote) → Weaknesses (fair, with why it matters) → Recommendation + verdict/rating.

**Review grammar:** present simple dominates ('the story follows…'); evaluative adjectives (compelling, uneven, luminous); concessive fairness ('although the plot is thin, the philosophy is profound'); soft hedging ('readers may find…').
**Never spoil the ending** — restraint reads as mature judgement.

data.title: Comprehension and paraphrasing
notes: **What it is:** extracting and restating passage information — the trap is copying whole sentences; the skill is locate-then-restate.

**Method:** skim for gist → scan for the question's keywords (the answer lives nearby) → answer in complete sentences with synonyms → match the question type (WH → answer the WH; 'Why' → 'Because…'; true/false → quote evidence) → verify against the text.

**Grammar of answers:** convert passage nouns into clauses ('its existence' → 'that it exists'); use report frames ('the passage states that…'); keep the passage's tense zone; quote marks ONLY when demanded.
**Length discipline:** 1-mark answers = one sentence; 2-mark answers = answer + reason/evidence.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.topicTitle: Grammar for writing — sentences, clauses, punctuation
notes: **Sentence types as tools:** simple (one clause — POWER), compound (two main clauses via and/but/so or a semicolon — equal weight), complex (main + subordinate clause via because/although/when/if — shows the relation between ideas). Mix them: examiners reward rhythm.

**Clauses vs phrases:** a phrase has no subject-verb pair and cannot stand alone; a dependent clause has one but leans on the main clause ('Because it rained.' alone is a fragment). Relative clauses (who/which/that) add noun detail — commas only for extra information.

**Punctuation logic:** full stop ends a thought; comma separates list items, follows openers, precedes and/but/so between full sentences; semicolon joins balanced sentences; colon introduces; apostrophe = possession or contraction (its vs it's is the classic trap). Comma splice = two full sentences joined by only a comma — fix it.

**Tense + agreement discipline:** pick a tense zone per paragraph (essays: present; reports: past); subjects agree with verbs ('Each of the students WAS present'); a/an by SOUND ('an hour', 'a university').
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Derivatives of Algebraic and Trig Functions
data.topicTitle: Derivatives of Algebraic and Trig Functions
notes: **Derivative definition:** f'(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h = lim(Δx→0) Δy/Δx.
**Geometric meaning:** f'(a) is the slope of the tangent line to y=f(x) at x=a.
**Basic derivatives:** d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹, d/dx(sin x) = cos x, d/dx(cos x) = -sin x, d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ, d/dx(ln x) = 1/x.
**Product rule:** (fg)' = f'g + fg'.
**Quotient rule:** (f/g)' = (f'g - fg')/g².
**Chain rule:** d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x))·g'(x).
**Higher order derivatives:** f''(x) = d/dx[f'(x)], f'''(x) = d/dx[f''(x)], etc.
confusion: ❌ 'd/dx(sin x) = cos x means the slope of sin at x=0 is 0.' ✅ At x = 0, sin(0) = 0, but d/dx(sin 0) = cos 0 = 1 — the tangent is steep, not flat.
❌ 'The derivative of a product is the product of the derivatives.' ✅ No! (fg)' = f'g + fg'. The 'product rule' is NOT 'differentiate each and multiply.'

❌ 'If f(x) = sin²x, then f'(x) = cos²x.' ✅ f'(x) = 2 sin x cos x = sin 2x. You must apply the Chain Rule: derivative of the *outer* function (u² → 2u) times the derivative of the *inner* function (sin x → cos x).
❌ 'd/dx(eˣ) = x·eˣ⁻¹ (power rule).' ✅ No — the power rule is for xⁿ where n is constant. For eˣ (constant base, variable exponent), d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ.

data.title: Higher Order Derivatives
notes: **Derivative definition:** f'(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h = lim(Δx→0) Δy/Δx.
**Geometric meaning:** f'(a) is the slope of the tangent line to y=f(x) at x=a.
**Basic derivatives:** d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹, d/dx(sin x) = cos x, d/dx(cos x) = -sin x, d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ, d/dx(ln x) = 1/x.
**Product rule:** (fg)' = f'g + fg'.
**Quotient rule:** (f/g)' = (f'g - fg')/g².
**Chain rule:** d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x))·g'(x).
**Higher order derivatives:** f''(x) = d/dx[f'(x)], f'''(x) = d/dx[f''(x)], etc.
**Fact.** Derivative f'(x) = lim_{h→0} [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h = tangent slope; rules: sum, product, quotient, chain.
**Fact.** d/dx xⁿ = nx^{n−1}; d/dx sin x = cos x; d/dx e^x = e^x; d/dx ln x = 1/x.

data.title: Applications of Derivatives
notes: **Derivative definition:** f'(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h = lim(Δx→0) Δy/Δx.
**Geometric meaning:** f'(a) is the slope of the tangent line to y=f(x) at x=a.
**Basic derivatives:** d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹, d/dx(sin x) = cos x, d/dx(cos x) = -sin x, d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ, d/dx(ln x) = 1/x.
**Product rule:** (fg)' = f'g + fg'.
**Quotient rule:** (f/g)' = (f'g - fg')/g².
**Chain rule:** d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x))·g'(x).
**Higher order derivatives:** f''(x) = d/dx[f'(x)], f'''(x) = d/dx[f''(x)], etc.

data.title: Integration as Inverse of Differentiation
notes: **Indefinite integral:** ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + C where F'(x) = f(x). C is the constant of integration.
**Basic integrals:** ∫xⁿdx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)+C (n≠-1), ∫1/x dx = ln|x|+C, ∫eˣdx = eˣ+C, ∫sin x dx = -cos x+C.
**Integration by substitution:** ∫f(g(x))g'(x)dx = ∫f(u)du where u=g(x).
**Integration by parts:** ∫u dv = uv - ∫v du.
**Definite integral:** ∫[a to b] f(x)dx = F(b)-F(a) where F'=f (Fundamental Theorem of Calculus).

data.title: Concept of Limit
notes: **Limit concept:** The limit of f(x) as x approaches a describes the value that f(x) approaches as x gets arbitrarily close to a (but not equal to a).
**Notation:** lim(x→a) f(x) = L means f(x) gets arbitrarily close to L as x approaches a.
**Direct substitution:** If f is continuous at a, then lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a).
**Indeterminate forms:** 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞-∞, 0⁰, 1^∞, ∞⁰ require special techniques.
**Standard limits:** lim(x→0) sin(x)/x = 1, lim(x→0) (1-cos x)/x = 0, lim(x→0) (eˣ-1)/x = 1, lim(x→0) ln(1+x)/x = 1.
**Algebraic properties:** lim[f±g] = lim f ± lim g, lim[f·g] = lim f · lim g, lim[f/g] = lim f / lim g (denominator ≠ 0).
**Continuity connection:** f is continuous at a if lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a).
confusion: ❌ 'The limit of a function at a point is always its value at that point' ✅ The limit only concerns values *near* a, not *at* a; f(a) might not even be defined.
❌ 'If the limit doesn't exist, the function is undefined' ✅ A function can be well-defined at a point, but the limit might not exist (e.g., jump discontinuities or oscillations).
❌ 'Indeterminate form 0/0 means the result is 0 or undefined' ✅ 0/0 is a signal to apply algebraic manipulation or L'Hôpital's Rule to find the limit, which may be a finite number.

data.title: Standard Limits and Evaluation
notes: **Limit concept:** The limit of f(x) as x approaches a describes the value that f(x) approaches as x gets arbitrarily close to a (but not equal to a).
**Notation:** lim(x→a) f(x) = L means f(x) gets arbitrarily close to L as x approaches a.
**Direct substitution:** If f is continuous at a, then lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a).
**Indeterminate forms:** 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞-∞, 0⁰, 1^∞, ∞⁰ require special techniques.
**Standard limits:** lim(x→0) sin(x)/x = 1, lim(x→0) (1-cos x)/x = 0, lim(x→0) (eˣ-1)/x = 1, lim(x→0) ln(1+x)/x = 1.
**Algebraic properties:** lim[f±g] = lim f ± lim g, lim[f·g] = lim f · lim g, lim[f/g] = lim f / lim g (denominator ≠ 0).
**Continuity connection:** f is continuous at a if lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a).
confusion: ❌ Applying limits directly when 0/0 form exists ✅ Must resolve 0/0 form using algebra, L'Hopital, or standard limits.
❌ Assuming lim(x→0) sin(x)/x is 1 in degrees ✅ Angle must be in radians for lim(x→0) sin(x)/x = 1.

data.title: Indeterminate Forms
notes: **Indeterminate Forms:** Limits that cannot be directly evaluated (0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞-∞, 0⁰, 1^∞, ∞⁰).
**L'Hopital's Rule:** For 0/0 or ∞/∞ forms: lim f/g = lim f'/g' if limit of derivatives exists.
**0/0 form:** Requires factoring, rationalization, or L'Hopital's rule.
**∞/∞ form:** Same techniques apply; divide by highest power of variable.
**0·∞ form:** Convert to 0/0 or ∞/∞ by rewriting as fraction.
**∞-∞ form:** Combine fractions or factor to resolve.
**Exponential forms (0⁰, 1^∞, ∞⁰):** Use logarithms: y = f^g → ln y = g·ln f.
confusion: ❌ Applying L'Hopital's rule to 0/1 or 1/0 forms ✅ L'Hopital only applies to 0/0 or ∞/∞ indeterminate forms.
❌ Forgetting to check indeterminate form before using L'Hopital ✅ Direct substitution first; only use L'Hopital if result is 0/0 or ∞/∞.

data.title: Continuity of Functions
notes: **Continuity at a point:** f is continuous at x=a if: (1) f(a) exists, (2) lim(x→a) f(x) exists, (3) lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a).
**Continuous on an interval:** f is continuous on [a,b] if continuous at every point in (a,b), right-continuous at a, left-continuous at b.
**Polynomial functions:** Continuous everywhere on ℝ.
**Rational functions:** Continuous everywhere except where denominator = 0.
**Trigonometric functions:** sin x, cos x continuous everywhere; tan x continuous except at x = (2n+1)π/2.
**Exponential and logarithmic:** eˣ continuous everywhere; ln x continuous for x>0.
**Intermediate Value Theorem:** If f is continuous on [a,b] and k is between f(a) and f(b), then there exists c∈(a,b) such that f(c)=k.
confusion: ❌ Assuming all functions with a hole are continuous ✅ A function is discontinuous at a point if f(a) doesn't exist or doesn't equal the limit.
❌ Continuity means the graph has no breaks ✅ Also requires f(a) to equal the limit value; removable discontinuity exists.

data.title: Differentiability
notes: **Differentiability at a point:** f is differentiable at x=a if f'(a) exists, i.e., lim(h→0) [f(a+h)-f(a)]/h exists.
**Differentiable implies continuous:** If f is differentiable at a, then f is continuous at a.
**Continuous does not imply differentiable:** |x| is continuous at x=0 but not differentiable.
**Smooth functions:** Differentiable everywhere (e.g., polynomials, sin x, cos x, eˣ).
**Corner/cusp points:** Non-differentiable points where left derivative ≠ right derivative.
**Vertical tangent:** Point where derivative approaches infinity (not differentiable).
**Fact.** Indeterminate forms 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞ → L'Hôpital: lim f/g = lim f'/g' (when applicable).
**Fact.** Standard limits: lim_{x→0} sin x / x = 1; lim_{x→0} (1 + x)^{1/x} = e; lim_{x→∞} (1 + a/x)^x = e^a.
**Fact.** Continuity: f continuous at c iff lim_{x→c}f(x) = f(c). Types of discontinuity: removable, jump, infinite.
confusion: ❌ Assuming continuous functions are always differentiable ✅ |x| at x=0 is continuous but has a corner (not differentiable).
❌ Differentiable implies the function is smooth ✅ Differentiable means derivative exists at that point; corners still exist elsewhere.

data.title: Conditional Probability
notes: **Probability definition:** P(E) = n(E)/n(S) for classical probability, where n(E) = favorable outcomes, n(S) = total outcomes.
**Axiomatic definition:** P(E)≥0, P(S)=1, P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B) for disjoint events.
**Complement rule:** P(E') = 1 - P(E).
**Addition rule:** P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)-P(A∩B).
**Conditional probability:** P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B), provided P(B)>0.
**Independent events:** A and B are independent if P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B).
**Multiplication theorem:** P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B|A) = P(B)·P(A|B).
**Bayes' theorem:** P(Aᵢ|B) = P(Aᵢ)·P(B|Aᵢ) / ΣP(Aⱼ)·P(B|Aⱼ).
**Fact.** P(E) = favourable/total. Additive law: P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). If mutually exclusive, P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B).
**Fact.** Multiplicative: P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B|A); independence: P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B).
**Fact.** Complement: P(A') = 1 − P(A). For discrete: ΣP = 1; expected value E(X) = Σxᵢpᵢ.

**Fact.** P(E) = favourable/total. Additive law: P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). If mutually exclusive, P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B).

confusion: ❌ 'Direction cosines are arbitrary' ✅ Direction cosines l, m, n are *fixed* values for a given vector: l = cos α, m = cos β, n = cos γ.

data.title: Vector Quantities and Types
notes: **Vector:** A quantity having both magnitude and direction. Represented as arrow or bold letter: **a** or a⃗.
**Scalar:** A quantity with magnitude only (mass, temperature, time).
**Vector addition:** Triangle law: place tail of b at head of a; resultant closes triangle. Parallelogram law: diagonal from common tail.
**Scalar multiplication:** ka has magnitude |k|·|a|. Direction same as a if k>0, opposite if k<0.
**Dot product:** **a**·**b** = |a||b|cosθ = a₁b₁+a₂b₂+a₃b₃. Result is scalar.
**Cross product:** **a**×**b** = |a||b|sinθ · n̂. Result is vector perpendicular to both a and b.
**Unit vector:** â = **a**/|**a**|. Standard unit vectors: î, ĵ, k̂ along x,y,z axes.
**Direction cosines:** cosα=a₁/|a|, cosβ=a₂/|a|, cosγ=a₃/|a|, where α,β,γ are angles with axes.
confusion: ❌ 'Vector magnitude can be negative' ✅ Magnitude is defined as the absolute length, so it is always ≥ 0.
❌ 'Adding vectors is same as adding scalar magnitudes' ✅ Vector addition must account for direction using head-to-tail or component methods; only scalar magnitudes can be added algebraically.
❌ 'A vector with zero magnitude points in a specific direction' ✅ A zero vector (null vector) has undefined direction because it doesn't have a distinct displacement.

data.title: Addition and Subtraction
notes: **Vector:** A quantity having both magnitude and direction. Represented as arrow or bold letter: **a** or a⃗.
**Scalar:** A quantity with magnitude only (mass, temperature, time).
**Vector addition:** Triangle law: place tail of b at head of a; resultant closes triangle. Parallelogram law: diagonal from common tail.
**Scalar multiplication:** ka has magnitude |k|·|a|. Direction same as a if k>0, opposite if k<0.
**Dot product:** **a**·**b** = |a||b|cosθ = a₁b₁+a₂b₂+a₃b₃. Result is scalar.
**Cross product:** **a**×**b** = |a||b|sinθ · n̂. Result is vector perpendicular to both a and b.
**Unit vector:** â = **a**/|**a**|. Standard unit vectors: î, ĵ, k̂ along x,y,z axes.

confusion: ❌ 'Vector addition is simply adding components' ✅ While true for components, the *geometric* interpretation requires head-to-tail placement; you must not just add scalar magnitudes.
❌ 'Subtraction is same as addition' ✅ Subtraction is vector addition of the first vector and the negative (reversed direction) of the second vector: A - B = A + (-B).
❌ 'The resultant vector's direction is always the average of the two vectors' ✅ The resultant depends on the relative magnitudes and directions (angles between vectors); it is not a simple average.

data.topicTitle: AC voltage applied to resistor, inductor, and capacitor
notes: When a sinusoidal voltage is applied to a pure resistor, the current follows the voltage with no delay. The rms current is the rms voltage divided by R, and the average power is the heating I_rms squared times R.

A pure inductor opposes a changing current. Its reactance is X_L = 2πfL, so a higher frequency or a larger inductance means a smaller current. The voltage leads the current by a quarter of a cycle, and the average power is zero.

A pure capacitor opposes a change of voltage. Its reactance is X_C = 1/(2πfC), which is large at low frequency and small at high frequency. The current leads the voltage by a quarter cycle, and again the average power is zero.
The three elements are drawn as phasors. The resistor voltage lies along the current. The inductor voltage is drawn 90° ahead of the current. The capacitor voltage is drawn 90° behind the current.
Household meters read rms values. A peak of 10√2 volts has an rms value of 10 V. Mixing a peak voltage with an rms current gives a wrong power.
A real coil is an inductor with resistance in series. The pure cases on this page are the pieces used later to build the impedance of an LCR circuit.

data.title: AC through R, L, C
notes: **AC through R, L, C:** This topic covers the behavior of AC circuits containing Resistors (R), Inductors (L), and Capacitors (C).
Understanding the phase relationships between voltage and current in R, L, and C components is essential for analyzing complex AC circuits.
Key concepts include impedance, reactance, and the conditions for electrical resonance.
An alternating voltage can be written v = V_0 sin ωt. In a pure resistor the current is i = (V_0/R) sin ωt, so voltage and current reach their peaks together and the average power is I_rms^2 R.

In a pure inductor the current lags the voltage by 90°. The opposition is the inductive reactance X_L = ωL = 2πfL, and it grows with frequency. A pure inductor stores energy in its magnetic field and returns it, so the average power over a cycle is zero.

In a pure capacitor the current leads the voltage by 90°. The capacitive reactance is X_C = 1/(ωC), and it falls as the frequency rises. The average power over a cycle is again zero because energy is stored in the electric field and then returned.
confusion: ❌ 'In an AC circuit, the voltage and current are always in phase' ✅ In a pure resistor, they are in phase. In an inductor, voltage leads current by 90°. In a capacitor, voltage lags current by 90°.
❌ 'Impedance (Z) is the algebraic sum of resistance (R) and reactance (X)' ✅ Impedance is the vector sum: Z = √(R² + (X_L - X_C)²).
❌ 'Resonance occurs when resistance is maximum' ✅ Resonance occurs when inductive reactance equals capacitive reactance (X_L = X_C), which minimizes impedance in a series circuit.
Voltage does not lead the current in a resistor.
X_L rises with frequency. X_C falls.
A pure inductor does not consume average power.
Peak and rms differ by √2. Do not mix them in one formula.

data.title: LC Oscillations
notes: **LC Oscillations:** This topic covers the oscillatory exchange of energy between a capacitor (storing electric field energy) and an inductor (storing magnetic field energy).
In an ideal LC circuit, electrical oscillations occur at a natural frequency determined by the values of L and C.
This is an analogy to a mechanical simple harmonic oscillator (mass-spring system).

If a charged capacitor is connected to a pure inductor, the capacitor discharges through the coil, the current builds a magnetic field, and that field then pushes charge back onto the capacitor with the opposite sign.
The charge on the capacitor is of the form Q = Q_0 cos ωt when it starts from rest at maximum charge. The current is the derivative and is maximum when the charge is zero.
The angular frequency of this exchange is ω = 1/√(LC). The frequency in hertz is f = 1/(2π√(LC)). It does not depend on the starting charge.
confusion: ❌ Thinking LC circuits lose energy immediately without resistance ✅ An ideal LC circuit (zero resistance) oscillates indefinitely; only practical circuits lose energy due to resistance (damped oscillations).

❌ Current is maximum when charge on capacitor is maximum ✅ When charge on the capacitor is maximum, the potential energy is maximum and the current is zero. When the current is maximum, the magnetic energy is maximum and charge is zero (energy transfer).
❌ Misinterpreting the oscillation frequency ✅ The angular frequency is ω = 1/√(LC), and the frequency is f = 1 / (2π√(LC)).
The frequency does not depend on the initial charge.
Maximum current and maximum charge do not happen together.
Energy is not lost in the ideal LC circuit.
ω here is 1/√(LC), not √(LC).
