data.title: LCR Series Circuit
notes: **LCR Series Circuit:** An AC circuit containing a resistor (R), inductor (L), and capacitor (C) connected in series.
The behavior is determined by the combination of resistance and reactance (inductive and capacitive).
It exhibits resonance when the net reactance is zero.
A series LCR circuit has one current through R, L and C. The resistor voltage is in phase with the current, the inductor voltage leads by 90°, and the capacitor voltage lags by 90°.

The two reactance voltages are opposite, so the net reactive voltage has size I|X_L − X_C|. With the resistor voltage IR, Pythagoras gives the supply voltage V = I Z, where Z = √(R^2 + (X_L − X_C)^2).
The phase angle satisfies tanφ = (X_L − X_C)/R. If X_L is larger, the current lags the supply voltage. If X_C is larger, the current leads.
At resonance X_L = X_C, Z falls to R, and the current is V/R, the largest series current for that supply. The frequency is f_0 = 1/(2π√(LC)), the same expression as the LC oscillation.
confusion: ❌ Believing resonance occurs at all frequencies ✅ Resonance occurs only at a specific frequency (f_r = 1 / (2π√LC)) where inductive reactance equals capacitive reactance (X_L = X_C).
❌ Misinterpreting phase angle as constant ✅ The phase angle φ (where tan φ = (X_L - X_C) / R) depends on the frequency of the AC source; it is zero at resonance.

❌ Assuming voltage across L and C is zero at resonance ✅ While the net voltage across the L-C combination is zero (because they are 180° out of phase), individual voltages across L and C can be non-zero and large.
Z is not R + X_L + X_C.
Resonance is not maximum resistance.
A lagging current means the circuit is inductive, not capacitive.
The large voltages on L and C are not added arithmetically to get the supply.

data.title: LCR series circuit and power factor
data.topicTitle: LCR series circuit and power factor
notes: The average power in a series LCR circuit is V_rms I_rms cosφ, not the product of the rms voltage and current alone. The extra factor cosφ is the power factor.
From the impedance triangle, cosφ = R/Z. A circuit that is almost a pure resistor has Z near R and a power factor near 1. A circuit dominated by reactance has a small power factor.

At resonance X_L = X_C, φ = 0 and the power factor is 1. All of the average power is then the heating I_rms^2 R in the resistor. The inductor and capacitor still exchange energy, but their average contribution is zero.
A power factor of zero means the current is 90° out of phase with the voltage, as in a pure inductor or a pure capacitor. Energy sloshes back to the source.
A lagging power factor is the inductive case, common with motors. Capacitors are added in industry to pull the power factor back toward 1 so that the current, for a given useful power, is smaller.
The instantaneous power oscillates. The average is what the meter records. Quoting V I without cosφ overstates the power whenever the phase is not zero.

data.title: Transformer
notes: **Transformer:** An electrical device based on mutual induction that changes the voltage level of an AC supply.
It works on the principle of electromagnetic induction: a varying current in the primary coil induces an EMF in the secondary coil via a common magnetic core.
Transformers can be step-up (increase voltage) or step-down (decrease voltage).

A transformer has two coils on an iron core. An alternating current in the primary changes the flux, and that changing flux induces an emf in the secondary. A steady direct current does not keep inducing a secondary emf.
If leakage is ignored, the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio: V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p. More turns on the secondary means a step-up of voltage. Fewer turns means a step-down.
An ideal transformer wastes no power, so V_p I_p = V_s I_s. A step-up of voltage is a step-down of current. Energy is not created.
The core is laminated so that eddy currents have short paths and less heating. A solid iron core would waste power as heat.
confusion: ❌ Assuming transformer works on DC ✅ Transformer only operates on AC as it requires a *changing* magnetic flux to induce EMF (DC has constant flux).

❌ Thinking voltage ratio is independent of current ratio ✅ According to the law of conservation of energy (P_in = P_out for an ideal transformer), voltage and current are inversely proportional: V_p/V_s = I_s/I_p.
❌ Forgetting eddy currents exist in the core ✅ Eddy currents are circular induced currents in the core that cause energy loss as heat; they are minimized by using laminated iron cores.
A transformer does not change DC.
Step-up voltage does not step up current.
The turns ratio is not the current ratio. The current ratio is inverted.
Laminations are about eddy currents, not about the turns ratio.

data.title: Elements of Communication
notes: A communication system moves a message from one place to another. The information source produces the message, which may be speech, music or data.
The transmitter converts that message into a signal that can travel. For radio this includes modulation, placing the message onto a high-frequency carrier so that the antenna can be a practical size.
The channel is the path: a wire, an optical fibre, or free space. Noise, which is unwanted electrical energy, is added along the channel and is not part of the message.
The receiver undoes the transmitter's work. It amplifies the weak signal and demodulates it, recovering a copy of the original message for the listener or the display.
Attenuation is the weakening of the signal with distance. Amplifiers along a long channel restore the level, but they cannot perfectly remove noise that was added earlier.
Bandwidth is the range of frequencies the message or the channel occupies. A wider message, such as video, needs a wider channel than speech.

data.title: Elements of a communication system
notes: The elements can be named as transducer, modulator and transmitter, medium, and receiver plus output transducer. This is the same chain as source, transmitter, channel and receiver, with the transducers made explicit.
A microphone is an input transducer: sound pressure becomes a voltage. A loudspeaker is an output transducer: the recovered voltage becomes sound again.
The message signal is often low frequency. Multiplying it with a carrier, or varying the carrier's amplitude or frequency, produces the modulated wave that the antenna launches.

The medium decides the loss. A copper pair, a fibre and a radio path have different attenuation and different noise. The link budget is the comparison of transmitted power with the power the receiver needs.
At the receiver a tuner selects the carrier, a demodulator strips it, and an amplifier raises the message to a useful level. Selecting the wrong carrier selects a different message.
Two-way radio uses the same elements in both directions. Each station is sometimes the source and sometimes the destination.

data.title: Modulation
notes: A speech or music signal changes too slowly to be radiated from a practical antenna. Modulation copies that message onto a high-frequency carrier so the antenna can be a reasonable length.

In amplitude modulation the carrier frequency stays constant and the amplitude rises and falls with the message. A louder message makes a deeper variation, up to the point where the envelope would cross zero.
The modulated wave contains the carrier and two sidebands, one at f_c + f_m and one at f_c − f_m. If the highest message frequency is f_m, the bandwidth occupied is 2 f_m.
Frequency modulation keeps the amplitude constant and shifts the carrier frequency with the message. It uses a wider band than AM and is less bothered by amplitude noise.
The modulation index in AM is the fractional change in amplitude. An index above 1 means overmodulation: the envelope no longer matches the message and the receiver distorts it.
Demodulation at the receiver strips the carrier and returns the message. A diode detector followed by a filter is the simple AM method taught with this page.

data.title: Bandwidth and propagation of electromagnetic waves
data.topicTitle: Bandwidth and propagation of electromagnetic waves
notes: Bandwidth is the range of frequencies a signal or a channel occupies. A wider message, such as television, needs a wider channel than speech. Two stations must be separated by at least their bandwidths or they overlap.

A ground wave travels along the surface of the Earth. The ground absorbs more energy at higher frequency, so ground-wave broadcast is used for the lower radio frequencies and does not reach around the world.

A sky wave is sent upward and can be returned by the ionosphere. That is how short-wave radio crosses long distances. The ionosphere is not a metal mirror at every frequency: above a critical frequency the wave passes through.
A space wave travels in a straight line from a high transmitting antenna to the receiver. Television and FM use it. The Earth's curve limits the range to a little beyond the geometric horizon.
For an antenna at height h above a spherical Earth of radius R, the horizon distance is about √(2 R h) when h is much smaller than R. A higher mast sees farther.
The same information can be sent in a narrow band by slowing it down, or in a wide band by sending it quickly. The channel must be at least as wide as the signal.

data.title: Electric Current and Drift Velocity
notes: Electric current is the rate at which charge passes a point. One ampere is one coulomb per second. In a metal the moving charges are electrons, but the conventional current is drawn in the direction positive charge would move.

Free electrons move fast in random directions. An electric field adds a small average velocity along the wire, the drift velocity. The random speed is kilometres per second. The drift speed is often a fraction of a millimetre per second.
If n electrons per unit volume, each of charge e, drift at v_d through area A, the current is I = n e A v_d. A larger density, a wider wire or a faster drift means a larger current.
The drift speed is e E τ / m, where τ is the average time between collisions. A stronger field or a longer free time means a faster drift. Collisions turn the ordered drift energy into heat.

The signal travels along the wire at a speed set by the electromagnetic field, close to the speed of light. That is not the drift speed of the electrons. A lamp comes on at once even though each electron drifts slowly.
Current density J is I/A, and J = n e v_d. Resistivity connects J to the field by E = ρ J in an ohmic metal.

❌ 'Electric current is the flow of electrons only.' ✅ By convention, current is defined as the *flow of positive charge*. In many cases (like electrolytes), negative charges also flow, but current is still in the opposite direction of electron flow.

❌ 'Drift velocity is the average velocity of all electrons at all times.' ✅ It is the *net average velocity* of the electrons due to an applied electric field, superimposed on their random thermal motion.

data.title: Ohm's law and its limitations
notes: Ohm's law says that the current in a metallic conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it, if the temperature and the physical state stay constant. The constant ratio V/I is the resistance.
Plotted with current vertical and voltage horizontal, an ohmic resistor is a straight line through the origin. The slope is 1/R. A steeper line is a smaller resistance.
The law is a limited description. A filament lamp heats as the current rises, its resistance increases, and the graph bends. You cannot take one R from a cold measurement and use it at white heat.
A semiconductor diode is non-ohmic in a stronger way. It conducts easily in forward bias and almost not at all in reverse bias. No single R describes it.
A thermistor and an electrolyte can also leave the straight line. Quoting V = I R for them without a stated temperature and a stated operating point is not justified.

Inside the range where the metal stays ohmic, the law is still the working tool for series and parallel circuits. The limitation is the range, not a reason to abandon the law for a carbon resistor at a steady temperature.

data.title: Ohm's Law
notes: Ohm's law says that the current through a metallic conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature and other physical conditions stay constant. The constant of proportionality is 1/R.
The working form is V = IR. R is the resistance. A steeper I–V line means a smaller resistance if I is plotted vertically, because the slope is 1/R.

The law is empirical for ohmic materials. A filament lamp's resistance rises as it heats, so its I–V graph curves. A semiconductor diode conducts very differently in the two directions and is non-ohmic.
Resistivity ρ is the material property in R = ρL/A. Ohm's law can hold while R still changes if the piece is stretched, because L and A change.
The ohm is the resistance that passes 1 A when 1 V is applied. Power in a resistor is I^2 R, or V^2/R, or V I, and that power becomes heat.
A circuit calculation uses Ohm's law on each ohmic element after the currents have been chosen. It is not a law of the battery's internal chemistry.
confusion: ❌ 'Ohm's Law applies to all conductors.' ✅ It is valid only for *ohmic conductors* (where V is proportional to I, like metallic resistors), not for non-ohmic devices like diodes or transistors.
❌ 'Ohm's Law defines Resistance (R=V/I).' ✅ Resistance is a *property* of the conductor (geometry/material); Ohm's law states that *for some materials*, R remains constant regardless of V or I.
❌ 'V is always proportional to I.' ✅ This holds true only when *temperature and other physical conditions* are kept constant.
Ohm's law is not true for every device.
The temperature condition is part of the statement.
Slope of I against V is 1/R, not R, in that plotting choice.
Resistivity and resistance are different.

data.title: Resistance and resistivity — temperature dependence
notes: Resistance is R = ρ L / A. A longer wire has more resistance. A thicker wire has less. Resistivity ρ is the material property, independent of the particular length and area.
The unit of resistivity is the ohm metre. A good conductor has a small resistivity. Glass and rubber have very large resistivities and are used as insulators.

For a metal over a moderate range, ρ = ρ_0 (1 + α ΔT), where α is the temperature coefficient. α is positive for metals, so heating raises the resistivity. More violent lattice vibrations scatter the electrons more often.
The same linear form is used for resistance if the size does not change: R = R_0 (1 + α ΔT). A copper winding in a hot motor has a higher resistance than the cold value on the label.

A semiconductor has a negative temperature coefficient. Heating frees more carriers, and the resistivity falls. That is why a thermistor can be used as a thermometer and why a semiconductor is not described by the metal formula with a positive α.

Alloys such as manganin are made so that α is nearly zero. They are used for standard resistors. Superconductors drop to zero resistance below a critical temperature, which is outside this linear formula.

data.title: Resistors in Combination
notes: Resistors in series carry the same current. The total voltage is the sum of the voltages, so the equivalent resistance is R = R1 + R2 + R3. The equivalent is larger than the largest single resistor.
Resistors in parallel have the same potential difference. The total current is the sum of the branch currents, so 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. The equivalent is smaller than the smallest branch.
Two parallel resistors have the shortcut R = R1 R2 / (R1 + R2). It is the product over the sum, and it is not used for three resistors without grouping.
A short string of series resistors can sit in parallel with another branch. Reduce the series string first, then combine the parallel pair.
The voltage divider is the series case: the larger resistor takes the larger share of the voltage, in proportion to its resistance, because the current is common.
Opening a parallel branch increases the equivalent resistance and decreases the total current from the source. Adding a parallel branch does the opposite.
confusion: ❌ 'Adding resistors in parallel increases the total resistance.' ✅ Parallel connections *decrease* total resistance, as they provide more paths for current to flow (1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2).
❌ 'In series, current changes across each resistor.' ✅ In a series circuit, the *current* remains the same through all components, while *voltage* splits proportionally.

❌ 'Total resistance in series is the average of individual resistances.' ✅ In series, the total resistance is the *sum* of individual resistances (Rs = R1 + R2), which is always greater than the largest individual resistor.
Parallel resistors do not add their ohm values.
The product-over-sum rule is for two resistors only.
Series current is the same. Series voltage is not.
A parallel equivalent is never larger than the smaller branch.

data.title: Kirchhoff's Laws
notes: Kirchhoff's first law, the junction rule, says that the sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum leaving it. Charge does not pile up at a steady junction, so Σ I = 0 if currents in are positive and currents out are negative.
Kirchhoff's second law, the loop rule, says that the algebraic sum of potential changes around a closed loop is zero. A walk that returns to the start cannot have gained energy.
A resistor drop is −IR when you walk with the current and +IR when you walk against it. A battery rise is +E when you walk from the negative plate to the positive plate inside the cell.
Unknown currents are given arrows before the equations. A negative answer means the real current is opposite to the arrow. You do not redraw and start again.
The number of independent equations matches the number of unknown currents. A junction equation and one or two loop equations are the usual set.
Internal resistance r is written as an extra resistor in series with the emf. The terminal voltage is then E − I r when the cell is supplying current.
confusion: ❌ 'KCL applies to open circuits.' ✅ KCL (junction rule) applies only at *nodes/junctions* where currents meet; it states ΣI_in = ΣI_out.
❌ 'KVL is valid for any loop including those with capacitors.' ✅ KVL applies to *closed loops*; for capacitors, you must include the potential difference V = q/C across the capacitor.

❌ 'Sign conventions for KVL don't matter as long as you're consistent.' ✅ While consistency is key, wrong sign conventions will flip *all* your results; the standard rule is: voltage rise = +, voltage drop = − when traversing the loop.
The junction law is not about voltages.
The loop law is not about currents adding to zero.
A negative current is a direction, not a mistake.
Walking against the current flips the IR sign.

data.topicTitle: Series and parallel combination of resistors
notes: A combination problem begins with a sketch of which resistors share a current and which share a node. Two resistors with no branch between them are in series even if the drawing is bent.
Replace each obvious series pair by one resistor, and each obvious parallel pair by one resistor, and redraw. The equivalent of the whole network is the last remaining resistor.
The source current is the source voltage divided by that equivalent. Then work backward. A series resistor carries the current of its string. A parallel branch takes V/R of that branch.
Power in each resistor is I^2 R using the current that actually flows through it. The powers add to the power leaving the source, V I, if the resistors are the only loads.

Three equal resistors can be all in series, all in parallel, or two in parallel with the third in series. Those three arrangements give 3R, R/3 and (3/2)R or a similar result depending on the drawing. The drawing decides.
A resistor that is shorted by a wire has zero voltage and carries no current. It is not part of the equivalent. A resistor in an open branch carries no current either.

data.title: Kirchhoff's laws and their applications
notes: An application starts with a circuit diagram and one arrow on every branch. At each junction write one current as the sum of the others so that the junction law is already built in.

For two loops, walk each loop and write Σ E = Σ IR, or the equivalent sum of rises and drops equal to zero. The shared resistor carries the difference or the sum of the loop currents, matching the arrows.
The two equations are linear. Eliminate one current by substitution. A negative result flips that arrow and is then used as a positive magnitude in later arithmetic.
A Wheatstone bridge is an application. If the bridge is balanced, the galvanometer branch has zero current, and the loop equations collapse to the ratio condition P/Q = R/S.
A potentiometer is another application: the working battery drives a long wire, and the balance length is the point where the loop containing the test cell has zero current.
After the numbers, check that every junction still satisfies in equals out, and that the power from the cells equals the sum of I^2 R. A failed check means a sign error.

data.title: Wheatstone and Meter Bridge
notes: A Wheatstone bridge has four resistances P, Q, R and S, with a galvanometer across one diagonal and the battery across the other. At balance the galvanometer current is zero and P/Q = R/S.

The metre bridge is that bridge with a uniform 100 cm wire as two of the arms. If the jockey balances at length l1 from the left, the left wire resistance is proportional to l1 and the right to l2 = 100 − l1.

If the known resistance R is in the left gap and the unknown X is in the right gap, the balance condition is X/R = l2/l1, or the swapped form if the gaps are swapped. The diagram decides which length is which.
A uniform wire is essential, because the ratio of resistances is the ratio of lengths only when the resistance per centimetre is constant.
End corrections add a few millimetres for the copper strips. A precise unknown repeats the measurement with the gaps swapped and averages the two values of X.
Heating the wire changes its resistance per centimetre, so the current is kept small and the balance is found with a light touch of the jockey.
confusion: ❌ 'A meter bridge can measure any resistance accurately.' ✅ It is accurate only for *moderate* resistances (≈1 Ω to 1 kΩ); very high or very low resistances give poor null points.

data.topicTitle: Electromotive force (emf), internal resistance, and cells in combination
notes: The emf of a cell is the work done per unit charge as charge is moved through the source. It is measured in volts. It is the open-circuit potential difference, when no current is drawn.
A real cell has internal resistance r. When current I flows, the terminal voltage is E − I r. The 'lost volts' I r heat the inside of the cell.

The current in a single loop is I = E / (R + r). A smaller external resistance draws a larger current and drops the terminal voltage further. Shorting a cell makes I = E/r, which can be large and damaging.
Two identical cells in series give emf 2E and internal resistance 2r, if they point the same way. The current in an external R is 2E / (R + 2r).
Two identical cells in parallel give emf E and internal resistance r/2. The parallel pair can supply a larger current before the terminal voltage sags, but the emf is still the emf of one cell.

Cells in opposition subtract their emfs. A 1.5 V cell set against a 1.5 V cell gives no net emf if they are identical, and a small difference of emf drives a current limited by both internal resistances.

data.title: Potentiometer
notes: A potentiometer is a long uniform wire carrying a steady current from a driving battery. The potential drop along the wire is uniform, so a length l corresponds to a potential difference k l, where k is the drop per unit length.

The test cell is connected so that it opposes the wire drop. At the balance length the galvanometer reads zero. The cell's emf then equals the wire drop, and no current is being drawn from the test cell.

Because the test cell is on open circuit at balance, the potentiometer measures emf rather than a terminal voltage under load. A voltmeter that draws current measures a slightly smaller terminal voltage.
Two cells can be compared: E1/E2 = l1/l2, since k cancels. The longer balance length belongs to the larger emf.
The driving cell's emf must be larger than the test emf, otherwise no point on the wire can balance. A rheostat in the driving circuit sets k.
For internal resistance, the balance length is l1 on open circuit and l2 when a known shunt R is across the cell. Then r = R (l1 − l2)/l2.
confusion: ❌ 'A potentiometer measures current directly.' ✅ It measures *potential difference (voltage)* by finding a null point where no current flows through the galvanometer.
❌ 'A potentiometer is the same as a voltmeter.' ✅ A voltmeter draws current and has finite resistance; a potentiometer draws *zero current* at balance, giving a more accurate measurement.
❌ 'A longer potentiometer wire always gives more accuracy.' ✅ Accuracy improves with a *longer* wire (smaller potential gradient), but only if the wire has uniform cross-section and material.
The potentiometer is a null method. It is not an ordinary voltmeter.
k cancels in a comparison.
No balance point means the driving emf is too small or the cell is connected the wrong way.
The longer length is the larger emf.

notes: This is the same bridge with the classroom names written out. P and Q may be the ratio arms of a box, while R is known and S is the unknown. Balance is still P/Q = R/S.
When the ratio arms are the wire, P is proportional to the left length and Q to the right length. A jockey at the centre means the two gaps are equal if the wire is uniform.
If the balance point is far toward one end, the percentage uncertainty in the short length is large. Changing the known resistor to bring the balance near 50 cm is good practice.
The battery key is closed before the galvanometer key, and opened in the reverse order, so that a self-induced kick does not throw the galvanometer.
The unknown can be a coil whose resistance changes with temperature. The bridge then measures that temperature effect, provided the wire itself stays cool.
A small series resistor added to one gap shifts the balance in a predictable direction. That shift is a check that the lengths have been assigned the right way.

data.title: Potentiometer and its applications
notes: The applications all use the same null. Comparing two cells uses E1/E2 = l1/l2. Measuring a thermocouple's small emf uses a small potential gradient so that the balance length is long enough to read.

Internal resistance uses two balance lengths. l1 is with the cell alone. l2 is with a known resistance R across the cell, so the cell now sends current and its terminal voltage is smaller. Then r = R (l1/l2 − 1).
A standard cell of known emf can set k. If that cell balances at l_s, then k = E_s / l_s, and an unknown balanced at l has E = k l. The standard cell must not be left on load.

Sensitivity improves when k is small, because a small change in emf moves the jockey a long way. That means a long wire or a small driving current, until the galvanometer can no longer see the unbalance.
The wire must stay uniform and at one temperature. A jockey scraped along a hot wire both damages the wire and shifts k.
The positive terminal of the test cell goes toward the high-potential end of the wire. Reversed terminals give no balance point.

data.title: Faraday's laws of electromagnetic induction
notes: Faraday found that an emf appears in a coil while the magnetic flux through it is changing. A bar magnet at rest in the coil, however strong, induces nothing.
The flux through one turn is B times the perpendicular area. For N turns the flux linkage is N times that flux. The induced emf equals the negative of the rate of change of flux linkage.
The flux can be changed by moving the magnet, by switching the field, by changing the area of the loop, or by rotating the coil. A generator uses the rotation.
A faster change produces a larger emf. Doubling N doubles the emf for the same change of flux per turn. That is why a search coil has many turns.
If the circuit is closed, the emf drives an induced current. If the circuit is open, the emf is still there and can be read by a voltmeter, but no current flows.
The direction of the induced current is fixed by Lenz's law so that it opposes the change of flux. Faraday's law supplies the size. Lenz's law supplies the direction.

data.title: Lenz's law and conservation of energy
data.topicTitle: Lenz's law and conservation of energy
notes: Lenz's law says the induced current takes the direction that opposes the change in flux which caused it. It is the reason for the minus sign in Faraday's law.
If the south pole of a magnet approaches a coil, the flux of that pole is increasing. The near face of the coil becomes a south pole so that it repels the approaching south pole.
If that south pole is pulled away, the flux decreases and the near face becomes a north pole, attracting the magnet and opposing the removal.
The opposition is to the change. A stationary magnet produces no change and no induced current, so there is no force from an induced current.

Pushing the magnet in against the repulsion takes mechanical work. That work is the energy which appears as the induced current's heating in the coil. If the induced current had attracted the magnet, the motion would accelerate and energy would appear from nowhere.
Eddy currents in a copper plate near a moving magnet oppose the motion and dissipate energy as heat. That is Lenz's law used as a brake.

data.title: Self-induction and self-inductance
notes: Self-induction is the emf induced in a coil by a change of its own current. The changing current changes the coil's own flux, and Faraday's law gives an emf.
The self-inductance L is defined by NΦ = L I, so L is the flux linkage per unit current. The induced emf is −L dI/dt. The minus sign is Lenz's law: the emf opposes the change in current.
When the current is increasing, the induced emf opposes the battery. When the current is decreasing, the induced emf tries to keep the current going. A spark at a switch is that attempt.
L increases with more turns, a larger area, and an iron core. A long solenoid has L = μ0 n^2 A l, with n turns per unit length, if the field is the ideal solenoid field.
The henry is the inductance that induces 1 V when the current changes at 1 A/s. Energy stored is (1/2) L I^2.
Two coils on one core have self-inductance each and mutual inductance as well. This page is only the self part.

importantStatements: Self-induction is the emf induced in a coil by a change of its own current. The changing current changes the coil's own flux, and Faraday's law gives an emf.

When the current is increasing, the induced emf opposes the battery. When the current is decreasing, the induced emf tries to keep the current going. A spark at a switch is that attempt.

data.title: Mutual induction and mutual inductance
notes: Mutual induction is the emf in one circuit caused by a changing current in a nearby circuit. The changing current changes the flux that links the second coil.
The mutual inductance M is defined so that the flux linkage in the secondary is M times the primary current. The induced emf is −M dI/dt.
M is the same either way: a current changing in coil 2 induces in coil 1 with the same M. That symmetry is M_12 = M_21.
M is large when the coils share flux, as on a common iron core, and small when they are far apart or at right angles so that little flux links across.
A transformer is mutual induction used continuously with alternating current. The secondary emf exists only while the primary current is changing.
The henry is again the unit. M = 1 H if 1 A/s in the primary induces 1 V in the secondary.

data.title: Growing and decaying current in LR circuits
data.topicTitle: Growing and decaying current in LR circuits
notes: When a battery is connected to a resistor and an inductor in series, the current starts at zero and rises toward I_0 = V/R. The self-induced emf opposes the rise, so the rise is gradual.
The growth equation is I = I_0 (1 − e^(−Rt/L)). At t = 0, I = 0. After a long time the exponential vanishes and I = I_0.
If the battery is then removed and the coil is left connected across the resistor, the current decays as I = I_0 e^(−Rt/L). It starts at I_0 and falls toward zero.
The time constant τ = L/R is the time for the growth to reach about 63% of I_0, because 1 − e^(−1) is about 0.63. In decay, one time constant leaves about 37% of the current.
A large L or a small R makes the change slow. The inductor behaves as an open circuit at the first instant and as a wire after a long time, for a steady battery.
Energy (1/2) L I^2 builds during growth and returns as heat in the resistor during decay. The spark when a large inductor is switched is that energy.

data.title: Coulomb's law and its applications
notes: Coulomb's law gives the force between two point charges: F = k |q1 q2| / r^2, with k = 9.0 × 10^9 in SI units. The force is along the line joining the charges. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
Doubling either charge doubles the force. Doubling the distance divides the force by four. The force on each charge has the same magnitude even when the charges are unequal.
A third charge feels the vector sum of the forces from the other two. If the charges are not on one line, resolve each force into components before adding.
In a uniform insulating medium the force is the vacuum force divided by the dielectric constant. The medium does not cancel the law. It reduces the force.
Spherical charge distributions, outside the sphere, act as if their charge were at the centre. Inside a uniform spherical shell the field is zero, so a charge there feels no net force from the shell.
The applications are the same law used twice: find one pair force, then add a second pair as a vector. A negative answer for a component means that component points opposite the axis you chose.

data.title: Coulomb's Law
notes: **Coulomb's Law:** The force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: F = k(q₁q₂)/r².
Understanding Coulomb's Law is essential for solving electrostatics problems and understanding electric fields.
Key definitions and principles related to Coulomb's Law should be memorized and practiced regularly.
Coulomb's law gives the force between two point charges at rest: F = (1/(4πε0)) |q1 q2| / r^2. The direction is along the line joining them. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
The constant 1/(4πε0) is 9.0 × 10^9 in SI units. Doubling one charge doubles the force. Doubling the separation divides the force by four.
The force on q1 due to q2 is equal and opposite to the force on q2 due to q1. They are a Newton's third-law pair, even though the charges may be unequal.
confusion: ❌ 'Coulomb's law force is always attractive.' ✅ Force is *attractive* for opposite charges, but *repulsive* for like charges.
❌ 'Coulomb force acts only in a vacuum.' ✅ It applies in any medium, but the force is *reduced* by the dielectric constant (relative permittivity) of the medium: F_medium = F_vacuum / εᵣ.

❌ 'Point charges must be stationary for Coulomb's law.' ✅ While electrostatic formulas assume static charges for simplicity, the law applies to charges at any instant; magnetic forces emerge only when charges are in motion.

❌ 'The force depends on the presence of other charges.' ✅ Coulomb's Law describes the interaction between *two* specific point charges; the presence of a third charge does not change this pair-wise interaction (Superposition Principle applies for net force).
practice: Solve at least 5 problems on Coulomb's law from your textbook.
Try to derive the electrostatic force for simple charge configurations.
Create a summary sheet with all important formulas and theorems.
Practice identifying which method/formula to apply in each problem type.
universalFacts: This topic is a cornerstone of the physics curriculum and appears consistently in examinations.

notes: Electric field intensity is the force on a small positive test charge divided by that charge. Its unit is the newton per coulomb. The test charge must be small enough not to disturb the sources.

A point charge Q produces E = k Q / r^2, outward if Q is positive. Two point charges need a vector sum. On the perpendicular bisector of an equal and opposite pair, the fields point the same way along the bisector.
A long straight line of charge uses Gauss's law. The field is radial and E = λ / (2 π ε0 r), so it falls as 1/r rather than 1/r^2. λ is the charge per unit length.

An infinite non-conducting sheet with surface charge density σ produces a field σ / (2 ε0) on each side, pointing away from the sheet if σ is positive. The field does not fall with distance in this ideal infinite case.

A conducting sheet with the same charge density on one outer surface has E = σ / ε0 just outside, because the conductor forces the field lines to leave from one side in the standard result for a thin charged conductor.
Field lines start on positive charge and end on negative charge. They do not cross. Closer lines mean a stronger field. The force on any charge q placed in the field is q E.

data.title: Electric Field Intensity
notes: The electric field intensity at a point is the force that a small positive test charge would feel there, divided by that test charge: E = F/q. The unit is N/C, or V/m.
The test charge must be small enough not to disturb the charges that produce the field. The field is a property of the place, not of the test charge.
A point charge Q produces E = k Q / r^2. The direction is outward if Q is positive and inward if Q is negative.
Field lines start on positive charge and end on negative charge. They do not cross, because the field at a point has one direction. Closer lines mean a stronger field.
The net field of several charges is the vector sum of the individual fields. On the perpendicular bisector of a dipole the fields are not along the same line, so components are required.
A uniform field, as between parallel plates, has the same vector everywhere in the central region. The force on a charge there is qE, constant in magnitude and direction.
confusion: ❌ 'Electric field intensity is the force on a charge.' ✅ It is the *force per unit positive test charge* at a point: E = F/q₀.

❌ 'Electric field lines represent the path of a particle.' ✅ They show the *direction* of the force on a positive charge; they don't necessarily represent the actual trajectory (except for stationary charges).
❌ 'Electric field is zero inside a conductor.' ✅ It is zero *inside the material of a static conductor*, but not necessarily inside a cavity within it or in non-static conditions.
E is not the force. Force is qE.
A negative charge feels a force opposite the field.
Field lines are not trajectories in every case.
You cannot add field magnitudes that point different ways.

data.title: Electric Potential
notes: Electric potential at a point is the work done by an external agent, without changing kinetic energy, in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point. It is a scalar. The unit is the volt.
A point charge Q gives V = k Q / r. A positive charge makes a positive potential. There is no direction to add, so potentials from several charges add as ordinary numbers.
The potential difference between two points is the work per unit charge to move a test charge between them. A charge q changes its potential energy by q ΔV.
Equipotential surfaces join points of equal potential. The field is perpendicular to an equipotential. No work is done moving a charge on an equipotential.
In a uniform field the potential falls along the field direction. Between plates, E = V/d if V is the potential difference and d is the separation, in the uniform region.
Potential can be zero where the field is not, as at the midpoint between equal and opposite charges. The two scalars cancel, but the two field vectors point the same way.
confusion: ❌ 'Electric potential is the same as electric potential energy.' ✅ Potential is *energy per unit charge* (J/C); potential energy is the *total energy* (J) required to assemble charges.
❌ 'Electric potential is zero where the electric field is zero.' ✅ Not always true (e.g., at the center of a charged ring, E=0 but V≠0).
❌ 'Electric potential is a vector quantity.' ✅ It is a *scalar* quantity; it has magnitude but no direction, though it can be positive or negative.
Potential is not a vector.
Zero potential does not mean zero field.
A negative charge is attracted toward higher potential.
Work on an equipotential is zero.

data.title: Capacitance
notes: Capacitance is C = Q/V, the charge stored per unit potential difference. The unit is the farad. A 1 F capacitor would store 1 C at 1 V, which is far larger than a classroom capacitor. Microfarads and picofarads are the usual sizes.
A parallel-plate capacitor in vacuum has C = ε0 A / d. A bigger plate area stores more charge for the same voltage. A wider gap lowers the capacitance.

Filling the gap with a dielectric of constant K multiplies the capacitance by K, if the dielectric fills the space. The molecules of the dielectric polarise and reduce the field for a given free charge.
Connecting a capacitor to a battery fixes V. The charge is then Q = C V. Disconnecting the battery fixes Q, and a later change of C changes V.
Capacitors in parallel add their capacitances because they share the voltage and the charges add. Capacitors in series add the reciprocals, and the equivalent is smaller than the smallest of them.
The energy stored is (1/2) C V^2. A capacitor does not conduct steady current once it is charged. It does pass changing current in an AC circuit.
confusion: ❌ 'Capacitors store charge.' ✅ They store *energy* in an electric field; the net charge is zero (q on one plate, -q on other).
❌ 'Capacitance depends on charge and potential.' ✅ It depends only on *physical geometry* (area, distance, dielectric) of the capacitor, not on the charge currently stored.
❌ 'Adding a dielectric decreases capacitance.' ✅ A dielectric *increases* capacitance by reducing the internal electric field (C = εᵣC₀).
❌ skip the key fact → ✅ capacitance c = q/v; parallel-plate c = ε₀a/d (larger with dielectric: c = ε₀εᵣa/d)..

data.title: Dielectric and dielectric constant
notes: A dielectric is an insulating material. Its molecules polarise in an electric field, so a thin layer of bound charge appears on the surfaces.

The dielectric constant K, also called the relative permittivity, is the factor by which the capacitance of a vacuum capacitor increases when the dielectric fills it: C = K C_0. For vacuum, K = 1. For water and many insulators, K is greater than 1.
With the charge on the plates held fixed, the polarisation opposes the field, so the net field and the potential difference fall. Since C = Q/V, a smaller V means a larger C.
The force between two charges in a uniform medium is the vacuum force divided by K. The medium does not remove the charges. It reduces the force.
A dielectric lets the capacitor be used at a higher voltage before sparking, up to the dielectric strength. That is a separate limit from the value of K.
If the capacitor stays connected to a battery, V is fixed and inserting the dielectric increases Q. If it is disconnected, Q is fixed and V falls. The two experiments are different.

data.title: Dielectrics
notes: Dielectrics are classified by their molecules. A non-polar molecule has no permanent dipole and acquires one by distortion in the field. A polar molecule already has a dipole and tends to line up with the field, against thermal jostling.
Either way, the field inside is the applied field minus the field of the bound surface charge. For a linear dielectric that fills the space, E = E_0 / K.
The bound charge is not free to flow in a wire. It stays on the dielectric surface. Leakage through a poor insulator is a separate, unwanted current.

The energy stored is Q^2/(2C) or (1/2) C V^2. These agree, but if you insert the dielectric at fixed Q, C rises and the energy falls. The difference is the work associated with pulling the dielectric in.
If you insert it at fixed V, C rises and the energy (1/2) C V^2 rises. The battery supplies that extra energy. Quoting the wrong case is a common exam error.
Above the dielectric strength the insulator breaks down and conducts. The working voltage must stay below that field times the thickness.
confusion: ❌ 'Dielectric constant is same as permittivity' ✅ Dielectric constant (relative permittivity) is a ratio (dimensionless), while permittivity has specific units (F/m).
❌ 'Dielectrics conduct electricity like metals' ✅ Dielectrics are insulators; they polarize in an electric field but do not conduct free charges like conductors.

❌ 'Polarization reduces the internal electric field' ✅ Polarization *creates* an opposing field, which results in a *net* reduction of the internal electric field compared to the external applied field.
Polar and non-polar both reduce the net field.
Bound charge does not flow around the circuit.
Energy falls at fixed Q and rises at fixed V.
E = E_0/K, not E_0 times K.

data.title: Energy stored in a capacitor
notes: Charging a capacitor means moving charge from one plate to the other against a rising potential difference. The work done is the energy stored.
At an intermediate charge q the voltage is q/C, so the next bit of charge dq costs (q/C) dq. Integrating from 0 to Q gives U = Q^2 / (2C). With Q = C V this is also (1/2) C V^2 and (1/2) Q V.
The factor one half appears because the voltage starts at zero and ends at V. The average voltage during charging is V/2, and charge Q times that average is (1/2) Q V.

A battery at constant V supplies energy Q V, which is C V^2. The capacitor stores only half of that. The other half is dissipated as heat in the resistance of the connecting wires during the charging current.
The stored energy can be written as a density in the field, (1/2) ε0 E^2 in vacuum. The energy is between the plates, in the field, not inside the metal of the plates.
If an isolated capacitor has its plates pulled apart, Q is fixed, C falls and the stored energy rises. The extra energy is the work you do against the attraction of the plates.

data.title: Faraday's Laws
notes: Faraday's first observation is that an emf appears in a circuit when the magnetic flux through it is changing. A steady flux, however large, induces nothing.
The flux through one turn is Φ = B A when the field is uniform and perpendicular to the area. At an angle, the perpendicular component B cosθ is used. Flux linkage for N turns is NΦ.
Faraday's law says the induced emf equals the negative of the rate of change of flux linkage. A faster change means a larger emf.
The flux can be changed by changing the field, by changing the area of the loop, or by rotating the loop. A generator rotates a coil so that the angle changes continuously.
The minus sign is Lenz's law. The induced current makes a field that opposes the change in flux that caused it.
If the circuit is open there is still an induced emf, but no induced current. Current needs a closed path.
confusion: ❌ 'Induced EMF depends only on magnetic field strength.' ✅ It depends on the *rate of change* of magnetic flux (dΦ/dt). A strong field that doesn't change induces no EMF.
❌ 'Faraday's law applies only to closed circuits.' ✅ The *law* defines the EMF induced in a loop; a physical current flows only if the circuit is *closed*.
❌ 'More turns always mean more flux.' ✅ More turns increase the *total flux linkage* (NΦ), which proportionally increases the induced EMF.
A steady field does not induce an emf.
Emf depends on the rate, not on the flux alone.
An open circuit can have an emf and no current.
Area, field and angle are three different ways to change the flux.

data.title: Lenz's Law
notes: Lenz's law says that the induced current flows so as to oppose the change in flux that produces it. It is the meaning of the minus sign in Faraday's law.
If the north pole of a magnet approaches a coil, the flux of that pole through the coil is increasing. The coil's near face becomes a north pole to repel the approaching magnet.
If the north pole is pulled away, the flux is decreasing, and the near face becomes a south pole to attract the magnet and oppose the removal.
The opposition is to the change, not to the field itself. A steady magnet in a coil induces nothing, so there is nothing to oppose.
The law is required by energy conservation. If the induced current helped the change, a tiny push would grow into a larger current and create energy.
You still need Faraday's law for the size of the emf. Lenz's law is only the direction. The right-hand grip then turns that opposing field into a current direction in the wire.
confusion: ❌ 'Lenz's Law creates energy.' ✅ It is a direct consequence of the *Law of Conservation of Energy*; the work done to move a magnet is converted into electrical energy.

❌ 'Lenz's law always opposes the magnetic field.' ✅ It opposes the *change in magnetic flux* that created the induced current, which may mean opposing the field or aiding it depending on the situation.
❌ 'Induced current only flows if the magnet moves.' ✅ It flows if the *magnetic flux* through the loop changes, which can happen by changing the magnet position, loop size, or field strength.
Lenz does not oppose the field. It opposes the change.
It does not give the number of volts.
A retreating pole is the opposite face from an approaching pole.
A steady magnet induces no opposing current.

data.title: Self and Mutual Induction
notes: Self-induction and mutual induction are the same Faraday effect with different flux. In self-induction the coil links its own changing flux. In mutual induction a second coil links flux from the first.
The self emf is −L dI/dt and it opposes the change of that coil's current. The mutual emf is −M dI_1/dt in the second coil.
A coil can have both at once. Its total induced emf is −L dI/dt from itself plus −M dI_other/dt from its neighbour.
L and M are both in henries. M cannot exceed √(L1 L2), and it reaches that limit only when every flux line of one coil links the other.
Opening a switch in a self-inductive circuit produces a large dI/dt and a spark. A mutual pair does the same in the second coil if the first current is interrupted.
The transformer, the induction coil and the coupled windings of a radio are mutual induction. The choke that opposes a change in a single circuit is self-induction.
confusion: ❌ 'Self-induction only happens in a coil.' ✅ It happens whenever the current *within* a conductor changes, creating a changing magnetic flux through itself.

❌ 'Mutual induction is the same as self-induction.' ✅ Self-induction is EMF induced by a coil's *own* current change; mutual induction is EMF induced in a *secondary* coil due to current changes in a *primary* coil.
❌ 'Inductance depends on the current flowing.' ✅ Like capacitance, inductance is a *geometric property* of the coil (turns, core material, shape), not dependent on the magnitude of the current.
Do not use M for a single isolated coil.
Do not use L for the emf in the neighbouring coil.
A steady current gives neither emf.
M is not added to L as if they were resistors.

data.title: LR Circuits
notes: An LR series circuit on a battery has a current that starts at zero. At that instant the entire battery voltage is across the inductor, because the resistor has no current and therefore no voltage.
As the current grows, the resistor voltage I R grows and the inductor voltage falls. After a long time the inductor voltage is zero and the resistor has the full battery voltage.
The current is (V/R) (1 − e^(−t/τ)) with τ = L/R. The voltages always add to V, with signs, which is the loop rule at every instant.
At t = τ the current is about 63% of the final value and the inductor still holds about 37% of the battery voltage.
If the battery is replaced by a short circuit, the current decays as I_0 e^(−t/τ). The inductor then drives the resistor, and both voltages fall together.
This file is the circuit view of the same law as the growth-and-decay file. The numbers here are a voltage split rather than a repeat of the earlier current.
confusion: ❌ 'Inductor instantly passes current.' ✅ Inductors *oppose* changes in current; at the moment of switching (t=0), current through an inductor remains zero.
❌ 'An inductor behaves like a resistor in DC steady state.' ✅ In DC steady state (t → ∞), an inductor acts as a *short circuit* (ideal wire with zero resistance).
❌ 'LR circuit decay time is infinite.' ✅ Current in an LR circuit decays exponentially; after $5\tau$ (where $\tau = L/R$), it is effectively zero.
The inductor does not keep the battery voltage forever.
At the first instant the resistor voltage is zero.
τ is L/R in seconds.
Decay is not a second growth formula.

data.title: Magnetic field and magnetic force on moving charges
data.topicTitle: Magnetic field and magnetic force on moving charges
notes: A charge moving in a magnetic field feels a force q v B sinθ. θ is the angle between the velocity and the field. The force is zero if the charge is at rest or if it moves parallel to the field.
The force is perpendicular to both the velocity and the field. A positive charge follows the right-hand rule. A negative charge is pushed the opposite way.
Because the force is always perpendicular to the velocity, it does no work. The speed stays constant. Only the direction changes.

If the velocity is perpendicular to a uniform field, the path is a circle. The radius is m v / (q B). A faster charge, or a heavier one, makes a larger circle. A stronger field makes a tighter circle.
If the velocity has a component along the field, that component is not changed and the path is a helix. The pitch is set by the parallel speed and the time to go once around.
The tesla is the field in which a charge of 1 C moving at 1 m/s perpendicular to the field feels a force of 1 N. Laboratory fields of a fraction of a tesla already bend electron beams.

data.title: Lorentz force and motion of charged particles in magnetic…
data.topicTitle: Lorentz force and motion of charged particles in magnetic fields
notes: The Lorentz force is the total electromagnetic force on a charge, q E plus the magnetic force q v B. The electric part can speed the charge up. The magnetic part only turns it.
If E and B are perpendicular to each other and to the velocity, the two forces can point in opposite directions. They cancel when q E = q v B, so v = E/B.

A velocity selector is a pair of crossed fields. Charges of the chosen speed go straight through. Faster charges are bent one way and slower charges the other way. The charge and the mass cancel, so the selected speed does not depend on them.
After the selector, a magnetic field alone bends the beam into a circle whose radius is m v / (q B). Measuring that radius at the known speed gives the mass-to-charge ratio.

A cyclotron uses the magnetic circle and an electric kick twice per revolution to increase the speed. The frequency of the orbit for a non-relativistic particle is q B / (2 π m), independent of the speed.
At speeds near the speed of light the mass effectively increases and the cyclotron frequency falls. The simple selector and the simple radius formula are for speeds well below that.

data.topicTitle: Biot-Savart law and its applications (straight wire, circular loop, solenoid)
notes: The Biot–Savart law gives the small field of a current element: it is proportional to I dl sinθ / r^2, and the direction is perpendicular to the element and to the line drawn to the point.
Integrating around a long straight wire gives B = μ0 I /(2π r). The field lines are circles around the wire, given by the right-hand grip. The field falls as 1/r.
At the centre of a circular loop of one turn, B = μ0 I /(2 R), along the axis. N turns wound together multiply the field by N.
A long solenoid is many circular turns in a row. Inside, the field is μ0 n I, nearly uniform, with n turns per metre. Outside an ideal long solenoid the field is negligible.
μ0 is 4π × 10^−7. The combination μ0 / 2π, used for the straight wire, is 2 × 10^−7. Using μ0 where the formula already contains 2π, or the other way round, is the usual slip.
Ampere's law reaches the wire and the solenoid faster when the symmetry is obvious. Biot–Savart is the law you start from when you have to build the field from elements.

data.title: Ampere's circuital law and its applications
data.topicTitle: Ampere's circuital law and its applications
notes: The applications are the reason the law is taught. You invent an Amperian path that follows the suspected field, write B times the length if B is constant, and set that equal to μ0 I_enclosed.

Outside a long straight wire the path is a circle and the whole current is enclosed. Inside a uniform cylindrical wire, at radius r smaller than the wire, only the current in the inner cross-section is enclosed, so I_enc = I (r^2/R^2).
That inner result makes B proportional to r inside the wire and proportional to 1/r outside. The two formulas meet at the surface.
A toroid uses a circular path inside the doughnut. The enclosed current is N I if the path threads all N turns. The circumference 2π r then gives B = μ0 N I /(2π r).
A path that threads no current, such as a circle outside a toroid, gives zero line integral. With the symmetry, B itself is zero there in the ideal case.
This is a different use from the solenoid card: here the worked case is the inside of a thick wire, not the solenoid interior.

data.title: Force between two parallel current-carrying conductors
data.topicTitle: Force between two parallel current-carrying conductors
notes: A long straight wire produces circles of magnetic field. A second wire, parallel to the first, carries current across that field and feels a force F = I L B sinθ. With the wires parallel, θ is 90°.
Substituting B = μ0 I1 /(2π r) gives the force per unit length F/L = μ0 I1 I2 /(2π r). The force is mutual: each wire feels the same magnitude.
If the currents are in the same direction the force is attractive. If they are in opposite directions the force is repulsive. The right-hand rule on one wire's field, then on the force, gives this.
The ampere was historically defined from this force: two long parallel wires, 1 m apart, carrying 1 A each, attract with 2 × 10^−7 N per metre of length.

The wires must be long compared with their separation, or the formula is only a middle-region estimate. The field is not uniform, but the result above is already the integrated force on a straight parallel wire.
Coils and bus bars use the same idea. Parallel turns of a solenoid attract. A short-circuit current in opposite bus bars pushes them apart.

data.title: Moving coil galvanometer, ammeter, and voltmeter
data.topicTitle: Moving coil galvanometer, ammeter, and voltmeter
notes: A moving-coil galvanometer carries a coil in a radial magnetic field. The torque is N I A B and does not change with angle, because the field is radial. A hairspring supplies a restoring torque k θ.
At rest, N I A B = k θ, so the deflection is proportional to the current. The scale can be marked in equal current steps.
The coil current must stay small. To measure a large current, a low-resistance shunt is connected in parallel with the galvanometer. Most of the current bypasses the coil.
If the galvanometer has resistance G and full-scale current I_g, and the ammeter is to read I, the shunt is S = I_g G / (I − I_g). A larger range needs a smaller shunt.

To make a voltmeter, a large resistor is connected in series. The instrument then draws little current and can be placed across a component. The series resistor is (V / I_g) − G for a full-scale voltage V.
The coil is damped, often by eddy currents in a metal frame, so the needle settles instead of swinging. Swapping the shunt and the series resistor builds the wrong instrument.

data.title: Magnetic Force on Moving Charges
notes: A charge moving in a magnetic field feels F = q v B sinθ, where θ is the angle between the velocity and the field. The force is zero if the charge is at rest or if it moves parallel to the field.
The direction is perpendicular to both v and B. For a positive charge the right-hand rule gives it. A negative charge feels the opposite force.
Because the force is always perpendicular to the velocity, it does no work and does not change the speed. It changes only the direction.
In a uniform field, motion perpendicular to the field is a circle of radius m v /(q B). Motion with a component along the field is a helix.
Combined electric and magnetic forces are the Lorentz force, qE + q v B in vector form. A velocity selector sets the two forces opposite and equal so that qE = q v B.
The tesla is the field that exerts 1 N on a charge of 1 C moving at 1 m/s perpendicular to the field.
confusion: ❌ 'A magnetic force can do work on a charged particle.' ✅ Magnetic force is always *perpendicular* to velocity, so it does *zero work*; it changes direction, not speed.
❌ 'A stationary charge experiences magnetic force.' ✅ The particle *must be moving* (v ≠ 0) and not parallel to B; a stationary charge feels no magnetic force.
❌ 'The force direction is given by the right-hand rule for negative charges too.' ✅ For *negative* charges (electrons), reverse the right-hand rule direction (or use left hand).
A stationary charge feels electric force but not magnetic force.
The magnetic force does not speed the charge up.
sinθ is not optional when the velocity is not perpendicular.
Negative charges reverse the rule.

data.title: Biot-Savart Law
notes: The Biot–Savart law gives the magnetic field due to a tiny current element: dB = (μ0 / 4π) I dl sinθ / r^2. The direction is perpendicular to the element and to the line from the element to the point.
A long straight wire is the integral of that law, and the result is B = μ0 I /(2π r). The field circles the wire, given by the right-hand grip.
At the centre of a single circular loop the result is B = μ0 I /(2 R), along the axis. A coil of N turns multiplies this by N if the turns are together.
On the axis of a loop, off centre, the field is along the axis and weaker. The perpendicular components from opposite elements cancel.
μ0 / 4π is 10^−7, and μ0 is 4π × 10^−7. Using the wrong one is the usual numerical slip.
The law is the magnetic analogue of Coulomb's law for a current element. It is the starting point. Ampere's law is the shortcut when symmetry is high.
confusion: ❌ 'Biot-Savart law gives the total magnetic field directly.' ✅ It gives the *contribution* dB from a tiny element dl; the total field requires integration over the entire conductor.
❌ 'The magnetic field is parallel to the current element.' ✅ dB is *perpendicular* to both dl and r̂ (given by the cross product dl × r̂).
❌ 'Biot-Savart law applies to moving charges but not currents.' ✅ A current is just moving charges; the law applies to *both* — for a charge: dB = (μ₀/4π)·(qv×r̂)/r².
The straight-wire field is not μ0 I /(2R). That is the loop centre.
The field circles a straight wire. It is not radial.
sinθ is zero for a point on the line of the element.
μ0 and μ0/4π are different.

data.title: Ampere's Circuital Law
notes: Ampere's circuital law says that the line integral of B around a closed path equals μ0 times the current enclosed by that path. It is useful when symmetry makes B constant on the path and parallel to it.
For a long straight wire, a circular path of radius r gives B times 2π r = μ0 I, so B = μ0 I /(2π r), the same answer as Biot–Savart.

For a long solenoid, a rectangular path with one side inside gives B = μ0 n I, where n is the number of turns per unit length. The field outside the ideal solenoid is zero, so that side of the rectangle contributes nothing.
A toroid, a solenoid bent into a ring, has B = μ0 N I /(2π r) inside the core and a very small field outside.
Currents outside the path are not enclosed, so they do not appear on the right-hand side. They may still shape the field if the symmetry is poor, which is why the law is then hard to use.
The law as stated here is for steady currents in vacuum. A displacement current is the later correction for changing electric fields.
confusion: ❌ 'Ampere's law works for any current distribution.' ✅ It is most useful for *highly symmetric* situations (infinite wire, solenoid, toroid); for arbitrary shapes, Biot-Savart is needed.
❌ 'The enclosed current must be at the center of the Amperian loop.' ✅ The current only needs to pass *through* the loop; its position inside the loop does not matter for the line integral.
❌ 'Magnetic field outside a solenoid is always zero.' ✅ For an *ideal infinite* solenoid it is zero, but a real finite solenoid has a weak external field.
n is turns per metre, not the total turns, in the solenoid formula.
Current outside the Amperian loop is not enclosed.
The outside of an ideal long solenoid is not a place of strong field.
The law does not replace Biot–Savart when there is no symmetry.

For a long straight wire, a circular path of radius r gives B times 2π r = μ0 I, so B = μ0 I /(2π r), the same answer as Biot–Savart.

For a long solenoid, a rectangular path with one side inside gives B = μ0 n I, where n is the number of turns per unit length. The field outside the ideal solenoid is zero, so that side of the rectangle contributes nothing.

data.title: Moving Coil Galvanometer
notes: A moving-coil galvanometer has a coil of N turns and area A in the radial magnetic field of a cylindrical pole piece. The field is radial so that the plane of the coil stays parallel to B in the useful sense and the torque is N I A B for any deflection.
A hairspring provides a restoring torque k θ. At equilibrium N I A B = k θ, so θ is proportional to I. The scale can be linear.

Current sensitivity is the deflection per unit current, N A B / k. Voltage sensitivity is the deflection per unit voltage. A large N, a large area, a strong field or a weak spring increases sensitivity.

To make an ammeter, a small shunt resistor is connected in parallel so that most of the current bypasses the coil. The galvanometer then reads a large current with only a small current through the coil.
To make a voltmeter, a large resistor is connected in series so that the instrument draws little current and can be placed across a component.
The coil is wound on a conducting frame, or has a separate damper, so that eddy currents stop the oscillation and the needle settles.
confusion: ❌ 'A galvanometer measures current directly like an ammeter.' ✅ A galvanometer detects *small* currents; an ammeter is a galvanometer with a *shunt resistor* added in parallel to measure larger currents.
❌ 'Increasing the number of turns reduces sensitivity.' ✅ Sensitivity is *directly proportional* to the number of turns (N): more turns = greater deflection for the same current.
❌ 'A galvanometer has zero resistance.' ✅ It has a *finite* resistance; an ideal ammeter has zero resistance, but the galvanometer itself does not.
The shunt is parallel, not series.
The voltmeter multiplier is series, not parallel.
Sensitivity is not the same as the range.
The radial field is what keeps the torque independent of angle.

data.title: Photoelectric Effect
notes: In the photoelectric effect, light falling on a metal can eject electrons. The effect starts at once, and it happens only if the frequency is above a threshold for that metal.

Einstein's explanation is that light arrives as photons of energy h f. A photon gives its energy to one electron. Part of that energy, the work function φ, is spent escaping the metal. The rest is kinetic energy.
K_max = h f − φ. Below the threshold, h f is less than φ and no electron escapes, however bright the light. Brightness is the number of photons, not the energy of each one.
A brighter beam above threshold ejects more electrons, so the current rises. It does not raise the maximum kinetic energy. That energy depends on frequency.
A stopping potential V_s is the retarding voltage that just cuts the current to zero. Then e V_s = K_max. Measuring V_s measures the fastest electrons.
A useful number is h c = 1240 eV nm, so a photon's energy in electronvolts is 1240 divided by the wavelength in nanometres.
confusion: ❌ 'Higher intensity light always causes photoelectric emission' ✅ Emission only occurs if the light frequency is *above* the threshold frequency, regardless of intensity.
❌ 'Photoelectric current increases with frequency' ✅ Current (number of electrons) increases with *intensity* (number of photons), not frequency.
❌ 'Stopping potential depends on light intensity' ✅ Stopping potential depends only on the *maximum kinetic energy* of emitted electrons, which is determined by the light *frequency*.
❌ skip the key fact → ✅ photoelectric effect: hν = φ + k_max; k_max = ev_s; stopping voltage v_s = (h/e)(ν − ν₀)..

data.title: de Broglie Waves
notes: Reading λ = h/p the other way, a measured wavelength gives the momentum p = h/λ. Electron diffraction fringes are therefore a momentum measurement.
An electron microscope forms an image with electrons rather than light. The shorter wavelength, at tens of kilovolts, gives a finer limit of resolution than a light microscope.

The wave packet that represents a localised particle is a spread of wavelengths. A narrow packet, a well known position, needs a wide spread of momenta. That is the idea behind the uncertainty principle.
A photon already had E = h f and p = E/c, which is the same λ = h/p. De Broglie's step was to give massive particles the relation that light already satisfied.
At higher voltage the electron is faster, the wavelength is shorter, and the non-relativistic √V formula starts to fail. Exam calculations at 100 to 200 V are still in the safe range.
The particle is not smeared into a wave in the detector. Many electrons build the diffraction pattern one impact at a time. Each impact is local. The pattern is the wave.
confusion: ❌ Wavelength is proportional to energy ✅ Wavelength is inversely proportional to momentum (λ = h/p), not energy directly.
❌ de Broglie waves apply only to charged particles ✅ Applicable to all matter, including neutral particles like neutrons, if they have momentum.
❌ Wave nature is observed in macroscopic objects ✅ Due to the extremely small value of Planck's constant (h), the wavelength of macroscopic objects is negligible and undetectable.
The microscope's advantage is the short wavelength, not a brighter lamp.
Uncertainty is a wave-packet fact, not a clumsy instrument.
Do not use the electron √V formula for a photon.
A single electron does not draw the whole fringe pattern.

data.title: Bohr's Atom
notes: Bohr kept the nuclear atom and added a quantum rule: the electron's angular momentum is n h / (2π), with n = 1, 2, 3, and so on. Only those orbits are allowed.
In those orbits the electron does not radiate, even though it is accelerating. Radiation happens only when the electron jumps from one allowed orbit to another.
The energy of hydrogen is E_n = −13.6 / n^2 electronvolts. The negative sign means the electron is bound. n = 1 is the ground state, the most tightly bound.
A jump from n2 down to n1 emits a photon with energy E_n2 − E_n1. The wavelength follows 1/λ = R (1/n1^2 − 1/n2^2), with R the Rydberg constant.
The Lyman series ends on n = 1 and is ultraviolet. Balmer ends on n = 2 and is the visible series. Paschen ends on n = 3 and is infrared.
Bohr's picture fails for atoms with many electrons and it has no wave reason for the quantum rule. It remains the right first model for hydrogen numbers.

Pay attention to the conditions under which formulas and theorems apply.
Practice with multiple examples to solidify your understanding.
The electron does not radiate in an allowed orbit.
−13.6 eV is the ground state, not an emitted photon.

data.title: Nucleus and Binding Energy
notes: The mass of a nucleus is less than the mass of its protons and neutrons weighed separately. The difference Δm is the mass defect.
Einstein's relation turns that mass into energy: binding energy = Δm c^2. In nuclear units, 1 atomic mass unit corresponds to 931 MeV.
The binding energy is the energy you must supply to separate the nucleus into individual nucleons. It is not an energy the nucleus has sitting as kinetic energy.
Binding energy per nucleon is the binding energy divided by the mass number A. It rises from the light nuclei, peaks near iron, and falls slowly for the heavy nuclei.

Fusion of very light nuclei moves them up the curve and releases energy. Fission of a very heavy nucleus also moves the pieces up the curve and releases energy. Both are movements toward higher binding energy per nucleon.
A calculated binding energy uses the actual masses, not the integer mass number. Using A as if it were the nuclear mass in u is the usual mistake.
confusion: ❌ Thinking nuclear mass equals sum of nucleons ✅ Nuclear mass is less than the sum of its constituents' masses; the difference is the mass defect, converted into binding energy (E = mc²).
❌ Misinterpreting binding energy per nucleon as total binding energy ✅ Binding energy per nucleon determines nuclear stability; higher values generally indicate a more stable nucleus.
❌ Confusing fusion and fission energy release ✅ Both processes release energy, but fusion involves combining light nuclei, while fission involves splitting heavy nuclei.
A larger mass defect means a more tightly bound nucleus, not a heavier one.
Binding energy is the energy to pull the nucleus apart.
Per nucleon, not the total, is what the stability curve plots.
1 u is 931 MeV, not 931 joules.

data.title: Semiconductors and Devices
notes: Silicon and germanium are semiconductors. At room temperature a few bonds break, giving a free electron and a hole. The conductivity lies between a metal and an insulator and rises with temperature.

Doping with a group-15 atom adds an extra electron. That is n-type, and electrons are the majority carriers. Doping with a group-13 atom leaves a hole. That is p-type, and holes are the majority carriers.

A p-n junction has a depletion layer. In forward bias the p-side is made positive, the barrier falls, and a large current flows. In reverse bias the barrier rises and only a tiny leakage current flows.
The diode is a one-way device. A rectifier uses that one-way behaviour to turn alternating voltage into a unidirectional voltage.
A bipolar transistor has two junctions, emitter, base and collector. A small base current controls a larger collector current. That is the current gain.
An LED is a diode that emits light when forward biased, as electrons and holes recombine. A solar cell is a junction that produces an emf when light creates pairs.
confusion: ❌ Assuming intrinsic semiconductors conduct well at room temperature ✅ Intrinsic semiconductors have very few free charge carriers; doping is required to significantly increase conductivity.
❌ Confusing P-type with positive charge ✅ P-type semiconductors are electrically neutral; they have "holes" as majority carriers, not a net positive charge.
❌ Misinterpreting the depletion layer as an insulator ✅ The depletion layer is a region depleted of free charge carriers, acting as a barrier, not an absolute insulator.
n-type is not negatively charged overall. It is still neutral.
Forward bias is p positive, not p negative.
Holes are missing electrons, not positive protons moving.
Temperature helps a semiconductor conduct. It usually hurts a metal.

data.title: Logic Gates
notes: A logic gate takes binary inputs, called 1 and 0, and gives a binary output. In a circuit, 1 is a higher voltage and 0 is a lower voltage. The exact voltages depend on the family of chips.
The AND gate outputs 1 only when every input is 1. The OR gate outputs 1 when at least one input is 1. The NOT gate has one input and outputs the opposite.
NAND is AND followed by NOT. It outputs 0 only when every input is 1. NOR is OR followed by NOT. It outputs 1 only when every input is 0.
NAND alone can build AND, OR and NOT. NOR alone can do the same. They are called universal gates.
A truth table lists every input combination. Two inputs give four rows: 00, 01, 10 and 11. Writing the output for each row is the whole definition of the gate.
Combinations make decisions: a NAND arrangement can add bits or store a bit in a latch. The exam usually stops at the truth table and a simple combination.
confusion: ❌ Confusing NAND/NOR as universal gates ✅ NAND and NOR are universal gates because any logic gate (AND, OR, NOT) can be constructed solely using them.
❌ Thinking logic levels are continuous ✅ Logic gates operate on discrete digital voltage levels (typically 0 or 1), not continuous analog signals.
❌ Misinterpreting Truth Tables for complex gates ✅ Truth tables must be evaluated step-by-step for complex gate combinations, not by guessing the output based on a single input.
OR is not exclusive. It is also 1 when both inputs are 1.
NAND is not 'both zero'. It is the opposite of AND.
NOT has one input.
1 is a voltage band, not necessarily 1 volt.

data.title: De Broglie wavelength and matter waves
data.topicTitle: De Broglie wavelength and matter waves
notes: De Broglie proposed that matter has a wavelength λ = h / p, where p is the momentum and h is Planck's constant. A faster or heavier particle has a shorter wavelength.
For an electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference V, (1/2) m v^2 = e V, so p = √(2 m e V) and λ = h / √(2 m e V).
In angstroms a useful electron form is λ ≈ 12.27 / √V when V is in volts. At 100 V the wavelength is about 1.23 Å, the size of atomic spacings, which is why electron diffraction is visible.
A cricket ball has a tiny wavelength because its momentum is huge. Its wave nature is real and undetectable. The effect shows up for electrons, neutrons and atoms.
Davisson and Germer diffracted electrons from a nickel crystal and found the wavelength that de Broglie predicted. That is the experimental anchor.
The wave is not the electron wiggling through a medium. It is the wave associated with the probability of finding the electron. The electron is still detected as a particle.

data.title: Atom — Bohr's model and hydrogen spectrum
data.topicTitle: Atom — Bohr's model and hydrogen spectrum
notes: Bohr's hydrogen atom keeps a positive nucleus and an electron in orbit, and adds the rule that the angular momentum is n h / (2π). Only integer n is allowed.
In an allowed orbit the electron does not radiate, even though it is accelerating. Radiation happens only when the electron jumps from one allowed energy to a lower one.
The energies are E_n = −13.6 / n^2 electronvolts. The ground state is n = 1, at −13.6 eV. The zero of energy is the electron removed to infinity.
The photon energy is the difference of the two levels. A jump from n = 3 to n = 2 is a Balmer line. Jumps that end on n = 1 are the Lyman series, in the ultraviolet.
The wave formula is 1/λ = R (1/n1^2 − 1/n2^2). R is the Rydberg constant. A larger jump gives a larger photon energy and a shorter wavelength.
The model gives the hydrogen numbers and fails for atoms with several electrons. It also does not explain why the angular momentum should be quantised. Later wave mechanics supplies that reason.
