data.summary: Convert measurements to moles, apply balanced-equation ratios, identify the limiting reactant, and convert the predicted amount to the requested quantity.

data.title: Biomolecules — Introduction and Functions
data.topicTitle: Biomolecules: Introduction and functions of carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, minerals, enzymes and water

mcqs.question: Which biomolecule is NOT a true polymer?
How many hydrogen bonds are present between G and C in DNA?
Insulin, haemoglobin and amylase all belong to which class of biomolecule?
The primary structure of a protein is determined by which bond?

notes: Biomolecules are organic molecules essential to life: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, plus minerals, enzymes and water.

Carbohydrates (CH2O)n: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, ribose), disaccharides (sucrose=glucose+fructose, lactose, maltose), polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose). Provide energy (4 kcal/g) and structural support.

Proteins: polymers of 20 standard amino acids (L-forms; glycine is achiral) joined by peptide (-CO-NH-) bonds. Four structural levels (primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary). Functions: enzymes, transport (haemoglobin), contraction, defence, structural.
Lipids: hydrophobic; triglycerides (fat storage, 9 kcal/g), phospholipids (membrane bilayer), steroids (cholesterol, hormones). Not true polymers.
Nucleic acids: DNA (double helix, deoxyribose, A=T 2 H-bonds, G=C 3 H-bonds) stores heredity; RNA (single strand, ribose, A=U) in protein synthesis (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA).
Enzymes: biological catalysts (mostly proteins); work by the lock-and-key / induced-fit model; denatured by high temperature or extreme pH; show high substrate specificity.
Water (major solvent, ~70% of cell) and minerals (Ca, P, K, Na, Fe, I) act as structural, catalytic and osmotic regulators; deficiency causes deficiency diseases.
confusion: Cellulose is a structural polymer in plant cell walls, not an energy reserve; glycogen (animal) and starch (plant) are the storage forms.
Starch is unbranched amylose + branched amylopectin; both yield maltose on hydrolysis.
Ribose and deoxyribose differ only by one oxygen atom on C-2; hence RNA vs DNA sugars.
Denaturation unfolds protein (loss of secondary/tertiary structure); it is often reversible at low temperature.
Lipids are not polymers; they do not have repeating monomers like the other three macromolecule classes.
A peptide bond forms between the -COOH of one amino acid and the -NH2 of the next, releasing one water (condensation).
practice: Match each biomolecule to a function: insulin (hormone), haemoglobin (transport), cellulose (structure), ATP (energy currency).
Draw a dipeptide from glycine + alanine and circle the peptide bond.
Differentiate DNA and RNA by sugar, bases, strands and function.
Explain why an enzyme is still present after catalysing a reaction.
Relate an enzyme deficiency (e.g. phenylalanine) to a disease (PKU).
universalFacts: Carbon makes up roughly a fifth of human body mass and forms the covalent backbone of every biomolecule.
Hemoglobin binds about 1.34 mL of oxygen per gram; fully saturated blood carries roughly 20 mL of oxygen per 100 mL.
Water has an anomalously high specific heat and acts as a biological thermostat.
Human insulin (51 amino acids) was produced by recombinant-DNA technology in 1978 and approved in 1982 — the first approved recombinant-DNA pharmaceutical.
examples: Starch in rice/potato is a storage polysaccharide; glycogen in liver/muscle is the animal reserve.
Cellulose (beta-glucose) forms the cell wall of green plants.
DNA replication and mRNA synthesis link nucleic acids to protein production.
Iodine deficiency enlarges the thyroid; iron deficiency causes anaemia.
practiceQuestions: How is a triglyceride different from a phospholipid in structure and function?
List the four structural levels of a protein with one example of a quaternary protein.
Describe the induced-fit model of enzyme action and its significance.
Why are essential amino acids called "essential"?
Differentiate amylose and amylopectin and state the test for starch.
formulas: General carbohydrate ratio: C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1, i.e. (CH2O)n
Endergonic polymerisation (condensation): monomer + monomer → dimer + H2O
Peptide unit: -C(=O)-NH-
DNA base pairing: A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds)
keyPoints: Functions: C=energy+structure, P=enzymes/transport/structure, L=storage+membrane, N=heredity+protein synthesis.
A hydrolysis breaks a bond + water; a condensation joins molecules - water.
Enzymes are specific, reversible regulators, not consumed in the reaction.
DNA is the gene; RNA is the messenger/scaffold in protein synthesis.
Essential amino acids (8 in adults, 9 in children) must come from food.
Deficiency of minerals leads to named diseases (Fe→anaemia, I→goitre, Ca→rickets).
enrichedContent.summary: Biomolecules are the chemical basis of life. Carbohydrates supply and store energy and form structural fibres; proteins (from 20 amino acids) act as enzymes, transporters, contractile and defence molecules in four structural levels; lipids store energy and build membranes; nucleic acids (DNA/RNA) store and express genetic information; enzymes, water and minerals complete the set. Mastery of structure-function links and enzyme kinetics is a frequent NEB examination focus.
specialNotes: In NEB written answers, pair every macromolecule with BOTH its monomer and its key function to earn full marks.
Protein denaturation is a favourite "application" question (cooking an egg, or fever denaturing enzymes).
Stress that enzymes lower activation energy; they do NOT supply energy.
importantStatements: All cells share the same basic biochemical machinery of DNA→RNA→protein (central dogma).
The 20 naturally occurring L-amino acids differ only in their R-group (side chain).
Phospholipid bilayers form spontaneously because the head is hydrophilic and the tail is hydrophobic.
Enzyme specificity is explained by the induced-fit model.
Water is the universal biological solvent and a participant in hydrolysis and condensation.
importantNotes: Memorise monomer → polymer: glucose→starch, amino acid→protein, fatty acid+glycerol→triglyceride, nucleotide→nucleic acid.
Learn base-pairing and hydrogen-bond counts (A=T=2, G=C=3).
Do 2–3 diagram questions: phospholipid bilayer, peptide bond, a DNA nucleotide ladder.
Link enzyme inhibitors (competitive vs non-competitive) to drug design.
examShortTricks: Remember C-H-O-N: C=energy, P=work, L=lipid, N=genetic.
A-T two H-bonds (think "A" has 2 strokes), G-C three.
Enzymes are proteins that END in "-ase".
Starch test: iodine → blue-black; reducing sugar: Benedict's → brick-red.
examNotes: High frequency: monomer/polymer matching tables, enzyme action and factors affecting enzymes.
Diagram-based marks: label a phospholipid bilayer and a DNA nucleotide.
Application: explain a disease caused by a biomolecule deficiency.
Do not confuse structural (cellulose) with storage (starch/glycogen) polysaccharides.

notes: Biomolecules are organic molecules essential to life: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, plus minerals, enzymes and water.

Carbohydrates (CH2O)n: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, ribose), disaccharides (sucrose=glucose+fructose, lactose, maltose), polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose). Provide energy (4 kcal/g) and structural support.

Proteins: polymers of 20 standard amino acids (L-forms; glycine is achiral) joined by peptide (-CO-NH-) bonds. Four structural levels (primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary). Functions: enzymes, transport (haemoglobin), contraction, defence, structural.
Lipids: hydrophobic; triglycerides (fat storage, 9 kcal/g), phospholipids (membrane bilayer), steroids (cholesterol, hormones). Not true polymers.
Nucleic acids: DNA (double helix, deoxyribose, A=T 2 H-bonds, G=C 3 H-bonds) stores heredity; RNA (single strand, ribose, A=U) in protein synthesis (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA).
Enzymes: biological catalysts (mostly proteins); work by the lock-and-key / induced-fit model; denatured by high temperature or extreme pH; show high substrate specificity.
Water (major solvent, ~70% of cell) and minerals (Ca, P, K, Na, Fe, I) act as structural, catalytic and osmotic regulators; deficiency causes deficiency diseases.
confusion: Cellulose is a structural polymer in plant cell walls, not an energy reserve; glycogen (animal) and starch (plant) are the storage forms.
Starch is unbranched amylose + branched amylopectin; both yield maltose on hydrolysis.
Ribose and deoxyribose differ only by one oxygen atom on C-2; hence RNA vs DNA sugars.
Denaturation unfolds protein (loss of secondary/tertiary structure); it is often reversible at low temperature.
Lipids are not polymers; they do not have repeating monomers like the other three macromolecule classes.
A peptide bond forms between the -COOH of one amino acid and the -NH2 of the next, releasing one water (condensation).
practice: Match each biomolecule to a function: insulin (hormone), haemoglobin (transport), cellulose (structure), ATP (energy currency).

universalFacts: Carbon makes up roughly a fifth of human body mass and forms the covalent backbone of every biomolecule.
Hemoglobin binds about 1.34 mL of oxygen per gram; fully saturated blood carries roughly 20 mL of oxygen per 100 mL.
Water has an anomalously high specific heat and acts as a biological thermostat.
Human insulin (51 amino acids) was produced by recombinant-DNA technology in 1978 and approved in 1982 — the first approved recombinant-DNA pharmaceutical.
examples: Starch in rice/potato is a storage polysaccharide; glycogen in liver/muscle is the animal reserve.
Cellulose (beta-glucose) forms the cell wall of green plants.
DNA replication and mRNA synthesis link nucleic acids to protein production.
Iodine deficiency enlarges the thyroid; iron deficiency causes anaemia.

formulas: General carbohydrate ratio: C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1, i.e. (CH2O)n

Peptide unit: -C(=O)-NH-

keyPoints: Functions: C=energy+structure, P=enzymes/transport/structure, L=storage+membrane, N=heredity+protein synthesis.
A hydrolysis breaks a bond + water; a condensation joins molecules - water.
Enzymes are specific, reversible regulators, not consumed in the reaction.
DNA is the gene; RNA is the messenger/scaffold in protein synthesis.

data.summary: Biomolecules are the chemical basis of life. Carbohydrates supply and store energy and form structural fibres; proteins (from 20 amino acids) act as enzymes, transporters, contractile and defence molecules in four structural levels; lipids store energy and build membranes; nucleic acids (DNA/RNA) store and express genetic information; enzymes, water and minerals complete the set. Mastery of structure-function links and enzyme kinetics is a frequent NEB examination focus.

The 20 naturally occurring L-amino acids differ only in their R-group (side chain).
Phospholipid bilayers form spontaneously because the head is hydrophilic and the tail is hydrophobic.
Enzyme specificity is explained by the induced-fit model.
Water is the universal biological solvent and a participant in hydrolysis and condensation.

# Cell: Introduction of cell, concepts of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells

## 1. Introduction
The **cell** is the structural and functional unit of life: the smallest thing that shows all seven life processes together. A bacterium, an onion peel cell, your cheek cell scraped with a toothpick — each is a membrane-bound compartment where biomolecules meet organisation, and organisation becomes life. Everything in this syllabus — tissues, organs, genetics, disease — is cells behaving singly or together.

The discovery story is short and examinable. Robert Hooke (1665) saw dead cork "cells"; Leeuwenhoek's lenses revealed living animalcules; Schleiden (plants, 1838) and Schwann (animals, 1839) declared all organisms cellular; Virchow (1855) added *omnis cellula e cellula* — every cell from a pre-existing cell. Then Chatton (1925) coined *prokaryote/eukaryote*, Dougherty (1957) proposed the two organisations as a deep divide, and Stanier and van Niel (1962) popularised the dichotomy that still frames this topic.

**What you will learn:** (i) the cell concept and cell theory; (ii) cell size range and why cells stay small; (iii) the prokaryotic organisation (correct, modern version — mesosomes retired); (iv) the eukaryotic organisation; (v) the full comparison; (vi) exceptions that prove the rule (viruses, RBCs).

**Learning outcomes.** You can: state cell theory with authors; compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells on eight features; explain the surface-area-to-volume reason for smallness; and correct the mesosome and "largest/smallest cell" statements.

## 2. Hierarchy body — the cell idea, then the two organisations

### What a cell is, and cell theory
1. **Definition.** A cell is the membrane-enclosed unit of structure and function of living organisms, containing hereditary material and the machinery to use it.
2. **Cell theory (exam core).** Schleiden and Schwann: all living things are made of cells and cell products; Virchow: all cells arise from pre-existing cells. Modern addition: the cell is the unit of heredity and the site of energy flow — genetics and metabolism live inside cell theory now.
3. **How big are cells?** Most are microscopic (bacteria ~1 µm, human cheek cell ~60 µm, human ovum ~0.12 mm — just visible). The largest known cell is the unfertilised ostrich ovum; mycoplasmas are among the smallest known free-living cells (~0.2–0.4 µm). A human body holds on the order of 3×10¹³ cells (published estimate; counts vary with body size).
4. **Why so small?** Surface area grows as the square, volume as the cube: a big cell starves at its centre because supply crosses the surface. Smallness is a transport law, not an accident — the surface-area-to-volume ratio is the standard 2-mark explanation.
5. **Not everything cellular is a cell.** Viruses are acellular (nucleic acid + protein coat, no metabolism outside a host); mature mammalian red blood cells and sieve-tube elements lose their nuclei to do their jobs better.

### The prokaryotic cell (modern account)
1. **Definition.** Organisation without a membrane-bound nucleus or organelles: DNA lies in a nucleoid, ribosomes are 70S, cell division is by binary fission.
2. **Envelope.** Capsule/slime layer (some) → cell wall (peptidoglycan in most bacteria; absent in mycoplasmas) → plasma membrane, across which respiratory electron transport occurs in aerobes.
3. **Validity note — mesosomes retired.** Older books (and older notes) said membrane folds called mesosomes are the sites of respiration. Mesosomes are now known to be fixation artifacts of electron microscopy — the correction tested in this unit. Write: respiration enzymes sit in the plasma membrane itself.
4. **Cytoplasmic kit.** 70S ribosomes, storage granules, plasmids (small extra DNA rings carrying antibiotic resistance), and in photosynthetic forms chromatophores/thylakoid membranes; flagella (simple filament) and pili/fimbriae in some.
5. **Examples.** *Escherichia coli* (gut), cyanobacteria (photosynthetic, e.g., *Nostoc*), mycoplasmas (wall-less, among the smallest free-living cells).

### The eukaryotic cell
1. **Definition.** Organisation with a true membrane-bound nucleus (nuclear envelope + nucleolus + chromatin) and membrane-bound organelles — mitochondria, plastids (plants), ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles.
2. **Ribosomes and division.** 80S ribosomes in the cytosol (70S inside mitochondria and chloroplasts — the endosymbiotic clue). Division is by mitosis/meiosis with a spindle, not simple fission.
3. **Two great lineages.** Plant cells add wall, large central vacuole and plastids; animal cells add centrioles and lysosomes and lack the wall — the next topic draws every organelle.
4. **Where the two meet.** Mitochondria and chloroplasts carry their own small DNA and 70S ribosomes: former free-living prokaryotes now living inside eukaryotes (endosymbiotic theory) — the bridge between this topic and the next.

### The comparison (learn as pairs, not lists)
Prokaryote ↔ eukaryote on eight fixed features: genetic material (naked nucleoid ↔ chromatin in nucleus); nuclear envelope (absent ↔ present); membrane organelles (absent ↔ present); ribosomes (70S ↔ 80S cytosolic); wall chemistry (peptidoglycan, or absent ↔ cellulose/chitin, or absent in animals); division (binary fission ↔ mitosis/meiosis); size (mostly 0.2–10 µm ↔ mostly 10–100 µm); examples (*E. coli*, cyanobacteria ↔ onion cell, cheek cell).

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Prokaryotic vs eukaryotic cells**

| Feature | Prokaryotic | Eukaryotic |
|---|---|---|
| Nuclear envelope | Absent (nucleoid) | Present (true nucleus) |
| Membrane-bound organelles | Absent | Present (mitochondria, ER, Golgi…) |
| Ribosomes | 70S | 80S in cytosol (70S in mitochondria/chloroplasts) |
| Cell wall | Peptidoglycan (absent in mycoplasmas) | Cellulose/chitin (absent in animal cells) |
| Division | Binary fission | Mitosis / meiosis |
| Size | Mostly 0.2–10 µm | Mostly 10–100 µm |
| Flagella | Simple filament | Complex 9+2 axoneme |
| Examples | *E. coli*, cyanobacteria | Onion peel, cheek cell |

**Table 2 — Cell sizes (validity-checked)**

| Cell | Size | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Mycoplasma | ~0.2–0.4 µm | Among smallest free-living cells |
| Typical bacterium | ~1–5 µm | *E. coli* ≈ 2 µm |
| Human cheek cell | ~60 µm | Squamous epithelium |
| Human ovum | ~0.12 mm | Just visible to the eye |
| Ostrich ovum (unfertilised) | ~15 cm shell | Largest known single cell |
| Human body total | ~3×10¹³ cells | Published estimate; varies |

**Table 3 — Instrument and stain links**

| Tool | What it shows | Example in this topic |
|---|---|---|
| Light microscope | Cells and nuclei | Cheek cell + methylene blue |
| Electron microscope | Membranes, ribosomes | 70S vs 80S, envelope |
| Staining | Contrast for parts | Gram stain splits bacteria |

**Table 4 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
|---|---|---|
| Cell theory | Schleiden/Schwann + Virchow | Authors + statement |
| Prokaryote | No nucleus, 70S, fission | Features + examples |
| Eukaryote | Nucleus + organelles, 80S | Features + plant/animal split |
| Comparison | Eight-feature table | The standard long answer |
| Mesosome/size facts | Artifact retired; 0.2 µm–15 cm range | Correction-type reason questions |

## 5. Worked examples and applications
1. **Cheek-cell mount.** Scrape inside of cheek, smear, methylene-blue stain, focus 10× then 40×: flat irregular cells, dark central nuclei — your own eukaryotes in ten minutes.
2. **Onion peel.** Peel epidermis, stain with safranin: brick-wall rectangular cells with walls and big vacuoles — the plant version in the same period.
3. **Curd under the lens.** A drop of curd shows *Lactobacillus* rods (~2 µm): prokaryotes you ate for breakfast, no nucleus in sight.
4. **Why no giant bacteria?** A 1 mm bacterium would have 1/1000th the surface per volume of a 1 µm one — diffusion could not feed it. Size answers structure.
5. **Antibiotic logic.** Penicillin blocks peptidoglycan wall-building (prokaryote-only structure); streptomycin hits 70S ribosomes (human cytosol uses 80S) — the comparison table is pharmacology.
6. **RBC design.** Mammalian red cells eject the nucleus to carry more haemoglobin — losing the defining eukaryotic feature for function; exceptions prove the rule.
7. **Yoghurt vs antibiotic.** Antibiotics kill gut bacteria (prokaryotes) while sparing gut lining (eukaryote 80S) — selective toxicity read straight off Table 1.

## 6. Key terms and statements
- **Cell** — membrane-bound structural and functional unit of life.
- **Cell theory** — all organisms are cellular; every cell comes from a pre-existing cell (Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow).
- **Prokaryote** — cell without membrane-bound nucleus or organelles; 70S ribosomes; binary fission.
- **Eukaryote** — cell with true nucleus and membrane organelles; 80S cytosolic ribosomes; mitosis/meiosis.
- **Nucleoid** — naked circular DNA region of prokaryotes (no envelope).
- **Mesosome note** — membrane folds once called respiratory sites are fixation artifacts; respiration enzymes sit in the plasma membrane itself.
- **70S vs 80S** — prokaryotic (and mitochondrial/chloroplast) vs eukaryotic cytosolic ribosomes — the antibiotic target difference.
- **Binary fission** — direct prokaryotic division: replicate DNA, split in two.
- **Omnis cellula e cellula** — Virchow's dictum: every cell from a cell.
- **Endosymbiotic clue** — organelle 70S ribosomes + own DNA point to prokaryote ancestors.

## 7. Exam Zone
**NEB map.** Cell theory (authors + statement) is a guaranteed short note. The eight-feature comparison table is the standard 5-mark long answer; add Fig. 4.1/4.3 as the labelled-diagram requirement. Reason questions target: why cells are small (surface/volume), why mesosomes are rejected, why RBCs lack nuclei, why antibiotics spare us.

**Short tricks.** "Schleiden–Schwann–Virchow 1838–39–55" (plant, animal, from-cells). "70-pro, 80-eu". "Naked, single and small = prokaryote". Size ladder: *mycoplasma → bacterium → cheek → ovum → ostrich*.

**Sources for the facts above:** Raven Biology §4.2.1 (prokaryotic structure); OpenStax Microbiology §8.3 (respiration); Sapp (2005) on the prokaryote–eukaryote dichotomy; Dougherty history (PMC4574257); BioNumbers (cell sizes); Bianconi/Sender–Milo (body cell counts); unit validation card (corrected claims kept verbatim in sense).

## 8. Summary and self-check
The cell is life's unit; cell theory (Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow) plus modern heredity/energy additions frames it. Prokaryotes pack naked DNA (nucleoid), 70S ribosomes and a wall into ~1 µm and divide by fission — with respiration across the plasma membrane (mesosomes retired as artifacts). Eukaryotes add a true nucleus, membrane organelles and 80S ribosomes at ~10–100 µm and divide by mitosis/meiosis. Size spans mycoplasma (~0.3 µm) to ostrich egg, ruled by surface-to-volume law. Organelle DNA/70S whispers the endosymbiotic past. Figures: comparison schematic, size scale, NCBI comparison plate, labelled animal cell.

**Self-check.** (1) State cell theory with one author per clause. (2) Reproduce the eight-feature comparison from memory. (3) A student writes "mesosomes respire" — correct her in two sentences. (4) Why can you see an ovum but not a mycoplasma? (5) How does the 70S/80S split explain antibiotic safety?

**Common confusions.** Prokaryote ≠ only bacteria (includes cyanobacteria; mycoplasmas lack walls) · nucleoid ≠ nucleus (no envelope) · 70S also inside mitochondria/chloroplasts · viruses are acellular, not prokaryotic · largest cell = ostrich ovum (unfertilised), not whale cells.

data.summary: The cell is life's structural and functional unit. Cell theory: Schleiden and Schwann (all organisms cellular) + Virchow (omnis cellula e cellula). Prokaryotes carry naked nucleoid DNA, 70S ribosomes and (usually) peptidoglycan walls at ~1 µm, dividing by binary fission, with respiratory enzymes in the plasma membrane — mesosomes retired as fixation artifacts. Eukaryotes add a true nucleus, membrane organelles and 80S ribosomes at ~10–100 µm, dividing by mitosis/meiosis. Sizes run from mycoplasma (~0.2–0.4 µm) to the ostrich ovum, ruled by the surface-area-to-volume law; the body holds ~3×10¹³ cells (estimate). Exceptions: viruses (acellular), RBCs (no nucleus). Organelle DNA + 70S point to endosymbiosis. Figures: comparison schematic, size scale, NCBI comparison plate, labelled animal cell.

notes: DETAILED ORGANELLE ANALYSIS (plant + animal cell).

Plasma membrane: phospholipid bilayer (heads out, tails in) + integral proteins (channels, pumps, receptors) + peripheral proteins + cholesterol + glycocalyx (cell recognition). Fluid-mosaic model (Singer & Nicolson, 1972).

Mitochondrion: double membrane; outer smooth, inner folded into cristae; matrix with Krebs enzymes; own DNA + 70S ribosomes (endosymbiosis); aerobic respiration: glycolysis (cytoplasm) → Krebs (matrix) → ETS (cristae) → ~34 ATP.

Chloroplast: double membrane; thylakoids stacked into grana; stroma with Calvin-cycle enzymes; chlorophyll a + b; own DNA + 70S ribosomes; light reactions (grana → ATP, NADPH, O2) + Calvin cycle (stroma → glucose).
Nucleus: nuclear envelope (4 nm, two membranes, pores); nucleoplasm; chromatin (DNA + histone proteins); nucleolus (rRNA + ribosome assembly).
Rough ER (RER): ribosomes on outer surface → protein synthesis (secretory + membrane proteins); continuous with nuclear envelope.
Smooth ER (SER): lipid synthesis, carbohydrate metabolism, detoxification (liver), Ca2+ storage (muscle — sarcoplasmic reticulum).
Golgi apparatus: cisternae + vesicles; modifies (glycosylation), packages, sorts, and secretes proteins; forms lysosomes + cell plate (plants).
Lysosomes: 8–12 nm vesicle, hydrolytic enzymes (acidic pH); digest food particles, worn organelles (autophagy); "suicide bags" when damaged.
Vacuole: plant — large central (turgor, storage); animal — small (excretion, osmoregulation, contractile in protozoa).
Cytoskeleton: microfilaments (actin), intermediate filaments, microtubules (tubulin); shape, movement, intracellular transport, division (spindle).
Centrioles (animal): microtubule rings; form the spindle during mitosis; absent in most plants.
Cell inclusions: storage granules (starch, fat, glycogen), pigments (leuco-, chro-, heterochromoplasts), crystalloids.
Cell wall (plant): cellulose microfibrils (primary wall) + pectin; secondary wall with lignin; fully permeable; provides rigidity + protection.
confusion: RER makes PROTEIN; SER makes LIPID. A cell secreting lots of protein has abundant RER + Golgi (e.g., pancreatic acinar cell).
The Golgi does NOT synthesise proteins; it MODIFIES, SORTS, and PACKAGES what the RER made.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their OWN DNA + 70S ribosomes — the key endosymbiosis evidence.
Lysosomes are animal-cell organelles; plants use the large vacuole for hydrolytic digestion.
Cilia and flagella share the 9+2 axonemal microtubule structure; centrioles (9+0) are related but lack the central pair.
The nucleus is NOT the only place with DNA: mitochondria + chloroplasts carry their own genomes.

enrichedContent.summary: A detailed examination of the eukaryotic cell shows how each membrane-bound organelle specialises a metabolic function. The fluid-mosaic plasma membrane controls transport; mitochondria and chloroplasts convert energy (and carry their own DNA, evidence of endosymbiosis); RER makes protein while SER makes lipid; the Golgi modifies and packages; lysosomes digest; the nucleus and nucleolus control heredity; and the cytoskeleton (microfilaments, microtubules) maintains shape and drives division. data.topicTitle: Cell division: concept of cell cycle, types of cell division (amitosis, mitosis and meiosis) and significances

mcqs.question: In Anaphase I of meiosis, what separates?

notes: DETAILED CELL DIVISION: the full cell cycle and every mitotic/meiotic phase.
Interphase (90% of the cycle): G1 (growth, organelle duplication, protein synthesis), S (DNA replication — each chromosome now has 2 sister chromatids), G2 (preparation for mitosis, checkpoint).
Checkpoints: G1/S (DNA damage, nutrients), G2/M (replication complete), M (spindle attachment) — failures cause cancer.

Mitosis phases (PMAT): Prophase (chromatin → chromosomes, spindle forms, nuclear envelope breaks), Metaphase (chromosomes align at the equatorial plate, spindle fibres attached to centromeres), Anaphase (centromeres split, sister chromatids pulled to opposite poles), Telophase (chromosomes decondense, nuclear envelopes reform, cytokinesis).
Cytokinesis: animal cells — cleavage furrow (actin); plant cells — cell plate → new wall.

Meiosis: two divisions. Meiosis I (reductional): Prophase I (chromosomes pair = synapsis; crossing over between non-sister chromatids), Metaphase I (homologous pairs at the equator; independent assortment), Anaphase I (homologs separate), Telophase I. Meiosis II (equational): like mitosis but no DNA replication; sister chromatids separate.
Outcome: meiosis → 4 haploid (n) genetically distinct cells; mitosis → 2 diploid (2n) identical cells.
Crossing over (Prophase I) + independent assortment (Metaphase I) = the two sources of meiotic variation.
Amitosis (direct division): simple karyokinesis; rare — described in some protozoans, yeasts/some fungi and certain pathological or regenerating cells.
Errors: mitotic errors → uncontrolled division = cancer; meiotic non-disjunction → aneuploidy (e.g., Down syndrome = usually trisomy 21).
Significance: mitosis = growth, repair, asexual reproduction; meiosis = gamete formation + genetic diversity.
NEB focus: the full cell cycle, all mitotic and meiotic phases, variation, and errors.
confusion: Mitosis maintains the chromosome number (2n → 2n); meiosis halves it (2n → n).
Crossing over and independent assortment occur in MEIOSIS only, not mitosis.
In Anaphase I of meiosis, HOMOLOGOUS chromosomes separate; in Anaphase of mitosis and Anaphase II of meiosis, SISTER CHROMATIDs separate.
DNA replication happens ONLY in the S phase; meiosis has one S phase then two divisions.
G2 is not a "resting" phase; DNA has already doubled in S and the cell is preparing for M.
Non-disjunction = a homologous pair (or chromatid pair) fails to separate → one cell gets both, the other gets none.

universalFacts: Interphase occupies ~90% of the cell cycle; mitosis is brief.
A human cell with 46 chromosomes yields two 46-chromosome cells after mitosis and four 23-chromosome cells after meiosis.
Crossing over can occur at multiple points per chromosome pair in Prophase I.
Cancer is fundamentally uncontrolled mitosis due to failed checkpoints (e.g., p53 mutations).
examples: Onion root tip: classic mitotic figures (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase).
Spermatogenesis: 1 primary (2n) → 2 secondary (n) → 4 spermatids (n) → 4 sperm.
Oogenesis: 1 primary (2n) → 1 secondary (n) + 1 polar body → 1 functional ovum (n) + usually 2–3 polar bodies (meiosis II completes only if fertilization occurs).
Down syndrome: usually full trisomy 21 from meiotic non-disjunction (~95% of cases; translocation and mosaic forms also occur).
Amitosis: direct division without a spindle; described in some protozoans and yeasts.

notes: DETAILED CELL DIVISION: the full cell cycle and every mitotic/meiotic phase.
Interphase (90% of the cycle): G1 (growth, organelle duplication, protein synthesis), S (DNA replication — each chromosome now has 2 sister chromatids), G2 (preparation for mitosis, checkpoint).
Checkpoints: G1/S (DNA damage, nutrients), G2/M (replication complete), M (spindle attachment) — failures cause cancer.

Mitosis phases (PMAT): Prophase (chromatin → chromosomes, spindle forms, nuclear envelope breaks), Metaphase (chromosomes align at the equatorial plate, spindle fibres attached to centromeres), Anaphase (centromeres split, sister chromatids pulled to opposite poles), Telophase (chromosomes decondense, nuclear envelopes reform, cytokinesis).
Cytokinesis: animal cells — cleavage furrow (actin); plant cells — cell plate → new wall.

Meiosis: two divisions. Meiosis I (reductional): Prophase I (chromosomes pair = synapsis; crossing over between non-sister chromatids), Metaphase I (homologous pairs at the equator; independent assortment), Anaphase I (homologs separate), Telophase I. Meiosis II (equational): like mitosis but no DNA replication; sister chromatids separate.
Outcome: meiosis → 4 haploid (n) genetically distinct cells; mitosis → 2 diploid (2n) identical cells.
Crossing over (Prophase I) + independent assortment (Metaphase I) = the two sources of meiotic variation.
Amitosis (direct division): simple karyokinesis; rare — described in some protozoans, yeasts/some fungi and certain pathological or regenerating cells.
Errors: mitotic errors → uncontrolled division = cancer; meiotic non-disjunction → aneuploidy (e.g., Down syndrome = usually trisomy 21).
Significance: mitosis = growth, repair, asexual reproduction; meiosis = gamete formation + genetic diversity.
NEB focus: the full cell cycle, all mitotic and meiotic phases, variation, and errors.
confusion: Mitosis maintains the chromosome number (2n → 2n); meiosis halves it (2n → n).
Crossing over and independent assortment occur in MEIOSIS only, not mitosis.
In Anaphase I of meiosis, HOMOLOGOUS chromosomes separate; in Anaphase of mitosis and Anaphase II of meiosis, SISTER CHROMATIDs separate.
DNA replication happens ONLY in the S phase; meiosis has one S phase then two divisions.
G2 is not a "resting" phase; DNA has already doubled in S and the cell is preparing for M.
Non-disjunction = a homologous pair (or chromatid pair) fails to separate → one cell gets both, the other gets none.

data.title: Biotechnology Applications and Ethical Considerations
notes: Biotechnology applies a living system to a product: a crop, a drug, a microbe or a test.
In agriculture the example is a crop given a gene that reduces insect damage, such as Bt cotton, and microbes that improve a fermentation.
In medicine the examples are recombinant insulin, safer vaccines and antibiotics originally found in microbes.
A genetic test can tell a family about a disease allele. The ethical requirement is consent, and the result must not become a reason to deny a person unfairly.
Releasing an engineered organism raises a safety question: will it cross with wild relatives, and who is watching.
Taking a gene or a crop variety from a community without consent or share of benefit is the ownership problem. Use and fairness are both part of the topic.
importantConcepts: CRISPR-Cas9: genome editing tool that allows precise DNA modifications
Recombinant DNA technology: combining DNA from different sources
Bioinformatics: computational analysis of biological data
Ethical issues: consent, equity, unintended consequences, designer babies
importantStatements: CRISPR enables targeted gene knock-out or knock-in in living organisms.
GMOs are genetically modified organisms with traits introduced through genetic engineering.
Ethical debates center on safety, accessibility, and potential misuse of biotech.

Applications range from medicine (insulin production) to agriculture (pest-resistant crops).

Germline editing (embryo modification) is highly controversial due to heritable changes.

data.title: Cell Structure and Organelles
notes: Cell theory: living things are made of cells, the cell is the unit of structure and function, and cells arise from cells.
A prokaryotic cell has a nucleoid, 70S ribosomes and no mitochondria. A eukaryotic cell has a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

data.title: Ecology and Ecosystems
notes: A population is the members of one species in a place. A community is the populations living together. An ecosystem adds the physical surroundings.
A niche is the role: what the organism eats, when it is active, and which conditions it tolerates. Two species do not keep identical niches for long.
Biotic factors are the living influences. Abiotic factors are light, temperature, water, soil and salinity.
A food chain moves energy from a producer to consumers. A food web is many chains joined. Decomposers return matter to the soil.
Only about ten percent of the energy at one level is available at the next. The rest is lost as heat and as work of staying alive. Chains therefore stay short.
A pond and a forest are both ecosystems. The pond's producers are algae and water plants. The forest's are trees. The structure differs. The energy rule does not.

data.title: Environmental Science and Sustainability
notes: A sustainable use takes no more of a resource, and dumps no more waste, than the system can replace or absorb.
Climate pressure, polluted air and water, loss of habitat and the using-up of freshwater and fertile soil are the four pressures named in this note.
Renewable resources renew if the harvest stays below the renewal. A forest cut faster than it grows is being used as if it were a mine.
Non-renewable resources, such as coal and oil, are not replaced on a human timescale. Sustainability then means using less and wasting less.
Reduce, reuse and recycle cut the demand and the rubbish. Community forestry in Nepal is a worked case of a renewable resource brought back under local rules.

data.title: Evolution and Natural Selection
notes: Individuals in a population differ from one another, and some of those differences are hereditary and can be passed to offspring.
More offspring are born than the resources can support, so not all of them survive and breed.
Individuals whose hereditary traits fit the conditions leave more offspring. That is natural selection.
Over generations the successful variants become more common. The population changes. That change is evolution by selection.
Darwin could not name the source of new variation. Mutation and the shuffling of genes, understood later, supply it. Selection only sorts what is already heritable.
Selection is not an animal trying to improve. A giraffe does not stretch into a new gene. Lamarck's acquired characters are the contrast, and they are not what selection uses.
importantConcepts: Selection pressure: environmental factors favoring certain traits
Adaptation: traits that increase survival and reproduction
Speciation: formation of new species from existing ones
Common ancestry: related species share common ancestors
importantStatements: Natural selection is the process by which beneficial traits become more common in a population over generations.

keyPoints: Variation is the raw material for natural selection.

specialNotes: The peppered moth example (Biston betularia) is a classic case of natural selection in action.

examNotes: Distinguish between natural selection and artificial selection (breeding).

data.title: Genetics and Inheritance
notes: A gene can exist as alleles. A diploid individual carries two alleles of each gene.
Dominance means that in a heterozygote, one allele's phenotype hides the other allele's phenotype.
Segregation: those two alleles separate when gametes form, so each gamete gets one.
A cross of two heterozygotes therefore gives a genotype ratio of 1:2:1 and, if dominance is complete, a phenotype ratio of 3:1.
Independent assortment: alleles of different, unlinked genes are sorted independently. Two such genes in a double heterozygote cross give 9:3:3:1.
A test cross with the homozygous recessive reveals whether a dominant phenotype hides a recessive allele. Linked genes are the exception this note only flags: they do not assort independently.
importantConcepts: Mendelian inheritance: traits follow predictable patterns
Punnett square: a method for predicting offspring genotypes
importantStatements: In a monohybrid cross (Aa × Aa), the genotypic ratio is 1:2:1 (AA:Aa:aa) and the phenotypic ratio is 3:1 (dominant:recessive).
Dominant alleles mask recessive alleles in heterozygous individuals.
Mendel's law of segregation states that alleles separate during gamete formation.
keyPoints: Mendelian ratios: 3:1 for dominant/recessive in monohybrid crosses.
Punnett squares are essential for predicting offspring genotypes and phenotypes.
Dominant traits appear in the phenotype even when recessive allele is present (heterozygous).
Recessive traits only appear in homozygous recessive individuals (aa).
specialNotes: Mendel worked with pea plants but his laws apply to all sexually reproducing organisms.
The concept of incomplete dominance (e.g., flower color in snapdragons) deviates from classical Mendelian ratios.
Sex-linked inheritance (X-linked traits) follows a different pattern due to sex chromosomes.
examShortTricks: 3:1 ratio in monohybrid cross = dominant:recessive phenotype.
Punnett square predicts 25% AA, 50% Aa, 25% aa in Aa × Aa cross.

data.summary: Mendelian inheritance tracks alleles. They segregate, one to each gamete, giving 1:2:1 genotypes and 3:1 phenotypes under complete dominance. Unlinked genes assort independently and give 9:3:3:1. A test cross uncovers a hidden recessive allele.

visualization.desc: Alleles segregate. Unlinked genes assort independently. Ratios 3:1 and 9:3:3:1.

notes: A gene can exist as alleles. A diploid individual carries two alleles of each gene.
Dominance means that in a heterozygote, one allele's phenotype hides the other allele's phenotype.
Segregation: those two alleles separate when gametes form, so each gamete gets one.
A cross of two heterozygotes therefore gives a genotype ratio of 1:2:1 and, if dominance is complete, a phenotype ratio of 3:1.
Independent assortment: alleles of different, unlinked genes are sorted independently. Two such genes in a double heterozygote cross give 9:3:3:1.
A test cross with the homozygous recessive reveals whether a dominant phenotype hides a recessive allele. Linked genes are the exception this note only flags: they do not assort independently.

data.title: Human Physiology and Homeostasis
notes: Homeostasis is the keeping of a steady internal state while the outside changes: temperature, blood glucose, pH, water and salts.
Negative feedback detects a change and starts a response that pushes the value back toward the set point. The response switches off as the set point is approached.
If body temperature rises, skin vessels widen and sweat increases heat loss. If it falls, vessels narrow and shivering produces heat.
If blood glucose rises after a meal, insulin promotes uptake and storage. If glucose falls, glucagon promotes release from liver glycogen. The two hormones pull in opposite directions.
The kidneys keep water and salts by varying how much is reabsorbed. Antidiuretic hormone saves water when the body is short of it.
Positive feedback, as in the intensification of labour contractions, drives a change further. It is the exception. Homeostasis of temperature and glucose is negative feedback.
importantConcepts: Negative feedback: deviation triggers response that reverses the change
Positive feedback: amplification of a response (e.g., childbirth)
Homeostatic variables: temperature, pH, glucose concentration, osmolarity
Regulatory centers: hypothalamus, pituitary gland, endocrine glands
importantStatements: Thermoregulation maintains body temperature around 37°C (98.6°F).
Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it.
The kidneys regulate fluid balance and electrolyte concentrations.
keyPoints: Homeostasis relies on sensor organs detecting changes and control centers responding.
Feedback loops are essential for maintaining stable internal environments.
Multiple systems work together (e.g., nervous, endocrine, muscular) to achieve homeostasis.

specialNotes: Body temperature is maintained by shivering (heat production) and sweating (cooling).

Osmoregulation prevents dehydration by adjusting water intake and kidney function.

Set point = normal value that the system tries to maintain.
Sensors detect changes, control centers respond, effectors implement changes.

data.title: Animal Adaptations — Aquatic, Terrestrial and Volant
data.topicTitle: Animal adaptation: Aquatic (primary and secondary), terrestrial (cursorial, fossorial and arboreal) and volant adaptation

mcqs.question: The streamlined (fusiform) body of a fish is an adaptation for:
Whales and seals are examples of:
Hollow bones in birds are an adaptation for:
Countercurrent exchange in fish gills allows:

notes: Animal adaptation: structural, physiological, and behavioural features that allow an animal to survive in a particular environment.
Aquatic adaptation: primary aquatic (fishes, fully aquatic) and secondary aquatic (whales, seals — originally terrestrial).
Aquatic features: streamlined (fusiform) body, fins, gills (countercurrent exchange), lateral line (fish), webbed feet, dense bones, salt glands.
Terrestrial adaptation: cursorial (running — cheetah, horse), fossorial (burrowing — earthworm, mole), arboreal (tree-dwelling — monkey, sloth).
Terrestrial features: waterproof skin (fur, scales, feathers), lungs, internal fertilisation, nitrogenous waste (urea/ammonia), strong limbs.
Volant adaptation: flight; features: wings (feathers), hollow (pneumatic) bones, air sacs (double respiration), strong pectoral muscles, streamlined body, beak.
Adaptations increase survival and reproduction in a given habitat; they are the result of natural selection.
NEB focus: aquatic (primary + secondary), terrestrial (cursorial, fossorial, arboreal), and volant adaptations.
Nepal examples: fish (Terai), rhododendron forest birds (volant), snow leopard (terrestrial cursorial), pangolin (fossorial).
confusion: Primary aquatic animals were ALWAYS aquatic (fishes); secondary aquatic animals (whales, seals) evolved FROM terrestrial ancestors.
A fusiform (streamlined) body REDUCES water resistance; it is an adaptation for fast swimming.
Countercurrent exchange in fish gills allows ~80% O2 uptake efficiency (blood and water flow in opposite directions).
Hollow bones in birds reduce weight for flight; they are still strong (internal struts).
Arboreal animals (monkeys) have grasping hands/feet, forward-facing eyes (stereoscopic vision), and a prehensile tail (New World monkeys).
Fossorial animals (moles, earthworms) have reduced eyes, strong forelimbs for digging, and cylindrical bodies.

Birds have a double respiration system (air sacs + lungs) that delivers fresh air through the lungs on BOTH in- and exhalation.
A hummingbird's wings beat ~50 times per second; some migrate thousands of km.

data.topicTitle: Animal behavior: Reflex action, taxes, dominance and leadership
notes: A reflex is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus. The path is a reflex arc: receptor, sensory neuron, a coordinator in the spinal cord or brain, motor neuron, and effector. The knee-jerk arc is handled in the spinal cord, so the leg extends before the brain has finished registering the tap.

Taxes are directed movements toward or away from a stimulus. Positive phototaxis is movement toward light. Negative phototaxis is movement away from it. Chemotaxis follows a chemical, geotaxis follows gravity, and thigmotaxis follows touch.

Kinesis is a change in speed or turning rate when a stimulus changes, without a fixed direction. An animal that simply moves faster in a dry patch, and slows down in a moist patch, shows kinesis. It is not a taxis, because it is not aimed.

Innate behavior is present without being taught, as in a reflex or a taxis. Learned behavior changes with experience. Most real behavior mixes the two: the ability to learn is innate, the particular lesson is not.

Dominance is a social ranking in which some individuals get priority to food, mates or resting sites. A pecking order in birds is a linear dominance hierarchy. Leadership is the tendency of a group to follow one individual when moving or fleeing. The leader is not always the most dominant animal.

These patterns matter in the wild because they decide who feeds, who breeds and how a herd escapes a predator. A reflex protects the body immediately. A taxis places the animal in a better spot. A hierarchy reduces constant fighting inside the group.

confusion: A taxis is directed. A kinesis is not. Calling every movement a taxis loses the distinction.
A reflex does not require a conscious decision. The brain may be informed afterwards, but the knee-jerk does not wait for that.
The dominant animal is not automatically the leader of every movement. Dominance is about priority. Leadership is about being followed.
Negative phototaxis is not a failure to respond to light. It is an active movement away from light.
keyPoints: Reflex arc: receptor, sensory neuron, coordinator, motor neuron, effector.
Taxis: directed movement, named by the stimulus and by the sign (positive or negative).
Kinesis: non-directional change in activity.
Dominance is a ranking for priority. Leadership is being followed during movement.
The knee-jerk coordinator is the spinal cord.
importantStatements: A reflex is fast because the arc is short and does not depend on conscious thought.
Taxes orient an animal in a gradient. Kinesis only changes how much the animal moves.
Social rank reduces repeated fights by making the outcome of a contest predictable.
examples: The knee-jerk: a tap on the tendon stretches a receptor, and the leg extends.
Maggots often move away from light, a negative phototaxis.
Woodlice move more in dry air and slow down in moist air, a kinesis that leaves them in the moist place.
universalFacts: The same reflex arc parts appear in vertebrates: a sensor, an incoming nerve, a central connection, an outgoing nerve and a muscle or gland.
Pecking order is the classic name for a linear dominance hierarchy, first described in flocks of hens.
formulas: Reflex arc order: receptor → sensory neuron → coordinator → motor neuron → effector.
Sign of a taxis: positive = toward the stimulus, negative = away from it.

exercises.question: Woodlice walk quickly in dry bright air and almost stop under a damp stone. Is this best called a taxis or a kinesis, and why?
steps: A taxis would be movement aimed toward or away from a stimulus, such as walking straight to the dark.
Here the animal changes its rate of movement as conditions change.
It slows where it is damp, so it spends more time there without steering along a compass direction.
A change in speed or turning, without a set direction, is kinesis.
exercises.answer: It is a kinesis: activity falls in the damp place, so the animal accumulates there without a directed path.

notes: Animal behavior: the actions and responses of animals to stimuli; includes innate (fixed) and learned behaviours.
Reflex action: an automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus, mediated by a reflex arc (receptor → sensory neuron → CNS → motor neuron → effector).
Taxes: orientation responses (movement toward or away from a stimulus). Phototaxis (light), chemotaxis (chemical), thigmotaxis (touch), geotaxis (gravity).
Taxis vs Kinesis: taxis is DIRECTIONAL movement toward/away from a stimulus; kinesis is NON-directional (random) movement in response to a stimulus.
Dominance and leadership: social hierarchies in group-living animals (primates, wolves, fish); the dominant individual has priority access to food, mates, and territory.
Fish migration: seasonal movement to feeding or breeding grounds; e.g., salmon (upstream spawning), mackerel (Nepal Terai rivers).
Bird migration: long-distance seasonal movement (e.g., Himalayan birds migrate to lower altitudes in winter; storks migrate to the Terai).
NEB focus: reflex action, taxes, dominance and leadership, fish and bird migration.
Migration is a behavioural adaptation; it is seasonal and genetically programmed.
confusion: A reflex arc is SHORT (spinal level); it does NOT involve the brain (faster response).
Taxis is DIRECTIONAL (toward/away from a stimulus); kinesis is NON-DIRECTIONAL (random movement).
Phototaxis: movement in response to light (positive = toward, negative = away).
Dominance hierarchies are ESTABLISHED through social interactions; they are not fixed by birth.
Fish migration is often seasonal (breeding, feeding); it is not random movement.
Bird migration is a BEHAVIOURAL adaptation; it is genetically programmed and often learned by first-year migrants.

Some salmon (e.g., Atlantic salmon) migrate thousands of km upstream to spawn in the stream where they were born.
Honeybees use a "waggle dance" to communicate the direction and distance of a food source to nestmates.
Migration is one of the most spectacular animal behaviours; some birds fly >10,000 km per year.
examples: Reflex: touching a hot object → hand withdraws (reflex arc: skin receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → muscle).
Phototaxis: earthworms move AWAY from light (negative phototaxis).
Chemotaxis: bacteria move toward a nutrient source (positive chemotaxis).
Dominance: a dominant male lion has priority access to females in the pride.
Fish migration: mackerel in the Kosi and Gandaki rivers migrate seasonally to feed and breed.
Bird migration: Himalayan birds (e.g., bar-headed goose) migrate to the Terai in winter; storks migrate to lowland lakes.

mcqs.question: Eutrophication is caused by excess:

notes: Environmental pollution: the addition of substances or energy to the environment at a rate that exceeds its capacity to dilute, degrade, or absorb them.
Air pollution: SO2 (coal), NOx (vehicles), CO (incomplete combustion), PM2.5/PM10 (particulates), ozone (ground-level), CFCs; sources: industry, vehicles, power plants, biomass burning.
Effects of air pollution: respiratory diseases (asthma, bronchitis), acid rain, smog, global warming, ozone depletion.
Kathmandu Valley: PM2.5 exceeds WHO limits ~10× in winter (stove smoke, vehicles, dust).

Water pollution: domestic waste, industrial effluent, agricultural runoff (pesticides, fertilisers), oil spills, thermal pollution; effects: eutrophication, oxygen depletion, disease (cholera, typhoid).
Soil pollution: heavy metals, pesticides, plastics, industrial waste; effects: reduced fertility, contamination of food, leaching to groundwater.
Pesticides: chemicals to control pests; types: insecticides, herbicides, fungicides, rodenticides; effects: biomagnification, resistance, non-target species death, soil/water contamination.
Control measures: reduce emissions, renewable energy, tree planting, waste treatment, organic farming, international agreements (Montreal, Paris).
NEB focus: sources, effects, and control measures of air, water, and soil pollution; pesticides and their effects.
Nepal: vulnerable to air (Kathmandu), water (river pollution), and soil (pesticide) pollution; deforestation and urbanisation are major contributors.
confusion: Acid rain (pH < 5.6) is caused by SO2 and NOx, NOT by CO2 alone.
Ozone is beneficial in the STRATOSPHERE (blocks UV) but harmful at ground level (smog, air pollutant).
Biomagnification: toxin concentration INCREASES at higher trophic levels (e.g., DDT in fish-eating birds).
Pesticide resistance: pests evolve resistance over time; higher doses are needed.
Eutrophication: excess nutrients (N, P) → algal bloom → O2 depletion → fish kill.
PM2.5 (fine particulates) are MORE harmful than PM10 because they penetrate deeper into the lungs.

DDT (banned in many countries) biomagnifies up food chains; it caused eggshell thinning in raptors (eagles, falcons).
Eutrophication is the #1 cause of "dead zones" (hypoxic zones) in lakes and coastal waters.
Nepal's community forestry program manages ~36% of the country's forest land.

data.title: Applications in agriculture and medicine
notes: ### 1. Agricultural Applications
- **Bt Cotton**: Contains Bacillus thuringiensis gene for insect resistance
- **Bt Corn**: Pest-resistant corn expressing Bt toxin
- **Golden Rice**: Enhanced with vitamin A (beta-carotene)
- **Herbicide-resistant crops**: Tolerant to specific herbicides
- **Delayed ripening tomatoes**: Flavr Savr tomato
- **Drought-resistant crops**: Modified for water stress tolerance
### 2. Medical Applications
- **Insulin**: Produced by E. coli using rDNA technology (replaced animal insulin)
- **Growth Hormone**: For treating dwarfism
- **Vaccines**: Hepatitis B vaccine (yeast expression system)
- **Gene Therapy**: Treating genetic disorders by replacing faulty genes
- **Monoclonal Antibodies**: Cancer treatment, diagnostic tests
- **CRISPR-Cas9**: Gene editing for therapeutic purposes
### 3. Transgenic Animals
- **GloFish**: Fluorescent zebrafish (research)
- **Transgenic mice**: Disease models (cancer, Alzheimer's)
- **Pharming**: Animals producing pharmaceutical proteins in milk
- **RoboCow**: Producing human proteins in milk
### 4. Biopiracy and Patents
- **Biopiracy**: Unauthorized commercial use of biological resources
- **Basmati rice case**: US patent on Indian basmati (later revoked)
- **Neem case**: EU patent on neem derivatives (revoked)
- **Wheat case**: US patent on Indian wheat (revoked)
- **Protected Biological Resources**: Nepal has traditional knowledge databases
### 5. Bioremediation
- Using microbes to clean up environmental pollutants
- Oil-spill cleanup: Pseudomonas putida degrades hydrocarbons
- Heavy metal removal: Bioaccumulation by certain microbes
### 6. Entrance Exam Focus
Applications of Bt crops; Insulin production; Biopiracy examples.
Agricultural biotechnology changes a crop or uses a microbe so the farm needs fewer sprays or yields more from the same land.
Bt cotton carries a bacterial gene, and the protein from that gene kills certain caterpillars that would otherwise eat the crop.
Medicine uses recombinant cells that carry the human gene to make human insulin for people who need it.
A vaccine can be a harmless antigen produced in a cultured cell, given so the body learns the antigen before infection.
Antibiotics first found in fungi and bacteria remain a medical use of microbes, and they treat a bacterial infection that is already underway.

x All transgenic animals are harmful. x Many provide medical benefits.
x Biopiracy is legal. x It's the unauthorized exploitation of indigenous knowledge.
Bt toxin is a protein aimed at certain insects. It is not a fertiliser.
Recombinant insulin is human insulin made by a microbe. It is not pig insulin by default.
An antibiotic does not vaccinate you. It treats a current bacterial infection.
A gene from a crop is not automatically unsafe, and it is not automatically owned by nobody.

data.summary: Biotechnology applies the use of living organisms and their products to make or modify useful products, and in modern practice this means recombinant DNA technology. In agriculture, Bt crops carrying Bacillus thuringiensis genes give insect resistance, Golden Rice supplies provitamin A, and herbicide-resistant, delayed-ripening and drought-tolerant varieties raise yields and food quality. In medicine, recombinant DNA gives human insulin, growth hormone and hepatitis B vaccine, while gene therapy, monoclonal antibodies and CRISPR-Cas9 treat and diagnose disease at the genetic level. Transgenic animals serve as disease models and as factories producing therapeutic proteins, and the same tools clean up pollution through bioremediation, although the unauthorised use of indigenous knowledge raises the ethical problem of biopiracy.
importantConcepts: A transgenic organism carries an artificially inserted gene from another organism, introduced through a suitable vector; Bt cotton, for example, expresses the cry gene of Bacillus thuringiensis.
The Bt toxin is a protein that becomes active only in the gut of susceptible insect larvae, which is why Bt crops are considered safe for humans and most other organisms.
Recombinant DNA technology produces human insulin and growth hormone in bacteria or yeast instead of extracting them from slaughtered cattle and pigs, as was done for earlier animal insulin.

Transgenic animals are used as disease models (transgenic mice for cancer and Alzheimer's), as producers of useful substances (pharming, with therapeutic proteins secreted in milk), and as aquarium or companion organisms (GloFish).
Biopiracy is the unauthorised commercial use of biological resources and traditional knowledge; the neem and basmati rice patent cases were challenged and the patents revoked.
Bioremediation uses organisms to remove pollutants — Pseudomonas species degrade oil hydrocarbons, and some microbes accumulate heavy metals such as mercury and cadmium.
importantStatements: Bt cotton contains the cry gene from Bacillus thuringiensis, whose toxin protein kills insect larvae that feed on the plant.
Golden Rice is engineered to accumulate beta-carotene (provitamin A) in the grain so that it can help combat vitamin A deficiency.
Human insulin made by recombinant DNA technology in Escherichia coli has the same biological activity as natural human insulin.
Monoclonal antibodies are produced by the fusion of a single antibody-producing B cell with a myeloma cell to form a hybridoma, and are used in cancer therapy and in diagnostic tests.
Gene therapy aims to correct a faulty gene by replacing, removing or silencing it using a suitable vector delivered to the affected tissue.
Biopiracy is the unauthorised commercial appropriation of biological resources and traditional knowledge without permission or benefit sharing, and it threatens national sovereignty.

Medical applications: insulin, growth hormone for dwarfism, hepatitis B vaccine made in a yeast expression system, gene therapy, monoclonal antibodies and CRISPR-Cas9.
Flavr Savr, engineered to delay softening of tomatoes, was the first commercial GM food approved for sale, in 1994 in the United States.
CRISPR-Cas9 is a gene-editing tool in which a guide RNA directs a nuclease to a chosen DNA sequence, so that sequence can then be changed precisely.

data.title: Principles of biotechnology
notes: ### 1. What is Biotechnology?
Biotechnology is the use of living organisms or their products to make or modify products for practical use. Modern biotechnology involves genetic engineering.
### 2. Core Techniques
- **Recombinant DNA (rDNA) Technology**: Combining DNA from different sources
- **PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction)**: Amplifying DNA segments
- **Gel Electrophoresis**: Separating DNA fragments by size
- **Gene Cloning**: Making copies of genes
### 3. Tools of Recombinant DNA Technology
- **Restriction Enzymes (Molecular Scissors)**: Cut DNA at specific sequences (palindromes)
- **Examples**: EcoRI (cuts at GAATTC), HindIII (cuts at AAGCTT)
- **Sticky ends**: Overhanging single-stranded ends after cutting
- **Blunt ends**: No overhang after cutting
- **Vectors (Molecular Vehicles)**: Carry foreign DNA into host
- **Examples**: Plasmids, bacteriophages, cosmids, Ti plasmid
- **Competent Host**: Modified to accept foreign DNA (CaCl2 treatment for bacteria)
### 4. Steps in rDNA Technology
1. Isolation of genetic material (DNA extraction)
2. Cutting DNA with restriction enzymes
3. Separation by gel electrophoresis
4. Insertion of DNA into vector
5. Transformation into host cell
6. Expression of desired gene
### 5. PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction)
- Amplifies specific DNA segment millions of times
- **Steps**: Denaturation (94°C), Annealing (50-65°C), Extension (72°C)
- **Enzyme**: Taq polymerase (heat-stable from Thermus aquaticus)
- **Components**: Template DNA, primers, dNTPs, Taq polymerase
- **Applications**: Forensics, disease diagnosis, genetic research
### 6. Gel Electrophoresis
- Separates DNA fragments by size using electric field
- DNA is negatively charged, moves toward positive electrode
- Smaller fragments move faster through agarose gel
- Visualized with ethidium bromide under UV light
### 7. Entrance Exam Focus
Identify restriction enzymes; Describe PCR steps; Explain vector requirements.
Biotechnology here means using a living system, or an enzyme taken from one, to make or change a product that people use.
A restriction enzyme cuts DNA at a short recognition site and can open a plasmid at that same site.
A vector, often a plasmid, carries the foreign DNA into a host cell so the host can copy it.
confusion: x Any enzyme can cut DNA. x Only specific restriction enzymes recognize specific sequences.
x PCR makes infinite copies. x Each cycle doubles DNA - limited by reagents.
x DNA moves to positive electrode because it's positive. x DNA is NEGATIVE, moves to POSITIVE.
A restriction enzyme cuts. It does not copy. Polymerase copies.
A plasmid is a vector in this story, not the disease.
The host does not have to be the organism the gene came from.
PCR multiplies DNA. It does not by itself make a field of cotton.

formulas: Biotechnology here means using a living system, or an enzyme taken from one, to make or change a product that people use.
A restriction enzyme cuts DNA at a short recognition site and can open a plasmid at that same site.
data.summary: Biotechnology is the use of living organisms or their products to make or modify products for practical use, and modern biotechnology is built on recombinant DNA (rDNA) technology. The essential tools are restriction enzymes, which cut DNA at specific palindromic recognition sequences such as EcoRI at GAATTC to give sticky or blunt ends, and vectors such as plasmids, bacteriophages and cosmids, which carry foreign DNA into a competent host. rDNA technology proceeds through six steps from isolation of DNA to expression of the gene, while PCR amplifies a chosen DNA segment using thermostable Taq polymerase and gel electrophoresis separates fragments according to size. These techniques together underpin every product of modern biotechnology.
importantConcepts: Recombinant DNA technology isolates DNA from two sources, cuts both with the same restriction enzyme and joins the fragments with DNA ligase to form recombinant DNA.

Restriction enzymes, called molecular scissors, recognise specific palindromic sequences and cut them — EcoRI at GAATTC, HindIII at AAGCTT — producing sticky ends with single-stranded overhangs or blunt ends.
Vectors, called molecular vehicles, carry foreign DNA into the host cell: plasmids, bacteriophages, cosmids, and the Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens for plant transformation.

The host cell must be made competent so that it will take up DNA, which in bacteria is achieved by treatment with CaCl2, and transformants are usually selected using an antibiotic-resistance marker on the vector.
PCR amplifies a chosen DNA segment from template DNA, two primers, dNTPs and Taq polymerase through repeated cycles of denaturation at about 94 °C, annealing at 50-65 °C and extension at about 72 °C.
Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size: DNA is negatively charged and migrates towards the positive electrode, and smaller fragments move fastest through the agarose gel.
importantStatements: Only specific restriction enzymes cut DNA, and each recognises its own sequence; a random nuclease such as DNase I cannot be used for rDNA work.
Sticky ends produced by the same restriction enzyme are complementary, so they base-pair with each other and DNA ligase then seals the backbone.
Each cycle of PCR approximately doubles the target DNA, so amplification is exponential but becomes limited by reagent quantity and primer exhaustion.
DNA carries a net negative charge on its phosphate backbone, so in an electric field it migrates towards the anode, the positive electrode.
Taq polymerase is used in PCR because it is thermostable and survives the 94-95 °C denaturation step that would denature an ordinary enzyme.
A good vector needs an origin of replication so it multiplies in the host, a selectable marker, and a cloning site containing single sites for the restriction enzymes used.
importantTasks: State the function of a restriction enzyme and give the recognition sequence and type of end produced by one example such as EcoRI or HindIII.
Describe the three steps of a PCR cycle, stating the temperature of each step and naming the enzyme used.
Explain why Taq polymerase is used in PCR and state what would happen if a heat-labile enzyme were used instead.
Explain how gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments of different sizes and how the bands are made visible.

keyPoints: DNA ligase seals the sugar-phosphate backbone after complementary sticky ends pair, forming the recombinant plasmid.
EcoRI cuts 5'-GAATTC-3' to leave 5' AATT overhangs, and HindIII cuts 5'-AAGCTT-3' to leave 5' AGCT overhangs.
The rDNA steps are: isolation of DNA, cutting with restriction enzymes, separation by gel electrophoresis, insertion into a vector, transformation of the host, and expression of the gene.
PCR components are template DNA, forward and reverse primers, the four dNTPs, Taq polymerase and a buffer containing Mg2+ ions.
Bands are visualised after staining with ethidium bromide under UV light; smaller fragments travel furthest from the wells.
Gene cloning in a vector produces many identical copies, that is clones, of a single DNA fragment.
specialNotes: Restriction enzyme recognition sites are palindromes, read the same 5' to 3' on both strands, which is what allows the enzyme to cut both strands of the double helix.
The same restriction enzyme must be used on both the vector and the insert, otherwise the ends will not be complementary and the fragments will not join.
Each PCR cycle doubles the target DNA, so after n cycles there are 2 to the power n copies of the target sequence (2 to the power 10 = 1024).
Ethidium bromide is a powerful mutagen, so safer dyes such as SYBR Safe are now preferred; the principle of visualising bands under UV light is unchanged.
A plasmid is chosen over a bacteriophage for many cloning jobs because it is small, easy to isolate, and its host cells can be grown in large numbers to give high yield.

DNA is negative so it runs to the positive electrode, and the smaller the fragment, the faster it travels.
Vector checklist: origin of replication, selectable marker, and a single cloning site.
Taq comes from Thermus aquaticus, a hot-spring thermophile, which is exactly why it survives 94 degrees.

mcs.question: EcoRI recognises and cuts the DNA sequence:
mcs.explanation: EcoRI cuts 5'-GAATTC-3' and leaves 5' AATT sticky ends. AAGCTT is the site recognised by HindIII and CTGCAG by PstI.

mcs.question: The enzyme used in PCR that survives the 94 degrees C denaturation step is:
mcs.explanation: Taq polymerase from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus is thermostable, so it survives repeated heating to about 94 degrees; other enzymes would denature.

mcs.question: In gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments move through the gel towards the:
options: Negative electrode, because DNA is negatively charged
Positive electrode, because DNA is negatively charged
Positive electrode, because DNA is positively charged
Both electrodes equally, whatever the fragment size
mcs.explanation: The phosphate backbone gives DNA a net negative charge, so it migrates to the anode, the positive electrode, and smaller fragments move fastest through the agarose.

mcs.question: Which of the following is a suitable vector for carrying foreign DNA into a bacterial cell?
mcs.explanation: A plasmid is small circular extra-chromosomal DNA with its own origin of replication, a selectable marker and a single restriction site, which makes it ideal for cloning in bacteria.

mcs.question: The enzyme that joins two DNA fragments by sealing the sugar-phosphate backbone is:
mcs.explanation: DNA ligase forms phosphodiester bonds to seal the nicks left after complementary sticky ends pair, producing recombinant DNA; a restriction endonuclease makes the cut in the first place.

notes: ### 1. What is Biotechnology?
Biotechnology is the use of living organisms or their products to make or modify products for practical use. Modern biotechnology involves genetic engineering.
### 2. Core Techniques
- **Recombinant DNA (rDNA) Technology**: Combining DNA from different sources
- **PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction)**: Amplifying DNA segments
- **Gel Electrophoresis**: Separating DNA fragments by size
- **Gene Cloning**: Making copies of genes
### 3. Tools of Recombinant DNA Technology
- **Restriction Enzymes (Molecular Scissors)**: Cut DNA at specific sequences (palindromes)
- **Examples**: EcoRI (cuts at GAATTC), HindIII (cuts at AAGCTT)
- **Sticky ends**: Overhanging single-stranded ends after cutting
- **Blunt ends**: No overhang after cutting
- **Vectors (Molecular Vehicles)**: Carry foreign DNA into host
- **Examples**: Plasmids, bacteriophages, cosmids, Ti plasmid
- **Competent Host**: Modified to accept foreign DNA (CaCl2 treatment for bacteria)
### 4. Steps in rDNA Technology
1. Isolation of genetic material (DNA extraction)
2. Cutting DNA with restriction enzymes
3. Separation by gel electrophoresis
4. Insertion of DNA into vector
5. Transformation into host cell
6. Expression of desired gene
### 5. PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction)
- Amplifies specific DNA segment millions of times
- **Steps**: Denaturation (94°C), Annealing (50-65°C), Extension (72°C)
- **Enzyme**: Taq polymerase (heat-stable from Thermus aquaticus)
- **Components**: Template DNA, primers, dNTPs, Taq polymerase
- **Applications**: Forensics, disease diagnosis, genetic research
### 6. Gel Electrophoresis
- Separates DNA fragments by size using electric field
- DNA is negatively charged, moves toward positive electrode
- Smaller fragments move faster through agarose gel
- Visualized with ethidium bromide under UV light
### 7. Entrance Exam Focus
Identify restriction enzymes; Describe PCR steps; Explain vector requirements.

data.topicTitle: National parks, wildlife reserves, conservation areas, biodiversity hotspots, wetlands and Ramsar sites
notes: National parks are legally protected areas established to conserve wildlife, biodiversity, and natural ecosystems, with strict restrictions on human activities such as hunting, logging, and settlement.
Wildlife reserves are protected areas focused primarily on the conservation of particular species or groups of wildlife, allowing limited sustainable use by local communities.
Conservation areas are regions where conservation of biodiversity is integrated with sustainable development and community participation, balancing ecological protection with human livelihoods.

Biodiversity hotspots are regions with exceptionally high species richness and endemism that are under severe threat from human activities; they cover only 2.3% of Earth's surface but harbor over 50% of endemic plant species.

Wetlands are ecosystems saturated with water, either permanently or seasonally, supporting rich biodiversity and providing critical services like water purification, flood control, and carbon storage.
Ramsar sites are wetlands of international importance designated under the Ramsar Convention (1971) for their ecological, botanical, zoological, limnological, or hydrological significance.
Nepal has 12 national parks, 1 wildlife reserve, 6 conservation areas, and 10 Ramsar sites, reflecting its commitment to in-situ conservation.

In-situ conservation protects species within their natural habitats (national parks, reserves), while ex-situ conservation protects species outside natural habitats (zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks).
Buffer zones around protected areas allow sustainable resource use by local communities, reducing pressure on core conservation zones.
Protected area management involves zoning, anti-poaching patrols, habitat restoration, community engagement, and monitoring of species populations.

data.title: Ecology — Concepts and Ecosystems
data.topicTitle: Ecosystem ecology: concept of ecology, biotic and abiotic factors, species interactions; concept of ecosystem, structural and functional aspects of pond and forest ecosystem
notes: Detailed notes on 01 ecosystem ecology concept of ecology biotic and abiotic factors species interactions concept of ecosystem structural and functional aspects of pond and forest ecosystem within the ecology unit.
Ecology: the study of the interactions between organisms and their environment (biotic + abiotic).
Biotic factors: living components (plants, animals, microorganisms); Abiotic factors: non-living (light, temperature, water, soil, pH, gases).
Species interactions: mutualism (+/+), commensalism (+/0), parasitism (+/-), predation (+/-), competition (-/-), amensalism (-/0), neutralism (0/0).
Ecosystem: a functional unit of biotic + abiotic components interacting; types: aquatic (pond, lake, ocean) and terrestrial (grassland, forest, desert).
Structural aspects: producers (autotrophs), consumers (herbivores, carnivores, omnivores), decomposers (bacteria, fungi); trophic levels.
Functional aspects: energy flow (unidirectional, sun → producers → consumers → heat), nutrient cycling (biogeochemical), and food chains/webs.
Pond and forest ecosystems: producers (phytoplankton / trees), consumers (zooplankton / herbivores / carnivores), decomposers; abiotic factors (light, temperature, water, soil).
Nepal: Terai, hills, and mountains each have distinct ecosystems (e.g., Chitwan Terai, temperate oak-rhododendron hills, alpine zone).
NEB focus: concept of ecology, biotic/abiotic factors, species interactions, and structural + functional aspects of pond and forest ecosystems.
In nature an organism does not exist in isolation, it is associated with organisms of its own and of different kinds as well as with the physical environment.
If the organism is plant, it depends for growth on the aerial environment for light, temperature and carbon dioxide, on the soil environment for inorganic nutrients and water.
If it is an animal it depends on the plants for food and shelter.
If it is a microorganism it depend on the dead organic matter from plants and animals for its food, and releases the nutrients tied in the organic matter for the reuse of plants.
Thus, there are continuous interactions among the organisms and between the organisms and the habitat resulting into an integrated, functional unit.
This functional unit is known as ecosystem.
It is the structural and functional unit of ecology.
Thus, ecosystem is defined as ‘the structural and functional unit of ecology where the living organisms interact with each other and the surrounding environment’.
confusion: ❌ Misconception about 01 ecosystem ecology concept of ecology biotic and abiotic factors species interactions concept of ecosystem structural and functional aspects of pond and forest ecosystem. ✅ Scientific explanation.
Predation (+/-) and parasitism (+/-) both harm one partner; predation usually KILLS the prey quickly, parasitism is long-term and usually does not kill the host immediately.
Mutualism (+/+) benefits both; commensalism (+/0) benefits one, affects neither; parasitism (+/-) benefits one, harms the other.
Competition (-/-) harms BOTH species (interspecific); intra-specific competition is within the same species.
An ecosystem is a FUNCTIONAL unit (energy flow + nutrient cycling); a community is just the assemblage of species.
Energy flows ONEDIRECTIONALLY through an ecosystem (sun → producers → consumers → heat); it is NOT cycled.
Nutrients (C, N, P) ARE cycled (biogeochemical); energy is not cycled.
