data.title: Immune system and immunity
notes: ### 1. Immune System Overview
The immune system protects the body against pathogens and foreign substances.
### 2. Innate Immunity (Non-specific)
- Present from birth
- First line of defense
- **Physical barriers**: Skin, mucous membranes
- **Chemical barriers**: Stomach acid, lysozyme in tears
- **Phagocytes**: Neutrophils, macrophages engulf pathogens
- **Inflammation**: Redness, swelling, heat, pain
- **Fever**: Elevated temperature inhibits pathogen growth
- **Natural Killer cells**: Destroy infected host cells
### 3. Adaptive Immunity (Specific)
- Develops over lifetime
- Specific to particular pathogens
- Has memory (immunological memory)
- **Humoral immunity**: B cells produce antibodies
- **Cell-mediated immunity**: T cells destroy infected cells
### 4. Antibodies (Immunoglobulins)
- **IgG**: Most abundant, crosses placenta, long-term immunity
- **IgM**: First responder, large pentamer
- **IgA**: Mucosal immunity (tears, saliva, breast milk)
- **IgE**: Allergic reactions, parasitic infections
- **IgD**: B cell receptor
### 5. Active vs Passive Immunity
- **Active**: Body produces its own antibodies (infection or vaccination)
- **Passive**: Receives pre-made antibodies (mother to baby, antivenom)
### 6. Vaccination
- Introduces weakened/killed antigen to stimulate active immunity
- Creates memory cells for faster response on re-exposure
- Herd immunity: When enough people are immune, disease spread is limited
### 7. Autoimmune Diseases
- Immune system attacks body's own cells
- Examples: Rheumatoid arthritis, Type 1 diabetes, Lupus, Multiple sclerosis
### 8. Allergies
- Hypersensitive response to harmless antigens (allergens)
- Mediated by IgE, mast cells release histamine
- Examples: Hay fever, asthma, food allergies, anaphylaxis
### 9. Entrance Exam Focus
Distinguish innate vs adaptive; Identify antibody types; Explain vaccination principle.
Innate immunity is ready at birth: skin, mucus, acid in the stomach, and phagocytes that engulf invaders without learning their identity.
Adaptive immunity learns one particular antigen. Lymphocytes do that work, and they leave memory cells after the first meeting.
B cells make antibodies, and each antibody fits one antigen, so the response is specific rather than a general barrier.
T cells kill infected body cells and help other cells of the immune system respond to the same antigen.
A vaccine shows the immune system an antigen, or a harmless form of it, so memory cells form before the real infection arrives.
confusion: x Innate immunity has memory. x Only adaptive immunity has immunological memory.
x Antibodies kill pathogens directly. x Antibodies mark pathogens for destruction.
x Vaccines cause the disease. x Vaccines use weakened/killed pathogens to build immunity.
An antibody is not an antibiotic. One is made by the body. The other is a drug.
Innate defence does not remember a particular measles virus.
A vaccine is prevention by memory. It is not a treatment given after the organs have already failed.
Fever can be a defence. It is not itself a pathogen.

data.summary: The immune system protects the body in two ways: innate (non-specific) immunity, which is present from birth and acts immediately, and adaptive (specific) immunity, which is acquired during life and carries immunological memory. Innate defences include physical and chemical barriers, phagocytes, inflammation, fever and natural killer cells, while adaptive immunity has a humoral branch in which B cells produce antibodies and a cell-mediated branch in which T cells destroy infected cells. Active immunity is the body's own antibody response to infection or vaccination, while passive immunity is the receipt of ready-made antibodies from a mother or from an antivenom. Failure of self-tolerance produces autoimmune disease and hypersensitivity to harmless antigens produces allergy.
importantConcepts: Innate immunity is the first, non-specific line of defence: physical barriers (skin, mucous membranes), chemical barriers (stomach acid, lysozyme in tears), phagocytes, inflammation, fever and natural killer cells.

Adaptive immunity is specific to particular antigens, develops over the lifetime, and has immunological memory; it has a humoral branch (B cells producing antibodies) and a cell-mediated branch (T cells killing infected cells).

Antibodies are immunoglobulins of five classes: IgG (most abundant, crosses the placenta, long-term immunity), IgM (first responder, large pentamer), IgA (mucosal immunity), IgE (allergy and parasites) and IgD (B-cell receptor).

Active immunity results from the body making its own antibodies after infection or vaccination — slow to start but long lasting; passive immunity is the receipt of ready-made antibodies — immediate but temporary.
Vaccination supplies a weakened, killed or subunit antigen that creates memory cells and herd immunity without causing the disease itself.
Autoimmunity is an attack on the body's own cells, while allergy is a hypersensitivity response to a harmless allergen mediated by IgE and histamine released from mast cells.
importantStatements: Only adaptive immunity has immunological memory; innate immunity responds in the same way every time and cannot be primed.
Antibodies do not normally kill pathogens directly — they bind and neutralise the antigen or tag the pathogen for phagocytosis and complement activation.
Vaccines do not cause the disease because they contain killed, weakened or non-pathogenic forms of the antigen.
IgM is the first antibody produced in a primary immune response and is a large pentamer with high binding strength.
IgG is the only immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta, giving natural passive immunity to the foetus and newborn.
Allergic reactions and defence against parasitic worms involve IgE, which triggers mast cells to release histamine.

keyPoints: Innate immunity: present at birth, non-specific, no memory. Adaptive immunity: acquired, antigen-specific, has memory.
The four classic signs of inflammation are redness, swelling, heat and pain, usually with some loss of function at the site.
Fever raises body temperature and slows the growth and reproduction of many pathogens.
IgG is the most abundant antibody in plasma, crosses the placenta and gives long-term immunity; IgA is found in tears, saliva, mucus and breast milk.
Natural passive immunity reaches the baby as maternal IgG through the placenta and as IgA in colostrum and breast milk.
Herd immunity arises when a large enough fraction of the population is immune, breaking the chain of transmission of infection.
specialNotes: Innate immunity has no memory, so the same innate response occurs on every exposure, which is why vaccination is needed for lasting protection.
Natural passive immunity from maternal antibodies is immediate but short-lived and creates no memory in the baby.
Only IgG crosses the placenta; IgA is instead transferred to the infant in colostrum and breast milk.
T lymphocytes do not produce antibodies — only plasma cells derived from B cells do; helper T cells coordinate the response instead.
Long-term protection is provided by memory cells rather than by antibody level alone, since antibody titres fall after an infection.
examShortTricks: 'Born versus built': innate immunity is present at birth, adaptive immunity is built during life.
If a question mentions memory cells, the answer is adaptive or specific immunity.
Antibody mnemonics: G goes through the placenta, M is the first major responder, A is in secretions, E is for allergy and parasites, D is the B-cell receptor.
Active means your own body makes the antibodies (slow, lasting, memory); passive means ready-made antibodies are given (fast, temporary, no memory).
Vaccine gives a weakened or killed antigen and builds memory; antivenom or anti-tetanus serum supplies antibodies and is passive.

Vaccination and herd immunity often form the last part of a 5-mark question on communicable disease.
Autoimmune disease and allergy questions test the difference between an attack on self and a response to a harmless antigen (2 marks each).

options: It acts as the first line of defence

mcs.explanation: IgM is secreted first because its large pentameric structure gives high binding strength; IgG follows and provides the long-term immunity.

mcs.explanation: The baby receives ready-made IgA instead of producing it, so the transfer is natural (mother to infant) and passive (no memory cells are formed).

mcs.explanation: IgE binds to mast cells; when the allergen binds to this IgE, the mast cells release histamine, producing sneezing, itching and rash, and in severe cases anaphylaxis.

options: Slow to act but long lasting
Immediate but temporary, with no memory cells formed
Effective only after the immune system makes memory cells
mcs.explanation: An antivenom supplies pre-formed antibodies, giving instant protection that is broken down over a few weeks. Immunity from a vaccine is slower to develop but produces memory cells.

mcqs.question: A virus contains:

notes: Viruses: acellular, obligate intracellular parasites; not classified in any kingdom; consist of a nucleic acid core (DNA or RNA) + protein coat (capsid); some have a lipid envelope.
Structure: capsomeres (protein subunits of capsid); bacteriophages have a head (icosahedral) + tail; animal viruses may have an envelope with glycoprotein spikes.
Types by nucleic acid: DNA viruses (e.g., T4 phage, smallpox) and RNA viruses (e.g., influenza, HIV, SARS-CoV-2).
Bacteriophage (T4): lytic life cycle — adsorption → injection → replication → assembly → release (lysogeny is the lysogenic cycle in lambda phage).
Replication: viruses hijack the host cell machinery; they cannot replicate independently.
Importance: many human and animal diseases (common cold, flu, HIV/AIDS, hepatitis, rabies, smallpox — eradicated in 1980).
Applications: viral vectors in gene therapy, bacteriophages in food safety testing, viruses in molecular biology tools.
NEB focus: virus structure, lytic cycle of T4 phage, and importance of viruses.
confusion: Viruses are NOT living organisms: they lack metabolism, cannot reproduce outside a host, and are not made of cells.
A virus has EITHER DNA or RNA, never both (with rare exceptions like some retroviruses that convert RNA to DNA).
Bacteriophages infect BACTERIA; animal viruses infect animals; plant viruses infect plants.
The capsid is protein; the core is nucleic acid; the envelope (if present) is lipid + glycoproteins from the host membrane.
Lytic cycle destroys the host cell; lysogenic cycle integrates viral DNA into the host genome (prophage) without immediate lysis.
Viruses are NOT visible under a light microscope; they require an electron microscope (~20–300 nm size).

universalFacts: The largest virus (Pithovirus) is ~1.2 µm in diameter — visible only under a light microscope.
Smallpox was the first human disease eradicated by vaccination (1980).
Retroviruses (e.g., HIV) carry RNA but use reverse transcriptase to make DNA in the host.
Viruses are ~1/100th the size of a typical bacterium.

Influenza virus — RNA virus, causes seasonal flu.
HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) — retrovirus, causes AIDS.
SARS-CoV-2 — RNA virus, causes COVID-19.

data.summary: Viruses are acellular, obligate intracellular parasites that contain either DNA or RNA enclosed in a protein capsid (and sometimes a lipid envelope). They cannot replicate outside a host cell and hijack host machinery. The T4 bacteriophage lytic cycle (adsorption, injection, replication, assembly, release) is the NEB model. Viruses cause many important diseases but are also valuable tools in gene therapy and molecular biology. data.title: Vegetation: Introduction, types of vegetation in Nepal
data.topicTitle: Vegetation: Introduction, types of vegetation in Nepal
notes: Vegetation is the plant cover of a place, set by temperature, rain, soil and height. Nepal's cover changes quickly because the land rises from the Terai to the high Himalaya.
Below about 1000 m the belt is tropical. Sal, Shorea robusta, dominates, with sisau along rivers. This is the Terai and the inner Terai.
From about 1000 to 2000 m the belt is subtropical. Chir pine, Pinus roxburghii, and Schima–Castanopsis forest are the markers.
From about 2000 to 3000 m the belt is temperate. Oak and Rhododendron arboreum, the national flower, are the markers. Rhododendron here is a flowering plant.
Toward 4000 m, fir, birch and juniper thin out. The timberline is the last trees. Above it, alpine herbs and grasses continue until the snowline, which is higher.

Forest and other wooded land cover about 45 percent of Nepal. The east is wetter than the west at the same height, so the species lists differ. Community forestry is a management success in the middle hills, not itself a belt.

notes: Organic chemistry: study of carbon compounds.
Carbon: tetravalent, forms 4 bonds.
Functional groups: -OH (alcohol), -COOH (carboxylic acid), etc.
Homologous series: same functional group, differ by CH₂.
confusion: ❌ All atoms are identical in an element. ✅ Isotopes have same protons but different neutrons.
❌ Atoms are indivisible. ✅ Atoms consist of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
❌ Electrons orbit in fixed paths like planets. ✅ Electrons exist in probability clouds (orbitals).
❌ Heisenberg uncertainty means we cannot measure position and momentum precisely simultaneously — not that we lack good instruments.
❌ de Broglie wavelength applies only to light. ✅ All matter has wave nature; detectable mainly for small masses like electrons.
❌ Quantum number l can be any integer. ✅ l ranges from 0 to n−1.
❌ Magnetic quantum number ml determines energy. ✅ ml determines orbital orientation, not energy (in absence of magnetic field).
❌ Spin quantum number ms can be ±½ or any value. ✅ ms is always +½ or −½.
❌ Aufbau principle means filling from bottom to top of the diagram. ✅ Fill lowest-energy orbitals first: 1s→2s→2p→3s→3p→4s→3d→4p→...
❌ Pauli exclusion allows two electrons per orbital with any spin. ✅ Two electrons in same orbital must have opposite spins.
❌ Hund's rule means pair electrons before spreading. ✅ Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first with parallel spins.
❌ The mole is just a number like dozen. ✅ 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ particles (Avogadro constant) — a bridge between atomic and macroscopic scales.
❌ Molar mass and molecular mass are the same thing. ✅ Molecular mass is in amu; molar mass is in g/mol — numerically equal but different units.
❌ Limiting reagent is the reactant with smallest mass. ✅ Limiting reagent is the one that produces the least product (determined by moles, not mass).
❌ % yield can exceed 100%. ✅ % yield >100% indicates impure product or incomplete drying.
❌ Molarity and molality are the same. ✅ Molarity = mol/L solution (changes with T); Molality = mol/kg solvent (temperature-independent).
❌ A strong acid completely ionizes in water. ✅ Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) are ~100% ionized; weak acids partially ionize.
❌ pH can be negative. ✅ pH < 0 is possible for concentrations >1M (e.g., 2M HCl has pH ≈ −0.3).
❌ Kc changes when concentration changes. ✅ Kc is constant at constant temperature; only temperature changes K.
❌ Adding catalyst shifts equilibrium position. ✅ Catalyst speeds both forward and backward reactions equally; no shift in equilibrium.
❌ High pressure always favors products. ✅ High pressure favors side with fewer gas moles (Le Chatelier).
❌ Exothermic reactions are spontaneous. ✅ Spontaneity depends on ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, not just ΔH.
❌ Endothermic reactions cannot be spontaneous. ✅ Endothermic reactions can be spontaneous if TΔS > ΔH (e.g., ice melting above 0°C).
❌ ΔH and ΔU are always the same. ✅ ΔH = ΔU + PΔV; they differ when gas moles change.
❌ Heat (q) and work (w) are state functions. ✅ q and w are path functions; only ΔU, ΔH, ΔS, ΔG are state functions.
❌ Oxidation and reduction happen separately. ✅ Oxidation and reduction always occur together (redox).
❌ Oxidizing agent gets oxidized. ✅ Oxidizing agent accepts electrons and gets reduced.
❌ Reducing agent gets reduced. ✅ Reducing agent donates electrons and gets oxidized.
❌ Faraday's laws apply only to metals. ✅ Faraday's laws apply to any substance deposited/dissolved at electrodes.
❌ Real gases obey PV=nRT at all conditions. ✅ Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature.
❌ van der Waals constants a and b are same for all gases. ✅ a (attraction) and b (volume) are gas-specific.
❌ Surface tension increases with temperature. ✅ Surface tension decreases as temperature increases.
❌ Viscosity decreases with temperature for liquids. ✅ Viscosity of liquids decreases with T; gases increase with T.
❌ Colligative properties depend on nature of solute. ✅ Colligative properties depend only on number of particles, not identity.
❌ Raoult's law applies to all solutions. ✅ Raoult's law is exact for ideal solutions; approximate for dilute real solutions.
❌ Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. ✅ Yes — π = CRT depends on solute particle concentration.
❌ All carbon compounds are organic. ✅ CO, CO₂, carbonates, and carbides are inorganic despite containing carbon.

data.summary:
Atomic structure: From Rutherford's nuclear model through Bohr's quantized orbits to the modern quantum mechanical model, understanding electron configuration using four quantum numbers is fundamental.

Stoichiometry: The mole concept bridges atomic and macroscopic scales; limiting reagent determines theoretical yield; concentration expressed as molarity or molality.

Chemical equilibrium: Dynamic equilibrium has equal forward and backward rates; Kc/Kp are temperature-dependent; Le Chatelier's principle predicts response to stress.

Thermodynamics: First law (energy conservation); enthalpy changes in reactions; Gibbs free energy determines spontaneity; entropy of universe always increases.

Oxidation-reduction: Redox involves electron transfer; oxidation numbers track electron flow; electrochemical cells convert chemical to electrical energy; Faraday's laws quantify electrolysis.

States of matter: Gas laws relate P, V, T, n; kinetic theory explains gas behavior; real gases deviate due to intermolecular forces and molecular volume.

Solutions: Molarity and molality express concentration; colligative properties depend on particle number; Raoult's law describes vapor pressure of ideal solutions.

Chemical bonding: Ionic bonds form from electron transfer; covalent bonds from sharing; VSEPR predicts molecular geometry; hybridization explains bonding orbitals.

Organic chemistry basics: Carbon's tetravalency and catenation enable millions of compounds; functional groups determine reactivity; IUPAC nomenclature provides systematic naming.

Hydrocarbons: Alkanes (CnH2n+2) are saturated; alkenes (CnH2n) have C=C; alkynes (CnH2n-2) have C≡C; aromatic compounds based on benzene ring.

Periodic table: Elements arranged by atomic number; periodic trends in radius, ionization energy, electronegativity; s, p, d, f blocks based on orbital type.

Applied chemistry: Petrochemical industry, polymer science, green chemistry principles; importance of sustainable chemical manufacturing for environmental protection.

Carbon forms 4 covalent bonds in all stable compounds.

Isomerism increases molecular diversity enormously.

data.topicTitle: Periodic trend and periodicity: atomic radii, ionic radii, ionization energy, electron affinity, electronegativity, metallic characters (general trend and explanation only)
notes: ### 1. Meaning of periodicity

Periodicity is the recurrence of similar physical and chemical properties at regular intervals when elements are arranged in order of atomic number. Its cause is the periodic repetition of the *valence-shell electronic configuration*: trends across a period follow from increasing Z_eff, trends down a group from increasing n and increasing shielding.
### 2. Atomic radii

Radius is measured as covalent radius (half the bond length in a homonuclear molecule), metallic radius (half the distance between neighbouring metal atoms) or van der Waals radius (from non-bonded contacts — the largest). **Across a period the radius decreases** (Li 152 → F 64 pm) because nuclear charge rises faster than shielding; **down a group it increases** (Li → Cs) because a new shell is added. Period 4 shows a normal contraction after the d-block, and the 5d series follows the 4d series closely — the lanthanide contraction (poor 4f shielding).
### 3. Ionic radii
• A cation is smaller than its parent atom (Na 186 pm → Na⁺ 95 pm); an anion is larger (Cl 99 pm → Cl⁻ 181 pm) because added electrons increase repulsion while the nuclear charge is unchanged.
• Down a group the ionic radius increases for the same charge (Li⁺ < Na⁺ < K⁺ < Rb⁺ < Cs⁺); across a period ions of the same charge get smaller.
• **Isoelectronic series** (same number of electrons): radius decreases as nuclear charge increases, N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Ne > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺; for one element Fe³⁺ < Fe²⁺.
### 4. Ionisation energy (IE)

The minimum energy needed to remove the most loosely bound electron from an isolated gaseous atom; measured in kJ mol⁻¹ or eV per atom (H: 1312 kJ mol⁻¹ = 13.6 eV). **It increases across a period** (Li 520 → Ne 2081 kJ mol⁻¹) because Z_eff rises and size falls, and **decreases down a group** as size increases. Anomalies: Be > B and N > O (2s² stability; 2p pairing repulsion in oxygen), repeated as Mg > Al and P > S. Successive IEs always increase (IE₁ < IE₂ < IE₃), and a large jump marks the end of a shell — Na IE₁ = 496, IE₂ = 4562 kJ mol⁻¹.
### 5. Electron affinity (EA)

The energy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron, X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g); EA is often reported as the energy *released*, so state the sign convention in answers. It generally becomes more exothermic **across a period** and less so **down a group** as size and shielding increase. Chlorine has a higher EA than fluorine (349 vs 328 kJ mol⁻¹) because F's very small 2p shell causes extra electron–electron repulsion. Noble gases have ~zero or positive EA, and Be and N have very small values because of filled/half-filled stability.
### 6. Electronegativity (EN)

The tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared electron pair. Pauling's scale takes F = 4.0 (highest), O = 3.5, N = 3.0, H = 2.1, Cs ≈ 0.7; the Mulliken scale uses (IE + EA)/2. **EN increases across a period and decreases down a group**; noble gases are assigned little or no value. Bond polarity follows from ΔEN: > 1.7 usually ionic, < 0.5 essentially non-polar covalent (HF, ΔEN = 1.9, is polar covalent).
### 7. Metallic and non-metallic character

Metallic character **decreases across a period** (Na → Cl) and **increases down a group** (Li → Cs): metals lose electrons easily (low IE), non-metals gain them (high IE, high EA/EN). Consequences: oxide character moves from basic → amphoteric → acidic across a period, and the diagonal pairs (Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si) show metallic character reappearing diagonally.
### 8. Applications
• Reactivity predictions: alkali metals become more reactive down the group (low IE); halogen oxidising power falls from F to I (high EA/EN mainly for F and Cl).
• Explains the acidic/basic character of oxides, the amphoteric behaviour of Al₂O₃ and the change from ionic NaCl to covalent AlCl₃ across period 3.
• Used in materials selection (semiconductors Si, Ge), in predicting bond polarity and dipole moments, and in understanding ion sizes for crystal packing and complex formation.
### 9. Limitations of the trends

All the trends are *general*, not exact: the Be/B, N/O, Mg/Al and P/S breaks come from penetration and pairing, and the d- and f-blocks show many irregularities (Cr, Cu, lanthanide contraction, poor 4f shielding, relativistic effects in heavy elements). Radii are not directly measurable and covalent, metallic and van der Waals values differ by 0.5–1 Å, so only one consistent type may be compared. Electron affinity depends on the stated convention, and electronegativity values differ between scales (Pauling, Mulliken, Allred–Rochow), with noble-gas values ill-defined. Above all, trends are qualitative — quantitative prediction needs quantum calculations or Z_eff with accurate shielding.
confusion: ❌ Atomic radius increases across a period. ✅ It decreases because Z_eff rises faster than shielding.
❌ An anion is smaller than its parent atom. ✅ It is larger — added electrons increase repulsion while nuclear charge stays the same.
❌ IE increases smoothly across a period. ✅ Be > B and N > O (also Mg > Al, P > S) are standard breaks from 2s² stability and 2p pairing.
❌ Fluorine has the highest electron affinity. ✅ Chlorine does (349 vs 328 kJ mol⁻¹) because of extra repulsion in F's tiny 2p shell.
❌ Electronegativity is directly measurable. ✅ It is a derived, scale-dependent parameter (Pauling, Mulliken, Allred–Rochow).

examples: **Problem:** Arrange Mg²⁺, Na⁺, F⁻, O²⁻ in decreasing size. **Solution:** they are isoelectronic (10 electrons), so the smallest nuclear charge gives the largest radius → O²⁻ (Z = 8) > F⁻ (9) > Na⁺ (11) > Mg²⁺ (12).

**Problem:** Which has the higher first ionisation energy, Be or B? **Solution:** Be (899 kJ mol⁻¹) > B (801 kJ mol⁻¹), since Be's 2s² is a filled subshell and its electron penetrates closer to the nucleus than B's 2p electron.

confusion: ❌ All atoms are identical in an element. ✅ Isotopes have same protons but different neutrons.
❌ Atoms are indivisible. ✅ Atoms consist of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
❌ Electrons orbit in fixed paths like planets. ✅ Electrons exist in probability clouds (orbitals).
❌ Heisenberg uncertainty means we cannot measure position and momentum precisely simultaneously — not that we lack good instruments.
❌ de Broglie wavelength applies only to light. ✅ All matter has wave nature; detectable mainly for small masses like electrons.
❌ Quantum number l can be any integer. ✅ l ranges from 0 to n−1.
❌ Magnetic quantum number ml determines energy. ✅ ml determines orbital orientation, not energy (in absence of magnetic field).
❌ Spin quantum number ms can be ±½ or any value. ✅ ms is always +½ or −½.
❌ Aufbau principle means filling from bottom to top of the diagram. ✅ Fill lowest-energy orbitals first: 1s→2s→2p→3s→3p→4s→3d→4p→...
❌ Pauli exclusion allows two electrons per orbital with any spin. ✅ Two electrons in same orbital must have opposite spins.
❌ Hund's rule means pair electrons before spreading. ✅ Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first with parallel spins.
❌ The mole is just a number like dozen. ✅ 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ particles (Avogadro constant) — a bridge between atomic and macroscopic scales.
❌ Molar mass and molecular mass are the same thing. ✅ Molecular mass is in amu; molar mass is in g/mol — numerically equal but different units.
❌ Limiting reagent is the reactant with smallest mass. ✅ Limiting reagent is the one that produces the least product (determined by moles, not mass).
❌ % yield can exceed 100%. ✅ % yield >100% indicates impure product or incomplete drying.
❌ Molarity and molality are the same. ✅ Molarity = mol/L solution (changes with T); Molality = mol/kg solvent (temperature-independent).
❌ A strong acid completely ionizes in water. ✅ Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) are ~100% ionized; weak acids partially ionize.
❌ pH can be negative. ✅ pH < 0 is possible for concentrations >1M (e.g., 2M HCl has pH ≈ −0.3).
❌ Kc changes when concentration changes. ✅ Kc is constant at constant temperature; only temperature changes K.
❌ Adding catalyst shifts equilibrium position. ✅ Catalyst speeds both forward and backward reactions equally; no shift in equilibrium.
❌ High pressure always favors products. ✅ High pressure favors side with fewer gas moles (Le Chatelier).
❌ Exothermic reactions are spontaneous. ✅ Spontaneity depends on ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, not just ΔH.
❌ Endothermic reactions cannot be spontaneous. ✅ Endothermic reactions can be spontaneous if TΔS > ΔH (e.g., ice melting above 0°C).
❌ ΔH and ΔU are always the same. ✅ ΔH = ΔU + PΔV; they differ when gas moles change.
❌ Heat (q) and work (w) are state functions. ✅ q and w are path functions; only ΔU, ΔH, ΔS, ΔG are state functions.
❌ Oxidation and reduction happen separately. ✅ Oxidation and reduction always occur together (redox).
❌ Oxidizing agent gets oxidized. ✅ Oxidizing agent accepts electrons and gets reduced.
❌ Reducing agent gets reduced. ✅ Reducing agent donates electrons and gets oxidized.
❌ Faraday's laws apply only to metals. ✅ Faraday's laws apply to any substance deposited/dissolved at electrodes.
❌ Real gases obey PV=nRT at all conditions. ✅ Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature.
❌ van der Waals constants a and b are same for all gases. ✅ a (attraction) and b (volume) are gas-specific.
❌ Surface tension increases with temperature. ✅ Surface tension decreases as temperature increases.
❌ Viscosity decreases with temperature for liquids. ✅ Viscosity of liquids decreases with T; gases increase with T.
❌ Colligative properties depend on nature of solute. ✅ Colligative properties depend only on number of particles, not identity.
❌ Raoult's law applies to all solutions. ✅ Raoult's law is exact for ideal solutions; approximate for dilute real solutions.
❌ Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. ✅ Yes — π = CRT depends on solute particle concentration.
❌ All carbon compounds are organic. ✅ CO, CO₂, carbonates, and carbides are inorganic despite containing carbon.

data.summary:
Atomic structure: From Rutherford's nuclear model through Bohr's quantized orbits to the modern quantum mechanical model, understanding electron configuration using four quantum numbers is fundamental.

Stoichiometry: The mole concept bridges atomic and macroscopic scales; limiting reagent determines theoretical yield; concentration expressed as molarity or molality.

Chemical equilibrium: Dynamic equilibrium has equal forward and backward rates; Kc/Kp are temperature-dependent; Le Chatelier's principle predicts response to stress.

Thermodynamics: First law (energy conservation); enthalpy changes in reactions; Gibbs free energy determines spontaneity; entropy of universe always increases.

Oxidation-reduction: Redox involves electron transfer; oxidation numbers track electron flow; electrochemical cells convert chemical to electrical energy; Faraday's laws quantify electrolysis.

States of matter: Gas laws relate P, V, T, n; kinetic theory explains gas behavior; real gases deviate due to intermolecular forces and molecular volume.

Solutions: Molarity and molality express concentration; colligative properties depend on particle number; Raoult's law describes vapor pressure of ideal solutions.

Chemical bonding: Ionic bonds form from electron transfer; covalent bonds from sharing; VSEPR predicts molecular geometry; hybridization explains bonding orbitals.

data.title: Ideal Gas and the Ideal Gas Equation: Universal Gas Constant and its Significance
data.topicTitle: Ideal gas and ideal gas equation; universal gas constant and its significance
notes: ### 1. Meaning of an ideal gas

An ideal (perfect) gas is a hypothetical gas that obeys the gas laws and PV = nRT exactly under all conditions. Its molecules are point masses with no volume and no intermolecular forces, and collisions are perfectly elastic. No real gas is ideal, but every gas approaches ideal behaviour at **low pressure and high temperature**.
### 2. The ideal gas equation

From Boyle (V ∝ 1/P), Charles (V ∝ T) and Avogadro (V ∝ n): $V\propto\frac{nT}{P}$, hence $PV=nRT$. Useful forms: $PV=\frac{m}{M}RT$ (mass m, molar mass M), $PM=dRT$ (density d) and $P=CRT$ for molar concentration C.
### 3. Meaning and value of R (universal gas constant)

For one mole of an ideal gas R = PV/T is the same for every gas — hence *universal*. Physically R is the work done when 1 mol of ideal gas expands at constant pressure per kelvin of temperature rise. Values: R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 8.314 × 10⁷ erg K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 0.0821 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 2 cal K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Related constant: Boltzmann constant k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ (R is per mole, k is per molecule).
### 4. Significance of R
• Independent of the nature of the gas, it links P, V, T, n with energy — the bridge between the gas laws and thermodynamics (ΔH = ΔU + ΔnRT).
• Mean kinetic energy of 1 mol of any gas = (3/2)RT; R also appears in the Arrhenius equation and in Cp − Cv = R.
• It fixes the molar volume: from V = RT/P, 1 mol occupies 22.4 L at STP.
### 5. Applications
• Determining molar mass and density of gases and volatile liquids (Dumas and Victor Meyer methods) using PM = dRT.
• Calculating gas volumes for stoichiometry, cylinder contents and gas storage, and calibrating flow meters and gas thermometers.
• Basis of chemical-engineering calculations (compressor design, pipelines, airbags), of the kinetic theory and of thermodynamic work terms for gases.
### 6. Limitations
• PV = nRT is exact only for an ideal gas; real gases deviate measurably, and grossly at high pressure or near the critical temperature.
• Both central assumptions are unattainable — molecules always have finite size and always attract one another (otherwise no gas could be liquefied).
• It cannot describe condensation, critical phenomena or the liquid state, and fails for associating (H-bonded) or highly polar gases even at ordinary pressure.
• R is constant only for an ideal gas; for a real gas PV/T varies with pressure, so the van der Waals equation or Z = PV/nRT corrections are needed.
**Fact.** Ideal gas equation PV = nRT; from kinetic theory P = ⅓ (Nm/m)⟨c²⟩, so PV = ⅓N m⟨c²⟩.
**Fact.** r.m.s. speed c_rms = √(3RT/M); mean kinetic energy per mole = 3RT/2, per molecule = 3k_BT/2.
**Fact.** Real gases deviate near condensation; Van der Waals: (P + a n²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT.
confusion: ❌ An ideal gas is merely a light gas such as hydrogen. ✅ Ideality is about behaviour (no forces, no molecular volume), not mass; hydrogen merely approaches it best.
❌ R changes from gas to gas. ✅ R is universal; only the real-gas constants a and b differ between gases.
❌ R and k are the same constant. ✅ k = R/N_A is the per-molecule (Boltzmann) constant.
❌ PV = nRT works at 100 atm without error. ✅ Deviation becomes severe (Z ≠ 1) and the van der Waals equation is required.

data.title: Liquid Crystals and their Applications
notes: ### 1. Meaning

Liquid crystals are substances that are simultaneously partly ordered like a crystal and partly mobile like a liquid — a mesophase intermediate between the crystalline solid and the isotropic liquid. They flow and take the shape of the container, yet their rod- or disc-shaped molecules retain positional/orientational order, so their optical, electrical and mechanical properties are **anisotropic** (direction-dependent). F. Reinitzer first observed this behaviour in cholesteryl benzoate (1888).
### 2. Characteristics
• Molecules are elongated (rod-like) or flat and disc-like with flexible end chains; shape anisotropy produces the ordered mesophase.
• Partial order gives birefringence (two refractive indices), anisotropic dielectric constant, viscosity, elasticity and magnetic susceptibility.
• Order-disorder change occurs over a narrow, well-defined **temperature range** — below it a solid, above it an ordinary liquid.
• **Thermotropic** LCs form on temperature change (displays); **lyotropic** LCs form in solution when concentration changes (soap, detergents, cell membranes).
### 3. Classified mesophases
• **Nematic:** molecules parallel, positions random — the display material.
• **Smectic:** parallel molecules arranged in layers (soaps, some polymers).
• **Cholesteric (chiral nematic):** layers twisted into a helix, strongly temperature-sensitive colours used in thermometers and mood strips.
### 4. How an LCD works

A thin nematic layer is sandwiched between transparent conducting electrodes and crossed polarisers. In the twisted-nematic cell the molecules untwist when a voltage is applied, changing the polarisation of the transmitted light, so each pixel switches from bright to dark. Millions of such cells form the pixels of calculators, watches, phones, monitors and televisions.
### 5. Applications
• **Displays:** LCD televisions, monitors, laptops, phones, digital watches, calculators and instrument panels — the largest use of liquid crystals.

• **Temperature measurement and mapping:** thermochromic LCs change colour with temperature — fever strips, aquarium thermometers, mood strips, non-destructive thermal mapping of electronic circuits and hot-spot detection in medicine and industry.
• **Sensors and optics:** pressure-sensitive LC films, optical switches and light valves, privacy glass, laser-beam steering and tunable lenses.
• **Materials:** liquid-crystal polymers such as Kevlar give very strong, stiff fibres (protective clothing, aerospace composites); LCs are also used in chromatography, lubricants and detergents.
### 6. Limitations
• The useful mesophase exists only in a narrow temperature window, so devices must stay within their rated range — LCDs fail in extreme cold and darken in strong heat.
• They are passive (non-emissive) and need a backlight, so brightness, contrast and viewing angle are limited compared with emissive displays.
• Response is slower than emissive technologies and polarisers absorb much of the light, so efficiency is moderate.
• They are sensitive to UV light, shock, contamination and moisture; some mesogens are chemically unstable or toxic and must be sealed carefully.
• The rigid-rod model explains mesophases only qualitatively; quantitative transition temperatures need statistical theories (Maier–Saupe, Onsager).
confusion: ❌ Liquid crystals are crystals that have partly melted. ✅ They form a distinct mesophase: molecules flow yet keep orientational order.
❌ Liquid crystals emit light. ✅ LCDs modulate transmitted light from a backlight — they are non-emissive.
❌ They are liquids containing suspended crystal particles. ✅ The order is molecular and inherent to the phase.
❌ Liquid crystal displays work by melting. ✅ They work by electric-field reorientation of molecules within the same mesophase.
❌ A liquid crystal thermometer measures heat capacity. ✅ It uses the temperature dependence of the helical pitch, which shifts the reflected colour.

data.title: Efflorescent, Deliquescent and Hygroscopic Solids; Crystallization, Crystal Growth and Water of Crystallization
data.topicTitle: Efflorescent, deliquescent and hygroscopic solids; crystallization and crystal growth; water of crystallization
notes: ### 1. Water of crystallisation — the concept behind the three classes

Water of crystallisation is water chemically combined in a fixed stoichiometric ratio inside a crystal lattice (not merely adsorbed). Examples: CuSO₄·5H₂O (blue vitriol), Na₂CO₃·10H₂O (washing soda), Na₂SO₄·10H₂O (Glauber's salt), MgCl₂·6H₂O, CaSO₄·2H₂O (gypsum), FeSO₄·7H₂O. It is usually driven off by heating, and the loss of mass gives the number of water molecules per formula unit (gravimetric determination); the anhydrous salt often differs in colour and crystal shape.
### 2. Efflorescent solids

Efflorescent substances lose their water of crystallisation (wholly or partly) spontaneously in dry air and crumble to a powder, because the vapour pressure of the hydrate exceeds the water-vapour pressure of the atmosphere. Examples: Na₂SO₄·10H₂O → Na₂SO₄ (white powder); Na₂CO₃·10H₂O → Na₂CO₃·H₂O; CuSO₄·5H₂O fades from blue towards pale blue/white; alum. Hot, dry weather speeds it up, so such salts must be stored in sealed containers.
### 3. Deliquescent and hygroscopic solids

**Deliquescent** solids absorb moisture from the air, dissolve in it and form a saturated solution (a puddle) — CaCl₂, MgCl₂, NaOH, KOH, FeCl₃·6H₂O, ZnCl₂. **Hygroscopic** substances absorb or adsorb moisture and become damp without dissolving — concentrated H₂SO₄, P₄O₁₀, CaO (quicklime), CuO, silica gel, glycerol. Hygroscopic materials are used as **drying agents/desiccants** (silica-gel sachets, conc. H₂SO₄ in desiccators, quicklime in packaging). Whether a salt deliquesces depends on humidity: the air must exceed its deliquescence relative humidity (NaCl ≈ 75% RH, CaCl₂ ≈ 30% RH), so a 'deliquescent' salt may simply effloresce or remain unchanged in dry air.
### 4. Crystallization and crystal growth

**Crystallisation** is the formation of a pure solid in crystalline form from a solution, melt or vapour: the solution is saturated and then supersaturated by cooling or slow evaporation, after which **nucleation** begins and **crystal growth** follows. Good crystals need slow, steady growth — slow cooling, a clean solution, a suitable solvent, undisturbed conditions and sometimes a seed crystal. Large single crystals are grown by slow evaporation (sugar, alum, KDP), by the Czochralski pulling technique from a melt (silicon and germanium for electronics), by zone refining, or from the vapour (sublimation and chemical vapour transport).
### 5. Applications
• Recrystallisation is the standard laboratory purification technique; soluble impurities stay behind in the mother liquor.
• Industrial crystallisation produces salt, sugar, urea, fertilisers and pharmaceutical crystals, where crystal habit and size control tablet manufacture and food texture.

• Single-crystal growth supplies semiconductor wafers, quartz oscillators, laser and detector crystals and gemstones; crystallisation is also used in water softening (scale removal) and freeze-drying.

• Desiccants and drying agents (silica gel, CaCl₂, P₄O₁₀, H₂SO₄) protect instruments and goods from moisture and are essential for analytical weighing, while anti-caking agents stop efflorescent salts from caking.
### 6. Limitations

• The three terms describe behaviour, not a rigorous classification: the same substance can deliquesce in humid air and effloresce in dry air (Na₂SO₄ and Na₂CO₃ hydrates both do), because humidity, temperature and the hydrate's vapour pressure decide the outcome.
• Efflorescence may stop at a lower hydrate rather than reach the anhydrous salt, so equations assuming complete dehydration can be wrong.
• Deliquescence occurs only above the substance's critical relative humidity; below it the solid merely adsorbs a little water.

• Determining water of crystallisation by heating fails if the substance decomposes or hydrolyses (MgCl₂·6H₂O loses HCl and water when heated strongly) or if the sample also picks up atmospheric moisture.
• Crystallisation cannot remove impurities that co-crystallise as mixed (isomorphous) crystals, is slow, and always loses some product in the mother liquor, lowering the yield.
confusion: ❌ Efflorescent, deliquescent and hygroscopic mean the same. ✅ Efflorescent solids *lose* water to the air, deliquescent solids *absorb water and dissolve*, hygroscopic solids *absorb water and become damp*.
❌ Deliquescence happens in any weather. ✅ It requires air humidity above the deliquescence relative humidity (≈30% for CaCl₂, ≈75% for NaCl).
❌ Water of crystallisation is moisture sticking to a crystal. ✅ It is chemically combined in a definite ratio and forms part of the crystal structure.
❌ Any solid that becomes damp is deliquescent. ✅ Hygroscopic solids only become moist; deliquescent solids dissolve into a solution.
❌ Fast cooling gives the best crystals. ✅ Slow, undisturbed growth gives larger, purer crystals; rapid cooling gives many small crystals.

data.title: Introduction to Unit Crystal Lattice and Unit Cell
data.topicTitle: Introduction to unit crystal lattice and unit cell
notes: ### 1. Meaning

A **crystal lattice** is the regular three-dimensional arrangement of points (lattice points) in space at which the constituent particles of a crystal lie. A **unit cell** is the smallest repeating portion of that lattice which, when repeated in three dimensions, generates the whole crystal — it is the building block or 'brick' of the crystal. Lattice + the atoms/ions/molecules at its points = the crystal structure.
### 2. Lattice parameters and crystal systems

A unit cell is described by six parameters: the three edge lengths a, b, c and the three interaxial angles α, β, γ. Depending on their relative values, crystals fall into **7 crystal systems** (cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, triclinic, hexagonal and rhombohedral) which give **14 Bravais lattices** when the four possible cell centreings are included.
### 3. Types of unit cell
• **Primitive (simple) cell:** particles only at the eight corners.
• **Body-centred cell (BCC):** corners + one particle at the body centre.
• **Face-centred cell (FCC):** corners + one particle at the centre of each of the six faces.
• **End/base-centred cell:** corners + particles at the centres of two opposite faces.
### 4. Share of each particle and atoms per cell

Because a cell shares its particles with neighbours: a corner particle contributes 1/8, one on an edge 1/4, one on a face 1/2 and one at the body centre 1. Hence the effective number of atoms per unit cell, Z, is 1 for simple cubic, 2 for BCC and 4 for FCC.
### 5. Geometry of the three cubic cells
• Simple cubic: coordination number 6, a = 2r, packing efficiency 52.4% (polonium, rarely found).
• Body-centred cubic: coordination number 8, √3a = 4r, packing efficiency 68% (Na, K, Fe, Cr, W).
• Face-centred cubic (cubic close-packed): coordination number 12, √2a = 4r, packing efficiency 74% (Cu, Ag, Au, Al, Pb) — the densest possible packing of spheres.
Density of a crystal follows from the cell contents: $\rho=\frac{ZM}{a^{3}N_{A}}$ where M is the molar mass and a the edge length.
### 6. Meaning and applications of the unit cell

The unit cell turns the microscopic structure into measurable quantities: from the edge length (measured by X-ray diffraction) and the cell contents, the **density** and the **Avogadro constant** can be determined; the cell also explains why FCC metals (Cu, Al) are soft and ductile while BCC metals (Fe, W) are stronger, why some crystals cleave along definite planes, and how doping works — substitutional or interstitial foreign atoms in the silicon lattice create n-type and p-type semiconductors.

Other applications: identification and purity testing of minerals, alloys and pharmaceutical polymorphs by X-ray diffraction; design of alloys and ceramics; gemstone identification; and understanding of ionic conductivity and diffusion in solids.
### 7. Limitations

The ideal lattice model is an idealisation: real crystals contain point defects (Schottky and Frenkel defects, vacancies, interstitials) and extended defects (dislocations, grain boundaries) that control important properties such as ionic conductivity, mechanical strength and colour, but are absent from the perfect-cell picture. The hard-sphere model treats atoms as rigid touching spheres, whereas electron density is diffuse and atoms are not hard spheres, so packing-efficiency values are approximate. The model describes only periodic structures — quasicrystals and modulated structures have no single repeating cell, and in solid solutions or alloys the cell parameters vary continuously with composition rather than having a fixed value for a 'unit cell'. Finally, the unit cell gives no direct information about bonding or electronic band structure.
confusion: ❌ A unit cell is the same as a crystal lattice. ✅ The lattice is the array of points; the unit cell is the smallest repeating block of that lattice with its contents.
❌ A corner atom belongs entirely to one unit cell. ✅ It is shared by eight cells, so it contributes only 1/8.
❌ BCC and FCC have the same number of atoms per cell. ✅ BCC has Z = 2, FCC has Z = 4 and simple cubic Z = 1.
❌ The closest packing of equal spheres reaches 100%. ✅ The maximum (FCC/HCP) is 74%; simple cubic reaches only 52.4%.
❌ Unit cell dimensions cannot be measured. ✅ They are measured routinely from X-ray diffraction patterns using Bragg's law.

$$\text{SC: }a=2r,\ Z=1,\ 52.4\%;\quad \text{BCC: }\sqrt{3}a=4r,\ Z=2,\ 68\%;\quad \text{FCC: }\sqrt{2}a=4r,\ Z=4,\ 74\%$$
$$\rho=\frac{ZM}{a^{3}N_{A}},\qquad n\lambda=2d\sin\theta\ (\text{Bragg})$$
universalFacts: Seven crystal systems combine with four centering types to give 14 Bravais lattices.
Coordination numbers: simple cubic 6, BCC 8, FCC (and HCP) 12.
Polonium is the standard 'real-life' example of a simple cubic metal; NaCl crystallises in a face-centred cubic array of ions.
answer pattern for "Introduction to unit crystal lattice and unit cell": define → method → result. Structure earns the marks on 6–10 mark questions.
examples: **Problem:** Copper (FCC, a = 361 pm, M = 63.5 g mol⁻¹) — find the density. **Solution:** Z = 4; ρ = ZM/(a³N_A) = (4 × 63.5)/((3.61×10⁻⁸ cm)³ × 6.022×10²³) ≈ 8.97 g cm⁻³, matching the known value for copper.
**Problem:** Show that the radius of an atom in a BCC lattice is r = √3a/4. **Solution:** along the body diagonal of length √3a, the atoms touch: √3a = 4r, hence r = √3a/4 ≈ 0.433a.
importantNotes: Quote the sharing fractions (1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 1) and Z values 1, 2, 4 — these are the most frequently asked points.
Use consistent units in the density formula: a³ in cm³ with N_A per mole gives g cm⁻³.
For any structural question, identify the lattice type first, then the values Z, r and packing efficiency follow.

data.title: Unit 1 — Education and Humanity
notes: ### 1. Meaning of Education
Education is the systematic process of facilitating learning, acquiring knowledge, skills, values, and habits. It is not merely schooling but a lifelong journey of personal and social development.
### 2. Types of Education
- **Formal Education**: Structured, curriculum-based learning in schools, colleges, and universities.
- **Non-Formal Education**: Organized learning outside the formal system (adult education, vocational training).
- **Informal Education**: Lifelong learning from family, peers, media, and life experiences.
### 3. Education and Humanity
True education must nurture humanity — empathy, ethical reasoning, and social responsibility. When education becomes purely job-oriented, it risks producing skilled but morally empty individuals.
### 4. Goals of Education
- Intellectual: Developing critical thinking and creativity
- Moral: Building character and ethical judgment
- Social: Fostering cooperation and civic responsibility
- Economic: Preparing for productive employment
### 5. Education in Nepal
Nepal's education system has evolved from traditional gurushekha to modern schooling. The National Education Plan 2019 emphasizes inclusive, equitable, and quality education for all.
### 6. Entrance Exam Focus
Common MCQs: Define education; Difference between formal and informal education; Role of education in nation-building.

data.title: Unit 2 — Communication
notes: ### 1. What is Communication?
Communication is the exchange of information, ideas, feelings, and meaning between two or more people through symbols, signs, or behavior.
### 2. Elements of Communication
- **Sender**: The person who initiates the message
- **Message**: The content being communicated
- **Channel/Medium**: The method of transmission (verbal, written, digital)
- **Receiver**: The person who gets the message
- **Feedback**: The response from the receiver
- **Noise**: Any interference that distorts the message
### 3. Types of Communication
- **Verbal**: Spoken or written words
- **Non-verbal**: Body language, gestures, facial expressions
- **Visual**: Images, graphs, symbols
- **Active Listening**: Fully concentrating on what is being said
### 4. Communication Barriers
Physical (distance, noise), Psychological (prejudice, emotion), Semantic (language differences), Cultural (norms, values).
### 5. Effective Communication Skills
Clarity, conciseness, correctness, courtesy, and confidence are the 5 Cs of effective communication.
### 6. Entrance Exam Focus
MCQs: Identify elements of communication; Differentiate verbal and non-verbal; List barriers to communication.

data.title: Unit 3 — Media and Society
notes: ### 1. Media: Definition and Types
Media refers to the channels through which news, entertainment, education, and opinion are delivered. Types: Print (newspapers, magazines), Broadcast (TV, radio), Digital (social media, websites).
### 2. Role of Media in Society
- Informing the public about current events
- Educating and raising awareness
- Providing entertainment
- Acting as a watchdog over government
- Shaping public opinion and culture
### 3. Media Ethics
Accuracy, fairness, independence, accountability, and minimizing harm are core principles of media ethics.
### 4. Impact of Social Media
Social media has democratized information but also spread misinformation. Critical media literacy is essential.
### 5. Media in Nepal
Nepal has a vibrant press with newspapers like Kailash, Online Khabar, and Gandaki. Radio and TV remain dominant in rural areas.
### 6. Entrance Exam Focus
MCQs: Functions of media; Difference between traditional and new media; Role of media in democracy.

notes: ### 1. Summary

The Selfish Giant is a tale about a giant who builds a wall around his beautiful garden, keeping children out. As a result, winter perpetually reigns in his garden. When the giant finally lets the children back in, spring returns. Through the story, Wilde explores themes of selfishness, redemption, and the transformative power of love and compassion.
### 2. Characters
- **The Giant**: Initially selfish, later becomes kind and selfless
- **The Children**: Symbolize innocence, joy, and renewal
- **The Little Boy**: Represents Christ-like figure; his tears bring spring back
### 3. Themes
- **Selfishness vs. Generosity**: The giant's transformation shows that sharing brings happiness
- **Redemption**: Anyone can change and find salvation through love
- **Nature and Morality**: The garden's seasons reflect the giant's moral state
- **Childhood Innocence**: Children represent purity and spiritual wisdom
### 4. Key Symbols
- **The Wall**: Separation, ego, and isolation
- **Winter**: Coldness of selfishness; **Spring**: Warmth of compassion
- **The Rose Tree**: Never blossoms for the giant until the little boy returns
- **The Little Boy**: Symbol of divine love and Christ
### 5. Moral of the Story
True happiness comes from sharing and loving others. Selfishness leads to isolation and spiritual winter.
### 6. Entrance Exam Focus
MCQs: Who built the wall? What did the children represent? Why did winter come? Short answers: Theme of redemption; Symbolism of the garden.

Wilde uses the changing seasons to mirror the giant's moral condition, and presents the little boy as a Christ-like figure whose tears restore the garden. notes: ### 1. Summary

The Oval Portrait is a framed story within a story. A narrator lies ill in an abandoned chateau in the Apennines. He finds an oval portrait of a young woman and reads a note explaining that it was painted by a young artist who loved his bride deeply. Consumed by his art, he neglected her, and as he painted, she slowly grew pale and died — her life force transferring into the portrait.
### 2. Narrative Structure
- **Frame narrative**: Story within a story
- **First-person narrator**: Provides objective observation
- **Artistic description**: The painter's account is embedded
### 3. Themes
- **Art vs. Life**: Art can consume and destroy life
- **Destructive Passion**: Obsessive love becomes self-destructive
- **Beauty and Death**: Beauty is transient; death gives permanence
- **The Artist's Sacrifice**: Creating art requires sacrifice
### 4. Gothic Elements
- Setting: Isolated chateau, stormy weather, shadows
- Mood: Melancholy, supernatural undertones
- Theme: Death and art intertwine
- Symbolism: The oval frame represents life's fragility
### 5. Literary Devices
- **Foreshadowing**: Early hints of the tragic ending
- **Symbolism**: The painting as a vessel of life force
- **Irony**: The artist's greatest work costs his wife's life
### 6. Entrance Exam Focus
MCQs: Who painted the portrait? Where was the story set? Short answers: Theme of art vs. life; Gothic elements; Symbolism of the oval frame.

data.title: Comprehension and Unseen Passage — answering in your own words
notes: **What it is:** extracting and restating passage information — the trap is copying whole sentences; the skill is locate-then-restate.

**Method:** skim for gist → scan for the question's keywords (the answer lives nearby) → answer in complete sentences with synonyms → match the question type (WH → answer the WH; 'Why' → 'Because…'; true/false → quote evidence) → verify against the text.

**Grammar of answers:** convert passage nouns into clauses ('its existence' → 'that it exists'); use report frames ('the passage states that…'); keep the passage's tense zone; quote marks ONLY when demanded.
**Length discipline:** 1-mark answers = one sentence; 2-mark answers = answer + reason/evidence.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

**The four-step comprehension method:** (1) SKIM — read the passage once quickly (60 seconds) to get the gist. Don't stop for unknown words. (2) SCAN — read the questions FIRST, then scan the passage for keywords related to each question. (3) LOCATE — find the exact sentence(s) that contain the answer. Underline them. (4) RESTATE — write the answer in YOUR OWN WORDS using complete sentences. Never copy the passage verbatim.

**Why copying is the #1 comprehension error:** Examiners explicitly penalise copied sentences. If the passage says 'The river was polluted with industrial waste,' and you write 'The river was polluted with industrial waste,' you get ZERO marks for that answer. You must PARAPHRASE: 'Industrial waste had contaminated the river.' This proves you UNDERSTOOD the meaning, not just your ability to copy.

**Paraphrasing techniques for exam success:** (1) *Synonym swap*: 'happy' → 'joyful', 'big' → 'large', 'sad' → 'sorrowful'. (2) *Word class change*: 'The government decided' → 'The government's decision was…' (3) *Voice change*: 'They built the bridge' → 'The bridge was built by them.' (4) *Clause reduction*: 'Although it was raining heavily, they went out' → 'Despite the heavy rain, they went out.' (5) *Active to passive*: 'The teacher gave the students homework' → 'The students were given homework by the teacher.'

**Question type mastery — WH questions:** (1) *What* — answer with a noun or clause: 'What caused the flood?' → 'Heavy rainfall caused the flood.' (2) *Why* — answer with a reason: 'Why did she refuse?' → 'She refused because she had lost faith in the system.' (3) *How* — answer with a method or manner: 'How did they solve the problem?' → 'They solved it by combining traditional knowledge with modern techniques.' (4) *When/Where/Who* — direct factual answers. ALWAYS use complete sentences unless told otherwise.

**Question type mastery — true/false/not given:** (1) *True* — the passage explicitly confirms the statement. (2) *False* — the passage explicitly contradicts the statement. (3) *Not Given* — the passage doesn't mention the information at all. 'Not Given' is different from 'False' — it means the information is simply absent, not wrong. This distinction is heavily tested.

**Question type mastery — short answer vs. long answer:** (1) *Short answer* (1 mark): one sentence, direct to the point. (2) *Long answer* (2-3 marks): answer + supporting evidence/reason from the passage. For 2-mark questions, always include BOTH the answer AND the evidence. Format: 'X happened because Y [evidence from passage].' Don't just state the answer — justify it.

**Vocabulary-in-context questions:** When asked 'What does the word X mean in the passage?', do NOT write a dictionary definition. Write what the word means IN THAT CONTEXT. 'In the passage, "reluctant" means unwilling or hesitating because the character had no choice but to agree despite her reservations.' Always anchor your answer in the passage's context.

**Inference questions — reading between the lines:** Inference questions ask you to deduce something NOT explicitly stated. 'What can you infer about the author's attitude?' Strategy: (1) Find the sentence with the relevant information. (2) Ask 'what does this imply?' (3) Write the implication as your answer. Don't go beyond the text — stay close to the passage. 'The author's use of the word "heartbreaking" suggests they feel deep sorrow about the situation.'

**Reference questions — what does 'it/this/that' refer to?** These questions ask you to identify what a pronoun or demonstrative refers to in context. Strategy: (1) Find the pronoun in the passage. (2) Look at the preceding sentence(s). (3) Identify the noun that the pronoun replaces. Answer: 'It refers to [the specific noun from the passage].' Never answer with another pronoun.

**Tone and attitude questions:** 'What is the author's tone?' Possible answers: formal, informal, objective, subjective, sympathetic, critical, sarcastic, hopeful, pessimistic, nostalgic, indifferent. 'What is the author's attitude towards…?' Possible answers: positive, negative, neutral, ambivalent, critical, admiring. Always support your answer with a specific word or phrase from the passage.

**Main idea and title questions:** (1) *Main idea*: Read the first and last sentence of each paragraph. The main idea is what connects ALL paragraphs. (2) *Title*: Choose a title that covers the WHOLE passage, not just one paragraph. A good title is specific but not too narrow. Bad title: 'Pollution in Kathmandu' (only covers one paragraph). Good title: 'Environmental Challenges in Urban Nepal' (covers all paragraphs).

**Comprehension time management:** For a 30-mark comprehension section with a 300-400 word passage and 10-12 questions: (1) Spend 2 minutes skimming. (2) Read questions in 1 minute. (3) Each question takes 2-3 minutes (locate + restate + verify). (4) Leave 2 minutes for review. Total: ~30 minutes. Don't spend 10 minutes on one question — move on and come back. Speed and accuracy matter.

**The verification check — your last step:** After writing every answer, go back to the passage and ask: (1) Does my answer match the passage? (2) Have I answered the question asked, not a different one? (3) Is my answer in my own words? (4) Is it in a complete sentence? (5) Does it fit the word limit? If any answer fails these checks, rewrite it. Verification catches 60% of comprehension errors.
confusion: Copying vs. paraphrasing: Copying = writing the exact words from the passage (0 marks). Paraphrasing = expressing the SAME MEANING in YOUR OWN WORDS (full marks). Example: Passage says 'The children played joyfully in the garden.' Copy: 'The children played joyfully in the garden' (wrong). Paraphrase: 'The kids had fun playing outdoors in the garden' (correct). Always paraphrase unless the question says 'quote from the passage.'

Inference vs. opinion: An inference is a LOGICAL conclusion drawn from evidence in the passage. An opinion is YOUR PERSONAL belief that may or may not be supported by the passage. Inference: 'The character was likely anxious because she kept checking her watch.' Opinion: 'I think the character was anxious because I get nervous too.' Inferences use passage evidence; opinions use personal experience. Examiners want inferences.

True vs. Not Given: True = the passage CONFIRMS the statement. False = the passage CONTRADICTS the statement. Not Given = the passage NEITHER confirms nor contradicts — the information is simply absent. Example: Passage says 'Rahul went to school.' Statement: 'Rahul walked to school.' This is NOT GIVEN — we know he went, but not HOW. Don't assume; stick to what's in the passage.

Short answer vs. long answer format: A short answer (1 mark) is one complete sentence that directly answers the question. A long answer (2-3 marks) is answer + evidence/reason. Format for long answers: 'The answer is X because Y [with reference to the passage].' For short answers, skip the 'because' — just state the answer directly. Over-answering short questions wastes time; under-answering long questions loses marks.

Main idea vs. topic: The TOPIC is what the passage is about (one word or phrase: 'deforestation'). The MAIN IDEA is what the passage says ABOUT the topic (a complete sentence: 'Deforestation in Nepal is accelerating due to population pressure and policy failures'). Don't confuse them — a topic is a label; a main idea is a claim.
practice: Read this passage (150 words) about 'The Benefits of Meditation' and answer: (a) in one sentence, what is the main idea? (b) paraphrase the sentence 'Regular meditation has been shown to reduce cortisol levels by up to 25%.' (c) infer the author's tone. (d) explain what 'mindfulness' means in the passage's context.

Read an unseen passage (200 words) on 'Urban Traffic Congestion'. Answer these questions: (1) What does 'it' refer to in the sentence 'This has led to increased pollution, which it exacerbates daily'? (2) True/False/Not Given: 'All vehicles contribute equally to pollution.' (3) What is the author's attitude towards government policy? (4) Summarise the main problem in 20 words.

Read the passage about 'The Changing Face of Nepali Education' and write answers to: (a) What does the word 'colonial' mean in paragraph 2? (b) Inference: What can you deduce about the author's educational background? (c) Main idea of paragraph 3 in your own words (no more than 15 words). (d) True/False: 'Technology has replaced the need for textbooks entirely.'

Practice with this 10-mark comprehension test: Read a 250-word passage on 'The Impact of Social Media on Teenagers'. Write answers to: (1) What is the passage mainly about? (2) In your own words, explain one negative effect mentioned. (3) True/False with reason. (4) What does the author imply about future trends? (5) Give a suitable title.

Read a passage about 'Climate Change in the Himalayas' and answer: (a) Paraphrase: 'Glacial melt has accelerated dramatically over the past decade.' (b) Inference: What impact does this have on downstream communities? (c) What does the passage suggest about human responsibility? (d) Choose the best title from: (i) Glaciers Melting (ii) Climate Change in the Himalayas (iii) Water Crisis.
universalFacts: Comprehension skills are tested in virtually every English examination worldwide — NEB, CBSE, ICSE, Cambridge IGCSE, IELTS, TOEFL. The 'locate-then-restate' method (find the answer in the text, express it in your own words) is the universal standard across all these exams.

In the NEB English exam, comprehension typically carries 15-20 marks out of 60-80 total. It is the single highest-weighted section. Mastering comprehension technique can add 5-8 marks to your total score — more than any other single skill.

Research by reading specialists shows that students who practice 'active reading' (predicting, questioning, visualising, summarising) score 25-30% higher on comprehension tests than students who read passively. The four strategies above (skim-scan-locate-restate) are a practical application of active reading.

The most common comprehension error across all levels is copying from the passage. Studies of examiner reports show that 40-60% of students who lose marks in comprehension do so because they copied sentences instead of paraphrasing. This single habit is the biggest barrier to high comprehension scores.

Paraphrasing is a transferable skill — it is used not just in comprehension but also in summarisation, note-making, essay writing, and even in professional contexts like research and journalism. Mastering paraphrasing in exam preparation benefits your overall English proficiency.

data.title: Essay Writing — argumentative, descriptive, narrative, expository
data.topicTitle: Essay Writing — argumentative, descriptive, narrative, expository
notes: **What it is:** an essay argues, describes, narrates or explains a topic in organised paragraphs. The examiner marks STANCE + STRUCTURE + evidence, not length.

**Universal skeleton:** Introduction (hook + thesis) → Body paragraphs (ONE reason each: topic sentence → explanation → example) → optional counter-argument (acknowledge, then rebut) → Conclusion (restate thesis + consequence).

**Four types:** *Argumentative* (clear side, reasons, admit the other side), *Descriptive* (5 senses, spatial order, show-don't-tell), *Narrative* (one incident: setup → conflict → climax → reflection), *Expository* (explain causes/process in numbered factors, no opinion).
**Tense logic:** essays live in PRESENT for general truths; past only inside narrative examples; predictions use will/would.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Formal Letter Writing — editor, application, complaint, inquiry
data.topicTitle: Formal Letter Writing — editor, application, complaint, inquiry
notes: **What it is:** a letter to someone you do NOT know (editor, manager, office). Half the marks are the fixed BLOCK LAYOUT; the other half is polite business tone.

**Block order:** Sender's address → Date → Recipient's designation + address → Subject line → Salutation ('Dear Sir/Madam') → Body (3 short paragraphs: who you are + purpose / details / polite request) → Complimentary close → Signature + full name in capitals.
**The pairing rule that trips everyone:** 'Dear Sir/Madam' → end **Yours faithfully**; 'Dear Mr/Ms Sharma' (real name) → end **Yours sincerely**.
**Tone grammar:** no contractions (*do not*, *I am*); polite modals (*would*, *could*, *may*); passive voice for formality ('the matter is being investigated').

**Variants:** *Editor* (public issue + call for action), *Job application* (post + skills + 'Enclosure: CV'), *Complaint* (what, when, defect + remedy + deadline), *Inquiry/Order* (price/availability/terms).
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Grammar for Writing — sentences, clauses, punctuation
data.topicTitle: Grammar for Writing — sentences, clauses, punctuation
notes: **Sentence types as tools:** simple (one clause — POWER), compound (two main clauses via and/but/so or a semicolon — equal weight), complex (main + subordinate clause via because/although/when/if — shows the relation between ideas). Mix them: examiners reward rhythm.

**Clauses vs phrases:** a phrase has no subject-verb pair and cannot stand alone; a dependent clause has one but leans on the main clause ('Because it rained.' alone is a fragment). Relative clauses (who/which/that) add noun detail — commas only for extra information.

**Punctuation logic:** full stop ends a thought; comma separates list items, follows openers, precedes and/but/so between full sentences; semicolon joins balanced sentences; colon introduces; apostrophe = possession or contraction (its vs it's is the classic trap). Comma splice = two full sentences joined by only a comma — fix it.

**Tense + agreement discipline:** pick a tense zone per paragraph (essays: present; reports: past); subjects agree with verbs ('Each of the students WAS present'); a/an by SOUND ('an hour', 'a university').
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Informal Letter Writing — personal letter format
notes: **What it is:** a letter to someone you know well — friend, family. Same skeleton, different temperature: warm, natural, personal.

**Block order:** Sender's address → Date → Salutation with first name ('Dear Rahul,') → Warm opening (ask about them / react to their letter) → Main body (news, invitation, reply) → Warm closing → 'Your loving friend,' + first name only.

**Tone grammar:** contractions welcome (it's, don't, I'm); question tags create warmth ('You remember that day, don't you?'); tenses mix naturally — past for news, present for feelings, future for plans.
**Exam check:** answer anything their last letter asked — examiners verify you responded; keep within ~130 words.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Paragraph Writing — topic sentence, cohesion, exam format
notes: **What it is:** ONE controlling idea in 4–6 sentences — the engine behind every essay, letter and report.

**Structure:** (1) *Topic sentence* — main idea + your angle, specific not generic. (2) *Supporting sentences* — each adds ONE fact/example/reason, logically ordered. (3) *Concluding sentence* — restates or lands a consequence; no new ideas here.
**Unity test:** if a sentence could belong to another paragraph, delete it. **Coherence test:** the reader follows without re-reading — via connectors and repeated key words.
**Exam discipline:** 90–120 words; start with the idea, not with 'The'; end with consequence.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Report Writing and Summarisation — news & event report format
notes: **What it is:** factual, third-person, past-tense reporting of an event (sports day, blood donation camp) — not a story, not an opinion.

**Structure:** Headline (short, factual) → Byline ('By a Staff Reporter') + dateline ('Kathmandu, 12 May:') → Lead paragraph answering WHO did WHAT, WHERE, WHEN, WHY in 2–3 sentences → Body in chronological order → a short quotation from the chief guest → closing outcome.
**Tense/voice grammar:** past simple for every event; passive voice is standard for ceremony facts ('trophies were distributed'); reported speech for quotes; third person only — never 'I'.
**Summarisation partner skill:** compress any passage into its core idea in your own words within the word limit — keep the author's viewpoint, drop examples and repetition.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Review Writing — book and film review format
notes: **What it is:** a balanced critical evaluation — what the work is, what it does well, what falls short, and whether it is worth the reader's time.

**Structure:** Title + basic details (title, author/director, year, genre) → Brief SPOILER-FREE summary (2–3 sentences) → Strengths (one concrete example/quote) → Weaknesses (fair, with why it matters) → Recommendation + verdict/rating.

**Review grammar:** present simple dominates ('the story follows…'); evaluative adjectives (compelling, uneven, luminous); concessive fairness ('although the plot is thin, the philosophy is profound'); soft hedging ('readers may find…').
**Never spoil the ending** — restraint reads as mature judgement.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Speech Writing — salutation, hooks, persuasive devices
notes: **What it is:** writing meant to be SPOKEN — short sentences, rhythm, direct address. The examiner checks 'speakability'.

**Structure:** Salutation in order of seniority ('Respected Chairperson, judges, teachers, and my dear friends —') → Self-intro (if required) → Hook (question/fact/quotation) → 2–3 clear points ('First… Second… Finally…') → Persuasive devices (triads, repetition, rhetorical questions) → Strong closing appeal + 'Thank you.'
**Grammar for the ear:** imperatives command action ('Let us pledge…'); rhetorical questions make the audience answer mentally; triads create rhythm.
**Test:** read your draft aloud — where you gasp, rewrite. Repeat your core phrase 2–3 times.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Story Writing — complete arc from a given outline
notes: **What it is:** a COMPLETE narrative arc judged on plot — situation → problem → turning point → resolution → (often) a quiet moral.

**Structure:** Opening (if the prompt gives a first line, USE it verbatim and continue) → Complication → Rising action → Climax (the decisive moment — slow down here) → Resolution + realisation/moral.

**Tense machinery:** past simple drives the plot; past continuous paints background ('I was dawdling home'); past perfect marks earlier events ('which she had lost'); direct speech at the climax adds life.
**Keep ONE tense zone and ONE narrator** — drifting between present and past, or I/he, breaks the story.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Summary and Note-making — condensing any passage
notes: **Summary:** read for gist → underline key ideas → draft (author's main idea first, then 2–4 key supports) → cut modifiers/examples to fit the word limit → verify meaning is unchanged and nothing is copied.

**Summary grammar:** four paraphrase moves — synonym swap (threat→danger), word-class change (pollute→pollution), voice change (active↔passive), sentence merge; report verbs frame it ('the passage argues…'). Never add your own opinion.

**Note-making:** TITLE in caps → numbered sub-headings (1, 2, 3 — noun phrases, one per paragraph) → compact key-phrase points (a, b, c) → abbreviations (&, →, e.g.) with an 'Abbreviations used' note.
**Note grammar:** nominalise verbs for headings ('agricultural expansion'); drop articles/auxiliaries in points; every point under 7 words.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Essay Writing
notes: ### 1. Types of Essays
- **Narrative**: Tells a story with a sequence of events
- **Descriptive**: Paints a picture with words
- **Expository**: Explains or informs objectively
- **Argumentative**: Presents a claim with evidence
- **Persuasive**: Convinces the reader to accept a viewpoint
### 2. Essay Structure
- **Introduction**: Hook + thesis statement
- **Body Paragraphs**: Topic sentence + evidence + analysis
- **Conclusion**: Restate thesis + summary + final thought
### 3. Argumentative Essay Tips
State a clear thesis, use credible evidence, address counterarguments, and conclude forcefully.
### 4. Descriptive Essay Tips
Use sensory details (sight, sound, smell, touch, taste). Show, don't tell.
### 5. Common Essay Topics
Education, Technology, Environment, Globalization, Youth Role, Health, Corruption, Tourism in Nepal.
### 6. Entrance Exam Focus
Write an essay on any one: 'Technology has made life easier' / 'Environmental protection is our duty'. Structure: 5-7 paragraphs, 250-300 words.
confusion: ❌ Argumentative = personal opinion. ✅ Must be backed by evidence and logic.
❌ Descriptive = listing facts. ✅ Should engage all five senses.
practice: Write an argumentative essay on 'Is technology beneficial or harmful?'
Describe your favorite place using sensory details.
Write an expository essay on 'The importance of education'.

It also gives type-specific technique, such as using credible evidence and answering counterarguments in argumentative writing, and appealing to the five senses in descriptive writing. For the entrance exam, expect an essay of 5-7 paragraphs and roughly 250-300 words on a familiar topic.
