specificConditions: **Field vs Potential Distinction:** Gravitational field $\vec{g} = -GM/r^2 \, \hat{r}$ is a *vector* (force per unit mass). Gravitational potential $V = -GM/r$ is a *scalar* (work per unit mass). The field is the negative gradient of the potential: $\vec{g} = -\nabla V = -dV/dr \, \hat{r}$.

**Superposition Advantage:** Potentials add as scalars ($V_{total} = \sum V_i$), which is simpler than adding field vectors. This makes potential calculations easier for multiple mass distributions, especially when symmetry is broken.

data.title: Gravitational Potential and Potential Energy

notes: **Gravitational potential V:** the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to a point, without acceleration. For a point mass M: $V = -\frac{GM}{r}$. At infinity $V = 0$, and everywhere else V is negative because gravity does positive work as the mass approaches — the field does the work, so potential decreases.

**Gravitational potential energy U:** the work done against gravity in assembling a system; for two masses separated by r: $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$. It is the energy of the whole system, not of one mass alone. U is negative because the system is bound — you must supply $GMm/r$ of energy to separate the masses to infinity.

**Why the minus sign matters:** potential energy is defined with zero at infinity. Since the force is attractive, energy is released (and PE decreases) as masses come together. A satellite in orbit at radius r has $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ — its total mechanical energy is $E = K + U = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$, which is negative, confirming a bound orbit.

**Near Earth's surface:** for small heights h above the surface, $U = mgh$. This is the constant-g approximation of $-\frac{GMm}{r}$: since $\Delta(1/r) \approx -h/R^2$, the change matches $mgh$. Use $mgh$ only for $h \ll R$; use $-\frac{GMm}{r}$ for large altitudes (satellites, rockets).

**Worked example — escape energy:** to launch a mass m from Earth's surface (R) to infinity you must supply $GMm/R$. Numerically for m = 1 kg: $\frac{6.67\times 10^{-11}\times 5.97\times 10^{24}}{6.37\times 10^6} \approx 6.25\times 10^{7} \text{ J} \approx 62.5 \text{ MJ}$ per kg. This energy corresponds to the escape speed 11.2 km/s.

**Potential vs potential energy vs field:** field $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ (the force per unit mass, a vector); potential V is a scalar (J/kg); potential energy $U = mV$. The field is the negative gradient of the potential: $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ radially.

**Equipotential surfaces:** surfaces of constant V. Moving along an equipotential surface requires zero work; the field is always perpendicular to these surfaces. For a point mass, equipotentials are concentric spheres.

**Superposition:** for multiple masses, $V = \sum\left(-\frac{GM_i}{r_i}\right)$ and $U = \sum\left(-\frac{GM_i m}{r_i}\right)$ — potentials add as scalars, which is much simpler than adding force vectors.
confusion: ❌ 'Potential and potential energy are the same.' ✅ Potential V is work per unit mass (J/kg); potential energy $U = mV$ (J). V belongs to a point in the field; U belongs to the mass–field system.
❌ 'Negative energy is unphysical.' ✅ Negative potential energy simply means the system is BOUND — energy must be added to separate it. It is a matter of the reference at infinity.
❌ '$U = mgh$ and $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ disagree.' ✅ They agree for small heights: $mgh$ is the CHANGE in $-\frac{GMm}{r}$ near the surface. Use the right one for the régime.
❌ 'Potential is maximum at Earth's surface.' ✅ Potential is most negative at the surface ($-\frac{GM}{R}$) and rises toward zero with altitude — at infinity it reaches the (higher) value 0.
❌ 'Doubling the distance doubles the potential energy.' ✅ $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ — doubling r halves the magnitude, so U becomes $-\frac{GMm}{2r}$ (less negative).

❌ 'A satellite far away has lots of potential energy.' ✅ A far-away satellite has potential energy near ZERO (least negative, but $U \approx 0$). It needs enormous kinetic energy (orbital speed) that comes from the launch energy.

**Zero at Infinity Convention:** $V=0$ and $U=0$ at $r=\infty$. Negative values mean the system is bound. Moving closer to a mass makes $V$ and $U$ *more negative* (energy released). The depth of the potential well is $|U| = GMm/r$ (binding energy).

**Approximation Boundary:** $U = mgh$ is valid only for $h \ll R$ (constant $g$ approximation). For $h \gtrsim R$, the exact $U = -GMm/r$ must be used. The crossover is typically around $h \sim 0.1R$ where the error exceeds 1%.

notes: **Gravitational potential V:** the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to a point, without acceleration. For a point mass M: $V = -\frac{GM}{r}$. At infinity $V = 0$, and everywhere else V is negative because gravity does positive work as the mass approaches — the field does the work, so potential decreases.

**Gravitational potential energy U:** the work done against gravity in assembling a system; for two masses separated by r: $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$. It is the energy of the whole system, not of one mass alone. U is negative because the system is bound — you must supply $GMm/r$ of energy to separate the masses to infinity.

**Why the minus sign matters:** potential energy is defined with zero at infinity. Since the force is attractive, energy is released (and PE decreases) as masses come together. A satellite in orbit at radius r has $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ — its total mechanical energy is $E = K + U = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$, which is negative, confirming a bound orbit.

**Near Earth's surface:** for small heights h above the surface, $U = mgh$. This is the constant-g approximation of $-\frac{GMm}{r}$: since $\Delta(1/r) \approx -h/R^2$, the change matches $mgh$. Use $mgh$ only for $h \ll R$; use $-\frac{GMm}{r}$ for large altitudes (satellites, rockets).

**Worked example — escape energy:** to launch a mass m from Earth's surface (R) to infinity you must supply $GMm/R$. Numerically for m = 1 kg: $\frac{6.67\times 10^{-11}\times 5.97\times 10^{24}}{6.37\times 10^6} \approx 6.25\times 10^{7} \text{ J} \approx 62.5 \text{ MJ}$ per kg. This energy corresponds to the escape speed 11.2 km/s.

**Potential vs potential energy vs field:** field $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ (the force per unit mass, a vector); potential V is a scalar (J/kg); potential energy $U = mV$. The field is the negative gradient of the potential: $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ radially.

**Equipotential surfaces:** surfaces of constant V. Moving along an equipotential surface requires zero work; the field is always perpendicular to these surfaces. For a point mass, equipotentials are concentric spheres.

**Superposition:** for multiple masses, $V = \sum\left(-\frac{GM_i}{r_i}\right)$ and $U = \sum\left(-\frac{GM_i m}{r_i}\right)$ — potentials add as scalars, which is much simpler than adding force vectors.
confusion: ❌ 'Potential and potential energy are the same.' ✅ Potential V is work per unit mass (J/kg); potential energy $U = mV$ (J). V belongs to a point in the field; U belongs to the mass–field system.
❌ 'Negative energy is unphysical.' ✅ Negative potential energy simply means the system is BOUND — energy must be added to separate it. It is a matter of the reference at infinity.
❌ '$U = mgh$ and $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ disagree.' ✅ They agree for small heights: $mgh$ is the CHANGE in $-\frac{GMm}{r}$ near the surface. Use the right one for the régime.
❌ 'Potential is maximum at Earth's surface.' ✅ Potential is most negative at the surface ($-\frac{GM}{R}$) and rises toward zero with altitude — at infinity it reaches the (higher) value 0.
❌ 'Doubling the distance doubles the potential energy.' ✅ $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ — doubling r halves the magnitude, so U becomes $-\frac{GMm}{2r}$ (less negative).

❌ 'A satellite far away has lots of potential energy.' ✅ A far-away satellite has potential energy near ZERO (least negative, but $U \approx 0$). It needs enormous kinetic energy (orbital speed) that comes from the launch energy.

data.title: Variation of g Due to Altitude and Depth
data.topicTitle: Variation in value of 'g' due to altitude and depth

notes: **g above the surface (altitude):** at height h above Earth's surface, $g' = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2} = g\left(\frac{R}{R+h}\right)^2$. As h increases, g decreases. For small h ($h \ll R$), a binomial expansion gives $g' \approx g\left(1 - \frac{2h}{R}\right)$ — a useful approximation.

**g below the surface (depth):** at depth d, only the mass inside the concentric sphere of radius ($R-d$) contributes: $g' = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)$ — gravity DECREASES linearly with depth. At the centre ($d = R$), $g' = 0$.

**Why they differ:** above the surface, whole-earth mass acts from a larger distance ($1/r^2$ law); below the surface, the shell above the point exerts zero net force (shell theorem) and only the inner sphere matters, whose mass scales as ($R-d$)^3 while distance scales as ($R-d$) — giving linear decrease.

**Worked example — altitude:** at $h = R$ (one Earth radius up), $g' = g\left(\frac{R}{2R}\right)^2 = g/4 = 2.45 \text{ m/s}^2$. At $h = 100$ km, using the small-h formula, the fractional decrease is $2h/R = 2\times 100/6400 = 0.031$, so $g' \approx 9.5 \text{ m/s}^2$.
**Worked example — depth:** at $d = R/2$ (3200 km deep), $g' = g(1 - 1/2) = g/2 = 4.9 \text{ m/s}^2$. At $d = R$ (centre) → $g' = 0$ (weightlessness, though pressure is immense).
**Graphs (NEB favourite):** $g$ vs $r$ rises linearly from 0 at the centre to g at the surface, then falls as $1/r^2$ beyond the surface. The maximum value of g on Earth is at the surface.

**Other causes of variation:** (1) rotation of Earth: g reduced by $\omega^2 R \cos^2 \lambda$ ($\lambda$ = latitude), maximum at the equator; (2) shape: Earth is an oblate spheroid — g is larger at the poles ($\approx 9.832$) than the equator ($\approx 9.78$); (3) local density anomalies (mountains, mineral deposits) cause tiny local changes used in geophysics.

**Altitude formula for satellites:** for an orbit at height h, effective $r = R + h$: $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{R+h}}$ and the orbital g is $g' = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2}$ — the same g formula used at that radius.
confusion: ❌ 'g increases with altitude.' ✅ Above the surface g DEcreases as $\frac{1}{(R+h)^2}$; below the surface it also decreases (linearly). g is max at the surface.
❌ 'From height h, g falls by $h/R$.' ✅ The small-h approximation is $2h/R$ (from the square), not $h/R$. At $h = 100$ km, that is ≈ 3%.
❌ 'Deep inside Earth, g keeps growing.' ✅ It decreases linearly: $g' = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)$, zero at the centre. The shell above you pulls equally in all directions (zero net).
❌ 'g is the same at poles and equator.' ✅ Rotation and the oblate shape make g slightly larger at the poles (~0.5% difference).
❌ 'At altitude 6400 km, g is half of surface.' ✅ At $h = R$, $g' = g/4$ — the height doubles the distance, so the square halves twice.
❌ 'Weightlessness in orbit means no gravity.' ✅ Astronauts at 400 km still feel ~88% of surface gravity — they float because they are in free fall around Earth.

specificConditions: **Altitude Formula:** Above the surface ($h \ge 0$), $g' = g(R/(R+h))^2$ follows the inverse-square law exactly. For $h \ll R$, the binomial approximation gives $g' \approx g(1 - 2h/R)$ — the factor of 2 comes from the square in the denominator.

**Depth Formula:** Below the surface ($d \le R$), only the mass interior to radius $R-d$ contributes (Shell Theorem). Since mass $\propto (R-d)^3$ and distance $\propto (R-d)$, $g' = g(1 - d/R)$ — a linear decrease to zero at the center.

**Surface Maximum:** $g$ reaches its maximum at Earth's surface. It decreases in both directions: $1/r^2$ outside, linear inside. The graph of $g$ vs $r$ is triangular-like: linear rise from center to surface, then inverse-square fall.

notes: **g above the surface (altitude):** at height h above Earth's surface, $g' = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2} = g\left(\frac{R}{R+h}\right)^2$. As h increases, g decreases. For small h ($h \ll R$), a binomial expansion gives $g' \approx g\left(1 - \frac{2h}{R}\right)$ — a useful approximation.

**g below the surface (depth):** at depth d, only the mass inside the concentric sphere of radius ($R-d$) contributes: $g' = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)$ — gravity DECREASES linearly with depth. At the centre ($d = R$), $g' = 0$.

**Why they differ:** above the surface, whole-earth mass acts from a larger distance ($1/r^2$ law); below the surface, the shell above the point exerts zero net force (shell theorem) and only the inner sphere matters, whose mass scales as ($R-d$)^3 while distance scales as ($R-d$) — giving linear decrease.

**Worked example — altitude:** at $h = R$ (one Earth radius up), $g' = g\left(\frac{R}{2R}\right)^2 = g/4 = 2.45 \text{ m/s}^2$. At $h = 100$ km, using the small-h formula, the fractional decrease is $2h/R = 2\times 100/6400 = 0.031$, so $g' \approx 9.5 \text{ m/s}^2$.
**Worked example — depth:** at $d = R/2$ (3200 km deep), $g' = g(1 - 1/2) = g/2 = 4.9 \text{ m/s}^2$. At $d = R$ (centre) → $g' = 0$ (weightlessness, though pressure is immense).
**Graphs (NEB favourite):** $g$ vs $r$ rises linearly from 0 at the centre to g at the surface, then falls as $1/r^2$ beyond the surface. The maximum value of g on Earth is at the surface.

**Other causes of variation:** (1) rotation of Earth: g reduced by $\omega^2 R \cos^2 \lambda$ ($\lambda$ = latitude), maximum at the equator; (2) shape: Earth is an oblate spheroid — g is larger at the poles ($\approx 9.832$) than the equator ($\approx 9.78$); (3) local density anomalies (mountains, mineral deposits) cause tiny local changes used in geophysics.

**Altitude formula for satellites:** for an orbit at height h, effective $r = R + h$: $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{R+h}}$ and the orbital g is $g' = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2}$ — the same g formula used at that radius.
confusion: ❌ 'g increases with altitude.' ✅ Above the surface g DEcreases as $\frac{1}{(R+h)^2}$; below the surface it also decreases (linearly). g is max at the surface.
❌ 'From height h, g falls by $h/R$.' ✅ The small-h approximation is $2h/R$ (from the square), not $h/R$. At $h = 100$ km, that is ≈ 3%.
❌ 'Deep inside Earth, g keeps growing.' ✅ It decreases linearly: $g' = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)$, zero at the centre. The shell above you pulls equally in all directions (zero net).
❌ 'g is the same at poles and equator.' ✅ Rotation and the oblate shape make g slightly larger at the poles (~0.5% difference).
❌ 'At altitude 6400 km, g is half of surface.' ✅ At $h = R$, $g' = g/4$ — the height doubles the distance, so the square halves twice.
❌ 'Weightlessness in orbit means no gravity.' ✅ Astronauts at 400 km still feel ~88% of surface gravity — they float because they are in free fall around Earth.

data.title: Motion of a Satellite — Orbital Velocity and Time Period
data.topicTitle: Motion of a satellite: orbital velocity and time period of the satellite

notes: **Orbital velocity (v₀):** a satellite stays in a circular orbit when the gravitational pull GMm/r² provides the required centripetal force mv²/r. Equating: GMm/r² = mv₀²/r → v₀ = √(GM/r). Near Earth's surface, v₀ = √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km/s.

**Why v₀ matters:** too slow → the satellite spirals in; too fast → it escapes to a higher ellipse. The orbital speed depends only on the radius (GM/r), not on the satellite's mass — heavy and light satellites share the same orbit speed.

**Time period (T):** T = circumference/velocity = 2πr/v₀ = 2π√(r³/GM) — Kepler's third law. Squaring: T² ∝ r³. A higher orbit has a longer period: the Moon (r ≈ 3.84×10⁸ m) takes ~27.3 days; the ISS (r ≈ 6.8×10⁶ m) takes ~92 minutes.

**Energy of an orbiting satellite:** K = ½mv₀² = GMm/2r, U = −GMm/r, so E_total = −GMm/2r. Notice K = −U/2 and E = U/2 — a signature of circular orbits. To raise a satellite to a higher orbit you must ADD energy, but the KE actually decreases (higher orbit = slower speed).
**Worked example — geostationary orbit:** for T = 24 h, r = (GMT²/4π²)^(1/3) ≈ 4.22×10⁷ m ≈ 35,800 km above the equator with v₀ ≈ 3.08 km/s.

**Low Earth vs geostationary comparison:** LEO (200–2000 km): v ≈ 7.8 km/s, T ≈ 90 min, covers Earth rapidly (imaging, ISS). Geostationary (35,800 km): v ≈ 3.07 km/s, T = 24 h, appears fixed over one spot (communications, weather).

**Orbit changes:** to transfer between circular orbits, a Hohmann ellipse uses two engine burns; near perigee/apogee speeds change by Δv = v₂ − v₁. Firing thrust ahead slows the satellite and lowers the orbit; firing backward raises it.
confusion: ❌ 'A satellite must be above the atmosphere to feel no gravity.' ✅ A satellite feels gravity at every altitude — it is in continuous free fall. It never falls to Earth because its forward speed curves its fall into an orbit.
❌ 'Weightlessness means g = 0 on the ISS.' ✅ g at 400 km is ≈ 8.7 m/s² (89% of surface). Astronauts float because both they and the station accelerate toward Earth together (free fall).
❌ 'Heavier satellites orbit slower.' ✅ Orbital speed is independent of the satellite's mass: v₀ = √(GM/r).
❌ 'Higher orbit → faster speed.' ✅ Higher orbit means SLOWER speed (v₀ = √(GM/r)) but a LONGER period. To reach a higher orbit you must speed up at launch; once there, the circular speed is lower.
❌ 'T is proportional to r.' ✅ T ∝ r^{3/2} — the period grows faster than the radius.

❌ 'A satellite's kinetic energy increases as it moves to a higher orbit.' ✅ KE = GMm/2r DECREASES with height; the added energy is stored as potential energy (+GmM·Δ(1/r)) making the total E = −GMm/2r less negative.

Satellites in low orbit experience tiny atmospheric drag; station-keeping burns periodically restore their altitude.

specificConditions: **Orbital Velocity Derivation:** $v_0 = \sqrt{GM/r}$ comes from equating gravitational force to centripetal force: $GMm/r^2 = mv_0^2/r$. This applies to *circular* orbits around a spherically symmetric mass. The satellite's mass cancels out — all satellites at the same radius have the same speed.

**Period Law:** $T = 2\pi\sqrt{r^3/GM}$ is Kepler's third law for circular orbits. Squaring gives $T^2 \propto r^3$, independent of satellite mass. This is valid only for bound circular/elliptical orbits — not for escape trajectories ($E \ge 0$).

**Energy Relations:** For circular orbits: $K = GMm/2r$, $U = -GMm/r$, $E = -GMm/2r$. Notice $K = -U/2$ and $E = U/2$. The negative total energy confirms a bound orbit. To raise an orbit, you ADD energy (thrust), but the orbital speed *decreases* because $v_0 \propto 1/\sqrt{r}$.

notes: **Orbital velocity (v₀):** a satellite stays in a circular orbit when the gravitational pull GMm/r² provides the required centripetal force mv²/r. Equating: GMm/r² = mv₀²/r → v₀ = √(GM/r). Near Earth's surface, v₀ = √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km/s.

**Why v₀ matters:** too slow → the satellite spirals in; too fast → it escapes to a higher ellipse. The orbital speed depends only on the radius (GM/r), not on the satellite's mass — heavy and light satellites share the same orbit speed.

**Time period (T):** T = circumference/velocity = 2πr/v₀ = 2π√(r³/GM) — Kepler's third law. Squaring: T² ∝ r³. A higher orbit has a longer period: the Moon (r ≈ 3.84×10⁸ m) takes ~27.3 days; the ISS (r ≈ 6.8×10⁶ m) takes ~92 minutes.

**Energy of an orbiting satellite:** K = ½mv₀² = GMm/2r, U = −GMm/r, so E_total = −GMm/2r. Notice K = −U/2 and E = U/2 — a signature of circular orbits. To raise a satellite to a higher orbit you must ADD energy, but the KE actually decreases (higher orbit = slower speed).
**Worked example — geostationary orbit:** for T = 24 h, r = (GMT²/4π²)^(1/3) ≈ 4.22×10⁷ m ≈ 35,800 km above the equator with v₀ ≈ 3.08 km/s.

**Low Earth vs geostationary comparison:** LEO (200–2000 km): v ≈ 7.8 km/s, T ≈ 90 min, covers Earth rapidly (imaging, ISS). Geostationary (35,800 km): v ≈ 3.07 km/s, T = 24 h, appears fixed over one spot (communications, weather).

**Orbit changes:** to transfer between circular orbits, a Hohmann ellipse uses two engine burns; near perigee/apogee speeds change by Δv = v₂ − v₁. Firing thrust ahead slows the satellite and lowers the orbit; firing backward raises it.
confusion: ❌ 'A satellite must be above the atmosphere to feel no gravity.' ✅ A satellite feels gravity at every altitude — it is in continuous free fall. It never falls to Earth because its forward speed curves its fall into an orbit.
❌ 'Weightlessness means g = 0 on the ISS.' ✅ g at 400 km is ≈ 8.7 m/s² (89% of surface). Astronauts float because both they and the station accelerate toward Earth together (free fall).
❌ 'Heavier satellites orbit slower.' ✅ Orbital speed is independent of the satellite's mass: v₀ = √(GM/r).
❌ 'Higher orbit → faster speed.' ✅ Higher orbit means SLOWER speed (v₀ = √(GM/r)) but a LONGER period. To reach a higher orbit you must speed up at launch; once there, the circular speed is lower.
❌ 'T is proportional to r.' ✅ T ∝ r^{3/2} — the period grows faster than the radius.

❌ 'A satellite's kinetic energy increases as it moves to a higher orbit.' ✅ KE = GMm/2r DECREASES with height; the added energy is stored as potential energy (+GmM·Δ(1/r)) making the total E = −GMm/2r less negative.

data.topicTitle: Meaning of thermal equilibrium and Zeroth law of thermodynamics
notes: The first law is energy conservation for a thermodynamic system. With heat Q positive into the system and work W positive when done by the system, ΔU=Q−W. Internal energy U is a state function; heat and work are energy transfers across the boundary.
For a gas expanding against constant pressure, W=PΔV. If 500 J of heat enters and the gas does 180 J of work, then ΔU=500−180=320 J.
At constant volume, boundary work is zero, so Q=ΔU if no other work is present. In an adiabatic process Q=0 and ΔU=−W. Over a full cycle ΔU=0, hence net Q=net W.
For a monatomic ideal gas ΔU=(3/2)nRΔT. For 2 mol heated by 10 K, ΔU≈(3/2)(2)(8.314)(10)=249 J, independent of the path between the states.
A p–V diagram makes work visible: work done by a gas is the area under the process curve, W=∫P dV. Expansion gives positive work under this convention; compression gives negative work.

The first law says the rise in internal energy equals the heat added to the system plus the work done on the system. A common school form writes ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW with ΔW the work done by the gas. The two forms agree if you keep the sign of W consistent. This note uses work done on the gas.
confusion: Some books define work on the system as positive and write ΔU=Q+Won; do not mix conventions.
At constant volume, Q=ΔU only if no other work is present.

specificConditions: **Energy Conservation Foundation:** The first law ($\Delta U = Q - W$) is energy conservation applied to thermodynamic systems. Internal energy $U$ is a state function; heat $Q$ and work $W$ are path-dependent energy transfers. The sign convention: $Q > 0$ when heat enters the system, $W > 0$ when work is done BY the system.

**Process Dependence:** $Q$ and $W$ depend on the thermodynamic path (isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric, isochoric), but $\Delta U$ depends only on initial and final states. For a cyclic process, $\Delta U = 0$ and $Q = W$ — net heat in equals net work out.

**Work in Thermodynamics:** Only $PV$-work is considered in the basic first law: $W = \int P_{ext} dV$. Reversible work uses the system pressure $W = \int P dV$. Other work forms (electrical, surface tension, magnetic) must be added as extra terms if present.

data.topicTitle: Thermal Energy, Heat, and Temperature: Cause and Direction of Heat Flow
notes: Thermal energy is the total kinetic energy of the molecules in a substance, which depends on the temperature and the number of molecules.
Heat is the energy transferred between two systems due to a temperature difference. It is a form of energy in transit, not a property of a system.
Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the molecules in a substance. It determines the direction of heat flow.

specificConditions: **Heat Flow Direction:** Heat always flows from a region of higher temperature to a region of lower temperature. This is a fundamental principle of thermodynamics.
**Thermal Equilibrium:** When two systems are in thermal equilibrium, there is no net heat flow between them, indicating that their temperatures are equal.

**Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics:** If system A is in thermal equilibrium with system C, and system B is in thermal equilibrium with system C, then system A is in thermal equilibrium with system B. This establishes temperature as a well-defined property.

**Thermal Expansion:** Most substances expand when heated and contract when cooled. The change in length (ΔL) of a substance due to thermal expansion is given by ΔL = L₀ α ΔT, where L₀ is the original length, α is the coefficient of linear expansion, and ΔT is the change in temperature.
**Heat Transfer Mechanisms:**
- Conduction: Heat transfer through conduction is given by Fourier's law: Q = -k A (dT/dx), where k is the thermal conductivity, A is the area, and dT/dx is the temperature gradient.

- Convection: Heat transfer through convection is given by Newton's law of cooling: Q = h A ΔT, where h is the convective heat transfer coefficient, A is the area, and ΔT is the temperature difference.

- Radiation: Heat transfer through radiation is given by the Stefan-Boltzmann law: Q = ε σ A (T⁴ - T_s⁴), where ε is the emissivity, σ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, A is the area, and T and T_s are the temperatures of the body and its surroundings.

**Thermal Energy and Internal Energy:** Thermal energy is related to the internal energy of a system, which includes the kinetic and potential energy of the molecules. The internal energy of a system depends on its temperature, pressure, volume, and the phase of the substance.

**Heat Transfer in Real Systems:** In real systems, heat transfer is often a combination of conduction, convection, and radiation. The overall heat transfer coefficient U combines these effects: 1/(U A) = 1/(h₁ A₁) + R_th + 1/(h₂ A₂), where R_th is thermal resistance.
**Temperature Gradient:** The temperature gradient is the rate of change of temperature with distance and is the driving force for heat conduction.
**Thermal Contact:** For heat transfer to occur between two systems, they must be in thermal contact. This means they must be able to exchange heat energy.
**Diathermic and Adiabatic Walls:** Diathermic walls allow heat to pass through, while adiabatic walls do not. Systems separated by adiabatic walls cannot exchange heat.

notes: Thermal equilibrium is a state in which two or more systems have the same temperature and there is no net heat flow between them.
When two systems are in thermal equilibrium, they are at the same temperature, and no heat is transferred between them.
The Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics states that if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
This law establishes temperature as a fundamental property that determines thermal equilibrium.
The Zeroth Law is essential for defining temperature and is the foundation for the other laws of thermodynamics.
Thermal contact is required for heat transfer between systems. When two systems are in thermal contact, they can exchange heat energy.
Diathermic walls allow heat to pass through, while adiabatic walls do not allow heat to pass through.

Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the molecules in a system.
The Zeroth Law is crucial for understanding the behavior of thermodynamic systems and is the basis for the definition of temperature.

The Zeroth Law is essential for the design and analysis of thermodynamic systems and devices.

specificConditions: **Thermal Equilibrium:** Two systems are in thermal equilibrium if there is no net heat flow between them when they are in thermal contact. This implies that their temperatures are equal.

**Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics:** If system A is in thermal equilibrium with system C, and system B is in thermal equilibrium with system C, then system A is in thermal equilibrium with system B. This establishes temperature as a well-defined property.
**Thermal Contact:** For heat transfer to occur between two systems, they must be in thermal contact. This means they must be able to exchange heat energy.
**Diathermic and Adiabatic Walls:** Diathermic walls allow heat to pass through, while adiabatic walls do not. Systems separated by adiabatic walls cannot exchange heat.
**Thermometers:** A thermometer measures the temperature of a system by bringing it into thermal equilibrium with the system. The thermometer's reading indicates the temperature of the system.

**Temperature Measurement:** Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the molecules in a system. It determines the direction of heat flow: heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature.
**Thermal Equilibrium and State Functions:** In thermal equilibrium, the macroscopic properties of a system (such as temperature, pressure, and volume) are constant and do not change with time.

**Applications of Zeroth Law:** The Zeroth Law is used to define temperature scales and to compare temperatures of different systems. It is essential for the design and analysis of thermodynamic systems and devices.

**Thermal Equilibrium in Real Systems:** In real systems, thermal equilibrium is achieved when the net heat flow between systems is zero, even though individual molecules may still be transferring energy.

**Temperature and Heat Flow:** Heat flows from a region of higher temperature to a region of lower temperature. When two systems are in thermal equilibrium, their temperatures are equal, and no net heat flow occurs.
**Thermal Equilibrium and Energy Transfer:** In thermal equilibrium, the total energy of the system remains constant, and there is no net transfer of energy between the systems.

data.title: Change of Phases and Latent Heat
data.topicTitle: Change of Phases and Latent Heat
notes: Phase change is the transition of a substance from one state of matter to another (solid, liquid, or gas).
Latent heat is the amount of heat required to change the phase of a substance without changing its temperature.
During a phase change, the temperature of the substance remains constant even though heat is being added or removed.
The heat required for a phase change is given by Q = mL, where m is the mass of the substance and L is the latent heat.
There are six common phase changes: melting, freezing, vaporization, condensation, sublimation, and deposition.
Melting: the process of a solid turning into a liquid (e.g., ice melting into water).
Freezing: the process of a liquid turning into a solid (e.g., water freezing into ice).
Vaporization: the process of a liquid turning into a gas (e.g., water evaporating into steam).
Condensation: the process of a gas turning into a liquid (e.g., steam condensing into water).
Sublimation: the process of a solid turning directly into a gas (e.g., dry ice turning into carbon dioxide gas).
Deposition: the process of a gas turning directly into a solid (e.g., frost forming on a cold surface).
Latent heat of fusion (L_f): the heat required to change 1 kg of a substance from solid to liquid (or vice versa) at its melting point.
Latent heat of vaporization (L_v): the heat required to change 1 kg of a substance from liquid to gas (or vice versa) at its boiling point.
Latent heat of sublimation (L_s): the heat required to change 1 kg of a substance from solid to gas (or vice versa).
The latent heat values depend on the substance and the phase change involved.
For water at 1 atm: L_f = 334 × 10³ J/kg, L_v = 2260 × 10³ J/kg.
The latent heat of vaporization is generally much larger than the latent heat of fusion for a given substance.
The latent heat of sublimation is approximately equal to the sum of the latent heat of fusion and the latent heat of vaporization.
Phase diagrams show the conditions of temperature and pressure under which a substance exists in different phases.
The triple point is the unique temperature and pressure at which all three phases (solid, liquid, gas) of a substance coexist in equilibrium.
The critical point is the temperature and pressure above which a substance cannot exist as a liquid, no matter how much pressure is applied.
Phase changes are important in many natural phenomena and technological applications, such as weather patterns, climate change, and refrigeration.
The latent heat of vaporization decreases with increasing temperature and becomes zero at the critical temperature.
The latent heat of fusion is generally less than the latent heat of vaporization.
Phase changes are accompanied by changes in volume and density.
The energy required for a phase change is used to overcome intermolecular forces and to do work against external pressure.
specificConditions: **Phase Change Definition:** Phase change is the transition of a substance from one state of matter to another without a change in temperature. The heat required or released during a phase change is called latent heat.

**Latent Heat:** Latent heat is the amount of heat required to change the phase of a unit mass of a substance without changing its temperature. It is given by Q = mL, where m is the mass and L is the latent heat.
**Common Phase Changes:**
- Melting: Solid to liquid (e.g., ice to water), L_f = 334 × 10³ J/kg for water
- Freezing: Liquid to solid (e.g., water to ice), L_f = 334 × 10³ J/kg for water
- Vaporization: Liquid to gas (e.g., water to steam), L_v = 2260 × 10³ J/kg for water
- Condensation: Gas to liquid (e.g., steam to water), L_v = 2260 × 10³ J/kg for water
- Sublimation: Solid to gas (e.g., dry ice to CO₂ gas), L_s ≈ L_f + L_v
- Deposition: Gas to solid (e.g., frost formation), L_s ≈ L_f + L_v
**Phase Diagrams:** A phase diagram shows the conditions of temperature and pressure under which a substance exists in different phases. It includes the triple point and critical point.
**Triple Point:** The unique temperature and pressure at which all three phases (solid, liquid, gas) coexist in equilibrium. For water, it is 273.16 K (0.01°C) at 611.657 Pa.
**Critical Point:** The temperature and pressure above which a substance cannot exist as a liquid, no matter how much pressure is applied. For water, it is 647 K (374°C) at 21.8 MPa.

**Energy Considerations:** During a phase change, the heat added or removed is used to overcome intermolecular forces and to do work against external pressure. The temperature remains constant during a phase change.
**Latent Heat Values:** Typical latent heat values: Water L_f = 334 kJ/kg, L_v = 2260 kJ/kg; Ice L_f = 334 kJ/kg; Steam L_v = 2260 kJ/kg; Copper L_f = 205 kJ/kg; Aluminum L_f = 397 kJ/kg.
**Phase Change and Volume:** Phase changes are often accompanied by changes in volume and density. For example, water expands when it freezes, which is why ice floats on water.
**Applications of Phase Changes:** Phase changes are important in many natural phenomena and technological applications, such as weather patterns, climate change, refrigeration, and air conditioning.
**Heat Transfer During Phase Changes:** During a phase change, the heat transfer rate is given by Q = mL/t, where t is the time taken for the phase change.

**Phase Change and Energy:** The energy required for a phase change is much larger than the energy required to change the temperature of a substance. This is why phase changes are important in energy storage and transfer systems.
**Phase Change and Temperature:** The temperature of a substance remains constant during a phase change, even though heat is being added or removed. This is a key characteristic of phase changes.

notes: Heat Q is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. For a temperature change without phase change, Q=mcΔT, where m is mass and c is specific heat capacity. A temperature difference has the same numerical size in kelvins and degrees Celsius.
Heat capacity C=Q/ΔT applies to the whole object; specific heat c=C/m is per unit mass. A 0.50 kg aluminium block with c=900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ heated by 20 K needs Q=0.50×900×20=9000 J.
During melting or boiling, temperature remains constant while latent heat changes phase: Q=mL. Melting 0.10 kg of ice at 0°C requires 0.10×334000=33400 J before the resulting water is warmed.
For an insulated calorimeter, energy conservation gives ΣQ=0: heat lost by hot parts equals heat gained by cold parts. Include the calorimeter and any phase changes when specified.
Example: 0.20 kg water heated by 15 K with c=4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ needs Q=0.20×4200×15=12600 J.

Heat that changes temperature is m c Δθ. Heat that changes state at constant temperature is m L, with no Δθ in the formula. A melting calculation often needs both: warm the ice to 0°C, melt it, then warm the water.

specificConditions: **Heat Capacity Definition:** Heat capacity $C = \Delta Q/\Delta T$ is the heat required to raise temperature by 1 K. Specific heat capacity $c = C/m$ is per unit mass (J/kg·K). Molar heat capacity $C_m = C/n$ is per mole (J/mol·K).

**Phase Change Latent Heat:** During phase change (melting, boiling), temperature is constant while heat is absorbed/released as latent heat: $Q = mL$. Latent heat of fusion $L_f$ (solid↔liquid) and vaporization $L_v$ (liquid↔gas) are material properties.

**Calorimetry Principle:** In an isolated system, heat lost by hot bodies = heat gained by cold bodies. This assumes no heat loss to surroundings and no phase changes unless accounted for. The final equilibrium temperature is found by equating $m_1 c_1 (T_f - T_1) = m_2 c_2 (T_2 - T_f)$.

data.title: Kinetic Molecular Model of an Ideal Gas
data.summary: The kinetic molecular model explains gas behavior through random motion of molecules. Key assumptions: point particles, elastic collisions, no intermolecular forces except during collision, negligible volume compared to container. Derives pressure P = (1/3)ρv²_rms and connects macroscopic properties (P, V, T) to microscopic molecular motion.
notes: Basic Postulates: (1) Gas consists of large number of identical molecules in random motion. (2) Molecular size ≪ mean separation (point masses). (3) Collisions with walls and between molecules are perfectly elastic. (4) No intermolecular forces except during brief collisions. (5) Time of collision ≪ time between collisions. (6) Newton's laws apply to each molecule.

Origin of Pressure: Pressure arises from momentum transfer when molecules collide with container walls. Each collision imparts impulse Δp = 2mv_x (for wall perpendicular to x-axis). Summing over all molecules and averaging gives P = (1/3)(N/V)m⟨v²⟩ = (1/3)ρv²_rms.
Root Mean Square Speed: v_rms = √(⟨v²⟩) = √(3RT/M) = √(3kT/m), where M is molar mass, m is molecular mass, k is Boltzmann constant. At same T, lighter molecules move faster.
Connection to Temperature: Average translational KE per molecule = (3/2)kT. Total translational KE of N molecules = (3/2)NkT = (3/2)nRT. Temperature is a measure of average molecular kinetic energy.
Ideal Gas Law Derivation: From P = (1/3)(N/V)m⟨v²⟩ and ⟨KE⟩ = (1/2)m⟨v²⟩ = (3/2)kT, we get PV = NkT = nRT — the ideal gas equation derived from microscopic mechanics.

Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution: Molecular speeds follow a statistical distribution f(v) = 4π(m/2πkT)^(3/2) v² exp(-mv²/2kT). Most probable speed v_mp = √(2kT/m), average speed v_avg = √(8kT/πm), rms speed v_rms = √(3kT/m). Ratio v_mp : v_avg : v_rms ≈ 1 : 1.13 : 1.22.
Degrees of Freedom: Monatomic gas has 3 translational DOF → C_v = (3/2)R. Diatomic adds 2 rotational DOF at room T → C_v = (5/2)R. Vibrational modes activate at high T.
Mean Free Path: Average distance between collisions λ = 1/(√2 πd² n), where d is molecular diameter and n = N/V number density. At STP, λ ≈ 68 nm for air.

Limitations of Model: Assumes point particles and no interactions — fails at high pressure (finite volume matters) and low temperature (intermolecular attraction matters). Real gases require van der Waals corrections.
specificConditions: Low Density Required: Model assumes molecular volume ≪ container volume. Valid when gas is dilute (low P, high T). Breaks down near condensation point.
Elastic Collisions Only: Energy conservation in collisions is essential. Inelastic collisions would cause temperature decay — not observed in equilibrium gases.
Large Number of Molecules: Statistical averaging requires N ≫ 1. Fluctuations become significant for very small systems (nanoscale).
Thermal Equilibrium Assumed: Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution applies only at equilibrium. Non-equilibrium flows require Boltzmann transport equation.
formulas: Pressure: $P = \frac{1}{3} \rho v_{rms}^2 = \frac{1}{3} \frac{Nm}{V} \langle v^2 \rangle$
RMS speed: $v_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}} = \sqrt{\frac{3kT}{m}}$
Average KE per molecule: $\langle KE \rangle = \frac{3}{2} kT$
Total translational KE: $E_k = \frac{3}{2} nRT$
Most probable speed: $v_{mp} = \sqrt{\frac{2RT}{M}}$
Average speed: $v_{avg} = \sqrt{\frac{8RT}{\pi M}}$
Mean free path: $\lambda = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2} \pi d^2 n}$
keyPoints: Gas pressure results from molecular collisions with container walls.
Temperature measures average translational kinetic energy: ⟨KE⟩ = (3/2)kT.
v_rms = √(3RT/M): lighter gases move faster at same temperature.
PV = nRT derives directly from kinetic theory postulates.
Speed distribution follows Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics.
Model valid for dilute gases; real gases need corrections at high P or low T.

Statement 2: Absolute temperature is proportional to average translational kinetic energy per molecule.
Statement 3: The ideal gas law PV = nRT is derivable from Newtonian mechanics applied to molecular motion.
Statement 4: Molecular speeds in equilibrium follow the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution.
Statement 5: Kinetic theory bridges macroscopic thermodynamics and microscopic mechanics.

At 300 K, nitrogen molecules have v_rms ≈ 517 m/s — supersonic yet no wind because motion is random.

Monatomic C_v = 3R/2 comes from 3 translational DOF × (1/2)R each.

universalFacts: Daniel Bernoulli first proposed kinetic theory in 1738, but it was ignored until Clausius, Maxwell, and Boltzmann developed it rigorously (1857–1870s).
Brownian motion (observed 1827, explained by Einstein 1905) provided direct experimental confirmation of molecular motion.

confusion: Thinking temperature measures total energy: It measures AVERAGE translational KE per molecule, not total internal energy.
Confusing v_rms with average speed: v_rms = √(⟨v²⟩) ≠ ⟨v⟩. They differ by ~8% for Maxwell distribution.
Believing molecules stop at 0°C: 0°C = 273 K; molecules still have substantial KE. Only at 0 K would classical motion cease.
Assuming all molecules move at same speed: Speeds follow a broad distribution; individual molecules constantly change speed via collisions.
Thinking pressure comes from molecular weight: Pressure arises from momentum transfer in collisions, not gravitational force on molecules.

data.title: Boltzmann Constant and RMS Speed
data.summary: The Boltzmann constant k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K links macroscopic temperature to microscopic molecular energy. RMS speed v_rms = √(3kT/m) = √(3RT/M) characterizes the typical molecular speed in a gas at temperature T. At the same temperature, lighter molecules move faster; v_rms determines diffusion rates, effusion, and kinetic energy.
notes: Boltzmann Constant Definition: k = R/N_A where R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. Value: k = 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J/K (exact since 2019 SI redefinition). It converts temperature (kelvin) into energy (joules) per particle.

Physical Significance of k: Average translational KE per molecule = (3/2)kT. At 300 K, ⟨KE⟩ = (3/2)(1.38×10⁻²³)(300) ≈ 6.21 × 10⁻²¹ J ≈ 0.039 eV. This is the thermal energy scale governing molecular motion.
RMS Speed Formula: v_rms = √(⟨v²⟩) = √(3kT/m) = √(3RT/M), where m = molecular mass, M = molar mass. Derived from equating pressure expression P = (1/3)ρv²_rms with ideal gas law PV = nRT.

Speed Hierarchy: For Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution: v_mp = √(2kT/m) < v_avg = √(8kT/πm) < v_rms = √(3kT/m). Numerical ratio: v_mp : v_avg : v_rms ≈ 1.41 : 1.60 : 1.73 (or 1 : 1.13 : 1.22 normalized to v_mp).
Temperature Dependence: v_rms ∝ √T. Doubling absolute temperature increases v_rms by factor √2 ≈ 1.414. Cooling to 1/4 original T halves the rms speed.
Mass Dependence: v_rms ∝ 1/√M. At same T, hydrogen (M=2 g/mol) moves √(32/2) = 4 times faster than oxygen (M=32 g/mol). This explains why light gases escape planetary atmospheres more readily.
Typical Values at 300 K: H₂: 1920 m/s; He: 1370 m/s; N₂: 517 m/s; O₂: 483 m/s; CO₂: 412 m/s. All supersonic yet no bulk flow due to random directions.
Connection to Kinetic Energy: Total translational KE of n moles = (3/2)nRT = (3/2)NkT. Internal energy of monatomic ideal gas U = (3/2)nRT depends only on T, not V or P.
Effusion and Graham's Law: Rate of effusion ∝ v_rms ∝ 1/√M. Lighter gases effuse faster through small openings. Used in uranium enrichment (²³⁵UF₆ vs ²³⁸UF₆).
specificConditions: Ideal Gas Assumption: Formulas assume point particles with elastic collisions and no intermolecular forces. Real gases deviate at high P or low T.
Thermal Equilibrium Required: Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution and well-defined v_rms apply only at equilibrium. Non-equilibrium flows have different velocity distributions.
Translational Motion Only: v_rms refers to center-of-mass translational speed. Rotational and vibrational energies contribute to total internal energy but not to v_rms.
Classical Regime: Quantum effects become significant when de Broglie wavelength λ = h/(mv) approaches interparticle spacing. For most gases above ~10 K, classical treatment is valid.
formulas: Boltzmann constant: $k = \frac{R}{N_A} = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \text{ J/K}$
RMS speed: $v_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3kT}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}$
Most probable speed: $v_{mp} = \sqrt{\frac{2kT}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{2RT}{M}}$
Average speed: $v_{avg} = \sqrt{\frac{8kT}{\pi m}} = \sqrt{\frac{8RT}{\pi M}}$
Average KE per molecule: $\langle KE \rangle = \frac{3}{2} kT$
Speed ratio: $v_{mp} : v_{avg} : v_{rms} = \sqrt{2} : \sqrt{8/\pi} : \sqrt{3}$
keyPoints: k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K bridges macroscopic T and microscopic energy.
v_rms = √(3RT/M): depends on T and M, not on P or V directly.
At same T, all gases have same ⟨KE⟩ but different v_rms.
v_rms > v_avg > v_mp always for Maxwellian distribution.
Lighter molecules move faster: v_rms ∝ 1/√M.
Graham's law of effusion follows directly from v_rms ∝ 1/√M.
importantStatements: Statement 1: Boltzmann constant relates temperature to average molecular kinetic energy via ⟨KE⟩ = (3/2)kT.
Statement 2: RMS speed is the square root of the mean of squared molecular speeds, not the arithmetic mean speed.
Statement 3: At identical temperatures, gases with lower molar mass have higher rms speeds.
Statement 4: The three characteristic speeds (v_mp, v_avg, v_rms) are distinct and ordered for any Maxwellian gas.
Statement 5: Graham's law of effusion is a direct consequence of the mass dependence of rms speed.
importantNotes: Since 2019, k is defined exactly as 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J/K, fixing the kelvin in terms of energy.
v_rms appears in pressure formula because pressure depends on ⟨v²⟩, not ⟨v⟩².

data.topicTitle: Kinetic-molecular model of an ideal gas
notes: **Postulates (Four fundamental assumptions):**
1. A gas consists of a large number of identical, point-like molecules with negligible volume (point particles).
2. The molecules are in constant, random motion. No two molecules occupy the same point in space.
3. There are no intermolecular forces between molecules except during perfectly elastic collisions.
4. Collisions between molecules (and with container walls) are perfectly elastic and take negligible time compared to the time between collisions.

**Why the model works:** The kinetic theory explains gas laws (Boyle's, Charles's, Gay-Lussac's) and pressure. It connects macroscopic properties (P, V, T) to microscopic behavior (molecular speed, collisions).

**Pressure origin:** Pressure arises from molecules colliding with container walls. Each collision delivers a tiny impulse (change in momentum). The average of many collisions over time creates a constant force on the wall, resulting in pressure.

**Temperature and kinetic energy:** Temperature is a direct measure of the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules. The average translational kinetic energy per molecule is $\langle K \rangle = \frac{3}{2}k_BT$, where $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant.

**Absolute temperature scale:** The Kelvin scale is an absolute temperature scale where $T = 0$ K means zero thermal motion (all molecular motion ceases). This is a fundamental limit of thermodynamics.

**Why temperature cannot be negative:** Kinetic energy is always non-negative ($\frac{1}{2}mv^2 \geq 0$), so $\langle K \rangle = \frac{3}{2}k_BT \geq 0$. Since $k_B > 0$, this requires $T \geq 0$. Negative temperature is not possible in the kinetic theory.

**Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution:** The distribution of molecular speeds in an ideal gas is a specific probability distribution. It shows that most molecules have speeds near the average, with fewer at very low or very high speeds. The shape is asymmetric with a long tail to high speeds.

**Degrees of freedom:** The number of independent ways a molecule can store energy. Monatomic gas: 3 translational DOF. Diatomic: 3 translational + 2 rotational DOF at room temperature (vibrational DOF not active). Polyatomic: more DOF including vibration.

**Internal energy:** For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature and is given by $U = \frac{f}{2}nRT$, where $f$ is the number of degrees of freedom. Monatomic: $f=3$, so $U = \frac{3}{2}nRT$.

**Degrees of freedom and heat capacity:** $C_V = \frac{f}{2}R$ for molar heat capacity at constant volume. Monatomic gas: $C_V = \frac{3}{2}R$. Diatomic gas: $C_V = \frac{5}{2}R$ (at room temperature).

**Elastic collision definition:** A collision where both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. In an elastic collision between two molecules, the relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation: $|\vec{v}_1 - \vec{v}_2|_{\text{after}} = |\vec{v}_1 - \vec{v}_2|_{\text{before}}$.
**Collision frequency:** The average number of collisions per unit time per molecule. Increases with higher density and higher temperature (faster molecules collide more often).

**Real gas approximation:** The kinetic theory works well for gases at low pressure and high temperature where intermolecular forces are negligible and molecular volume is small compared to container volume. Real gases deviate at high pressure/low temperature.

confusion: Temperature is a measure of AVERAGE kinetic energy, not the kinetic energy of any single molecule. A hot object has higher average KE per molecule, but individual molecules have a range of speeds.
The kinetic theory assumes perfectly elastic collisions. In reality, some kinetic energy is lost to internal excitation (vibration, rotation) or radiation, especially in gases with complex molecules.

Temperature can be defined for any system in thermal equilibrium, but the kinetic energy definition $\langle K \rangle = \frac{3}{2}k_BT$ applies specifically to translational kinetic energy in ideal gases. Rotational and vibrational energy also contribute to temperature.

The mean free path is inversely proportional to number density (n) and collision cross-section (σ). At higher pressure (lower volume), molecules are closer together and collide more frequently, reducing the mean free path.

The mean free path decreases with increasing temperature because molecules move faster and cover more distance between collisions, even though number density may change. $\lambda = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}n\sigma}$, and $n \propto P/T$.
practice: A gas sample has a number density of $10^{25}$ molecules/m$^3$. Calculate the mean free path if the collision cross-section is $10^{-19}$ m$^2$. Solution: $\lambda = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2} n \sigma} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2} \times 10^{25} \times 10^{-19}} = \frac{1}{1.414 \times 10^6} = 7.07 \times 10^{-7}$ m $= 707$ nm.

Calculate the average translational kinetic energy of a nitrogen molecule ($N_2$) at 300 K. Solution: $\langle K \rangle = \frac{3}{2}k_BT = \frac{3}{2} \times 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 300 = 6.21 \times 10^{-21}$ J. Convert to eV: $6.21 \times 10^{-21} / 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 0.039$ eV.

A gas expands isothermally (constant T) from 1 L to 3 L. If the initial pressure is 2 atm, find the final pressure. Solution: Boyle's law: $P_1V_1 = P_2V_2 \rightarrow P_2 = P_1V_1/V_2 = 2 \times 1 / 3 = 0.67$ atm.

Calculate the root-mean-square speed of oxygen molecules ($O_2$, $M = 32$ g/mol) at 300 K. Solution: $v_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M} = \sqrt{3 \times 8.314 \times 300 / 0.032} = \sqrt{7482.6 / 0.032} = \sqrt{233,831} = 484$ m/s.

Why does the kinetic theory predict that all ideal gases at the same temperature have the same average kinetic energy? Because $\langle K \rangle = \frac{3}{2}k_BT$, which depends only on T, not on molecular mass or identity.
universalFacts: The kinetic theory was first proposed by Daniel Bernoulli in 1738 in his work 'Hydrodynamica', but it was largely ignored until revived by Clausius, Maxwell, and Boltzmann in the 19th century.
Maxwell and Boltzmann independently developed the distribution of molecular speeds in the 1860s-1870s. The distribution is now called the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution.

At room temperature, a nitrogen molecule has an average speed of about 500 m/s, but its most probable speed (peak of the distribution) is about 470 m/s, while the rms speed is about 517 m/s. The distribution is asymmetric with a long tail to high speeds.
The kinetic theory explains why sound travels faster in solids (molecules are closer together, so momentum transfer is more efficient) than in gases, despite gases having faster individual molecules.

The third law of thermodynamics (Nernst's theorem) states that the entropy of a perfect crystal at absolute zero is zero. This is related to the fact that at $T = 0$ K, molecular motion ceases, so there is only one possible microstate.

data.title: Derivation of Pressure Exerted by Gas
data.topicTitle: Derivation of pressure exerted by gas
notes: **Setup:** Consider a cubical container with side length $L$ containing $N$ molecules of mass $m$. The volume is $V = L^3$.

**Momentum change in one collision:** When a molecule with x-component of velocity $v_x$ hits the wall perpendicular to the x-axis, it rebounds with velocity $-v_x$. The change in momentum is $\Delta p = p_f - p_i = m(-v_x) - m(v_x) = -2mv_x$. The magnitude is $2mv_x$.
**Time between collisions:** The molecule travels a distance $2L$ (to the opposite wall and back) at speed $|v_x|$. Time between collisions with the same wall is $\Delta t = 2L/|v_x|$.

**Force from one molecule:** $F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \frac{2mv_x}{2L/|v_x|} = \frac{2mv_x}{|v_x|} = \frac{mv_x^2}{L}$. (Note: $|v_x| = v_x$ if $v_x > 0$, but we use magnitude for force magnitude).

**Pressure contribution:** Force per unit area is $P = F/A = \frac{mv_x^2}{L} / L^2 = \frac{mv_x^2}{L^3} = \frac{mv_x^2}{V}$. This is the pressure contribution from a single molecule with x-velocity $v_x$.

**Averaging over all molecules:** The total force is the sum of forces from all molecules. Since the wall is perpendicular to x-axis, only $v_x$ components matter. Total pressure $P = \frac{1}{A} \sum F_i = \frac{1}{L^2} \sum (mv_{ix}^2/L) = \frac{m}{L^3} \sum v_{ix}^2 = \frac{m}{V} \langle v_x^2 \rangle$.

**Relating to total kinetic energy:** The total kinetic energy is $K = \frac{1}{2}m \sum v_i^2 = \frac{1}{2}mN\langle v^2 \rangle$. Since $\langle v^2 \rangle = \langle v_x^2 \rangle + \langle v_y^2 \rangle + \langle v_z^2 \rangle$ and by symmetry $\langle v_x^2 \rangle = \langle v_y^2 \rangle = \langle v_z^2 \rangle$, we have $\langle v_x^2 \rangle = \frac{1}{3}\langle v^2 \rangle$.

**Final result:** Substituting back, $P = \frac{m}{V} \cdot \frac{1}{3}\langle v^2 \rangle = \frac{1}{3} \frac{mN}{V} \langle v^2 \rangle = \frac{2}{3} \frac{N}{V} (\frac{1}{2}m\langle v^2 \rangle) = \frac{2}{3} \frac{N}{V} \langle K \rangle$. Since $\langle K \rangle = \frac{3}{2}k_BT$, we get $P = \frac{N}{V} k_BT = \frac{n}{V} RT = \frac{nRT}{V}$.

**Pressure in terms of average KE:** $P = \frac{2}{3} \frac{N}{V} \langle K \rangle$. This shows the direct link between pressure and microscopic kinetic energy. The factor 2/3 comes from the 3 spatial dimensions (1/3 per dimension).
**Derivation steps recap:**
1. Momentum change: $\Delta p = 2mv_x$
2. Time between collisions: $\Delta t = 2L/|v_x|$
3. Force on wall: $F = \frac{2mv_x^2}{L}$
4. Pressure: $P = F/A = \frac{mv_x^2}{L^3} = \frac{mv_x^2}{V}$
5. Average over all molecules: $P = \frac{m}{V} \langle v_x^2 \rangle$
6. Relate to total KE: $\langle v_x^2 \rangle = \frac{1}{3}\langle v^2 \rangle$, so $P = \frac{m}{3V} \langle v^2 \rangle$
7. Substitute $\langle K \rangle = \frac{1}{2}m\langle v^2 \rangle$: $P = \frac{2}{3} \frac{N}{V} \langle K \rangle$

confusion: The derivation assumes the wall is perpendicular to the x-axis. For a wall at an angle, the momentum change and force calculation would be different.
The factor 1/3 comes from the three spatial dimensions. In 2D, it would be 1/2, and in n-dimensions, it would be 1/n. Students often forget this geometric factor.
The derivation assumes the wall is stationary. If the wall were moving (e.g., piston), the relative velocity would need to be used, and the derivation would be more complex.
The derivation applies to ideal gases where collisions are perfectly elastic. In real gases with inelastic collisions, energy is lost and the derivation needs modification.
practice: A gas molecule with mass 3.34 × 10⁻²⁶ kg (mass of N₂) has an x-component of velocity of 500 m/s. Calculate the force it exerts on a wall of area 0.01 m². Solution: $F = \frac{mv_x^2}{L}$. First find $L = V^{1/3} = (0.01)^{1/3} = 0.215$ m. $F = \frac{3.34 \times 10^{-26} \times 500^2}{0.215} = \frac{3.34 \times 10^{-26} \times 250000}{0.215} = \frac{8.35 \times 10^{-21}}{0.215} = 3.88 \times 10^{-20}$ N. Pressure = $F/A = 3.88 \times 10^{-20} / 0.01 = 3.88 \times 10^{-18}$ Pa.

A gas container has side length 0.1 m. A molecule with x-velocity 400 m/s hits the wall. Calculate the time between collisions with the same wall. Solution: $\Delta t = 2L/|v_x| = 2 \times 0.1 / 400 = 0.2 / 400 = 0.0005$ s = 5 × 10⁻⁴ s.

If the average kinetic energy per molecule is 6.21 × 10⁻²¹ J (from previous problem), what is the average vₓ²? Since $\langle K \rangle = \frac{1}{2}m\langle v^2 \rangle = \frac{1}{2}m(3\langle v_x^2 \rangle)$, then $\langle v_x^2 \rangle = \frac{3\langle K \rangle}{m}$. For m = 3.34 × 10⁻²⁶ kg, $\langle v_x^2 \rangle = \frac{3 \times 6.21 \times 10^{-21}}{3.34 \times 10^{-26}} = 5.57 \times 10^5$ m²/s².

A container with 1000 molecules has total kinetic energy 6.21 J. What is the average kinetic energy per molecule? Solution: 6.21 J / 1000 = 6.21 × 10⁻³ J per molecule. This is $\langle K \rangle = \frac{3}{2}k_BT$, so we can find T if needed.

A molecule with mass 28 u (N₂) has rms speed of 480 m/s. Calculate its average kinetic energy. Solution: $K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$. Mass in kg: 28 × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ = 4.648 × 10⁻²⁶ kg. $K = 0.5 × 4.648 \times 10^{-26} \times 480^2 = 0.5 × 4.648 \times 10^{-26} \times 230400 = 5.35 × 10^{-21}$ J.
universalFacts: The kinetic theory was developed in the 19th century by Rudolf Clausius (1850s), James Clerk Maxwell (1860s), and Ludwig Boltzmann (1870s). Maxwell's equations for the distribution of speeds were a major breakthrough.

The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution was first derived by James Clerk Maxwell in 1860 for gas molecules. Ludwig Boltzmann later provided a statistical interpretation and connected it to entropy (S = k_B ln Ω).

At room temperature (300 K), the average speed of a nitrogen molecule (N₂, molar mass 28 g/mol) is about 517 m/s, while the most probable speed is about 470 m/s. The distribution has a long tail to high speeds.

The kinetic theory explains why the speed of sound is higher in solids and liquids than in gases: in solids, molecules are closer together, so momentum transfer (sound waves) is more efficient even though individual molecules move slower.

The kinetic theory is foundational to statistical mechanics, which connects microscopic behavior to macroscopic thermodynamics. It was a key step in establishing thermodynamics as a branch of physics rather than just engineering.

data.title: Heat Capacities of Gases
data.summary: Gases have two principal specific heats: C_v at constant volume and C_p at constant pressure. For ideal gases, C_p − C_v = R (Mayer's relation). The ratio γ = C_p/C_v depends on molecular degrees of freedom: monatomic γ = 5/3, diatomic γ = 7/5. These values govern adiabatic processes, sound speed, and thermodynamic cycles.
notes: Specific Heat Definition: Amount of heat required to raise temperature of unit mass by 1 K. For gases, value depends on process conditions because gases expand significantly when heated.
C_v (Constant Volume): Heat added increases only internal energy (no work done since dV = 0). Q = nC_vΔT = ΔU. For monatomic ideal gas: C_v = (3/2)R. Diatomic at room T: C_v = (5/2)R.
C_p (Constant Pressure): Heat added increases internal energy AND does expansion work against external pressure. Q = nC_pΔT = ΔU + PΔV. Always C_p > C_v because extra energy goes into work.
Mayer's Relation: C_p − C_v = R for one mole of ideal gas. Derived from H = U + PV and ideal gas law. Per unit mass: c_p − c_v = R/M where M is molar mass.
Adiabatic Index γ: γ = C_p/C_v. Monatomic: γ = 5/3 ≈ 1.67. Diatomic (room T): γ = 7/5 = 1.40. Polyatomic: γ ≈ 1.33. Determines adiabatic process behavior: PV^γ = constant.

Degrees of Freedom f: Each quadratic DOF contributes (1/2)R to C_v per mole. Monatomic: f = 3 (translational) → C_v = 3R/2. Diatomic: f = 5 (3 trans + 2 rot) → C_v = 5R/2. Vibrational modes add R each (kinetic + potential) but activate only at high T.

Temperature Dependence: At very low T, rotational/vibrational modes freeze out (quantum effect). C_v decreases below classical prediction. At high T, vibrational modes activate, increasing C_v toward equipartition limit.

Experimental Measurement: C_v measured in bomb calorimeter (fixed volume). C_p measured in flow calorimeter or derived from C_v + R. Adiabatic expansion methods (Clement-Desormes) determine γ directly.
Applications: γ determines speed of sound v = √(γRT/M), adiabatic lapse rate in atmosphere, efficiency of Carnot and Otto cycles, and shock wave properties.
specificConditions: Ideal Gas Assumption: Mayer's relation C_p − C_v = R holds exactly only for ideal gases. Real gases show deviations at high P or low T.
Temperature Range Matters: Degrees of freedom activated depend on T. Room-temperature diatomic values assume rotation active but vibration frozen.
Per Mole vs Per Mass: Molar heat capacities use R; specific (mass-based) use R/M. Always check units in problems.
Quasi-static Processes: Definitions assume reversible, quasi-static heating. Rapid non-equilibrium heating gives different effective heat capacities.
formulas: Mayer's relation: $C_p - C_v = R$
Adiabatic index: $\gamma = \frac{C_p}{C_v}$
Monatomic: $C_v = \frac{3}{2}R$, $C_p = \frac{5}{2}R$, $\gamma = \frac{5}{3}$
Diatomic (room T): $C_v = \frac{5}{2}R$, $C_p = \frac{7}{2}R$, $\gamma = \frac{7}{5}$
General: $C_v = \frac{f}{2}R$, $C_p = \left(\frac{f}{2}+1\right)R$
Speed of sound: $v = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT}{M}}$
keyPoints: C_p > C_v because constant-pressure heating includes expansion work.
Mayer's relation: C_p − C_v = R for ideal gases.
γ = C_p/C_v determines adiabatic behavior and sound speed.
Degrees of freedom dictate heat capacity values via equipartition.
Monatomic γ = 5/3; diatomic γ = 7/5 at ordinary temperatures.
Vibrational modes increase C_v at high temperatures.
importantStatements: Statement 1: Molar heat capacity at constant pressure exceeds that at constant volume by the gas constant R.
Statement 2: The ratio γ = C_p/C_v is always greater than unity for any gas.
Statement 3: Heat capacity values reflect the number of active molecular degrees of freedom.
Statement 4: Adiabatic processes obey PV^γ = constant where γ depends on molecular structure.
Statement 5: Speed of sound in a gas is proportional to √γ, linking thermodynamics to acoustics.
importantNotes: For air (mostly N₂ + O₂), γ ≈ 1.40 at STP — matches diatomic prediction.
Steam (H₂O, polyatomic) has γ ≈ 1.33; helium (monatomic) has γ ≈ 1.67.
At cryogenic temperatures, H₂ behaves as monatomic (rotation frozen): γ → 5/3.

Monatomic: f=3 → γ=5/3; Diatomic: f=5 → γ=7/5.
Higher γ → steeper adiabat → faster sound speed.
If given C_v, get C_p = C_v + R; if given γ and C_v, get C_p = γC_v.

examples: Argon (monatomic): C_v = 12.47 J/(mol·K), C_p = 20.79 J/(mol·K), γ = 1.67. Difference = 8.32 ≈ R.
Nitrogen at 300 K: C_v = 20.8 J/(mol·K) ≈ 5R/2, C_p = 29.1 J/(mol·K) ≈ 7R/2, γ = 1.40.
Speed of sound in air at 20°C: v = √(1.4 × 8.314 × 293 / 0.029) ≈ 343 m/s.
Adiabatic compression: Air compressed from 1 atm to 8 atm. T₂/T₁ = (P₂/P₁)^((γ−1)/γ) = 8^(0.286) ≈ 1.81. If T₁ = 300 K, T₂ ≈ 543 K.

universalFacts: Julius Robert von Mayer first stated C_p − C_v = R in 1841, contributing to energy conservation principle.
Einstein and Debye models explain low-temperature heat capacity anomalies using quantum statistics.
Atmospheric adiabatic lapse rate (~9.8 K/km dry) derives directly from γ and gravitational acceleration.
Supersonic flight creates shock waves whose strength depends on γ of the surrounding gas.
confusion: Thinking C_p and C_v are material constants independent of process: They are defined FOR specific processes (constant P or V).
Using R without checking molar vs mass basis: Molar uses R = 8.314; specific uses R/M.
Assuming γ is always 1.4: Only true for diatomic gases near room temperature. Monatomic and polyatomic differ.
Believing vibrational modes always contribute: They activate only above characteristic temperatures (e.g., ~2000 K for N₂).
Confusing heat capacity with thermal conductivity: Heat capacity stores energy; conductivity transfers it. Different physical quantities.

data.title: Instantaneous Velocity and Acceleration
notes: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version complements the original note with the limit-definition approach, calculus forms and graphical slope reasoning for instantaneous velocity and acceleration.

**Average quantities first:** average velocity $v_{avg} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$ uses the whole interval; average acceleration $a_{avg} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$ likewise. They smooth out everything that happened in between — a car doing 100 km in 2 h has $v_{avg} = 50$ km/h regardless of traffic.

**The limit idea:** instantaneous velocity is the average velocity as $\Delta t \to 0$: $v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{dx}{dt}$. It answers 'how fast RIGHT NOW' — exactly what a speedometer reads.
**Instantaneous acceleration:** $a = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}$. Acceleration is the derivative of velocity — the 'slope of the slope'.

**Graphical meaning:** on an $x$–$t$ graph, velocity = slope of the tangent at the instant (not the chord); on a $v$–$t$ graph, acceleration = slope of the tangent, and the AREA under the curve between two times gives the displacement.

**Sign reasoning:** $v > 0$ → moving forward; $v < 0$ → moving backward; $a > 0$ with $v > 0$ → speeding up; $a > 0$ with $v < 0$ → slowing down (a negative velocity becoming more negative). 'Slowing down' means $v$ and $a$ have OPPOSITE signs — the classic exam trap.

**Worked calculus example:** $x(t) = 5t^2 - 3t$. Then $v = dx/dt = 10t - 3$ and $a = dv/dt = 10\,\text{m/s}^2$ (constant). At $t = 2$ s: $v = 17$ m/s; the particle is momentarily at rest when $t = 0.3$ s.

**Uniform vs non-uniform acceleration:** if $a$ is constant the SUVAT equations apply; if $a$ varies with time, position or velocity, only the calculus definitions (or graphs) work. This is why the derivative definition is the more general and more fundamental one.

**NEB exam focus:** define instantaneous velocity/acceleration as limits; differentiate a given $x(t)$; find when a particle is at rest or reverses; convert between $x$–$t$, $v$–$t$ and $a$–$t$ graphs (slopes and areas).

confusion: ❌ 'Instantaneous velocity equals average velocity.' ✅ Only when motion is uniform. In general $v_{inst} = dx/dt$ while $v_{avg} = \Delta x/\Delta t$; they coincide only if the $x$–$t$ graph is a straight line.

❌ 'Negative acceleration always means slowing down.' ✅ Slowing means $v$ and $a$ have OPPOSITE signs. A ball thrown upward (up = positive) has $v > 0$ with $a = -g$ — it slows going up and speeds up coming down, with the SAME downward acceleration throughout.
❌ 'The area under an $x$–$t$ graph gives velocity.' ✅ The SLOPE of $x$–$t$ gives velocity; the AREA under a $v$–$t$ graph gives displacement. Mixing these up is the classic graph-question error.
❌ 'At the turning point, acceleration is zero.' ✅ At a reversal, $v = 0$ but $a$ is NOT zero (e.g. a ball at the top of its flight has $v = 0$, $a = g$ downward). Zero velocity ≠ zero acceleration.
❌ 'Speed can be negative.' ✅ Speed is $|v|$, always non-negative; velocity carries the sign (direction).
❌ 'If $v = 0$ at an instant, the particle has stopped permanently.' ✅ $v = 0$ can be a momentary pause (top of a throw) — check the acceleration to know what happens next.
practice: Given $x(t) = 4t^3 - 2t^2 + 5$ (m): find $v(t)$ and $a(t)$; evaluate at $t = 1$ s. — $v = 12t^2 - 4t = 8$ m/s; $a = 24t - 4 = 20$ m/s².
A particle's velocity is $v(t) = 6t - 3t^2$ (m/s). When is it instantaneously at rest, and what is its acceleration then? — $t = 0$ or $2$ s; at $t = 2$: $a = 6 - 6t = -6$ m/s².
From a $v$–$t$ graph consisting of a straight line from (0, 4) to (4, 12) m/s, find the acceleration and the displacement in 4 s. — $a = 2$ m/s²; displacement = area $= \frac{4+12}{2}\times4 = 32$ m.
A stone is thrown up at 20 m/s ($g = 10$ m/s²). Find its velocity and acceleration at the highest point. — $v = 0$; $a = 10$ m/s² downward — zero velocity, non-zero acceleration.
The position of two trains is $x_1 = 20t$ and $x_2 = 5t^2$ (m). When are their instantaneous velocities equal, and where? — $20 = 10t$ → $t = 2$ s at $x = 40$ m.
universalFacts: Calculus was invented (Newton and Leibniz, 1660s–70s) precisely to handle instantaneous quantities — physics and calculus were born together, and Newton's name for the derivative was the 'fluxion'.
Car speedometers show instantaneous speed, while trip computers computing distance ÷ time show average speed — the two can differ enormously in city traffic.

Radar guns and GPS speed trackers estimate instantaneous velocity by measuring position over very small time windows — a physical implementation of the limit $\Delta x/\Delta t$ with $\Delta t \to 0$.
In relativity and quantum mechanics, instantaneous velocity remains fundamental: particle accelerators track beam particles through billions of instantaneous velocity updates per second.
examples: Example 1: $x(t) = 3t^2$ m → $v = 6t$ m/s; at $t = 2$ s the instantaneous velocity is 12 m/s, while the average velocity over 0–2 s is $\frac{12-0}{2} = 6$ m/s — different because the motion speeds up.
Example 2: A metro train's $v$–$t$ graph: trapezoid of acceleration, cruise, braking. Displacement = area of trapezoid; acceleration = slope in each segment.
Example 3: $v(t) = 8 - 4t$: the particle reverses at $t = 2$ s where $v = 0$ but $a = -4$ m/s² throughout — illustrating reversal with constant acceleration.
Example 4: Two instants with equal speeds but different velocities: $v = +10$ m/s at $t_1$ and $v = -10$ m/s at $t_2$ — same speed, opposite direction of motion.
Example 5: From $a = 6t$ and $v(0) = 2$ m/s: integrate to $v = 3t^2 + 2$ and, with $x(0) = 0$, $x = t^3 + 2t$ — showing how derivatives run downward ($x \to v \to a$) and integrals run upward.

Q2. Distinguish between average acceleration and instantaneous acceleration with one example each.

formulas: Instantaneous velocity: $v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{dx}{dt}$
Instantaneous acceleration: $a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}$
Displacement from velocity: $x_2 - x_1 = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} v\,dt$ (area under $v$–$t$ curve)
Velocity from acceleration: $v_2 - v_1 = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} a\,dt$
Rest condition: $v = \frac{dx}{dt} = 0$; reversal check: sign change of $v$ around that instant
keyPoints: Instantaneous velocity is the slope of the tangent of the $x$–$t$ graph; instantaneous acceleration is the slope of the $v$–$t$ graph.
Displacement is the area under the $v$–$t$ graph; change in velocity is the area under the $a$–$t$ graph.
$v = 0$ does not imply $a = 0$ — turning points have zero velocity but non-zero acceleration.
Speeding up ⟺ $v$ and $a$ share the same sign; slowing down ⟺ opposite signs.
Derivatives go down the chain $x \to v \to a$; integrals go up $a \to v \to x$, using initial conditions.
The limit definition is valid for ANY motion — SUVAT equations are special cases of constant acceleration only.
data.summary: Instantaneous velocity and acceleration are defined as limits: $v = dx/dt$ and $a = dv/dt = d^2x/dt^2$. Graphically, $v$ is the tangent slope of the $x$–$t$ curve and $a$ the tangent slope of the $v$–$t$ curve, while areas under $v$–$t$ and $a$–$t$ curves give displacement and velocity change. These definitions work for all motion — uniform or not — making them more fundamental than the constant-acceleration equations. Key exam skills: differentiating given $x(t)$, locating rest/reversal instants, and reading slopes and areas correctly with attention to signs.
specialNotes: Note 1: Carry units through calculus: if $x$ is in metres and $t$ in seconds, $v$ is m/s and $a$ is m/s² automatically.
Note 2: NEB graph questions award marks for BOTH slope reasoning and area reasoning — label which you used.
Note 3: When integrating acceleration, always determine integration constants from given initial conditions.
Note 4: In 'is the particle speeding up?' questions, compare signs of $v$ and $a$ at that instant — not the sign of $a$ alone.
importantStatements: Statement 1: Instantaneous velocity is the limit of average velocity as the time interval tends to zero: $v = dx/dt$.
Statement 2: Instantaneous acceleration is the derivative of velocity with respect to time: $a = dv/dt$.
Statement 3: On a position–time graph the slope of the tangent at any instant gives the instantaneous velocity at that instant.
Statement 4: The area under a velocity–time curve between two instants equals the displacement in that interval, regardless of whether the acceleration is constant.
importantNotes: Note 1: Zero instantaneous velocity does not imply zero acceleration (turning points).
Note 2: Instantaneous speed equals the magnitude of instantaneous velocity, but never carries a direction.
Note 3: For constant acceleration only, $v_{avg} = (u+v)/2$; this shortcut fails when $a$ varies.
Note 4: The calculus definitions apply to ALL motion; SUVAT equations are the special case of constant $a$.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: 'At rest' ⇒ set $dx/dt = 0$ and solve for $t$; then check the sign of $v$ on both sides to classify pause vs reversal.
Trick 2: In graph MCQs, remember: slope of $x$–$t$ = $v$; slope of $v$–$t$ = $a$; area of $v$–$t$ = $x$; area of $a$–$t$ = $v$.
Trick 3: If $x(t)$ is a polynomial, differentiate term-by-term ($d(t^n)/dt = nt^{n-1}$) — no formula sheet needed.

Trick 5: Units self-check: differentiate $x$ in metres → $v$ in m/s → $a$ in m/s²; if your units don't cascade, recheck the algebra.
