data.title: Big Bang, Hubble Law and Expansion of the Universe
data.topicTitle: Universe: Big Bang and Hubble law — expansion of the Universe
notes: **Big Bang theory:** The prevailing cosmological model describing the origin and evolution of the universe. The universe began approximately 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense initial state — the Big Bang singularity — and has been expanding and cooling ever since. All matter, energy, space, and time originated from this event.

**Hubble's law:** The recessional velocity $v$ of a galaxy is directly proportional to its distance $d$ from an observer: $v = H_0 d$. This linear relationship is the observational cornerstone of an expanding universe. The constant of proportionality $H_0$ is the Hubble constant, currently measured as $H_0 \approx 70\,\text{km/s/Mpc}$.

**Hubble parameter and time:** The Hubble time $t_H = 1/H_0 \approx 14$ billion years gives an approximate age of the universe. This is consistent with the independently measured age of 13.8 billion years from the cosmic microwave background.

**Cosmological redshift:** Light from distant galaxies is redshifted (wavelengths stretched) because the space between the source and observer is expanding during the light's travel time. The redshift $z = (\lambda_{obs} - \lambda_{emit})/\lambda_{emit}$ directly measures how much the universe has expanded since the light was emitted.

**Doppler redshift vs. cosmological redshift:** For nearby galaxies ($z < 0.01$), recession velocity is given by the special-relativistic Doppler formula $v \approx cz$. For distant galaxies, cosmological redshift is due to the expansion of space itself, not the motion of galaxies through space — they are at rest in the expanding space.

**Evidence for the Big Bang:** (1) Hubble expansion (1929): galaxies recede at speeds proportional to distance. (2) Cosmic microwave background (1965): Penzias and Wilson discovered uniform 2.7 K radiation — relic from hot early universe. (3) Big Bang nucleosynthesis predictions: ~25% helium abundance matches observations. (4) Galaxy evolution: lookback time shows younger galaxies in the distant past.

**Cosmic microwave background (CMB):** The cooled relic radiation from ~380,000 years after the Big Bang, when the universe became transparent to photons. Originally at ~3000 K (emitting visible light), it has redshifted to 2.725 K. The CMB is uniform to 1 part in 100,000 — tiny temperature fluctuations reveal the seeds of all cosmic structure.

**Scale factor:** The relative expansion of the universe is described by the scale factor $a(t)$, where distances scale as $d(t) = a(t) d_0$. Hubble's law in general form: $\dot{a}/a = H(t)$, where $H(t)$ is the Hubble parameter that varies with cosmic time. Currently $H \approx H_0$, but in the past $H$ was much larger.

**Friedmann equations:** The dynamics of an expanding universe are governed by Einstein's field equations: $H^2 = (\dot{a}/a)^2 = \frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho - \frac{kc^2}{a^2} + \frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}$. The curvature parameter $k$ can be $-1$, $0$, or $+1$ (open, flat, or closed universe). Current observations show the universe is spatially flat ($k = 0$).

**Dark energy and accelerating expansion:** In 1998, observations of distant Type Ia supernovae showed the expansion of the universe is ACCELERATING. This requires a dominant form of energy with negative pressure — dark energy — acting as a cosmological constant $\Lambda$. Dark energy makes up ~68% of the total energy density of the universe.

**Timeline of the universe:** Planck epoch (< 10⁻⁴³ s) → Grand unification epoch → Inflationary epoch (10⁻³⁶ to 10⁻³² s, universe expanded by factor ~10²⁶) → Electroweak epoch → Quark epoch → Hadron epoch → Photon epoch → Nucleosynthesis (3 min, formed H, He) → Recombination (380,000 yr, CMB released) → Galaxy formation → Solar system (9 Gyr) → Today (13.8 Gyr).

**NEB exam focus:** State and explain Hubble's law $v = H_0 d$. Calculate recession velocities and distances using the Hubble constant. Distinguish between Doppler redshift and cosmological redshift. Explain the evidence for the Big Bang theory. Calculate the age of the universe from $H_0$.

**Olbers' paradox:** If the universe were infinite, static, and uniformly filled with stars, the night sky should be as bright as the surface of a star. The resolution is that the universe has a finite age and is expanding — stars have finite lifetimes and light from distant stars hasn't had time to reach us.

**Critical density:** The density that makes the universe spatially flat: $\rho_c = 3H_0^2/(8\pi G) \approx 9.5 \times 10^{-27}\,\text{kg/m}^3$. Current density: ordinary matter ~5%, dark matter ~27%, dark energy ~68%. Total density equals critical density to within 0.5% — the universe is flat.

**Grandfather paradox and causality:** The finite age of the universe (~13.8 Gyr) and the finite speed of light mean that there is a cosmological horizon — regions of space from which light has not yet had time to reach us. We cannot observe the entire universe.

**Inflationary cosmology:** In the first 10⁻³² seconds, the universe underwent exponential expansion by a factor of at least 10²⁶. This explains the uniformity of the CMB (horizon problem), the flatness of space (flatness problem), and the absence of magnetic monopoles (monopole problem). Inflation was driven by a scalar inflaton field.
confusion: ❌ The Big Bang was an explosion in space. ✅ The Big Bang was the BEGINNING of space and time itself. There was no pre-existing space into which the universe exploded. Space, time, matter, and energy all came into existence together.

❌ Hubble's law applies to all galaxies in the same way. ✅ Hubble's law $v = H_0 d$ applies to galaxies that are not gravitationally bound to each other. Galaxies within the same cluster can have peculiar velocities that deviate from the Hubble flow.

❌ Redshift means galaxies are moving through space away from us. ✅ Cosmological redshift is caused by the EXPANSION OF SPACE ITSELF. Galaxies are at rest in their local frame; space expands and stretches the wavelength of light as it travels.

❌ The universe was always expanding at the current rate. ✅ The expansion rate has changed dramatically over cosmic history. In the early universe, expansion was decelerating due to gravity; around 4 billion years ago, dark energy began to dominate and expansion began accelerating.

❌ The CMB is the leftover heat from the Big Bang explosion. ✅ The CMB is the thermal radiation from the hot plasma that filled the universe 380,000 years after the Big Bang, when it cooled enough to become transparent. It is not from the initial explosion but from the state of the universe at recombination.

❌ Dark energy and dark matter are the same thing. ✅ Dark matter (27%) interacts gravitationally but not electromagnetically. Dark energy (68%) is a property of space itself causing accelerated expansion. They are completely different phenomena with different effects.

❌ The Hubble constant has been measured precisely and is not changing. ✅ $H_0$ (the current value) is measured precisely (~70 km/s/Mpc), but the Hubble parameter $H(t)$ varies with cosmic time. Dark energy causes $H(t)$ to decrease at first, then stabilize as dark energy dominates.
practice: A galaxy is observed to have a recession velocity of 14,000 km/s. Using $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc, find its distance. $d = v/H_0 = 14,000/70 = 200$ Mpc. At 1 Mpc = 3.26 million light years, this galaxy is $200 \times 3.26 = 652$ million light-years away.

A galaxy at distance 400 Mpc has a redshift $z = 0.095$. Find the recession velocity. For small $z$, $v \approx cz = 3 \times 10^5 \times 0.095 = 28,500$ km/s. Using Hubble's law: $v = H_0 d = 70 \times 400 = 28,000$ km/s. Good agreement! At larger $z$, the linear approximation breaks down and relativistic formulas are needed.

A galaxy has redshift $z = 2$. How much has the universe expanded since the light was emitted? $1 + z = a_{now}/a_{then}$, so the scale factor was $a_{then} = a_{now}/(1+z) = a_{now}/3$. The universe was 3 times smaller when the light was emitted. Light took billions of years to reach us.

The age of the universe estimated from the Hubble constant is $t_H = 1/H_0$. If $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc, show this gives ~14 billion years. $1/H_0 = 1/(70\,\text{km/s/Mpc}) = (3.09 \times 10^{19}\,\text{km})/70\,\text{km/s} = 4.41 \times 10^{17}$ s $= 14.0 \times 10^9$ yr = 14 billion years. This is a rough estimate because expansion was different in the past.

If the universe doubles in size in the future, what will happen to the Hubble parameter? For a matter-dominated universe, $H \propto a^{-3/2}$, so doubling $a$ reduces $H$ by $2^{-3/2} \approx 0.35$. But dark energy-dominated universes have constant $H$. Observations suggest $H$ will approach a constant ~57 km/s/Mpc.

Why do we see the cosmic microwave background coming from all directions at the same temperature? During inflation, regions that are now far apart were in causal contact — they exchanged information and thermalized. When inflation expanded them apart faster than light could communicate between them, they lost contact. The uniformity we see today reflects their early thermal equilibrium, preserved in the CMB.
universalFacts: The cosmic microwave background was discovered accidentally by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson in 1965 while working on radio communications. They received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1978. The CMB is the most perfect black body in nature, matching Planck's law to extraordinary precision.

The 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Perlmutter, Schmidt, and Riess for the 1998 discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe — implying that ~68% of the universe consists of dark energy. This was one of the most shocking discoveries in cosmology.

The Planck satellite (2009-2013) measured the CMB temperature fluctuations to microkelvin precision, determining the universe's age (13.82 Gyr), composition (68.3% dark energy, 26.8% dark matter, 4.9% ordinary matter), and geometry (flat to 0.4%).

The Hubble Space Telescope was named after Edwin Hubble, who in 1929 published his landmark paper establishing the linear relationship between distance and recession velocity for galaxies — the observational foundation of modern cosmology.

The concept of an expanding universe was first suggested by Alexander Friedmann in 1922 and independently by Georges Lemaître in 1927, who proposed a 'primeval atom' — essentially the Big Bang — as the origin of the universe.

data.topicTitle: Universe: Big Bang and Hubble law — expansion of the Universe
data.summary: The Big Bang theory describes the universe originating from an extremely hot, dense state ~13.8 billion years ago and expanding ever since. Hubble's Law v = H₀d states that galaxies recede at speeds proportional to their distance, providing direct evidence for cosmic expansion. The Hubble constant H₀ ≈ 70 km/s/Mpc quantifies the current expansion rate.
notes: Big Bang Theory: The universe began as a singularity of infinite density and temperature approximately 13.8 × 10⁹ years ago. Space itself expanded, cooling the universe and allowing formation of subatomic particles, atoms, stars, and galaxies over time.

Cosmic Timeline: t = 0: Singularity. t < 10⁻⁴³ s: Planck epoch (quantum gravity). t ~ 10⁻³⁶ s: Inflationary epoch (exponential expansion). t ~ 3 min: Nucleosynthesis (H, He, Li formed). t ~ 380,000 yr: Recombination (CMB released). t ~ 400 Myr: First stars. t ~ 9 Gyr: Solar system forms.

Evidence for Big Bang: (1) Hubble's Law — galaxies receding proportionally to distance. (2) Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) — 2.725 K blackbody radiation, uniform to 1 part in 10⁵. (3) Abundance of light elements — H:He ratio ~3:1 matches nucleosynthesis predictions. (4) Large-scale structure — galaxy distribution matches gravitational growth from initial fluctuations.

Hubble's Law: v = H₀d, where v is recession velocity, d is proper distance, and H₀ is Hubble constant. Discovered by Edwin Hubble in 1929 using Cepheid variable stars as standard candles. Current best estimate: H₀ ≈ 67–74 km/s/Mpc (tension between CMB and local measurements).

Interpretation of Redshift: Cosmological redshift z = Δλ/λ is NOT Doppler shift from motion through space. It results from stretching of photon wavelengths as space expands during transit. For small z: v ≈ cz; for large z: relativistic cosmology required.

Hubble Time and Age: t_H = 1/H₀ ≈ 14.4 Gyr gives rough age estimate assuming constant expansion. Actual age differs due to deceleration (matter domination) then acceleration (dark energy). Current age: 13.8 Gyr from ΛCDM model fitting.

Expansion of Space vs Motion Through Space: Galaxies are not flying apart through pre-existing space. Space itself is stretching, carrying galaxies with it. No center exists — every observer sees others receding. Analogy: dots on inflating balloon surface.

Dark Energy and Accelerated Expansion: Type Ia supernovae observations (1998) revealed expansion is accelerating, not slowing. Attributed to dark energy (Λ in Einstein's equations), constituting ~68% of total energy density. Fate: eternal accelerated expansion ('Big Freeze').

Limitations and Open Questions: Singularity problem (quantum gravity needed). Horizon problem (solved by inflation). Flatness problem (solved by inflation). Nature of dark matter (~27%) and dark energy (~68%). Multiverse speculation from eternal inflation.

specificConditions: Homogeneity and Isotropy: Cosmological principle assumes universe looks same everywhere (homogeneous) and in all directions (isotropic) on large scales (>100 Mpc). Validated by CMB uniformity and galaxy surveys.
General Relativity Framework: Expansion described by Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker metric derived from Einstein's field equations. Newtonian mechanics insufficient for cosmological scales.
Redshift-Distance Relation Linear Only Locally: v = H₀d holds for z < 0.1. Higher redshifts require full relativistic treatment with scale factor a(t) and cosmological parameters Ω_m, Ω_Λ.

Hubble Constant Tension: Local distance ladder (Cepheids + SNe Ia) gives H₀ ≈ 73 km/s/Mpc; CMB (Planck satellite) gives H₀ ≈ 67.4 km/s/Mpc. Discrepancy unresolved — possible new physics or systematic errors.
formulas: Hubble's Law: $v = H_0 d$
Redshift: $z = \frac{\lambda_{obs} - \lambda_{emit}}{\lambda_{emit}} = \frac{a(t_{now})}{a(t_{emit})} - 1$
Hubble time: $t_H = \frac{1}{H_0}$
Scale factor relation: $1 + z = \frac{a(t_0)}{a(t)}$
Friedmann equation: $H^2 = \frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho - \frac{kc^2}{a^2} + \frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}$
Critical density: $\rho_c = \frac{3H_0^2}{8\pi G}$

data.title: Universe and Big Bang
notes: **Big Bang model.** The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago in an extremely hot, dense state and has been expanding and cooling ever since; space itself expands, galaxies recede from each other.
**Hubble's evidence.** Galaxies show redshift proportional to distance (v = H₀d) — the expansion law that founded observational cosmology.
**Cosmic microwave background.** The faint 2.7 K microwave glow filling the sky is the cooled remnant of the fireball, released when atoms formed about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
**Primordial nucleosynthesis.** In the first minutes, nuclear fusion made hydrogen, helium and traces of lithium; all heavier elements were forged later inside stars.
**Timeline.** Inflation → matter–radiation equality → recombination and CMB → first stars and galaxies → solar system (about 9 Gyr later) → planets and life.

Hubble's observation is that distant galaxies recede, and the recession speed is roughly proportional to the distance. Running that expansion backward leads to a hot, dense early state. The cosmic microwave background is the leftover radiation from that state, now cooled to about 2.7 K.

data.title: Dark Matter, Black Holes and Gravitational Waves
data.topicTitle: Dark matter, black hole and gravitational wave
notes: **Dark matter:** A form of matter that does not emit, absorb, or reflect electromagnetic radiation — it is completely invisible to all telescopes. Its presence is inferred solely from gravitational effects on visible matter, light, and the large-scale structure of the universe. Dark matter comprises approximately 27% of the universe's total energy density.

**Evidence for dark matter — galaxy rotation curves:** Stars in spiral galaxies orbit the galactic center. Newtonian mechanics predicts orbital velocity should decrease with distance from the center ($v \propto 1/\sqrt{r}$). Instead, rotation curves remain FLAT at large radii — stars maintain the same orbital speed far from the visible disk. This requires additional invisible mass (dark matter halo) extending far beyond the visible galaxy.

**Evidence — gravitational lensing:** Dark matter bends light from background galaxies through gravitational lensing. The pattern and strength of lensing arcs around galaxy clusters reveal the total mass distribution, which is consistently much larger than the visible mass. The Bullet Cluster (two colliding galaxy clusters) provides the most direct evidence: the hot gas (visible) has been separated from the dark matter (detected via lensing).

**Evidence — large-scale structure and CMB:** Dark matter was essential in the early universe: its gravity pulled matter together to form the first stars and galaxies. Without dark matter, the universe would look very different. CMB measurements precisely constrain the dark matter density to 26.8% of the critical density.

**Candidates for dark matter:** (1) WIMPs (Weakly Interacting Massive Particles) — hypothetical particles that interact only through gravity and the weak force. (2) Axions — very light particles proposed to solve the strong CP problem. (3) Primordial black holes — black holes formed in the early universe. All remain undetected as of 2026.

**Black hole definition:** A region of spacetime where gravity is so overwhelmingly strong that nothing — not even light or any other form of information — can escape once it crosses the event horizon. Black holes are solutions to Einstein's field equations of general relativity.

**Schwarzschild radius (event horizon):** The radius of the event horizon for a non-rotating, uncharged black hole: $R_s = \frac{2GM}{c^2}$. For a one solar mass black hole: $R_s \approx 3$ km. For a billion-solar-mass supermassive black hole: $R_s \approx 3 \times 10^9$ km (~20 AU).

**Types of black holes:** (1) Stellar-mass black holes ($3-100 M_\odot$) formed from collapsed massive stars. (2) Intermediate-mass black holes ($100-10^5 M_\odot$) — formation mechanism uncertain. (3) Supermassive black holes ($10^6-10^{10} M_\odot$) found at the centers of most galaxies, including the Milky Way's Sagittarius A* ($4 \times 10^6 M_\odot$).

**Hawking radiation:** Stephen Hawking predicted in 1974 that black holes emit thermal radiation due to quantum effects near the event horizon. The temperature is $T = \frac{\hbar c^3}{8\pi G M k_B}$ — extremely tiny for astrophysical black holes. For a solar-mass black hole: $T \approx 6 \times 10^{-8}$ K. Black holes lose mass over time and eventually evaporate.

**Gravitational waves (gravitational radiation):** Ripples in the fabric of spacetime caused by accelerating masses, propagating at the speed of light. Predicted by Einstein in 1916 as a consequence of general relativity. Unlike electromagnetic waves, gravitational waves are quadrupolar and interact extremely weakly with matter — they pass through everything essentially unimpeded.

**Gravitational wave detection — LIGO:** The Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory detected its first gravitational wave (GW150914) on September 14, 2015 from two black holes (~36 and 29 solar masses) merging 1.3 billion light-years away. The signal lasted 0.2 seconds, with peak strain $h \approx 10^{-21}$.

**LIGO interferometer principle:** Each LIGO detector is an L-shaped Michelson interferometer with 4 km arms. A passing gravitational wave stretches one arm and compresses the other alternately, changing the arm length difference by ~10⁻¹⁸ m (one-thousandth the diameter of a proton). Laser interferometry detects this tiny change.

**Gravitational wave sources:** (1) Binary black hole mergers — most massive, detectable to billions of light-years. (2) Binary neutron star mergers — also produce optical counterparts (kilonovae), observed in GW170817. (3) Supernovae — asymmetric explosions produce detectable bursts. (4) Pulsars — rapidly rotating neutron stars with tiny asymmetries. (5) Primordial gravitational waves — from cosmic inflation, detectable in the CMB B-mode polarization.

**Multi-messenger astronomy:** GW170817 (August 2017) was detected by LIGO and Virgo, and 1.7 seconds later, the Fermi GBM detected a gamma-ray burst from the same location. This confirmed that neutron star mergers produce short gamma-ray bursts and heavy elements (gold, platinum) through r-process nucleosynthesis.

**NEB exam focus:** State the evidence for dark matter. Calculate the Schwarzschild radius. Explain gravitational wave generation and detection. Distinguish between dark matter, dark energy, and black holes. Solve problems using $R_s = 2GM/c^2$.

**Black hole information paradox:** In quantum mechanics, information cannot be destroyed. But Hawking radiation causes black holes to evaporate, seemingly destroying information. This paradox — whether information is lost or preserved — remains one of the deepest unsolved problems in theoretical physics.

**Event horizon telescope:** In 2019, the EHT collaboration released the first image of a black hole — the supermassive black hole in galaxy M87 (6.5 billion solar masses) — as a silhouette against surrounding hot gas. The image confirmed predictions of general relativity about the shadow's size and shape.
**Dark matter.** About 27% of the universe is invisible matter detected only through its gravity; it neither emits nor absorbs light and outweighs visible matter roughly five to one.

**Evidence for dark matter.** Galaxy rotation curves stay flat far from the centre (Kepler's law fails), gravitational lensing is stronger than visible mass allows, and the CMB pattern fixes its share of the energy budget.
**Black holes.** Where gravity is so strong that the escape velocity reaches c, nothing — not even light — can leave; the horizon radius is the Schwarzschild radius r_s = 2GM/c².
**Signatures.** A black hole is revealed by its effects: stars orbiting an invisible companion, X-rays from a glowing accretion disc, and gravitational waves from merging black holes (LIGO).
**Modern imaging.** The Event Horizon Telescope photographed the shadow of M87's central black hole, testing general relativity in the strong-field regime.

Dark matter is unseen mass inferred because galaxies rotate too fast in their outer parts for the bright stars to be all the mass. A black hole is a mass so compact that the escape speed at its horizon is the speed of light. Gravitational waves are ripples of spacetime, detected as a tiny stretching and squeezing of a distance.

confusion: ❌ Dark matter is the same as dark energy. ✅ Dark matter (27%) is a form of mass that exerts gravitational attraction — it clumps and forms structure. Dark energy (68%) is a property of space itself that causes accelerated expansion and does not clump. They are fundamentally different.

❌ Black holes suck in everything around them. ✅ Outside the event horizon, black holes behave like any other object of the same mass. A black hole's gravity at the distance of Earth's orbit is identical to the Sun's. Black holes are dangerous only if you get very close.

❌ Nothing can escape from inside a black hole, not even light. ✅ This is the DEFINITION of an event horizon. Nothing, not even light, can escape once inside $R_s$. This is why they are called black holes.

❌ Gravitational waves are made of matter. ✅ Gravitational waves are ripples in SPACETIME ITSELF — not made of any material substance. They propagate through empty space at the speed of light, carrying energy.

❌ Dark matter is composed of familiar particles we just haven't detected yet. ✅ Most dark matter cannot be composed of Standard Model particles (electrons, protons, neutrons, neutrinos). Known neutrinos are too light and too abundant in the wrong way. Dark matter must be a new type of particle or form of matter beyond the Standard Model.

❌ Black holes are infinitely dense singularities. ✅ The singularity at the center is a breakdown of general relativity where density becomes infinite — but this is likely a mathematical artifact. In quantum gravity (not yet fully developed), the singularity would be replaced by something finite.

❌ Gravitational waves are easy to detect because they are so energetic. ✅ Gravitational waves interact extremely weakly with matter. The strain is $h \approx 10^{-21}$ — LIGO measures changes in arm length of one part in $10^{21}$. They pass through the Earth without any interaction, which makes detection both fascinating and extremely challenging.

practice: Calculate the Schwarzschild radius for (a) a 10 solar mass black hole, (b) the Earth. For (a): $R_s = 2GM/c^2 = 2(6.67 \times 10^{-11})(2 \times 10^{31})/(9 \times 10^{16}) \approx 30$ km. For (b): $M = 6 \times 10^{24}$ kg, $R_s = 2 \times 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24} / (9 \times 10^{16}) = 8.9$ mm. The Earth would become a black hole if compressed to the size of a pea!

A galaxy cluster has a total mass of $10^{14} M_\odot$ but visible mass of only $3 \times 10^{13} M_\odot$. What fraction is dark matter? Dark matter fraction = $(10^{14} - 3 \times 10^{13})/10^{14} = 70\%$. Dark matter is 7 times the visible mass — this is typical for galaxy clusters.

Two black holes, each of mass $M$, merge to form a black hole. What is the mass of the final black hole? The final mass is LESS than $2M$. During merger, energy is radiated away as gravitational waves. For a non-rotating head-on merger, $\Delta M/M \approx 5.7\%$. This energy can be detected as gravitational waves billions of light-years away.

The LIGO detector has arm length 4 km. If a gravitational wave of strain $h = 10^{-21}$ passes, how much does each arm change in length? $\Delta L = h \times L = 10^{-21} \times 4000 = 4 \times 10^{-18}$ m = 0.000004 femtometers. This is $1/1000$ the diameter of a proton. Advanced LIGO achieves this by measuring laser phase differences over hundreds of reflections.

The supermassive black hole at the center of M87 has mass $6.5 \times 10^9 M_\odot$. Calculate its Schwarzschild radius. $R_s = 2GM/c^2$. Using $R_{s,\odot} = 3$ km: $R_s = 3 \times 6.5 \times 10^9 = 1.95 \times 10^{10}$ km $\approx 130$ AU $\approx$ the size of Pluto's orbit. The event horizon is enormous.

A dark matter particle has mass $m$. Estimate its characteristic size if it is a Compton wavelength-sized primordial black hole. The Compton wavelength is $\lambda_C = h/(mc)$. If $R_s = 2Gm/c^2 = \lambda_C/2$, then $m = \sqrt{hc/(2G)} \approx m_P/\sqrt{2}$, where $m_P = \sqrt{\hbar c/G} \approx 21.7$ μg is the Planck mass. This gives $m \approx 15$ μg — suggesting Planck-mass dark matter candidates.

A neutron star has mass $2 M_\odot$ and radius 10 km. Calculate its surface gravity. $g = GM/R^2 = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 4 \times 10^{30} / (10^5)^2 = 2.67 \times 10^{12}$ m/s² $\approx 2.7 \times 10^{11} g$. The escape velocity from the surface is $v = \sqrt{2GM/R} \approx 0.6c$ — almost the speed of light!

universalFacts: The 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish, and Kip Thorne for LIGO's detection of gravitational waves — confirming a prediction Einstein made in 1916 and opening a completely new window on the universe.

The Event Horizon Telescope (2019) imaged the black hole shadow in M87, showing a ring of radio emission surrounding a dark center. The image matched general relativistic predictions to high precision, confirming black hole properties predicted by Einstein's theory.

The Higgs boson discovery at CERN in 2012 confirmed that mass arises from interaction with the Higgs field. However, the mass of the Higgs (125 GeV) is far below the natural scale suggested by quantum corrections — the 'hierarchy problem', potentially solved by supersymmetry or other BSM physics.

The LIGO-Virgo collaboration has detected over 100 gravitational wave events from binary black hole and neutron star mergers since 2015. Each detection opens a new channel for studying the universe — gravitational wave astronomy is now a mature field.

Dark matter detection experiments (XENON, LUX, PandaX) use ultra-sensitive underground detectors looking for WIMP-nucleus scattering. As of 2026, no dark matter particle has been directly detected, ruling out much of the WIMP parameter space and motivating alternative candidates.

data.topicTitle: Dark Matter, Black Holes and Gravitational Waves
notes: **Dark matter.** About 27% of the universe is invisible matter detected only through its gravity; it neither emits nor absorbs light and outweighs visible matter roughly five to one.

**Evidence for dark matter.** Galaxy rotation curves stay flat far from the centre (Kepler's law fails), gravitational lensing is stronger than visible mass allows, and the CMB pattern fixes its share of the energy budget.
**Black holes.** Where gravity is so strong that the escape velocity reaches c, nothing — not even light — can leave; the horizon radius is the Schwarzschild radius r_s = 2GM/c².
**Signatures.** A black hole is revealed by its effects: stars orbiting an invisible companion, X-rays from a glowing accretion disc, and gravitational waves from merging black holes (LIGO).
**Modern imaging.** The Event Horizon Telescope photographed the shadow of M87's central black hole, testing general relativity in the strong-field regime.

data.title: Mirror Formula
notes: A spherical reflecting surface acts as a spherical mirror. For paraxial rays, a concave mirror converges parallel rays to a real focus; a convex mirror makes them diverge from a virtual focus.
The centre of curvature C is distance R from pole P; paraxial focus F is halfway between, so f=R/2. Wide-angle marginal rays do not meet this approximation exactly.
Using Cartesian distances positive to the right, a concave mirror has f=−15 cm. For u=−30 cm, 1/v=1/f−1/u=−1/15+1/30=−1/30, so v=−30 cm and m=−v/u=−1.

Construct an image with a ray parallel to the principal axis (reflected through F for a concave mirror) and a ray through C (retraces itself). Their intersection locates a real image; backward extensions locate a virtual image.
Spherical aberration occurs when marginal rays focus differently from paraxial rays. A smaller aperture reduces it by excluding marginal rays.

When an object is closer to a concave mirror than the focus, the formula gives a positive v. In the Cartesian convention that positive image distance is behind the mirror, and the image is virtual, upright and enlarged. The same formula covers both the real and the virtual cases. The sign does the work.

data.title: Laws of Refraction and Refractive Index
notes: **Snell's law (First law of refraction):** When light passes obliquely from one medium to another, $\frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \text{constant} = \frac{n_2}{n_1}$, where $i$ is the angle of incidence, $r$ is the angle of refraction, and $n_1$, $n_2$ are the refractive indices of the first and second media respectively. This law is the basis of all refraction phenomena.

**Refractive index definition:** $n = \frac{c}{v}$, where $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ is the speed of light in vacuum and $v$ is its speed in the medium. Since $v < c$ always, $n > 1$ for all real materials. Higher $n$ means light travels slower in that medium.

**Relative refractive index:** $n_{21} = \frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{v_1}{v_2}$. This is the refractive index of medium 2 as seen from medium 1. When light enters a denser medium ($n_2 > n_1$), it bends TOWARD the normal. When entering a rarer medium, it bends AWAY from the normal.

**Laws of reflection (concurrent with refraction):** The incident ray, reflected ray, and normal all lie in the same plane. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection ($i = r$). These laws apply at both the reflecting and refracting surfaces.

**Dispersion of light:** White light splits into its constituent colors when refracted because different wavelengths travel at different speeds in a medium. Red (long λ) has $n_{red} < n_{blue}$ (short λ). This is why prisms disperse white light into a spectrum.

**Rainbow formation (primary rainbow):** Water droplets act as spherical prisms. Light enters, refracts, reflects once inside the droplet, then refracts again on exit. Red emerges at about 42° and violet at about 40° from the backscattering direction. The secondary rainbow (24°) forms from two internal reflections.

**Dispersive power of a material:** $\omega = \frac{n_F - n_C}{n_D}$, where $n_F$, $n_C$, $n_D$ are the refractive indices for blue (Fraunhofer F), red (Fraunhofer C), and yellow (Fraunhofer D, sodium D line) light respectively. Higher ω means more dispersion.

**Abbe number:** $V_D = \frac{n_D - 1}{n_F - n_C}$. This is the reciprocal of dispersive power, scaled and shifted. Gases have $V_D \gg 1$ (negligible dispersion). Crown glass has $V_D \approx 60$, flint glass $V_D \approx 30$.

**Limiting cases of Snell's law:** When $i = 0°$: $r = 0°$ (normal incidence, no bending). When $n_2 \ll n_1$: the ray undergoes total internal reflection if $i > 90°$, which is impossible, so this explains why very high-index materials can guide light.

**Critical angle derivation:** At the critical angle, $r = 90°$, so $\sin i_c = \frac{1}{n_2/n_1} = \frac{n_1}{n_2}$. In terms of refractive indices: $\sin i_c = \frac{n_{rarer}}{n_{denser}}$. For glass ($n = 1.52$): $i_c = \arcsin(1/1.52) \approx 41.1°$.

**Total Internal Reflection (TIR):** When $i > i_c$, no refracted ray exists. 100% of the light is reflected back into the denser medium. This is COMPLETELY different from ordinary reflection at a surface where typically 85-95% is reflected.

**NEB exam focus:** Apply Snell's law to find angles of incidence and refraction. Calculate refractive indices from speed of light data. Understand the conditions for TIR and calculate critical angles. Draw accurate ray diagrams showing refraction at plane surfaces.

**Evanescent wave and frustrated TIR:** Just below the critical angle, an evanescent wave penetrates the rarer medium and decays exponentially. If another medium is brought within ~1 wavelength, this wave can transfer energy — this is the principle behind atomic force microscopy and photon tunneling sensors.

**Practical applications — prisms:** At least 40° apex angle prisms rely on TIR (as in Porro prisms and binocular roof prisms). Right-angle prisms use TIR at two internal surfaces. This provides 100% reflection without coating, unlike mirrors which lose 10-15% per reflection.

**Astronomical applications — refractive index of air:** Even air has $n \approx 1.0003$ at STP. This causes atmospheric refraction, making stars appear ~0.5° higher than their true positions. This effect must be corrected in precise astronomical measurements.

**Biological applications — eye lens:** The human crystalline lens has varying refractive index from center to periphery and from front to back, allowing it to focus light onto the retina for all distances. The cornea contributes ~70% of the eye's refractive power ($n_{cornea} \approx 1.376$).

**Wave optical interpretation:** The phase change upon reflection depends on the relative indices. When reflecting off a medium with higher $n$, there is a 180° phase shift (equivalent to a path difference of λ/2). This determines whether thin film interference is constructive or destructive.
confusion: ❌ Snell's law is $n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2$ with no mention of which is larger. ✅ Snell's law shows that when $n_2 > n_1$: $\sin\theta_2 < \sin\theta_1$, so $r < i$ (ray bends toward normal). When $n_2 < n_1$: $r > i$ (ray bends away from normal). The direction of bending is determined by the relative densities.

❌ The refractive index $n$ can be less than 1. ✅ For real materials at optical frequencies, $n > 1$ because $v < c$. In some special cases (metamaterials at microwave frequencies), engineered materials can have $n < 1$, but this doesn't apply to standard optical media.

❌ A larger refractive index means faster light in that medium. ✅ LARGER refractive index means SLOWER light. The relationship is $n = c/v$: larger $n$ means smaller $v$. Diamond ($n \approx 2.4$) is optically the fastest glass.

❌ The critical angle formula is $\sin\theta_c = \frac{n_1}{n_2}$. ✅ The correct formula is $\sin\theta_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1}$ where $n_1 > n_2$ (denser to rarer). Using $\frac{n_1}{n_2} \approx \frac{1.52}{1} = 1.52 > 1$ would give $\sin\theta_c > 1$, which is impossible for real angles.
❌ Total internal reflection means all light is absorbed and disappears. ✅ TIR means ALL light is REFLECTED back. No transmission occurs, but the light energy is preserved in the reflected beam.

❌ Dispersion only happens with prisms. ✅ Dispersion occurs at EVERY refracting surface. Prisms make dispersion visible because they have large apex angles, but rainbows form from millions of tiny atmospheric droplets acting as prisms.

❌ The angle of refraction is always greater than the angle of incidence. ✅ Refraction angle is SMALLER than incidence angle when entering denser medium, and LARGER when entering rarer medium. The ray bends toward normal in denser medium, away in rarer medium.
practice: A ray of light in water ($n = 1.33$) is incident on a water-to-air interface at 35°. Find the angle of refraction. Since light is going from water to air (denser to rarer), $n_1 = 1.33$, $n_2 = 1$, $i = 35°$. $\sin r = n_1\sin i / n_2 = 1.33 \times \sin 35° / 1 = 1.33 \times 0.574 = 0.763$. $r = \arcsin(0.763) = 49.7°$. The ray bends away from the normal (49.7° > 35°).

Find the critical angle for diamond ($n = 2.42$) in air. $\sin\theta_c = n_{air}/n_{diamond} = 1/2.42 = 0.413$. $\theta_c = \arcsin(0.413) = 24.4°$. This is why cut diamonds are so brilliant — many possible paths for light undergo TIR.

A ray strikes a glass slab ($n = 1.5$) at 60° to the normal. (a) Find the angle inside the glass. $\sin r = \sin 60°/1.5 = 0.866/1.5 = 0.577$, so $r = 35.3°$. (b) The emergent ray makes what angle with the normal? Since the slab has parallel faces, the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, so it emerges at 60° to the normal.

A fiber optic cable uses glass with core index 1.48 and cladding index 1.46. Find the critical angle at the core-cladding interface. $\sin\theta_c = n_{clad}/n_{core} = 1.46/1.48 = 0.986$. $\theta_c = \arcsin(0.986) = 80.4°$. Light incident at angles greater than 80.4° to the normal undergoes TIR and is guided down the fiber.

White light (λ = 400 nm to 700 nm) enters a glass prism ($n_{blue} = 1.53$, $n_{red} = 1.51$). Calculate the dispersion angle (the angle between blue and red rays after one refraction). For incident angle 45°: $\sin\theta_{blue} = \sin 45°/1.53 = 0.463$, $\theta_{blue} = 27.6°$. $\sin\theta_{red} = \sin 45°/1.51 = 0.470$, $\theta_{red} = 28.1°$. Dispersion = 0.5° per interface. With two refractions in a prism, total dispersion is larger.

A glass window has refractive index 1.5. An object 30 cm behind the glass appears to be how far behind the glass? The apparent depth formula when viewing perpendicular to the surface: $d_{apparent} = d_{real}/n = 30/1.5 = 20$ cm. The object appears 20 cm behind the glass instead of 30 cm. For oblique viewing, both lateral shift and apparent depth occur.

Light travels through 2 m of glass ($n = 1.5$), then 3 m of water ($n = 1.33$), then air. Find the total optical path length (in wavelengths). Optical path length = $\sum n_i d_i$. OPL = $1.5 \times 2 + 1.33 \times 3 + 1 \times 0 = 3 + 3.99 = 6.99$ m. The optical path is the same as if the light had traveled 6.99 m in vacuum.
universalFacts: Snell's law was first quantitatively formulated by Willebrord Snellius (Snell) in 1621, though the law was known to Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) in the 11th century. Fermat's principle of least time provides the variational derivation of Snell's law.

The refractive index varies with wavelength (dispersion) because the polarization response of matter to electric fields depends on frequency. This is fundamental to fiber optics, laser technology, and understanding celestial atmospherics.

In special relativity, vacuum ($n = 1$) is the only medium where phase velocity equals the universal speed limit $c$. In other media, $v = c/n < c$, but signal velocity can still propagate at speeds approaching $c$.

Metamaterials engineered at optical frequencies can have negative refractive index ($n < 0$), leading to backwards radiation where the wave vector points opposite to the energy flow. This enables perfect lenses and novel waveguides.

The Abbe number $V_D$ is the primary specification for choosing optical glass. High-dispersion (low $V_D$) glasses like flint are used for prisms. Low-dispersion (high $V_D$) glasses like crown minimize chromatic aberration in lenses.

data.title: Laws of Refraction
notes: **Refraction.** Light bends while crossing obliquely between media of different optical density because its speed changes; it bends towards the normal entering a denser medium and away from it leaving.
**Snell's law.** For a ray crossing the boundary, n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r, with the incident ray, refracted ray and normal all in one plane and sin i/sin r constant for the pair of media.
**Refractive index.** The absolute index of a medium is n = c/v; the relative index of medium 2 w.r.t. 1 is n₂₁ = v₁/v₂ = sin i/sin r = 1/n₁₂.
**Apparent depth.** Viewed normally, a depth t appears as t/n; the normal shift is t(1 − 1/n) — the standard numerical on river depth and pooled objects.
**Dispersion's origin.** Because v depends on wavelength, n_violet > n_red; white light refracting at a surface separates colour — the seed of the prism spectrum.

Refraction bends a ray toward the normal when it enters a slower medium. The index is the vacuum speed divided by the speed in the medium, and Snell's law uses that index. Frequency stays the same, so a higher index means a shorter wavelength.

data.title: Lateral Shift
notes: **Lateral Shift:** This topic covers the fundamental concepts of lateral shift in the physics curriculum.
Understanding lateral shift is essential for solving problems and building higher-level mathematical skills.
Key definitions and theorems related to lateral shift should be memorized and practiced regularly.

**Definition:** When a ray of light passes through a parallel-sided transparent slab (like a glass slab), it emerges parallel to the original direction but displaced sideways. This perpendicular displacement is called the lateral shift (or lateral displacement).
**Formula:** $d = t \cdot \frac{\sin(i - r)}{\cos r}$, where $t$ is the thickness of the slab, $i$ is the angle of incidence, and $r$ is the angle of refraction.

**Derivation:** Inside the slab, the ray travels at angle $r$ to the normal. The horizontal distance traveled inside the slab is $t/\cos r$. The lateral shift is this distance multiplied by $\sin(i - r)$: $d = (t/\cos r) \cdot \sin(i - r)$.
**Special case — normal incidence:** When $i = 0°$, $d = 0$. The ray passes straight through without any lateral shift. This is consistent with Snell's law: $r = 0$ when $i = 0$.
**Dependence on thickness:** The lateral shift is directly proportional to the slab thickness $t$. A thicker slab produces a larger shift. Doubling the thickness doubles the shift.

**Dependence on angle of incidence:** As $i$ increases from 0°, the lateral shift increases. At grazing incidence ($i \to 90°$), the shift approaches the thickness $t$ (the ray travels almost parallel to the slab faces).

**Dependence on refractive index:** For a fixed angle of incidence, a higher refractive index means a larger refraction angle $r$ is smaller, so $(i - r)$ is larger, and the shift is larger. Denser materials produce more lateral shift.

**No angular deviation:** The emergent ray is PARALLEL to the incident ray. The slab causes a lateral displacement but no change in direction. This is because the two refractions (entry and exit) cancel each other's angular effect.

**Apparent shift of objects:** When you look through a glass window at an angle, objects appear slightly displaced from their true positions. This is due to lateral shift. The effect is small for thin windows but noticeable with thick glass blocks.

**Multiple slabs:** If light passes through multiple parallel slabs of different materials, the total lateral shift is the sum of individual shifts: $d_{total} = \sum t_k \cdot \frac{\sin(i_k - r_k)}{\cos r_k}$, where each $i_k$ and $r_k$ is determined by Snell's law at each interface.

**NEB exam focus:** Derive the lateral shift formula. Calculate the shift for given values of $t$, $i$, and $n$. Explain why the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray. Draw ray diagrams showing the shift.

**Numerical example:** A glass slab ($n = 1.5$) of thickness 10 cm is illuminated by a ray at $i = 60°$. First find $r$: $\sin r = \sin 60°/1.5 = 0.866/1.5 = 0.5774$, so $r = 35.3°$. Then $d = 10 \cdot \frac{\sin(60° - 35.3°)}{\cos 35.3°} = 10 \cdot \frac{\sin 24.7°}{0.816} = 10 \cdot \frac{0.418}{0.816} = 5.12$ cm.

**Why the emergent ray is parallel:** At the first interface, the ray bends toward the normal by angle $(i - r)$. At the second interface, it bends away from the normal by the same angle $(i - r)$ because the surfaces are parallel and the geometry is symmetric. Net angular change = 0.

**Application — periscopes and binoculars:** Parallel-sided glass blocks are used in optical instruments to displace the light path without changing its direction. This allows compact instrument design while maintaining the line of sight.

**Connection to prism:** A prism has non-parallel faces, so the emergent ray is NOT parallel to the incident ray — it is deviated by angle $\delta = i + e - A$. The lateral shift formula does not apply to prisms.
confusion: Carefully distinguish between similar-looking concepts in lateral shift.
Pay attention to the conditions under which formulas and theorems apply.
Practice with multiple examples to solidify your understanding.
❌ The emergent ray is deviated from the original direction. ✅ The emergent ray is PARALLEL to the incident ray. A parallel-sided slab causes lateral shift but NO angular deviation.

❌ Lateral shift depends on the refractive index of the slab material only. ✅ Lateral shift depends on ALL THREE: thickness $t$, angle of incidence $i$, AND refractive index $n$ (through the refraction angle $r$).
❌ At normal incidence, there is a lateral shift. ✅ At normal incidence ($i = 0°$), the lateral shift is ZERO. The ray passes straight through without any displacement.

❌ The lateral shift formula $d = t\sin(i-r)/\cos r$ works for prisms. ✅ This formula is ONLY for parallel-sided slabs. Prisms have non-parallel faces, so the emergent ray is deviated, not just shifted.

❌ A thicker slab always produces a proportionally larger shift for the same angle. ✅ Yes, the shift IS directly proportional to thickness: $d \propto t$. But the proportionality constant depends on $i$ and $n$.

❌ The lateral shift is the same as the deviation angle. ✅ Lateral shift is a DISTANCE (measured in cm or m). Deviation angle is an ANGLE (measured in degrees). They are completely different quantities.

❌ Light passing through a glass slab changes its frequency. ✅ The frequency of light does NOT change when it passes through any medium. Only the speed and wavelength change: $v = c/n$ and $\lambda = \lambda_0/n$.

A glass slab of thickness 5 cm ($n = 1.5$) is struck by a ray at $i = 45°$. Find the lateral shift. $\sin r = \sin 45°/1.5 = 0.7071/1.5 = 0.4714$, so $r = 28.1°$. $d = 5 \cdot \frac{\sin(45° - 28.1°)}{\cos 28.1°} = 5 \cdot \frac{\sin 16.9°}{0.883} = 5 \cdot \frac{0.291}{0.883} = 1.65$ cm.

Show that for small angles of incidence, the lateral shift is approximately $d \approx t \cdot i \cdot (1 - 1/n)$. For small $i$ and $r$: $\sin(i-r) \approx i - r$ and $\cos r \approx 1$. From Snell's law: $r \approx i/n$. Therefore $d \approx t(i - i/n) = t \cdot i \cdot (1 - 1/n)$. This linear approximation is useful for paraxial optics.

A ray passes through a glass slab and emerges with a lateral shift of 2 cm. If the slab thickness is doubled to 10 cm (same material, same angle of incidence), what is the new lateral shift? Since $d \propto t$, doubling the thickness doubles the shift: $d_{new} = 2 \times 2 = 4$ cm.

A transparent slab of thickness 3 cm produces a lateral shift of 1 cm for a ray incident at 60°. Find the refractive index of the slab. $d = t\sin(i-r)/\cos r$. $1 = 3\sin(60°-r)/\cos r$. $\sin(60°-r) = \cos r/3$. Using the identity $\sin(60°-r) = \sin 60°\cos r - \cos 60°\sin r$: $0.866\cos r - 0.5\sin r = \cos r/3$. Solving: $r \approx 30°$. Then $n = \sin 60°/\sin 30° = 0.866/0.5 = 1.73$. This is a high-index glass or crystal.

Why does a fish in water appear displaced when viewed from above at an angle? Light from the fish refracts at the water-air interface. The emergent ray appears to come from a point closer to the surface (apparent depth effect) AND laterally shifted. The combined effect makes the fish appear at a different position than its actual location.

A ray enters a parallel-sided slab of refractive index $n$ at angle $i$. Show that the lateral shift is maximum when $i \to 90°$ (grazing incidence). As $i \to 90°$, $r \to \arcsin(1/n)$. The shift $d = t\sin(i-r)/\cos r \to t\sin(90°-r)/\cos r = t\cos r/\cos r = t$. The maximum lateral shift equals the slab thickness.
universalFacts: This topic is a cornerstone of the physics curriculum and appears consistently in examinations.
Understanding lateral shift builds the foundation for more advanced topics in mathematics.
Real-world applications of lateral shift span engineering, physics, economics, and computer science.

The lateral shift through a parallel-sided slab is a fundamental result in geometrical optics. It demonstrates that refraction at parallel interfaces produces displacement without deviation — a principle used in many optical instruments.

In architectural glass, lateral shift is usually negligible for thin panes (a few mm). But in thick glass blocks used in art installations or optical tables, the shift can be several centimeters and must be accounted for in precise alignments.

The concept of lateral shift generalizes to any number of parallel interfaces. In a multi-layer coating (anti-reflective coatings on lenses), each layer contributes a small lateral shift, and the total effect determines the phase relationship between reflected waves.

In fiber optics, the concept of lateral shift is related to the "beam wander" that occurs when light enters a fiber at an angle. Proper coupling requires minimizing the lateral displacement at the fiber end face.

Leonhard Euler studied the optics of parallel-sided plates in the 1740s, deriving the lateral shift formula and showing its relationship to the delay introduced by the plate — a precursor to modern optical path length calculations.

A glass slab of thickness 5 cm ($n = 1.5$) is struck by a ray at $i = 45°$. Find the lateral shift. $\sin r = \sin 45°/1.5 = 0.7071/1.5 = 0.4714$, so $r = 28.1°$. $d = 5 \cdot \frac{\sin(45° - 28.1°)}{\cos 28.1°} = 5 \cdot \frac{\sin 16.9°}{0.883} = 5 \cdot \frac{0.291}{0.883} = 1.65$ cm.

Show that for small angles of incidence, the lateral shift is approximately $d \approx t \cdot i \cdot (1 - 1/n)$. For small $i$ and $r$: $\sin(i-r) \approx i - r$ and $\cos r \approx 1$. From Snell's law: $r \approx i/n$. Therefore $d \approx t(i - i/n) = t \cdot i \cdot (1 - 1/n)$. This linear approximation is useful for paraxial optics.

A ray passes through a glass slab and emerges with a lateral shift of 2 cm. If the slab thickness is doubled to 10 cm (same material, same angle of incidence), what is the new lateral shift? Since $d \propto t$, doubling the thickness doubles the shift: $d_{new} = 2 \times 2 = 4$ cm.

A transparent slab of thickness 3 cm produces a lateral shift of 1 cm for a ray incident at 60°. Find the refractive index of the slab. $d = t\sin(i-r)/\cos r$. $1 = 3\sin(60°-r)/\cos r$. $\sin(60°-r) = \cos r/3$. Using the identity $\sin(60°-r) = \sin 60°\cos r - \cos 60°\sin r$: $0.866\cos r - 0.5\sin r = \cos r/3$. Solving: $r \approx 30°$. Then $n = \sin 60°/\sin 30° = 0.866/0.5 = 1.73$. This is a high-index glass or crystal.

Why does a fish in water appear displaced when viewed from above at an angle? Light from the fish refracts at the water-air interface. The emergent ray appears to come from a point closer to the surface (apparent depth effect) AND laterally shifted. The combined effect makes the fish appear at a different position than its actual location.

A ray enters a parallel-sided slab of refractive index $n$ at angle $i$. Show that the lateral shift is maximum when $i \to 90°$ (grazing incidence). As $i \to 90°$, $r \to \arcsin(1/n)$. The shift $d = t\sin(i-r)/\cos r \to t\sin(90°-r)/\cos r = t\cos r/\cos r = t$. The maximum lateral shift equals the slab thickness.

data.title: Total Internal Reflection
notes: **Total Internal Reflection:** This topic covers the fundamental concepts of total internal reflection in the physics curriculum.
Understanding total internal reflection is essential for solving problems and building higher-level mathematical skills.
Key definitions and theorems related to total internal reflection should be memorized and practiced regularly.

**Definition:** Total internal reflection (TIR) occurs when a ray of light traveling in a denser medium strikes the boundary with a rarer medium at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle. All the light is reflected back into the denser medium — no refraction occurs.
**Two essential conditions:** (1) Light must travel from a DENSER medium to a RARER medium ($n_1 > n_2$). (2) The angle of incidence must EXCEED the critical angle ($i > \theta_c$).

**Critical angle formula:** $\sin\theta_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1}$, where $n_1$ is the refractive index of the denser medium and $n_2$ is the refractive index of the rarer medium. At the critical angle, the refracted ray travels along the boundary ($r = 90°$).

**Critical angle for common materials:** Glass-to-air ($n = 1.52$): $\theta_c = \arcsin(1/1.52) = 41.1°$. Water-to-air ($n = 1.33$): $\theta_c = \arcsin(1/1.33) = 48.8°$. Diamond-to-air ($n = 2.42$): $\theta_c = \arcsin(1/2.42) = 24.4°$.

**What happens at different angles:** If $i < \theta_c$: partial reflection + refraction (most light transmits). If $i = \theta_c$: refraction at 90° (along the boundary). If $i > \theta_c$: TOTAL internal reflection (100% reflection, no transmission).

**Why TIR is 	otal:** Unlike mirror reflection (which absorbs 5–15% of light), TIR reflects 100% of the light. This makes it far more efficient than metallic mirrors for bending light paths in optical instruments.

**Optical fibre principle:** An optical fibre consists of a core (high $n$) surrounded by cladding (lower $n$). Light entering the core at angles greater than the critical angle undergoes repeated TIR, traveling kilometers with minimal loss. This is the basis of modern telecommunications.

**Diamond sparkle:** Diamond's high refractive index ($n = 2.42$) gives a very small critical angle (24.4°). Light entering a well-cut diamond undergoes multiple TIR events before exiting, creating the characteristic brilliant flashes of color (fire).

**Mirage phenomenon:** On a hot road, air near the surface is hotter and less dense (lower $n$) than air above. Light from the sky bends away from the normal as it passes through increasingly rarer layers. At a certain height, the angle exceeds the critical angle and TIR occurs, creating the illusion of water on the road.

**Prism binoculars:** Porro prisms in binoculars use TIR at the hypotenuse face (glass-to-air at 45°, which exceeds the critical angle of ~42° for glass). This provides reflection without the need for a silvered coating — brighter images with no degradation.

**NEB exam focus:** State the two conditions for TIR. Derive the critical angle formula. Calculate critical angles for common material pairs. Explain optical fibres and mirages using TIR. Draw ray diagrams showing TIR in prisms and fibres.

**Fibre optic numbers — acceptance angle:** The maximum angle at which light can enter an optical fibre and still undergo TIR is called the acceptance angle. $\sin\theta_a = \sqrt{n_{core}^2 - n_{clad}^2}$. For typical fibres ($n_{core} = 1.48$, $n_{clad} = 1.46$): $\theta_a \approx 16°$.

**Optical fibre types:** (1) Step-index fibre: core and cladding have uniform but different indices. (2) Graded-index fibre: the core's index gradually decreases from center to edge, causing light to follow curved paths and reducing modal dispersion.

**Applications of TIR:** (1) Optical fibres for communication and endoscopy. (2) Prism reflectors in binoculars and periscopes. (3) Diamond cutting for maximum brilliance. (4) Automotive rain sensors (TIR is disrupted by water droplets on the windshield). (5) Fiber-optic sensors for temperature and pressure.

**Partial reflection at TIR:** In reality, at angles just above the critical angle, a small evanescent wave penetrates into the rarer medium (decaying exponentially over a distance of about one wavelength). This is the principle behind frustrated TIR and near-field optical microscopy.

**Energy conservation in TIR:** Since no light is transmitted, all the incident energy is reflected. The intensity of the reflected ray equals the intensity of the incident ray (ignoring absorption in the medium). This is why TIR prisms are preferred over silvered mirrors in precision optics.
confusion: Carefully distinguish between similar-looking concepts in total internal reflection.
Pay attention to the conditions under which formulas and theorems apply.
Practice with multiple examples to solidify your understanding.

❌ TIR can occur when light goes from rarer to denser medium. ✅ TIR ONLY occurs when light travels from DENSER to RARER medium ($n_1 > n_2$). From rarer to denser, the ray always bends toward the normal and always enters the second medium.

❌ The critical angle exists for any pair of media. ✅ The critical angle only exists when $n_1 > n_2$. If light goes from air to glass ($n_1 < n_2$), there is no critical angle — refraction always occurs.

❌ At the critical angle, all light is reflected. ✅ At the critical angle ($i = \theta_c$), the refracted ray travels ALONG the boundary ($r = 90°$). TIR begins only when $i > \theta_c$, not at $i = \theta_c$.
❌ TIR produces a dimmer reflection than a mirror. ✅ TIR reflects 100% of the light — it is BRIGHTER than any metallic mirror, which typically absorbs 5–15% of incident light.

❌ Optical fibres work because light is "trapped" by the cladding. ✅ Optical fibres work because of TIR at the core-cladding interface. The cladding has a LOWER refractive index than the core, creating the condition for TIR.

❌ The critical angle for diamond is about 42°. ✅ Diamond's critical angle is about 24.4° (much smaller than glass's 42°). This small critical angle is what makes diamonds so brilliant — light undergoes multiple TIR events before exiting.

❌ TIR can occur at any interface, including solid-solid interfaces. ✅ TIR requires a boundary between two media with DIFFERENT refractive indices. It can occur at any such boundary (glass-air, water-glass, fibre core-cladding) as long as light travels from the higher-index to the lower-index medium.
practice: Solve at least 5 problems on total internal reflection from your textbook.
Try to derive the key formulas from first principles.
Create a summary sheet with all important formulas and theorems.
Practice identifying which method/formula to apply in each problem type.

Find the critical angle for light going from glass ($n = 1.52$) to water ($n = 1.33$). $\sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1 = 1.33/1.52 = 0.875$. $\theta_c = \arcsin(0.875) = 61.0°$. Light going from water to glass would not have a critical angle (it's going to a denser medium).

A ray in water ($n = 1.33$) strikes the water-air interface at 40°. Does TIR occur? The critical angle is $\theta_c = \arcsin(1/1.33) = 48.8°$. Since $i = 40° < 48.8°$, TIR does NOT occur. The ray is partially reflected and partially refracted into the air.

A ray in water ($n = 1.33$) strikes the water-air interface at 60°. Does TIR occur? Since $i = 60° > 48.8° = \theta_c$, TIR DOES occur. All light is reflected back into the water. This is why underwater swimmers looking up see a mirror-like surface at steep angles.

Calculate the critical angle for a diamond ($n = 2.42$) in air. $\sin\theta_c = 1/2.42 = 0.4132$. $\theta_c = \arcsin(0.4132) = 24.4°$. This small critical angle means light entering a diamond at most angles undergoes TIR, contributing to its brilliance.

An optical fibre has core index 1.48 and cladding index 1.46. Find the acceptance angle. $\sin\theta_a = \sqrt{n_{core}^2 - n_{clad}^2} = \sqrt{1.48^2 - 1.46^2} = \sqrt{2.1904 - 2.1316} = \sqrt{0.0588} = 0.2425$. $\theta_a = \arcsin(0.2425) = 14.0°$. Light must enter within 14° of the fibre axis to be guided.

Explain why a crack in a glass window appears silvery when viewed from certain angles. Light traveling inside the glass reaches the crack (which is filled with air) at angles that may exceed the critical angle for glass-air ($\theta_c \approx 42°$). When this happens, TIR occurs at the crack surface, making it appear shiny and silvery — like a mirror.
universalFacts: This topic is a cornerstone of the physics curriculum and appears consistently in examinations.
Understanding total internal reflection builds the foundation for more advanced topics in mathematics.
Real-world applications of total internal reflection span engineering, physics, economics, and computer science.

The phenomenon of total internal reflection was first observed and described by Augustin-Jean Fresnel in 1818. His mathematical treatment of TIR predicted the evanescent wave that penetrates into the rarer medium.

Optical fibre communication, invented by Charles Kao in the 1960s, revolutionized global communications. Kao won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2009 for his work. A single fibre can carry terabits of data per second over thousands of kilometers.

The "sparkle" of a cut diamond is directly related to its small critical angle (24.4°). A poorly cut diamond allows light to escape through the bottom, making it appear dull. Expert cutters angle the facets to maximize TIR and light return to the viewer's eye.

Frustrated total internal reflection occurs when a third medium is brought very close (within a wavelength) to the interface where TIR is occurring. The evanescent wave can then couple into the third medium, allowing a small amount of light to "tunnel" across the gap.

TIRprisms are used in high-quality binoculars because they reflect 100% of the light (compared to ~95% for silvered mirrors). This makes the image significantly brighter, especially in low-light conditions.

A prism has angle $A = 60°$ and refractive index $n = 1.5$. Find the angle of minimum deviation. Show that at minimum deviation, $r = A/2$. At minimum deviation, $i = e$ and by symmetry $r_1 = r_2$. From the prism geometry: $A = r_1 + r_2 = 2r$. Therefore $r = A/2$. For $A = 60°$, $r = 30°$.

A glass prism ($n = 1.6$) has minimum deviation $\delta_{min} = 40°$. Find the prism angle $A$. From $n = \frac{\sin\frac{A+\delta_{min}}{2}}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}$: $1.6 = \frac{\sin\frac{A+40}{2}}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}$. Let $x = A/2$: $1.6 \sin x = \sin(x + 20°)$. Solving numerically: $x \approx 30°$, so $A \approx 60°$.

Why is the minimum deviation method more accurate than measuring deviation at arbitrary incidence? At minimum deviation, the ray path is symmetric, making the measurement less sensitive to small errors in reading the angles. Also, the deviation is at a stationary point (minimum), so small errors in prism orientation have minimal effect on the measured angle.

A ray passes through a prism with $A = 50°$ and $n = 1.52$. Find the angle of incidence that produces minimum deviation. At minimum deviation: $r = A/2 = 25°$. By Snell's law at the first face: $\sin i = n \sin r = 1.52 \times \sin 25° = 1.52 \times 0.4226 = 0.6424$. $i = \arcsin(0.6424) = 40.0°$.

Prove that for a given prism, the angle of incidence that gives minimum deviation is unique. The deviation function $\delta(i)$ is convex (U-shaped) with a single minimum. This can be shown by taking the derivative $d\delta/di$ and showing it equals zero at exactly one value of $i$ (where $i = e$).

data.title: Minimum Deviation Condition
notes: **Minimum Deviation Condition:** This topic covers the fundamental concepts of minimum deviation condition in the physics curriculum.
Understanding minimum deviation condition is essential for solving problems and building higher-level mathematical skills.
Key definitions and theorems related to minimum deviation condition should be memorized and practiced regularly.

**Deviation angle (δ):** When a ray of light passes through a prism, it bends at both faces. The total angle between the incident ray's original direction and the emergent ray's direction is called the angle of deviation, $\delta$.
**Formula for deviation:** $\delta = i + e - A$, where $i$ is the angle of incidence, $e$ is the angle of emergence, and $A$ is the prism angle (refracting angle).

**Minimum deviation (δ_min):** As you vary the angle of incidence $i$, the deviation $\delta$ changes. There is a unique value of $i$ that gives the SMALLEST possible deviation, called the angle of minimum deviation, $\delta_{min}$.

**Symmetric path condition:** At minimum deviation, the ray passes SYMMETRICALLY through the prism: $i = e$ (angle of incidence equals angle of emergence) and $r_1 = r_2 = r$ (angles of refraction at both faces are equal).
**Geometric consequence:** At minimum deviation, the ray inside the prism is parallel to the base of the prism (for an isosceles prism). This is the shortest path through the prism.

**Finding δ_min experimentally:** Rotate the prism on a spectrometer table while viewing the emergent ray. The deviation angle decreases to a minimum and then increases. The minimum point is marked by the ray momentarily stopping and reversing direction.

**Why minimum deviation matters:** At $\delta_{min}$, the prism formula $n = \frac{\sin\frac{A+\delta_{min}}{2}}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}$ is exact and doesn't require knowing the internal ray path. This makes it the most accurate way to measure refractive index.

**Curve of δ vs. i:** Plotting deviation $\delta$ against angle of incidence $i$ gives a U-shaped curve. The lowest point is $\delta_{min}$. The curve is symmetric about the minimum point (since swapping $i$ and $e$ gives the same deviation).

**Physical intuition:** At minimum deviation, the light takes the "path of least resistance" through the prism. Any deviation from the symmetric path increases the total bending because one face does more bending while the other does less, and the net effect is larger.

**Small prism approximation:** For a thin prism (small $A$), the minimum deviation is approximately $\delta_{min} \approx (n - 1)A$. This is useful for estimating deviation without precise measurements.

**Dispersion at minimum deviation:** Since refractive index $n$ depends on wavelength ($n_{violet} > n_{red}$), each color has a different $\delta_{min}$. Violet light deviates more than red light, producing a spectrum.

**Spectrometer measurement:** In a laboratory spectrometer, $\delta_{min}$ is found by rotating the prism table until the image of the slit stops moving and reverses direction. The angle between the incident and emergent ray at this point is $\delta_{min}$.

**NEB exam focus:** State the condition for minimum deviation ($i = e$, $r_1 = r_2$). Draw the ray diagram showing the symmetric path. Explain why minimum deviation gives the most accurate refractive index measurement.

**Connection to prisms in optics:** Minimum deviation is used in spectrometers, monochromators, and prism-based optical instruments. It provides the most well-defined relationship between angle and refractive index.

❌ Minimum deviation occurs when the ray passes straight through the prism without bending. ✅ Minimum deviation still involves bending — it's the SMALLEST possible total deviation, not zero deviation. The ray still refracts at both surfaces.

❌ At minimum deviation, the ray is perpendicular to both prism faces. ✅ At minimum deviation, the ray inside the prism is parallel to the BASE (for an isosceles prism), not perpendicular to the faces. The angles of incidence and emergence are equal but not necessarily 90°.

❌ Any angle of incidence gives the same deviation. ✅ Deviation varies with angle of incidence. Only at one specific value of $i$ does the deviation reach its minimum. For other values of $i$, the deviation is larger.

❌ The angle of minimum deviation is zero for a prism. ✅ For a prism with $A > 0$ and $n > 1$, the minimum deviation is always positive. Zero deviation would require no refraction, which is impossible for a prism in air.
❌ Minimum deviation means the ray doesn't bend at all. ✅ "Minimum" means the smallest possible, not zero. The ray still bends — it's just the configuration that produces the least total bending.
❌ At minimum deviation, $r_1 \neq r_2$. ✅ At minimum deviation, $r_1 = r_2 = A/2$. This is one of the key conditions that defines minimum deviation.

❌ You can find δ_min without a spectrometer. ✅ While you can approximate δ_min with a simple setup, precise measurement requires a spectrometer to accurately measure the angle between incident and emergent rays.

A prism has angle $A = 60°$ and refractive index $n = 1.5$. Find the angle of minimum deviation. At minimum deviation: $n = \frac{\sin\frac{A+\delta_{min}}{2}}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}$. $1.5 = \frac{\sin\frac{60+\delta_{min}}{2}}{\sin 30°} = \frac{\sin\frac{60+\delta_{min}}{2}}{0.5}$. So $\sin\frac{60+\delta_{min}}{2} = 0.75$. $\frac{60+\delta_{min}}{2} = \arcsin(0.75) = 48.59°$. $\delta_{min} = 97.18 - 60 = 37.18°$.
Show that at minimum deviation, $r = A/2$. At minimum deviation, $i = e$ and by symmetry $r_1 = r_2$. From the prism geometry: $A = r_1 + r_2 = 2r$. Therefore $r = A/2$. For $A = 60°$, $r = 30°$.

A glass prism ($n = 1.6$) has minimum deviation $\delta_{min} = 40°$. Find the prism angle $A$. From $n = \frac{\sin\frac{A+\delta_{min}}{2}}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}$: $1.6 = \frac{\sin\frac{A+40}{2}}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}$. Let $x = A/2$: $1.6 \sin x = \sin(x + 20°)$. Solving numerically: $x \approx 30°$, so $A \approx 60°$.

Why is the minimum deviation method more accurate than measuring deviation at arbitrary incidence? At minimum deviation, the ray path is symmetric, making the measurement less sensitive to small errors in reading the angles. Also, the deviation is at a stationary point (minimum), so small errors in prism orientation have minimal effect on the measured angle.

A ray passes through a prism with $A = 50°$ and $n = 1.52$. Find the angle of incidence that produces minimum deviation. At minimum deviation: $r = A/2 = 25°$. By Snell's law at the first face: $\sin i = n \sin r = 1.52 \times \sin 25° = 1.52 \times 0.4226 = 0.6424$. $i = \arcsin(0.6424) = 40.0°$.

Prove that for a given prism, the angle of incidence that gives minimum deviation is unique. The deviation function $\delta(i)$ is convex (U-shaped) with a single minimum. This can be shown by taking the derivative $d\delta/di$ and showing it equals zero at exactly one value of $i$ (where $i = e$).

The minimum deviation condition was first studied systematically by Isaac Newton in his optical experiments. He used a prism to separate white light into colors and measured the deviation of each color.

Spectrometers used in chemistry and physics labs are designed to measure angles of minimum deviation with high precision (to within 1 arcminute or better). This allows determination of refractive index to 4-5 significant figures.
The concept of minimum deviation applies not just to prisms but to any refracting or reflecting system. Mirrors, lenses, and diffraction gratings all have similar minimum-deflection configurations.
In fiber optics, the concept of minimum deviation is related to the critical angle and total internal reflection. Light entering an optical fiber at certain angles experiences minimum loss.

The minimum deviation angle depends on the wavelength of light (dispersion). This is why prisms produce rainbows — different colors have different refractive indices and therefore different minimum deviation angles.

data.title: Prism Formula
notes: **Geometry of a prism.** The refracting angle of the prism equals the sum of the internal angles, A = r₁ + r₂, whatever the incidence.
**Angle of deviation.** The ray turns through δ = (i₁ + i₂) − A, where i₁ and i₂ are the angles at the two faces.
**Minimum deviation.** Deviation is least when the ray passes symmetrically (i₁ = i₂, r₁ = r₂ = A/2); then δ_m = 2i − A — the setting used in all prism measurements.
**Prism formula.** At minimum deviation the refractive index is n = sin[(A + δ_m)/2] / sin(A/2) — how n of a glass prism is found experimentally.
**Dispersion and thin prisms.** For a thin prism δ = (n − 1)A; violet deviates most and red least, and the angular dispersion is θ = δ_v − δ_r, giving the dispersive power ω = θ/δ_y.

The deviation produced by a prism is i + e − A. It is smallest when the ray passes symmetrically, and that minimum is the setting used to measure the index. The index is then the sine of half of A plus δ_m, divided by the sine of half of A.
