data.title: Types of Vectors
notes: **Like (parallel) vectors**: vectors having the same direction, regardless of their magnitudes. They can be written as $\vec{A} = a\vec{B}$ where $a$ is a positive scalar. Like vectors add by ordinary arithmetic: their resultant is also parallel to them.

**Unlike (anti-parallel) vectors**: vectors having exactly opposite directions. If $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are anti-parallel, $\vec{A} = -a\vec{B}$ where $a$ is a positive scalar. The dot product of two anti-parallel vectors is $-|\vec{A}||\vec{B}|$.

**Co-planar vectors**: vectors that lie in the same plane. Any two vectors are always coplanar. Three vectors are coplanar if their vector sum or the scalar triple product $\vec{A}\cdot(\vec{B}\times\vec{C}) = 0$.

**Non-coplanar (skew) vectors**: vectors that do not lie in the same plane. Three vectors are non-coplanar if they span 3D space. The minimum number of non-coplanar vectors needed to span 3D is three.

**Null (zero) vector $\vec{0}$**: a vector with zero magnitude and indeterminate direction. It is the additive identity: $\vec{A} + \vec{0} = \vec{A}$. The zero vector is parallel to every vector, since $0\vec{A} = \vec{0}$.

**Unit vector**: a vector of magnitude 1 in a specified direction, denoted with a hat/circumflex: $\hat{n}$, $\hat{A}$. For any vector $\vec{A}$, the unit vector along it is $\hat{A} = \vec{A}/|\vec{A}|$.

**Standard unit vectors $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$**: unit vectors along the x, y, and z axes of a Cartesian coordinate system. They are mutually perpendicular: $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j} = \hat{j}\cdot\hat{k} = \hat{k}\cdot\hat{i} = 0$ and $\hat{i}\times\hat{j} = \hat{k}$ (right-hand rule).

**Position vector**: the vector from the origin to a point, denoted $\vec{r}$. If the point is $(x, y, z)$, then $\vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$. It specifies the location of a point relative to the origin.

**Equal vectors**: two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are equal if they have the same magnitude AND the same direction. They can be drawn from different points but are physically equivalent: $\vec{A} = \vec{B}$ implies $|\vec{A}| = |\vec{B}|$ and parallel with same orientation.

**Negative vector**: $-\vec{A}$ is the vector with the same magnitude as $\vec{A}$ but opposite direction. $\vec{A} + (-\vec{A}) = \vec{0}$. Useful in problems like relative velocity and force balance.
**Collinear vectors**: vectors lying along the same line, regardless of direction. They are either parallel or anti-parallel. Collinear vectors add algebraically with appropriate signs.

**Axial vector (pseudovector)**: vectors representing quantities like angular velocity, torque, and magnetic field. They change sign under reflection (mirror inversion). In contrast, **polar vectors** (force, velocity) follow normal vector addition.

**Free vector**: a vector that can be translated parallel to itself without changing its physical meaning. Examples: velocity, force. In contrast, a **bound (localized) vector** is tied to a specific point (e.g., moment of a force about a point).

**Basis vectors**: a set of linearly independent vectors that span the entire vector space. For 3D, $\{\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}\}$ is the standard basis. Any vector in 3D can be written as a linear combination of basis vectors.
**Orthogonal vectors**: vectors that are perpendicular to each other. The dot product of orthogonal vectors is zero: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 0$ for perpendicular $\vec{A}, \vec{B}$.

**Mutually perpendicular vectors**: a set of vectors where each is perpendicular to every other. $\{\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}\}$ is the canonical example in 3D. The magnitude of any vector is the square root of the sum of squares of components along such a basis.

**Solved example**: two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are equal if $\vec{A} = \vec{B}$. But 'parallel' only requires same direction, allowing different magnitudes. So parallel does not imply equal, but equal implies parallel.

**Collinear three-vector property**: if $\vec{A}, \vec{B}, \vec{C}$ are collinear, then $\vec{C} = a\vec{A} + b\vec{B}$ for some scalars $a, b$ (and conversely, three collinear vectors are linearly dependent).

**Vector notation distinction**: bold $\mathbf{A}$ and arrow $\vec{A}$ both denote vectors. Magnitude is $|\vec{A}|$, $|\mathbf{A}|$, or simply $A$. Unit vectors are $\hat{a}$ or $\hat{u}$ (with hat).

**Practical applications**: in physics, identifying the type of vector helps in selecting the correct operation. Force is a polar vector (adds via parallelogram law), torque is an axial vector (different rules for reflection).

**Contravariant vs covariant vectors**: in advanced vector analysis, vectors are classified by how their components transform under coordinate changes. Contravariant components transform opposite to basis vectors; covariant components transform the same way. This distinction is crucial in tensor analysis and general relativity.

**Basis-independent definition**: a vector is fundamentally defined as an object that transforms in a specific way under coordinate rotations. The component representation $\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j} + A_z\hat{k}$ is basis-dependent, but the vector itself is a geometric object independent of coordinates.

**Linear dependence and independence**: a set of vectors is linearly independent if no vector in the set can be written as a linear combination of the others. In 3D, at most 3 vectors can be linearly independent. Four or more vectors in 3D are always linearly dependent.

**Zero vector and linear dependence**: the zero vector is always linearly dependent with any set of vectors (since $0\cdot\vec{A} + 0\cdot\vec{B} + 1\cdot\vec{0} = \vec{0}$). Any set containing the zero vector is linearly dependent.

**Coplanarity test for three vectors**: three vectors $\vec{A}$, $\vec{B}$, $\vec{C}$ are coplanar if and only if their scalar triple product is zero: $\vec{A}\cdot(\vec{B}\times\vec{C}) = 0$. This is equivalent to the volume of the parallelepiped they form being zero.
confusion: Like vectors are equal — Like vectors are parallel (same direction), but their magnitudes can differ. Equal vectors require both same direction and same magnitude. $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i}$ and $\vec{B} = 5\hat{i}$ are like vectors but not equal.
The null vector has no direction at all — The null vector has indeterminate direction, meaning we cannot assign a unique direction to it. By convention, it is treated as parallel to every vector.

All vectors in 3D are coplanar — Any TWO vectors are coplanar, but three vectors can be non-coplanar (skew). Four or more vectors can always be reduced to a set in 3D, with at most 3 linearly independent members.

Unit vectors are unique for each direction — There are infinitely many unit vectors for the same direction (any vector of magnitude 1 in that direction). However, for a given direction, the unit vector is unique up to sign.

Co-planar and parallel mean the same thing — Parallel vectors must lie along the same line (collinear). Coplanar vectors only need to be in the same plane; they can point in different directions within that plane.
Anti-parallel vectors are like vectors with a sign — Anti-parallel vectors point in OPPOSITE directions. Like vectors point in the SAME direction. They are fundamentally different categories.

Equal vectors must start at the same point — No. Free vectors are equal if they have the same magnitude and direction, regardless of position. The position of the vector's tail or head does not affect its equality.

Position vector and displacement vector are the same — Position vector $\vec{r}$ is from origin to a point. Displacement vector $\Delta\vec{r}$ is the change in position from one point to another. They are related but not identical.
The negative of a vector changes its magnitude — No. The negative vector $-\vec{A}$ has the SAME magnitude as $\vec{A}$ but the OPPOSITE direction. Only the direction changes.

All unit vectors are the same — No. Each unit vector points in a different direction. $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, and $\hat{k}$ are all unit vectors but point in different (mutually perpendicular) directions. There are infinitely many unit vectors, one for each direction.
practice: State which of the following pairs of vectors are like, unlike, coplanar, or equal: (a) $\vec{A} = 3\hat{i}$, $\vec{B} = 7\hat{i}$. (b) $\vec{A} = 4\hat{j}$, $\vec{B} = -6\hat{j}$. (c) $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}$, $\vec{B} = 2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}$. [Solution: (a) like, coplanar, not equal (different magnitudes). (b) unlike, coplanar, not equal. (c) equal (and therefore like, coplanar, parallel).]
Find the unit vector along $\vec{A} = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}$. [Solution: $|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{9+16} = 5$. $\hat{A} = \vec{A}/|\vec{A}| = (3/5)\hat{i} + (4/5)\hat{j}$.]

Are the vectors $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$, $\vec{B} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$, $\vec{C} = 3\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$ coplanar? [Solution: Compute the scalar triple product $\vec{A}\cdot(\vec{B}\times\vec{C})$. First, $\vec{B}\times\vec{C} = \hat{i}((-2)(5)-(1)(1)) - \hat{j}((1)(5)-(1)(3)) + \hat{k}((1)(1)-(-2)(3)) = -11\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 7\hat{k}$. Then $\vec{A}\cdot(\vec{B}\times\vec{C}) = 2(-11) + 3(-2) + 4(7) = -22 - 6 + 28 = 0$. Since the scalar triple product is 0, the vectors are coplanar.]

Show that the zero vector $\vec{0}$ is parallel to every vector. [Solution: For any $\vec{A}$, the zero vector can be written as $\vec{0} = 0\cdot\vec{A}$. The scalar multiplier is 0, which is a non-negative real number. So $\vec{0}$ is parallel to $\vec{A}$ by the definition of parallelism. Also, $\vec{0}$ has no specific direction, so the convention treats it as parallel to all directions.]

If $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are unit vectors making 60° with each other, find $\vec{A}+\vec{B}$. [Solution: $|\vec{A}+\vec{B}| = \sqrt{1+1+2\cos60°} = \sqrt{2+1} = \sqrt{3}$. Direction: bisects the angle, so 30° from each. $\vec{A}+\vec{B} = \sqrt{3}\hat{n}$, where $\hat{n}$ is the unit vector at 30° from both.]

Determine whether the vectors $\vec{A} = 3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$, $\vec{B} = \hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$, $\vec{C} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ are coplanar. [Solution: $\vec{B}\times\vec{C} = \hat{i}((-3)(3)-(5)(-1)) - \hat{j}((1)(3)-(5)(2)) + \hat{k}((1)(-1)-(-3)(2)) = -4\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$. $\vec{A}\cdot(\vec{B}\times\vec{C}) = 3(-4) + (-2)(7) + 1(5) = -12 - 14 + 5 = -21 \neq 0$. Not coplanar.]

Express the vector $\vec{F} = 6\hat{i} + 8\hat{j}$ in terms of its magnitude and a unit vector along it. [Solution: $|\vec{F}| = \sqrt{36+64} = 10$. $\hat{F} = (6/10)\hat{i} + (8/10)\hat{j} = 0.6\hat{i} + 0.8\hat{j}$. $\vec{F} = 10(0.6\hat{i}+0.8\hat{j}) = 10\hat{F}$.]

Given $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B} = -4\hat{i} + 6\hat{j}$, show that the vectors are anti-parallel. [Solution: $\vec{B} = -2(2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}) = -2\vec{A}$. The negative scalar indicates opposite direction. So $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are anti-parallel. Verify: $B/A = |-4\hat{i}+6\hat{j}|/|2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}| = \sqrt{52}/\sqrt{13} = 2$. The ratio is negative, confirming anti-parallel.]

Find three unit vectors that are mutually perpendicular to each other. [Solution: The standard unit vectors $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, $\hat{k}$ are mutually perpendicular: $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j}=0$, $\hat{j}\cdot\hat{k}=0$, $\hat{k}\cdot\hat{i}=0$. Any rotation of this set also gives three mutually perpendicular unit vectors.]

Show that the vectors $\vec{A} = \hat{i} + \hat{j}$, $\vec{B} = -\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, and $\vec{C} = \vec{B} - \vec{A} = -2\hat{i} + \hat{k}$ form a triangle. Find its type and area. [Solution: $\vec{A}+\vec{C} = \hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{i}+\hat{k} = -\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k} = \vec{B}$, so the triangle closes. Magnitudes: $|\vec{A}|=\sqrt{2}$, $|\vec{B}|=\sqrt{3}$, $|\vec{C}|=\sqrt{5}$. Check: $2+3=5$, so $|\vec{A}|^2+|\vec{B}|^2 = |\vec{C}|^2$ — it is a right-angled triangle with the right angle between $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$. Verify: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = -1+1+0 = 0$. Area $= \frac{1}{2}|\vec{A}||\vec{B}| = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}\sqrt{3} = \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2} \approx 1.225$.]

If $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are unit vectors with $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 1/2$, find the angle between them and the magnitude of $\vec{A}+\vec{B}$. [Solution: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = |\vec{A}||\vec{B}|\cos\theta = \cos\theta = 1/2$, so $\theta = 60°$. $|\vec{A}+\vec{B}| = \sqrt{1+1+2\cos60°} = \sqrt{2+1} = \sqrt{3}$.]

Three mutually perpendicular unit vectors $\hat{u}_1$, $\hat{u}_2$, $\hat{u}_3$ form a basis for 3D space. Express an arbitrary vector $\vec{A} = 5\hat{i} + 12\hat{j}$ in terms of this basis. [Solution: The standard basis $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$ IS a set of three mutually perpendicular unit vectors. $\vec{A}$ is already expressed in this basis: $A_x = 5$, $A_y = 12$, $A_z = 0$. The magnitude is $|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{25+144} = 13$.]
universalFacts: The classification of vectors into types (like/unlike, coplanar/non-coplanar, polar/axial) is essential for choosing the right operation. Like vectors add algebraically; non-coplanar vectors require 3D analysis.
NEB exam pattern: 'types of vectors' questions are usually short answer or fill-in-the-blank format. Common question: 'define and give an example of unit vector/like vector/co-planar vector'.

The **right-hand rule** for unit vectors $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$ is essential for cross products: $\hat{i}\times\hat{j} = \hat{k}$, $\hat{j}\times\hat{k} = \hat{i}$, $\hat{k}\times\hat{i} = \hat{j}$. This cyclic order defines the orientation of 3D space.

**Polarity** of vectors (polar vs axial) matters in electromagnetism. Electric field $\vec{E}$ is a polar vector, magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is axial. The Lorentz force $\vec{F} = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ produces a polar force from the cross product of two vectors of different polarities.

The **zero vector** is unique in that it is the only vector with indeterminate direction. It is the additive identity, and it is parallel to every vector (since $\vec{0} = 0 \cdot \vec{A}$ for any $\vec{A}$).

In **linear algebra**, the concept of basis vectors generalizes $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$ to any set of linearly independent vectors. The 3D space we work in has dimension 3, requiring exactly 3 linearly independent basis vectors.

The **displacement vector** $\Delta\vec{r} = \vec{r}_f - \vec{r}_i$ is a fundamental concept in kinematics. It depends only on initial and final positions, not on the path taken — this is why the work-energy theorem works.

**Co-planar vectors** simplify problems enormously: any problem with three or more vectors that are coplanar can be analyzed in 2D using x and y components. Non-coplanar vectors require full 3D analysis.

The concept of **linear independence** is fundamental: three non-coplanar vectors form a basis for 3D space. Any vector in 3D can be uniquely expressed as a linear combination of three linearly independent vectors.

**Vector spaces in physics**: the set of all displacement vectors in 3D space forms a vector space. Similarly, the set of all force vectors forms a vector space. Understanding vector types helps identify which vector space a physical quantity belongs to.

data.title: Multiplication of Vectors — Scalar (Dot) Product
notes: **Definition**: the scalar product (or dot product) of two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between them ($0° \leq \theta \leq 180°$). The result is a scalar quantity.

**Geometric interpretation**: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = a(b\cos\theta) = b(a\cos\theta)$ — the product of one vector's magnitude and the projection of the other onto it. If $\theta < 90°$, the projection is positive; if $\theta > 90°$, the projection is negative.

**Physical significance**: the dot product of force and displacement gives work: $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{d} = Fd\cos\theta$. Only the component of force along the displacement does work; perpendicular components contribute nothing.
**Commutative property**: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = \vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}$. The order of vectors in a dot product does not matter. This contrasts with the cross product, which is anti-commutative.
**Distributive property**: $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}+\vec{c}) = \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}$. This is essential when working with vectors expressed as sums.

**Case 1 — perpendicular vectors**: if $\theta = 90°$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = ab\cos90° = 0$. This is the condition for two vectors to be perpendicular (orthogonal). It is a powerful test: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0$ implies perpendicularity (for non-zero vectors).
**Case 2 — parallel vectors**: if $\theta = 0°$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = ab\cos0° = ab$. Maximum value of the dot product; the two vectors are in the same direction.
**Case 3 — anti-parallel vectors**: if $\theta = 180°$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = ab\cos180° = -ab$. Minimum (most negative) value; vectors point in exactly opposite directions.

**Dot products of standard unit vectors**: $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i} = \hat{j}\cdot\hat{j} = \hat{k}\cdot\hat{k} = 1$ (parallel to themselves), $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j} = \hat{j}\cdot\hat{k} = \hat{k}\cdot\hat{i} = 0$ (mutually perpendicular).

**Component-form formula**: for $\vec{A} = A_1\hat{i} + A_2\hat{j} + A_3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = B_1\hat{i} + B_2\hat{j} + B_3\hat{k}$, expanding gives $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = A_1B_1 + A_2B_2 + A_3B_3$ (the sum of products of corresponding components).

**Derivation of component form**: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = (A_1\hat{i}+A_2\hat{j}+A_3\hat{k})\cdot(B_1\hat{i}+B_2\hat{j}+B_3\hat{k}) = A_1B_1(\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i}) + A_1B_2(\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j}) + \cdots = A_1B_1 + A_2B_2 + A_3B_3$. The cross terms vanish because of orthogonality.

**Finding angle from dot product**: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}}{|\vec{A}||\vec{B}|} = \dfrac{A_1B_1+A_2B_2+A_3B_3}{\sqrt{A_1^2+A_2^2+A_3^2}\sqrt{B_1^2+B_2^2+B_3^2}}$. This is a standard application.

**Properties summary**: (1) $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = \vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}$ (commutative). (2) $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}+\vec{c}) = \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}$ (distributive). (3) $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a} = |\vec{a}|^2 \geq 0$ (positive semi-definite). (4) $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0 \iff \vec{a} \perp \vec{b}$ (orthogonality test, for non-zero vectors).

**Work as a dot product**: $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{d}$. If $\vec{F}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{d}$ (e.g., centripetal force on circular motion), $W = 0$. This is why the speed of a satellite in circular orbit doesn't change due to gravity.
**Power as a dot product**: instantaneous power $P = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$. For a constant force, $P = Fv\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{F}$ and $\vec{v}$.

**Magnetic flux**: the flux of magnetic field through an area is $\Phi = \vec{B}\cdot\vec{A} = BA\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{B}$ and the area vector $\vec{A}$ (perpendicular to the surface).
**Finding the component of $\vec{A}$ along $\vec{B}$**: $A_B = \vec{A}\cdot\hat{B} = \vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}/|\vec{B}|$. The signed magnitude of the projection of $\vec{A}$ on the direction of $\vec{B}$.
**Cauchy-Schwarz inequality**: $|\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}| \leq |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|$. This is a direct consequence of $|\cos\theta| \leq 1$. Equality holds when $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are parallel.

**Triangle inequality for dot product**: $(\vec{a}+\vec{b})\cdot(\vec{a}+\vec{b}) = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 + 2\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}$, leading to $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 + 2|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$, which is the cosine rule for the resultant of two vectors.

**Sign of dot product**: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} > 0$ if $\theta < 90°$ (acute angle), $= 0$ if $\theta = 90°$, $< 0$ if $\theta > 90°$ (obtuse angle). This sign tells you whether the angle between vectors is acute or obtuse.

**Definition**: a unit vector is a vector with magnitude exactly 1 that specifies a direction. It is denoted by a letter with a hat/circumflex overhead, e.g., $\hat{n}$, $\hat{A}$, $\hat{u}$. The hat indicates that the magnitude is unity.

**Mathematical relation**: any non-zero vector $\vec{A}$ can be written as $\vec{A} = |\vec{A}|\hat{A}$, where $\hat{A}$ is the unit vector in the same direction. The unit vector is $\hat{A} = \vec{A}/|\vec{A}|$.

**Property**: since $\hat{A}$ has magnitude 1, $\hat{A}\cdot\hat{A} = |\hat{A}|^2\cos0° = 1$. This makes unit vectors the 'building blocks' for expressing other vectors with direction and magnitude as scalars times direction.

**Standard unit vectors $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$**: these are unit vectors along the x, y, and z axes of a Cartesian coordinate system. They satisfy $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i} = \hat{j}\cdot\hat{j} = \hat{k}\cdot\hat{k} = 1$ and $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j} = \hat{j}\cdot\hat{k} = \hat{k}\cdot\hat{i} = 0$.

**Any 3D vector in terms of standard unit vectors**: $\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j} + A_z\hat{k}$. The components are the projections of $\vec{A}$ on the axes, and the magnitude is $|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{A_x^2+A_y^2+A_z^2}$.

**Worked example**: find the unit vector of $\vec{A} = 3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$. Magnitude: $|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{3^2+2^2+5^2} = \sqrt{9+4+25} = \sqrt{38}$. Unit vector: $\hat{A} = \vec{A}/|\vec{A}| = (3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+5\hat{k})/\sqrt{38} = (3/\sqrt{38})\hat{i} + (2/\sqrt{38})\hat{j} + (5/\sqrt{38})\hat{k}$.
**Verification**: $\hat{A}\cdot\hat{A} = (3/\sqrt{38})^2 + (2/\sqrt{38})^2 + (5/\sqrt{38})^2 = (9+4+25)/38 = 38/38 = 1$ ✓. So $\hat{A}$ is indeed a unit vector.
**Approximating $\sqrt{38}$**: $\sqrt{38} \approx 6.164$. So $\hat{A} \approx 0.487\hat{i} + 0.324\hat{j} + 0.811\hat{k}$. The sum of squares of these coefficients: $0.237 + 0.105 + 0.658 = 1.0$ ✓.

**Direction in spherical coordinates**: in 3D, the unit vector at angles $(\theta, \phi)$ (polar and azimuthal) is $\hat{r} = \sin\theta\cos\phi\,\hat{i} + \sin\theta\sin\phi\,\hat{j} + \cos\theta\,\hat{k}$. This represents the direction from the origin to the point on a unit sphere.

**Unit normal vector $\hat{n}$**: a unit vector perpendicular to a surface. For a surface $f(x,y,z) = 0$, the gradient $
abla f$ gives a vector perpendicular to the surface, and $\hat{n} = 
abla f/|
abla f|$ is the unit normal.
**Unit tangent vector $\hat{t}$**: a unit vector along the direction of motion of a particle along a curve. If position is $\vec{r}(t)$, then $\hat{t} = d\vec{r}/dt / |d\vec{r}/dt|$.
**Application in dot product**: the component of $\vec{A}$ along $\hat{u}$ is $\vec{A}\cdot\hat{u} = |\vec{A}|\cos\theta$. This is how unit vectors simplify extracting directional information.

**Application in cross product**: the vector component of $\vec{A}$ perpendicular to $\hat{u}$ is $\vec{A}\times\hat{u}$, which gives a vector perpendicular to both $\vec{A}$ and $\hat{u}$, with magnitude $|\vec{A}|\sin\theta$.
**Position vector as a unit vector**: a point at distance $r$ from origin in direction $\hat{r}$ has position vector $\vec{r} = r\hat{r}$. This is the cleanest way to express a position.

**Unit vector in terms of components**: if $\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j} + A_z\hat{k}$, then $\hat{A} = (A_x/|\vec{A}|)\hat{i} + (A_y/|\vec{A}|)\hat{j} + (A_z/|\vec{A}|)\hat{k}$. The coefficients are the **direction cosines**.

**Direction cosines** of $\hat{A}$: $\cos\alpha = A_x/|\vec{A}|$, $\cos\beta = A_y/|\vec{A}|$, $\cos\gamma = A_z/|\vec{A}|$. They satisfy $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$ (since $\hat{A}$ is a unit vector).
**Zero vector has no defined unit vector**: you cannot find a unit vector along $\vec{0}$ because the direction is indeterminate. The formula $\vec{0}/|\vec{0}|$ is undefined.

**Unit vector notation**: in textbooks, unit vectors are written with hats ($\hat{i}$), tildes ($\tilde{A}$), or in bold ($\mathbf{e}$). All represent the same concept. The hat is most common in NEB curriculum.
**Negative unit vector**: $-\hat{A}$ is also a unit vector (magnitude 1) but in the opposite direction. Unit vectors come in pairs, one for each direction along a line.
confusion: Dot product is just multiplication of magnitudes — Dot product is $|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$, NOT just $|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|$. The cosine factor accounts for direction. If $\vec{a} \perp \vec{b}$, the dot product is 0 even though both are non-zero.
Dot product is commutative only sometimes — Dot product is ALWAYS commutative: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = \vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}$. There are no exceptions for non-zero vectors.

A negative dot product means one of the vectors is negative — A negative dot product means the angle between the vectors is obtuse ($> 90°$). Both vectors can be entirely positive (e.g., 5 N and 10 N at 120° give $-25$).
The dot product depends on the order — The dot product is independent of order. $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = \vec{B}\cdot\vec{A}$. Only the cross product has order dependence.
The dot product formula $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = ab\cos\theta$ works for parallel vectors too — Yes, for $\theta=0°$, $\cos0°=1$ and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=ab$. The formula is general for all angles.

A larger dot product means the vectors are more parallel — Yes, the dot product increases as $\theta$ decreases. Maximum at $\theta=0°$ (parallel), minimum at $\theta=180°$ (anti-parallel, negative dot product), zero at $\theta=90°$.

You can dot product any two vectors regardless of type — You can compute the dot product of any two vectors, but the result is meaningful only for vectors in the same dimensional space. You cannot dot-product a 2D vector with a 3D vector without embedding one in the other's space.

$\vec{A}\cdot\vec{A}$ is the same as $\vec{A}\cdot|\vec{A}|$ — $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{A} = |\vec{A}|^2$ (magnitude squared), not the product of magnitude and magnitude. The dot product of a vector with itself is always a non-negative scalar.

A unit vector has zero magnitude — A unit vector has magnitude EXACTLY 1, not 0. The zero vector $\vec{0}$ has magnitude 0 and indeterminate direction; a unit vector has magnitude 1 and a specific direction.

Every vector is a unit vector — Only vectors with magnitude 1 are unit vectors. A general vector $\vec{A} = 3\hat{i}$ has magnitude 3, not 1. To get a unit vector, you must divide by the magnitude: $\hat{A} = \vec{A}/|\vec{A}|$.
There is only one unit vector in space — There are infinitely many unit vectors, one for each direction in space. In 3D, unit vectors form a unit sphere (all vectors of magnitude 1).
Unit vectors add to give a vector with the sum of magnitudes — Unit vectors add via the parallelogram law, considering their direction. $\hat{i} + \hat{j}$ has magnitude $\sqrt{2}$, not 2.

The unit vector is just the direction — The unit vector encodes ONLY the direction, but it is itself a vector (with magnitude 1). Saying 'just the direction' is informal — formally, the unit vector is a vector in 3D space with magnitude 1.
The unit vector $\hat{A}$ equals $\vec{A}$ — $\hat{A}$ equals $\vec{A}$ only if $|\vec{A}| = 1$. For a general vector, $\hat{A} = \vec{A}/|\vec{A}|$, which is the unit vector in the same direction.

Direction cosines are the same as components — Direction cosines are the components of a unit vector. They are the cosines of the angles the vector makes with the coordinate axes, and their squares sum to 1.
A unit vector along an axis is the same as the axis — The unit vector along the x-axis is $\hat{i}$, which has magnitude 1. The x-axis itself is an infinite line, not a vector.
practice: If $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = 3\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$, find $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}$. [Solution: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 2(3) + (-3)(1) + 4(-2) = 6 - 3 - 8 = -5$.]

Find the angle between $\vec{A} = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B} = 5\hat{i} + 12\hat{j}$. [Solution: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 15 + 48 = 63$. $|\vec{A}| = 5$, $|\vec{B}| = 13$. $\cos\theta = 63/(5\cdot13) = 63/65 \approx 0.969$. $\theta \approx 14.3°$.]
If $\vec{F} = 10\,\text{N}$ and $\vec{d} = 5\,\text{m}$ at $\theta = 60°$, find the work done. [Solution: $W = Fd\cos\theta = 10 \cdot 5 \cdot 0.5 = 25\,\text{J}$.]

Show that $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ are perpendicular. [Solution: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 2(1) + 3(-2) + (-1)(4) = 2 - 6 - 4 = -8 \neq 0$. Wait — they are NOT perpendicular. Let me redo: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = -8$, so not perpendicular. Try $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}$ again: $2-6-4 = -8$. Not zero. To be perpendicular, need a different pair.]

Verify: the dot product of $\vec{A} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ with itself gives $|\vec{A}|^2$. [Solution: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{A} = 1(1) + 2(2) + 3(3) = 1+4+9 = 14$. $|\vec{A}|^2 = 1^2+2^2+3^2 = 14$. ✓]

Find the projection of $\vec{A} = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}$ on $\vec{B} = 5\hat{i} + 12\hat{j}$. [Solution: $\text{proj} = \vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}/|\vec{B}| = (3\cdot5+4\cdot12)/13 = (15+48)/13 = 63/13 \approx 4.85$.]
If $|\vec{A}|=5$, $|\vec{B}|=12$, and $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = -30$, find the angle between them. [Solution: $\cos\theta = -30/(5\cdot12) = -30/60 = -0.5$. $\theta = 120°$.]

A force $\vec{F} = (3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 5\hat{k})\,\text{N}$ displaces an object by $\vec{d} = (2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k})\,\text{m}$. Find the work done. [Solution: $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{d} = 3(2) + 4(-1) + (-5)(1) = 6 - 4 - 5 = -3\,\text{J}$. The work is negative, meaning the force opposes the motion.]

Find the unit vector along $\vec{A} = 6\hat{i} + 8\hat{j}$. [Solution: $|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{36+64} = 10$. $\hat{A} = (6/10)\hat{i} + (8/10)\hat{j} = 0.6\hat{i} + 0.8\hat{j}$. Check: $0.36 + 0.64 = 1$ ✓]
If $\hat{u} = (3/5)\hat{i} + (4/5)\hat{j}$, find the vector of magnitude 25 in the direction of $\hat{u}$. [Solution: $\vec{A} = 25\hat{u} = 25((3/5)\hat{i}+(4/5)\hat{j}) = 15\hat{i}+20\hat{j}$.
Find the unit vector along $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$. [Solution: $|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{4+9+36} = \sqrt{49} = 7$. $\hat{A} = (2/7)\hat{i} - (3/7)\hat{j} + (6/7)\hat{k}$.
If $\hat{A} = (1/\sqrt{3})(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})$, show that $\hat{A}$ is a unit vector. [Solution: $|\hat{A}|^2 = (1/3)(1+1+1) = 1$. So $|\hat{A}| = 1$. Yes, $\hat{A}$ is a unit vector.]

Find the unit vector along the position vector $\vec{r} = 4\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$. [Solution: $|\vec{r}| = \sqrt{16+16+4} = \sqrt{36} = 6$. $\hat{r} = (4/6)\hat{i} - (4/6)\hat{j} + (2/6)\hat{k} = (2/3)\hat{i} - (2/3)\hat{j} + (1/3)\hat{k}$.

Given $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$, find the unit vector in the direction opposite to $\vec{A}$. [Solution: $|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{4+36+9} = \sqrt{49} = 7$. $\hat{A} = (2/7)\hat{i} - (6/7)\hat{j} - (3/7)\hat{k}$. Opposite: $-\hat{A} = -(2/7)\hat{i} + (6/7)\hat{j} + (3/7)\hat{k}$.

Find the direction cosines of the vector $\vec{A} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$. [Solution: $|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{1+4+4} = 3$. Direction cosines: $\cos\alpha = 1/3$, $\cos\beta = 2/3$, $\cos\gamma = -2/3$. Check: $1/9+4/9+4/9 = 9/9 = 1$ ✓]

A unit vector makes angles 30° with the x-axis and 60° with the y-axis. Find its components and the angle with the z-axis. [Solution: $\cos30° = \sqrt{3}/2$, $\cos60° = 1/2$. Let $\cos^2\gamma = 1 - 3/4 - 1/4 = 0$, so $\gamma = 90°$. Unit vector: $(\sqrt{3}/2)\hat{i} + (1/2)\hat{j} + 0\hat{k}$.
universalFacts: The dot product was introduced by **Hermann Grassmann** in 1844 and independently by **William Kingdon Clifford** in 1878. It is the foundation of the **inner product** in linear algebra, generalizing to higher dimensions.
**Work-energy theorem** in its vector form: $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{d} = \Delta K$. The dot product of force and displacement gives the work, which equals the change in kinetic energy.

NEB exam tip: problems involving the dot product of 2D/3D vectors are very common. The fastest method is the component form $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z$. Then find the angle using $\cos\theta = \vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}/(|\vec{A}||\vec{B}|)$.

In **electromagnetism**, the dot product appears everywhere: electric potential $V = \vec{E}\cdot\vec{d}$ for a uniform field, magnetic flux $\Phi = \vec{B}\cdot\vec{A}$, and power delivered $P = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$.
The dot product of **normal force** with **velocity** is always zero (since they are perpendicular). This is why normal forces do no work — they cannot change kinetic energy, only redirect motion.

In **3D graphics**, the dot product is used to determine whether two surfaces face each other (dot product of normals > 0) or away from each other (< 0). This is critical for lighting calculations (Lambert's cosine law).

The **Cauchy-Schwarz inequality** ($|\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}| \leq |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|$) is one of the most powerful inequalities in mathematics. It follows directly from $|\cos\theta| \leq 1$ in the dot product formula.

The dot product is the basis of **linear regression** in statistics and machine learning: the projection of data onto a direction vector (a unit vector) extracts the component of data along that direction.

Unit vectors are the foundation of **vector calculus** — the gradient $
abla f$, divergence $
abla\cdot\vec{F}$, and curl $
abla	imes\vec{F}$ are defined using unit vectors and partial derivatives.

NEB exam tip: problems asking to 'find the unit vector' are extremely common. The steps are always: (1) find the magnitude, (2) divide each component by the magnitude. Always verify the answer has unit magnitude (sum of squares of components = 1).

The notation $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$ was introduced by **Josiah Willard Gibbs** in his 1881 vector analysis textbook, building on earlier work by Hamilton and Heaviside. The choice of 'i, j, k' (not 'i, j, l' to avoid confusion with '1') is intentional.

In **computer graphics**, unit vectors are called **normalized vectors** or **direction vectors**. The 'normalize' function in any graphics library converts a vector to a unit vector to preserve direction while simplifying calculations.

**Spherical and cylindrical coordinates** use unit vectors $\hat{r}, \hat{\theta}, \hat{\phi}$ and $\hat{r}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{z}$ respectively. These unit vectors change direction as you move, unlike the constant $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$ of Cartesian coordinates.
The **direction cosines** of a unit vector give the angles it makes with the coordinate axes. They are useful in crystallography for specifying the orientation of crystal planes (Miller indices).

In **electromagnetic wave theory**, the unit vector along the direction of propagation $\hat{k}$ and the polarization unit vectors $\hat{E}_0, \hat{B}_0$ form an orthonormal basis. They are mutually perpendicular and unit magnitude.

Any **rotation matrix** $R$ has the property that its columns are unit vectors (in 3D) and they are mutually perpendicular. This makes rotation matrices a powerful tool for describing orientation changes.

data.title: Power
notes: Power is the rate of energy transfer: average P=ΔW/Δt and instantaneous P=dW/dt. Its SI unit is watt, 1 W=1 J s⁻¹.
For translation, dW=F⃗·dr⃗ gives P=F⃗·v⃗=Fv cosθ. Only the force component parallel to velocity transfers energy; a perpendicular centripetal force does no work in uniform circular motion.

Worked example: a 200 kg load rises steadily at 0.50 m s⁻¹. The lifting force is mg=1960 N for g=9.8 m s⁻², so useful power is Fv=980 W. In 10 s the load rises 5 m and gains 9800 J, confirming P=W/t=980 W.
At constant speed, net power is zero because engine power balances resistive forces. For rotation, P=τ⃗·ω⃗; efficiency η=Pout/Pin distinguishes useful output from input.
A 50 N force at 60° to a crate moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ transfers energy at P=50×3×cos60°=75 W, not 150 W.

Power is the rate of doing work. When a force stays along the velocity, power is the force times the speed. A larger engine can do the same work in less time, which is a larger power, not a larger store of energy.

data.title: Work-Energy Theorem — Kinetic and Potential Energy
data.topicTitle: Work-energy theorem; kinetic and potential energy
notes: **Work-Energy Theorem (statement):** The net work done by all forces acting on a particle equals the change in its kinetic energy: $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = K_f - K_i = \frac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv_i^2$. This is a scalar equation — direction is handled through the dot product in work.

**Derivation from Newton's Second Law:** $F = ma = m \frac{dv}{dt}$. Multiply both sides by $v = dx/dt$: $F v = m v \frac{dv}{dt} = m \frac{d}{dt}(\frac{1}{2}v^2)$. Integrate over time: $\int F v dt = \int F dx = W = \Delta(\frac{1}{2}mv^2) = \Delta K$. This shows the theorem is mathematically equivalent to $F=ma$.

**Kinetic energy definition:** $K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$. Always positive (since $v^2 \ge 0$). Scalar quantity — depends on speed, not velocity direction. A 1 kg mass at 10 m/s has $K = 50$ J. Doubling speed quadruples KE (v² dependence).

**Potential energy — general concept:** Potential energy $U$ is energy stored due to the position or configuration of a system in a conservative force field. It is defined ONLY for conservative forces. The change in potential energy is the negative of the work done by the conservative force: $\Delta U = -W_{\text{conservative}}$.

**Gravitational potential energy (near Earth):** $U_g = mgh$, where $h$ is height above an arbitrarily chosen reference level (usually ground or lowest point in problem). $\Delta U_g = mg\Delta h$. Work by gravity: $W_g = -\Delta U_g = mg(h_i - h_f)$. Only HEIGHT difference matters, not the path taken.

**Elastic potential energy (spring):** For a spring obeying Hooke's law $F = -kx$, $U_s = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$ where $x$ is displacement from natural length. Work by spring: $W_s = -\Delta U_s = \frac{1}{2}kx_i^2 - \frac{1}{2}kx_f^2$. $U_s$ is always $\ge 0$ (minimum at $x=0$).

**Mechanical energy:** $E = K + U = K + U_g + U_s + \dots$. When ONLY conservative forces do work, $W_{\text{net}} = W_{\text{conservative}} = -\Delta U$. Then $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = -\Delta U$, so $\Delta K + \Delta U = 0$, meaning $E = \text{constant}$. This is conservation of mechanical energy.

**Non-conservative forces and the general work-energy relation:** When non-conservative forces (friction, air resistance, applied forces) are present: $W_{\text{nc}} = \Delta E = \Delta K + \Delta U$. This is the most general form. $W_{\text{nc}}$ is the work done by ALL non-conservative forces. If $W_{\text{nc}} = 0$, mechanical energy is conserved.

**Kinetic energy in different frames:** KE is frame-dependent. In lab frame: $K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$. In CM frame: $K_{\text{CM}} = \frac{1}{2}\mu v_{\text{rel}}^2$ where $\mu$ is reduced mass. The total KE = $K_{\text{CM}}$ (motion of CM) + $K_{\text{rel}}$ (internal motion). Only internal KE can be converted to heat in inelastic collisions.

**Potential energy reference point is arbitrary:** $U = mgh$ uses $h$ measured from any reference. Changing reference adds a constant to all $U$ values, which cancels in $\Delta U$. Always choose the reference to simplify the problem (e.g., $U=0$ at ground level, or at equilibrium of spring).

**Energy approach vs force approach:** Force approach: $F=ma$, solve for acceleration, integrate for velocity/position. Energy approach: $W_{\text{nc}} = \Delta E$, solve directly for speed or height. Energy is often simpler when forces vary or path is curved, but it gives speeds, not trajectories or times.

**Work done by gravity in a closed loop:** Zero. $W_g = -\Delta U_g$, and for a closed loop $\Delta U_g = 0$ (you return to the same height). This is why gravity is conservative. Work done by friction in a closed loop: NEGATIVE (energy lost to heat). Friction is non-conservative.

**Power and the work-energy theorem:** $P = \frac{dW}{dt} = \frac{dK}{dt} = Fv$ (when $F$ and $v$ are parallel). The rate of change of kinetic energy equals the power delivered by the net force. For a particle moving in a circle at constant speed, $\Delta K = 0$, so net work = 0, and centripetal force does zero work ($F \perp v$).

confusion: The work-energy theorem uses NET work (sum of work by ALL forces). A common error is using work by just one force. If you push a block at constant speed on a rough floor, your work is positive, friction's work is negative, NET work = 0, $\Delta K = 0$ — the theorem holds perfectly.

Potential energy is NOT defined for non-conservative forces. You CANNOT write $U_{\text{friction}} = \mu mg x$. Friction dissipates energy as heat; there is no 'friction potential' to store and recover energy. This is a fundamental distinction.

Mechanical energy conservation ($K+U=\text{constant}$) ONLY applies when $W_{\text{nc}}=0$. If there is ANY friction, air resistance, or external pushing/pulling, mechanical energy is NOT conserved. You MUST use $W_{\text{nc}} = \Delta E$ instead.

The reference point for potential energy does NOT affect the physics. $\Delta U$ is what matters. If you set $U=0$ at the table vs floor, the KE at the bottom is the same. Students often waste time 'finding the right' reference — any reference works if used consistently.

Kinetic energy can NEVER be negative ($v^2 \ge 0$). Potential energy CAN be negative (e.g., $U = -GMm/r$ for universal gravity). Total mechanical energy can be negative (bound systems like planets in orbit). Only ENERGY DIFFERENCES are physically meaningful.
practice: A 0.5 kg ball is dropped from height 20 m. Find its speed at 5 m above ground using energy conservation. Solution: $U_i = mgh_i = 0.5 \times 9.8 \times 20 = 98$ J. $U_f = 0.5 \times 9.8 \times 5 = 24.5$ J. $\Delta U = -73.5$ J. $\Delta K = +73.5$ J. $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 73.5 \rightarrow v = \sqrt{147/0.5} = \sqrt{294} = 17.1$ m/s.

A 2 kg block compresses a spring ($k = 400$ N/m) by 0.1 m on a frictionless surface and is released. Find its max speed. Solution: Initial: $U_s = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 = 200 \times 0.01 = 2$ J, $K=0$. Final: $U_s = 0$, $K_{\text{max}} = 2$ J. $\frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times v^2 = 2 \rightarrow v^2 = 2 \rightarrow v = 1.41$ m/s.

A 1 kg block slides on a rough horizontal surface ($\mu_k = 0.3$) with initial speed 10 m/s. How far does it go before stopping? Solution: $W_{\text{nc}} = W_f = -\mu_k mg d$. $\Delta K = 0 - \frac{1}{2} \times 1 \times 100 = -50$ J. $W_{\text{nc}} = \Delta K \rightarrow -0.3 \times 1 \times 9.8 \times d = -50 \rightarrow d = 50 / 2.94 = 17$ m.

A 3 kg mass is attached to a vertical spring ($k = 200$ N/m) and released from the spring's natural length. Find the max extension. Solution: Let $x$ be extension. Initial: $U_g = 0$ (reference), $U_s = 0$, $K = 0$. Final: $U_g = -mgx$, $U_s = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$, $K = 0$. Energy: $0 = -mgx + \frac{1}{2}kx^2 \rightarrow x = 2mg/k = 2 \times 3 \times 9.8 / 200 = 0.294$ m.

A 1000 kg car goes up a 10° hill at constant 20 m/s. Engine power? Assume 20% losses. Solution: Force to overcome gravity: $F_g = mg \sin 10^\circ = 1000 \times 9.8 \times 0.174 = 1705$ N. Useful power $P = F_g v = 1705 \times 20 = 34,100$ W. With 20% loss, input power = $34,100 / 0.8 = 42,625$ W ≈ 57 hp.
universalFacts: The work-energy theorem was developed by Leibniz, Bernoulli, and Coriolis in the 17th-19th centuries. The concept of 'vis viva' (living force, $mv^2$) by Leibniz (1686) was a precursor — he argued $mv^2$ (not $mv$) was the conserved quantity in mechanical systems.

Noether's theorem (1918) proves that conservation of energy is a consequence of time translation symmetry: the laws of physics don't change with time. If physics were different tomorrow, energy wouldn't be conserved. This is one of the deepest connections in physics.

Kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ is NOT a relativistic formula — it's the low-speed approximation of $(\gamma - 1)mc^2$. At $v = 0.1c$, the error is about 0.5%. At everyday speeds, Newtonian KE is exact for all practical purposes.

Potential energy is a property of the SYSTEM, not a single object. A ball alone doesn't have gravitational PE; the ball-EARTH system does. The energy is stored in the gravitational field. Similarly, spring PE is stored in the spring's deformed configuration.

The total energy of the universe (if well-defined) is constant. In general relativity, energy conservation is subtle — in an expanding universe, energy of photons decreases (redshift), and there's no global energy conservation law. But locally, energy conservation is exact and tested to extraordinary precision.

data.title: Conservation of Energy

notes: **Work done by a constant force:** W = F·d·cos θ = Fd cos θ, where F is the magnitude of the force, d is the displacement, and θ is the angle between the force and displacement vectors. Work is a scalar quantity (SI unit: joule, J = N·m). Work is positive when the force has a component in the direction of displacement (θ < 90°), negative when opposite (θ > 90°), and zero when perpendicular (θ = 90°).

**Work done by a variable force:** when force varies with position, work is the area under the F-x graph, or mathematically, W = ∫ F(x) dx from x₁ to x₂. For a spring force F = −kx, the work done by the spring when stretched from x₁ to x₂ is W = ½k(x₁² − x₂²).

**Work-energy theorem:** the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy: W_net = ΔK = ½mv² − ½mu². This is one of the most powerful results in mechanics — it connects forces (through work) to motion (through kinetic energy).

**Work done by gravity:** W_g = mgΔh = mg(h_i − h_f), where Δh is the change in height. Gravity does positive work when the body falls (h decreases) and negative work when it rises (h increases). The work done by gravity is independent of the path — only the vertical displacement matters.

**Work done by a spring:** W_s = ½kx² (work done ON the spring to stretch/compress it by x). The spring does work W = ½k(x_i² − x_f²) when it returns from x_i to x_f. At the natural length (x = 0), the spring does maximum work.

**Work done by friction:** W_f = −f_k·d = −μ_k·N·d. Friction always does negative work (it opposes motion), converting mechanical energy into heat. The work depends on the path length d, not just the displacement — friction is non-conservative.

**Zero work situations:** (1) Force perpendicular to displacement (e.g., normal force on a horizontal surface, centripetal force in circular motion). (2) No displacement (pushing a wall). (3) Force applied to a body that doesn't move.

**NEB exam focus:** work done by constant force (W = Fd cos θ), work done by a spring (W = ½kx²), work-energy theorem (W_net = ΔK), area under F-x graph for variable forces, and identifying zero-work situations.
confusion: ❌ 'Work and energy are different concepts.' ✅ Work is a TRANSFER of energy. When you do work on a body, you transfer energy to it. The work-energy theorem (W_net = ΔK) makes this precise.
❌ 'Work is a vector because force and displacement are vectors.' ✅ Work is a SCALAR — it is the dot product of force and displacement (W = F·d·cos θ). It has magnitude but no direction.

❌ 'If a body moves, work must be done.' ✅ Work is done only if the force has a component along the displacement. Centripetal force does zero work in circular motion (always perpendicular to velocity).
❌ 'Work done by gravity depends on the path.' ✅ Gravity is a conservative force — work depends only on the vertical displacement (mgΔh), not on the path taken.
❌ 'A spring does work W = ½kx² when stretched by x.' ✅ The work done ON the spring to stretch it is ½kx². The work done BY the spring when it returns is also ½kx² (energy is recovered).
❌ 'Friction always does negative work.' ✅ Static friction can do positive work — e.g., the static friction on your feet pushes you forward when walking. Kinetic friction always does negative work.

notes: **Work done by a constant force:** W = F·d·cos θ = Fd cos θ, where F is the magnitude of the force, d is the displacement, and θ is the angle between the force and displacement vectors. Work is a scalar quantity (SI unit: joule, J = N·m). Work is positive when the force has a component in the direction of displacement (θ < 90°), negative when opposite (θ > 90°), and zero when perpendicular (θ = 90°).

**Work done by a variable force:** when force varies with position, work is the area under the F-x graph, or mathematically, W = ∫ F(x) dx from x₁ to x₂. For a spring force F = −kx, the work done by the spring when stretched from x₁ to x₂ is W = ½k(x₁² − x₂²).

**Work-energy theorem:** the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy: W_net = ΔK = ½mv² − ½mu². This is one of the most powerful results in mechanics — it connects forces (through work) to motion (through kinetic energy).

**Work done by gravity:** W_g = mgΔh = mg(h_i − h_f), where Δh is the change in height. Gravity does positive work when the body falls (h decreases) and negative work when it rises (h increases). The work done by gravity is independent of the path — only the vertical displacement matters.

**Work done by a spring:** W_s = ½kx² (work done ON the spring to stretch/compress it by x). The spring does work W = ½k(x_i² − x_f²) when it returns from x_i to x_f. At the natural length (x = 0), the spring does maximum work.

**Work done by friction:** W_f = −f_k·d = −μ_k·N·d. Friction always does negative work (it opposes motion), converting mechanical energy into heat. The work depends on the path length d, not just the displacement — friction is non-conservative.

**Zero work situations:** (1) Force perpendicular to displacement (e.g., normal force on a horizontal surface, centripetal force in circular motion). (2) No displacement (pushing a wall). (3) Force applied to a body that doesn't move.

**NEB exam focus:** work done by constant force (W = Fd cos θ), work done by a spring (W = ½kx²), work-energy theorem (W_net = ΔK), area under F-x graph for variable forces, and identifying zero-work situations.
confusion: ❌ 'Work and energy are different concepts.' ✅ Work is a TRANSFER of energy. When you do work on a body, you transfer energy to it. The work-energy theorem (W_net = ΔK) makes this precise.
❌ 'Work is a vector because force and displacement are vectors.' ✅ Work is a SCALAR — it is the dot product of force and displacement (W = F·d·cos θ). It has magnitude but no direction.

❌ 'If a body moves, work must be done.' ✅ Work is done only if the force has a component along the displacement. Centripetal force does zero work in circular motion (always perpendicular to velocity).
❌ 'Work done by gravity depends on the path.' ✅ Gravity is a conservative force — work depends only on the vertical displacement (mgΔh), not on the path taken.
❌ 'A spring does work W = ½kx² when stretched by x.' ✅ The work done ON the spring to stretch it is ½kx². The work done BY the spring when it returns is also ½kx² (energy is recovered).
❌ 'Friction always does negative work.' ✅ Static friction can do positive work — e.g., the static friction on your feet pushes you forward when walking. Kinetic friction always does negative work.

notes: **Work done by a constant force:** W = F·d·cos θ = Fd cos θ, where F is the magnitude of the force, d is the displacement, and θ is the angle between the force and displacement vectors. Work is a scalar quantity (SI unit: joule, J = N·m). Work is positive when the force has a component in the direction of displacement (θ < 90°), negative when opposite (θ > 90°), and zero when perpendicular (θ = 90°).

**Work done by a variable force:** when force varies with position, work is the area under the F-x graph, or mathematically, W = ∫ F(x) dx from x₁ to x₂. For a spring force F = −kx, the work done by the spring when stretched from x₁ to x₂ is W = ½k(x₁² − x₂²).

**Work-energy theorem:** the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy: W_net = ΔK = ½mv² − ½mu². This is one of the most powerful results in mechanics — it connects forces (through work) to motion (through kinetic energy).

**Work done by gravity:** W_g = mgΔh = mg(h_i − h_f), where Δh is the change in height. Gravity does positive work when the body falls (h decreases) and negative work when it rises (h increases). The work done by gravity is independent of the path — only the vertical displacement matters.

**Work done by a spring:** W_s = ½kx² (work done ON the spring to stretch/compress it by x). The spring does work W = ½k(x_i² − x_f²) when it returns from x_i to x_f. At the natural length (x = 0), the spring does maximum work.

**Work done by friction:** W_f = −f_k·d = −μ_k·N·d. Friction always does negative work (it opposes motion), converting mechanical energy into heat. The work depends on the path length d, not just the displacement — friction is non-conservative.

**Zero work situations:** (1) Force perpendicular to displacement (e.g., normal force on a horizontal surface, centripetal force in circular motion). (2) No displacement (pushing a wall). (3) Force applied to a body that doesn't move.

**NEB exam focus:** work done by constant force (W = Fd cos θ), work done by a spring (W = ½kx²), work-energy theorem (W_net = ΔK), area under F-x graph for variable forces, and identifying zero-work situations.

data.title: Transformer — principle, types, and losses
notes: A transformer has a primary coil and a secondary coil on an iron core. Alternating current in the primary changes the flux, and that changing flux induces the secondary emf. Direct current does not keep the flux changing, so a transformer does not pass steady DC.
The voltage ratio equals the turns ratio when leakage is ignored. More secondary turns raise the voltage and, in the ideal case, lower the current so that input power equals output power.
A step-up transformer raises voltage. A step-down transformer lowers it. The names refer to voltage, not to power and not to current.

Copper loss is the heating I squared R in both windings. It grows with the load current. Core loss is eddy-current heating plus hysteresis, and it is present whenever the flux is alternating, even if the secondary is open.
Laminating the core and using soft iron cut those core losses. The efficiency is useful output power divided by input power. It is less than 1 once either loss is present.
A small transformer on no load still draws a little primary current to supply the core loss and the magnetising flux. That no-load current is not the load current.
